Jim Chalmers flags savings package and downplays chance of cost-of-living relief
In short:
Treasurer Jim Chalmers says a budget savings package will be delivered before the end of the year.
The prime minister had indicated this week that cost-of-living relief measures could be on the way for households.
What's next?
Mr Chalmers warned the cost of servicing government debt would rise by billions of dollars as borrowing costs around the world increase.
Treasurer Jim Chalmers has vowed there will be more savings in the mid-year budget update but downplayed the prospect of more cost-of-living relief for Australians.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had indicated this week help was on the way for households, but Mr Chalmers said the government was looking to run a "tight ship" because of sustained pressure on the budget.
He told Insiders a savings package would feature in the budget update, which is due in mid-December.
"One of the primary influencers on the mid-year update will be the need to find more savings,"
he said.
"There is very, very substantial and intensifying pressure, not just on our budget but on budgets around the world."
The treasurer said the package would be influenced by the inflation challenge and the "helpful and responsible role" the government "intend to play" to see that figure come down over time.
"So we can get real wages growing again and so some of this pressure can come off people," he said.
On Wednesday, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised interest rates to a 15-year high.
Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said she would not "play the blame game", but warned inflation "isn't all about the Middle East conflict".
On Sunday, Mr Chalmers said "no serious observer" would disagree the war in the Middle East was putting "very substantial" pressure on the Australian economy.
He said additional government spending had been concentrated in areas such as bulk billing, to ease pressure on family budgets.
The Coalition had argued the government was spending too much and had contributed to inflation.
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson labelled Mr Chalmers a "disastrous treasurer" and called for him to step down.
"He's actively stoked inflation, and he's fundamentally undermined the success of this country," Mr Wilson said.
Cost of government debt to rise by billions
The treasurer also warned the cost of servicing government debt would rise by billions of dollars as borrowing costs around the world increased.
US government bonds were heavily sold off last month, in a sign investors were demanding higher returns to lend money.
Bonds are essentially IOUs issued by governments to borrow money and are bought and sold by large investment funds as well as individual investors.
The bond market is generally seen as safer than the share market, but big swings in bond prices can be an early warning sign of financial stress.
Mr Chalmers said the government's trillion-dollar debt burden would balloon as cheaper debt is paid off, and the government is forced to turn to new, more expensive borrowing options.
"This spike in borrowing costs in the major economies will also play out here," he said.
"The pressure will still come to Australia, unfortunately, and you'll see in the billions of dollars the magnitude of pressure, coming from those bond yields which are changing so quickly."

After failed execution, health workers say Tennessee's method flouts medical ethics
This story describes the lethal injection procedure used in a death penalty.
In May, a group of healthcare workers spent about an hour trying to establish complete IV access so they could inject Tony Carruthers, an inmate at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville, with a lethal dose of sedative.
Maria DeLiberato, an attorney for Carruthers, was in the room. She said the workers stuck his arms and feet with needles, to no avail. A doctor then tried to insert a central line through his collarbone and shoulder. That didn't work, either.
Carruthers groaned in pain and blood oozed from puncture wounds, DeLiberato said in a news briefing.
After more than an hour, Gov. Bill Lee called the warden, ordering him to halt the execution attempt. He later granted Carruthers a one-year reprieve.
Now, as another death row inmate's execution approaches, doctors and nurses in the state say they want medical professionals removed from the execution process. They've also joined defense attorneys and nine Republican state lawmakers in demanding a moratorium on the death penalty and an overhaul of the state's execution methods.
The doctors' arguments echoed those the American Medical Association (AMA) has made before the U.S. Supreme Court and in its code of ethics.
The death penalty in the U.S.
Tennessee is among 27 states where the death penalty is legal, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, a nonprofit that offers data and analysis on issues surrounding capital punishment.
Governors in four of those states have halted all executions, citing moral concerns and logistical ones, such as being unable to obtain lethal injection drugs amid pharmaceutical companies' refusal to sell them for use in executions. Lethal injection is still the primary execution method nationwide, but some states may use gas, a firing squad, or electrocution.
Since the beginning of 2020, 170 people have been executed in 17 states, with most occurring in Florida, Texas, and Oklahoma. In that time, six states have had botched lethal injections, according to the Death Penalty Information Center, which defines those as executions that include a departure from the protocol because of unanticipated problems and that cause more pain for the prisoner than anticipated, whether they ultimately end with a death or not. Several of the stories read like Carruthers' — protracted but ultimately failed attempts to establish IV access.
Tennessee doctors' concerns
The IV team gave up on trying to place a peripheral IV line into Carruthers after several failed attempts, according to DeLiberato's account. Following protocol, physician Mark Fowler, a contractor for the state's prison system, then tried to insert a central line in a deeper vein. That's a quasi-surgical procedure in which a plastic tube is inserted in the chest, groin, or neck. Fowler used a series of syringes, trying to insert the tube under Carruthers' collarbone and then through his shoulder.
In an October 2025 deposition, Fowler said he hadn't done such a procedure in the 12 years since he had stopped working in an emergency room, and didn't know that placing a central line could be among his execution duties.
Fowler told NPR by phone on Sept. 24 that "the doctor does not participate in the execution. The only thing the doctor does is declare the person dead." He did not have further comment.
Two months after the halted lethal injection, more than 40 doctors and nurses sent a letter to Gov. Lee, calling on him to pause executions and redesign the protocol to omit health workers from the process.
The letter said that Tennessee's rules requiring the participation of pharmacists, physicians, and other healthcare workers in executions are at odds with medical ethics, as well as guidelines explicitly laid out by groups such as the American Medical Association. The AMA code says doctors are to preserve life when there is hope of doing so and bars participation in executions.
"This means that the health care professionals who agree to take part in Tennessee's executions are those willing to set aside their professional ethics," the letter to Lee reads. "The problems that we have seen, such as in Mr. Carruthers's case, are the predictable result of working with such unscrupulous actors."
Dr. John Greer, a retired Nashville hematologist, said in a news conference about the letter that he wasn't surprised the central line placement went awry.
"Placing a central line is not just sticking a needle in a person's arm," he said.
Greer said the doctor has to tap a large vessel above the heart. He said that it's a risky procedure in which an error could cause a collapsed lung or heavy bleeding — and that only those with specific training and routine practice should attempt.
"And I cannot imagine that there would be someone who's doing these routinely who would be involved in this procedure," Greer said.
Some Republican state senators also called for a hold on executions and an overhaul of the process, saying that "incompetent administration" of capital punishment gives its critics more ammunition.
This summer, Lee said he didn't want a pause.
"The Department of Correction did exactly what they should," he said. "It should not affect executions in the future."
"It's one of the most difficult things that we do in this state," Lee said later. "But I am committed to making sure that it is done in the way that it should be."
The state's lethal injection protocol orders the prison to keep a curtain over the media witnesses' viewing window until the IVs are established, so none of them could offer a visual account of the failed execution attempt.
A lawsuit challenging that policy has been filed by the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and news outlets, including NPR Member station WPLN. The lawsuit argues the lack of transparency during the IV placement process obscures problems like the ones that happened
in Carruthers' case.
There's a broad understanding in the U.S. that the medical establishment doesn't participate in executions, said Dr. Matthew Wynia, director of the Center for Bioethics and Humanities at the University of Colorado's medical school.
"We came out of World War II with a whole bioethics and medical ethics enterprise that is really strongly opposed to medicine serving as an arm of the state and using specialized medical skills to hurt people or kill people," Wynia said.
A history of medical abuses by government doctors — such as forced sterilizations and unethical studies of untreated syphilis in the U.S., and murder and torture in Nazi Germany — forged that consensus, he said.
Wynia mentioned other nations where medical professionals still participate in executions.
"But they are, you know, Iran and Saudi Arabia and Russia, sort of authoritarian states, where medicine is an arm of the government," Wynia said. "Medical involvement in executions ends up happening because medicine is unable to say, 'No, we don't do that.'"
Medical issues loom over upcoming execution
Tennessee was scheduled to execute Christa Pike on Sept. 30, who was 18 years old when she and her boyfriend killed Colleen Slemmer. A federal appeals court halted it about an hour before.
Pike's attorneys this year raised several concerns that the state's lethal injection protocol would violate her rights. Among them is their contention that because she suffers from a platelet disorder, it's likely she will need a central line placed. They also argued that she was at risk of needless suffering, alleging Carruthers' execution showed that Fowler — who has confirmed publicly that he will oversee Pike's execution — is incompetent at placing central lines.
In June, they put all of those concerns in a request to the Tennessee Supreme Court, asking for a special investigator to collect evidence and hold hearings to determine whether they warranted an order to delay her execution and design a method for only her.
The court did appoint a special investigator, a senior judge named Mark Ward. He held a series of hearings in Knoxville last month. Ward said he didn't believe Pike's rights would be violated by the process and submitted his report to the court.
On Sept. 23, the Tennessee Supreme Court denied Pike's stay, agreeing with Ward, saying none of the concerns amounted to a constitutional violation. On Sept. 28, Lee announced he would not grant her clemency.
But on the morning of the scheduled execution on Sept. 30, the execution was halted by a federal appeals court.
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with WPLN and KFF Health News.

DA in Cornell rape investigation declined to review some evidence, including interviews: report
Prosecutors agreed not to pursue criminal charges based on Jane Doe’s six-page statement

A New York district attorney declined to review additional evidence gathered by Cornell University police before deciding not to pursue criminal charges in a gang rape investigation, according to newly obtained records.
The records, obtained by the New York Times, show that on November 25, 2024, a Cornell investigator told a member of the Tompkins County district attorney’s office that campus police had conducted additional interviews. Prosecutors did not ask to review the evidence and instead agreed that, based on a six-page statement from the former student known as Jane Doe, “criminal charges would not be pursued in this case.”
But before prosecutors declined to pursue charges, Cornell police had conducted interviews, reviewed messages, logged tips and contacted people connected to the case. The investigation continued through January 2025, but prosecutors did not review the additional evidence, a decision not previously reported, according to The Times.
The case stems from a civil lawsuit filed last month by Jane Doe, who alleges she was drugged and gang-raped by seven Chi Phi fraternity members in October 2024. All of the men have denied wrongdoing, and none has been criminally charged. New York officials are now reviewing the case in light of the civil lawsuit.
A spokesperson for the Tompkins County D.A.’s Office pushed back on The Times’ report in a statement to The Independent Saturday, saying: “The ‘interviews’ being cited were essentially each of the seven suspects telling the police that they would not speak to them on the advice of counsel.”
After the civil lawsuit, there was strong reaction from many questioning why the fraternity members weren’t charged, raising questions about rape on the nation’s college campuses and whether Cornell officials handled it properly.
The handling of the case is now under renewed scrutiny and criticism that has made national headlines. On Friday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul criticized Cornell police and the district attorney before appointing Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor with the authority to bring criminal charges.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten reportedly told The Times Thursday that additional records gathered by Cornell police were “not pertinent to our analysis because we had Jane Doe’s comprehensive account of the events.”
Van Houten has defended his decision not to prosecute, saying Jane Doe’s police statement “described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious and consensual.” The statement did not establish a crime under New York law, he claimed.
Former prosecutors and legal experts have questioned the decision to rely primarily on the campus police investigation.
“We would never rely on a campus police investigation,” Rick Trunfio, a former upstate New York sex crimes prosecutor and Syracuse University law professor, told The Times. “There are too many problems with that.”
Trunfio said the case should have been handled by a specialized police or prosecution team.
“You think Cornell University wants to report something like that?” he added.
A Cornell representative who speaks for campus police declined The Times’ request for comment, citing pending litigation.
The Independent has contacted Cornell for comment.
According to Jane Doe’s account, she went to the Chi Phi fraternity house after being invited by a fraternity member she had romantic feelings for. She said she initially consented to sex with him and another man, but then became increasingly intoxicated after drinking alcohol, smoking marijuana and taking a drug she was told was ketamine, which she said she was pressured to take.
She said the ketamine, which she had never taken before, left her in a state of “vague consciousness” and that she was largely unable to defend herself or understand what was happening. As more men entered the room – some after a Snapchat message advertised that a woman was available for sex – she said she felt trapped and “cornered” while naked in the bed, she told investigators.
Doe alleged that multiple men sexually assaulted her without her consent, including two men who she said performed sex acts on her while she was partially incapacitated. She also said another man kissed her without consent, while two others stood nearby watching. She told investigators that some men snorted drugs from her unclothed body.
“I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in," she told investigators.

The Allahabad High Court has initiated suo motu proceedings on noise pollution following reports of the death of a 7-year-old Class 2 student at a school in Balrampur while a procession carrying loudspeakers and a music system was passing nearby.
The incident occurred on September 22 at Divine Public School on City Palace Road in Bhagautiganj, Balrampur. The deceased was identified as Vaishnavi Tiwari. According to reports, the procession was part of the 10-day Ganpati Utsav, which started on September 14.
Observing that the incident raises larger questions over the unchecked menace of noise pollution, a Division Bench of Justice Rajan Roy and Justice Manjive Shukla on Wednesday (September 28) ordered the registration of a separate suo motu PIL while hearing an existing case concerning the use of pressure horns, modified silencers and hooters.
The court, however, clarified that it had not established any connection between the alleged loud noise and the child’s death.
The Bench maintained that the broader problem of noise pollution and the enforcement of statutory safeguards required separate consideration. It observed that violations of the Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000, were frequently witnessed in public spaces despite the existing legal framework.
The PIL will examine the authorities responsible for controlling noise pollution, the enforcement measures currently in place, and whether regular monitoring is required, The Bench said.
The court also stressed the need for greater public awareness, observing that a lack of awareness may contribute to violations. At the same time, the Bench said continued violations despite enforcement measures should attract accountability under the applicable law.
The court made the Uttar Pradesh Director General of Police, the Uttar Pradesh Pollution Control Board (UPPCB), the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), Lucknow civic authorities and officials from key government departments parties in the matter. The Balrampur District Magistrate, Superintendent of Police and Chief Medical Officer were also directed to be impleaded. The State was asked to obtain reports on the incident and submit details of measures taken or proposed to enforce noise-control laws.
The court also expressed hope that the child’s parents and school authorities would not face unnecessary pressure or interference. The matter will now be heard on October 12.

They call it the “world’s first parcel locker for abortion pills”. Polish campaigners have launched a new means of distribution as part of their ongoing effort to skirt the country’s near-total ban on abortion.
Painted pink and framed by zebra-striped curtains, the 22-compartment “AbortOmat” in Warsaw allows women to access the pills swiftly and anonymously using a six-digit code. The service was envisaged for those who cannot or do not want to wait days for mail delivery due to a missed miscarriage or health complications, or who worry about receiving the pills at home.
“And why not?” said Kinga Jelinska, the director of the Women Help Women foundation and co-founder of the Abortion Dream Team, the two groups behind this week’s launch.
“You can order underwear, cosmetics, mascara, whatever and receive it practically the same or next day,” she said. “Why not abortion pills, where in some cases there might be more urgency?”
The innovation comes six years after people across Poland took to the streets to protest against the tightening of abortion laws that already ranked among the strictest in Europe, setting off the country’s largest demonstrations since the fall of communism. In 2023, the protests were credited with helping to propel Donald Tusk, and his promises to overhaul the laws within 100 days, into power.
Since then, political stagnation has set in, said Jelinska, citing comments made last year by Tusk in which the prime minister said there was “simply no majority” to change the laws to allow abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy. Tusk instead hinted that his government was intent on doing things differently, telling reporters that it would not prosecute those who helped to facilitate abortions.
While the possession or ingestion of abortion pills is not outlawed in Poland, provision of the medication or helping someone to obtain it is considered a crime punishable by up to three years in prison.
The locker offers a novel way to challenge these restrictions, said Jelinska. “It’s a little bit of a hack on the law,” she said. “The law is about directly giving to someone. So here we have a machine in between, which makes the legality of everything much more vague.”
The locker sits inside the abortion centre that was opened in March 2025 by the Abortion Dream Team. Described as the first of its kind in democratic Poland, it offers a safe space for people to consult on abortion options or receive support while they take the pill.
Symbolically located across the street from the Polish parliament, the centre has allowed campaigners to shine a spotlight on the continued need for abortion access in Poland while also providing services to a wide array of people, said Jelinska. “It has exceeded our expectations.”
But it had also laid bare how few in power were willing to stand up for them, she said. “The one thing that has surprised us, and it speaks to the political situation, is that there are protests in front of the centre; three, sometimes four times a week.”
While usually less than a dozen people turn up, the protesters regularly use sirens and vuvuzelas to make their point, leaving campaigners worried that the noise levels would eventually result in neighbours asking the centre to relocate. “Neither the city or the police have reacted. So that has been a big disappointment to us,” said Jelinska.
It was a glimpse of how these organisations had increasingly felt abandoned by politicians, even as about 50,000 people in Poland contacted the wider network of pro-choice organisations last year seeking help, said Jelinska. “I think in Poland, abortion access won’t be solved by politics but by women and communities,” she said. “We cannot trust politicians with our own bodies.”

Baby bonuses fail to address the fear of falling behind
In highly competitive societies like Hong Kong and Singapore, subsidies and parental leave can’t overcome the cultural pressure keeping young couples from starting families
When one of my seniors from medical school was pregnant during her surgical residency, she planned the exact date of her C-section so she could complete her training on time. When I asked why she didn’t consider taking maternity leave to recuperate afterwards, she said she couldn’t bring herself to lag behind her peers. “I didn’t want motherhood to slow me down,” she said.
In medicine, it is common for women to delay childbearing until after their early career years, often into their mid-thirties or later. When I speak to friends in professional careers such as law, accounting and consulting, they echo a similar sentiment.

United Nations, Sep 23: President Donald Trump said US and Iranian officials met Tuesday, an unexpected engagement that came even as he threatened in his address to the UN General Assembly that he may “annihilate” the Islamic Republic if a deal isn't reached soon to end the nearly seven-month war.
Trump told reporters that his chief envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met with the Iranian officials on the sidelines of the annual gathering of world leaders but he offered few details about how the discussions transpired or the substance of the exchange.
“It was a very good meeting,” Trump said. The president later added that the Iranian officials were “not the highest level, but it's something.”
The engagement comes after months of US-Iran communications languishing following the collapse of a short-lived ceasefire that was brokered in June.
US and Iranian negotiators met separately with Qatari and Pakistani mediators in Doha in early July for indirect talks.
Earlier Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Trump is open to meeting with Iran's president, Masoud Pezeshkian, while he's in New York for the General Assembly.
“This is a president that will meet with anybody for the most part, because he believes that engaging with people is important if you're going to solve problems,” Rubio said on NBC's “Today” show. “It doesn't mean you're going to end up agreeing with them, but it's important.”
Trump also met on Tuesday with leaders and senior officials from Gulf Cooperation Council nations - Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates - as well as Jordan to discuss the way ahead with the war in Iran.
In his address to the General Assembly, Trump made the case that he's shown fortitude while other leaders have equivocated as he defended his decision to start a war with Iran.
But Trump also suggested that he could be at a crossroads in the conflict even as he called on the Islamic Republic to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz and return to the negotiating table to find a settlement to end the conflict.
“I have a big decision to make,” Trump said. “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before, maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world. Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
The president's comments came in his wide-ranging address to the international body in which he also celebrated this year's US military operation to oust Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from power, a new agreement to expand the US military presence in Greenland, and pushed back against calls for greater regulation of the artificial intelligence industry.
But at the heart of the address was a fulsome defence of the war and pushback on the notion that Iran has shown a measure of resilience.
“The terrorist regime is behaving badly, not because they are strong and confident, but because they are weak and desperate," Trump said.
Most of Iran's delegation walked out of the chamber as Trump railed against the Islamic Republic.
After his speech, Trump gathered with Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen on the sidelines of the General Assembly to sign a new security agreement.
The deal, announced last week, came together after Trump repeatedly threatened to “take over” Greenland, a territory of NATO-ally Denmark, by military force if necessary.
Trump said Tuesday the US will immediately begin the process of developing a larger military presence in Greenland including “building two very major military bases”.
Under the deal, Greenland remains Denmark's territory.
Trump also held talks with new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
He's expected to hold a more informal meeting on Tuesday evening with Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez, according to the White House.
Trump also took part in an event on the Shield of Americas, an initiative Trump launched with Latin American countries earlier this year focused on combatting violent cartels.
The visit to the UN comes as Trump's foreign policy approach - particularly his decision to start a war with Iran - has become a drag on his fellow Republicans' hopes of retaining control of both chambers of Congress during the coming midterm elections.
Nevertheless, Trump made the case in his speech that the world is better off for his leadership.
“I have no interest in leaving dangers to grow for another day," Trump said.
In last year's address at the UN, Trump claimed the US had “demolished” Iran's nuclear capabilities after he ordered the June 2025 bombardment of three key facilities.
He returned to the General Assembly nearing the seven-month mark of a new war against Iran that he insists is necessary to address a nuclear threat posed by Iran.
The war has grown more complicated even though strikes by the United States and Israel have killed much of Iran's top leadership and destroyed its air force and navy, while a US blockade of Iranian oil has left Tehran in economic shambles.
The energy market continues to be spooked by the war and oil prices remain elevated.
Saudi Arabia earlier this month shuttered a key pipeline that acted as a relief valve for oil blocked in the Gulf. The kingdom made the move after the pipeline came under attack by Iran-backed militants in Iraq.
At the same time, territorial grabs by the Yemen-based Houthi rebels, another Iranian-backed group, near the Bab al-Mandab Strait has now made it treacherous for oil carriers to use that Red Sea shipping lane.
In his address, the president also touched on Russia's continuing war against Ukraine - a conflict that during his 2024 campaign he predicted would be resolved on Day One of his second term. He once again expressed hope that the conflict will soon be resolved.
Trump hasn't obscured that his patience is being tested by Ukraine's targeting of Russia's diesel refineries - an issue that's added to the global oil markets' volatility - and Russia's targeting of Ukraine's energy grid.
Trump last week asserted that he got the two sides to agree to not target each other's energy infrastructure.
Zelenskyy had said he was willing to go along with Trump's plan if Russia abided by it. Russia said it could only go along with Trump's energy truce proposal if Western energy sanctions on Moscow were lifted first.
The two sides have continued carrying out strikes on refineries and other energy infrastructure.
Trump noted that last week he signed a new sanctions bill targeting Moscow. It empowers him to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas.
The legislation includes an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. Trump, however, has yet to enact the stiff penalties.
“If necessary, I will have to use them,” Trump said. “It's time to stop the killing.”

Jio Financial Services (JFS) and German insurance major Allianz have cumulatively infused ₹640.1 Cr ($66.5 Mn) into their general insurance joint venture, Jio Allianz General Insurance, as the companies move to operationalise the business. According to a regulatory filing by JFS, the companies each invested ₹320.05 Cr in the JV via a rights issue, subscribing 32 Lakh shares apiece. Jio Financial and Allianz continue to hold the JV equally, with their ownership remaining at 50% each. The funds raised through the rights issue will be used by Jio Allianz General Insurance to fund its business operations. Jio Financial said its cumulative investment in Jio Allianz General Insurance has now reached ₹375 Cr. Jio Allianz General Insurance Ltd (JAGIL) is a 50:50 joint venture between Jio Financial Services and Allianz Europe B.V. Launched on May 12, 2026, the JV was formed to offer general insurance, including health insurance, in India, targeting individuals and businesses. JAGIL is part of Jio Financial's broader insurance strategy, which also includes Jio Insurance Broking and its 50:50 reinsurance JV, Allianz Jio Reinsurance, with Allianz. Allianz Jio Reinsurance in its first full quarter of operations (Q1 FY27) underwrote gross written premiums of ₹266 Cr during its first full quarter of operations. The latest capital infusion comes as Jio Financial continues to expand its fintech ecosystem, with insurance forming one of the key areas of its broader push beyond its core consumer-facing financial products. JFS houses a broad fintech ecosystem spanning lending, payments, insurance, investments and wealth management. Its businesses include Jio Credit for lending, Jio Payments Bank for banking services, Jio Payment Solutions for payment aggregation, Jio Insurance Broking, Jio Leasing and Jio Finance Platform for distributing financial products. Via its 50:50 JV with BlackRock, JFS operates asset management and wealth management businesses, with broking also being developed. More recently, it also entered a proposed JV with Bank of America, which could acquire up to 49.9% in Jio Credit. On the financial front, Jio Financial Services’ net profit zoomed 2.6X to ₹830.3 Cr in the first quarter (Q1) of FY27 from ₹324.7 Cr in the year-ago period. Operating revenue crossed the ₹2,000 Cr mark during the June quarter, surging 227% YoY to ₹2,004.5 Cr. Shares of JFS ended today’s trading session 2.17% lower at ₹211.90 on the BSE.

Convicted murderer Christa Pike is unconscious, intubated and receiving breathing assistance from a ventilator after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute her, her attorneys said on Friday (October 2, 2026), providing the first detailed account of the extent of injuries she suffered during the lethal injection.
Hospital staff are working to save Pike’s life and clear the lethal drug pentobarbital from her system, her attorneys said in an emergency court filing seeking an order requiring Tennessee’s Department of Correction to preserve evidence from Wednesday night’s botched execution.
Pike remains in critical condition, her lawyers said, two days after the state administered two doses of pentobarbital but failed to kill her. She has suffered significant injuries to both arms, they added.
“At no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body,” Pike’s lawyers said in a filing in the Chancery Court for the State of Tennessee Twentieth Judicial District.
The filing provides the fullest picture yet of the medical consequences of an attempted execution that Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said followed the state’s established protocol. It was the state’s second botched execution this year and Lee has halted any further state killings for the rest of 2026 and ordered an independent review of what happened.
Pike’s attorneys have said the execution team’s difficulties administering the drug were related to intravenous access, an issue they had warned the state and courts about before the execution.
Pike, 50, was convicted of killing her 19-year-old classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995, when Pike was 18. She had been scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than two centuries.

With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a massive $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court, and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilisational norms”.
Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while likely angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which makes up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire human rights and democracy fund (HRDF).
Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe, and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa.
“The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.”
The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human-rights defenders and civil-society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, migration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance.
“Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations.
“The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.”
The largest award of $40m was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation.
In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant).
Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus, and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI.
The state department did not comment on individual grants but told the Guardian the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals.”
“Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.”
Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. Shaheen, the ranking member of the Senate foreign relations committee, has put a partial “hold” on giving the grants to some of the controversial awardees – setting up a showdown with the State Department with just hours left for the money to be obligated.
ProPublica first reported that Trump officials had drawn up at least a dozen no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe and advocates for white South Africans.
The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped.
A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned Justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president.
A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches.
One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria.
And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations.
The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year).
The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and is enforced by Ofcom, its age-verification rules – which took effect last year – have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship.
The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News.
The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, on issues from online safety law to migration that are live in British politics.

What are amplifiers for and how important are they to your sound system's quality?
You probably already have a few hiding in plain sight.
Gear makers will gladly sell you a hundred different add-ons to improve your sound system. To this day, it's possible to buy gold-plated audio cables, even though they can't really improve digital audio — you're either getting a clean data signal or you're not. On the short list of products to take seriously is an amplifier, whether you're building a home theater or your own private music sanctuary. There's a reason your local boutique audio store has been selling them for decades.
You shouldn't automatically pick up an amplifier alongside a new set of speakers, however. It's critical to understand what an amplifier does, how much it can improve sound quality in the real world and whether you need to buy a separate one at all. If you're a newcomer to "serious" audio, you might be surprised to learn that you probably have several amps in your home, hidden in plain sight. That speaks to the underlying importance of the technology.
It's also worth tackling some fundamental misconceptions along the way. Those include not just the necessity of separate amps, but notions like the inherent superiority of tube amps to solid-state models. Don't buy into the temptation to spend hundreds of dollars on something just because it might look good on your shelf. Presumably, your goal is high-quality audio, rather than just showing off to your friends — and there may be more cost-effective ways to upgrade your system.
How amplifiers can improve your sound system
On their own, most audio signals aren't strong enough to be heard clearly. For a demonstration of this, all you need is a turntable with its speakers disabled. If you listen closely, you'll hear something called "needle talk" — the stylus running along the vinyl grooves. This is quiet, and it may not even be distinguishable as music. For you to hear anything meaningful, all sound systems need an amplifier to increase the strength of a signal before output. It's important to match an amp to the power and impedance specs of your speakers, measured in watts and ohms, respectively.
Amps accomplish more than just an increase in volume. Any quality amp will let you adjust gain (the amount of signal boost) and shape sound to your preferences via its equalizer (EQ). You might tweak frequencies for heavier bass or clearer vocals, for example. It's important to get gain and EQ settings right not just for pleasing sound, but to prevent clipping, distortion or even hardware damage.
Let's take a moment to distinguish between amps and preamps. The latter simply raise audio up to line level for correct gain throughout your sound system, meaning that you still need an amp to power your speakers. Some amps have a preamp built-in, streamlining the audio chain.
That leads us to the question of whether you need to buy an amp at all. The truth is that in many cases, you don't. Many, if not most, consumer speakers are active, meaning that they already have integrated amps, as evidenced by their individual power cords. Only passive speakers require external power sources, and even then, you may not need a dedicated unit. Receivers often incorporate both amp and preamp functions, making them a one-stop shop. Exceptionally power-hungry systems may demand an amp on top of that. For example, elaborate Dolby Atmos setups that exceed the number of channels your receiver can power simultaneously will need an amp.
Most people should probably opt for a solid-state amp rather than a tube-based one. While tube models famously provide a "warmer" sound and are visually slick — especially for fans of Fallout's brand of retrofuturism — they typically deliver 50W or less apiece, making them unsuited to surround-sound configurations unless you're willing to spring for several of them. Tubes also require more maintenance, namely swapping them as they wear out. Trying to run a home theater based on tube amps would be an expensive exercise in futility.
More cost-effective sound upgrades
More often, it's the quality of the speakers you have that could stand to be upgraded. If you've got a basic stereo soundbar or speaker pair, jumping to a high-powered, all-in-one Atmos bar will make a world of difference. If you've already got that, it might be time to add rear and side channels for enhanced sound separation. Adding ceiling channels is the endgame for an audiophile, yet they can potentially be more trouble than they're worth, given that you need to both mount and wire them.
A lot of improvements are far cheaper. Unwanted rattling can be solved by add-ons like mats or speaker stands. You can reduce unwanted reverb with acoustic panels, and sometimes muddy bass can be fixed by moving speakers farther away from your walls. If you've got smart speakers with automatic room calibration, you should be running that process whenever you make significant space alterations.
As we've said, amps do have a place in sound systems. It's just that if you have active speakers or a receiver, they're probably redundant until you reach high-end territory. In other words, if you don't have a 7.2.4-channel home theater, or an entire wall devoted to kicking back with Pink Floyd and Dr. Dre, you can probably tuck your wallet away.

At any gathering, you could easily spot him by his colourful printed shirt or jacket. His tall stature, smiling face, and warm handshakes have put generations of students, researchers, and scientists at ease.
Since 1956, when he joined the founding faculty of the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, he has never stopped working at the bench. Along the way, he developed the world’s first leprosy vaccine and a hormonal birth control vaccine, founded India’s first immunology institution, mentored hundreds of students, and continues his research work at a private R&D institution he established after retirement. That’s Gursaran Prasad Talwar, Pran to friends and colleagues, who turns 100 on October 2, today.
Gaining experience
Talwar had a troubled childhood. His mother passed away a week after delivering him in 1926, at her mother’s place in Hisar, then in undivided Punjab. His father, a science postgraduate from the Indian Institute of Science, Bangalore (now Bengaluru), ran a small pharmacy and dispensary in Lahore, where he shifted after remarrying. After a few years of schooling at a madrasa in Hoshiarpur, his father admitted Talwar to the Central Model School in Lahore. His excellent performance in the matriculation exam got him into the Government College Lahore, where he did his BSc Honours and MSc (tech).
As part of the postgraduation course, Talwar came to work at a pharmaceutical manufacturing unit in the Kangra Valley in the summer of 1947 but was caught in the communal frenzy that followed the partition of Punjab. He somehow made it to Lahore only to find that his family had migrated to India. Thus he landed in Delhi in late 1947 and started looking for jobs.
At this time, European countries began offering scholarships for higher education to Indian students via the Government of India. Talwar applied, and he was shortlisted and given a choice. “I chose France. Their national echo ‘Liberté, Égalité, Fraternité’ appealed to my leftist leanings,” Talwar recalled. He joined the fermentation laboratory of the Pasteur Institute, but soon shifted to the biochemistry wing. He completed his Docteur es Sciences degree in 1953. After two years of postdoctoral work in Germany and working in an industrial concern in Milan in Italy, Dr. Talwar returned to India in 1955. His idea was to gain necessary experience for starting a pharmaceutical or chemical business in India.
Great excitement
But life took a different turn as Dr. Talwar was selected to join the proposed biochemistry department of AIIMS as an associate professor in 1956. “In medical colleges, biochemistry was then a minor part of physiology. I tried against all odds and succeeded in making it an independent course with a separate compulsory paper,” Dr. Talwar said. Simultaneously, he established a research lab and began working on growth-promoting hormones like estradiol. He published papers on mechanisms that enable hormones to activate gene transcription and translation.
The 1960s were a period of great excitement in modern biology, with landmark discoveries being made. Pushpa Mitra Bhargava, then at the Regional Research Laboratory Hyderabad, teamed up with Dr. Talwar to form what came to be called the Guha Research Conference. Bhargava organised an international symposium on nucleic acids at the Regional Research Laboratory, Hyderabad, in January 1964, which several newly minted and future Nobel laureates, such as Francis Crick, Gerhard Schramm, Charles Heidelberger, Seymour Benzer, and Roger Monier, attended. The trio of Bhargava, Dr. Talwar, and Obaid Siddiqui themselves constituted the rising stars of modern biology in India.
In 1970, the World Health Organization (WHO) proposed to start a regional training centre in immunology and initiate research in leprosy at AIIMS. Dr. Talwar was hesitant since his work on hormones was going on satisfactorily. “Howard Goodman, who was leading the WHO team, said India had the largest burden of leprosy in the world and asked me bluntly: ‘Do you think Americans will come and solve this problem?’ I knew nothing about leprosy but then started studying why people get leprosy and found that it was their inability to react immunobiologically to some key antigens of M. leprae,” Dr. Talwar said.
This fundamental understanding eventually led to the first curative vaccine against leprosy. It was a long process but resulted in an effective vaccine that not only cured the disease but also healed the scars. It also has the ability to react with key antigens of M. tuberculosis. The mycobacterium used to make the vaccine was later sequenced and named MIP or Mycobacterium indicus pranii, combining Pran and ‘National Institute of Immunology’, or NII.
Founding NII
Another landmark contribution by Dr. Talwar was the birth control vaccine, which has undergone extensive human trials and has been found to be safe, but is still to go into commercial production. “I found that all available birth control methods like vasectomy and intra-uterine devices were not yielding desired results because of various reasons. I wanted to develop a vaccine which could prevent pregnancy without derangement of menstrual regularity and hormonal profiles. So the target molecule should have a key role in sustaining pregnancy,” Dr. Talwar explained as to why he chose human chorionic gonadotropin to develop the vaccine.
Dr. Talwar revealed that the idea of the NII emerged from a discussion with Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. In 1980, the Jawaharlal Nehru Memorial Fund selected Dr. Talwar as a Nehru Fellow; during the fellowship, Indira Gandhi, who was the Fund’s chairperson, used to meet the Fellows to learn about their work. Dr. Talwar told her about the leprosy vaccine and also explained how childhood immunisation could save millions of lives. She asked Dr. Talwar if India had enough vaccines, and he said ‘no’. Ms. Gandhi told him to give him a one-page note in ten days on how India could develop new vaccines.
Dr. Talwar happened to travel to New York the next day for a scientific meeting. “While sipping champagne along with caviar, on the plane, I wrote a note and submitted it to her upon my return. It was this note that became the basis for founding NII just two years later, in 1983,” Dr. Talwar said.
After retiring from the NII and a stint with the International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology, New Delhi, Dr. Talwar founded the Talwar Research Foundation in 1999, where he continues to work with a small band of researchers on hormones, antigens, and antibodies. He says he has no regrets in life as he begins his second century.
Dinesh C. Sharma is a New Delhi-based journalist and author.
