On a bright, sunny day last May, I stood on a boat surrounded by the turquoise waters of the island nation of Palau. I was there in the western Pacific watching scuba divers as they prepared to bring up evidence of a mysterious aquatic world.
Palau is famous for its spectacular and rich coral reefs. But these divers were planning to descend past those sun-lit marine communities and down into a lesser-known twilight zone known as the “mesophotic coral ecosystem.”
Mesophotic essentially means “middle” and “light,” which is where these ecosystems are—not quite in the bright daylight, not quite in the profound darkness, but somewhere in between. For simplicity’s sake, we’ll call these communities, which range from some 30 meters to 150 meters below the surface, the “deep reefs.”
One of the divers on the boat with me was a zoologist and curator at the California Academy of Sciences named Luiz Rocha, who has spent decades studying these deep reefs and their secrets.
“Anything between 30 meters and 150 meters is really, really unknown,” he told me.
Because these deep reefs are so unknown, researchers like Rocha are left with big questions. They want to get a baseline picture of what is going on in these ecosystems—even just who lives there!—so that they can better understand how they function. They’ve also tried to work out whether (or not) these deep reefs might provide a refuge for species living in shallower coral reefs.
I was in Palau for Vox’s Unexplainable podcast because, in an effort to gather more information about these mysterious places, Rocha left some scientific structures down in these twilight depths back in 2016. Those structures then spent almost a decade becoming encrusted with all kinds of marine life. And now, Rocha was back to retrieve them, hoping that he—along with many other scientists — would be able to open them up, like a box of scientific puzzle pieces, full of clues about this under-understood marine world.
One thing that’s often acknowledged in papers about mesophotic coral ecosystems is that scientists don’t know as much as they’d like to. A National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration article about them from 2019 is full of “mays,” as in: They may “serve as essential fish habitat for economically and ecologically important species.
Researchers do know some things, of course. They know that these deep reefs can be found in many of the same regions as shallower coral reefs—so mainly the tropical and subtropical parts of the world, like Micronesia, the Caribbean, and even the Gulf of Mexico. They’ve found that there are many species that seem to be unique to these places, and recent research points to their potential susceptibility to climate change.
Researchers have also gotten a sense of some of the key differences between these deep reefs and their shallower coral neighbors. In shallow reefs, hard corals team up with photosynthesizing algae. The algae provide the corals with nutrients, and the corals secrete a calcium-carbonate matrix that helps create the architecture of the reef.
As you go deeper, though, the light begins to fade, and the opportunities for photosynthesis start to fade with it. The temperature also drops. So the animals living down in the deep reefs are ones that can survive in a dimmer, cooler world.
Scientists can dive into the deep reefs to try to learn more about these understudied places—as Rocha has—but exploring down at 100 meters requires more difficult, riskier technical diving than exploring at shallower depths. The deeper you dive, for example, the faster gases get pushed into your tissues, which imposes limits on these really deep dives.
“We have a very, very short time,” Rocha says, “And by short time, I mean five minutes. Six, seven minutes.”
Scientists can take some pictures in that time, make some measurements, or collect a few samples, but then they have to move back upwards—a process that can take hours, since they must rise slowly to avoid decompression sickness.
It is, obviously, not particularly efficient to study an ecosystem in five- to seven-minute intervals. People have also used remote-operated vehicles and submersibles to explore the deep reefs, but those have their own issues, and cameras can’t always capture all the detail you might want, or photograph more secretive, cryptic animals. So huge gaps remain in scientific knowledge about these ecosystems.
“Whenever we go somewhere,” Rocha says, “the first thing we find is new species. It’s the most basic thing in science you can do.” But this effort goes beyond just cataloging new species of fish, sponges, or sea slugs.
Rocha wants to answer fundamental questions like: What is the main energy source for everything down here in the dim light? What does the food chain look like? How have things evolved to live at these depths? How similar are they to the shallow ecosystems, and how different? How are they affected by climate change—and what’s the most efficient way to protect them?
But Rocha says that “in some ways, we don’t even know what questions to ask. We really only know what the crucial questions are when we have a baseline understanding of the ecosystem. And for deep reefs, we don’t have that yet.”
Rocha is not deterred by the enormous number of question marks that surround these deep reefs. For years now, he has been gathering bits of basic information about them, often via those very short dives.
About a decade ago, though, Rocha got interested in another method for sampling the biodiversity of this sort of marine ecosystem—a technique involving “autonomous reef monitoring structures” or ARMS.
Basically, each ARMS is a stack of several PVC plates, separated at uniform intervals and attached to a base plate. They look like little gray, featureless hotels. You take them to a place that you want to study, bring them down, secure them, and then leave them alone for a while to let them collect … life.
“As soon as you drop any kind of clean structure on a reef,” Rocha says, “it starts getting colonized by larvae of everything around it—of sponges, gorgonians, corals. And then, because there’s a lot of hiding spots between the plates—so between the floors of the hotel—they start getting colonized by shrimp, by mollusks, by ascidians, by anything you can imagine in the ocean. And it becomes this stable, diverse mini reef, if you will, packed with a lot of biodiversity that would be very hard to collect all at once in any given reef.”
A few years after that initial drop, you come back, collect the ARMS, and then study the mini reef that has grown on them. You can sample and touch and analyze things to your heart’s content.
It’s not only a very effective way to collect lots of creatures, all at once, but also a great way to do so in a standardized way. If you went down—or sent a robot down—to collect an encrusted rock from a reef, you could learn a lot about the life on it, but it would be hard to compare the life on that rock to life on other rocks from other reefs, or even the same reef, because each rock would have its own unique characteristics. Not so for ARMS.
“ Every one’s the same,” Chris Meyer, director of the Smithsonian Global ARMS program, told me. “It’s prefab housing, and then you just look to see who moves in.”
To Rocha, this seemed like a great way to get a really good, long look at the deep reefs instead of the brief glimpses he was getting from diving. It was also, he told me, fairly cheap to deploy them. So from 2016 to 2018, with some private funding, he and his colleagues left ARMS in some of the deep reefs around Palau—as well as in Guam, the Marshall Islands, and French Polynesia. They installed some around 50 meters, and some around 100, and then some around 10 meters, so he could compare the deep reefs to their shallower neighbors.
After that, he waited.
In fact, he waited a little longer than he would have liked, because the retrieval of ARMS is more expensive than deploying them, so he had to work out more funding.
Eventually, private funders agreed to underwrite the retrieval of the ARMS that Rocha had left. Which is how he and his fellow divers finally found themselves on a boat in Palau again, ready to pull up these structures from the deep.
Over the course of a few days, I watched a whole team of people pull several ARMS out of the deep reefs of Palau. Some of the ARMS were relatively sparse, but others were almost fuzzy with organisms—vibrant with red and orange and green and pink and white. One had a massive sponge attached to it; another had several delicate fronds dangling from it like coralline ferns. The ARMS collected each day traveled to the Palau International Coral Reef Center in bins full of seawater, where the scientists quickly got to work—seeing and touching (and smelling) this mysterious ecosystem right up close.
The process was, as it turned out, equal parts magical excitement and well-oiled, Cheez-It–fueled disassembly line. After the plates were taken apart, Meyer took photographs of the plates—what he called a “time capsule of the place.” Others in the lab picked carefully through trays of debris, hunting for tiny crabs and worms and mollusks, or scraped samples off the plates and deposited them in tubes.
They collected sea squirts, said to be our closest invertebrate relatives. They collected sponges—flat ones that felt dry underwater, thick ones with bristles like tiny, unmoving caterpillars, one as thin as a flake of skin and shot through with silver filaments. They collected strange, soft corals known as octocorals, and they collected colonies of animals called bryozoans, which created what looked like swirling, two-dimensional honeycombs.
“We’re looking for every unique thing, which we call a morphospecies,” a Smithsonian research biologist named Sarah Tweedt explained. “And we’re trying to get some representative tissue samples from all of these things so that we can sequence the DNA—and match the DNA to the organism.”
That is, of course, assuming there is already a known genetic match in our existing DNA libraries.
On the first day that I spent with the team, a Cal Academy curator named Terry Goslinger identified several potential new species. He is an expert on colorful, delightful sea slugs known as nudibranchs, and so, because of his deep knowledge (and because nudibranchs’ bright hues and patterns make them somewhat easier to tell apart than some other underwater creatures), he was able to make some on-the-spot calls about whether or not certain species were likely to be new to science, pending genetic testing to confirm.
Many of the animals were trickier to pin down, though. The researchers did their best to identify the creatures they were finding, but even now, several months out, there’s still a lot of work to be done. Of the close to 3,000 specimens, only a small fraction were identified at a species level. The numbers are a little bit inexact because researchers are still processing the data, but when I checked in with a Cal Academy postdoc working on the project, Susanne Bähr, in July, she told me that only 3 percent of samples had been ID’d by species, and a little less than 20 had a genus designation. Many, many more were only identified at higher, broader taxonomic levels. Genetic testing of the samples, paired with photographs and descriptions of the samples, will help people work out more specific species, and also help them identify whether certain species are new to science.
The most important parts of this work will involve more than just identifying species. In fact, the more time I spent with these researchers in the lab (including one evening spent with them as they worked past midnight), the more I got the sense that, while they seemed excited about seeing new species, they seemed equally excited to witness relationships between animals.
When I walked into the lab one day, for example, several people urged me to go over and look through a microscope at a creature known as a pompom crab—a tiny yellow crustacean holding purple anemones in its modified front claws. Tweedt was extremely jazzed when she found something referred to as a “skeleton shrimp,” which looked to me like the marine equivalent of a stick insect, blending in on something called a hydroid. She pulled me aside another time, around 1 in the morning, to show me “the frosting on the cake” of the day, which turned out to be some bright red sea snails and the bright red octocorals they seemed to live on
As she put it in a later conversation, these relationships are, in many ways, the key takeaway from this ARMS project, and what distinguishes it from efforts to bring up a few individual samples at a time. Studying them, or even just looking at the fuller picture ARMS provide, is what will let researchers tackle some of the outstanding questions about these ecosystems. Bähr, for example, is already working with the data from ARMS retrieved in Guam, trying to analyze how much overlap (or lack thereof) there is between species at different depths in the deep reefs.
Really, though, this is all just the beginning. In one of our conversations, Rocha compared the work they are doing now to ecology work done in the mid-20th century to understand how species’ vertical distribution changes as you go up a mountain. This drove home for me how far behind researchers working on the mesophotic deep reefs are compared to their colleagues working on, say, shallower coral reefs. I asked him what kept him working on such a difficult puzzle.
“It’s the reward at the end of it,” he said. “If it’s a hard puzzle, at the end of it, the reward is always bigger.”
“But in our lifetimes, will we assemble the deep reef puzzle?” I asked.
“No, we will not assemble the puzzle, no,” Rocha said, “but we’ll generate some good pieces for the next generation to assemble.”

Anthropic vs. the pope
Claude’s creators are worried the LLM could be conscious. The Catholic Church disagrees.
Hi readers, happy Friday! It’s been a big week for the AI debate — not the one about whether it will cause the robot apocalypse, though there’s still plenty to worry about there, but instead about whether the technology is conscious.
The folks at Anthropic, the AI company behind the large language model Claude, certainly seem to think it is — or at least, they’re extremely open to the possibility.
As the New York Times reported earlier in the week, the company has spent the last year grappling with the question by speaking with religious thinkers from many faith traditions in an effort to chart a moral course for the LLM (that is, to keep it from killing us all, so maybe it is all one big debate).
In the process, the Times reports, some of those thinkers observed that members of the Anthropic team were “relating to [Claude] like a conscious being” and even, according to it, a degree of “moral status.”
On the flip side of this debate is Pope Leo XIV, who decidedly does not seem to buy into AI consciousness arguments. His “Magnifica Humanitas” encyclical earlier this year argued that AI will never be able to replace humanity — and reportedly “alarmed” Anthropic’s co-founder, Christopher Olah.
Since then, Pope Leo has continued to emphasize the differences between humans and machines this week. “There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others,” he posted on Friday. “Algorithms lack the spark of humanity.”
Loneliness machines
Conscious or no (and that’s a no from me), it’s hard to argue that tech companies don’t want you to interact with their models like people. That includes OpenAI and Meta, both of whom introduced “cute” new AI agents — called Dots and Muse, respectively — last month.
As my colleague Adam Clark Estes reported this week, though, the promise of a companionable, always-there AI might not be the best idea in the world — especially for children. A new study, still under review, suggests that AI use may be causing loneliness in middle schoolers.
Adam spoke with the lead researcher on the study, UNC Chapel Hill professor Anne Maheux, who explained that “middle school students using AI for emotional intimacy and companionship developed greater loneliness over time.”
According to Maheux, one big point where AI chatbots fail compared to human beings is “friction,” or the complicated push-and-pull dynamic of any connection with a real human being. By contrast, chatbots are “sycophantic, highly agreeable, anthropomorphized,” she says, which can lead to kids “developing expectations or understandings of interactive relationships that are actually fundamentally at odds with a normal human relationship.”
People, in other words, still matter, no matter how much the AI companies want us to build our lives around machines instead.

Pakistan launches deadly air strikes on Afghanistan
- Published
Pakistan has conducted further air strikes on Afghanistan, killing nine civilians and injuring 11 others, the Taliban government said.
Islamabad's information ministry confirmed the strikes, which it said killed twenty-two militants.
Zabihullah Mujahid, the chief spokesman of the Afghan Taliban, said the strikes hit homes in the Kunar and Helmand provinces bordering Pakistan. Women and children are among the dead, he said in an X post.
"We condemn this act as an aggression and crime in violation of all accepted principles," he said.
Pakistan had very different claims, saying that the "well-planned and calibrated" attack targeted "terrorist camps" in Afghanistan, where large quantities of weapons and ammunition were stored.
Maximum precautions were taken to ensure no collateral damage occurred, Pakistan's information ministry said.
Pakistan has repeatedly accused the Afghan Taliban of harbouring militant groups that carry out and plan attacks on it from inside Afghanistan's territory.
The Afghan Taliban deny it, saying Pakistan's militancy is an internal problem, but it has led to a significant deterioration in the relationship between the two neighbours.
Fighting between the allies-turned-foes escalated dramatically in February this year, with Pakistan declaring that it's in an "open war" with Afghanistan after a surge in deadly clashes and cross-border airstrikes.
Talks mediated by China established a fragile ceasefire in March.
Last month, a deadly attack on a police facility in north-west Pakistan, which killed 24 people, rekindled tensions between the two countries.
Last week, Pakistan launched air strikes in Afghanistan which hit Kandahar, the Taliban's base of power, among other provinces. This earlier attack killed four civilians, according to the Afghan Taliban government.

Forward-deployed engineers are one of the hottest jobs in AI. Finding them isn't easy.
"These are unicorns," Asa Kalavade, vice president of forward-deployed engineering at Amazon Web Services, told Business Insider.
Like its rivals, Amazon has made a big bet on the future of FDEs. In June, AWS announced a $1 billion investment to create a dedicated AWS FDE organization.
Popularized by Palantir, FDEs are often embedded with companies to integrate AI into their workflows and to build more customized solutions.
Anthropic, OpenAI, and Microsoft have announced major initiatives in recent months to compete for the lucrative enterprise AI business. Forrester estimates that between May and July alone, the three companies and Amazon pledged roughly $9 billion to FDE-related ventures.
"FDE hiring is sort of the rage in town these days," Kalavade said. "Everybody wants to be an FDE."
Amazon is being selective as it builds the team, Kalavade said, initially focusing on engineers who can hit the ground running.
"Our initial seed is what I call the insurgents, the frontier engineers who've been there, done this before," she said.
Kalavade said it's "a really hard role," and that those best positioned to succeed have a startup mindset. She said Amazon is essentially looking for three things: a product customer mindset, deep software expertise, and agentic experience.
"Different people will have different strengths, but at the end of the day, that's the package that we think makes the most successful FDEs," she said.
Part of the issue, Kalavade said, is that colleges and universities are still developing FDE training programs. She said that recent groups of applicants have improved, especially in their familiarity with AI.
"The batch that came out this summer was the first one that grew up with more AI native thinking," she said.
Kalavade said AI models alone can get customers "halfway," but she said FDEs are needed to turn that into a customized solution.
"Anyone can build an agent now, but how do you make sure the agent has the right guardrails?" she said. "How do you figure out, 'OK, what's the best underlying model that I can use from a cost-based perspective?' What do I need to do to update to the next model? How do I make sure that the right security policies are applied? So all of those things are areas that are needed around the model."
Amazon wants to make AI integration easier, Kalavade said, while also making sure companies can become more self-sufficient.
"We want them to look and co-build with us for one or two, or six months," she said, "but then the only way we can create long-lasting change is if they co-build and they adopt these methodologies to do more."

Breaking up forests is just as bad for global warming
How broken up a forest is can affect local temperatures as much as the forested area, a new study has found. Using satellite data, researchers found that in tropical and temperate zones, dividing continuous forests into smaller, isolated patches significantly raised surface temperature. In high-altitude boreal forests, however, fragmentation had a cooling effect because it exposed more open ground to snow cover, which reflects sunlight. The findings mean climate action needs to track fragmentation, too.
Radio jets from colossal black holes light up gas clouds
Astronomers have wondered how large black holes affect the gas halos surrounding their host galaxies. An Indian team combined hundreds of observations to find a glow of ionised hydrogen only along the path of radio-frequency energy blasting from the galaxies’ centres. Magnesium, a marker of cool gas, was however found scattered around the galaxies. This meant the jets don’t create the halos; instead, as they shoot out, they crash into existing gas clouds and light them up.
Flying butterflies use wing patterns to confuse predators
The striking wing patterns of butterflies may be a visual defence. By studying high-speed videos of butterfly flights and using 3D computer models, scientists found the combination of flapping wings and contrasting patterns, such as stripes and bright edges, creates an optical illusion that tricks a predator’s eyes and confuses its judgment of the insect’s speed and direction. The team said this “potentially represents one of the most successful visual defence strategies in moving animals”.

The Supreme Court on Monday (September 28, 2026) questioned the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) over its proposed deadline – of nearly two years — for implementing front-of-pack warning labels (FoPL) on packaged foods, asking why it wanted to “waste so much time” on fresh public and industry consultations when the issue concerned citizens’ health.
The court’s remarks came as it pressed the food safety regulator to expedite the introduction of warning labels on packaged foods high in sugar, salt and saturated fat.
Responding to the court’s September 10 order, which raised several questions over the size, colour, and placement of the proposed labels as well as the timeline for their implementation, the FSSAI said in an affidavit filed last week that the draft regulations would require a four-month process of consultation and finalisation. It proposed notifying the labelling norms by July 1 next year, following which food business operators would be given another 365 days to transition to the new regime to ensure minimal hardship.
“Why voluntary compliance for a year? Why do you need so much time? Why do you want to start afresh with the exercise of hearing and calling for objections? You started in 2022. What did you do in the last four years?” a Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K. Vinod Chandran asked while reserving its order in the matter.
PIL petition
The top court was hearing a public interest litigation (PIL) petition filed by non-profit organisation 3S and Our Health Society, seeking the introduction of FoPL guidelines on the lines of those in force in foreign jurisdictions. The petitioner, represented by advocate Rajiv Shankar Dwivedi, has argued that such labels are necessary to warn children and other consumers about packaged foods containing high levels of salt, sugar and saturated fat, and their potential adverse health effects.
Additional Solicitor-General Brijender Chahar, appearing for the Centre and the FSSAI, explained that the exercise initiated in 2022 concerned the Indian Nutrition Rating (star-rating) system and was based on a different yardstick from the warning-label regime now under consideration.
“Today, the yardstick is completely different. We have set four months for drafting the regulations. The rest we leave it to my Lords — how much time should be given for compliance,” Mr. Chahar submitted.
Public health goal
Justice Pardiwala appreciated the steps taken by the regulator so far, but said much more remained to be done to give meaningful effect to the court’s objective of protecting public health. The Bench also indicated that it would seek to strike a “balance” while fixing a reasonable timeline to roll out the warning labels.
“We appreciate whatever you have done so far, and we appreciate your initiative, but there is a lot which is required to be done to give meaningful effect to what we want to achieve… We are undertaking this entire exercise for the good of the nation, for the good of the citizens, so we expect the authority to accept our order in its true spirit,” the Bench said.
The Bench further made it clear that its forthcoming directions would be binding on the regulator and said it expected the FSSAI to implement them “scrupulously” and in their “true spirit”. The court also indicated that it would keep the matter pending to monitor compliance with its directions.
“We will now pronounce the final order. We will again keep it for some time to ensure due compliance with each and every direction. Do not disappoint us on the day when the matter comes up for reporting compliance,” the Bench told the regulator.
Single-phase proposal
In its affidavit filed earlier, the FSSAI had told the top court that it was prepared to roll out FoPL for packaged foods in a single phase, departing from its earlier proposal for a two-stage implementation based on the number of “nutrients of concern” present in a product.
“The FSSAI proposes to adopt a single-phase approach for the implementation of Front-of-Pack Nutrition Labelling. To finalise the draft regulations, it requires a four-month period, and there shall be a ‘voluntary implementation period of 365 days’ by Food Business Operators (FBOs),” the affidavit had stated.
On the design of the warning label, the regulator modified its earlier proposal for a red hexagon and suggested placing the hexagon against a white, square-shaped background, drawing from the labelling format followed in Canada.
The FSSAI also clarified that the warning requirement would not be confined to products containing high levels of two or more nutrients of concern. Packaged foods exceeding the prescribed threshold for even one such nutrient would carry the warning.
Under the proposed framework, the warning label would be prominently placed on the top-left corner of the front of the package for greater visibility. The warning would also appear in a font larger than that used for the nutritional information displayed on the back of the pack.
Note of caution
Earlier, the top court had also flagged a possible unintended consequence of the proposed regime. It had noted that requiring manufacturers to reduce salt, sugar and fat — ingredients that add to taste, texture, and shelf life — could prompt greater reliance on artificial preservatives, emulsifiers and other additives.
The Bench had therefore asked the FSSAI to examine this possibility and consider corresponding regulatory safeguards to ensure that reducing one set of potentially harmful ingredients does not result in their substitution with other additives that could pose health concerns.
For determining the products that would require such warnings, the FSSAI has proposed adopting threshold values for added sugar, added fat used in cooking, and salt per 100 g/ml, as prescribed in the Dietary Guidelines for Indians, 2024, issued by the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition (NIN).

House Republicans are reportedly in "triage mode" heading into the 2026 midterm elections, according to a new report.
Republicans have reportedly become fearful of their chances in the midterms as President Donald Trump's approval rating has been consistently and historically low heading into election season, according to CNN. Recent Associated Press polling shows Trump with a 69 percent disapproval rating.
As a result, some Republicans have shifted their focus from gaining power in Congress to mitigating the damage they expect to see this November.
Part of the alleged "triage mode" involves Republicans moving money away from races that they view as difficult to win, according to the report.
Among those seats that might be subject to abandonment are reportedly races against Congresswoman Mariannette Miller-Meeks in Iowa and Tom Kean in New Jersey, as well as an open seat in Nebraska.
A day before CNN's report, Semafor reported that the GOP-backing Senate Leadership Fund is stopping a $30 million ad campaign meant to back Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley in North Caroline and moving that money to Senator Roger Marshall's re-election campaign in Kansas.
Republicans are also reportedly putting significant funding into newly redrawn districts in both Texas and Florida, which could help mitigate other losses, according to an anonymous GOP leadership aide who spoke to CNN.
“At the end of the day, redistricting could be the lifesaver either way – either minimizing the losses or the reason we potentially hold onto the majority," the aide reportedly said.
Despite the gloom and doom reportedly being felt among the GOP's congressional leadership, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said he is "absolutely still convinced" that Republicans will retain control of the House.
Republicans speaking to CNN were apparently less confident, telling CNN's Sarah Ferris and David Wright that they're focused on minimizing the Democrats' potential majority. Multiple sources told CNN they hoped to hold the Democrats to a 10-seat advantage or fewer.
“They [said] their strategy is now focused on how to limit Democrats to the slimmest majority possible," according to the report.
Even Trump has voiced some concern ahead of the midterms. He has twice promised to send Americans $5,000 checks if Republicans come out ahead in the midterm elections, though many, including Republicans, are skeptical that he will make good on the bribe.
During a rally in Oklahoma on Thursday, Trump told a crowd that he was concerned about races in Michigan, Texas and elsewhere.
We’re worried about Michigan. We’re worried about Texas. We’re worried about a few states," Trump said during the address.
He said his concern extended to about 35 or 40 races.
"But we have to get the word out because we have to win in those 35. Maybe you could even say 40 places, 40 races," Trump said. "You have many, you have hundreds of races, but it’s all about 40."

- Hegseth suggested the Office of Religious Affairs would address urgent spiritual needs among the troops, which he said had long been neglected. He said the office would report directly to him and that budgets would be guaranteed both for chaplaincy and infrastructure, such as "base chapels."

In October 2026, a rumor spread that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth had announced the creation of an Office of Religious Affairs at the Pentagon.
The claim spread on social media, including X. One X post included a video of Hegseth speaking on a stage with a U.S. flag background (archived):
"Today, at my direction, I am establishing the Office of Religious Affairs," Hegseth says in the video. "Starting today, and for secretaries of war after me, the Office of Religious Affairs will report straight to the top. No staff filters. No bureaucratic dilution. A direct line to the secretary."
Meanwhile, several Snopes readers searched the website seeking more information about the supposed Office of Religious Affairs.
It is true that on Sept. 30, 2026, Hegseth gave a speech he called the "State of the Force" address. In this speech, he said he had ordered the creation of an office dedicated to religious affairs, which Department of Defense spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed in an X post (archived):
We reached out to the DOD seeking more details about the initiative and will update this story if we learn more.
Here's what we know about the new DOD office so far:
Office of Religious Affairs
In his speech, Hegseth said the initiative would address what he described as long-neglected spiritual needs among the troops (starting around the 50:25 mark of the DOD's recording of the speech):
After describing how significant the loss of a religious community could be for military personnel assigned to a new location or deployed abroad, Hegseth said that "political correctness and secular humanism" had allowed budgets for religious support to dwindle and infrastructure such as "base chapels" to go into disarray.
Religious diversity in the force
Hegseth said that "less than 5% of our force identifies as non-religious," without citing his source for the number. A 2019 congressional report found that while 2.3% of the force identified as agnostic or atheist, the affiliation of 24.4% of active duty personnel fell under "Other/Unclassified/Unknown" (PDF Page 51).
Meanwhile, the Military Association of Atheists and Freethinkers, an organization that advocates for nonreligious military members but is not associated with the DOD, said 2.05% of the force identified as "Humanists" in 2018 (Humanism is a non-theistic belief; Humanists believe in a moral and ethical code without believing in God). That report also said the chaplaincy did not represent the religious diversity of the military, with an overrepresentation of evangelistic Christians, when only 13.31% of the troops identified as such.
We reached out to the MAAF for comment on the creation of the office. A spokesperson told us the group was in the process of dissolving and directed us to the American Humanist Association, a nonprofit that advocates for secular humanism. We will update this story if the AHA returns our request for a statement on the possible impact of the creation of the office on nonreligious service members.
In May 2026, the DOD released a list of recognized religions in a memorandum signed by Undersecretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness Anthony Tata. The memo included 31 religions, down from 211, according to Military.com, the news outlet dedicated to reporting on the U.S. Military. Twenty-two of those 31 were Christian denominations.
Hegseth then announced the creation of the Office of Religious Affairs, designed to report directly to him in the Pentagon organizational chart. In his announcement, he said (around 52:32 of the video embedded above):
This won't be a paper pushing shop. It will have real teeth. It will protect budgets, demand infrastructure, and strengthen religious support. The experts, our chaplains, will finally have an advocate at the highest levels. Policy and resources will serve the mission, not smother the mission.
'Spiritual readiness' and 'spiritual resilience'
A memo issued on the same day confirmed the creation of the office. It read, in part:
The Department of War is committed to fulfilling its duty to support the Department's Service members, their families, and the Department's civilian personnel in the free exercise of religion as protected by the Constitution of the United States and applicable Federal law. While the Department accomplishes this mission primarily through the chaplaincies of the Military Departments established under title 10, U.S. Code, the establishment of the ORA will ensure resources are adequately provided and, where necessary, policy is properly aligned to prioritize the free exercise of religion and the spiritual readiness across the Total Force.
Still, Hegseth's memo said, this effort to support the spirituality of military personnel should not "be construed to compel religious participation or to diminish the free exercise rights of any Service member, civilian employee, or family member of any faith or no faith."
The memo also said the new office had 90 days to present a plan of action to rebuild the spiritual force of the military:
Within 90 days of the date of this memorandum, the Secretaries of the Military Departments, in coordination with their respective Chiefs of Chaplains, will submit to the Director a comprehensive baseline report of all unfunded and underfunded religious affairs requirements, including, but not limited to, delivery ofreligious ministry, facilities and infrastructure, logistics, chaplain-led programs, chapel youth programs, faith-based homeschool support for military families, programs related to suicide reduction, and contracted services from faith-based non-Federal entities; research, technology, and analytical tools to support spiritual fitness, spiritual readiness, and spiritual resilience; chaplain in-service procurement programs, chaplain and religious support team training and education.
For further reading, Snopes examined another announcement Hegseth made that day, the launch of "Project Meridian," set to study the "future of warfare."

Lyrical Animation is developing a new animation series based on “RuneScape” in partnership with creator Charlie “MoistCr1TiKaL” White and game developer Jagex, the company’s CEO Jon Bellamy announced on stage at RuneFest in Birmingham, UK, on Saturday.
The project will bring the world of Gielinor to the screen, and marks a new step in Jagex’s ambition to expand the “RuneScape” world beyond the gaming ecosystem.
“For 25 years, our players have helped shape ‘RuneScape’s’ extraordinary world, its characters and its stories,” said Bellamy. “When we talk about the future of ‘RuneScape,’ we don’t just mean games. We see huge potential to bring Gielinor to life in new ways, both for the millions who already know and love it and for a whole new audience. It’s early days, but we’re excited to explore that potential with Charlie and the team at Lyrical Animation, and we wanted our players to be the first to know.”
Popular on Variety
Jagex first released “RuneScape” in 2001, and it has grown into a massively popular fantasy multiplayer online role-playing game. Through quests, combat, exploration and cooperative adventures, players can forge their own paths through the medieval fantasy world of Gielinor. The franchise now includes “RuneScape,” “Old School RuneScape” and “RuneScape Dragonwilds.”
White is a longtime member of the “RuneScape” community and has amassed more than 25 million followers across his channels and platforms. “I’ve been playing RuneScape for 22 years, and it’s one of my favorite IPs ever,” said White. “I’m so excited to be working with the team on this project.”
“RuneScape has such a unique storytelling voice, at once laugh-out-loud funny and effortlessly insightful,” said Daniel Dominguez, creative director of Lyrical Animation. “To be allowed to help bring that to life for its millions of fans alongside our dear friend Charlie again is a dream come true.”
Lyrical Animation will produce the project alongside White’s Meatier Productions. Development is in its early stages, and the company expects to reveal more details in 2027.

US Coast Guard finds ‘debris field’ from missing medical plane traveling from Bermuda to Boston
‘Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?’ a controller can be heard asking the pilot

Searchers found a “debris field” off the coast of Nantucket, Massachusetts, from an air ambulance that was carrying six people when it vanished over the Atlantic on Saturday during a flight from Bermuda to Boston, the U.S. Coast Guard said.
Four Canadians and two Bermudian nationals were aboard, and their next of kin were notified as the search continued, the Coast Guard said in a statement.
It added that one of its cutters would keep searching the water overnight and into Sunday.
According to the Coast Guard, the Federal Aviation Administration reported that the Gulfstream G100 lost contact very early Saturday morning.
Air traffic audio indicates that it may have been “coming in blind” when a storm loomed ahead shortly before it vanished.
The pilot reported electrical problems and declared an emergency as the jet approached the coast, according to air traffic control audio posted by LiveATC.net.
“Roger, you said you’re coming in blind. Is that what you said?” a controller can be heard asking the pilot.
That makes Mary Schiavo, who is a former Inspector General of the Transportation Department, think the plane may have lost its navigational instruments just as a storm moved across its path on radar.
The plane also descended sharply from its cruising altitude of around 24,000 feet to around 10,000 feet, according to preliminary data from flight tracking site FlightRadar24.
“Something bad happened with this big drop, and they flew into this big storm. It’s a terrible place to have a loss of your instruments and be flying blind,” said Schiavo, who is an aviation attorney.
“It’s very easy to get disoriented and not know if you’re turning, climbing, descending, etc.”
The Canadian-registered air ambulance jet had four crew members and two passengers aboard when it departed Bermuda’s L.F. Wade International Airport for the nighttime flight to Massachusetts, according to a statement from the Bermuda airport's operator, Skyport.
Transport Canada was closely monitoring and working with authorities on search and rescue efforts, the country’s Minister of Transport Steven MacKinnon said on the social platform X.
The National Transportation Safety Board said it was gathering information about the situation, but it did not say immediately if it would investigate.
"Our thoughts are with those on board and their loved ones as the search continues," a spokesperson from Massport, which operates Boston’s airport, told NBC 10.
The aircraft is owned by Latitude Air Ambulance of Hamilton, Ontario, Canada, the station reported.
Latitude has been operating medical flights since 2009, according to the company. Its Gulfstream jets are equipped with full ICU supplies, patient stretchers and can travel over 3,000 miles.

Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”
Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”
Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.
Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.
She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”
In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.
Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”
In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.
In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.
Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.
In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.
Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

The disclosure of BJP’s West Bengal election expenditure has sparked a storm on social media after revealing a Rs 2.5 lakh payment to Bengali actor and vlogger Sayak Chakraborty, who was involved in a controversial beef-steak incident at Kolkata’s Olypub in January 2026.
The report, published on the party’s letterhead and signed by office secretary at the BJP headquarters Mahendra Kumar Pandey details the party’s expenditure between March 15, the date of announcement of West Bengal assembly elections, and May 6, 2026, the official completion of the polls. The report shows that the BJP paid Rs 2,50,000 to a person named Sayak Chakraborty.
The payment appears under Schedule 3, titled “Expense(s) on Media Advertisement (print and electronic, bulk SMS, cable, website and TV channel etc.) on General Party propaganda authorised/incurred by Party Central Headquarters”. Chakraborty is listed at serial number 23 under the “electronic media” category.
The disclosure has drawn particular attention because Chakraborty was involved in a beef-related controversy at the iconic Park Street pub, Olypub, on January 30, 2026.
Following the publication of the expenditure report, Chakraborty acknowledged that he had been paid by the BJP, but claimed it had nothing to do with the Olypub incident.
The Olypub Incident & Why the Expenditure Disclosure Raises Eyebrows
On January 30, Chakraborty alleged that he had been served beef steak instead of a mutton dish at the restaurant. He subsequently lodged an FIR against Olypub and the concerned waiter who allegedly served him beef.
Sayak recorded the heated interaction on a live video and posted it on his Facebook page. His page, ‘Sayakk’, has 1.5 million followers. The 3-minute-47-second video has since been deleted from the page but remains available across social media. The clip can be watched here:
According to Chakraborty, while having dinner at Olypub, he and two friends ordered a mutton steak. The server placed a plate of food on their table without telling them what it was. Unaware of what they had been served, they ate it. After they had finished the dish, the waiter returned with another plate and said, “This is your mutton steak.” When they questioned him about the earlier dish, the waiter allegedly said it had been a beef steak.
Trouble started after that.
In the viral video, Chakraborty can be heard saying, “I ordered mutton steak; how could you mess it up and serve me beef instead? How could you hear beef instead of mutton? Do you know I am a Brahmin? I ate beef instead of mutton because of you!”
He also asked the server, Nasimuddin Sheikh, about his religion, before saying, “You made me eat Go-Mata!”
Following the altercation with the server, the actor lodged an FIR at Park Street police station. Kolkata Police arrested Nasimuddin based on the complaint. He was released on bail four days later.
The disclosure of the BJP’s expenditure immediately raised questions about whether Chakraborty had been paid by the party for his role in the Olypub episode. The questions gained further significance given that the incident had the potential to fuel a communal debate around beef, religion and Hindu identity — ideas that could serve the BJP’s broader political messaging.
They also arose because the immediate relatives of another person who was with Sayak during the incident appear in the BJP’s expenditure list.
At Olypub, while the beef controversy was unfolding, Sayak was accompanied by fellow social media influencer Sukanta Kundu and Kundu’s female friend. The BJP’s list includes the names of Sikha Kundu and Subrata Kundu, identified as Sukanta’s parents. Sikha and Subrata were paid Rs 4,50,000 and Rs 3,00,000 respectively.
Sayak Chakraborty’s Disclosure
As social media posts questioning Chakraborty’s association with the BJP gained traction, and media reports on the issue emerged, Sayak made a Facebook post on the morning of September 26, admitting that he had received a payment from the party.
He, however, claimed that his reaction at Olypub was a genuine outburst and not paid promotion.
He pointed to Olypub’s statement apologising for the meat mix-up as evidence that the episode was not scripted to evoke emotions. According to him, the BJP and others who shared his views simply supported him after the incident.
Chakraborty said the BJP and a few other political parties had subsequently approached him to make promotional content. He accepted the BJP’s offer and made several videos, including content on the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), possible reasons behind Narendra Modi’s silence during the conflict, and a congratulatory message for Suvendu Adhikari after he became chief minister.
He reiterated that these videos were made between March and May, the period covered by the BJP’s expenditure report, while the Olypub incident took place in January. Alt News tried calling up Chakraborty on his mobile number, but his phone was switched off.
Kundu, too, shared a Facebook post on September 26, acknowledging that the payment details being linked to him were indeed genuine. At the same time, he asserted that the Olypub incident was not part of his political campaign.

Congress members on the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs have written to committee chairman Radha Mohan Das, seeking an examination into conduct of the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) in West Bengal and police action against workers and supporters of the opposition party after the results for the assembly elections were declared on May 4.

“The discussion on the SOP to be followed by the Police Forces that the Chairman of the Committee assured on 25 August 2026 be held at the next sitting, that the pellet gun firing on innocent students at Jantar Mantar be taken up in it…and that the demand of Shri Derek O'Brien of 23 September 2026 be taken up with it, as one subject,” the letter said.

- On Sept. 30, 2026, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth delivered what he called a "State of the Force" address. During it, he announced the launch of "Project Meridian," which he described as "an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare."
- Hegseth named Tesla and Space X CEO Elon Musk, former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, as heads of Project Meridian.
- In a memorandum published the same day, Hegseth wrote, "Project Meridian's primary function will be to map the trajectory of future warfare, identify critical capability gaps, and propose actionable solutions in furtherance of the identified goals in the 2026 National Security Science and Technology Strategy."
- Snopes will update this report if additional information surfaces about what, specifically, Project Meridian will do. We have reached out to the Department of Defense, Musk, Gingrich and Luckey asking for more details about what the project will entail and are waiting for responses.
In late September 2026, a rumor spread online that Tesla and Space X CEO Elon Musk and former Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich had joined a new effort announced by the U.S. Department of Defense called "Project Meridian."
Several social media posts made the claim, including on Reddit and X. One X post (archived) said Musk, Gingrich and Palmer Luckey, founder of defense technology company Anduril Industries, had been recruited to lead the project "to focus on developing future warfare and autonomous weapons systems for battlefields 'from under the Earth to beyond the moon'":
The official X account of the DOD's chief technology officer confirmed the story (archived):
"From under the earth to beyond the moon, our warfighters will have technological superiority," the post read. "PROJECT MERIDIAN: THE FUTURE OF WARFARE."
Here's what we know so far about the initiative, its goals and the people involved:
Hegseth's announcement
On Sept. 30, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth delivered what he called a "State of the Force" address — meant to evoke the State of the Union address, which the president delivers annually to Congress — and announced the launch of Project Meridian, which he described as "an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare."
Hegseth began to describe Project Meridian roughly midway through his address (at 34:45 in the video):
Today we are leveraging a unique source of American advantage. One our adversaries do not have: our innovators, our senior leaders and our technologists — big thinkers who will forecast the creative solutions for tomorrow's conflicts. That's why today at my direction I am announcing Project Meridian, an effort led by America's best minds to study the future of warfare. Under the leadership of the department's chief technology officer, Emil Michael, Project Meridian will be co-led by three of our nations best minds. Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey and Newt Gingrich, all of whom are up in the audience with us today.
Shortly after he named them, Musk, Luckey and Gingrich stood up to applause from the crowd.
Musk, Gingrich and Luckey
Hegseth said the three men would lead a group of "subject-matter experts from across our nation's unmatched innovation, academic and policy ecosystems." The goal, he said, would be to develop "absolute technological superiority," by focusing on, among other things, "autonomous warfare" — in other words, weapons and equipment capable of functioning autonomously.
Musk was previously involved in President Donald Trump's administration as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency, which spearheaded drastic spending cuts to government programs. (The Government Accountability Office said in August 2026 that DOGE incorrectly reported or failed to substantiate some of its purported savings.) Musk's xAI technology has reportedly been used by U.S. forces in the Iran war.
Gingrich has consistently defended the war with Iran (archived), which has proved unpopular with U.S. voters, according to polls.
Luckey described himself as a "radical Zionist" during "The Shawn Ryan Show" podcast in February 2025, saying he defended Israel's right to exist. Asked directly by Axios what he thought of the war in Iran, he declined to answer.
Autonomous warfare
During the address, Hegseth also announced the creation of a new combatant command: "Today, with Autonomous War Command — AutoWarCom — we institutionalize and we supercharge the era of SI, robotics, and autonomous systems. All in order to win," Hegseth said. ("SI" refers to "super intelligence," what the federal government began calling artificial intelligence in September 2026.)
Hegseth appeared to present Project Meridian as the way to identify the technologies best suited to arm AutoWarCom. He said the group led by Musk, Gingrich and Luckey would render its first conclusions in 120 days.
The same day, the Pentagon published a memorandum that further outlined the goal of Project Meridian. It read:
Project Meridian will leverage critical perspectives from outside the Pentagon, drawing upon a group of top technologists, innovators, business leaders, policy makers, and national security experts. Project Meridian's primary function will be to map the trajectory of future warfare, identify critical capability gaps, and propose actionable solutions in furtherance of the identified goals in the 2026 National Security Science and Technology Strategy.

UAE had shared details about FlyDubai flight with Israel, including pilots' names and nationalities
Regional officials say authorities in the United Arab Emirates shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of last week's FlyDubai flight on which a pilot attempted to seize control of the Israel-bound aircraft and crash it
TEL AVIV, Israel -- Authorities in the United Arab Emirates shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of the FlyDubai flight on which a pilot attempted to seize control of the Israel-bound aircraft and crash it, regional officials said Sunday, raising new questions over how the attacker evaded detection.
While the investigation continues, preliminary details about the incident have highlighted several major security lapses. Officials already have said the Omani co-pilot had been barred from flying by his own country because of concerns about his extremist views. It also remains unclear how a citizen of Oman, an Arab country that has no diplomatic relations with Israel, was allowed to fly a planeload of Israelis to Tel Aviv.
The United Arab Emirates, which is leading the investigation, said the co-pilot attacked the flight's captain with the cockpit’s crash ax and tried to take control of the plummeting plane in a “terrorist attack” Wednesday. His actions nearly crashed the flight with 182 people on board before the Indian captain managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and others to rush in and subdued the attacker.
The regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities. Israel hadn’t raised red flags on any passenger or member of the crew, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters about the probe.
The passengers who halted the attack and helped regain control of the aircraft have been hailed as heroes in Israel.
But officials have begun to raise difficult questions and trade accusations about the security blunders that could have led to a major disaster.
The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the Transportation Ministry is responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights. Transportation Minister Miri Regev told Israel’s public broadcaster Kan that the security agencies are responsible for flight security and that her ministry wasn’t given a list of passengers or any warnings.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that Israel has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel.
It also remains unclear how FlyDubai, a low-cost Emirati airline that operates flights between Israel and the UAE, had failed to identify the Omani pilot as a security risk. Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England who wrote a book about aircraft hijackings and bombings, said background check systems differ from country to country and there are limits on what types of information can be shared.
“In terms of aviation security itself, obviously we want to have as robust background checks as possible. But there are huge limitations on doing background checks in any case, especially in cross-border checks,” he said.

'Rock, paper, scissors' decides London Marathon dates

A game of rock, paper, scissors was used to determine when the elite female and male races will take place during next year's unique two-day London Marathon.
After confirming they were playing for the right to race on the traditional Sunday, women's wheelchair world record holder Catherine Debrunner beat men's world record holder Sabastian Sawe - both 2026 London Marathon champions in their respective races - in the contest.
As a result, the elite men and men's wheelchair races are set for Saturday, 24 April, with the women's races the following day.
Hugh Brasher, chief executive of London Marathon Events, said: "Sabastian and Catherine's rock, paper, scissors battle was an entertaining way to decide which day would host each elite race.
"Splitting the elite races will allow us to shine an even brighter spotlight on the extraordinary athletes taking part."
Earlier this year, organisers of the event confirmed the London Marathon will be held across two days in what is said to be a momentous one-off edition of the event.
The decision was made to enable more people to take part, after a record 1.33 million people entered the ballot for next year.
In 2027 a record-breaking 100,000 participants will take part and it is estimated that more than £150m will be raised for charitable causes.
The women's championship categories will line-up behind the women's elite field for the first time in the London race.

India had the highest number of children with no sanitation service in schools, with 50 million out of the world total of 244 million as of 2025, according to a new global report. Only Nigeria (34 million), Ethiopia (26 million), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11 million) or Indonesia (8 million) had a comparatively large number of schoolchildren who had no access to sanitation service.
The data from ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’ shows the progress as well as the challenges India is facing in meeting the water, sanitation and hygiene goals that are part of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) set for 2030.
14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service
The report can also be seen as a decadal report card on the Swachh Bharat Mission, which was launched in India on October 2, 2014. The report cites the achievement of India which saw a 14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service.
Lack of hygiene service
The WHO/UNICEF report that is part of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) shows that globally, 362 million children still had no hygiene service at their school in 2025. Of these, 20 million were from India.
It is not just lack of access that the WHO report flags about India but also gaps in data. “There is now sufficient data to estimate trends in basic hygiene coverage between 2015 and 2025 for all SDG regions except Central and Southern Asia where there were insufficient recent data to generate estimates for India, and therefore the region, beyond 2024.”
Drinking water
On the brighter side, India is among the 28 out of 62 countries that are on track to achieve universal coverage of basic drinking water in schools by 2030.
As of 2025, there were 258 million children who still had no drinking water service at their school. The number of children from Indian schools made up 12 million of this number or about 1 out 20 children in the world. The report shows that India has made a big progress in basic drinking water services in 2025 and average rates of change between 2015 and 2025. India, Panama, Syrian Arab Republic, Togo and Tuvalu increased coverage by over 4% per year, “demonstrating that rapid progress is possible”.
However, the report found that while gaps in basic water coverage persists between school levels and between rural and urban areas, this did not apply to India, Cambodia and Fiji.

Splice CEO Kakul Srivastava thinks AI emails are killing conversations
As head of Splice, Kakul has tried to carefully thread the line on AI music tools. She also hates her cup warmer.
Splice CEO Kakul Srivastava thinks AI emails are killing conversations
As head of Splice, Kakul has tried to carefully thread the line on AI music tools. She also hates her cup warmer.
Before that, Kakul held executive roles at Flickr, Yahoo, GitHub, and Adobe. Throughout her career, Kakul has found herself at the intersection of Silicon Valley and creatives. That’s been especially true at Splice, where she’s not just expanded the platform’s footprint by acquiring Spitfire Audio, but also overseen its forays into the world of generative AI.
Last year, she was very outspoken on an episode of Decoder about avoiding the sort of “push-button, get-song” AI that has made companies like Suno so controversial. And based on her answers to our questionnaire, it doesn’t seem like her skepticism has waned. When it comes to Splice, the company has made a point of trying to offer AI products that still keep the human at the center of the creative process. And when it comes to communicating with colleagues, Kakul sees the same need to keep AI at bay.
What is your most indispensable tool?
A well-written document and a real conversation about it.
Splice is remote-first, so we don’t have a hallway. What we have instead is somebody sitting down and actually thinking something through, and then a bunch of people arguing with it. Almost everything good that’s happened here started that way.
Which is why I’m careful about AI-written documents. Once you can’t tell whether there’s a person behind the words, the conversation you have about it becomes a different conversation, and a worse one. And you can’t really go back from that. I think the same thing is true of music.
What is your happy place online?
Instagram, which I know is not the fashionable answer. My feed has turned into almost entirely people making music in ways I would never have thought of. There’s gothic western, which I did not know was a thing. There’s a woman in Russia who organizes street dancing. There’s a guy playing modern hits on a hammered dulcimer. The Indian chai-wala rapping. I could watch it all, all day.
What game do you have the fondest memories of?
Antakshari. It’s an Indian game — you sing a bit of a song, and whatever letter the line ends on is the letter the next person has to start their song with. You play it on long car rides, at weddings, any time a group of people is stuck somewhere together.
I love that the whole game is made out of music and none of the players are musicians. You just have to remember, and you have to be willing to sing in front of your family, which for most people is the harder part. And then when you watch people’s faces get soft when the song really hits — even when it’s sung badly. That’s the power of music.
What’s the most disappointing gadget you’ve owned?
A cup warmer. It warms the cup. It does not warm the coffee. I want to be clear that it works exactly as designed.
What creation are you most proud of?
I can’t not say my kids. Watching a person go from nothing to a fully formed human with opinions you did not give them is the most amazing thing I have been anywhere near. And the strange part is that it isn’t rare. It’s happening in every house on the street. We all just watch it happen and then go about our day.
Which are you least proud of?
I was on the early team at Tiny Speck, the company that later became Slack. Before Slack, we made a game called Glitch — a massively multiplayer open world — and it was one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever worked on. The art, the sound, the writing, the way the world actually worked. Some of the most talented people I’ve ever been around.
It failed, and it failed for reasons that were sitting right there in front of us. It was built on Flash, and Adobe had already stopped investing in Flash. It was a PC experience at the exact moment the whole world was moving to playing games on a phone. Two enormous tectonic trends, and we didn’t account for either one in time to do anything about them. I feel like I let down the creativity of the people who built something beautiful.
What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?
Say the thing, then explain it. Don’t lay all your proof out first, hoping it earns you the right to make your point. Nobody is listening to the proof yet. They’re listening for whether you sound like you believe it. The confidence you say it with is what makes room for the explanation.
What is your current obsession?
Cooking my mother’s food. She died before I learned most of it from her, so I’ve been reconstructing her recipes off YouTube — strangers in their own kitchens, making the thing the way their mothers made it. It takes a lot of tries. I got one of them right last year, and the taste put me straight back to being eight years old with my mom by my side.
This is what I think about when people ask me what technology is for. Some guy uploaded a video of his family’s recipe and gave me my mother’s cooking back. He will never know that.
What do you think is worth splurging on?
Live jazz. There is nothing else like being in a room where people are making decisions in real time and can’t take them back. I travel a lot for work, and if there’s any way to get to a show in whatever city I’m in, I’ll do it, even when it means I’m useless the next morning.
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
A heist movie where nothing gets stolen and everybody gets paid.
