Why Windows 11 is always using so much RAM
High RAM usage isn't always a problem that needs a fix.
Open Task Manager on a Windows 11 PC, and it's easy to panic no matter how much RAM you have. Even without many apps open, your computer will likely be using more than 50 percent of its memory. And while this seems like a problem, most of the time it isn't. While 16GB of RAM is the standard for modern computers, that doesn't mean it's no longer enough just because your PC is using almost all of it. This has more to do with how modern versions of Windows manage memory.
First, it's worth taking a look at what RAM is used for. Your computer's memory temporarily stores data that your processor needs to run apps and open files. It offers much faster speeds than your hard drive or SSD, so it's much quicker to access data from. The more RAM you have, the more items your computer can keep open and ready for you to switch between. Multitasking gets a lot better with more RAM.
What's actually using your RAM
The latest versions of Windows treat RAM as something to be used, not something to conserve. In the past, your computer would use only the RAM needed to run the programs you currently have open. However, unused RAM doesn't do anything for you — it ends up being a waste of resources. What Windows does now is figure out what you might need to run soon and keep that in RAM. That could be an app you open often, or a file you're regularly working on. This makes your computer feel a lot faster, because Windows has already preloaded what you need.
All of this happens under a process called SysMain (or SuperFetch in older versions of Windows). It learns your computer usage habits to keep important parts cached in standby memory. If you open Chrome every morning, there's a good chance Windows will keep it in RAM for you. The time it takes to open an app that's preloaded in RAM is significantly shorter than loading it from your storage drive. As a result, you may notice that your PC is using more than half of its available RAM, or sometimes almost 100 percent.
To see what's going on, press Ctrl + Shift + Esc to open Task Manager. Then go to the Performance tab on the left and select Memory — ignore In use and look at Available instead. Cached data counts as available because Windows can reclaim it instantly. The more RAM you have, the more Windows can use to keep your apps and files cached. That's why you shouldn't worry about how much RAM is being used in standby.
When high RAM usage becomes a problem
Despite this smart management, excessive RAM usage can still sometimes be a problem. If you've noticed your computer running slowly or apps crashing, or you're getting alerts that your computer is "low on memory," there might be something else going on.
In that case, check the Processes tab in Task Manager to see which apps are using the most RAM, and close any you don't need. Restart your PC if it's been a while, too. This will fix memory leaks (an issue where a program doesn't return memory it's done using to the available pool). Be sure to disable startup apps you don't use so they aren't hogging memory in the background.
Some third-party "memory cleaner" apps claim to help reduce RAM usage, but there are generally not worth using. While they might reduce the percentage of memory in use, having apps switch to the page file (part of your storage drive Windows uses as backup, pretend RAM) makes them slower. These apps also aren't a long-term solution, since the system will eventually reload everything again.
Some people choose to disable SysMain entirely and revert to the old RAM management system. While we wouldn't recommend this in most cases, on an older PC with a mechanical hard drive, the constant preloading can keep the disk busy and make the system sluggish. If that's the case for you, press Win + R, type services.msc and look for SysMain. Open its Properties, click Stop and set the startup type to Disabled. This will prevent Windows from preloading files and apps into your RAM.
But again, we don't recommend this unless you're on an old system with an HDD that's starved for RAM. If you're still stuck with 8GB of RAM (or less), the proper solution is upgrading to 16GB or more — even though RAM is more expensive than ever. In the meantime, you can also try changing a few settings to improve your experience on Windows 11 PCs.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

AAP's Priyanka Kakkar joins Congress: 'No need to let votes scatter now'

In a setback to the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), the Arvind Kejriwal-led outfit's chief national spokesperson, Priyanka Kakkar, joined Congress on Saturday, saying that there was “no need to let votes scatter votes now”.

Who is Priyanka Kakkar?
Priyanka Kakkar served as the AAP chief national spokesperson in her most recent assignment, having been appointed in April 2023.
She joined the party in 2013 and, over the years, managed various organisational duties, including serving as the Telangana Observer, legal head for the South Delhi parliamentary constituency, and advisor to Rajya Sabha MP Sanjay Singh.
Kakkar holds a Master’s Degree in Law (LLM) from the University of Pennsylvania and has practised law for nearly two decades..

South Korean president orders probe into data leaks across financial industry
SEOUL: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung ordered a thorough investigation and response measures over recent personal data leak incidents at banks, finance companies and public agencies, Seoul's presidential office said on Sunday (Oct 4).
Financial Services Commission (FSC) Chairman Lee Eog-weon convened an emergency meeting with financial industry associations, regulators and executives from affected institutions on Sunday, warning that the sector must respond with the highest level of vigilance, the FSC said in a statement.
The FSC's Lee said authorities could not rule out the possibility that artificial intelligence was used in the attacks and called for an "AI attacks defended by AI" approach, while also signalling broader upgrades to the financial sector's cybersecurity framework.
Sunday's meeting came after similar talks on Friday, when the FSC said Shinhan Bank, KB Kookmin Bank and others had reported cyberattacks, while Yonhap news agency reported that Hana Bank and Woori Bank had also suffered breaches.
The banks could not immediately be reached for comment outside regular working hours on Sunday.
The financial regulator said authorities had launched on-site investigations after Shinhan Bank reported a breach on Sep 30 and had since expanded probes into other reported incidents.
The regulator directed financial institutions to carry out comprehensive security inspections, tighten access controls, minimise external system access and strengthen consumer protection measures.
It also said attack methods, internet protocol addresses and other threat information would be rapidly shared across the industry to prevent further incidents.
Yonhap news agency said regulators believe the attacks may have broadly scanned multiple financial companies for vulnerabilities rather than targeting a single institution.
Attack traffic was reported to have originated from IP addresses across several countries including the United States, Japan, Singapore, Vietnam and Britain, Yonhap said, citing bank data submitted to lawmakers.
Sunday's emergency meeting was brought forward from Oct 7 after additional breaches were discovered at second-tier financial institutions, according to multiple Korean media reports.
The country's main opposition People Power Party said authorities should also investigate the possibility of North Korean involvement, citing past cyberattacks attributed to Pyongyang against South Korean financial institutions.

At about 9.30 on Wednesday morning local time, Tali Manes was taking her six-year-old daughter, Nina, to the toilet on the regular flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when she heard a series of heavy blows against the cockpit door.
Manes, an Israeli bank executive, immediately told a flight attendant seated nearby that something was wrong. When he did not react, she shouted at him: “Something is happening in there!” Seconds later, the man “simply went to the [cockpit] door and opened it”, Manes told Israel’s Channel 12 TV.
Inside, the scene was the stuff of travellers’ nightmares: blood spattered over the cockpit walls and a brutal struggle in progress between the badly injured pilot and the co-pilot, who was armed with some kind of sharp weapon. There was no one at the controls of the Boeing 737.
Manes shouted again: “He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!”
Many of the details of what happened on flight FZ 1073 are still unclear, but what happened next is well documented by witness testimony and videos.
As the plane went into a steep dive, losing 16,000ft of altitude in about a minute, most of the 182 passengers screamed, prayed and tried desperately to reassure panicking children. But a small group rushed to the cockpit and overpowered the co-pilot. One, a plumber, copied an action seen on TV documentaries about plane crashes to pull the aircraft out of its dive.
Two off-duty pilots on the flight, both among the handful of non-Israeli passengers, then took over the controls of the now almost rudderless aircraft to guide it eventually to a landing 90 minutes later in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia. In the meantime, Manes had helped truss the co-pilot with a telephone cord while a dentist treated the injured Indian pilot, Smit Machchhar. It was a “great miracle”, Manes said on eventually reaching Tel Aviv on an emergency flight 10 hours later.
In a video call with Narendra Modi, the Indian prime minister, broadcast live by TV networks, Machchhar, who is recovering in an Abu Dhabi hospital, said he had been “fighting for my life”.
The pilot successfully sent an alarm to air traffic control signalling the attack and then, as his strength ebbed, managed to unlock the cockpit security door.
“I had so many wounds. I had fallen down,” Machhchar said. “At one point, I realised that if I didn’t get up … then passengers would lose their lives.”
For the moment, the identity of the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar is unknown, though regional sources said he was an Omani national who had joined flydubai – which is owned by the United Arab Emirates (UAE) government – between five and nine months ago.
The co-pilot was barred from flying in Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, the Associated Press quoted a source as saying on Saturday, and was subsequently hired by flydubai.
In Israel, there is little doubt about the co-pilot’s intentions. “The co-pilot is a terrorist who tried either to hijack the plane or bring it down as a suicide. The worst scenario is he was trying to get into Israel,” said Arik Arad, the chair of the aviation cybersecurity consultancy Cyviation and El Al’s former head of security at Ben Gurion airport
Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, has claimed the co-pilot was exposed to “Islamist radical indoctrination”, saying Israeli investigators had found evidence on social media accounts that he wanted to “kill Jews”.
“The attacker, he calls out to the aircrew: ‘Kill me, kill me,’” Netanyahu told Fox News, adding it was “clear he was suicidal”.
Experts said there have been only a handful of instances of suicide by plane – cases where the pilot’s motivation is primarily to kill him or herself by crashing the plane, rather than using the plane as a weapon, as in the 9/11 attacks.
In 2015, the co-pilot of a low-cost German airline flight who had hidden evidence of psychiatric illness from his employers deliberately crashed, killing himself and 150 others. Suggestions that the crash of an AirIndia 787 in Ahmedabad last year was the result of a pilot deliberately cutting fuel to engines have been fiercely disputed.
Terrorism experts are sceptical that the flydubai co-pilot’s only motivation was to end his own life. “The odds that a pilot would decide to commit suicide and just happen to be flying a plane full of Israelis are pretty low,” said Colin Clarke, a terrorism expert at the respected Soufan Center in New York.
“Netanyahu has a big interest in this being terrorism, but the best explanation is probably the most obvious one [ie terrorism],” he said. “The question … is: was [the co-pilot] recruited by a group or an organisation … or was he radicalised alone? In which case, what was hyping him up, given he was flying a planeload of Israelis? Could that be Gaza?”
Security services have been warning of a wave of radicalisation across the Middle East prompted by the war in Gaza, which came to an inconclusive halt with a fragile ceasefire a year ago. But there has been limited evidence as yet that any violent Islamist extremist groups have gained support as a consequence of the conflict.
Terrorism experts said the most obvious group that might be involved in such an attack would be al-Qaida in the Arabian Peninsula (AQAP), which is based in Yemen and has a history of efforts to bring down planes. They said AQAP had recently sought to launch or inspire violence internationally.
“Aviation remains the classic propaganda by deed,” Clarke said. “It’s been said that terrorism is theatre, and nothing is more theatrical than taking down an airplane. You get a body count, media coverage, you get your message across, and this makes a plane the ultimate spectacular terrorist attack.”
There are now many questions for aviation security. Changes made to plane design after 9/11, which allowed pilots to lock cockpit doors from the inside, have long been controversial among experts. If Machchhar’s desperate efforts to allow access to the flight deck had been unsuccessful, there is little doubt all onboard FZ 1073 would have died.
There are also questions about screening of pilots. This can be expensive for airlines and could deprive them of valuable crew if too many fail more rigorous efforts to expose psychiatric illness or extremist views. Pilots may be reluctant to fly routes where they undergo greater screening, and some may hide physical or psychological problems for fear of being grounded.
Arad said: “The important issue … is that obviously pilots are not being screened enough. Lots needs to be done.”
Dubai international airport, the world’s busiest airport for international passenger traffic, has built some of its appeal on a reputation for safety in a volatile region, said Philip Baum, a visiting professor of aviation security at Coventry University in England.
“They are very conscious of the fact – a little bit like Israel in many respects – that they cannot afford to have a terrorist attack happening on a flight out of there,” he said.
The UAE has ordered investigators to “collect information and evidence to determine the truth of the incident, its circumstances, details and motives, and to verify the extent of its connection to any terrorist activity or purpose, or the existence of prior planning or direction for it,” its attorney general, Hamad Saif al-Shamsi, said on Thursday.
Arad foresees growing threats to civilian aviation from cyber-attacks and the malevolent use of AI, which could allow the targeting multiple planes simultaneously. But other experts pointed out there was no need for such sophistication to pose a threat.
Clarke said: “Whether or not it involves an attacker who was self-radicalised or part of a group, keeping things simple is always the best way to carry out an attack, and this came pretty damn close.”

The Frenemy: How Australia navigates superpower rivalry
- Published
Snipers shatter the silence of the Australian bush. Then the missiles hit, the smoke rising in the distance. The buzz of drones starts up, soon to be drowned out by helicopters flying overhead.
Every piece of hardware is being deployed, no expense spared. But this is no war zone – the last time Townsville saw conflict was during World War Two. This is a show of military might.
" We live in a volatile world," says Australian Army Brigadier Ben McLennan.
"Training an army to be prepared to fight a war that is potentially more likely than it has been previously, [is] very important."
War is no longer an abstract concept for Australians who often feel removed from the problems facing other parts of the world. Thousands of miles from active conflict, the country, like everywhere else, is facing the knock-on effects of Iran and Ukraine such as higher fuel prices and rising inflation.
With China's military capabilities also on the rise and its increasing influence in the Pacific, there's also more concern about the threat it represents. Australia has responded by deepening its relationship with the US, its security ally and China's rival superpower.
But that also puts Australia in a tricky position - for China's rise has also given Australia its biggest trading partner.
It's a paradox that most people are well aware of - which is probably why we've been invited to report on what Australia is doing to protect itself but nobody is willing to say whom they're preparing to fight.
"We're rehearsing for a war - the worst type of war - a World War Two-like war, a World War One-type war, a total war," says Brigadier McLennan, preferring to remain vague when asked who the enemy is.
Binding tighter to the US
The war scenario playing out before us is part of a major joint exercise known as "Southern Jackaroo" - a training programme involving the Australian, American and Japanese armed forces aimed at strengthening defence co-operation across the Indo-Pacific.
"We like to call ourselves America's 911 response force," US Marine Kevin Hicks says.
And in terms of numbers, they are more prepared than ever. In 2012, just 200 US Marines were deployed to Australia for an annual six-month deployment. Today, that figure has risen to around 2,500.
A quick read of Australia's 2026 National Defence Strategy gives you an easy answer as to why these numbers are growing.
"Intense competition between major powers – principally the United States and China – will be an enduring feature of our strategic environment," it said.
"China continues to undertake the largest military build-up in the world today, without the transparency or strategic reassurance the region expects."
The military tie-ups aren't just being seen in terms of troops but in bases too - most obviously in the north of the country such as RAAF Tindal air base in the Northern Territory which has been upgraded to support long-range American B52 bombers.
But the security partnership between the US, the UK and Australia - Aukus - arming Australia with nuclear submarines, is arguably the biggest example of deepening ties.
The Australian approach differs from that of its fellow middle powers. While Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney has talked about middle powers reorganising their priorities in light of an increasingly unreliable US, Australia seems to be intent on tying itself ever closer.
But that comes as Australians themselves increasingly doubt their relationship with the US.
"Only 31% of Australians trust the United States to act responsibly in the world, and a mere 28% of Australians trust China to do the same," says Charles Lyons-Jones, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute, citing their annual poll.
"Those are striking findings when you consider the level of trust that the Australian government has with the United States."
The 'frenemy'
While Australia's alliance with the US is changing, so too is its relationship with China.
Armed forces might be prepping for a potential military conflict but the fact remains China is Australia's most important economic partner.
Australia and China have had diplomatic relations since 1972 but it was only in the early 2010s that China became Australia's biggest trading partner, hungry for all the commodities it had to offer.
Australia opened up its economy and encouraged business and trade, Chinese President Xi Jinping was invited to address parliament. And it culminated in the signing of a free trade agreement in 2015.
The golden era didn't last long though. When Australia suggested an investigation into the origins of Covid in 2020, China objected to this line of questioning and retaliated with tariffs.
And then in 2021, Australia became the first nation to perform a U-turn on China's Belt and Road Initiative - its massive global infrastructure plan - when they cancelled the state of Victoria's agreement with the Chinese government three years after signing up.
A number of Australians have also been detained in China, including journalist Cheng Lei, who was released in 2023 after more than three years.
Relations have improved in recent years under the Labor government of Anthony Albanese, but it's not without challenges.
In June this year for example, China slapped 55% tariffs on beef to protect its own domestic market - despite the free trade agreement.
Even with these hiccups, this year's Lowy Institute Poll found that a majority of Australians (61%) saw China more as an economic partner than a security threat. That was an 11-point increase from last year. When it comes to China investing in Australia though, they are more wary.
"There are a number of European countries which are larger investors in Australia than China, and that is because our jurisdictions are much more similar, and there is a greater level of trust between our governments," says Lyons-Jones.
This year's Lowy Institute Poll also showed that for the first time, a majority of Australians (51%) believed that Australia's relationship with China was more important than its relationship with the US.
Rise and fall of superpowers
Earlier this month, former Prime Minister Kevin Rudd – a fluent Mandarin speaker - gave an address in which he talked of "radical changes" now reshaping Australia's national security, including "the rise and rise of China at a time when America continues to debate what sort of global power it wants to be".
Dr Marina Yue Zhang, an Associate Professor at the University of Technology Sydney agrees Australia's relationship with its closest ally is changing.
"The US is really doing something dramatic and more and more people in Australia - and I think globally - have realised 'is this the big brother we can all trust and put all our faith in?' " she says.
But old rivalries live on. With Australia caught between two superpowers, every exchange between their leaders carries weight. And in Beijing earlier this year, when Xi met Trump, the Chinese president invoked the idea of the "Thucydides Trap", the theory that conflict can become almost inevitable when a rising power challenges an established one.
"This is, if not the transition of great powers, at least [it's] power struggles of great powers, says Zhang.
And in that competition, Australia is inevitably affected. The US is a security ally that while more unreliable than in the past is still its mainstay. But economically so too is China. It's not an either/or relationship, it's a balancing act.
"There's no way Australia will choose one side and [dump] the other- it's not in their interests," Zhang says.
"It's getting harder and harder to maintain, but Australia has to do it."

As Brazil goes to the polls on Sunday (October 3), will the country join the "rightward shift" seen in Latin America in recent years?
The election in Brazil has been deemed "deeply polarising" as voters choose between two starkly different visions for the country proposed by leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing senator Flavio Bolsonaro.
Incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and his challenger, Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, are the frontrunners in Brazil's presidential election on Sunday.
Polls showed Lula and Flavio in a neck-and-neck fight. Reuters reported that an October 25 runoff is likely.
In Brazil, Lula's victory is expected to keep the country a major leftist bastion in the region, alongside Mexico, while a Flavio Bolsonaro win would see the country join the rightward-shifting tide.
The battle in Brazil comes as Latin America has swung sharply to the right in recent years.
Right-wing candidates and conservative allies of US President Donald Trump won seven major presidential elections in Latin America in the past few years, most of them since Trump's inauguration in January 2025.
Here is a look at the Latin American countries that elected conservative presidents recently:
Trump-endorsed Abelardo de la Espriella secured a narrow victory in Colombia's June presidential election. A lawyer and business owner, Espriella pledged to reduce the size of the state, broaden the tax base, cut corporate taxes and restart oil exploration.
De la Espriella is nicknamed “The Tiger." His election marked a pivotal moment for Colombia, which was governed for the past four years by a former member of a rebel group, who was critical of the Trump administration’s immigration and anti-drug policies, the Associated Press reported.
In Peru, Conservative Keiko Fujimori secured victory in a razor-thin June race. Ratings agency Moody's said a Fujimori government would preserve policy continuity, bolster investor confidence and boost economic growth.
A business-friendly conservative politician who campaigned on a tough-on-crime platform, Fujimori is the daughter of late former President Alberto Fujimori, whose government defeated the Shining Path violent extremist group in the 1990s but also took an authoritarian turn.
She took office in July. According to AP, she promised to build four new prisons, including a mega-prison modeled after El Salvador’s CECOT facility, militarise Peru’s borders to curb drug trafficking and deport migrants working in the country without legal residency.
Javier Milei, nicknamed “The Lion,” won Argentina’s presidential election in November 2023 by promising to slash government spending and tackle the South American nation’s decades-long inflation problem.
An economist and television commentator, Milei has reportedly stopped the nation’s central bank from printing money to finance the government deficit and has cut government spending by firing civil servants and halting investment in public infrastructure programs, while reducing subsidies for public utility bills.
Daniel Noboa winning the election in Ecuador with 56 percent of the vote, and was reelected to a four-year term in April 2025.
A member of one of Ecuador’s wealthiest families, Noboa has given the military a more prominent role in providing security in coastal cities overrun by drug gangs fighting over the control of ports and drug trafficking routes. But the strategy has not substantially reduced homicide rates.
Under her watch, Ecuador’s military started to conduct joint operations against drug traffickers with the US Noboa also pushed for the reopening of a US military base in Ecuador, but the proposal was struck down in a referendum last year.
Nasry Asfura narrowly won the presidential election in Honduras in November, defeating his closest rival by less than a percentage point.
A real estate investor and former city mayor of the National Party, Asfura belongs to the same party as former President Juan Orlando Hernández, who was pardoned by Trump for a drug trafficking conviction.
Asfura was endorsed by the US president, who threatened to cut off aid to the small Central American country if Asfura was not elected.
José Antonio Kast, a conservative and a devout Catholic, won Chile’s presidential election in December 2025, defeating a progressive government that had been in power for the previous four years.
In his campaigns, Kast capitalised on fears over increasing crime rates in Chile and said he would expel migrants from countries like Venezuela and Haiti who had been working in Chile without residency permits.
One of his first moves after taking office has been to expand a trench along Chile’s borders with Peru and Bolivia in a bid, his government says, to stop drug trafficking and migration.
Laura Fernández won Costa Rica’s election in February with 48 percent of the vote, defeating her closest rival by 15 percentage points and surpassing the 40 percent of votes needed to avoid a runoff election.
She was an economy minister under conservative ex-President Rodrigo Chaves.
The winner of the Brazilian elections will determine Brazil's foreign policy.
Flavio Bolsonaro's father and far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro is an ally of US President Donald Trump.
Meanwhile, Lula, who at 80 is one of the world's oldest heads of state, is running in his seventh presidential election and has strengthened Brazil's ties with China.
Notably, Lula has accused the Trump administration of using tariffs and other means to interfere with Brazilian affairs. Bolsonaro has portrayed Trump as an ally, and is expected to strengthen ties with Washington if elected.
The Trump administration has imposed tariffs on Brazilian products and sanctions on judges and other officials.
If Leftist Lula wins, Washington will likely continue resorting to threats and targeted tariffs to curb ties with China, Regiane Bressan, a professor of International Relations at the Federal University of Sao Paulo, told AFP.
The US is Brazil's second-largest trading partner, behind China.
A Flavio Bolsonaro presidency would have more alignment with Washington, "at least rhetorically," said Bressan.
The latest Latinobarómetro poll, taken in 17 countries and published exclusively by The Economist, showed that Latin Americans’ views of the United States have soured since Trump came to power.
The share with a favourable opinion fell from 73 percent in 2024 to 63 percent, the report published on September 30, 2026, claimed.
The poll revealed that, for the first time in a historically pro-American region, Latin Americans view China’s influence in a better light than America’s: 65% call it positive, compared with 57% for the United States.
“This reflects Mr Trump’s aggressive stance towards a region he believes his country should dominate,” the report added.
Will this mean Leftist Lula's comeback in the 2026 Brazilian elections? The next president will be known once the results of the ongoing polls are released.
The electoral court (TSE) will start publishing results at 5 pm Brasília time on Sunday, October 4, 2026, as soon as polling places close. A runoff between both is expected on October 25, if neither passes 50 percent of votes. Sunday’s results will offer the first real measure of the candidates’ support beyond polls.

(In the weekly Health Matters newsletter, Athira Elssa Johnson writes about getting to good health, and staying there. You can subscribe here to get the newsletter in your inbox.)
A treatment can make a difference only when patients can access it. The cost of medicines, their safety and regulation, and whether people can get the care they need are all part of that question. This week, our coverage also looks at vaccination, infectious diseases, artificial intelligence, prevention and new medical research.
Questions around the cost of medicines came into focus after the Supreme Court described the overpricing of essential cancer drugs as “broad daylight dacoity”. The report examines concerns around medicine prices and what they mean for access to treatment.
A regulatory warning against the indiscriminate use of painkillers and antibiotics highlighted the risks of inappropriate medicine use, including kidney disease. India has also ordered a crackdown on nicotine pouches, citing health risks.
Food regulation also featured this week. Krishnadas Rajagopal reports on FSSAI telling the Supreme Court that front-of-pack nutrition labelling will be rolled out in a single phase.The regulator has also proposed that only milk-derived products be represented as ‘paneer’. Bindu Shajan Perappadan explains what analogue paneer is and why FSSAI is acting against it.
Vaccination and infectious diseases
Vaccination has been another focus, with attention on missed doses, vaccination records, catch-up vaccination, adult immunisation and changing needs across different stages of life.
In our Health Webinar, experts discussed childhood and adult vaccination, travel vaccination and common concerns around vaccines. The discussion also looked at the importance of maintaining vaccination records and understanding changing immunisation needs.
Ahead of winter, Sayesha Gupta, Megha Jacob and Karan Babbar looked at vaccination among older adults and why Delhi’s grandparents may need protection alongside their grandchildren.
The wider question of preparedness also remains important. India stressed the need for resilient health systems and pandemic preparedness at the United Nations.
On the infectious disease front, reports showed that the Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to two new health zones. An mpox case has also been confirmed in a northeastern Congolese city at the centre of the Ebola outbreak.
In India, C. Maya reports on scientists at IAV, Keralam developing a dengue early-warning system to forecast trends and help anticipate outbreaks.
AI and healthcare
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being used in medical imaging, clinical decision-making and drug and vaccine development. Its expanding role also raises questions around patient safety, inaccurate information, data and the potential misuse of AI in biology.
The latest Health Wrap examines these issues in ‘AI in healthcare: promise, risks and patient safety’.
Other developments include a partnership between Anthropic and OpenEvidence to expand access to medical AI; Afshan Yasmeenreported on HEADS, an initiative using AI to help address gaps in mental healthcare. In Assam, inputs from ASHAs are being used to develop an AI-enabled training platform for cervical cancer screening.
Health data is also coming under scrutiny, with the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic called to appear before an Australian AI probe following a breach involving a health database.
Nutrition and prevention
Nutrition and preventive health also featured prominently. A study found that consuming an additional 100 grams of ultra-processed food a day was associated with a 14% higher risk of a heart event. The findings add to research examining the relationship between ultra-processed food and cardiovascular health.
Suparna Mukherjee looks at what people should know about artificial sweeteners and health, particularly as their use becomes more common.
Managing conditions, new research
Several stories this week examine conditions that can be difficult to recognise, diagnose or manage.
I look at GERD and why persistent reflux symptoms need to be distinguished from what is commonly described as heartburn.
Another report looked at research linking pregnancy-related forgetfulness, popularly called ‘momnesia’, to disruption in a brain circuit, offering another possible explanation for cognitive changes during pregnancy.
Swagata Yadavar reported on village health centres in Haryana screening people for heart disease and identifying those who need further care.
Divya Gandhi reports on a study found that deaf adults have distinctly superior peripheral vision, adding to research into how sensory systems adapt to differences in sensory input.
Dr. V. Divya Sai looks at what happens when cancer treatment is no longer working and treatment options change. Dr. C. Aravinda examines why male contraception continues to lag behind other forms of contraception.
Researchers at RGCB in Keralam have developed nanopore sensors aimed at detecting biomarkers associated with neurodegenerative diseases, while IIT Palakkad researchers have developed sensors for faster heparin monitoring.
Another report looks at the U.S. FDA’s approval of an AbbVie drug for Parkinson’s disease. The Health Ministry’s latest advisory on stem cell therapy for autism has also drawn attention, read our explainer here.
More from the health desk
In our all you need to know series, Meenakshy S. explains Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, a group of connective tissue disorders that can affect multiple systems of the body
President’s call puts spotlight on celebrity endorsements of harmful products
Serish Nanisetti reports on a UN finding that five crore Indian children still lack access to sanitation services in their schools.
Rajlakshmi Ghosh explains how the new NCAHP regulations could affect allied and healthcare professionals.
Sanjukta Sharma writes on why is everything linked to inflammation now
Vikas Vasudeva reports on researchers documenting the first human deaths from Caspian cobra bites in India.

Rogo, a US-based financial-services AI startup, raised $30 Mn this month. What made this unique was that some of the world's largest banks, including Barclays, BNP Paribas, Citi, MUFG and Société Générale, invested in this company, even though it has VC backing too. Nine global banks are now on Rogo’s cap table, representing nearly $20 Tn in combined assets. Rogo isn't an isolated case. Large banks and their venture investment arms are increasingly taking big bets on AI companies. Such investments have grown at a compounded annual rate of 21% since 2023, per an Evident AI analysis of the 50 biggest global banks, with Wells Fargo, Citi and Goldman Sachs the most active US bank investors. Recent deals around the world and in India back this trend. Citigroup and Spain's Santander have both taken stakes in Tokyo-based Sakana AI, which builds foundational models and custom AI for financial services. In India, examples include HDFC Bank and Canara Bank’s investments in CoRover as well as IDFC Bank’s partnership with Sarvam to build an R&D lab with the aim of developing the world’s first self-improving bank. Three forces seem to be pushing banks past the old vendor relationship. Deep integration into regulated, high-stakes workflows requires more trust and customisation than an arm's-length license can provide. Owning a stake or co-building the R&D gives banks influence over a roadmap they're increasingly dependent on. And for BFSI institutions sitting on enormous proprietary data and distribution, contributing that data to jointly built AI systems can be more valuable than a services contract. “License provides a means to access technology, while investment or co-development may result in a more profound collaboration between a bank and a startup. Cocreation gives the bank an ability to affect product architecture and work flows instead of simply fitting the bank’s processes into a ready-made solution,” said Mukesh Pandey, founder of consultancy firm Rupyaa Paisa. Whether this becomes the default model for bank-AI relationships, or stays concentrated among the largest, most AI-forward institutions, is still an open question. So is what this means for smaller AI startups negotiating with a bank that is simultaneously their client, their investor and increasingly their co-developer. The ones that end up without any bank partnerships or strategic investments may struggle to get the same access to data, distribution and trust. Banking On AI HDFC Bank's move on CoRover, the Bengaluru-based conversational AI firm behind BharatGPT, was described as the first investment by a leading private bank in a model maker. That isn't CoRover's only investor with a bank. Canbank Venture Capital Fund, the wholly owned VC arm of Canara Bank, had already invested in CoRover. CoRover’s founder and CEO Ankush Sabhrawal said that the association between the company and the banking ecosystem has moved from being a typical startup-investor partnership to a strong technological and domain collaboration. Further, Sarvam's partnership with IDFC FIRST Bank is a particularly interesting example. The companies said they would work towards building what they describe as a "self-improving bank." Their collaborative R&D lab will focus on frontier AI research, post-training and AI safety, with systems designed to learn from customer interactions, human corrections, exceptions and eventual outcomes. The partnership is intended to bring AI research closer to the bank's own operating environment, allowing models and systems to be tested against the institution's specific problems and improved using production outcomes. Sarvam has also built a growing footprint across financial services through more deployment-oriented partnerships. With Mahindra Finance, the startup's voice AI has been used across customer-facing workflows, and Sarvam's current enterprise portfolio lists Mahindra Finance alongside IDFC FIRST Bank, Tata Capital and SBI Life among its financial-services customers. While not a bank, Bajaj Finance recently picked up a 5% stake in Delhi NCR-based TrueFan AI, a generative-video startup whose avatars Bajaj was already using at scale for customer engagement and dealer communication. The deal sits under the NBFC’s new Finserv Intelligence programme, which plans to invest ₹1,500–2,000 Cr into early stage AI, cybersecurity and fintech startups. For banks and indeed NBFCs, AI is increasingly becoming more than another technology procurement category. Besides just being mere customers, banks and NBFCs are becoming financial stakeholders in the company building the technology. India's banking and financial-services sector is beginning to show early signs of the same shift. Are Indian Banks Moving Fast? Beyond financial resources, bank-led investments bring with them insights into the operational nature of financial services, including areas where AI technologies could be applied effectively in the area of customer support, employee assistance, knowledge management, multilingual engagement, etc. “The feedback provided by banks becomes useful for determining specific areas where AI needs more accuracy, context, security, and compliance. It is crucial for BharatGPT, as the majority of banking transactions involve multilingual clients and difficult financial terms. The company views the controlled customization as a use of the client’s approved knowledge reference points, algorithms, and mechanisms instead of utilising proprietary information in a standard solution,” CoRover’s Sabharwal added. That kind of close, iterative feedback loop is easier to justify when the sector on the other end of it is already AI's biggest spender. BFSI holds the largest share of India's AI market, largely on the back of early adoption for fraud detection, risk management, customer service, and personalised financial solutions. The sector's focus on digital transformation and data-driven decision-making has made it a key driver of AI demand — reaching a market size of over $1 Bn in 2025, and projected by research firm IMARC Group to grow to $9.4 Bn by 2034 at a CAGR of 26.5%. A more significant change may actually be happening outside the cap table. Indian banks and financial institutions are increasingly working directly with AI startups to adapt technology to specific banking workflows, rather than simply purchasing a general-purpose AI product. The logic behind these tie-ups was laid out plainly by Axis Bank's Prasad Lad, the head of the bank’s business intelligence unit. He said Axis is working with startups across voice AI, document reading and rapid UI/UX prototyping, adding that this isn't an area where the bank can build everything in-house. “Startups such as Sarvam bring capabilities, particularly across Indian languages, that would be difficult for a bank to develop internally,” he added. Kotak Mahindra Bank, on the other hand, has started leveraging AI across software development, employee productivity, customer service and experience, credit decisioning, and marketing. While most of the AI work is done by in-house team, the bank leans on startup partners for niche requirements, said Vijay Narayanan, Head of Innovation and AI, without specifying the startups Kotak Mahindra Bank is currently working with. Humans In The Banking Loop That same efficiency the AI partnerships are built to deliver is already showing up in headcount. Axis Bank reported a decline of over 3,100 employees in FY26, which it attributed to sustained investments in technology and productivity enhancements. HDFC Bank, Kotak Mahindra Bank and ICICI Bank have seen similar headcount reductions, directly or indirectly tied to AI-led automation. In some cases, roles are being revised. "We expect 50-60% of our employees to be repurposed into sales and relationship roles over the next two years, with no layoffs as part of this transition but we continue to hire, especially for specialised technology talent,” Salee S Nair, MD and CEO, Tamil Nadu Small Mercantile Bank. As with other layoffs in recent times, many have wondered whether these strategic investments are resulting in less humans in the banking loop. Axis Bank CEO Amitabh Chaudhry told Bloomberg that investments in AI and technology would let the bank expand its business without a proportional rise in staff, signalling slower hiring even as operations scale up. This is not a new experience for Indian banks by any means. Every step taken by Indian banks in the past two decades has come with such cutbanks — whether it is internet banking, mobile banking and digital payments or indeed the AI banking future that banks are rushing to embrace. But with every new technology jump, there have been teething pains, bugs and major tech gaps, which is why the buck always stops at the humans leading the banks. With AI, this human responsibility will grow by magnitudes because fewer humans will be running the banks. So even if banks are ready for an AI future as they are demonstrating today with their investments, the next major discussion has to cover what the role of humans will be in this future.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision of voters' list, officials said on Wednesday.
The officials made the remarks in the wake of a media report that the two Election Commissioners had objected to the Election Commission's steps 14 times in 10 months amid the SIR.
Responding to queries, the officials said the two commissioners had flagged decisions related to deletion of names in various states during the poll roll cleanup and handling of voter database.
EC sources maintained that all decisions of the Election Commission of India, including SIR, have been unanimous and with the approval of both the Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner.
Officials said the law governing the functioning of the Election Commission and a Supreme Court judgment underline that as much as possible, decisions should be taken unanimously and if need be, majority view should prevail.
The Indian Express reported that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners, Sandhu and Joshi.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Opposition parties have slammed the EC over the SIR, claiming it was meant to target electors not aligned to the BJP and its allies.

Centre's AI and copyright committee falls silent, second paper overdue by months
A second working paper on the AI-copyright issue, which the government had earlier said would be out by February this year, is also yet to be prepared.
A government panel formed last year to examine how Artificial Intelligence (AI) fits within India's copyright framework has not met since June, three of its members told HT, adding that official interest in the issue appears to have waned.
A second working paper on the AI-copyright issue, which the government had earlier said would be out by February this year, is also yet to be prepared, the members added.
The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT) set up the committee on April 28, 2025, to examine the legal and policy questions around AI and copyright, and to assess whether the Copyright Act, 1957 is adequate to address them.

The members said that when the first working paper was completed in December 2025, the committee said the second would follow in two months. Nearly 10 months have passed but there is neither any paper nor a new timeline from the DPIIT, they said.
"The fizz has gone out from the government's side. They are not prioritising this issue," one of the members said, asking not to be named. This member added the panel's last consultation was held before the beginning of the Monsoon Session of Parliament.
The first paper examined the use of copyrighted material in training AI models. The second looks at the content AI generates. The panel members said discussions held on the second paper covered who owns AI-generated work, who is liable for it, what counts as originality, and whether AI-generated work should get copyright at all.
Opinion | India must urgently get its own AI Safety Institute
"Deliberations took place on the second part after the release of the first report, however, they were sporadic in nature," said another committee member, also asking not to be named. Members said the committee met every two weeks when they were charting out the first paper but the sessions reduced for the work on the second one.
The first paper proposed a mandatory blanket licence that would let AI developers train their models on all lawfully accessed copyrighted content in India without seeking permission from each creator. Copyright owners would instead be paid through a new central collecting body.
DPIIT invited public comments on the proposal and extended the deadline by a month to February 6. Since then, no revised or final version has been released.
The first member quoted above said the issue has lost its urgency. "At that time it was a major issue as people were complaining about AI training and its liability. I guess it's become the status quo now. There is also not a lot of pushback from the public," the member said.
While the policy work has stalled, the courts are dealing with the issue. In the case between news agency ANI and OpenAI – who was one of the first in India to question whether a news outlet's content can be used to train tools like ChatGPT – the Delhi High Court passed an interim order in July. It held that OpenAI's use of ANI content for training was protected as fair dealing, and refused to grant an injunction in the matter. ANI has since appealed against the single judge's decision.
The committee's members include DPIIT additional secretary Himani Pande, DPIIT director Simrat Kaur, IT ministry scientist Anurag Kumar, Nasscom's Chockalingam M and Sudipto Bannerjee, IP lawyers Ameet Datta and Adarsh Ramanujan, and Delhi University professor Raman Mittal.
HT sent emails to Himani Pande and Simrat Kaur but did not get a response at the time of filing this report.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Canada bet billions on an EV boom. Was it too much, too soon?
Volkswagen battery plant in Ontario latest major project to be delayed
The federal and provincial governments bet billions on the rapid rise of the electric vehicle industry. But major EV and battery projects in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia have since been delayed, cancelled, suspended, substantially changed — and in one case, gone bankrupt — as automakers and suppliers adjust to weaker-than-anticipated demand.
The latest is Volkswagen's massive PowerCo battery plant in St. Thomas, Ont., where production has been pushed back two years to 2029, because of "evolving market demand."
The setbacks are raising questions about whether Canada bet too big on how quickly the EV market would grow. Critics say demand may never reach the levels needed to support the scale of battery production governments sought to attract, while others argue these are temporary delays in the decades-long shift toward electrification.
A million batteries, but for what?
Grieg Mordue, a former Toyota executive and retired McMaster University professor who studied the auto industry, says the St .Thomas plant illustrates two problems with Canada's EV investment strategy: scale and location.
When the project was announced in 2023, PowerCo said the plant would eventually make enough battery cells for roughly one million EVs a year.
Mordue says that seemed inefficient since Volkswagen's major assembly operations are in the southern United States and Mexico, meaning batteries produced in St. Thomas would have to travel long distances to reach the vehicles they're intended to power.
Europe isn't the obvious destination either, he says, because Volkswagen (VW) already has battery production capacity there.
Even together, VW's North American plants don't produce enough vehicles to provide an obvious market for a million batteries a year.
"They got a million batteries," he said. "What are they going to do with them?"
VW and its PowerCo subsidiary did not respond to a request for comment.
VW has said the plant remains a cornerstone of its North American battery strategy and is continuing construction even as it pushes production back.
VW also said the delay will allow it to incorporate newer battery technology and scale production as demand develops.
It could also have an upside for taxpayers, Mordue said — in the form of a smaller subsidy bill.
Much of the support promised to Volkswagen is still tied to how many batteries the plant produces. With production now set for 2029 and with those incentives scheduled to start declining in 2030 and ending in 2032, Mordue says governments will likely pay "a whole lot less" than the original maximum.
Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada said in a statement that the federal government has so far contributed $700 million to the construction of the St. Thomas battery plant, noting Ontario is responsible for one third of the $13.2 billion governments have agreed to in production subsidies.
"The government remains engaged with PowerCo on their updated timelines," the statement said.
Ontario's Ministry of Economic Development Job Creation and Trade did not respond by deadline.
A bet on the long-term
Still, others argue that looking at today's EV demand misses the time scale on which investments such as St. Thomas were made.
"These investments are meant to last 50 to 70 years or more," Joanna Kyriazis, directory of policy and strategy at Clean Energy Canada told CBC News.
She said the current slowdown should be seen as growing pains in an industry that is still transitioning, rather than evidence Canada built too much battery capacity.
There are signs Canada's EV market may already be recovering after a slowdown.
New restgistrations of battery-only EVs rose 37.4 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, compared with the same time last year, according to Statistics Canada. When hybrids are included, Canadians registered 58,811 new zero-emission vehicles during the quarter, up 26.7 per cent.
Kyriazis says the investments are about keeping Canada relevant as the global auto industry undergoes a historic shift from gasoline-powered vehicles.
"It's not a question of maintaining a place in the North American auto indstury. It's — is Canada going to have an auto industry that survives in the 21st century at all?" she said.
"There's a clear direction that the global auto sector is going and if Canada wants to have a competitve auto sector into the future, we've got to be able to make and sell competitively priced electric vehicles and the parts that go into them."
Kyriazis says the potential market for these batteries also extends beyond electric vehicles. As electricity grids expand, batteries will increasingly be needed to store power and help balance supply and demand.

The St. Thomas site and a NextStar plant in Windsor, she said, "were looking at a short-term strategy of building batteries that would be used for grid-scale storage while EV update in North American started to sort of even out."
Kyriazis argues the current U.S. retreat from electric vehicles could prove temporary and that Canada shouldn't base a decades-long industrial strategy on policies that could change again under a future administration.
There is evidence the EV battery bet may have been early rather than fundamentally misplaced. The wider justification for building domestic battery capacity hasn't disappeared either.
China produced more than 80 per cent of the world's battery cells last year, according to the International Energy Agency, leaving governments in North America and Europe to build domestic supply chains in an industry that remains heavily concentrated in Asia.
Will buyers catch up?
University of Guelph economics professor Ross McKitrick is less convinced that time will solve the problem. He said EVs have an established market, but argues governments built their policy around expectations of demand far greater than what has so far emerged.
"What the government's been trying to do is force that market into existence," he said. "The numbers just don't add up."
McKitrick points to the billions governments offered manufacturers to build EVs and batteries, while simultaneously offering consumers incentives to buy the vehicles as evidence the industry wasn't able to sustain itself on the scale governments envisioned.
In a 2024 paper published in the Canadian Journal of Economics, McKitrick warned that if Canada's EV sales requirements rise faster than buyers' willingness to purchase them, it could hurt automakers and the wider economy.
