Sixty-three per cent of the 3,253 Water Supply Schemes (WSS) taken up under the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) in Jammu and Kashmir are non-operational despite expenditure of around Rs 7,000 crore, a House Committee of the Jammu and Kashmir Legislative Assembly has found, raising serious questions over planning, execution, procurement, quality control and monitoring of the flagship rural drinking-water programme.
The findings are contained in the voluminous 1253-page report of the House Committee constituted to examine alleged irregularities in the implementation of JJM in the Union Territory. The report was laid before the Legislative Assembly on September 21 by committee chairman Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. The committee was constituted on April 9, 2025, to examine alleged irregularities in implementation of the Mission.
“The result is that 63 per cent of 3253 WSS involving an expenditure of Rs. 7000.00 crore are non-operational,” the report states. It adds that even the 37 percent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were “not fully operational”.
The committee said the institutional mechanism established to oversee JJM had failed to discharge its responsibilities effectively, resulting in inadequate planning, supervision and monitoring.
“The House Committee is of the considered view that there has been complete abdication of authority,” the report said, referring to the Apex Level Committee, Executive Committee and District Level Committees.
The panel attributed the failure to achieve the Mission’s objectives within the stipulated timeframe to what it described as “gross negligence” on the part of these committees and the officers who manned them.
According to the report, 37 per cent of schemes claimed by the Jal Shakti Department to be functional were also “not fully operational” in several cases.
The committee also questioned official figures relating to Functional Household Tap Connections (FHTCs), saying discrepancies emerged between departmental records and ground conditions during field inspections.
The panel said records supplied to it contained what it described as “false claims” regarding the number of FHTCs provided in habitations and the number of habitations covered.
“On spot visits, the House Committee came to know that far less than the number of FHTC indicated in the record, have actually been provided benefit of the Safe and Adequate Drinking Water of the prescribed quality,” the report said.
The committee also questioned the department’s claim that 81 per cent of rural households in J&K had tap-water connections as of March 2025, saying the figures required physical verification.
The House Committee was headed by Justice (Retd) Hasnain Masoodi. Its 13 members were Mohammad Yousuf Tarigami, Ali Mohammad Dar, Altaf Ahmad Wani, Aijaz Ahmad Jan, Rajiv Jasrotia, Ranbir Singh Pathania, Tanvir Sadiq, Javaid Riyaz Bedar, Muzaffar Iqbal Khan, Rafiq Ahmad Naik, Arjun Singh Raju and Iftikar Ahmad.
The committee subsequently undertook field inspections to assess the implementation of JJM works. It inspected schemes in Rajouri and Poonch, among other areas, before finalising its findings.
One of the major concerns highlighted by the committee was the failure to establish the sustainability and adequacy of water sources before executing schemes.
The panel found instances where expenditure had been incurred on pumping systems, storage facilities, transmission networks and distribution infrastructure without adequately establishing the viability of the underlying water source.
In WSS Shirpora Bangil, the committee found high sulphur and iron content in the source and said this had rendered the scheme useless. It termed the expenditure “unfruitful” and directed fresh testing of the source.
“Providing of FHTC is immaterial in absence of safe and viable source,” the committee observed.
The report also cited schemes affected by land and source disputes. These included WSS Dachnipora in Pahalgam, WSS Lelhara, WSS Syed Mantaqi Khrew and WSS Greenland Wuyan. In WSS Bugam Dooniwari, the committee said Rs 10 crore had been spent without benefiting the targeted population because of a source dispute.
The committee has also scrutinised the decision to shift from GI pipes to HDPE pipes during JJM implementation.
It noted that the Jal Shakti Department, Jammu, authorised Executive Engineers in April 2023 to use HDPE pipes instead of GI pipes depending on site feasibility. However, an earlier technical committee had recommended modification of DPRs before the change.
The panel said the national-level communications cited in support of the shift did not mandate compulsory replacement of GI pipes with HDPE pipes and questioned why the decision was taken several years after the Mission’s launch.
It said the decision had significant financial and operational implications and “ought to have been taken by the Apex Level Committee”.
The report also records allegations made by retired IAS officer Ashok Parmar concerning procurement orders and changes in pipe specifications. Parmar alleged that procurement orders worth Rs 4,000 crore were placed without approval and that HDPE pipes were ordered in violation of approved DPRs. The committee recorded these as allegations and evidence presented before it, rather than independently establishing every allegation.
The committee separately examined tube-well projects and raised concerns over tendering, technical qualifications, quality assurance and functionality.
It said some tube wells had failed to meet desired standards and noted submissions that water from certain sources was unsuitable for human consumption. The committee observed that quality-assurance mechanisms appeared to have been inadequately enforced.
The panel also questioned the effectiveness of third-party monitoring agencies hired for audit and inspection of JJM works. It said field observations regarding faulty execution indicated that such agencies had failed to discharge their obligations adequately despite being paid for monitoring and audit work.
The committee has recommended constitution of a High-Level Committee to conduct a comprehensive audit of JJM and retrofitting schemes, including procurement of DI, GI and HDPE pipes and execution of civil works.
It has recommended identifying officers and engineers responsible for irregularities and initiating action against those found responsible under applicable rules.
The panel has also called for scrutiny of officers who served on the Apex Level, Executive and District Level Committees from their constitution until March 31, 2025, with their actions and omissions examined against the respective terms of reference.
A comprehensive technical, financial and administrative review of tube-well projects has also been recommended, covering functionality, water quality, payments released, pending liabilities and possible additional expenditure.
The committee said the problems identified were not confined to isolated technical failures but indicated “possible systemic deficiencies in planning, procurement, quality control, contract administration and project oversight”.
Its central finding is that the success of JJM cannot be measured merely through construction figures or tap connections recorded in official databases. The ultimate test, the committee said, is whether households are actually receiving safe and adequate drinking water.

As Mangaluru bade farewell to Southern Railway (SR) to embrace South Western Railway (SWR) on October 1, the Dakshina Kannada District Rail Users, an online forum of railway patrons emotionally recalled the over a Century-long association of the coastal city with the SR and the Zone’s contribution to the railway infrastructure development in the region.
“We have demanded more. We have criticised shortcomings. We have fought for Mangaluru whenever we felt it deserved better,” the Forum said adding criticism does not erase history. It said since the formation of Southern Railway in 1951 and the subsequent establishment of Palakkad Division, they have been an important part of Mangaluru’s railway story — from infrastructure and freight to iconic trains, passenger connectivity and the modern Vande Bharat services.
Thanking every railway officer, engineer, technician, loco pilot, station staff, track maintainer, and railway employees who served Mangaluru for being a part of Mangaluru’s railway history, the Forum said, “As a new chapter begins, we carry forward the infrastructure, services, memories and legacy of this long association.”
Infrastructure creation
Over the decades, the SR has contributed to the development of Mangaluru Central as a major terminal and coaching centre while developing Mangaluru Junction as an important railway junction. It has also provided coaching, stabling, pit-line and carriage maintenance facilities at Central along with platform and terminal infrastructure and other operational assets. Progressive doubling and electrification of Mangaluru-Shoranur corridor, railway connectivity and sidings to New Mangalore Port and major industries were also done.
Iconic trains
The Forum said SR’s association with Mangaluru would also be remembered through many iconic trains, including Mangaluru Central-MGR Chennai Central Mail, Mangaluru Central-Thiruvananthapuram Central Maveli and Malabar Express, Mangaluru Central-Kanniyakumari Parasuram Express, Mangaluru Central-Mumbai LTT Matsyagandha Express and many more.
Mangala Express, which originally operated from Mangaluru Central, was later extended to Ernakulam Junction and subsequently evolved into today’s Mangala Lakshadweep Express (Ernakulam-Hazrath Nizamuddin).
SR also operated Vande Bharat Express services between Mangaluru Central-Madgaon and Mangaluru Central-Thiruvananthapuram Central.

For better or for worse, romance lovers have never been hornier for hockey. Now, the National Hockey League wants to cash in.
As part of its new “Hot for Hockey,” campaign, the NHL is rolling out romance novel-inspired short stories starring the league’s players on audiobook platforms. According to the Sports Business Journal, the league contacted popular hockey romance writers to write and narrate the 60 to 90 second stories, and will tap creators on BookTok, the romance-heavy literary subculture on TikTok, to promote the content.
The first batch of short stories, which dropped this week, feature players including the Philadelphia Flyers’ Trevor Zegras, the Carolina Hurricanes’ Sebastian Aho, and the Las Vegas Golden Knights’ Jack Eichel. They’re written by Pucking Wrong author C.R. Jane and more closely resemble back-cover summaries than actual romance novels. And, despite the nods to genre tropes, the players aren’t paired with romantic partners. Much more boringly, the stories appear to be a bid to get people to watch the actual games. The entirety of The Summer I Turned Gritty with Trevor Zegras is as follows:
“Trevor Zegras came to Philly looking for a fresh start. But after battling with Pittsburgh in the playoffs last year, he found out how gritty things could get. One heated summer later, Philly’s pretty boy is looking a whole lot grittier.”
Not all romance readers are thrilled about the campaign. Some argue that it makes players targets for sexual harassment. Others see the stories as cheap pandering that fails to engage with female and LGBTQ hockey fans’ concerns about homophobia and toxic masculinity in the sport.
“I cannot begin to describe the depths of my rage that this is actually happening,” Emily Rath, a best-selling hockey romance novelist, posted on Threads. “Yes, the NHL contacted me to participate. And I have never turned down an offer so fast.”
“They See Dollar Signs”
Romance novels focused on hockey players have been on the rise for years—the New York Public Library first highlighted the trend in 2019. Hockey romance burst into the mainstream with the massive success of romance novel-turned-streaming series Heated Rivalry, followed by Off Campus.
Jon Weinstein, a spokesperson for the NHL, tells WIRED in a statement that the campaign is a “playful nod to something that’s clearly going on in the cultural zeitgeist.”
“We were very proud to partner with real hockey authors, illustrators and voice actors in the space, and we’re grateful the players were willing to have a little fun with it too,” he says.
Yet many hockey romance fans applauded Rath and Chelsea Curto, the author of the steamy D.C. Stars series, for their refusal to participate in the campaign.
Rath, whose Jacksonville Rays series recounts a myriad of sexual relationships involving a fictional NHL team, said on Threads that the league’s slide deck for the campaign was filled with jokes she considered to be mockery of the genre, as well as what she alleged were AI cover renders. Curto also clocked the AI graphics, writing on Threads that it was probably for the best that she declined to be involved, as her books “can be very critical of the league.”
“They’re just encouraging the idea that women only care about hockey if it’s packaged like a romance novel,” Rath posted. “And they’re using popular authors and our credibility to launder their tarnished brand and lure in our readers.”
In Rath’s opinion, the NHL has failed to take accountability for or take action to address “racism, homophobia, and misogyny” in the league—a view shared by several hockey fans who spoke with WIRED. Lacey Conine, the founder of Double Hockey Stix—a clothing brand aimed at underrepresented hockey fans—says she initially thought news of the romance-centric campaign was satire.
“I had so many comments,” she says, “of people just being like, ‘This is disgusting. We hate this. What is this? How is the NHL this tone deaf?’”
In its current iteration, Conine says, the campaign feels like the NHL is “mocking you, and pandering to you, and making fun of you,” while failing to address fans’ concerns about aspects of hockey culture that can be hostile for fans that break the straight, white, male mold.
“I think that they see dollar signs,” Conine says. “They're trying to bring in Heated Rivalry fans—and then canceling Pride Nights. That tells you where they're at.”
While NHL commissioner Gary Bettman told reporters earlier this year that “every team does a Pride Night,” a handful of teams have moved away from themed nights that celebrate the LGBTQ community. That includes the Dallas Stars, which will not host a Pride Night this season, the team’s first time in five years without one. The Stars—which will host a night focused on romantic fantasy novel Iron Flame—did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment. A portion of the Iron Flame event’s proceeds will go to the Trevor Project, a nonprofit focused on suicide prevention among LGBTQ youth.
The NHL banned players from wearing specialty-themed uniforms, such as Pride sweaters and tape, in June 2023. The decision on tape was later reversed, with the league emphasizing that it does not single out Pride specifically in its ban. The NHL also highlighted other partnerships with the LBGTQ groups, such as the annual Pride Cup.
Several female hockey fans say the NHL’s attempt to cater to romance readers falls flat because of how the sport’s governing bodies approach sexual assault allegations. Echo, a 35-year-old fan of the Montreal Canadiens who asked to be referred to by her first name to protect her privacy, says she believes the league aims to use “romanticized narratives to whitewash the insidious aspects of hockey culture and its players.”
The Globe and Mail reported in 2022 that Hockey Canada, the sport’s national governing body, had used players’ registration fees to build funds that covered certain expenses—among them, sexual assault claims, as well as other lawsuits. (A spokesperson for Hockey Canada, Jeremy Knight, said in an email that the organization has taken “considerable action to help drive systemic change” in the sport over the last four years.) Last year, five former Canadian Junior Hockey players were deemed eligible to play in the NHL after being acquitted in a high-profile sexual assault case. Three currently play in the league.
Players Can Face Sexual Harassment
NHL teams’ past hockey romance-centric campaigns have also raised concerns about the sexual harassment of players. In 2023, a player on the Seattle Kraken, Alexander Wennberg, and his wife, Felicia, posted about an influx in “predatory and exploiting” comments after the team’s social-media account published content aimed at BookTok.
The NHL said that players approved all content for the new campaign, which will be exclusively focused on hockey. (The NHL Players’ Association did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.) Still, Conine and other fans question if romance-inspired marketing focusing on specific players fuels an uncomfortable brand of sexualization and parasocial relationships.
“Fans are going to do what fans are going to do in their spaces and their time,” Conine says. But, when the league is “literally creating these narratives—I think there's a line there. And, I think they crossed it.”
Jess Rauchberg, a lecturer in the school of media and communication at the University of Leeds, notes that the campaign is essentially league-approved real-person fiction. Hockey RPF has existed since at least the late ’90s and often involves romantically or sexually coupling hockey players with other players.
“Breaking the fourth wall”—discussing RPF outside of fandom spaces or with players—has historically been seen as poor form. But as the NHL’s marketing efforts increasingly encourage fans to feel a personal connection with players, Rauchberg says, the division between RPF and marketing material has blurred.
A hockey fan herself, Rauchberg believes that hockey RPF and romance are popular because they allow fans to imagine a reality where their desires are represented. Sometimes that desire is for players to make out. Other times, it’s a league where players push back against rape culture and toxic masculinity.
“I describe them as fantasy novels,” Rauchberg says. “In real life, the players probably aren't like Ilya Rozanov, consent king.”

Welcome back to Power Play! Each week, senior writer Molly Taft tackles a topic around this midterm season’s biggest issue: data centers. If you’ve got a question or thought for the column, feel free to shoot Molly an email at [email protected] or reach them securely on Signal at mollytaft.76.
On January 1, a new tax windfall will kick in that could benefit scores of rural data center projects—all thanks to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
Starting next year, projects sited in tracts of rural land across the country will be newly eligible for a set of specific corporate tax benefits under a program expanded by the bill. The new rules “may significantly lower barriers for large-scale, capital-intensive projects in rural areas—most notably hyperscale data centers,” said a statement from Ways and Means Committee chair Jason Smith last year. “The economic case for building data centers in designated rural opportunity zones becomes far more compelling” with the new program, he continued.
But experts warn that the results for rural communities could be mixed.
“Right now, the only requirement to get the benefits is capital investment,” says Emily Kraschel, a tax policy analyst at the Searchlight Institute, a public policy think tank. “However, that doesn't guarantee that that money is necessarily creating jobs or creating a local economic boost. You'd be more sure of that with a more traditional factory that requires lots of workers. But with a data center, that assumption goes a little wonky.”
During the first Trump administration, a bipartisan group of lawmakers proposed the creation of the opportunity zone program, which offers tax benefits for companies that choose to build projects in certain low-income census tracts. Last year, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made a number of changes to open up the program in order to attract more investment to rural areas.
Kraschel and her colleagues from Searchlight have been researching data center projects that might qualify for these tax benefits, comparing the locations of data center projects in development with rural census tracts eligible for the new program. WIRED exclusively reviewed the research compiled by Searchlight and found more than 100 data centers under various stages of development in rural areas that could be eligible.
Searchlight used a very conservative database of under 700 data center projects that are planned or under construction to compile its research; other datasets put the number of data centers in development in the US at closer to 1,500. It’s very likely that the number of newly eligible projects is bigger, especially since more data centers are decamping from urban areas. Separate research from Pew found that while just 13 percent of operating data centers are located in rural areas, a majority of planned facilities—around 67 percent—are going rural.
Searchlight’s research comes as the backlash against data centers—including from rural and GOP voters—is reaching a fever pitch. Tax breaks for data centers being built by some of the most powerful companies in the world have become a flashpoint in these debates: Amazon recently made headlines for attempting to negotiate for a lower tax bill on one of dozens of data centers it plans to open in Mississippi, while The New York Times reported last week that Meta is writing off data center equipment under a federal tax break intended for research and experimentation.
In the scramble to try to regulate the industry, the opportunity zones aren’t going unnoticed. Last month, Senator Josh Hawley introduced legislation that would eliminate opportunity zone funding for data centers, claiming that he would help “ensure Big Tech companies don’t get tax breaks to build data centers on farmland.”
A project simply existing in a rural opportunity zone doesn’t mean the company automatically will get the tax benefits; the company has to create a specialized investment vehicle to kickstart the process. Because the tax break can be considered confidential IRS data, it’s next to impossible to know which companies are pursuing the benefits unless they voluntarily disclose.
The research Searchlight compiled shows some big names that could stand to benefit from the program. But high-profile tech companies, when contacted for comment on the program, seemed eager to distance themselves from yet another tax break story. WIRED reached out to Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, all of which are developing data centers in areas that could be eligible for the new program, to ask about their plans to take the tax benefits.
Microsoft, Meta, and Amazon all denied using the program. In a statement, Microsoft’s general counsel of infrastructure legal affairs, Rima Alaily, told WIRED that the company “does not use the opportunity zone program to invest in the purchase or construction of its data centers.” Similarly, Amazon spokesperson Julia Lawless said the company “does not actively seek out” land in opportunity zones for development, and that it has not claimed the tax benefit for its projects.
“If we locate in one of these areas, it's because our site selection criteria—from available land to access to talent—aligns with tracts that governments across all levels have previously identified for economic development; not because we utilized the OZ benefit,” says Lawless. “We have not used this program for our site selection and have no plans to add it to our criteria for our future decisionmaking process." Google did not respond.
There are many reasons why data center builders may be choosing rural areas, from moving away from community opposition to pursuing cheaper land. But it’s not out of the question that companies with lower corporate profiles than Microsoft or Amazon developing data centers may choose to opt in to tax benefits.
Nathan Jensen, a government professor at the University of Texas-Austin, says that he would be “very surprised” if some companies were not considering siting in rural opportunity zones as part of their decisionmaking process.
“It’s essentially free money,” he says.
Giving tax advantages to companies to build stuff to spur local economies is a good idea in theory. But the opportunity zone program has had mixed results in execution. There’s some evidence that the program has done little to actually drive investment to disadvantaged areas, and that many of the projects getting federal kickbacks would have happened even without the tax boost. (Overall, the government says the expansion of the opportunity zone program to rural areas will cost an estimated $40.9 billion over the next decade.)
There is no requirement for projects getting opportunity zone benefits to create jobs; the assumption is that they will do so, simply by siting in the community itself. This isn’t always the case for projects like storage facilities and warehouses, which, Jensen says, have been popular choices for developers working in opportunity zones. Data centers may create a number of jobs in the short term for their construction, but there’s an ongoing debate about whether or not they create a lasting new workforce over the longer term.
“Lawmakers need to decide what they really want out of these investments,” says Kraschel. “Do you want to use this as a way to get data centers away from population centers? Are they just looking for capital investment, or are they wanting things like jobs?”
Jensen, for his part, thinks it’s “interesting we have this program that's incentivizing an investment while states are trying to de-incentivize or even ban it.”
What We’re Writing
On Friday, Amazon rolled out a series of commitments in communities where it’s building its data centers, pledging $1 billion in investments in initiatives like free community college programs over the next five years. Importantly, the company also confirmed that it is no longer using nondisclosure agreements with public officials in communities where it’s building data centers. NDAs have been a huge flashpoint in the public backlash to data center development across the country.
I wrote about Amazon’s announcement; it will be interesting to see if this changes public opinion! (If you live in a community near an Amazon data center and have thoughts about this, I’m all ears: [email protected], or reach me on Signal at mollytaft.76.)
What We’re Reading
- There was a flurry of data-center-related activity on the Hill this week. First up: a long-awaited new bipartisan permitting bill has some big implications for data centers; Bloomberg has more.
- And a bill echoing the White House’s Ratepayer Protection Act failed in the Senate, after Democrats claimed it was simply lip service to help Republican senator Jon Husted. Husted is facing a tough reelection battle against Sherrod Brown in Ohio, where data centers have played a starring role. NBC covers the battle.
- In Pennsylvania, a data center is still struggling with local opposition even after offering residents $10,000 each to accept the project. The Wall Street Journal reports.
- There’s a new tool that estimates the energy use and carbon emissions from data centers, created by Sustainable AI Group. (We spoke to cofounder Boris Gamazaychikov about AI agents and energy use for a newsletter a few weeks back.) You can read all about it in Heatmap.

On July 19, as Sahida Fakir stepped out of her Navi Mumbai home to buy dinner, she was allegedly picked up and detained by Mumbai police’s Chembur crime branch. Four days later, her husband Jumman Fakir learnt that she was forcibly pushed across the border into Bangladesh on suspicion being an illegal immigrant.
Even as Sahida remains steeped in uncertainty, away from her family in Bangladesh to this day, a writ petition filed in the Supreme Court was heard by a Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana on September 17. The court sought a response from the Centre within four weeks.
A native of Gobindapur village, Swarupnagar block in West Bengal’s North 24 Parganas district, Sahida was not given any opportunity to established her Indian citizenship before being detained, her husband alleged.
Alt News spoke to Sahida Fakir, who narrated to us the harrowing experience of being pushed into no-man’s land at midnight and wading through a marsh to reach the Bangladesh side. According to her, she was picked up by the Mumbai police and kept in a detention centre for four days before being pushed out of India. In this duration, the police didn’t produce her before a magistrate.
“When I was pleading with Mumbai police officials to let me go, they just sneered at me and said we need to fill up the empty seats of the deportation airplane,” she alleged, asking, “How can they be so inhumane? What is my fault? Being a Muslim who speaks Bengali?”
Jumman told Alt News that he reached Chembur crime branch office on July 19 and attempted to prove his wife’s citizenship by furnishing her documents. “The police said that they would need few days to verify her documents and, if necessary, would ask for additional documents. I went to the office again on July 22 with more papers, but the next day, they informed me that she had been pushed into Bangladesh. When I asked how they could do such a thing without giving us any opportunity to prove our citizenship, I was thrown out of the office,” he claimed.
According to Jumman, after almost a week, Sahida called from Bangladesh to inform him that she had allegedly been expelled from India through either the Assam or the Northeast border, and that she was currently living with a family from Satkhira that provided her shelter. “She called me from an unknown number and was crying inconsolably. A family from Bhadiyali village in Kalaroa Upazila of Satkhira was sheltering her, and the Bangladesh police posted two armed guards for her protection outside the residence,” he said. “I get to speak to her occasionally by calling the Bangladeshi family’s number. She is a thyroid patient. Local journalists had arranged some food, clothes and medicines for her, however, that stock is fast depleting.”
The couple has lived in Mumbai for the last 20 years — Jumman works as a car cleaner while Sahida worked as a domestic help. Their elder son Sahin Fakir lives in their native village in Bengal’s North 24 parganas district while 13-year-old Samim Fakir lived with his parents in Mumbai. After Sahida’s pushback, Jumman and Samim left Mumbai and returned to Swarupnagar.
ALSO READ: Jalil Akhtar: Valid Indian documents, cleared SIR in 2002 & 2026, yet arrested as a ‘Bangladeshi’
What The Documents Say
According to Sahida’s citizenship documents, including her birth certificate, her Aadhar card, voter card, PAN card, accessed by Alt News, she was born in November 1988. On October 19, 1995, the Bithari-Hakimpur Gram Panchayat, under the Swarupnagar Block, issued her birth certificate (serial number 6382).
Sahida’s father, Aminuddin Gazi, is listed in the 2002 SIR electoral roll (Part 89, Serial 514, Swarupnagar assembly); her grandfather, Badsha Gazi, is also listed in the 1952 electoral roll for Swarupnagar assembly. See below:
On January 29 this year, the Bithari-Hakimpur Gram Panchayat issued a family genealogy stating that Badsha Gazi’s son, Aminuddin Gazi, had 14 children, including Sahida. Sahida’s name also appears in land records accessed by Alt News. Although Jumman’s name appeared in the final SIR list, Sahida was placed in the “under adjudication” category. However, she had appealed against her exclusion.
Following her ‘unofficial deportation’ to Bangladesh in July, Sahida’s family was able to obtain a certificate from Swarupdaha Free Primary School on August 9, which states that she studied there from 1994 to 1998. Her transfer certificate, issued by Jamia Islamia Girls’ High Madrasa located in Swarupnagar block for Class 8 in 2008, is also available.
Sahida’s Account
Speaking to Alt News, Sahida said, “I was kept at the Chembur detention camp for four days. My phone, the money that I was carrying to buy chapatis for my family and my Aadhaar card — everything was snatched away. I begged the police, fell at their feet to let me contact my family, only then did they allow me to make a call for a few seconds. After I informed my husband, he came to the Chembur crime branch office to furnish all the documents to prove my Indian citizenship, but the police didn’t even bother to see or check them,” she alleged.
“After spending four days at the detention centre, they stacked several others and me onto a bus with dark curtains, so we couldn’t see where we were going. If anybody even tried to pull the curtains slightly, the Border Security Force men would beat and abuse them. We later realised that it was the airport. From there we were boarded onto an aircraft, and they took us somewhere on the Assam or Northeast border. I don’t know any of these places, but heard it from other people in our group,” she further alleged.
According to Sahida, she was placed in a group of around 200 people who were also pushed into Bangladesh.
“After we landed, we were taken to a detention centre. From there, we were packed into buses in batches. The bus took us to several other camps. They kept us waiting in some camps for 10 hours, and in some for about 3-4 hours before moving us out. Finally around 1 am, the BSF pushed all of us back into no man’s land,” she claimed.
“We were in a marsh with the muck reaching my neck in some places. I had to wade through the mud on no man’s land to finally reach the Bangladesh side of the border by daybreak,” she added.
The others told Sahida that they could be at the Feni border, near Chattogram of Bangladesh.
Following this, according to the petition submitted in the Supreme Court by her son, Sahin, Sahida somehow managed to reach the Petrapole-Benapole border area after a few days. There, the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) apprehended her, but due to humanitarian reasons, she was provided shelter and was finally able to contact her family on July 31, the petition said.
“A farming family from Bhadiyali village has sheltered me, and despite their financial constraints, they are doing their best to feed me. But do I deserve this hopeless situation? Why do I have to survive on other people’s grace? I have diabetes and thyroid issues. Since July 19, I haven’t had my medicine. My family’s life has been turned upside down. My husband had to flee Mumbai, leaving his meagre employment and my younger son had to leave his studies,” she lamented.
Alt News contacted an officer from Chembur crime branch, who refused to comment on the matter, stating that they are “officially required not to speak on such matters.”
We also reached out to the officer-in-charge of Kolaroa police station in Bangladesh. He refused to comment.
Legal Tangle: Contentious SOP, Loopholes in Govt Order
On August 17, Sahin moved the apex court with a petition challenging his mother’s apprehension, detention and forcible expulsion to Bangladesh, demanding that she be brought back to India. The petition argued that the Mumbai police’s actions directly contradicted the provisions of Article 21 of the Constitution.
The petition also challenged the legality of the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) dated May 2, 2025, titled ‘Procedure for deportation of illegal Bangladeshi nationals/Rohingyas’, and the ‘Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025’, insofar as it permits or facilitates removal of persons apprehended within India without the safeguards prescribed by law and the Constitution.
The SOP from May 2025, published by the Union ministry of home affairs (MHA), establishes guidelines for ‘deportation/removal/expulsion’ of Bangladeshi nationals and Rohingyas. According to the SOP: “All State Governments/UT Administrations shall set up a Special Task Force in each District under the police of the State/UT to detect, identify and deport/send-back illegal immigrants from Bangladesh/Myanmar settled in the State/UT concerned.”
“If the suspected Bangladesh/Myanmar national claims Indian citizenship and residence of a place in any other Indian State/UT, the concerned State Government/UT would send to the Home Secretary of the State/UT and District Collector/District Magistrate of the District from where the suspected person claims to hail, the details including name, parentage, residential address, details of near relatives etc. The State Government/ UT/Collector/District Magistrate concerned in turn will ensure that an appropriate report is sent to the deporting State Government/UT after proper verification within a period of 30 days,” the SOP reads.
It is important to note here that the SOP doesn’t mandate an FIR under the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, if a suspected Bangladeshi or a Rohingya is apprehended and due investigation, enabling anybody under suspicion of being an illegal immigrant to be simply expelled from India.
A Supreme Court advocate, requesting anonymity, told Alt News that the SOP is inhumane as it empowers the State and the border guarding forces such as the BSF to push back suspected ‘Bangladeshi and Rohingya’ infiltrators into ‘no man’s land’ without any judicial process. The SOP also mandates the handover of suspects to the relevant border guarding forces of Bangladesh and Myanmar, thus enabling the Indian border guarding forces to exercise their powers arbitrarily.
As contention around this SOP rose, the Indian government initiated ‘The Immigration and Foreigners Order, 2025’ — published in the Gazette of India on September 1, 2025, effectively overriding the provisions of the earlier SOP. According to this order, if a suspected foreign national is apprehended without his/her travel document, such as a passport, then that person’s nationality has to be first ascertained by that person’s Nation. After it has been proved beyond doubt that the person is an illegal immigrant, the deportation process will take place.
As per Chapter 3, Article 12(4)(c) of the said Order, it is clearly mentioned: “In the absence of a valid passport or other travel document, the authorities referred to in sub-paragraph (3) may immediately take appropriate steps for getting the nationality verified and for issuance of travel document in favour of the illegal migrant from the Embassy or High Commission of the country concerned in India through the Ministry of External Affairs and necessary steps shall be taken by such authorities to deport the illegal migrant from the country as soon as the travel document is received.”
Based on Sahida’s account of her ‘deportation’, however, it becomes clear that provisions of the Order were not followed. Further, even though certain provisions of the previous SOP were applied, the process, or rather the lack of it, in which she was pushed into Bangladesh, contradicts the rest of it.
In a similar case reported by Scroll.in, 66-year-old Dablu Sheikh and his three sons were picked up from their home in Suti, Murshidabad, under suspicion of being Bangladeshis. They have been missing for over 40 days. Sheikh’s father, Sk Samjani, was also a voter in the Suti Assembly constituency in 1966 and 1995, the report stated, adding that the inspector-in-charge of Suti police station said the four persons were illegal Bangladeshi infiltrators, and thus had been deported to Bangladesh. The officer further said that no FIR was registered against the four men under the Foreigners Act, as they were detained following the Union government circular from May 2025, and directly sent to the Jangipur holding centre. The report suggests that they were deported to Bangladesh from the holding centre.

Iran says Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until conditions are met
Iran presented a proposal during the UN General Assembly that would allow the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened within seven days if the conditions were met.
DUBAI: The Strait of Hormuz will not reopen until seven Iranian conditions set out in a June interim agreement with the United States are met, state media reported Iran's parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf as saying on Sunday (Oct 4).
Iran presented a proposal during the United Nations General Assembly under which the Strait of Hormuz waterway could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if the conditions were met, with the US replying to this proposal last week via Qatari intermediaries.
"The position of the Islamic Republic of Iran is completely clear and firm, and the Strait of Hormuz will not be opened until our seven conditions, based on the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, are met," Qalibaf, who is Iran's top negotiator, was quoted as saying.
He said Washington "must understand that the period of dragging out the (diplomatic) process and dictating one-sided demands is over".
IRAN SAYS NO NUCLEAR DISCUSSIONS
A Foreign Ministry spokesperson said on Sunday that Tehran had clarified its broad positions via mediators to the US response but that additional points remained to be communicated to Washington.
"The Americans' propositions are more or less in line with their previous positions, specifically on the nuclear issue. We told them our focus in this stage is the issue of the Strait of Hormuz and the return to security in this waterway requires clear steps from the US," spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said.
He also denied Tehran had offered UN nuclear watchdog inspections of its nuclear facilities in exchange for US sanctions relief, saying Iran had not entered into nuclear discussions with Washington.
The document being circulated outlines a seven-day period of trust-building aimed at returning the two sides to an enhanced version of the memorandum of understanding agreed in June, including concrete steps on Iran's nuclear programme, an official briefed on the talks said last week.
The disagreement centres on the sequencing of the steps rather than the components of the plan, the official added.
WARNING FROM ARAQCHI
Qatar has been shuttling messages between Washington and Tehran in an effort to end the conflict and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the conduit for a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas before the war that began at the end of February with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.
The June memorandum of understanding led to a brief ceasefire and included provisions on the strait and Iran's nuclear programme.
Separately, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told foreign ambassadors and diplomats in Tehran on Sunday that Tehran hoped Washington would choose diplomacy but warned that Iran was prepared to respond if the US again chose military action.
On Thursday, sources told Reuters that Iran was preparing a broader and more forceful response if Washington resumed large-scale military attacks.
“If they again move towards military solutions, we are more prepared than before and will take whatever action is necessary to defend ourselves,” Araqchi said on Sunday.
Army spokesperson Mohammad Akraminia told Fars news agency on Sunday Iran would upgrade the range of its missiles.

Watching a film in Mumbai could cost more per ticket. The possible increase follows a proposed rise in the city's entertainment tax on shows. Exhibitors and producers shared their estimates with The Economic Times (ET). The Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) proposes raising the levy from ₹60 to ₹400. That means an additional ₹340 for each film show. The proposed amount is nearly seven times the existing charge. However, the increase remains a proposal rather than an implemented change to the ticket price. This tax applies per show, not per ticket. A theatre would pay the fixed amount regardless of how many people attend. Exhibitors expect to pass the additional burden on to customers through higher ticket prices. The proposed levy could also reduce earnings shared by theatres and distributors. These earnings are calculated after taxes and other deductions from ticket collections. A higher tax leaves less money available for both sides. ET cited data from Karmic Films to explain the possible impact across seven shows. It assumes total ticket collections of ₹1 lakh. The combined show tax rises from ₹420 to ₹2,800. The money available for sharing decreases from about ₹83,326 to ₹80,946. Under an equal split, each side's share drops by ₹1,190. The example shows how collections can remain unchanged while earnings after deductions decline. Karmic Films co-founder Suniel Wadhwa highlighted this concern in his comments to ET. Poor attendance could make the burden harder to absorb. The same fixed tax applies even when only a few tickets are sold. Consequently, the tax burden per ticket increases during less crowded shows. Film trade analyst Girish Wankhede linked the proposal's impact directly to theatre occupancy. Mumbai is an important market for the film business. According to the ET report, it contributes 20-25% of India's gross box-office collections. Its average ticket prices are also significantly-above the national average. Industry representatives worry that other regions could introduce similar levies. Cinepolis India MD Devang Sampat criticised the proposal's timing and policy approach. According to him, India's cinema exhibition business has not fully recovered to its pre-COVID levels. For viewers, the concern is a potentially costlier cinema outing. For theatres and distributors, it is another squeeze on earnings amid weak attendance. The proposed tax would rise from ₹60 to ₹400 per show. Theatre owners would therefore pay ₹340 extra for every screening. This amount stays fixed, whether 20 people attend or 200. Theatres cannot know the final attendance when setting ticket prices. They may, therefore, choose a standard increase based on expected attendance. However, the same increase would produce different collections at different shows. An exhibitor quoted by ET estimated an increase of ₹5-10 per ticket. The exhibitor, while requesting anonymity, explained how the extra tax could be passed on to consumers. This is an industry estimate, rather than a confirmed increase across all Mumbai cinemas. Suppose a movie theatre adds ₹5 to every ticket. With 100 paying viewers, it collects ₹500 in additional revenue. That exceeds the additional tax by ₹160. With 68 viewers, it collects exactly ₹340, covering the increase. But a show with 50 viewers collects only ₹250 extra. The theatre would still fall short by ₹90. With just 20 viewers, it collects ₹100, leaving a ₹240 shortfall. Now, suppose the theatre increases each ticket price by ₹10. It would need 34 paying viewers to collect the additional ₹340. With only 20 viewers, it collects ₹200 and remains ₹140 short. These examples exclude GST and other deductions to keep the calculation simple. The BMC has increased the tax by nearly sevenfold. But that doesn’t mean your ticket price will also cost seven times more. It will probably be more expensive, possibly by around ₹10. Google Workspace is that ubiquitous modern business tool that almost feels invisible. We use it every day here at WIRED, whether that's for writing first drafts of articles in Docs, analyzing data in Sheets, or sharing files in Drive. And recently, I've been using the Gemini AI implementation that's built right into these tools, which is handy in all sorts of ways.
Google Workspace grants access to all kinds of productivity features that can help streamline processes and increase communication within a team or organization. It's not free, but here's the good news: If you're looking at a Workspace account for yourself (or for your team), Google is offering discounts until the end of 2026 using one of the Google Workspace coupon codes below. You can save up to 14 percent on plans for the first three months, whether you're signing up as an individual or as a business. Either way, the Google Workspace promo code down below is what you want to use.
Save up to 14% Off These Google Workspace Promo Codes 2026
There are some notable differences between each Workspace plan – I’ll dig into them in the next section – but all three plans come with access to the full slate of Workspace apps. You get Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and Meet, of course, but even the cheapest Starter plan includes basic access to Google’s other apps, such as NotebookLM and Gemini inside the Workspace suite. If you want to save, make sure to click one of the promo codes at the top of this page to secure your discount.
What Is the Best Google Workspace Plan?
Google offers four different Workspace plans, though only three are relevant for most people. There’s Starter, Standard, and Plus, as well as Enterprise, which is only available if you contact Google’s sales team. There isn’t a minimum number of users on any of the plans, but the bottom three options (Starter, Standard, and Plus) support up to 300 users. If you need more than that, you’ll need an Enterprise plan.
Although you have access to all the apps regardless of the plan you choose, there are some important differences, particularly between the Starter and Standard plans. Both include secure storage through Google Drive, but Starter comes with 30GB per user while Standard comes with a massive 2TB per user. Plus bumps that up to 5TB per user. Across all plans, storage is in a shared pool, so each additional user adds to the total pool of storage your organization can use.
Gemini is also a big difference between Starter and Standard. Although both have access to the Gemini app, Starter only has Gemini in Gmail and Vids. Standard (and Plus) includes Gemini across the full suite, including in Docs, Sheets, Slides, Drive, Meet, and Chat.
Starter is a great option for anyone just getting started, regardless of whether you’re a freelancer or a small business with a handful of employees. In addition to 30GB per user and limited access to Gemini, Starter comes with a few other limitations. It doesn’t support e-signatures in Docs, nor advanced features of Meet, such as noise cancellation. The bread and butter of Workspace is all here, though. You get a custom domain in Gmail, up to 100 participants in Meet, and the full Google suite of productivity apps.
Standard, as the name suggests, is Workspace proper, and it’s built for teams that need room to grow. That shows up most clearly in storage space, jumping from 30GB to 2TB per user. Standard basically cuts all the red tape on Starter. There aren’t any limitations on Gemini (it’s available across the full suite), Meet features like noise cancellation are available, and you can host up to 150 participants in a Meet call. Standard even comes with expanded access to NotebookLM, Google’s AI-driven note and research tool, with different chat modes and up to 20 generative audio overviews per day.
At the top of the range is Plus, which is focused on larger businesses. You don’t get any extra apps with this plan, but you do get 5TB of storage per user, along with up to 500 participants in Meet calls. The real reason to upgrade to Plus is security and admin controls, however. It includes Vault for data retention, along with LDAP access—basically a server for centralized account management, if you aren’t familiar.
Most people should use the Standard plan, not only for the large amount of storage space over Starter, but also due to the extra Gemini functionality. If you need to upgrade to Plus down the line, you can. And, more than likely, you’ll have a member of your IT team begging you to do so.
Why Teams Love Using Google Workspace Flows with Google Workspace
Google has updated Workspace a lot over the past several months, building in new functionalities via Gemini throughout the suite. But earlier this year, Google announced that it’s bringing all of those functionalities together through Workspace Flows. It’s a no-code automation tool that lets you build automatic workflows; i.e., update a Sheet when there’s a new email in Gmail from a particular address. The interesting thing about Flows, however, is that Gemini is built into it.
You can set up basic automations, which is great given how interconnected Google’s Workspace apps already are, but Flows become powerful when you throw Gems into the mix. Gems are AI agents built with Gemini, and you can create them with specific parameters.
Let me give you an example. Say you need a marketing plan, and an employee sends you a draft. You can have a workflow set up with a Gem that’s been trained on the budget, requirements, and tone of the campaign to quickly know if it can be approved or not. Or, you can create a Gem to scan your email, trained on your organization chart and role responsibilities, to notify you whenever you receive an email that has action items for you.
Flows give you a way to add a bit of context and reasoning to the often rigid constraints of simple automation systems, and they can save you a lot of time in the process. You may be able to gather customer feedback and put it into Sheets easily, for example, but Gemini can automatically sort, summarize, and categorize that feedback so you know what you should tackle first. Flows are centralized in Workspace, as well; you don’t need to install add-ons or configure anything outside of setting up your Workspace account.
Google Workspace Flows is a new tool integrated with Google Workspace. It is powered by Google’s Gemini AI and helps you get tasks done with Gmail, Docs, Sheets, Calendar and Chat. It can fix up emails, make plans, correct sheets, or write a follow-up message. No apps or links are needed.

French director Pierre Le Gall’s passionate love story “Flesh and Fuel,” which world premiered in Cannes’ Critics’ Week, won the top prize, the Golden Eye, at the 22nd Zurich Film Festival on Saturday.
The Golden Eye for best documentary went to Pete Muller’s “Bucks Harbor,” which premiered at the Berlin Film Festival in the Panorama section, where it won the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury.
Both categories are restricted to first, second or third directorial works.
“Flesh and Fuel,” Le Gall’s feature debut, follows French long-distance truck driver Étienne. When he meets Bartosz, a fun-loving Polish truck driver, his lonely daily routine is turned upside down. What starts as a brief encounter blossoms into a romance that transcends national borders.
Popular on Variety
The film stars Alexis Manenti, who won a César for Most Promising Actor for “Les Misérables.”
The jury stated, “At a time when isolation has become a means of protecting ourselves from the world and from one another, ‘Flesh and Fuel’ offers a compelling and deeply cinematic reflection on the fundamental human need for connection. With exquisite sensitivity, the film explores how the desire to love and be loved demands that we confront and ultimately break through the physical and emotional boundaries we construct around ourselves.”
The narrative film jury was comprised of directors Cary Joji Fukunaga and Fernando Eimbcke, actress Ella Rumpf, producer Julie Billy and Walter Fasano, director, film editor and screenwriter.
Special mentions went to Mads Mengel’s “The Guest” and Zou Jing’s “A Girl Unknown.”
“Bucks Harbor” centers on Downeast Maine, a U.S. fishing village where boys “are shaped by harsh winters and strict parental rules,” according to the festival. The film offers a “glimpse into the inner lives of the villagers.”
The jury said, “Merging the world of humans and extreme nature ‘Bucks Harbor’ is a raw indepth portrait of fragile masculinity in an underprivileged community in rural North America facing climate change and the loss of livelihood. While in times of polarization people are often presented stereotypically, this film provides a much-needed counter narrative in an empathetic way. It provides a deeply human story at eye level with its protagonists, in an impressively convincing visual style.”
The documentary jury was comprised of Sine Plambech, director and anthropologist, Alfredo de Juan, cinematographer, Anne Köhncke, producer, Jela Hasler, director, and Nikolas Geyrhalter, director, cinematographer and producer.
Special mentions went to “One in a Million,” by Itab Azzam and Jack Macinnes, and “My Home of Wind and Sand,” by Patrick Wally.
The Audience Award was won by Andrina Mračnikar’s “Mila/Marija,” and the Critics Jury Award went to Heinz Bütler’s “Ebjä! Adolf Wölfli.” The Science Award was picked up by “We Are Stardust” by Elisabeth Rasmussen.
Reta Guetg, festival director, said, the winners “show just how much courage and originality there is in filmmakers presenting one of their first works.”
She also noted the presence at the festival of international directing heavyweights such as Danny Boyle, Richard Linklater, Martin McDonagh, Jean-Pierre Jeunet, Jesse Eisenberg and Anton Corbijn.
“It is precisely these encounters between generations that define our festival,” she said.
During the festival, honorary awards were presented to Julianne Moore, Tom Hiddleston, Naomi Watts, John Turturro and other luminaries.

Jim Chalmers has warned of “very substantial and intensifying” economic pressures on the horizon but insists he’s not planning for a recession, as he prepares to find new ways to cut the budget ahead of its mid-year update.
The treasurer on Sunday called on critics of government spending to name the services that should be cut, as he points the finger at the private sector for driving up inflation in Australia amid the protracted conflict in the Middle East.
Chalmers said the US-led eight-month war against Iran, which has severely curtailed global oil supplies from the region, has been “disastrous” for cost-of-living pressures.
He also said there was “very substantial and intensifying pressure” on the federal budget.
“No serious observer of what’s going on right now would conclude anything other than [that],” he told ABC’s Insiders. “The longer this thing drags out, the bigger the impact on the global economy and on the Australian economy, whether it’s … on inflation or downward pressure on growth.
“We’re not anticipating [a recession] here in Australia, but certainly it is weighing on global growth, and we’re not immune from that.”
Inflation has jumped to 4% in the year to August, from 3.5%, while the Reserve Bank lifted its key interest rate to 4.6%, the highest figure since 2011.
Chalmers said the government was working on finding further savings to the budget in the mid-year economic and fiscal outlook, due in December, after cuts of $44.9bn over four years were identified in the May budget.
The treasurer said cuts to government spending weren’t the only factor driving up inflation in the economy, and cutting larger sums would impact essential services.
“If people don’t want us to strengthen Medicare, for example, or cut income taxes, or provide cost-of-living relief in other ways, then they should nominate where that should be cut,” he said on Sunday.
Beyond the war’s impact on driving up prices in Australia, Chalmers said the private sector was partly to blame.
“For every $5 of demand in our economy, $1 is public, $4 is private,” he said.
“Budget settings are not the primary driver of prices in our economy. There’s a whole bunch of other things going on.”
But the shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, said Chalmers should be sacked, claiming his decisions have increased inflation to generate tax windfalls.
“He’s actively stoked inflation, and he’s fundamentally undermined the success of this country, and now he’s announced today he’s on a sort of Argo-style salvation trip for investment, because he’s created a problem of sovereign risk,” he told News24.
The assistant science and digital technology minister, Andrew Charlton, said the consequences of having a recession, which would ease inflation, would be devastating.
“If you have a recession, you throw hundreds of thousands of people on to the unemployment queues, and that pulls a huge amount of demand out of the economy,” he told News24.
“It’s pretty easy to have low interest rates and low inflation if your economy goes through a recession.
“As a Labor government, that is a big priority for us to make sure that we don’t go into a recession that drives a lot of people into unemployment.”

Guillermo Del Toro is publicly declaring his love for “Digger.”
Del Toro took to X to call out naysayers of Alejandro G. Iñárritu’s film ahead of its Friday release. “Entirely Petty headline,” the director wrote in response to a review of Warner Bros.’ R-rated black comedy. “Love it or not. And yes, I do. “Funny, I go into the platform and without even scrolling down, these are popping at the top of my timeline…” he wrote alongside the repost. “So… I will just keep posting them. Tune in or drop out—” In another repost, he wrote, “Dig or Die – c’mon!”
