In October 2024, students at Cornell University received a campus crime alert about a reported sexual assault. At the time, it was just a campus story. Nearly two years later, on September 16, the victim, known only as “Jane Doe,” filed a civil lawsuit that brought national attention to her story. People across the country are asking what happened and why criminal charges never followed.
How did the Cornell rape case go so wrong?
A former sex crimes prosecutor explains where the Cornell case should go next.
Doe alleges that seven men drugged and sexually assaulted her at the Chi Phi fraternity house two years ago. Her lawsuit also accuses the university, fraternity and sorority organizations, and a local bar of failing to protect her.
The lawyers for several of the men have denied the allegations and any wrongdoing. Cornell says its disciplinary actions led to suspensions and expulsions for some of the young men, and that the Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from campus.
Doe went to campus police in November 2024, and the district attorney’s office reviewed her account and declined to bring charges. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said that what she described to Cornell police didn’t meet the state’s requirements for criminal charges.
Van Houten reopened the investigation late last month while continuing to defend his original decision to not pursue charges, but it’s now out of his hands: On Thursday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul named the state attorney general, Letitia James, as special prosecutor to investigate the allegations, saying she had “lost faith” in Van Houten.
To break down why Van Houten didn’t pursue the case at the time and what should have happened instead, Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with Lauren Hersh, a former Brooklyn prosecutor who led the office’s sex trafficking unit and CEO of World Without Exploitation, about how authorities handled Jane Doe’s allegations, the limits of New York’s consent laws, and what needs to change.
Hersh also explains where she believes the case should go next and what a special prosecutor can do to investigate (the interview took place prior to James’s appointment).
Below is an excerpt of Hersh’s conversation with Noel edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
I want to start with what we know in 2024. A young woman who we know as “Jane Doe” goes to the Cornell campus police and says she had gone to a frat house while under the influence of alcohol.
At the frat house, she was given more alcohol and ketamine. Several men had sex with her while she was intoxicated. This is what she tells Cornell campus police. What, in your view, is supposed to happen next?
There are a number of things that could happen. What I would say about these cases is there is no perfect scenario of what is supposed to happen, because what is critically important is we listen to the desire of the survivor.
We want to take this at her pace. We want to be guided by her wishes. We want her to decide if she is ready to go forward, if she wants to speak to campus police, the Title IX office, if she wants to speak to the local law enforcement. There are a lot of variables here, but for me, what is critically important is that we’re listening to the survivor and what she ultimately wants to happen.
In the present day, the district attorney who was involved has said that his office reviewed Jane Doe’s statement at the time and found at the time that what she described didn’t meet the legal definition of a crime.
I think people want to understand, Lauren, how is that possible?
To be really candid with you, Noel, this is an area that seems super unclear to me because the role of the district attorney in that moment is to investigate.
When you first get a case file, you first get a victim statement, and especially with facts as horrific as these facts are, or our understanding of this six-page document that the DA read — I would never say that this is a clear-cut case where there’ll be a conviction at the end. We never know that.
What I can say with 100 percent certainty is if you get a document like that, as a prosecutor, that is a significant investigative lead. And so, as a prosecutor, what I believe to be good practice is starting to pull the layers back, trying to understand what transpired here. Interviewing the victim. That feels critical. That never happened. We now know that there are all these text messages that were shared between these boys, and the prosecutor’s now saying, “I didn’t know about the text messages.”
It’s my understanding that there were a lot of boys on that particular text thread. And so a good investigator would have gone to that fraternity house and tried to interview some of those boys, tried to understand what were the contemporaneous statements made at that time. Were there any text messages? Was there any social media activity? And I believe that had they done that in a timely fashion, they likely would have come up with these text messages at that time and not two years later.
What you’re saying is interesting because the DA has come out publicly and defended himself by saying, essentially, the details of this lawsuit, which was filed in September of this year, are different from the details in the young woman’s 2024 statement to the police.
He has used that in his defense, right? “Here’s what I knew at the time versus what this young woman is saying today.” I think I hear you saying that maybe that’s not an excuse?
You’re asking about the inconsistent statements, and I find it troubling that the DA is leading with this notion that the victim has inconsistent statements because that feels to me like here we are making excuses and blaming the victim.
To my knowledge, the DA has not yet interviewed this victim. Perhaps he’s talking about the civil complaint, which I would think is written in a way where she has worked with her lawyer to put this together. And the initial statement, the initial six-page document that the DA read, my understanding is that it is basically a summary of a conversation.
Inconsistencies come in all shapes and sizes, so it’s hard to know exactly what we’re talking about here, but it is very common for there to be some inconsistencies. That is not a dealbreaker, despite the fact that this prosecutor wants the public to believe that it is.
What do you make of the prosecutor speaking publicly in the way that he is at this moment?
I find it rather confusing. I’m not really understanding why he is doing a media tour rather than sitting in his office doing the work, interviewing this particular victim, interviewing witnesses, seeing what evidence actually exists.
It seems to me that the DA has gotten to a conclusion before he’s done the work in actually investigating the case, and it is deeply troubling. And I think the governor should consider appointing a special prosecutor because I am not certain, based on this media tour, that this DA is able to give this particular survivor a full and fair investigation of the facts.
Drugs and alcohol are central to this case, right? The young woman admits she had been drinking and she was using ketamine. Under New York law, how does that affect whether or not someone is believed to be capable of consenting to sex?
New York law is actually really problematic here. It’s a place where I believe we are desperate for a legislative fix. I think that there have been a lot of advocates who’ve been championing a correction to this voluntary intoxication loophole for a lot of years, and we’ve not been able to get it.
New York law makes it very, very hard to prosecute a person when the victim is voluntarily intoxicated, but not unconscious, and this new law would allow the prosecutors the ability to bring cases when the victim is so severely intoxicated but not physically helpless and where a reasonable person should have known the victim’s condition.
In this particular case, based on what we’re hearing, she was in a condition where a reasonable person should have known her condition. And so in this particular instance, the DA is right. This is a very, very hard case to prove in this moment, but I’m a big believer. We don’t not prosecute cases because they’re hard cases. But at the same time, we know that a change to the law is critically important.
You clearly want more investigation here. What questions do you want asked? Who do you want to be [interviewed]?
Before I say who and how and what that investigation looks like, I think it’s really important to say that when two years have passed and the DA did not investigate these cases immediately, we have a big problem on our hands.
The fact that the DA did not investigate this from the moment he found out about this, it’s really problematic because as we know, evidence disappears, memories fade. When you’re dealing on a college campus with a specific culture, there may be a narrative that takes hold. And so it’s important to talk about the time lapse and how that harms the case.
That said, I still believe that the investigation is critically important. I don’t believe that this DA is the right person to do the investigation. I think a special prosecutor should be appointed. And then I think that the prosecutor and law enforcement should be interviewing everybody who was in that fraternity on that night. Anybody who saw this victim before, saw this victim after. Were there any statements in the immediate aftermath of her leaving that fraternity? Was there an outcry witness? We know that some text messages have come to light. Are there other text messages? I suspect that there are.
I’d want to interview as many of those boys as possible to understand what was going on because some of those text messages that have come to light — one says, “Free pussy” — don’t sound like a mindset that is engaging in consensual sex.
I think it is critically important that we understand all of the correspondence of that night. I think we want to see what is out there that helps us get closer to understanding what transpired that night.
I’ve seen two lines of thinking about this. One is that this is a horrific incident that never should have happened, but it is in some ways singular. But I’ve seen another line of thinking that says, “No, this is a systemic failure. This kind of thing goes on on college campuses, and the steps that follow the outcomes are often the same.”
I wonder if you think this is a systemic failure, and if you think it is, what would need to be done to fix this problem?
That’s a big question. I do think it’s a systemic failure. I also think it’s a cultural failure. And the reason that I would say this is because I don’t think this is isolated to this specific college campus. I think that sexual assault is happening across the country on college campuses everywhere.
In terms of additional systemic failures, I’ve been working with the Epstein survivors for the last year and a half, so I’ve seen so many systemic failures, so many prosecutorial failures, so much failure with law enforcement. I think that this is yet another example of prosecutorial failure.
I think the law enforcement failed this young person — the fact that there’s no investigation that happened immediately in the aftermath of this incident, no investigation. We just continue to fail survivors all over the place, and we have to start doing better.

G7 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel after Trump export ban threat
- Published
The G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.
The group of advanced economies, including the US, said the move would include a "substantial release" of diesel in the coming days.
President Donald Trump had threatened to ban diesel exports in a move which would have eased pressure on prices for US consumers ahead of November's midterm elections, but pushed up prices elsewhere.
In a joint statement, the G7 said member countries had now agreed to "refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products" on one another.
The G7 includes the US, UK, Canada, Japan, Germany, Italy and France, with the EU also represented at its meetings.
Trump had warned he would ban diesel exports from the US if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.
On Friday, he said on social media: "Europe has just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil. The process will begin immediately."
His Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had argued US farmers, truckers, and businesses "should not be left carrying the burden" as prices soar.
Diesel is used heavily by the haulage industry and in agriculture, meaning rises in the cost of the fuel feed through into essentials such as food.
But, following a meeting of G7 leaders, French President Emmanuel Macron said the bloc had agreed to release reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months under the coordination of the International Energy Agency (IEA).
The UK was represented at the meeting by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who said the measures would "stabilise energy supplies, build resilience in supply chains and shield households and businesses from price shocks".
Macron said the coordinated action would "bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel". Highlighting the agreement not to pursue export bans, Macron said "President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point".
Speaking at the White House, Trump later said an export ban on diesel was "never really on the table".
In the joint statement, G7 leaders said: "We will implement our commitments with a coordinated release through the IEA of 100 million barrels to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days by G7 members and partners."
It is not yet clear which partner countries will release stocks, nor how quickly.
The 100 million barrels will comprise a mix of diesel and crude oil. The price of global benchmark Brent crude oil briefly dropped below $100 a barrel, but rose back to around $102 by Friday evening. Before the US and Israel invaded Iran, it was trading at around $73.
Matt Smith, director of commodities research at Kpler, said oil had risen again due to renewed strikes between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.
"Oil prices were selling off strongly due to the announcement of strategic stock releases in Europe, but they reversed course on rumours of Saudi Arabia planning an offensive into Yemen as it looks to re-establish a safe path via Bab-Al Mandeb," he said.
European countries had pushed back against US threats to turn off American diesel, against a backdrop of the US-led war in the Middle East and reduced supplies from Russia and China.
The G7 leaders said they will also coordinate maintenance schedules to avoid multiple refineries being shut down at the same time, while encouraging countries with the capacity to do so to ramp up refining of diesel in particular.
Avoiding a ban on US diesel exports will offer significant relief to countries which are reliant on imports of the fuel, including the UK, where prices at the pump topped £2 a litre for the first time on Friday.
Over half of the UK's diesel is imported, with 31% of those imports coming from the US.
The US is one of the world's leading diesel suppliers, with domestic refineries churning out roughly four to five million barrels every day, according to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Americans consume about 3.6 million barrels of that. Refiners export the remaining 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels per day, making the US a vital supplier to the global market.
- Why UK diesel prices have breached the £2 per litre mark 
  - Published8 hours ago
Supplies of diesel internationally have been heavily constrained by the conflict in the Middle East, which has restricted the flow of both crude oil and refined diesel onto global markets.
Russia, which is also a major producer, has implemented its own export ban on diesel, following attacks on its refineries by Ukraine, further limiting supply. The G7 leaders stressed that they will maintain sanctions against Russia amid its ongoing war in Ukraine.
Diesel is harder to refine than petrol and, because of its use in the haulage industry and agriculture, it is very difficult to reduce demand.

The government has raised the ceiling price for natural gas produced from difficult fields, such as the KG-D6 block of Reliance Industries and BP, to $9.89 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) for the six months beginning October 1, 2026, from $8.90 previously, while keeping the ceiling for gas produced from the legacy fields of state-run Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC) and Oil India Limited (OIL) at $7 per MMBtu.
The new ceiling for gas from deepwater, ultra-deepwater and high-pressure, high-temperature discoveries is applicable for the period from October 1, 2026, to March 31, 2027, according to a notification by the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) of the oil ministry.
Gas produced from such difficult areas enjoys marketing and pricing freedom under the government's policy, but is subject to a government-notified ceiling.
The higher ceiling could provide some relief to producers developing India's more technically challenging offshore gas resources, where production costs are generally higher than those from mature onshore and legacy fields.
For gas produced by ONGC and OIL from their nomination fields, the government has notified an Administered Price Mechanism (APM) price of $11.22 per MMBtu for October, but the actual price remains capped at $7 per MMBtu, according to PPAC.
The APM gas price applies to gas produced from the legacy fields of the two state-owned companies and is used by priority sectors including city gas distribution, fertiliser and power.
For gas produced from new wells of ONGC and OIL in their nomination blocks, the government allows a 10% premium over the prevailing APM gas price, subject to the applicable ceiling. With the APM price for October capped at $7 per MMBtu, the effective price for new-well gas would accordingly be up to $7.70 per MMBtu.
The higher price for new-well gas is aimed at incentivising ONGC and OIL to invest in developing additional reserves and bringing new production on stream, while maintaining the existing ceiling for gas from their older, legacy fields.
India follows separate pricing mechanisms for gas from legacy fields of national oil companies and newer discoveries in difficult areas.
In April 2023, the government shifted pricing of gas from legacy fields to a formula linked to 10% of the monthly average crude oil import price, subject to a floor and ceiling. The ceiling was initially fixed at $6.50 per MMBtu and was subsequently raised by $0.25 annually after a two-year freeze.
The APM ceiling was raised to $6.75 per MMBtu from April 2025 and moved to $7 in April 2026.
Before the 2023 reform, APM gas prices were revised every six months based on international gas benchmarks and had fluctuated sharply, ranging from $1.79 per MMBtu in 2021 to $8.57 in the six months ended March 2023.
The separate regime for deepwater and other difficult fields was introduced to encourage investment in India's technically challenging hydrocarbon resources by allowing producers greater pricing and marketing flexibility.
Reliance Industries and its partner BP produce gas from the KG-D6 block in the Krishna-Godavari basin, one of India's key deepwater gas-producing areas.
Natural gas is a key feedstock for fertiliser production and is also used in power generation and by city gas distributors to supply compressed natural gas (CNG) and piped natural gas (PNG). Changes in domestic gas prices can therefore affect input costs across these sectors.

What to expect from school protests rattling France's government
High school students in France are expected to continue their protests this week, challenging President Emmanuel Macron's government
PARIS -- After a weekend lull, high schoolers in France are expected back at the barricades this coming week in their protest movement that is rattling the government of President Emmanuel Macron.
A key question is whether violence on the margins of the demonstrations will worsen, blurring the lines between protest and rioting, and whether Macron's government will ratchet up the already muscular response by police. According to the interior minister, officers made more than 5,000 arrests last week, 85% of them minors. Hundreds have been injured.
A test of the movement's endurance and appeal will come Tuesday, when the influential CGT labor union is urging workers to demonstrate, too.
Here's what to know:
Protests first erupted in the Paris region in mid-September. Teachers and students mobilized against a lack of staff at a lycée, or high school, in Creteil, in the southeastern outskirts of the French capital. From there, class strikes, blockades and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and then nationwide, with protests even in high schools of smaller towns.
Hundreds of schools have had to close because of damage or attacks that targeted staff, according to the education minister. More than 170 pupils and 65 staff members have suffered injuries, he says.
From the outset, pupils focused on perceived inequalities in the school system, saying that teaching, facilities and opportunities for advancement aren’t as good for students in disadvantaged neighborhoods — despite the promise of France's national motto: “Liberty, Equality, Fraternity.”
Placards held up by the first protesters in Creteil read “Too many inequalities, we’re disgusted,” “Education is a right, not a privilege,” and “Sorry to bother, it’s for our future,” according to photos posted by Clémence Guetté, the district's lawmaker at the National Assembly, France's parliament.
Pupils elsewhere complained that during summer heat waves, they roast in classrooms without air-conditioning, and they freeze in winter. French media broadcast videos of scampering rats, collapsed ceilings, leaks, broken furniture and other woes filmed in dilapidated schools.
"The public needs to know that conditions for studying are no longer what they were for us,” said Sophie Bordy, a 50-year-old literature teacher in Paris. "It has deteriorated significantly.”
Still, spending on education is one of the costliest items in the state budget that Macron’s government is proposing for 2027. It earmarked 65.5 billion euros ($74 billion) for schools, more than the 63.4 billion euros for defense.
Pupils also complain of long hours. In high schools, classes often start at 8 a.m. and can last to the early evening. French high schoolers’ compulsory school hours are among the highest in Europe, according to European Union figures.
“I see the teachers more than my family,” read one young girl's placard photographed by Le Parisien newspaper.
Guetté, the lawmaker who posted photos of herself meeting with the first protesters in Creteil, bullhorn in hand, is a rising star of the far-left France Unbowed party. Other France Unbowed lawmakers and elected officials also quickly identified with the protests, meeting with pupils and backing their demands.
France Unbowed leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon urged party members and supporters to protect pupils from the police, by putting themselves in between the two sides.
Mélenchon has denounced what he called the “savagery” of police officers who have liberally used tear gas and their batons to break up crowds. Police riot-control projectiles are suspected in some facial injuries that young protesters suffered.
Critics of Mélenchon accuse France Unbowed of stoking and manipulating the pupils for political gain. Mélenchon, a fiery anti-capitalist, says his party supports the movement but isn’t organizing it and wants it to be non-violent.
Mélenchon, 75, is making his fourth run for the French presidency and is wooing young voters. They tended to vote less than other age groups in the last presidential election in 2022 but could potentially help Mélenchon qualify for the decisive second-round runoff in May — a success that has always escaped him — if he can mobilize them to turn out.
“What we want is for this country’s young people to emerge from this episode with their heads held high, having won something and learned something, and to remember it when they cast their ballots,” Mélenchon said Thursday.
——
Associated Press journalist Oleg Cetinic in Paris contributed.

You can get Microsoft 365 for free through an eligible Education plan, free web and mobile versions of Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and other apps, or a 30-day Microsoft 365 trial with full desktop apps and 1 TB of OneDrive storage.
Microsoft 365 (formerly Office 365) is a subscription service that gives you access to various Microsoft products. This includes productivity apps like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, and OneNote; 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage; and tools like Teams, Forms, and Loop.
As of writing, a paid subscription starts at $1.99 a month or $19.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Basic and goes up to $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year for Microsoft 365 Premium. Whether getting a subscription is justified depends on which of the included apps and services you use and how much.
If you’re not too sure about that and don’t want to buy a subscription right away, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the following methods. Which method to pick depends on whether you’re a student/educator and your requirements.
Get the Microsoft 365 Education Plan
Microsoft 365 Education is a special plan for students and educators that provides free access to Microsoft 365 apps and services. You need a valid school, college, or university email address to be eligible. You’d have one if you’re a student or educator at an accredited institution with a Microsoft Education license.
To check if you qualify, visit the Microsoft 365 Education portal, type your institution-issued email address, and hit Next. If you’re eligible, you’ll be prompted to log in with the same email address. Or you may receive a verification link in your inbox. Subsequently, you’ll be able to use the Microsoft 365 apps within the browser or download them to your devices, based on the plan your institute offers.
Microsoft 365 Education is currently available in three plans: A1, A3, and A5. Your institute will most likely offer an A1 plan since it’s free, though some may offer an A3. The major difference between them is that A1 is web-only, whereas A3 supports downloads, so you can use the apps even when you’re offline.
If you don’t have an institute-provided email address or it isn’t eligible for the Education plan, you can get Microsoft 365 for free using the next method.

Use Microsoft 365 for the Web or Native Mobile Apps
Unless you have advanced needs — creating and running macros (VBA) in Excel, multi-device installation rights, or fully offline mode — you don’t really need a Microsoft 365 subscription. The online version of Microsoft 365, which offers access to basic versions of its apps, along with 5GB of free cloud storage, should serve your needs just as well.
All you need for this method is a Microsoft account and a web browser. In your preferred browser, visit the Microsoft 365 online portal and sign in with your Microsoft account. Create a new Microsoft account if you don’t have one.
Next, click the app launcher icon in your dashboard and select the app you want to use. This will open the app in a new browser tab, where you can create a new document or work on an existing one in your OneDrive storage. Any changes you make to the document are automatically saved to the cloud. Keep in mind, though, that the app’s functionality halts completely when you lose the internet connection.
Just like Microsoft 365 for the web, Microsoft also offers mobile apps for many of its productivity apps. So, if you just want to work on a Word, Excel, or PowerPoint document, you can download their mobile apps on your phone or tablet and use them. Just note that these apps offer limited functionality, similar to the web version. However, unlike their web versions, mobile apps support some offline functionality, allowing you to view a cached version of the document or edit local documents, even without an active internet connection.
Get the Microsoft 365 Free Trial
Microsoft offers a 30-day free trial to Microsoft 365. This trial gives you full, unrestricted access to the service, including complete offline capabilities and the ability to download desktop apps to your PC or Mac. You also get 1 TB of OneDrive cloud storage.
A free trial is great for someone who wants full-blown access to Microsoft’s productivity suite for a brief period. It also makes sense for those who want the Microsoft 365 service without committing to an upfront payment.
To subscribe to a 30-day Microsoft 365 free trial, you need a Microsoft account and a valid payment method. Open a browser and go to the official Microsoft 365 free trial page. Click the Start Free Trial button, and log in with your Microsoft account when prompted. If you haven’t taken a free trial with this account previously, you’ll be asked to add a valid payment method. Complete the checkout process. You now have complete access to Microsoft 365.
Set a reminder to cancel the subscription before the 30 days are up. If you forget, Microsoft will convert the trial to a monthly or annual subscription and charge you for the same on your added payment method.
Identify Your Use Case to Find the Right Method
You can use any of the above methods to get Microsoft 365 for free. However, not all of them offer the same level of access. As such, it’s important to identify your use case before choosing a method.
For example, if you want a full-blown Excel experience for a few weeks, the free 30-day trial makes more sense. Meanwhile, you might want to subscribe to the Microsoft 365 Education plan if you’re a student or educator and want desktop access to productivity apps for a longer period. Or use their mobile apps on your phone or tablet if you only need to view or maintain a few Excel sheets.

“Rendering Doom in a database is obviously a bad idea,” Lukas Vogel writes in a lengthy blog post explaining how exactly he managed to render Doom using an SQL database.
OK, that’s not entirely accurate. The SQLDoom project uses a small Python client to handle input and output, drive the game’s timing, and display each frame to the screen. Behind that, a series of CedarDB tables tracks the game geometry and state, while about 1,300 lines of SQL queries spread across 89 common table expressions implement the game logic and generate 35 bitmap framebuffers per second.
In this, SQLDoom is a major improvement over Vogel’s previous DoomQL project, which last year set out to build “a multiplayer Doom-like shooter entirely in SQL.” Unfortunately, that effort ended up with raycasting-based, grayscale ASCII graphics that were more akin to the simplistic 90-degree-angled maps of Wolfenstein 3D. The newer SQLDoom, on the other hand, generates full-color 640×480 frames that look like they could have come from the original Doom executable.
It’s all just data, man
Converting Doom‘s classic WAD files to a relational database was relatively simple and straightforward, Vogel writes, because of the way the original game broke levels down into vertices, lines, sectors, and so on. Even Doom‘s famous binary-space partition trees can be broken down into SQL using a sort_key for objects that’s pre-computed for each position at load time. With this set in your table, a simple “ORDER BY” statement can determine every frame which parts of walls to display and which to ignore, vastly improving performance.

'I've lost my peace' - Cape Verde hero Vozinha on newfound fame
- Published
Cape Verde's heroic World Cup goalkeeper Vozinha says he craves the "peace and tranquillity" of the life he led before he shot to fame.
The 40-year-old shot to global prominence in June when he almost single-handedly kept Spain at bay as Cape Verde drew 0-0 with the European champions on their World Cup debut.
Vozinha's follower count on social media sky-rocketed over the course of the game, from about 50,000 to more than one million.
But his fame shot up even further when Argentina needed extra time to beat Cape Verde in the round of 32.
Vozinha says his life was easier before his World Cup heroics.
"I've lost my peace and tranquillity," he told the Observer., external
"I no longer have any privacy, or at least much less than I used to.
"Now I go out, I go to a restaurant, and there's always someone who wants to take a photo with me or asks me for an autograph. Or, worse, someone is filming me.
"That's what has changed most in my life, and I don't think there's anything I can do about it."
Vozinha's mother became part of the fairytale too. After he revealed that she had could not afford a visa to watch his World Cup debut, US House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries announced that the visa fee had been waived.
Now Vozinha has revealed that his mother is visited on a daily basis by fans wanting to talk or to take photographs with him.
"A lot of people want to be famous and have a public profile, but they only see the positive side of that reality," said Vozinha.
"To be honest, if I were offered the life I have today or the life I had before, I'd choose the one I had before."
His World Cup performances for Cape Verde, a West African island nation with a population of 525,000, earned Vozinha a nomination for men's goalkeeper of the year at the Ballon d'Or awards.
"It's nice to feel like a kind of ambassador, but I want to make it clear that what we achieved was a collective effort," Vozinha said.
"We made history and the best news would be if we could harness that momentum to develop our country and improve the living conditions of our people."

The winter season in Delhi usually results in poor air quality, outbreaks of seasonal influenza, a heavy burden on hospitals and increasing medical expenses. Hidden within the yearly air quality reports is a health problem that is preventable, and yet costs the city’s citizens lakhs. Among the elderly, especially those who have diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, heart disease or a suppressed immune system, a viral infection can develop into bacterial pneumonia and require hospitalization. Industry estimates suggest that the average cost of a hospital stay is about ₹50,000, while intensive care can amount to ₹1 lakh. A single such incident can erase months’ worth of income and cause households relying on pensions and daily wages to slip down the income scale.
The battle against pneumonia
India has achieved real advances in the fight against pneumonia, mainly as a result of introducing the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV) as part of the Universal Immunisation Programme in 2017 and through Mission Indradhanush. Free three-dose vaccinations are provided to infants, and by 2023, vaccination rates among infants in India had reached 83%, according to the WHO/UNICEF Estimates of National Immunization Coverage (WUENIC).
The grandparents of these infants, however, are almost completely unprotected: National Sample Survey Office (NSSO) 80th Round Data on Health reveals that vaccination coverage among people aged 60 and over is only 0.40 per cent. While one generation is covered by the national programme, the other is left to avail of vaccines from a private market they may struggle to afford.
This gap is most significant in Delhi, since in the winter, the conditions can turn common respiratory infections into serious health issues.
Toxic winters
In December 2025, the city experienced its most toxic month in six years, with an average Air Quality Index of 351. Colder months naturally place a greater strain on the respiratory system. Winter air, which tends to remain stagnant, traps particulate matter near the ground: prolonged exposure compromises the lungs’ defensive abilities.
Government records show that there were more than 2,00,000 cases of acute respiratory illness and 30,000 hospital admissions in just six Delhi government hospitals between 2022 and 2024. When the pollution lasted throughout December 2025, doctors reportedly noted a 20% to 30% increase in the number of patients with respiratory problems, including some who had never before had such a condition.
These figures do not reflect the full extent of the problem, as they exclude people treated in private clinics, those who take medication on their own, infections that have never been confirmed by a laboratory test, and cases recorded as pneumonia rather than influenza.
Vaccine present, policy absent
What makes the number of hospitalisations and their resultant expenditure tragic, is that a a significant portion of this could perhaps be avoided with a vaccine that is already available. The 2026 Indian consensus guidelines concerning immunisation in adults recommend pneumococcal vaccination based on age and level of risk. It recommends the PCV20 vaccine for all adults between the ages of 18-49 years with chronic medical conditions or those considered at risk based on their health and lifestyle, or a single dose of the vaccine for all adults aged 50 and above. The guidelines also include adults who have immunosuppression and chronic diseases. For residents of Delhi, in winter when pollution makes the air toxic, this could mean the difference between a minor ailment an episode of hospitalisation.
India has no National Adult Immunisation Policy, and as a result, vaccination rates rely on individual awareness, access to a doctor, and the ability to pay out of pocket, a situation that systematically excludes older people in lower-income families. While this a critical problem ahead of winter in Delhi, it is not merely a Delhi problem: in 2022, India was estimated to whom were 149 million people aged 60 and over, a large number of whom are still economically active and support households.The Longitudinal Ageing Study in India (2017-18) showed that of Indians aged 45 and over, only around 0.6% had received a pneumococcal vaccine, a figure that has not changed much since then.
The burden in lives
The figure for deaths due to pneumonia recorded by India’s Medical Certification of Cause of Death in 2024 was 35,987, making it the leading cause of respiratory deaths, although it remains relatively out of the spotlight compared to other causes. Even this figure is an under estimate since the system covers only about one fifth to one quarter of all registered deaths nationally, and older people who die at home rather than in a hospital where certification takes place almost never get included at all.
Data on a year-by-year basis from Delhi shows that this is not an isolated occurrence but a consistent pattern, affecting precisely the group for whom a vaccine is already available but for whom no public system provides it.
Pollution raises the stakes
It is impossible for Delhi to solve its problem of air pollution by vaccination, and there is no suggestion here that it should. Reducing emissions at the source must continue to be the main course of action. However, the two measures operate at different stages of the same risk pathway. In the winter of 2025, the AQI reached 450 at a number of monitoring stations and people suffering from respiratory and cardiac conditions were told to remain indoors, a recommendation that is not a policy. When pollution increases baseline vulnerability, the removal of an additional infectious trigger becomes all the more important.
Before winter sets in this year, there is a concrete option available. Delhi could provide free pneumococcal vaccination to adults aged 60 and over who have recorded comorbidities via its present dispensary and mohalla clinic network and then assess both the uptake and the hospitalisation outcomes. The cost of each dose, at a few thousand rupees, is significantly lower compared to ₹65,000 for a hospitalisation episode.
Delhi already vaccinates the grandchildren; the medical case for vaccinating the grandparents is no different, it is merely administratively missing.

BCCI President Mithun Manhas on Saturday lauded the Indian men’s cricket team for retaining its Asian Games gold with a win over arch-rival Pakistan, and said the Shreyas Iyer-led outfit handled a high-pressure final well.
India defeated Pakistan by 19 runs in the final at Nisshin, Japan, emulating the women’s team which had also defended its gold medal last week.
“By far the best team of the tournament. We are the defending champions, and the performance they have shown this time is commendable,” Manhas told reporters here.
He was delighted to see the way the team handled pressure.
“They defeated arch-rivals Pakistan, who I feel don’t offer much competition anymore, and the way our team handled pressure situations…no other team in the world can do that,” he said.
He praised Tilak Varma and Abhishek Sharma for coming up with important knocks in the medal clash. “This is a team sport. Tilak Varma batted brilliantly, and Abhishek Sharma set the tone for the game. The job of openers is to build the game, and the middle order finishes the game. So, openers basically set the tone.

“Team India’s batting has been tremendous, and bowling…I would say that everyone defended a good total together,” he said.
The former Delhi cricketer also thanked ICC chief Jay Shah for doing commendable work to strengthen men’s and women’s teams during his tenure as BCCI secretary.
“I would like to thank Jay Shah once again here. He was the then (BCCI) secretary and his contribution has been significant in building this team.
“Not just for the men’s team, our women’s team has also won the World Cup. His contribution has been very big. So, a special thanks to him too,” he added.
Manhas dedicated the Asian Games victory to cricket fans and the Armed Forces.
“This victory, I believe, we should dedicate to the thousands of crores of fans who pray for the Indian team, and especially to those soldiers who sacrificed their lives for the country,” he said.
On cricket becoming an attraction in the Asian Games, Manhas said the sport is gaining some global traction.
“Different teams from around the world are participating, every country is getting involved in cricket, and it’s a very good thing that cricket is becoming global,” he said.
Manhas, who has close ties with cricket in the Valley, hoped to see more players from the region represent the country in future.
“Aquib Nabi, who comes from Baramulla, has reached here through a lot of hard work. When he played (in local cricket), BCCI was running it (J&K cricket) then. The BCCI has given its full support to this association now.
“We have promised to continue providing it in the future as well. There are a lot of talents here, and they just need to be nurtured and backed,” he said.

Snapchat’s distinct navigation uses custom icons across its main features: the bottom bar accesses Snap Map, Chat, Explore, Stories, and Spotlight. In chats, color-coded arrows and squares signal message types (pink for audio-less snaps, purple for video/audio snaps, and blue for text chats), while outlined versions show opened status or screenshots.
Snapchat successfully positioned itself as “the social media platform for Gen Z”. With its ephemeral nature and best retention features such as Snapstreaks, Snapchat is one of the most popular social media platforms currently.
However, I took my time to understand the platform better and finally became a user. But still, I am far from being a snapper, a word I use for those who are obsessed with Snapstreaks, including my close friends.
Despite being a user for months, I still find the Snapchat interface harder to navigate. Part of the reason is that it is completely detached from the common interfaces used in other social media platforms.
Moreover, Snapchat uses its own terms, such as Planets, Best Friends, and Chats, which can confuse new users. So, as part of our icon explanation series, in this guide you will learn everything about icons and their meanings on Snapchat. For quick reference, here is the Snapchat legend, followed by various icons on each screen and what they mean.

Snapchat Icons and Symbols and Their Meanings
Snapchat Bottom Navigation Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Open Snapchat > View the bottom navigation bar
Snapchat is still one of the apps that uses a bottom navigation bar, which lets you switch between different Snapchat core features such as Snap Map, Chat, Stories, Discovery, and Spotlight
- Snap Map: Snap Map is an interactive feature that lets you see your friends’ current locations and also locations with the most Snap activity
- Chat: The chat icon lets you switch to the Chats tab
- Explore: Using this icon, you can browse various Snapchat lenses and filter options
- Stories: Takes you to the Snapchat stories tab
- Spotlight: Spotlight is another name for the short video feed in the Snapchat app, just like Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts
Snapchat Chat Screen Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon
Now, moving on to the chat feed, which many of us also spend more time on, you will find various icons and symbols. This screen can be confusing for the user with various symbols. Here is what each symbol means.
- Add Friends: This is the same add button that you see on other screens, where it lets you discover or add new friends
- More Options: This option opens additional chat screen options, including the ability to create new chats, create new groups, manage them, manage friendships, and also customize friend emojis and more.
- Viewed Snap Without Audio: This means you have viewed your snap without audio
- Snap Reply: If you see a reply, it means you can reply to a friend with a snap again
- Unopened Snap With Audio: If you see this icon, it means it is an unopened snap with audio
- Chat: The chat icon lets you start a new conversation with your friend.
- New Chat: The new chat icon lets you create a new chat with any of your friends
Snapchat Chat Status Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon
Snapchat also uses various colored arrows and squares to represent the type of snaps. If you see a pink arrow icon, it means you sent a snap without audio. If you see a purple arrow, it means you sent a video snap; in other words, you sent a snap with audio or video.
If you see blue, it means the chat was sent; in other words, you sent a chat message. If you see gray, it means your chat is waiting for the person to accept you.
If the arrow turns into an outline pink arrow, it means the recipient has opened your Snapchat without audio. If you see purple, it means the recipient opened your Snapchat with audio or video, and it’s the same for the blue outline arrow.
If you see a square-shaped icon in pink, it means you received a new snap without audio. If you see a purple square box, it means you received a new snap with audio or video.
If you see a blue square-shaped icon, it means you received a chat message. If you see the outline messages, it means you have viewed all the chats and messages.
If you see a double-arrow outline pink arrow, it means someone took a screenshot of the snap without audio, and it is the same for the other arrow types, including video and chat.
If you see a reload symbol, it means someone replayed your snap without audio. If you see a purple arrow, it means someone replayed your snap with audio or video.
Snapchat Chat Call Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation

- Camera: It opens the camera to send a snap as a reply
- Voice Call: Snapchat also supports voice calls. Tapping on this icon, you can make a voice call to your friend.
- Video Call: Along with the voice call, Snap also supports video calls. You can tap on the video icon to start a video call with your friend.

How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation

- Camera: It opens your camera to send a snap quickly
- Voice Note: You can also quickly record a voice note and send it as a message
- Stickers: This is a sticker icon that lets you add stickers, Bitmoji, and other reaction options

Snapchat Friendship Profile Icons and Symbols Explained
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Chat icon > Open a conversation > Tap on your friend’s profile
Snapchat friends’ profiles can also be confusing for new users. It also consists of various icons similar to your profile page. Here is what each of them means.

Snapchat Snap Map Icons and Symbols Explained

- Friend Finder: It lets you search for and find friends who are visible on a Snap Map.

How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Camera icon

Snapchat Camera Screen Icons
How to access this screen: Home > Tap on the Camera icon

Prashant Bhushan, Neha Bora among 160 detained on Day 2 of anti-CEC stir; Yogendra Yadav calls march on October 4
A day after over 1,000 protesters were detained, several lawyers, activists and students gathered at the protest site for a second consecutive day.
The Delhi Police on Saturday detained 160 protesters, including senior advocate Prashant Bhushan, political activist Yogendra Yadav, AISA president Neha Bora and activist Anjali Bhardwaj, during a protest march demanding CEC Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
A day after over 1,000 protesters were detained, several lawyers, activists and students gathered at the protest site as the agitation continued for a second day. AISA had issued a call for people to join the protest at 1 pm on Saturday. Meanwhile, Yogendra Yadav has called for a citizen's march again on Sunday, October 4.
Police said no permission had been granted for any protest on October 3, and that “no prior intimation” of any such stir was received by the cops. Prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 also remained in force in the New Delhi district for a second consecutive day, with cops saying this was to ensure public safety, maintain public order and facilitate smooth traffic movement.
Protest began with two-hour delay, protesters detained within 15 minutes
Deep Dive
Student activists from AISA and other organisations returned to Jantar Mantar on Saturday, and protesters initially gathered on the Ashoka Road at 1 pm. The route to the backside of the protest site was sealed, with multiple layers of barricades and hundreds of security personnel deployed across the area.
Nearly two hours after the scheduled time of the protest, AISA national president Neha Bora, Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal, Swaraj India leader Yogendra Yadav, Supreme Court lawyer Prashant Bhushan and RTI activist Anjali Bhardwaj began leading the march amid heavy security presence in and around Jantar Mantar.
The Delhi Police made announcements and attempted to disperse the crowd, eventually detaining several protesters. “Nearly 160 people were detained and were taken to different police stations,” a police official said, requesting anonymity.

Verstappen wins Bahrain GP in Malaysia after long delays
- Published
Max Verstappen took his and Red Bull's first win of the year with a dominant drive in a dramatic Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia that started amid chaotic and unprecedented scenes.
Verstappen led home the Mercedes of Kimi Antonelli, who took a giant leap towards his first world title when team-mate George Russell retired from third place with a power unit failure with five laps to go.
Antonelli now leads Russell by 84 points with either six or seven races remaining.
Lewis Hamilton drove an extraordinary race after dropping towards the back with an incorrect tyre choice for a wet start to fight back to pass Red Bull's Isack Hadjar for third place with three laps to go.
All that came after a delay of an hour and a half caused initially by heavy rain and then by a series of bizarre technical problems that left several cars crawling as they completed formation laps on the wet track behind the safety car.
After that problem, it took some time for governing body the FIA to decide the order in which the cars should take the start.
The key stories of a madcap afternoon were:
- Verstappen's dominant win in a revived Red Bull
- The effective death knell for Russell's already faint title hopes
- A stunning recovery by Hamilton
- A series of questions over race organisation, particularly over the start
1 of 5
Once the race got under way, with the cars in their original order, Verstappen and Hamilton on the front row immediately lost ground and the Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell swept past them into first and second places.
Verstappen and the Mercedes drivers took the start on intermediate tyres on the still-wet track after a torrential tropical downpour had delayed the start.
Hamilton chose soft-compound slicks and immediately regretted the decision as it became apparent that the track was still far too wet for that option. He and others who chose slicks immediately dropped to the back of the field, and lost nearly a minute to the leaders in the early laps.
Meanwhile, Verstappen repassed Russell for second place on lap six, and was on Antonelli's tail when a safety car was deployed to allow marshals to recover the Cadillac of Valtteri Bottas, who had spun off at Turn 13 on lap nine.
The leaders took the opportunity of the safety car to pit for slick tyres, and when the race resumed four laps later, Verstappen immediately passed Antonelli at Turn Four, the Italian also losing out to Russell on the exit of the corner.
From that moment on, Verstappen was total in control and he edged away into a race of his own.
Behind him, Antonelli had pace on Russell and passed him on lap 21 at Turn Four, the move seemingly settling the top three positions.
A late safety car caused by Alex Albon's stricken Williams led to everyone switching to fresh tyres for a four-lap dash to the flag, but again Verstappen was supreme and remained unchallenged.
Even then, there was drama, as Russell pulled off just before Turn One with five laps to go before the safety car had even ended.
In the immediate aftermath, Lando Norris was apparently distracted by Russell's car and had to take to the gravel at Turn One to avoid running into the back of team-mate Oscar Piastri, dropping from eighth to 11th.
He recovered to ninth by the end, immediately behind Fernando Alonso, who scored points for Aston Martin for only the third time this year after their strongest performance of the year.
Strong recovery by Hamilton
Hamilton and the others who chose to use dry tyres at the start immediately lived to regret their decision, as they were passed by all the cars on intermediates.
Within a few laps, Hamilton was nearly a minute behind the leaders and down in 17th place, his race apparently over.
But he stayed out during the safety car, sticking with the soft tyres he had chosen for the start, and when the race restarted he began to pick off the cars in front of him, driving an excellent race to get back into contention for serious points.
Hamilton passed car after car until by lap 24 he was on the tail of Isack Hadjar's fourth-placed Red Bull.
They pitted together on lap 31, Hadjar sticking to soft tyres, and Hamilton having no choice but to move to mediums.
Hamilton trailed the Frenchman for lap after lap, right on his tail, but was never quite able to get close enough to pass, despite a number of attempts, before the late safety car.
That gave Hamilton the chance to switch to the preferred soft tyres, and a lap after the restart he passed Hadjar into Turn One to take the final podium position.
Ferrari's Charles Leclerc also passed Hadjar in the closing laps, with Oscar Piastri taking sixth after a dispiriting weekend for McLaren, ahead of Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson and Alonso.
Norris and the second Racing Bulls of Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.
What happened before the start?
After the tropical downpour, the race was initially started with formation laps behind the safety car. But immediately the problems started.
Verstappen and Hamilton were the first of a number of cars that were afflicted by a software issue that left them unable to do more than crawl along.
Initial indications were that this was caused by a software update issued to teams by governing body the FIA during the start delay. The FIA has yet to respond to requests for comment on the matter.
Most teams who were afflicted managed eventually to get their cars going, but the field order was jumbled, and that led to a debate as to the positions in which the cars should take the restart.
The rules did not cover the situation, which was unprecedented. And although they outline positional penalties for any driver who is not able to regain his position by a certain place on the track having lost it on a formation lap, this was ignored in restarting the race in its original order.

'The Night of the UFOs': Remembering the Oct. 4, 1967, skies over Nova Scotia
Besides Shag Harbour, sightings were reported in Dartmouth, Sambro, Wedgeport and elsewhere
Chris Styles was just 12 years old on a clear night when he looked out his bedroom window and spotted a strange light moving along the shoreline a few blocks from his house.
He grabbed his grandfather's binoculars to get a better look and then ran out of the house, much to his dad's dismay, down to the water's edge.
"There's this huge sphere and it was a very dull orange, and it was glowing just like a poker in a fireplace," said Styles about what he saw on Oct. 4, 1967, around 10 p.m. AT.
While that date is best known for a UFO sighting in Shag Harbour in southwestern Nova Scotia, Styles was in Dartmouth, N.S.
Primarily between the Halifax area and southwestern Nova Scotia, people recorded seeing things in the sky that night, which has led ufologists to call it "The Night of the UFOs."
"If you were outside that ... night and you looked up, and for some hours afterwards, you would have seen something," said Styles. "It was a clear night. People were seeing the faintest stars without binoculars."
Styles has written or co-written three books about UFO sightings, including Impact to Contact: The Shag Harbour Incident. He said coverage of Shag Harbour meant other sightings fell out of the press, such as what the crew of the MV Nickerson saw in the waters off Sambro.
Around 9 p.m., Capt. Leo Mersey said he spotted an object with three flashing red lights. The object, which showed up on radar, was about 25 kilometres away.
"It was very clear that night and we could see the lights of Halifax," Mersey said in a statement he filed with the RCMP.
The radar also showed three objects about 10 kilometres away, but he could not see them.
Around 11 p.m., the object he could see went into the air, but by then had only one red flashing light.
"I had never seen anything like that before but it sounds like the thing they are looking for down off Shelburne or Barrington Passage," Mersey said in the statement, which was taken Oct. 7, 1967.
The RCMP statement, taken by a corporal with the Lunenburg detachment, noted: "Capt. Mersey is considered to be a reliable type individual and bears a good reputation in his community."
But Shag Harbour has long remained the focus, said Styles, in part because of the large witness pool, what authorities said at the time, and the subsequent paper trail left behind.
In Shag Harbour, an object with flashing lights crashed into the waters off the tiny fishing village.
Besides the many eyewitnesses, adding credence to the account was that a responding RCMP officer, Const. Ron O'Brien, described seeing a light from the object floating about 800 metres offshore.
"It was being carried out to sea by the tide and disappeared before we could get a boat to it," he told the Chronicle-Herald in an Oct. 7, 1967, article.
Styles said RCMP officers commandeered two fishing boats to see what was in the water and if there were any survivors, assuming a plane had crashed. They were joined on the boats by local fishermen and other residents.
He said depending on who you talk to, the object either disappeared or submerged, but there was a yellow foam on the water that some say smelled of sulphur.
On Friday, Oct. 6, a naval diving team was brought in, and seven divers searched through the weekend, but reported finding nothing.
The investigation reached the highest levels of National Defence.
An Oct. 6, 1967, memo by Col. W.W. Turner, the director of operations at National Defence headquarters, noted: "The Rescue Co-ordination Centre conducted [a] preliminary investigation and discounted the possibilities that the sighting was produced by an aircraft, flares, floats, or any other known objects."
His son, John Turner, told CBC News his father often mentioned to the family that he received reports of alleged UFO sightings.
"Many were easily discounted as photos of a Frisbee or a hubcap, but he often said others simply could not be explained," Turner wrote by email.
Styles wasn't the only person to see something in Dartmouth on Oct. 4, according to the Chronicle-Herald on Oct. 7, 1967. The newspaper reported that a woman on her way home from work saw a bright, round object in the sky moving from the Halifax-Dartmouth ferry terminal.
"She described it as brighter, more vivid than a star, with an orange hue like a halo around the circumference," the reporter wrote.
The woman looked at it through binoculars when she got home and saw it was not a star.
The newspaper checked with CFB Shearwater's control tower to see if anything was on the radar during the window the woman described. Control tower personnel said no one was monitoring the radar at the time.

Ethiopian federal forces retake Mekelle airport from Tigrayan fighters, residents say
Ethiopian federal forces have retaken Mekelle’s airport from Tigrayan fighters
KAMPALA, Uganda -- Ethiopian federal forces have taken the airport in Mekelle, the capital of the northern Tigray region, according to people in the city who spoke to The Associated Press on Saturday, reversing a takeover by Tigrayan fighters that prompted the suspension of commercial flights last month.
It wasn't immediately clear when federal forces recaptured Alula Aba Nega Airport. Those who provided the information declined to be identified for fear of retribution amid uncertainty over who controlled the city.
Severe disruptions to internet and cellphone networks have made gathering and verifying information from Tigray difficult. Details of how the airport changed hands, including whether fighting took place there, remained unclear.
“The military is in full control of the airport. That much I can confirm,” an Ethiopian general said on condition of anonymity.
Neither the Ethiopian government nor the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF, had issued an official statement on the airport’s reported capture. It wasn’t clear who controlled Mekelle itself. An AP contributor in the city said residents feared looting amid the uncertainty.
“Many reports indicate that the government and allied forces have begun to control Tigray’s capital,” said Jalale Getachew Birru, an Ethiopia analyst for ACLED, an independent global monitor that collects, analyzes and maps data on conflict.
The AP could not independently verify those reports.
TPLF fighters seized the airport on Sept. 23, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to Mekelle and the Tigrayan cities of Axum and Shire. The African Union urged restraint, warning that renewed tensions threatened the peace agreement signed in 2022.
Federal troops are fighting alongside allied Tigrayan forces against the TPLF. The AP previously reported that the Tigray Peace Force, a breakaway faction of the Tigrayan rebels, was operating alongside federal forces in the neighboring Afar region.
The reported change in control follows a sharp deterioration in relations between Ethiopia and neighboring Eritrea. Ethiopia on Thursday ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave and announced the closure of its embassy in Eritrea. Eritrea said that it would sever diplomatic ties.
Ethiopian authorities have accused Eritrea of supporting the TPLF, an allegation Eritrea has denied.
The government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, if it takes control of Mekelle, is very likely to leave regional security in the hands of the Tigray Peace Force, which comprises former members of the Tigray Defense Forces, Birru said.
Abiy has tried and failed to subdue Tigray’s rebellious leaders in recent months, with TPLF Chairman Debretsion Gebremichael openly challenging him. Renewed fighting has shattered a 2022 peace deal that ended a devastating two-year war between federal troops, backed by Eritrea and allied militias, and the TPLF.
“This is an extraordinary and largely unexpected turn in a war whose direction looked very different only days ago,” Getachew Temare, an independent attorney and human rights defender who is from Ethiopia, said of the possible fall of Mekelle in an analysis posted on X. “But the most consequential question is not whether Mekelle falls. It is what this fall means politically.”
He said the emergence of the Tigray Peace Force makes the current conflict different from the previous one. When Mekelle fell to federal forces in November 2020, the TPLF “retained something far more important. A substantial political and social constituency for armed resistance remained intact. Within months, Tigrayan forces returned to Mekelle and the military balance was dramatically reversed.”
The fighting has brought renewed hardship to civilians still recovering from the previous 2020-2022 war. Residents of Mekelle told the AP earlier this week that communications, banking and other essential services had been disrupted.
In September, residents described fears of renewed isolation following the suspension of flights. They also reported that roads connecting Tigray and Afar had been closed to civilian traffic, although the AP couldn't independently verify the closures.

The British Sikh activist Jagtar Singh Johal has been released from a Delhi prison after the Indian high court warned the government it would be found in contempt of court if it continued to attempt to keep him in jail despite an 18 September court order releasing him on bail. Johal has been incarcerated for nine years without any full trial.
The court order was issued after Johal’s lawyers issued a writ of habeas corpus alleging he was being detained against the express direction of the court.
Johal’s nine-year detention on alleged terrorist offences, has been a cause of diplomatic tension between the UK and India, but campaigners have claimed the British government has not been active enough to secure his release or, alternatively, a full trial.
The campaign group Reprieve says his case has never come to full trial largely because of the inability of the Indian government to assemble credible witnesses to back their claim that Johal transported £3,000 to France to fund a multinational extremist plot involving targeted killings in the Punjab in 2016-17.
On Thursday morning, the high court in Delhi instructed the Indian government to release Johal by 2.30pm Indian time, giving government officials three hours to comply or find themselves risking contempt proceedings. In the end, he was released in the late afternoon wearing a red T-shirt to be greeted by friends, family and flowers.
Documents shown to the court by Johal’s lawyers on behalf of his father-in-law as petitioner revealed that messages from the prison to the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking permission for his release had been left unanswered.
His lawyers in their petition stated he had met all the bail conditions yet “the detainee has nevertheless not been released, and is being held in custody without the authority of any court, pending a ‘clarification’ sought by the jail from the Ministry of Home Affairs”.
The petition added that no clarification from the ministry had been forthcoming, explaining: “Every day of such detention is a continuing violation of the detainee’s fundamental rights under article 21 of the constitution of India.”
Johal has been detained by Indian authorities since 4 November 2017. He is facing eight charges of terrorism in the federal court, but had been cleared of largely similar charges by a Punjab court. He claims any initial confessions he gave were extracted under torture.
The bail terms last week imposed 11 conditions, including surrender of passport, a personal bond of 500,000 Indian rupees (£3,930) with two sureties, fortnightly reporting to the investigating officer, prior intimation of any change of residence and a ban on travelling to the Punjab. He was also restricted from talking to media about the case directly or indirectly.
The Indian government has alleged the Khalistan Liberation Force undertook the killings and Johal had “complete knowledge of the conspiracy” and was a KLF member.
His Dumbarton-based brother Gurpreet Singh Johal said: “There have been so many setbacks and disappointments in the last nine years that I didn’t dare to believe it until I saw Jagtar walking out of the prison gates with my own eyes. The last two weeks have been torture – knowing that Jagtar had been granted bail, but the authorities were refusing to let him out. I’ll sleep well tonight, knowing that he’s not behind bars.
“Tomorrow morning, the fight continues, because he’s still on trial and facing the death penalty for something he didn’t do, trapped in a sham legal process designed to punish him for standing up for human rights”.
Reprieve’s deputy executive director, Dan Dolan, said: “While tonight is the first night in almost nine years that Jagtar Singh Johal is not caged in a prison cell, he still has the threat of a death sentence hanging over him. It should also be noted that, despite bail being ordered, the prison refused to release Jagtar until his family brought a habeas corpus petition and a judge warned the jail they’d be found in contempt of court”.
The UK Foreign Office is understood to have been supporting recent calls for his release on bail after last week’s court order, as have two campaign groups in the UK Redress and Reprieve.

Prem* is a young mathematics graduate from a village in Jharkhand. He was known as an energetic and supportive young person. Children from the village often approached him when they had difficulties with mathematics. When he was selected for a job with the Indian Railways, it was expected to be a moment of happiness. But the thought of leaving his parents, friends, village and the life he shared with them was difficult for him.
In the weeks following the job offer, Prem began having sleepless nights, worrying about how he would cope with a new life and new responsibilities. Gradually, he stopped talking to his family. He began to feel helpless and worthless, lost interest in everyday life and reached a point where he attempted to end his life.
What helped was having people around him who could understand not only what he was going through, but also the world he was coming from. A neighbourhood facilitator working in a community-based organisation was able to sit with him, listen to his worries and share his dukh-sukh. They understood why leaving his parents, friends and village felt so difficult and gave him space to talk about the fears he was carrying.
The support was not about asking him simply to adjust or move on. It helped him think about what mattered to him, what he wanted for his future and how he could remain connected to the people and place that were important to him while taking up the new opportunity. He eventually wrote to the department asking for another opportunity to join. He was invited again and went to work, while continuing to receive support.
Prem’s experience highlights that what looks like a positive life event from the outside can sometimes become overwhelming. A suicidal act can often happen suddenly, during a moment of intense crisis. But the distress behind that moment may have been building for much longer.
For Adivasi communities, distress can be shaped by circumstances that may never appear in a psychiatric consultation.
When distress is accumulates
A recent study in Jharkhand examined psychosocial distress and help-seeking among Adivasi Ho adolescents. It found that distress was often linked to family conflict, pressure around education and work, financial hardship, violence, separation and loss, and difficulties in relationships. Some adolescents withdrew and stopped sharing what they were going through; for some, this included thoughts of self-harm or suicide
These accounts do not offer a single explanation for suicide among Adivasi communities. They show how distress can accumulate across everyday life — in family conflict, having to leave school temporarily or reduce schooling to help with agricultural or household work, substance use, untreated illness, violence, displacement, loss of livelihood, lack of mentorship, identity-related stigma and self-doubt, or the erosion of community and belonging.
When communities are disrupted
Belonging is an important part of suicide prevention. Stereotypes, exclusion, humiliation, discrimination and pressure to hide one’s identity can affect how people see themselves and how connected they feel to society. Historically, Adivasi communities stayed together. But modern development, alongside education and employment opportunities, have in some cases, uprooted Adivasi people from their culture. Mainstream schools do not teach Adivasi children in their own mother tongue; their history is woefully under-represented in the school curricula.
Sandip Sing, a radiologist from the Munda community practising in rural West Bengal and a first-generation learner, says, “There is a rapid transition in accessing and navigating educational and professional spaces, often amid gaps in resources, networks, and institutional familiarity. Bridging these gaps can be challenging, particularly with unfamiliar systems.”
Many educated Adivasis may also have had fewer opportunities to engage with their community’s history, culture, language and traditions, and may have complex or evolving relationships with their Adivasi identities. This matters for mental health because belonging itself is a source of strength. When people are uprooted without finding a new sense of belonging, distress can deepen.
This does not mean that development itself causes mental illness or suicide. The concern is what happens when rapid social change is accompanied by displacement, loss of livelihood, cultural disconnection and weakening social support.
Collective strength, mentoring
The strength of Adivasi life also lies in ways of expressing emotions and sharing knowledge. Songs and dances are not simply cultural performances; they are ways of expressing emotions, maintaining connection and making sense of life. The Adivasi dance itself is a powerful metaphor. People dance in a chain, holding one another. The village headman, Majhi Baba, dances alongside everyone else. An 80-year-old and an eight-year-old can dance together. There is no hierarchy; the strength is in the circle. For suicide prevention, this collective strength matters.
Young people also need places where they can be themselves without constantly having to explain or defend who they are. Lilibiti Saren, a medical officer from the Santhal community working in tribal areas of Bankura, West Bengal, notes that she often finds young people in these communities lacking direction. “There is a need for proper mentorship,” she says.
Locally organised Adivasi youth spaces can help. Such spaces can offer young people opportunities to speak in their own language, share experiences, learn from peers and elders and explore what Adivasiyat — identity, history, relationships and belonging — means to them.
Access and pathways in care
Clinical care remains essential. A person experiencing suicidal thoughts may need assessment for depression, substance use, trauma, psychosis, previous attempts, suicidal intent, access to means and immediate safety. Treatment and follow-up can save lives.
But access to mental health care is itself a major challenge in many Adivasi areas. Services are often limited, distant and unevenly available.
And even when services are available, the pathways into care may not be optimal. An Adivasi person with lived experience of mental healthcare says: “I felt like the psychiatrists and the psychologists were not speaking to me. They were judging me for what I had done and they were trying to find symptoms instead of trying to understand me, my pain and my situation.”
This raises an important question: are our mental health systems listening as carefully as they are diagnosing?
When formal services are scarce, difficult to reach, or experienced as unfamiliar or judgmental, people may seek support elsewhere—including from family, community networks, faith healers or indigenous systems. These spaces may offer something that the formal system does not: familiar language, relationships, cultural understanding and a sense of belonging.
Adivasi mental health therefore cannot be treated simply as another category within rural health. Representation matters — from schools to healthcare institutions and policy making.
Models that could work
In Adivasi communities of Jharkhand, particularly among the Ho, Munda and Santhal communities, Madait refers to a tradition of voluntary help and collective support for someone who needs it or is in distress. It reflects an understanding that some difficulties are too large for one household to manage alone.
This may be a useful way to think about mental healthcare too. The question is not simply how services can be delivered to Adivasi communities, but how communities themselves can shape, participate in and lead the care they need.
The same principle can be seen in Dukhu-Sukhu Baithaki — community support group meetings where people experiencing mental health difficulties and their families can meet, share experiences and support one another. This model works in West Singhbhum, Jharkhand, where people living with mental health conditions come together each month. These spaces do not replace professional care. They bring community knowledge, relationships and mutual support into the process of recovery.
Education without a knowledge of one’s roots; development that comes with displacement and mental healthcare that does not see or hear the people who need help is no longer enough. For suicide prevention, we must ask not only, “What is wrong with the individual?”, but also, “ Where is the community support? Where is the system that understands them?”
Perhaps suicide prevention in Adivasi communities must begin there — not by doing things for Adivasis, but by doing them with Adivasis.
