The Indian startup ecosystem continued to mature in FY26, with 22 new-age tech companies making their public market debut as against 13 in FY25. At the same time, a growing number of startups turned profitable or moved closer to profitability after years of cost rationalisation to adjust to the new funding realities. Despite a tough Q4 for many startups due to geopolitical uncertainties, Indian startups are expected to improve their top and bottom line numbers in FY26. Of the 98 startups in the tracker, 65, or about 67%, reported profits in FY26. However, the profitability picture remained uneven. Together, these 65 startups generated a net profit of ₹14,511.8 Cr, while the remaining 33 posted a cumulative loss of ₹21,459.4 Cr, underscoring that sustainable profitability remains a work in progress for a section of the ecosystem. Even so, the scale of India’s startup ecosystem continued to expand. The 98 companies generated ₹3.22 Lakh Cr in operating revenue in FY26, a sharp 44.26% increase from ₹2.23 Lakh Cr in FY25. To help you track the financial health of new-age tech companies, Inc42 has launched the FY26 Financial Tracker, bringing together key financial metrics in one place. Andhra Pradesh Roads and Buildings Minister B.C. Janardhan Reddy has said various development works are being taken up in Banaganapalle town in Nandyal district with the aim of providing better infrastructure to the public and finding permanent solutions to long-standing issues faced by the residents.
The Minister on Sunday (October 4, 2026) inspected various ongoing development projects and reviewed the progress and quality standards of the works with officials. He inspected the new RDO office building under construction in Banaganapalle. He said that once the building became operational, administrative services would be more conveniently accessible to the public. After inquiring about the progress of the construction, he directed officials to ensure high-quality work in accordance with prescribed standards and to expedite the completion of the project.
Mr. Janardhan Reddy also inspected the drainage construction works under way on Anjaneya Swamy Street. He instructed officials to develop an efficient drainage system, keeping in mind the difficulties residents face because of water stagnation and sewage issues during the rainy season. He ordered the swift completion of the construction works and directed that measures be taken to ensure the public faced no inconvenience.
The Minister also inspected the ongoing construction of the bypass road on the Yaganti Palle route. He said the bypass road would play a crucial role in easing traffic congestion on main roads and managing the town’s increasing vehicular movement, and provide better transportation facilities for the public.
Mr. Janardhan Reddy said the government’s objective was to comprehensively develop Banaganapalle town across all sectors and transform it into a model town in terms of infrastructure.
The Minister also performed the groundbreaking ceremony for the construction of a new shed at the Dastagiri Swamy Dargah in Banaganapalle town. He is undertaking the project with his own funds. The Dargah is located near the four-road junction on the road leading to Pandlapuram.

Probe launched into luxury One Stanley project over alleged steel bar shortage
Buildings Department pulls in developer and contractors after report claims house has up to 75 per cent fewer steel bars than approved
Authorities have launched a probe into the building quality of a luxury residential development in one of Hong Kong’s most expensive neighbourhoods in the Southern district after receiving a complaint from an owner that insufficient steel bars were used during construction.
The Buildings Department said on Saturday it was “very concerned about the matter” relating to One Stanley in Stanley, but stressed that its previous inspections did not find any imminent danger.
The department said it would summon meetings with the developer, contractors and other relevant parties responsible for the development.
Public concerns have been brewing since Friday after a report by the online property news platform WuChatProp alleged that an on-site inspection of a house found insufficient steel bars had been used in some parts of the property. The number fell short by as much as 75 per cent of the approved building plans, according to the report.

United Nations, Sep 23: In his inaugural speech at the UN General Assembly, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said world leaders must set up global standards to oversee artificial intelligence because “fundamental decisions on this technology are too important to be left to chance”.
Burnham said the UK will try to persuade other countries to adopt rules on transparency and access to AI models - and, even tougher, to get tech companies to sign on, too.
He said AI has immense potential but will also be “a source of disruption to the way we live and work - and a multiplier of risk”.
Burnham also said Russia and other states are using AI-augmented misinformation and disinformation to corrode democracy, something he said Britain has faced in the decade since it voted to leave the European Union.
He said he has asked British security chiefs to set up a National Centre for Information Defence to counter the threat.
Burnham also chaired a meeting at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday on the Israel-Palestine issue, alongside French President Emmanuel Macron, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan.
He said the two-state solution to Israel-Palestinian conflict must be kept alive.
Burnham said failure to deliver a two-state solution will “corrode trust” in politicians who have talked about the issue but not taken action.
He told delegates from dozens of countries that the UK has banned trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank because the “E1” settlement expansion plan is “a deliberate attempt to block a two-state solution.”
“We all live in an era of low trust in politics. Many people in this room, many politicians around the world, have spoken for decades about a two-state solution. But if we fail to back those words with deeds, we will further corrode trust in the political, diplomatic and international process,” the UK prime minister said. (AP)

The Embassy of the State of Palestine to India has questioned the description of the 1918 Battle of Haifa as the “liberation of Haifa”, saying that Indian soldiers who participated in the battle were serving under British command as part of an imperial military campaign that resulted in the occupation of Palestine.
In a five-page position paper titled “Rewriting of India–Palestine history: The battle of Haifa: liberation or occupation?”, the Palestinian Embassy said the terminology surrounding the battle required “careful and scholarly reflection” and argued that the event should be understood within the historical context of British military occupation of Palestine.
The Embassy said Palestine, including Haifa, was under Ottoman rule before 1918 and that British forces defeated the Ottoman Empire during the First World War, bringing Palestine under British occupation. Indian soldiers participated in the campaign as part of the British Indian Army, under British command.
It argued that describing them retrospectively as having “liberated Haifa” risked attributing to India a sovereign military decision that the country did not possess in 1918, when it was still under British rule.
The paper pointed to contemporary British terminology, saying military and parliamentary records referred to the operations in Palestine using terms such as “capture”, “take”, “fall” and “conquer”. It also noted that following the British military campaign, Palestine was administered under the Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (OETA) until its replacement by a civil administration in July 1920.
The Embassy also cited India’s own historical records, including the 2014 publication Indian War Memorials Around the World, saying it does not describe the event as the “liberation of Haifa”.
According to the paper, the publication records that the “fortified town of Haifa fell to a cavalry charge by the Jodhpur Lancers” and that the 15th Imperial Service Cavalry Brigade “broke through and took the town”.
It also referred to the Teen Murti Memorial in New Delhi, stating that the memorial was established during British colonial rule to commemorate Indian soldiers who served and died during the First World War, and was not originally intended to commemorate relations between India and Israel.
The Embassy said the memorial refers to “Palestine and some of its cities” among the places associated with the military campaigns in which Indian soldiers served.
The paper further cited official Indian records to state that 491 Indian soldiers are recorded at Ramleh War Cemetery, 109 at the Gaza and Deir el Balah War Cemeteries and 47 at the Haifa Indian Cemetery, besides soldiers commemorated at other cemeteries and memorials across historical Palestine.
The Embassy questioned why Haifa had become the centre of a commemorative narrative when Indian soldiers had fought across a much wider region, including the Suez Canal, Gaza, Jerusalem, the Jordan Valley, Damascus and Aleppo.
It also said the first formal Israeli public ceremony commemorating the Indian soldiers was held in 2010, nearly a century after the battle.
The paper argued that Britain, rather than India, was the principal military power behind the campaign, as it financed, armed and commanded the operation. It questioned why the “liberation of Haifa” narrative centred on Indian soldiers while Britain’s role was not similarly emphasised.
The Embassy also stressed that the soldiers described as “Indian soldiers” served in the British Indian Army and came from different regions, communities and religions across British India, whose geographical and political boundaries differed from those of the present-day Republic of India.
The position paper placed the soldiers’ participation within the wider history of British colonial rule, noting that Indian troops were deployed in military campaigns far from their homeland.
It also referred to the Rowlatt Act and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, arguing that the broader record of British rule should be considered when interpreting the role of Indian soldiers in the First World War.
The Embassy cited Mahatma Gandhi’s opposition to the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine at the expense of its indigenous population, including his statement that “Palestine belongs to the Arabs in the same sense that England belongs to the English.”
It further pointed out that India voted against UN Resolution 181 in 1947, which proposed partition and allocated Haifa to the proposed Jewish state, and questioned how the 1918 battle could subsequently be presented as a foundation for India-Israel historical ties.
The Embassy said describing the 1918 occupation of Haifa as a liberation “raises serious questions and concerns in Palestine”. It maintained that Haifa should be recognised as a Palestinian city at the time and that the battle took place in the context of the British military occupation of Palestine.
At the same time, the Embassy said its position was expressed with “full respect” for the sacrifice and memory of Indian soldiers and for India’s sovereign right to commemorate its history and fallen soldiers.
It called for historical remembrance of the Battle of Haifa to remain grounded in accuracy, balance and respect for the historical experiences of all concerned, while emphasising that the document represented the Palestinian Embassy’s perspective and was intended to contribute to discussion on the historical and legal questions surrounding the battle.

Concerns over the safety of drinking water have resurfaced in parts of Uri area of north Kashmir’s Baramulla district after residents of Gawalta village found a dead snake inside a pipeline supplying water to the locality, raising questions over the maintenance and monitoring of the public water supply network.
The incident comes weeks after a similar complaint from Karkroo Mohalla in Nambla, where residents had reported finding dead rats inside a water storage tank and supply pipelines.
Both incidents have generated severe resentment among the local population, who accused the Jal Shakti Department of not taking care of the water tanks, pipelines and other components of the supply network.
In the fresh incident, the residents said the Sokad-Gowlta Water Supply Scheme had remained non-functional for several days, leaving the village without regular drinking water.
They said that despite repeated requests to employees of the Jal Shakti Department, the problem was not addressed promptly.
“With the supply remaining disrupted, the local residents inspected the pipeline themselves on Monday and found a dead snake lodged inside it,” said Arif Hussain, a local resident.
The presence of the snake triggered concern among residents over the possibility of contamination and the overall hygiene of the water distribution system.
The residents of Gowlta have now urged the department to conduct an immediate inspection of the entire supply network, clean and disinfect the pipeline and ensure that only safe water is supplied to households.
They have also sought an inquiry into how the reptile entered the pipeline and demanded preventive measures, including regular inspection and sanitation of water infrastructure.
Residents said repeated complaints involving contamination or poor maintenance were a major issue in the area and the concerned authority should ensure monitoring of drinking-water schemes in the Uri area.

The OpenAI leader who just quit and issued a stark warning about safety says that, like other recent Big Tech defectors, he plans to help solve the problem from the outside.
David Robinson worked at OpenAI for three and a half years and ran transparency for the safety team. In an essay published Saturday in The Atlantic, he said he oversaw the company's "preparedness framework" and the writing of a slew of safety reports.
"Perhaps I should have stayed and fought for fundamental shifts in our staffing and culture, but in practice, my colleagues and I were so busy sprinting that we seldom had the chance to consider big changes, much less to actually make them," he wrote.
"That's why I concluded that stronger incentives for safety — coming from outside the company — are a big part of getting this right."
Robinson said he hired a PR firm, Spitfire Strategies, to help him with the public attention he'll receive following his departure. "But the decision to speak out is mine alone," he added.
That might be aimed at claims from some that public resignations by workers from companies, including Anthropic and Google, are part of a coordinated effort to spread mistrust of AI and foment government regulation. Elon Musk, for instance, said that former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon's resignation and subsequent public appearances seem "like a setup," which Coxon denied.
In response to Robinson's essay, an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement that the company is working to ensure AI models don't outpace the safety measures they've implemented.
"As our models become more capable, we continue to strengthen our safety and security practices to address the risks we see today while building safety cases to anticipate the risks of future advances," the spokesperson said. "We're making sure our models don't become more capable than we can safely manage and secure, and we pause training or hold back models when we need to slow down."
The spokesperson said OpenAI is taking steps to improve security for its AI models.
"We're making significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, expand our work with third-party evaluators, and improve real-time monitoring so we can detect and respond to concerning behavior earlier in the training process," the spokesperson said.
Robinson's departure comes two months after OpenAI agents escaped their system and hacked another AI company, Hugging Face, in July. OpenAI is not the only company struggling to balance the AI race with calls for guardrails. Last month, a small AI startup said it used Anthropic's Claude to hack into OpenAI's codebase, and The Wall Street Journal reported that Google's Gemini had hacked three companies this spring.
More recently, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said an OpenAI agent hacked a government website in June.
Robinson's PR reps did not respond to an inquiry from Business Insider about his next steps. In The Atlantic, he suggested his game plan is in flux.
"Now I plan to work on the outside, in the hope that I can help more people understand the risks I saw, and strengthen the incentives OpenAI and other firms have to be safer," he wrote. "Like other colleagues, I'm figuring out exactly what that means."

The White House has defended the ad campaign as ‘educational’ and ‘unapologetically patriotic’

Taxpayer-funded ads featuring President Donald Trump are hitting the airwaves with fighter jets, military footage, glowing praise and one striking declaration: “God made Trump.”
CNN obtained 12 of the 13 ads, which the Trump administration calls “public service announcements,” offering a look at a government-funded campaign focused heavily on Trump and his record, the outlet reported Friday.
The spots feature Trump alongside fighter jets and Marine One, tout his military actions in Iran and efforts to arrest Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, and even celebrate the UFC event he hosted on the White House lawn.
The ads range from 15 seconds to three minutes and end with the disclaimer “Paid for by the U.S. Government.” One, titled “God Made Trump,” was shown at a Republican midterm convention in Dallas last month.
In the ad, a narrator declares: “I need somebody with arms strong enough to rustle the deep state. So God made Trump.”
Another spot, titled “Final Battle,” was not among the ads CNN obtained but has also aired as the administration expands the campaign ahead of the November midterm elections.
The campaign has drawn scrutiny over its use of taxpayer money and Trump’s prominent role in the ads. Critics have questioned whether the spots violate federal laws governing government resources, while their timing, just weeks before the midterms, has also raised concerns.
The White House has reportedly allocated $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security for the campaign, with at least $2.5 million already spent on airtime. More ads are expected to run in the weeks ahead.
Trump has reportedly taken a hands-on role in the campaign, personally selecting some of the government-funded ads that will air. Former Trump White House communications director Mike Dubke also suggested the administration may have given CNN access to the ads knowing the network would air clips, effectively giving Trump additional television exposure.
The use of taxpayer money has prompted criticism from lawmakers in both parties.
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said Sunday on CBS’ "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan”: “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves.”
Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.” Raskin’s statement is an allegation and does not represent an established legal finding.
The White House has defended the campaign, telling The Independent in a statement earlier this week: “These public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
“The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country,” the White House added.

Burundi has agreed to join a clutch of other African nations in receiving migrants from other countries deported from the US under Donald Trump’s hardline immigration policy.
However, the authorities in Bujumbura, the country’s economic capital, said Burundi will only accept those not accused of crime or terrorism links, said Nancy Ninette Mutoni, a spokesperson for the country’s president, Évariste Ndayishimiye. Tuesday’s announcement gave no details of numbers, timing or financial details.
Washington has sent so-called “third-country deportees” to some half a dozen African nations as well as many other countries, often where they have no ties, have never been and find themselves detained indefinitely, under opaque deals that Senate Democrats say have cost tens of millions of dollars.
In many cases, deportees had secured legal protections from immigration courts in the US against repatriation. But rights groups say the third-country deals allow the US to circumvent those protections.
Mutoni said preparations were underway to arrange accommodation, living conditions and integration into local communities in Burundi. “Receiving them requires serious planning – where they will stay, what they will eat and how they will live alongside the local population,” she said.
“If they choose to join Burundian citizens and make a valuable contribution to national development, the law will be respected,” she said, regarding potential citizenship.
Burundi aimed to both strengthen diplomatic relations and provide hospitality to people in need, the spokesperson added.
The US state department did not immediately respond to requests for comment while a spokesperson for the Burundi foreign ministry said details of the agreement were not yet available.

One missing Google Docs feature has a pretty easy workaround
If you go a little out of your way, you can make Google Docs much easier on the eyes.
Google Docs is an incredibly convenient application, and it's one that receives constant support and updates. Recently, Google has been releasing more and more new features to the word processor, bringing Gemini-powered content creation tools to Docs — alongside a myriad of other AI updates. However, there's one long-requested feature that has historically escaped (and continues to escape) Google Docs' repertoire.
Google's own word processor has a lot going for it, what with the way it seamlessly bridges between its different host platforms (as opposed to Microsoft Word, which is much clunkier on mobile). Interestingly, though, one of the features missing from Docs exposes a divide between versions of the product. That missing feature is dark mode — which is present on mobile but missing on the web version. Dark mode is a glaring omission on the website version of Google Docs, so it's lucky that there are ways to get around this shortcoming both within and without Google's direct remit.
Official routes to dark mode on Google Docs
Google began to make dark mode available to Docs on mobile in 2020, first with Android and later with the Apple version of the application. In either version, you can find dark mode via Menu > Settings > Theme (or Choose Theme if you're using Android). From there, you can choose Dark, Light or System Default.
Unfortunately, you won't find this range of brightness options on Google Docs' own website. Google hasn't listed an official reason for this favoritism toward the mobile end of its offerings, but it has at least offered a single in-house workaround via Chrome's experimental features. By searching chrome://flags in Chrome, you can access these features and search for "Auto Dark Mode for Web Contents" — but be warned: these features are experimental and could compromise browser data and device security, so you're taking a risk by toggling this feature.
Dark mode on Google Docs via browser extensions
Luckily, there are ways of accessing dark mode without risky experimental toggles. You don't have to wait for the future of Google Docs to access browser extensions today — and that includes Google Docs Dark Mode in the Chrome Web Store (or an alternative for your browser of choice, such as DocsAfterDark on Firefox). It's not the only extension that covers this area, but it's a great choice, and it's easy to get working.
A free download of this browser extension will automatically activate dark mode in Google Docs. However, if you want to change up your dark mode settings (or disable the extension entirely), you'll want to hit the Extensions icon next to the search bar (which looks like a puzzle piece and is in the top-right of the screen). Here, you can not only disable the mod, but you can also select a color theme and tweak individual sepia, contrast, grayscale and brightness settings. In addition, this extension will automatically disable dark mode for prints — so don't worry about toggling it on and off all the time.

Ukraine's intelligence services has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a "new doctrine" of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, president Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to a new policy of airstrikes by Moscow designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, he said.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelensky told Reuters in an interview.
The Kremlin was not available to comment. But the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
Earlier, the Northern Bridge across the Dnipro river in the capital Kyiv was hit during a Russian air attack, mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Emergency services were deployed to the scene and traffic across the bridge from the east to the west bank was suspended following damage to the road surface and the overhead trolleybus cables.
Germany's Merz visits Kyiv as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian cities
German chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv Sunday in a show of support as Russia intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian cities.
The aerial war has intensified, with Moscow menacing cities across Ukraine with hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, while Kyiv has been striking Russia’s oil industry and businesses.
“Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I traveled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us,” Merz wrote on X, noting that Germany’s own security “also depends on the outcome of this war”.
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said Merz would hold talks with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky. Writing on X, Sybiha said the agenda would focus on "strengthening Ukraine, our defence and resilience, and our shared European security.”
Ukraine describes India's proposal for possible ceasefire with Russia as the 'broadest'
Ukraine has described India's proposal for a possible ceasefire with Russia as the "broadest" among four offers received by Kyiv, according to reports.
Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said: “We have four proposals. The broadest one is India’s proposal. We are ready for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, but only in this combination.”
Sybiha was speaking to reporters in Kyiv, according to European Pravda newspaper.
The other proposals were from Turkey, Egypt and the US.
Russia has stockpiled ballistic missiles ahead of winter onslaught, officials warn
Ukrainian officials warn Russia has stockpiled hundreds of ballistic missiles ahead of an expected winter onslaught against electricity and water infrastructure.
Last winter, the worst of the war, Russian strikes left swathes of the country without electricity and heating for days at a time.
Since the summer, Moscow has also begun launching dozens of fast and relatively cheap jet-powered Shahed drones a day at Ukraine, whose air defence teams have struggled to cope because their interceptor drones were too slow to catch them.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had been forced to rely heavily on its fighter aircraft – F-16s and MiGs – to down around 60 per cent of the Russian jet-powered drones, but supplies of 20mm ammunition for the planes were running low.
Kyiv was urgently working on other solutions – including boosting its electronic jamming capabilities, he said. In the second half of October, it would receive the first shipment of small, cheap air defence missiles capable of hitting the new Shaheds.
Last week, Zelensky said Ukraine was developing five models of new interceptor drones capable of downing the jet Shaheds.
Fresh from a meeting with his defence chiefs, he said tests on two of those models showed a modest success rate of around 30 per cent.
"We'll have to scale it," he said. "I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way."
Zelensky says 'not fair to normalise' ties with Russia before return to peace
After the Trump administration invited Vladimir Putin to attend a G20 summit in Miami in December and discussed business deals with Russian envoys, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky urged Washington not to normalise relations with Russia before ensuring a return to peace.
Zelensky said he would be happy to meet Putin for peace talks at the G20, but he warned the US not to believe in "illusions" that Russia would simply end hostilities if it gained control of Donbas.
"It's not fair just to normalise," said Zelensky, dressed in his trademark black T-shirt and military-style jacket.
Any resumption of economic and diplomatic ties with the West had to be in return for Russia ending hostilities, he said: "Because peace is more important than any kind of economy."
While the US has proposed a resumption of trilateral talks in the coming weeks in the UAE, Zelensky noted that an exact date and location for the technical-level conversations had still not been set.
German chancellor arrives in Kyiv
Germany's chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv today, pledging support for Ukraine.
Merz arrived along with the chiefs of German defence companies, in a show of support for president Volodymyr Zelensky amid escalating Russian attacks.
"I travelled to Kyiv today because Ukraine needs all our support in the coming weeks," the German chancellor said.
"If Russia is not stopped, sooner or later its war machine will turn against us,” he said, adding that Ukraine can “count on our help”.
Latvia's pro-Ukraine prime minister wins election
Latvia’s pro-Ukraine prime minister Andris Kulbergs' United List party has won the country’s parliamentary election held yesterday by a wide margin.
The election was held in the shadow of the Russia-Ukraine war, with many voters on edge amid warnings of potential Russian aggression.
Baltic countries have warned for months that Russia is mounting sabotage, cyber and other hybrid attacks across Europe to erode support for Ukraine and sow fear.
But Western officials dismiss concerns that Moscow is capable of launching a direct assault on Nato, of which Latvia is also a member.
Russia has dismissed such accusations as baseless and the result of anti-Russian hysteria.
Ukrainian counteroffensive 'Vivaldi' ongoing in Donbas
Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said a successful Ukrainian counteroffensive, code-named "Vivaldi", had recaptured around 140sqkm (54sqm) of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region and was still ongoing.
Russia has said it must control Donbas in its entirety as a condition for any peace deal.
In recent weeks, US president Donald Trump's administration has sought to revive talks to end the four-year-old conflict – Europe's bloodiest since Second World War.
The US leader last month urged Ukraine to refrain from hitting Russian oil installations, saying that was sending global diesel prices surging.
But Zelensky, speaking as air raid sirens blared outside the gilded halls of the presidential offices, said he had received no indications from Russia that Putin was interested in peace talks, or discussing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.
Putin has issued 'new doctrine' of striking civilian targets in Ukraine, Zelensky says
Ukraine's intelligence services has obtained documents showing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin had issued a "new doctrine" of military attacks on a much broader range of civilian targets ahead of this winter, president Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Ukraine will double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in response to the new policy of airstrikes designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities, but will not target civilians, Zelensky said.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelensky told Reuters in an interview.
"To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation."
The Kremlin was not available to comment on Saturday. But in a statement urging foreign nationals to leave Kyiv, the Russian Foreign Ministry said Moscow would continue to systematically hit targets in what it said were retaliatory strikes for Ukrainian attacks on Russia in recent months.
EU warns situation in Russia-occupied Oleshky is 'appalling'
The situation of civilians in the Russia-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky is “appalling”, the European Union has warned.
"What is happening in Oleshky, Ukraine, is appalling. Civilians are trapped under siege by Russian forces without access to food, medicine, clean water and basic care,” EU commissioner Hadja Lahbib said yesterday.
“This is unacceptable...Russia, as occupying power, has clear obligations under international humanitarian law: civilians must be protected, and humanitarian assistance must be facilitated," she said.
Ukraine seeks missiles and ammunitions for its jets
Poland, Belgium and Spain have agreed to supply 20mm rounds for cannons on Ukraine's F-16 jet fighters, Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Ukraine is anticipating a potential agreement on the supply of "several million" rounds of this ammunition in the near future, Sybiha said, adding that Kyiv also needed at least 300 Patriot interceptor missiles to bring down Russia's ballistic missiles.
The foreign minister said Moscow could be making 120 to 140 ballistic missiles each month, with 600 already in its stocks.

The latest figures were released by the health ministry on Thursday (October 1, 2026). They show that 4,018 people have died from among 8,300 confirmed cases, making up for nearly half of the confirmed cases in what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.

The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm regarding the rapid geographical spread of the virus into new health zones, stretching limited resources.

Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after deadly wildfires
- Published
Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country.
Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday.
Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993.
The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher.
Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa.
Under the law, anyone convicted of deliberately setting fire to forests, woods or fields could face execution.
The death penalty has also been extended to child kidnappings that involve torture, sexual assault or mutilation.
According to news agency AFP, Justice Minister Lotfi Boudjemaa told parliament: "The adoption of the death penalty for these acts is the appropriate legal response to curb these crimes."
The tougher penalties were justified because arson had reached "the level of organised crime", with investigations suggesting links to "foreign parties", Boudjemaa said.
The upper house, the Council of the Nation, will review the law before it is officially ratified by the president.
Investigative journalist Nozha Khelalef has been gathering the names of those believed to have died in the fires from death notices posted by families and information shared by some local authorities.
Her tally, listed on the independent news website Twala, external, puts the death toll at 200.
While Algeria regularly experiences forest fires in the summer, climate change has exacerbated the intensity and severity of recent wildfires in the country.

SBI Mutual Fund, under its various schemes, acquired an additional 1.18 Cr equity shares of Swiggy via open market transactions on Tuesday, the foodtech major informed the bourses earlier today. Business Insider spoke with four investors who found creative ways to use assets they already had — from retirement savings to a paid-off truck — to help finance their first deals.
Lucy Zheng borrowed from her 401(k)
When Lucy Zheng wanted to buy her first rental in 2023, she was cash-strapped and living in California, where prices felt unaffordable. She began looking at cheaper Midwest markets, eventually focusing on Detroit, where she found homes selling for about $60,000.
To fund the purchase, Zheng put in about $15,000 of her own money and borrowed the rest from her 401(k), allowing her to buy the property in cash. Under the rules of her employer-sponsored plan, she could borrow up to $50,000 or 50% of her vested account balance, whichever was less.
For Zheng, the appeal was speed and cost. She said she received the money within a few business days, paid a $75 fee, and closed on the property within two weeks.
She also liked that the interest on the loan went back into her own retirement account. To make the monthly repayments manageable, she temporarily reduced her regular 401(k) contributions so the loan payments roughly replaced what she had already been setting aside from each paycheck.
The major caveat, she noted, was the job-related risk: If she left or lost her job, she would have had to repay the balance immediately.
Mark Kearney used a HELOC to buy his first rental
Florida-based investor Mark Kearney never earned more than $52,000 a year and didn't think real-estate investing was a viable path to wealth, but he was able to use a home equity line of credit, or HELOC, to help fund his first investment property.
A HELOC lets homeowners borrow against the equity in their primary residence — the difference between what the home is worth and what they still owe on it — and it works similarly to a credit card: The lender approves a maximum credit line, and the homeowner can draw from it as needed during a set period.
Kearney said his paid-off home was worth about $200,000 at the time. Rather than borrow close to the maximum amount available, he opened a $30,000 line of credit — about 15% of his home's value — to help purchase a $100,000 single-family house in Virginia's Shenandoah Valley.
After finding a tenant, Kearney said the rental generated about $220 a month in profit. He used some of that cash flow to pay down the HELOC balance and put some into savings.
Kent He took out a home-equity loan to fund a short-term rental
Kent He tapped into the value of his San Diego home using a different product: a home-equity loan.
He and his wife bought their primary residence in 2019. As it appreciated, they built substantial equity and eventually took out a home-equity loan, which provides a fixed amount of cash upfront.
"When we bought, our home was $800,000, but it went up $200,000 in value," he said. "Because we're able to take out 80% of that, we could take out up to $160,000 of home equity to use it towards whatever we wanted." They chose to use the money to invest in a short-term rental.
A home-equity loan is similar to a HELOC in that both products let homeowners tap their home equity, but they distribute the money differently. A home-equity loan provides a lump sum upfront, while a HELOC provides a credit limit that borrowers can draw from during a set period.
Think of your primary home as "another tool in your tool belt," said He. "With all this equity, maybe you can take it out and put it into an investment, as long as the investment makes sense and it fits your risk appetite."
Mike Savage took a loan against his paid-off truck
Mike Savage used a more unconventional asset to fund his first deal: his paid-off truck.
After using retirement savings to relocate his family to Charleston, South Carolina, Savage said he and his wife had little left in the bank, but he owned his truck outright.
When he found a three-bedroom, one-bath house in South Carolina for $49,000, he took out a loan against the truck to cover the roughly $10,000 down payment. It gave him a way to enter the market without waiting years to save the money in cash.
Like borrowing against a home or retirement account, the strategy created another debt obligation tied to an asset he already owned. Still, Savage was determined to find a way into real estate.
His mindset, he said, was: "This is what I want to do. I just have to figure out how to make it happen."

In 2021, the Japanese government set out an ambitious plan for offshore wind: 10 gigawatts (GW) of power generation by 2030 and between 30 and 45 GW by 2040.
Hopes were high. According to one study published in Nature, resource-poor Japan has enough potential wind power to meet all domestic energy demand eight times over.
Throughout 2021, the first auctions for offshore wind sites saw significant interest from Japanese and foreign developers alike, including Mitsubishi Corp. and Norway’s Orsted.
Five years later, progress has been slow.
Only seven projects, with a total of 253.4 megawatts (MW), are operational so far, according to data from the Japan Wind Power Association. Many blame supply chain issues, including higher costs for raw materials. Others point to failures by the government to properly incentivize developers. This is what led Mitsubishi to completely exit the field in mid-2025, abandoning three projects due to construction prices nearly doubling, in a massive blow to Japan’s offshore wind ambitions.
But the loss of momentum for offshore wind is not just a matter of financing.
Concerns from fishers, environmentalists and local communities have also played a role, especially in Tohoku, Hokkaido and along the Sea of Japan coast, where most of Japan’s offshore wind resources lie. These groups have had projects suspended or delayed in Fukui, Shiga and Hokkaido prefectures and are raising concerns about other projects in Fukuoka and Shizuoka prefectures.
Some see a potential role for technology.
In Hokkaido, at two wind farms near eagle habitats, Nvbird bird detection and monitoring systems are already showing potential promise in preventing harm to endangered birds. Another system, AI Bird, developed by the Japan Weather Association, integrates video, infrared data and radar sensors to develop turbine-specific bird maps and automatically adjust operations to reduce conflicts.
As Japan looks to revive its offshore wind plans, addressing issues raised by environmentalists will be key in ensuring the rapid build-out needed to meet climate and energy demand goals.
“Offshore wind power stands as one of the most promising opportunities to harness the country’s vast marine resources and accelerate the expansion of renewable energy,” said Takeshi Matsuki, Japan country manager at the nonprofit Global Wind Energy Council. It is, he added, an opportunity to “demonstrate innovation, collaboration and leadership.”
Offshore wind and net zero
For many experts, the only way Japan can meet both its Paris Agreement and 2050 net-zero plans is by rapidly expanding offshore wind. Moreover, extra capacity might be even more crucial due to the rapid build-out of energy-intensive data centers to power ever-more sophisticated artificial intelligence.
In Tokyo, climate and energy organizations fear that any delays in expanding wind could open the door to the expanded use of fossil fuels, such as coal and natural gas, or controversial sources such as nuclear power, with far more worrying environmental impacts.
“Offshore wind is a key to achieving carbon neutrality and driving a new economy in Japan,” said Mika Ohbayashi, the director of the Tokyo-based Renewable Energy Institute, which is pushing for a more rapid wind expansion.
While countries such as Spain, the United Kingdom and Denmark have become offshore wind hot spots in recent years, Japan faces a unique hurdle. The country’s coastline has become a refuge for species that have lost habitats in other Asian countries, including China, North Korea and Russia, due to pollution, deforestation and industrialization. The issue is not just about how many birds offshore wind can impact, but instead, it’s the impact on the dwindling numbers of several iconic, threatened and endangered species that live in specific habitats.
“In Japan, suitable locations for constructing offshore wind farms often overlap with locations favored by birds,” said Tatsuya Ura, chief researcher with the Wild Bird Society of Japan. “We are concerned that large seabirds, particularly rare species, will be significantly affected.”
Japan’s strong wind currents are mostly along the remote northern and western coasts. And this landscape is dotted with numerous endangered and migratory bird habitats, including those for white-tailed eagles, red-throated loons, sea eagles, streaked shearwaters and ospreys. Local bird lovers, environmentalists and groups like Japan Bird Life and the Wild Bird Society of Japan are concerned that, in a rush to develop wind, bird habitats might be neglected.
“When selecting sites for offshore wind power generation, it is essential to avoid significant impacts on the natural environment,” added Ura. “However, Japan has very little data on marine birds and mammals, raising concerns about how appropriately such site selection can be carried out.”
The initial rush to develop offshore wind was concerning to Ura and other environmentalists, who say they found shortcomings in environmental impact assessments, such as ignored nesting sites or planned construction on breeding areas for several proposed offshore wind projects. Moreover, engagement from the developers of offshore wind has been lacking, environmentalists say.
“Companies do not consult with or negotiate with us about their plans, which means we cannot be involved in project planning from the early stages,” Ura said.
Despite concerns about impacts on specific species, there is consensus that climate change itself is a bigger threat to marine wildlife than wind turbines.
The nonprofit Audubon Society notes that two-thirds of bird species in North America will face extinction unless we tackle climate change. The Wild Bird Society of Japan agrees, stating that they don’t oppose offshore wind as a whole but want to see bird protection taken more seriously by developers.
There are economic concerns at play, too. If a wind farm is built without proper understanding of its impacts on birds and is found to threaten or harm birds, it could be forced to shut down or reduce operations, resulting in higher costs or potential losses.
In fact, that is just what happened to a planned wind farm along the Shiga and Fukui prefectural borders in 2023. A faulty environmental impact assessment — a common problem, according to Ura — ignored that a nearby forest was home to two endangered bird species, golden eagles and mountain hawk-eagles, of which less than 500 and 1,800, respectively, are estimated to still live in Japan. The project ended up being suspended, at a high cost to the developers.
Eurus Energy, one of Japan’s largest utilities, also said by email that they’ve had to cut operations at the Hamasato Offshore Wind Farm in Hokkaido due to multiple bird strike incidents. For several months during migration season, the farm could only operate for a few hours at night, limiting its ability to produce clean energy.
Tech solutions
One tool already being used at two offshore wind farms in Hokkaido last year is Nvbird, which uses AI and thermal imaging to mitigate the risks of bird strikes from offshore wind farms.
So far, the results are hopeful, says Lampros Argyris, business development manager at the Greece-based Nvisionist, the company behind Nvbird.
“Our first systems in Japan were installed onshore in Hokkaido in 2024,” said Argyris. “They have operated reliably, detecting at‑risk birds and triggering proportionate responses to monitor and reduce collision risk while minimizing unnecessary downtime.”
Birds present at those two sites include Steller’s sea eagles, white-tailed sea eagles, red-crowned cranes and Saunders’ gulls, all of which are considered vulnerable or near threatened by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
Nvbird uses cutting-edge sensors, which are adaptable and can gather data from each specific device. Nvbird then analyzes the data via an autonomous local processing AI. This allows it to constantly monitor and detect birds and slow or shut down operations when birds are present.
It’s not a simple process, says Argyris.
“Specific challenges for a bird detection system in Hokkaido are the very harsh weather conditions, heavy snowfall, fog, low temperatures, communication issues and difficulty in accessing sites in winter for maintenance,” said Argyris. To address that, the company is expanding local capacity, making the technology more weather-resilient and looking to train their systems on Japanese datasets.
According to Argyris, Nvbird has “operated reliably, detecting at‑risk birds and triggering proportionate responses to monitor and reduce collision risk while minimizing unnecessary downtime.”
Ura also sees potential for integration of satellite and broader bird monitoring to place turbines away from migration or nesting areas.
“This system … could be useful to some extent in monitoring the occurrence of bird collisions,” said Ura, especially “if it is linked to an emergency shutdown system for the turbines.”
Social acceptance
The developers of AI Bird, the tool created by the Japan Weather Association (JWA), see their tool playing a role in increasing social acceptance of wind power.
“The sustainable development of wind power must account for its environmental footprint, and mitigating harm to birds is crucial,” said Bich Ngoc Ho, an engineer with JWA. “Protecting these species aligns with international conservation commitments and helps maintain public support for renewable energy.”
AI Bird is a collaboration between JWA, academia and the Leadedge Technology corporation and uses high-resolution video and AI detection to identify certain species of flying birds, including white-tailed eagles and Steller’s sea eagles. According to JWA, they’ve achieved a 94% success rate in identification in trials. The system, however, has yet to be deployed at a commercial farm.
“The basic research and development has been completed,” said Ho. “By providing continuous, automated monitoring of bird activity, AI Bird can help operators make informed decisions, such as adjusting turbine operations during peak migration periods or high-risk events.”
Both Nvbird and AI Bird can be added to existing offshore wind farms or ones being planned, making it an additive solution. But Ura sees a problem with this approach — it relies on data, and thus far, Japan’s data on bird migration routes, nesting sites and potential conflicts is lacking. For environmental groups such as Ura’s, merely adding tools like AI Bird and Nvbird to a project located in a sensitive area is not enough.
“With the current method of site selection, it is highly likely that more and more locations will emerge where wind power generation projects and the protection of birds and marine life cannot be compatible,” said Ura. “On the other hand, if site selection involves marine spatial planning and strategic environmental impact assessment, it will be possible to select sites that are compatible.”
In fact, Ura’s organization has created a sensitivity map regarding offshore wind power and birds, which they hope can be the basis for better planning around offshore wind.
The time for proper planning and data gathering is now, because offshore wind in Japan is still in its infancy, with just seven offshore wind farms online producing 253 megawatts (MW) of power, including the two using Nvbird. These tools could limit the threats posed to some of Japan’s most precious and iconic bird species, raising support for the struggling industry.
“AI Bird is a proactive step to balance clean energy goals with environmental conservation,” said Ho. “While no solution is perfect, technologies like AI Bird are a crucial step toward responsible wind energy development.”

Hudson Williams wore this cardigan. Then the Indigenous designer's business went viral
Designer saw online sales spike and the $350 cardigan quickly sold out
When Canadian actor Hudson Williams stepped out wearing a piece by Canadian Indigenous designer Justin Jacob Louis on Wednesday, Louis didn't expect to go viral.
In fact, he nearly forgot it was happening.
The Samson Cree Nation-born designer was spending National Day for Truth and Reconciliation away from work. He was with his family, unplugged and out paddling on the lake.
And then he checked his phone.
"There was, like, a whole bunch of sales and the social media was lighting up and I was just like, 'What is going on? Did something happen?'" he said in an interview with CBC News.
"I realized that, like, every cardigan had sold out. At that time, there was like $12,000 in sales in a matter of an hour. And I was like, 'What the hell?'"
The Heated Rivalry star wore Louis's blue-and-black journey knit cardigan to the Kate Spade New York Global Summit on Women's Mental Health, along with an orange ribbon on his chest marking National Day for Truth and Reconciliation.
For Louis, seeing his work worn that day by a prominent Canadian actor made the moment "pretty special."
"There was intention and genuine interest in supporting us behind it, so that made it more meaningful for me," Louis said.
The cardigan, which costs $350, was designed by Louis, founder and creative director of Section 35 and the Justin Jacob Louis label. And it made its way to Williams as part of a last minute request.
How they connected
Louis said someone from Williams's team initially contacted him by email and over Instagram about the actor's interest in buying the piece — just last weekend.
Shipping it from his warehouse wasn't feasible within the timeframe, but he happened to have the right size at his studio in the Fraser Valley in Chilliwack, B.C.
Someone from Williams's team drove from Vancouver to Louis's studio that Sunday to pick it up.
Months of sales in two days
That choice had an immediate impact on Louis's small business.
The brand gained hundreds of new followers throughout the day. The cardigan sold out and other pieces began selling, too.
Louis estimates the shop did two to three months worth of sales in just two days.
While the brand hadn't planned on restocking the cardigan, the huge surge in demand persuaded Louis to open up pre-orders.
"For an independent small business, it helps out so much," he said. "It's just been kind of a whirlwind."
Design based on a dream
Louis says the design came to him in a dream he had while feeling disconnected and homesick and living about 12 hours from the community where he grew up.
In the dream, he was back at his father's place, walking across the pasture in winter under the night sky, wondering where his ancestors were.
"The stars in the sky lit up and then they turned into eyeballs and looked right at me," Louis said.
"It was just kind of like this reminder that they're always with you wherever you are, no matter how far from home you are."
Louis says Williams messaged him directly to thank him for the cardigan. They've stayed in touch, and the designer says he'd love to work with Williams again.
But for now, he's focused on continuing to design and build his labels.
Here's his advice to other designers and small businesses: stay intentional and true to your values and culture.
"That makes us who we are," he said. "Showcasing the beauty that exists within our communities. I think there's so much talent and the storytelling that comes from our people and our stories. It's what sets us apart. And I think staying true to that is so important."

Kyiv bridge hit in further Russian drone attack as German chancellor makes surprise visit
- Published
A major bridge in Kyiv has been targeted by Russian strikes for the second day in a row, coinciding with a surprise visit from German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's to the city.
The Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge was hit on Sunday morning, a day after it was first struck by drones in an attack that damaged the road surface and led to traffic disruption.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said Sunday's strike had also damaged a heating main, adding that there would be a temporary lack of hot water in the north-eastern Desnyanskyi district as a result.
Major bridges have been targeted in Kyiv over the past four days as Moscow ramps up attacks on critical infrastructure in the capital.
Unverified video footage of Sunday's strike shows cars moving on the bridge as a drone crashes into it before exploding, creating a ball of fire. A cloud of black smoke can be seen rising above the bridge.
Klitschko reported the strike on Telegram, writing: "Hitting the roadway on the North Bridge. Emergency services are on their way to the scene."
As emergency services responded to the incident, Germany's Merz reaffirmed his country's support for Ukraine and pledged further assistance to bolster Ukrainian air defences.
He wrote on X: "Ukraine is facing decisive weeks. That is why I travelled to Kyiv today with the message: You can rely on us.
"Germany's security also depends on the outcome of this war. That is why we are helping out of our own self-interest as well."
The first Russian strike on the Northern Bridge took place on Saturday, injuring two people and damaging the road surface and overhead trolleybus wires, Klitschko said.
Just days before, the Pivdennyi (Southern) Bridge was hit multiple times by Russian drones.
The Pivdennyi and Pivnichnyi bridges across the Dnipro River link the western and eastern parts of the capital and had not been hit before Thursday.
Russia said its drones had hit the two bridges used to transfer Ukrainian troops and military cargo. It also repeated a warning for foreign citizens, including diplomats, to leave Kyiv.
Earlier attacks on the Pivdennyi Bridge prompted Kyiv's defence council to hold a crisis meeting on Friday.
Klitschko warned that the city was now in a "very dramatic situation" as Moscow was battering its "critical infrastructure, logistics, housing" and other key facilities.
Experts say Russian drones are unlikely to bring down the bridges - but repeated attacks will force their closure and risk weakening their structure, making them unusable.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Russia is acting in response to Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, despite the fact that it was Moscow that had first launched such attacks.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Gloucester thrashed a limp Harlequins at Kingsholm to go to the top of the early Prem standings.
The Cherry and Whites ran in eight tries to make it two wins from two in the league and three on the bounce in all competitions.
Gloucester, who named three new signings in their starting line-up including Wales internationals Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake, completely outplayed their opponents in all facets of the match.
Visitors Quins, who handed a debut to England full-back George Furbank, struggled to get a handle on the game from the outset and remain bottom of the table without any points after failing to get on the scoreboard.

A progressive move down the right gave Gloucester fly-half Charlie Atkinson – three days after he signed a new deal committing his long-term future with the club - the opportunity to find Ben Loader free on the left with a pinpoint kick, and the winger dotted down to open the scoring.
