He’s the Oscar Wilde of infectious disease, I’m telling you. Or, like, Damian.
The need-to-know this morning
- Sanofi and Regeneron Pharmaceuticals, the duo behind the hugely successful drug Dupixent, are re-upping their partnership, with the companies announcing an expanded collaboration on a new series of antibodies for immunological diseases.
A journey to witness China’s biotech boom up close
It’s no secret that China’s biotech industry is increasingly setting the pace for science. But STAT’s Jason Mast traveled to Shanghai to get an up-close look at the competition that’s making Americans nervous.
There, at Jefferies’ first life sciences conference in China, executives boasted about developing drugs faster and cheaper than their American counterparts. They walked through their pipelines in English, as local Mandarin-speaking representatives from hulking multinationals like GSK, Merck, and Sanofi roamed the halls, scouting potential prospects between bites of duck sandwiches and dragonfruit.
Chinese-designed drugs now account for roughly half the global pipeline and more than half the potential value of licensing and collaboration deals — and Morgan Stanley projects they could represent 35% of FDA approvals by 2030.
“The best minds will all go there,” one China-focused investment banker told STAT. “Because the big pharma senior R&D guys are there, the general perception is, OK, ‘I might have the infrastructure, CRO work, whatever here but I still want my CSO to be in Kendall Square.’”
HHS wants AI to reinvent clinical trials
HHS announced yesterday that it is launching a new five-year effort to speed up clinical trials by using artificial intelligence, computational modeling, and more flexible study designs that blur the traditional boundaries between trial phases.
The ARPA-H program, dubbed SURPASS, will solicit ideas from teams from the realms of statistics, AI, clinical trial operations, and regulation. Neurodegenerative diseases of particular interest, STAT’s Margaret Manto writes.
The idea is to perhaps gradually replace some human control group data with in silico information — and develop AI systems that could streamline trial operations. HHS also announced initiatives to expand the number of clinical trial sites, build a national research data resource, and let patients contribute their own data. The details — including how much money is behind the effort — remain fuzzy.
Can Eric Cantor fix PhRMA’s woes in Washington?
Eric Cantor, the former House majority leader, is taking over PhRMA at a challenging moment for the drug industry, STAT’s Daniel Payne writes. Among other things, populist anger over medicine prices has scrambled the old political alliances that once made Republicans reliable allies of pharma.
Cantor built a reputation as a savvy GOP strategist before a stunning primary defeat in 2014. Now, he’ll have to navigate President Trump’s push to strongarm drugmakers into lowering prices. Democrats, meanwhile, plan to approach the industry with scrutiny of their own.
Cantor’s bipartisan relationships and dealmaking experience make him well suited to the job, many industry folk say. But there’s a certain irony here. Cantor will be defending drugmakers against a populist backlash — the same force that ended his congressional run.
A Huntington’s patient isn’t fazed by new UniQure data
When UniQure released data this week showing its gene therapy for Huntington’s disease slowed progression of the condition after four years by 44%, down sharply from 75% at three years, its stock tank. At least one patient took another view.
“This isn’t a cure,” advocate Lauren Holder, who is living with early-stage disease, told STAT’s Adam Feuerstein, explaining why she was not discouraged by the latest data on AMT-130. To her, even a few years of substantially slower decline would mean precious additional time with quality of life.
But Holder is far less sanguine about UniQure’s proposed confirmatory study, which would randomize roughly 200 Huntington’s patients to AMT-130 or standard treatment for three years if the gene therapy wins accelerated approval. Holder called that design “not ethical,” arguing that patients assigned to the control group would lose years without an effective treatment while also being unable to join other research.

Hospitals across the State are up against a shortage of drugs for treating non-communicable diseases (NCDs). Several commonly prescribed drugs for blood sugar management (metformin), hypertension (telmasartan), and cholesterol (atorvastatin) are in short supply in hospitals, even as authorities have assured that these will be back in stock within a week.
“It is not as though we are running short on all drugs. But NCD drugs are medicines that people should be taking without fail as a matter of routine and disruptions in its supply can be worrying. We anticipated this shortage last month and moved fast to make local purchases so our patients do not miss the medication,” the medical officer at a family health centre in Thiruvananthapuram said.
“NCD drugs are in short supply but we have not had any issues because our hospital management committee has adequate funds, apart from the substantial resources that our block panchayat sets aside every year for purchasing drugs, for making local purchases. If a substantial amount of drugs has to be purchased, then we float a tender. However, there are also health institutions in smaller panchayats which might be struggling to make local purchase because of insufficient funds,” the superintendent at a taluk hospital in the suburbs said.
Ideally, when a patient registered at the NCD clinic of a particular healthcare institution comes for review, the hospital should have at least 30 days’ stock of the NCD drugs for the patient to take home. In the present situation, many hospitals are not able to ensure that.
Medical officers said this year, the Kerala Medical Services Corporation Limited (KMSCL) released only the drug supplies of the first quarter and that the second quarter release of June did not happen at all which led to the shortage of some drugs, including NCD drugs.
The KMSCL purchases around ₹700-800 crore worth of medicines every year for supplying to around 8,000 government healthcare institutions. In its last procurement exercise, 180 items reportedly received no bids, while suppliers quoted higher prices for another 171 items. This resulted in re-tendering and delays in placing fresh orders.
According to sources, the supply orders given in January-March, for some 18 non-bidder drugs, were cancelled by the new government because the prices quoted were considered far too high, which triggered the present shortage. However, fresh procurement orders have been placed and the supplies are expected to arrive within a week, it was pointed out.
The fact that the KMSCL owes over ₹2,200 crore to various pharma firms, for drugs purchased for hospitals as well as the drugs purchased by hospitals for patients under the Karunya Arogya Suraksha Padhati, has not helped the situation. The massive delays in payment is one of the reasons why many pharma forms do not respond to tenders floated by the KMSCL.
Health Minister K. Muraleedharan had directed that the procurement procedures for the next financial year begin in October itself and that the entire process be completed by the end of December.
He also directed that middlemen be removed from the tender processes and that agencies dealing directly in imported medicines also be allowed to take part in tenders. He said a comprehensive overhaul was under way at the KMSCL
According to sources, there are also efforts to form a consortium with medical service corporations of other States so that common purchase tenders can be floated, which might likely bring prices further down.

Bellingham unlocks new level and potential to be 'one of the greatest'
- Published
Just a year ago, Jude Bellingham's place in the England squad was up in the air. Now he is being talked about as having the potential to be one of football's "greatest of all time".
The Real Madrid man was left out of Thomas Tuchel's Three Lions squad in October 2025 and his place at the World Cup was called into question, with the German head coach saying Bellingham wouldn't get star treatment.
But Bellingham did of course make the squad for the World Cup and was arguably his team's standout performer, finishing as England's top scorer with seven goals as they reached the semi-finals and finished third.
He has already shown that he is world class with starring performances for club and country, but the way he helped England to dismantle Croatia 7-0 in the Nations League on Saturday looked like someone perhaps reaching a new level.
The 23-year-old was instrumental in Rijeka, scoring as well as registering a hat-trick of assists. He even ended the match wearing the captain's armband as England inflicted the heaviest defeat in Croatia's history.
"Bellingham can go on to be one of the greatest players of all time," former Manchester United and Republic of Ireland midfielder Roy Keane said on ITV after the game.
"At this moment in time, he is an amazing footballer. The package – his running power, his delivery, his goal threat. The way he is progressing as a player, I still think there is a lot more to come from him."
Bellingham, recently voted England's player of the year for the second year in a row, is now "nailed on as the 10" for the future, former England defender Matt Upson told BBC Radio 5 Live.
Keane added: "He has been fantastic in possession, but what he does out of possession lifts all these other players.
"If you have a player that good in your team, who is amazing in possession and he's playing for Real Madrid and doing brilliant things, but his work rate off the ball... that will just inspire other players. He is a huge leader for them."
'Push for next level or other teams will catch up'
England's front four will share praise for the way in which they demolished the Croatian backline.
Record goalscorer Harry Kane scored twice, as did Bukayo Saka, with Anthony Gordon scoring and assisting too.
And Kane will be back in the spotlight on Tuesday when he can equal Peter Shilton's all-time England men's appearance record against the Czech Republic at Wembley.
In moving to 89 goals for his country, the 33-year-old again showed how irreplaceable he is for England, but, when he was rested with 20 minutes to go, it was Bellingham who took the captain's armband.
And that highlighted the younger man's importance as a leader within the squad.
Bellingham was also directly involved in more than two goals in an England game for the first time, and he became the first player to record three assists in a game for the Three Lions since Trent Alexander-Arnold against San Marino in November 2021.
It was Bellingham's performance in front of goal that impressed former England striker Ian Wright.
"When Bellingham is on the pitch, he is always driving forward and going again and again," Wright said.
"He was involved in everything. His athleticism, his technical ability, his intensity. He never lets up, the way he gets in the box, he is always in there unmarked. He is always in there."
Bellingham showed every aspect of his game against Croatia and Tuchel was asked by BBC Sport if he had gone to another level.
"Yes, at the moment it seems like it, and you always need to," Tuchel said.
"It's like you can never stand still. You have to develop and you have to push for the next level, otherwise other teams will catch up."
Tuchel, who said the performance was a way to "move on" after the disappointment of England's World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina, said that he "adjusted some things" following the tournament, giving players, including Bellingham, "a lot of responsibility".
Saka was part of the front four and Bellingham assisted his first goal with a high quality cross.
"He was amazing tonight," Saka said of Bellingham.
"He deserved player of the year and he deserved man of the match tonight too. He was special.
"[I'm] happy to play with him and happy to have him in the England team."

In late September 2026, an image spread online claiming to show a herd of wild bison surrounding a hiker. According to a Facebook post (archived) with the image, the wild bison were protecting the "stranded hiker" from a wildfire:
A wild bison herd formed a tight circle around a stranded hiker during a wildfire, and firefighters say the formation was the only reason she wasn't overtaken by the flames.
Rachel had been hiking a remote section of the reserve when the wind shifted without warning, turning a controlled burn nearly six miles away into a fast-moving wildfire cutting off her only route back to the trailhead. She had no cell signal, no clear path around the advancing smoke, and less than twenty minutes before the fire line would reach her position on an open grassy ridge with nowhere to shelter.
That's when the bison found her.
A herd of nearly thirty animals, moving away from the fire themselves, suddenly changed direction as they passed her position, slowing and gathering into a tight defensive ring around her exact spot on the ridge, facing outward, the way herds typically only form when protecting newborn calves from predators.
Rachel said she didn't understand what was happening at first, terrified she was now trapped between fire and a wall of two-thousand-pound animals. But the herd held its formation as the fire's smoke rolled over them, and she realized, watching the ash fall around the massive bodies surrounding her, that their sheer size and the churned, trampled earth beneath the herd was creating a wide buffer of bare ground the flames couldn't easily cross.
The fire burned around the herd's position rather than through it. When air support finally spotted the unusual circular formation from above and redirected a rescue team, they found Rachel unharmed at the center, the herd only breaking formation and moving on once the helicopter's rotors got close enough to disperse them.
Wildlife officials say bison herds have never been documented forming protective circles around a human being before, only around their own young. They have no explanation for why this herd made the exception.
(Facebook user "Wonder Paws")
The above image is fake, and the story accompanying it is not true. The image contains numerous signs it was generated using artificial intelligence. There also was no available evidence of bison legitimately protecting a hiker in this manner.
The first sign that the image was artificially generated was visible in the top portion showing the circle of bison. Several of them are facing outward but also appear to have heads on both sides of their bodies. The hiker is also not visible in the top portion. Furthermore, the bison in the lower portion of the image, showing the alleged rescue, appear to be copy-and-pasted versions of the same animal. Some bison in the lower portion also appear to have heads on both sides of their bodies.
The post appears to have first ben shared by a Facebook account that has a history of posting AI-generated material.
The "photograph" was allegedly taken in August 2025, according to the timestamp at the top left. We looked for evidence of news coverage around that time about a rescue involving a woman named Rachel and found no reporting from trustworthy outlets such as The Associated Press and Reuters. The story in the post also did not contain information that would be included in legitimate reports about such an incident, such as the specific location of the wildfire.
The image and accompanying story are an example of AI slop: low-quality content that's easy to create thanks to AI tools. Such content overwhelms social media feeds, leaving users unsure of what's real and what's not.
For further reading, Snopes has covered numerous examples of AI slop.

It rounds out a fairy-tale story for Wakefield who were relegated in 2023, returned to Super League in the 2025 season, and have now written themselves into the history books as champions.

Wakefield complete the fairy tale with stunning Grand Final win
In front of an electric and sold-out Old Trafford, it was a flawless first 40 from Wakefield Trinity.
They thought they had opened the scoring on the sixth minute when Johnstone went over in the corner. However, on review, it was clear he had been held up then forced into touch.

While it was end-to-end stuff, metres were coming much more easily to Wakefield with their pack proving too strong. That meant every set ended in pressure.
In the 25th minute, a brilliant Jake Trueman pressure kick saw Johnstone jump highest and find Vagana on his shoulder to walk in. Jowitt added the extras once again.
Just over 10 minutes later, Tyson Smoothy went close and then was followed by Tevaga who threw a dummy and then used his power to barrel over. Jowitt stayed perfect with the boot to extend Wakefield's lead further.
With less than two minutes remaining of the opening half, Jack Sinfield used some big-game nous to send over a drop goal to give Wakefield a more than three-score lead, and left Warrington with a mountain to climb at 19-0 down.
There was drama immediately in the second half when Wakefield's Corey Hall was sent to the sin bin for a high shot on Arron Lindop to give Warrington their opportunity to hit back, and they did.
Irwin threw a lovely dummy and then passed to open up the space and with a player advantage, Lindop had all the room to walk over in front of the Warrington faithful. Irwin converted to bring the scoreline to 19-6.
Warrington thought they had gone in again through Matty Ashton just minutes later, but a forward pass ruled out what would have been a score that brought the game right back in the balance
However, with numerical parity restored, it did not take long for Wakefield to get back on top once again and off the back of huge metres from Caleb Hamlin-Uele, they sent it out to Johnstone who used his step to pull off a sensational finish and with a 23-6 lead and 20 minutes to play, the Wakefield end was bouncing.
Warrington would not give up and with eight minutes left on the clock they kept the last tackle alive; Irwin sent over a looping pass and Lindop was in for his second. However, this time Irwin could not convert and the score was 23-10.
However the clock quickly ran away, Wakefield stayed strong, and immortality was theirs as the full-time hooter went and their name was etched onto the Super League trophy.

Allahabad High Court rejects bail pleas of 4 cops in 2021 custodial death case
The Allahabad High Court has rejected bail pleas of four UP Police personnel accused in the custodial death of Jaunpur man Krishna Kumar Yadav in 2021. The order underscores the gravity of the CBI's murder case and pushes the trial towards a quicker conclusion.
The Allahabad High Court has rejected the bail pleas of four Uttar Pradesh police personnel accused in the 2021 custodial death of Krishna Kumar Yadav, also known as Pujari, in Jaunpur district.
In its order dated September 30, the court cited the CBI chargesheet, which alleged that the policemen caused grievous injuries to Yadav to extract a confession and then murdered him by inflicting injuries sufficient to cause his death.
Justice Samit Gopal also took note of the Supreme Court's March 12, 2024 order cancelling bail granted to co-accused Jitendra Singh.
The top court had observed that the case involved allegations of custodial death against a police officer and that a stricter approach was needed while considering bail. It had also noted the gravity of the charge under Section 302 of the IPC and directed the accused to surrender before the CBI court.
The four accused whose bail applications were rejected are Jaysheel Tiwari, Ramkrit Yadav, Raj Kumar Verma and Angad Prasad Chaudhary. According to the CBI, false records were also created to show Yadav's death as an accident or an assault by unknown persons, instead of physical torture in police custody.
The agency filed a chargesheet against 11 police personnel after an FIR was lodged on February 12, 2021 at Baksha village in Jaunpur district under Sections 302, 34, 120-B and other provisions of the IPC. The Special CBI Judge in Lucknow later framed charges on September 18, 2024.
As per the FIR, Krishna Kumar Yadav was taken from his house at around 3 am on February 11, 2021 by a Special Operation Group team and later by the Baksa SHO along with other police personnel. A relative alleged in the FIR that Krishna was unable to stand and shouted to his mother to save him, saying the police would kill him.
The family was later informed that he had died in police custody. On September 8, 2021, a division bench of the high court transferred the investigation to the CBI, which then registered its own FIR and filed a chargesheet against 11 policemen.
The CBI relied on the opinion of an AIIMS-Delhi medical board, which said the victim had suffered multiple blunt-force injuries and that the cause of death was shock caused by the cumulative effect of those injuries.

On July 15, Raj Rani, 52, an ASHA worker in Yamunagar, Haryana had just completed her tasks for the day when she felt a throbbing pain in her left arm and in the middle of her chin. Since this pain had persisted for a few days, she went to the Community Health Centre (CHC) in Vyaspur to get an electrocardiogram (ECG) done.
The Additional Senior Medical Officer at the centre, Gunjeet Singh, saw the results of the ECG, gave her a dose of drugs including blood thinners and clotbusters, called a ‘loading dose’, and asked her to rush to the district hospital at Ambala Cantonment, two hours away, for further treatment.
Raj Rani had single-vessel disease, with a major coronary artery blocked. “At the district hospital, they scheduled my angioplasty the next day and I got one stent in my heart,” said Raj Rani. “I told my doctors to give me good treatment so I could resume my work as an ASHA. They reassured me that I would be able to do my duties, because I was lucky: I came in time,” she said.
Had this happened even two months ago, Raj Rani would not have received the diagnosis that would have led to quick treatment. Even though the Vyaspur CHC had an ECG machine, there was no technician to conduct it and while the medical officers could interpret the results, they were not very confident.
What changed
On May 29 this year, the Haryana government tied up with Sunfox Technologies, a health-tech startup, as part of Public-Private Partnership (PPP), to set up a tele-ECG network called Spandan One. Each medical centre in Haryana received a tele-ECG device that connects to smartphone and tablets, can be operated by frontline workers and gives a clinician-reviewed result in less than three minutes.
To date, nearly 600 government health facilities including primary health centres (PHCs), CHCs, sub-divisional hospitals and district hospitals have been equipped by a tele-ECG device along with training in using it. As of September 17, 33,854 ECG tests were conducted; 9,287 ECGs were abnormal and 1,342 critical cases were detected according to the Spandan dashboard.
In the remote Ranjitpur PHC in Yamunagar district, there is a steady increase in the footfall of patients due to the tele-ECG service available. “This is a new building we started using just six months ago; there is no fixed nurse or staff or even furniture,” said Varun Singh, medical officer who has been running the centre with staff on deputation and through borrowed furniture from other centres. “Ever since we got the tele-ECG, people have been coming to the centre asking for it,” he said.
One recent morning, Ram Saran, 75, come to the PHC with his son Mangaram to get his reports examined by Dr. Singh. Mr. Saran had been experiencing a feeling of his heart racing and breathlessness for many months. He had gotten an ECG and blood tests for ₹1200 at a private hospital at Vyaspur but wanted confirmation from the government doctor. The nursing officer at the PHC put the electrodes on Mr. Saran and an ECG graph formed in the tablet in her hands, with a message that the report was being analysed. Two and half minutes later, the report was ready to be downloaded. Mr. Saran had an ‘abnormal ECG’ and he was asked to consult a cardiologist and a copy of the report was sent to his mobile phone.
Dr. Singh then consulted with Mr. Saran and his son and told them to visit the hospital at Ambala Cant. at the earliest. “Before this initiative, I would not be able to interpret ECGs with this level of sophistication. The patient would need to visit a cardiologist available two hours away and wait a long time in the OPD for the diagnosis,” said Dr. Singh. For patients who are diagnosed with critical ECGs, an alarm goes off in the tablet to draw the attention of the healthcare worker and a prescription is generated so that patients receive life-saving medicines while the referral to a higher centre is being made.
“We never thought that we would get results within a few minutes of doing the ECG. This tele-ECG service is available in all centres in Yamunagar and is available in even other remote locations in the districts. This is a very welcome step,” said Shama Parveen, senior medical officer, Yamunagar CHC.
Primary care matters
Even though PHCs are the first point of contact of medical care for rural patients, they often do not have the necessary equipment or manpower to diagnose and treat heart ailments. A 2024 pre-print that assessed the availability of cardiac care in Vadodara district in Gujarat found only 44.11% of the surveyed PHCs had functional ECGs and employed them where indicated. In most cases patients were simply referred to higher centres for treatment. The time lost due to travel between centres can prove to be fatal for patients.
The impact of Haryana’s initiative has been incredible, said Kuldeep Singh, former Director General, Health Services (DGHS), Haryana who spearheaded the partnership. ECGs and early treatment for heart attacks is now available in rural centres that had earlier not registered a single heart attack due to lack of diagnosis. “We are already witnessing a 20% reduction in deaths in the emergency departments of district hospitals because patients are being stabilised before rushing here,” he said, adding that these are early assessments and more data is still being collected.
After primary care
Once the patient is stabilised with a loading dose, they are sent to higher centres such as district hospitals with Catherisation Labs where angiographies and angioplasties are performed. “Given the geography of Haryana, most patients reach the higher centre within one hour of the diagnosis, saving lives and heart muscles,” said Dr. Singh.
The Haryana government is also in a PPP with private providers to equip and run cath labs in four locations in the State–Panchkula, Gurugram, Faridabad and Ambala Cant. and is planning to soon expand to more locations.
As part of the agreement with the Haryana government, Sunfox Technologies provides equipment, training and on-going support for its tele-ECG system apart from maintaining a live dashboard monitoring cases. “Through the dashboard, we have real-time patient information which has given us rich insights–for example we now know that patients between 30-49 years have a higher incidence of cardiac issues than those over 50 years,” said Rajat Jain, CEO of the startup. Data has also shown that the incidence of critical ECGs among women in the age group of 30-49 is as much as men and greater than men in the age group of 70+, dispelling the belief that men have a greater risk for heart disease than women. “These kinds of insights are very important for policymakers but were never accessible before,” he said.
Challenges in the process
While the project is picking up steam in Haryana, there are some teething issues – many of the centres have to conduct repeat ECGs to get accurate ECG readings if they were not conducted properly the first time. A bump in the road was that the State’s nursing union had issued a diktat stating that nurses should not be conducting the ECGs as the post of ECG technicians has remained vacant in most health centres. The DGHS, however, later issued a letter stating that healthcare workers cannot deny conducting life-saving diagnosis and would face disciplinary action if they failed to do so. There is also the question of what happens when the partnership between the government and Sunfox Technologies ends: would the pathway to diagnosis and treatment change or would it have improved by then?
Looking ahead
Making ECGs available at PHCs is a great start but we need to do much more to improve the public health system as a whole to respond well to non-communicable diseases and their complications, said Chetanya Malik, a doctor who practices in Surguja, a remote district in Chattisgarh for the non-profit Sangwari. In Chhattisgarh, an ECG facility is only available at the district hospital, revealing the vastness of the need and the unevenness of primary care provided within the country. Dr. Malik also noted the need for patients to be given support in finding transport and for referrals to higher centres to be seamless to help solve the problem of cardiac emergencies.
India’s public health systems have, for decades now, remained focused on infectious diseases and maternal and child health — both still important, but the time has come to also realign the systems to care for non-communicable diseases. Heart disease alone is estimated to account for nearly 27% of all deaths in India. The need is enormous, and the technology is available. It is time all States implement such programmes, pointed out Dr. Kuldeep Singh.

Puducherry: Seam-bowling all-rounder Suryansh Shedge has been drafted into the India A squad as a replacement for injured Hardik Pandya for the upcoming three-match one-day series against Australia A, starting here on Tuesday.
Hardik, who was named in the squad last month, but subject to fitness clearance, was ruled out after experiencing discomfort in his right calf on September 19. An MRI scan later revealed that he has very mild intramedullary edema, which is equivalent to suffering right medial tibial stress syndrome.
“Yes, Shedge has joined the India A squad as a replacement for injured Hardik. Shedge had a quadriceps injury and was recovering from it at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru,” a source tracking developments told IANS on Sunday.
Shedge, 23, made his international debut during India's T20I tour of Ireland in June this year and featured in the T20I series against England and Zimbabwe, though he’s yet to take a wicket. He also impressed during the India A 50-over tri-series in Sri Lanka in June this year, scoring 147 runs in five matches while chipping in two scalps in 23 overs.
His inclusion in the India A team means Shedge will miss Mumbai's opening Ranji Trophy game against Chandigarh at the Wankhede Stadium, starting on October 11. Middle-order batter Naman Dhir will also miss the 50-over series against Australia A after being drafted into India's T20I squad for the upcoming five-match series against the West Indies as a replacement for Washington Sundar.
Sundar, the off-spin bowling all-rounder who was a member of the Asian Games gold medal winning team in Japan, has been released from the T20I squad to play Ranji Trophy for Tamil Nadu as part of preparation for the Tests against New Zealand, to be played in November.
Ruturaj Gaikwad will lead the India A side in the 50-over matches scheduled to be played on October 6, 9, and 11 respectively. The first one-day match will now begin at 2 PM, with gates opening for fans at 1pm, while the second and three matches will begin at 9am.
Updated India A squad: Ruturaj Gaikwad (captain), Priyansh Arya, Sai Sudharsan, Devdutt Padikkal (vice-captain), Rajat Patidar, Kumar Kushagra (wk), Nishant Sindhu, Vipraj Nigam, Arshin Kulkarni, Arshad Khan, Prabhsimran Singh (wk), Gurjapneet Singh, Yash Thakur, and Suryansh Shedge.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

Shortly after his controversial speech to the United Nations general assembly in September, Donald Trump gathered a dozen like-minded Latin American leaders and boasted that rightwing candidates had won all seven presidential elections held in the region since he began his second term.
“Everybody I’ve endorsed has won,” the US president said in New York to most of the leaders of the Shield of the Americas, an anti-drug cartel coalition of 15 countries governed by the right or far right.
Those electoral victories – and the US takeover of Venezuela after capturing Nicolás Maduro – have left just six Latin American countries under leftwing governments: regional heavyweights Brazil and Mexico, small Uruguay and Guatemala, and the isolated regimes of Cuba and Nicaragua.
On Sunday, Brazilians go to the polls in a presidential election that many believe will determine more than Latin America’s largest country’s fate for the next four years.
Given Mexico’s geographic proximity and unique economic relationship with the US, analysts see Brazil as perhaps the last country in the region still capable of saying “no” to Trump’s whims – something that could change dramatically depending on the election result.
Polls indicate a neck-and-neck race between Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old leftist incumbent who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term, and Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, the far-right senator son of former president Jair Bolsonaro.
“Trump really does take seriously the idea that the Americas should be his back yard,” said Pedro Telles, a professor at the School of International Relations at Brazil’s FGV university.
“Mexico will remain relevant, and its president, Claudia Sheinbaum, is one of the most popular leftwing leaders. But if Flávio wins, it would be a real blow to the left and a major boost to the far-right agenda globally,” added Telles.
“There is a lot at stake,” said Sandra Borda Guzmán, an associate professor of political science at Colombia’s Universidad de los Andes. “Instead of taking the opportunity to expand our region’s autonomy, a far-right victory would align the region unconditionally with the dictates of the US,” she added.
Lula and Bolsonaro differ sharply on the US, including over what has become Trump’s main foreign policy for the region: the so-called “war on drugs” used to justify dozens of airstrikes on boats that have killed more than 230 people and joint operations involving US military personnel on land.
While Bolsonaro has pledged to join the Shield of the Americas and to follow an “iron fist” approach to crime, Lula has raised concerns about sovereignty and said it is “sad to see the inferiority complex of Latin American presidents” who are part of the Trump-created coalition.
Lula and Trump’s relationship has swung between not speaking and public displays of warmth, but it is currently at a low point, with the Brazilian president and Democratic members of the US Congress accusing Washington of trying to interfere in Bolsonaro’s favour.
“Brazil is a big prize,” said Michael Shifter, adjunct professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service, adding that amid endless conflicts in Iran, Ukraine and Israel-Palestine, “US foreign policy is going very badly in the rest of the world.”
A victory for Bolsonaro in Brazil, he said, would be used “triumphantly” by Trump for producing an “almost completely aligned region”.
At the latest Shield of the Americas meeting, Trump made clear that it was not all about security. The US president also referred to the “tremendous natural wealth” of Latin American countries, which he said could not “be taken over by hostile outside powers” – widely understood as a reference to China.
Privileged access to Brazil’s rare earths and critical minerals was one of the conditions Washington imposed in exchange for not applying tariffs, which Lula rejected. Bolsonaro, on the other hand, has offered those natural resources as the “solution” to help the US “break its dependence on China”.
“Democracy is also kind of on the line here,” added Shifter, noting that Bolsonaro was only running because his father cannot – Jair Bolsonaro is under house arrest after being convicted of attempting a coup to overturn his defeat by Lula in the 2022 election.
“So it’s not just a question of one more country moving to the right, but of a right that has a very problematic relationship with democracy,” he said.
As in recent elections across Latin America, the race includes other candidates but is polarised between two leading candidates. Lula and Bolsonaro have alternated as frontrunners in the final stretch, making the outcome unpredictable; if neither wins 50% plus one of the votes, there will be a runoff on 25 October.
Bolsonaro’s only previous bid for an executive role in government ended ignominiously when he took fourth place in Rio’s 2016 mayoral race. But analysts say there are several reasons why a congressman best known for his family name and corruption allegations – some shelved, others still under investigation – has emerged as a serious challenger to a three-time president.
Unemployment, poverty and inflation have fallen, and average incomes have risen, but so has household debt – something many attribute to online betting, which the older Bolsonaro left unregulated and Lula banned days before the vote.
The incumbent’s campaign has also been hit by corruption allegations – still under investigation – involving his son and a former aide, while a scandal involving supreme court justices with no connection to Lula may have rubbed off on the president.
Many therefore see Bolsonaro’s support as coming both from a simple transfer of his father’s voter base and from an anti-Lula vote.
“I’m going to vote for Flávio, but not because I think he’s the best option,” said Bruna Arguello, 34, a businesswoman from Santana de Parnaíba, whose first choice would be Ronaldo Caiado, a far-right former governor of Goiás, polling at 4%. “Unfortunately, he has no chance of winning, so I’m going with Flávio so we can get Lula out,” she said.
Actor Docy Moreira, 59, will vote for Lula. In 2018, she was so dismayed by Jair Bolsonaro’s election that she decided to leave her home town of Belo Horizonte, where two-thirds of voters backed the far-right leader. “I couldn’t understand how people, including the vast majority of my family, were choosing so much violence and authoritarianism,” she said.
She Googled which cities had given Bolsonaro the lowest share of the vote, chose one about 1,550 miles away and moved north to Luís Correia, in Piauí.
She eventually returned home, and most of her family will now vote for Bolsonaro’s son. Still, Moreira remains confident Lula will win.
“If not, it will be devastating, but I’m not going to move again. I’m stronger now. I’ve learned that I can find refuge within myself,” said Moreira.

Apple says it is changing its macOS privacy settings to stop third-party app developers from misusing them to access message histories.
Friday’s announcement comes two weeks after tech columnist Jason Aten said that Meta’s new general-purpose AI agent Muse sent him an unsolicited notification referencing a thread between him and a co-worker over Apple Messages. Aten said he never granted Muse permissions to read his messages and had assumed they were off-limits. Social media last week blew up with masses of people who agreed and said the incident showed that AI assistants given access to calendars, emails, messages, shopping accounts, and other resources are akin to a skill saw or other power tool. While potentially useful, they can do real damage if not used carefully.
He said/she said
Meta CTO David Singleton joined the fray with a rebuttal that appeared solid. For Muse to access Apple Messages, a user must manually give it two privileges. One is full-disk access, a macOS system-level permission. The other is to enable a Messages connector setting in Muse.
“The Messages integration in the Muse Mac app is opt in,” Singleton said. “Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”
Singleton’s implication was clear. Muse could have read Aten’s Messages communications only if he had enabled both settings, and if so, the columnist had only himself—and certainly not Meta—to blame.
Earlier this week, I spoke to macOS security expert Patrick Wardle, who questioned Singleton’s denial. His reasoning: “From a technical point of view, with FDA (full-disk access), any (non-root file), is readable, browsing history, browser cookies, chats, etc etc etc.” I asked Meta how Muse couldn’t read messages when the app had full disk access, while every other app with that privilege could. Meta PR’s only response was to requote Singleton saying: “The Messages integration in the Muse Mac App is opt-in. Your Muse can only read Messages content if macOS system-level Full Disk Access is granted and the Messages connector is enabled.”

A major political row has erupted in Kerala following remarks made by a former legislator during an extended committee meeting, describing Malappuram district as a hotbed of communal and fundamentalist elements. The comments have drawn sharp criticism and sparked outrage, with concerns raised regarding political motives and stances on secularism. The development follows recent election setbacks and committee discussions held across districts. Critics and political figures have questioned the targeting of a minority-dominated district, while public reactions continue to surface across social media platforms, leading to wider debate within the state.
Scheduled Caste devotees entered a temple in Kallakurichi, Tamil Nadu, under police protection, ending a 50-year-long exclusion. Police personnel broke open the temple lock to permit entry and over 50 cops were deployed to prevent any clashes or untoward incidents as tensions arose. Adhidravidar devotees offered prayers after decades of denial. The temple had been under private maintenance for 50 years before the government assumed control two years ago, though local villagers previously restricted Dalit community members to worshipping at the gates.
Dangerous bike stunts performed late at night in a prime area of Chennai have triggered fear on the roads. The incidents, reported from the Valluvar Kottam stretch in the centre of the city, posed serious risks to motorists and two-wheeler riders. While three youths have been apprehended, police teams have launched a manhunt to identify and track down others involved in performing the illegal stunts. Questions have also emerged over the absence of traffic police personnel at the spot when the stunts occurred.
The Bharatiya Janata Party has launched a sharp attack on the Congress leadership over its silence regarding hero pilot Captain Smith. The party questioned the absence of any statements or posts from Sonia Gandhi and Rahul Gandhi praising the pilot's bravery, while leaders internationally, including the Prime Minister of India, have commended his actions in saving lives. The ruling party alleged that the principal opposition's stance is driven by vote bank considerations and pointed to previous statements regarding Gaza and historical terror incidents. A formal response from the Congress leadership on the allegations is awaited as political reactions continue to unfold.
A massive protest march unfolded in Mumbai on October 4, led by Uddhav Thackeray and Raj Thackeray, demanding the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Opposition parties, including the Congress and the Nationalist Congress Party Sharad Pawar faction, joined the demonstration after personal invitations from the Thackeray brothers. Senior leaders, including Vijay Wadettiwar, Balasaheb Thorat, and Jayant Patil, participated in the united stir despite past political differences. The march commenced from Metro Cinema and moved toward the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation headquarters, drawing large crowds of party workers and unaffiliated citizens, including youth from Mumbai, Thane, and Navi Mumbai. Demonstrators carried the Indian national flag rather than party banners, holding placards, slogans, and caricatures targeting the Election Commission over concerns regarding electoral transparency, logical discrepancies, and the alleged deletion of votes.

The Bharatiya Janata Party on Sunday (October 4, 2026) nominated former Trinamool Congress MP Rukmini Mallick alias Koel Mallick to Rajya Sabha.
Ms. Mallick was elected to the Upper House by Trinamool Congress in April this year. On July 16, 2026, the actor turned politician submitted her resignation to Vice President and chairman of the Upper House C. P. Radhakrishnan.
She is the fourth Trinamool Congress MP who has been nominated to Rajya Sabha by the BJP, after resigning from the Upper House.
Elections for 12 Rajya Sabha seats are scheduled on October 16.
On July 9, 2026, the BJP had nominated three former Trinamool Congress Rajya Sabha MPs Sushmita Dev, Sukhendu Sekhar Ray and Prakash Chik Baraik to the Upper House of Parliament, hours after the three former MPs joined the BJP in Kolkata.
While the three MPs had officially joined the BJP, Ms. Mallick had met BJP leaders including Union Home Minister Amit Shah after she had resigned from Rajya Sabha.
The nomination of former Trinamool Congress MPs to Rajya Sabha has sparked a debate about “Trinamoolisation of the BJP” with a section of party leaders saying that the party was accommodating those who faught against the BJP before the party came to power in WB.

‘Amit Shah ji, where are you’: Oppn slams Centre, Delhi Police as women journalists await FIR in harassment case
Rahul Gandhi, flagged the alleged police “misconduct at Jantar Mantar” on Saturday, asking why the government “fears registering a woman's complaint.”
Opposition leaders from the Indian National Congress and Aam Aadmi Party on Sunday questioned the Centre and Delhi Police after no FIR was registered over sexual harassment claims made by three women journalists. The Opposition maintained that it was their “basic duty” to register an FIR in the matter.
Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, flagged the alleged police “misconduct at Jantar Mantar” during the protests on Saturday, asking why the government “fears registering a woman's complaint.” He further said that the Delhi Police comes under the ministry of home affairs, adding that Union home minister Amit Shah would “have to answer for this.”
Deep Dive
Three women journalists have accused senior Delhi police officers of sexual harassment during the protest against the Election Commission (EC) at Jantar Mantar on Saturday. Their complaints have been forwarded to the crime branch for a detailed probe, the city police said on Sunday.
Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi too launched criticism against Prime Minister Narendra Modi and home minister Shah, saying it was the police's “job to provide security”. Aam Aadmi Party leader Saurabh Bharadwaj, who also joined the protest outside the Parliament Street Police Station where the journalist and her lawyer were present, said “failure” to register the FIR was “not merely a procedural lapse” but could constitute “a punishable offence.”
What have the Opposition leaders said?
Lok Sabha LoP Rahul Gandhi, in a post on X, said, it was the “police's basic duty” to register an FIR in the matter, saying hundreds of journalists had been sitting outside the police station with this demand.
“There are allegations of misconduct with women protesters. Cameras were snatched, journalists were dragged. And this isn't the first time—we've seen video evidence before of police officers engaging in disgusting misconduct with women,” he said, highlighting that hundreds were taken into custody on Saturday during the protest in Delhi.

“Women across Delhi, students, are gripped by fear for their safety, staging satyagraha—but the very police responsible for protecting women are raising hands against them. And a government that fears registering even one woman's complaint—what exactly is it protecting?” he questioned. “Delhi Police comes under the Ministry of Home Affairs. Amit Shah ji, where are you? You have to answer for this,” the Congress leader added.
Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi too said that “no concrete action was taken” in the matter. “. Women engaged in peaceful protests also allege that the police are behaving very indecently with them. The very police whose job it is to provide security is making women feel threatened. From college students to journalists—women are facing insecurity everywhere," she said. “Is this the right way to treat women? If not, then why don't you take notice of it?” she asked, tagging Shah and PM Modi.
AAP leader Bharadwaj said not registering the FIR could constitute a punishable offence “under Section 199(c) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, carrying rigorous imprisonment of 6 months to 2 years, along with fine.”
What has the Delhi Police said?
The Delhi Police acknowledge receiving the complaints from women journalists, and said they had been transferred to Crime Branch “for fair and impartial enquiry.” DCP Neha Yadav the three women had lodged a complaint at around 6 pm on Saturday “alleging manhandling by Delhi Police officers and staff during their detention.”
“Their complaint has been registered, medical examinations have been conducted, and the matter has been referred to the Crime Branch. We request anyone possessing relevant footage to share it with the Crime Branch,” Yadav told ANI news agency. She said AISA and other organisations had staged a protest on October 3 “despite the imposition of Section 163 of the BNSS” in the New Delhi district.

LUDHIANA: Former sarpanch of village Mannewal was shot dead by some unidentified bikers near Ladhowal Bypass on Saturday late evening.
The victim Navjeet Singh Neetu, 57, was driving his Toyota Innova car back home in Krishna Nagar when the incident occurred.
The Dashcam of his car captured the entire incident which the police seized.
It is said that Neetu had gone to visit his land in village Mannewal as per his daily routine.
At night when he was returning a bike borne masked assailants fired multiple gunshots at his car. The sources suggest that the victim sustained nearly 10 bullets.
The victim was rushed to the hospital however could not survive.
ACP West Jatinderpal Singh said that the victim was travelling alone when some bikers shot at him.
The victim suffered multiple gunshots and died at the spot. The police will lodge an FIR after recording the statements of the victim's family.
The police said that land dispute is suspected to be the reason behind the killing of former sarpanch.

Leicester hold off Newcastle for first Prem win
- Published
The Prem
Newcastle (5) 19
Tries: Ene, McGuigan, Jordan Cons: Connon, Henry
Leicester (17) 24
Tries: Moli, Radwan, Hurd Cons: Searle 3 Pens: Searle
Leicester Tigers picked up their first win of the season with a tense and hard-fought victory at Newcastle Red Bulls.
Former Newcastle winger Adam Radwan scored on his return to Kingston Park as the Tigers won for the first time in seven matches in all competitions, following a dismal run which stretches back into last season.
After being edged out by two points in a high-scoring thriller by Saracens six days ago, Leicester had to show their grit and determination to cling on to victory against a Newcastle side who threatened a late comeback.
Newcastle took the lead through Obi Ene's early score but, despite putting in a positive showing, they ultimately came up just short in their first home match of the season.

Ene scored three minutes into his Prem debut after Newcastle moved the ball left. The former Sale winger weaved inside, having collected fly-half Brett Connon's excellent cut-out pass, to dive over for the opener.
But Leicester hit back when hooker Samiuela Moli launched himself over at the back of a driving maul and Billy Searle popped over the conversion to give Tigers a slender advantage.
Gabriel Hamer-Webb had an opportunity to go over for Leicester soon after but was pushed into touch by an excellent try-saving tackle from Christian Wade, before Hamer-Webb made his own outstanding score-stopping challenge as Newcastle's Harrison Obatoyinbo threatened to break clear.
That moment proved to be pivotal as former Newcastle winger Radwan latched on to Freddie Steward's exquisite grubber kick to touch down. After Searle kicked the conversion, the fly-half then added a penalty in front of the sticks.
Newcastle missed two presentable opportunities to score a second try before half-time and the match restarted in a scrappy manner after the break - until Ene was prevented from scoring a second try of the match thanks to a textbook challenge from Leicester replacement Will Wand.
Radwan spurned a good opportunity to score his second, kicking the ball dead when he had a whole half of the field to run into. Leicester were made to pay for their profligacy when George McGuigan's pick-and-go enabled him to drive over from close range to help pull the deficit back to five points.
Leicester got a vital third try of the night when Will Hurd's quick tap let him barrel over, and Searle kicked the conversion to make it a two-score game once more with 12 minutes remaining.
Newcastle carved through Leicester with just under seven minutes left when Ollie Leatherbarrow's bold carry saw him break a tackle as Cameron Jordan went over with Zack Henry adding the extras.
With the clock ticking down, Wade carried Newcastle forward with a trademark burst down the wing, but the home side were eventually guilty of holding on as Leicester gratefully kicked to touch to claim victory.
'We were not accurate enough' - reaction
Newcastle Red Bulls director of rugby Dan McFarland told BBC Radio Newcastle:
"I'm really disappointed, to be honest. It was a game we could have won. Really pleased with the way we approached the game. I thought we were full of effort, full of energy.
"Most importantly, we were full of the endeavour that we wanted to put in, in terms of the way we wanted to play the game.
"Unfortunately, we were not accurate enough in key areas - but that will grow.
"We are trying not to play in a boring way. Today, we weren't where we wanted to be. In the first half, we gave away penalties at set-piece and let them into our 22. I thought we improved in that area as the game went on."
Leicester Tigers head coach Geoff Parling told BBC Radio Leicester:
"Gritty and dogged. Defensively, some good resolve and they're [Newcastle] going to break some teams this year with their quality attack and good speed.
"You go all pre-season and you try to build some real cohesion and you lose a lot of guys in the same position, but no excuses, we've just got to be better. I've got to help those guys to be able to execute in those moments.
"There's loads to improve on. The general feeling in the changing room is disappointment, which is great for me.
"Accuracy in the second half, especially at set-piece, we didn't allow ourselves to build up some pressure."

Djamal Ziane is a three-time league champion – but he does not always feel like it.
This summer, for the second year in a row and for the third time in seven seasons, the Lokomotive Leipzig captain hoisted the trophy into the air having led his team to the title in the Regional League Northeast, the fourth tier of German football.
But the memory is tinged with frustration because, just as in 2025 and 2020, Lokomotive's league title did not lead to promotion.
While the other regional champions in the German fourth division were promoted to the nationwide 3. Liga, "Lok" faced a play-off against a representative of the Regional League Bavaria, Wurzburger Kickers. Ziane scored, but an injury-ravaged Leipzig lost 3-1 on aggregate.
"Euer System ist krank," read a simple protest banner displayed by the 2,000 travelling supporters – "your system is sick".
"It's the worst thing – injury aside – that you can experience as a footballer," Ziane tells BBC Sport.
"Catastrophe doesn't cut it. It doesn't make any sense. If they really wanted to change it, they could do tomorrow."
But it's not that simple.
Germany's football pyramid has a bottleneck.
Beneath the Bundesliga, 2. Bundesliga and 3. Liga, the fourth tier is split into five regional divisions (North, West, Southwest, Northeast and Bavaria), each of which produces a league champion.
So far, so good. But with only four teams being relegated from the 3. Liga each season, the sums don't add up.
An unsatisfactory solution is currently in place: the champions in the West and Southwest go up automatically while a third automatic promotion spot is rotated among the other three leagues in a three-year cycle. The fourth spot is allocated via a play-off between the winners of the remaining two leagues.
One champion always misses out and, increasingly, it's the champion from the Regional League Northeast, covering the territory of the former eastern German Democratic Republic (GDR).
In addition to Lok Leipzig's triple tragedy, former serial GDR Oberliga winners Dynamo Berlin fell short in 2022 and Energie Cottbus drew the short straw in 2023. This season, there is only one eastern German club in the 3. Liga: Hansa Rostock.
The struggles of the regions' football clubs are, to some degree, a result of continuing socio-economic disparities between east and west, which were also reflected in the success of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in recent state elections.
Even in 2026, not one of the 40 leading companies listed on Germany's DAX stock exchange is based in the former east (outside Berlin). Salaries remain lower, unemployment remains higher and the population is older and shrinking as young people move west.
The reason that automatic promotion spots are handed to the champions in the West and Southwest is simply because there are more men's football teams registered in those jurisdictions - because more people live there.
It is an argument that Ziane is tired of hearing.
"In that case, you might as well give us the automatic promotion spot because we attract bigger crowds," he says.
Indeed, the average attendance in the Regional League Northeast last season (3,125) was around twice as high as that in the other leagues. Lok Leipzig themselves had the fourth highest (6,352). More than 11,000 attended the local derby against city rivals Chemie Leipzig.
"Unfortunately, you don't get any points for tradition, crowds and history," says 39-year-old Lok chief executive Toni Wachsmuth, who does not have access to sponsors with the same financial firepower as his counterparts further west.
"The [western] leagues do have better economic foundations but everyone agrees that the current system is nonsense. Everyone needs to compromise but some officials are clearly putting their own interests and positions above the general good of German football."
It comes as little surprise, therefore, that the latest push for change has come from the east, with clubs launching a new campaign in March 2025 with the slogan: "Meister mussen aufsteigen!" – champions must go up!
Their proposal: a reduction from five leagues to four, with the precise geographical borders to be determined anew each season with the help of artificial intelligence, taking into account factors such as distance of travel to away games and attractive derbies.
They call it the compass model. Because it can go in all directions. In return, the Regional League Northeast is prepared to compromise by giving up its emotional attachment to the territory of the former East Germany.
"I want to get away from this east-west debate," says Tommy Haeder, the 35-year-old chief executive of Chemnitzer FC and figurehead of the reform campaign. "We've had a change of generation. Many older officials have retired and been replaced by younger people who don't have this nostalgia for the GDR."
Haeder also emphasises the benefits that a fairer promotion system would bring for German football as a whole, arguing that eastern clubs would be better equipped to continue nurturing youth talent.
"It's not in the interest of talent development when young footballers from Chemnitz are torn away from their homes and families at the age of 10 to join academies in Hamburg, Dortmund or Stuttgart," he tells BBC Sport.
"The compass model is a model in which every region sacrifices a little bit to solve a much bigger problem. We're organised, we have a plan, we've made suggestions. Now it's up to the federations to act."
The campaign has since gained the support of more than 80 clubs across Germany, from east to west and up and down the pyramid.
Union Berlin, who were playing in the fourth tier as recently as the 2000s, became the first Bundesliga club to officially back the initiative, with club president Dirk Zingler saying: "The current set-up contradicts our understanding of sporting competition."
Borussia Dortmund president – and Bundesliga chairman – Hans-Joachim Watzke added his influential voice, stating: "Champions must go up and we think the compass model with four regional leagues is the best option."
Support also has also come from Bournemouth head coach Marco Rose who, drawing on his past as both a player and coach at Lok Leipzig, said: "I know what it's like for clubs trying to work within their means, or lack of means, at that level. Everything is on a knife edge.
"You have to give the clubs and their fans the belief that their efforts and sacrifices will be rewarded with promotion."
Momentum was growing before a key vote at the end of June when, after months of discussions, clubs were finally set to vote on the compass model – but the ballot descended into farce when, at the last minute, the regional federations conducting the vote announced two key changes:
Suddenly, the four new leagues would consist of only 18 teams rather than 20 (thus making the compass model less attractive because 10 more teams would miss out), and a stipulation was added that a majority be reached in each of the five regions for the model to pass.
An overall majority (50.9%) in favour of the compass model was still reached (including 60.9% in the West, 61.5% in the North and 76.3% in the Northeast) but the Southwest voted for an alternative option in which the northeastern league would be dissolved and its clubs reallocated, while the Southwest and West would simply remain the same.
"The move from a functioning system to a complex, insecure and economically riskier model without an obvious benefit doesn't make any sense to me," Robert Lempka, chief executive of Regional League Southwest side FSV Frankfurt told local public broadcaster Hessischer Rundfunk this summer. "I find it unsettling that an untransparent algorithm should decide a club's future."
The Bavarians, meanwhile, voted vaguely for "further talks", with Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) President Christoph Kern telling Munich's Abendzeitung newspaper in August: "We've gathered our clubs together on several occasions and none of the suggested models have majority support. I'm not prepared to simply give up the Regional League Bavaria like that."
For Haeder in Chemnitz, the vote was "an absolute catastrophe – completely amateurish". And he's not alone.
This season, protests have erupted across German football. In the Regional League Northeast, almost every game has begun with a delay as players have simply refused to play for the first minute.
On the opening day, Lok Leipzig supporters, their team still stranded in the same division, threw hundreds of plastic trophies on to the pitch, symbolising the worthlessness of their club's back-to-back titles.
Down in Bavaria, Bayern Munich's ultras attended a reserve team game in the regional league and produced an intricate choreography criticising the Bavarian Football Federation (BFV) for what they perceive to be an unco-operative stance.
"You've taken us for fools long enough," read a banner beneath a display depicting BFV officials using a magnet to pull a compass needle towards them. The ultras then set off red pyrotechnics which turned the compass needle back in the direction of the fans.
And before the international break, fans of clubs across the Bundesliga used their platform to call for reform with co-ordinated banners reading: "Clubs and fans betrayed! Champions must go up! Compass model now!"
The compass, it would appear, may finally be pointing towards a resolution after the German Football Federation (DFB) announced the convening of an extraordinary general meeting on 18 December.
"[The issue] must be resolved," said President Bernd Neuendorf. "The compass model received the most votes and offers the best chance for a concentration of elite performance and therefore better development of talent."
Any changes would only be implemented in the 2028-29 season – too late for Ziane who, now 34, has embarked on his 13th season with Lok Leipzig. Back-to-back champions, but still in the fourth division.
"You can never completely get over it because, at our level, the 3. Liga is probably the pinnacle. Promotion with my hometown club would have been the most wonderful thing in the world for me," he says before heading out for training.
"It's a shame that we have to force ourselves to remember what we've achieved. It's so hard to win this league and we did it twice in a row! You can't take that for granted."

Retired rugby league star Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles has been given a tribute prior to the NRL grand final.
Both men were diagnosed with motor neuron disease this year.
Australian artists Amy Shark, Dave Gleeson and Phil Jamieson performed while Arrow and Charles completed a lap of the ground.
Tens of thousands of fans have united by making the arrow gesture during a moving pre-grand final lap by the NRL's Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles, who were both diagnosed with motor neuron disease this year.
Arrow, who had the month of July dedicated to him when NRL players would make the arrow gesture after scoring, was forced into retirement following his diagnosis, rocking the Australian sporting community.
The pair were driven around Stadium Australia before the NRL grand final, with Australian music artists Amy Shark, Dave Gleeson and Phil Jamison performing.
Shark began with a rendition of You'll Never Walk Alone as Arrow and Charles began their lap.
Thousands in the crowd did the arrow gesture as they drove past, as prompted in a pre-packaged video by NRL Hall of Fame member Ray Warren.
"Jai's fight against MMD has reached far beyond the football field," Warren said.
"He has and continues to inspire others facing difficult times.
"The way Jai has faced this challenge with his head held high is showing us what true bravery really looks like.
"This is what our game is about. Strength, courage, community and making sure when life gets tough someone is there beside you."
After Shark sang You'll Never Walk Alone, Newcastle legend Dave Gleeson walked onto Stadium Australia to sing What's Up? by 4 Non Blondes.
Grinspoon's Phil Jamieson then joined Shark and Gleeson to end the tribute with the famous Tina Turner rugby league anthem, The Best.
The NRL has pledged $1 million, which was to be spent on pre-match entertainment, to help underprivileged kids who can not afford to play rugby league play rugby league," Australian Rugby League Commission chair Peter V'Landys told the ABC this week.
