Wolverine sits comfortably as my favorite Marvel hero right beside Spider-Man. I grew up with Hugh Jackman’s portrayal of Wolverine in the X-Men movies, along with Steve Blum and Cal Dodd’s masterful interpretation of the ol’ canucklehead across various Marvel media.
So, when Insomniac announced Marvel’s Wolverine back in September 2021 at the PlayStation Showcase, I was pumped. After countless hours swinging through the Marvel’s Spider-Man series with both Peter and Miles, I was eager to see their take on Logan, since he’s an incredibly complex character.
I expected Insomniac to take a similar approach to the 2009 X-Men Origins: Wolverine tie-in game with the combat. The story was messy, sure, but the combat was visceral, brutal, and perfectly showcased Wolverine’s violent power fantasy, which is exactly why I think it’s still an enjoyable game.
After spending 25 hours with it, I can confirm that Marvel’s Wolverine is a solid action game in my review. It’s nowhere near as bad as some of the criticism would have you believe, but it’s also far from the ultimate Wolverine game that many, including me, were hoping for. It has plenty going for it, but significant flaws keep it from reaching the heights of Insomniac’s Spider-Man series.
Wolverine’s Origin Gets More Complicated than It Needs to Be
Insomniac takes some big creative swings with the story in Marvel’s Wolverine, and not all of it lands. On the surface, Logan is dealing with amnesia, and he needs help to regain his memories and remember who he was before he became a weapon, while doing what he does best, a.k.a. tearing enemies to shreds.
You have your usual Marvel MacGuffin, the Helix Engine, a device capable of activating dormant mutants. Nathaniel Essex wants the engine to grow the mutant population and build a better future for his own kind.
Of course, in the middle of it all, there’s Bolivar Trask, an anti-mutant figurehead, who kidnaps mutants with the Reavers, deploys Sentinels, and delivers the usual “the world isn’t big enough for the both of us” brand of villainy.
That’s what the first act of Marvel’s Wolverine deals with. In the second act, you start to uncover Logan’s true origins, and it’s a far cry from Barry Windsor-Smith’s Weapon X comic, changing how Wolverine becomes the killing machine. The Helix Engine becomes priority number one for endgame villains like Lady Deathstrike and Essex.
However, the final act takes a nosedive, turning a solo Wolverine outing into an X-Men setup game. I’ll slice into spoilers now: Insomniac draws inspiration from comic writer Chris Claremont’s unused idea, bringing popular X-Men villain Apocalypse into the fray and making him the mastermind behind Logan’s adamantium-infused origin.
It’s incredibly bold, but doesn’t quite land for a Wolverine-focused game. The writing falls flat when the game introduces these larger-than-life elements. By the end, the story is revealed to be built on a centuries-long conflict between the Phoenix Force, Jean’s ultimate avatar, and Apocalypse’s Horseman of Death, which in this case is Wolverine.
It’s anything but grounded, but rich in spectacle, which, to me, doesn’t quite fit for an introductory Wolverine story. As the narrative grows ambitious, it loses much of the personal charm and intimacy that made the first act so compelling.
The balance between Logan’s personal stakes and the overarching X-Men story never quite comes together. But thanks to incredible performances from Liam McIntyre, Krizia Bajos, and Troy Baker, I remained hooked until the very end, even as I found myself conflicted by some of Insomniac’s narrative choices.
Had Insomniac taken a more grounded route like Larry Hama’s Wolverine stories in Madripoor, the story might have been better executed. I’m a sucker for character studies and less interested in a ‘jingling keys’ approach or endless fan service, so I was more invested in Logan’s personal journey before the bombastic spectacle took over.
However, I did appreciate that Insomniac didn’t play it safe with the story, even if its ambitious direction doesn’t always land.
Combat Is Where the Ol’ Canucklehead Gets Mean
What Insomniac misses with the story of Marvel’s Wolverine, they make up for in the combat. The combat system is ridiculously good, and very reminiscent of the X-Men Origins: Wolverine game. It’s brutal, fluid, responsive, and gives you multiple ways to slice through enemies.
The primary attacks with Square and Triangle start a combo, while parrying staggers enemies to perform a satisfying Barrage, which you can use to build your Rage Tier or restore health, depending on the skills you have unlocked.
The Skill Tree, while not as extensive, still works wonders in combat, giving you opportunities to implement many Special Techniques. “Overwhelm” and “Tornado Spin” were by far my favorite Special Techniques, offering a quick way to isolate enemies while controlling entire crowds with adamantium-coated swirls.
The most enjoyable part of Wolverine’s combat is building up to Rage Tier 3, which bathes the screen in greyscale and lets Logan go completely feral, ripping the hands and legs off Reavers and the Hand with continuous Critical Strikes.
Seeing chunks of Logan get blown off with Insomniac’s new blood technology was genuinely impressive, especially when it feeds directly into his Last Stand ability at Rage Tier 2, allowing him to recover from a fatal blow in exchange for his Rage Tier bars.
Adaptations and passive buffs kept combat fresh, as I built Logan to generate and maintain his Rage mode longer, unlocking AP by completing Nightmare Trials and finding Whisky Bottles in Marvel’s Wolverine.
Playing on “The Best There Is” difficulty is no joke, especially when multiple enemies or mini-bosses gang up on you. But it also pushes the combat beyond run-of-the-mill button mashing, forcing you to use every shiny trick in Wolverine’s adamantium arsenal.
Madripoor and Japan Are Gorgeous Wastes of Space
Every location in Marvel’s Wolverine is stunning, from Madripoor to Japan and Canada. The problem is that these beautiful hubs feel strangely hollow when there’s so little opportunity to explore them. You’re largely confined to dense streets and the occasional rooftop, following a one-note linear path through environments that feel like they were built to be explored more freely.
For the majority of my playthrough, I stopped to appreciate the world and capture clicks with Insomniac’s vastly updated Photo Mode, which only made me more frustrated that these locations weren’t explorable.
I’m not saying they should be as open as New York in the Marvel’s Spider-Man series. But given how Logan can jump, slide, and launch from one building to another, these hubs feel criminally wasted, with little to discover beyond Material Crates and Whisky Bottles.
This brings me to another problem with the Marvel’s Wolverine world design: Logan’s smooth traversal is extremely underutilized. You have Launch Points throughout Madripoor and Japan, yet you can’t use them because you have to stick to a one-note world design. Moreover, Logan can only climb certain surfaces with his claws, which makes the “exploration” all the more limited.
Sliding across rooftops, leaping from building to building via Launch Points, and using ziplines to traverse densely packed areas are some of Wolverine’s most enjoyable movement mechanics. But invisible walls and level boundaries will get in your way too often.
Just Follow the White Paint, Bub
The most controversial element of Marvel’s Wolverine is how far it takes handholding players with white cloth/paint. What makes it even more egregious is that it’s a linear game with only a handful of exploration opportunities, which makes the white markers stick out like a sore thumb. Meanwhile, the blue scent trail isn’t nearly as bad.
Sections with white paint/cloth markings where there’s nowhere to go but forward, especially during the traversal Nightmare Challenges, feel like Insomniac is afraid to let players off the hook. There’s a fine line between helpful guidance and excessive handholding, and Insomniac paints that line with white markings so you don’t lose track.
On the other hand, the blue scent trails or the Marvel’s Wolverine “fart gas trail” represent Logan’s feral senses, guiding him to characters during specific story sections or collectibles such as Whisky Bottles.
It’s still handholding, yes, but they aren’t as intrusive as the white paint/cloth markers, and only appear in a handful of sections. Thankfully, Insomniac reduced their opacity in a quick hotfix, and they now look the way they should have from launch.
Additionally, Marvel’s Wolverine is rated 18, so it’s targeted towards adults and mature audiences. Yet, the handholding made me feel like I wouldn’t know where to go without it. I’d have much preferred they remove the white markings and relegated Logan’s senses to R3 on the controller.
Despite everything, the blue scent trails didn’t bother me as much as the white cloth/paint, since it only appears when Logan’s picking up someone’s scent or a collectible is nearby. It’s a linear experience, yet the game feels the need to guide you every step of the way.
Liam McIntyre Carries Wolverine with a Standout Performance
Despite all the game’s faults, Liam McIntyre’s performance as Wolverine is nothing short of spectacular. Logan is an inherently complex character, balancing a deeply human vulnerability with the violence and rage that have defined him for decades, making him no easy character to portray.
McIntyre handles that duality remarkably well, delivering a nuanced performance that captures Logan’s humanity and his yearning for belonging without ever losing sight of the monster lurking beneath the surface.
Even though I’m not a fan of Logan and Jean as a couple (I’m more of a Logan and Mariko shipper), McIntyre and Bajos have incredible chemistry from the moment they meet, making their relationship worth rooting for.
Not much needs to be said about Troy Baker’s performance as Mister Sinister; he’s incredible as always. However, Brett Gipson’s portrayal of Sabretooth surprised me. He’s so compelling, even while tearing Logan apart, that I’m excited to see him return in a Wolverine sequel, if there is one, or even the X-Men game.
For all my qualms with the game, its performances remain a standout, with Liam McIntyre’s portrayal of Wolverine ranking alongside Yuri Lowenthal’s iconic performance as Peter Parker in Insomniac’s Spider-Man series.
Performance: An Adamantium-Smooth Frame Rate on My Base PS5
Marvel’s Wolverine is easily Insomniac’s best-looking and best-performing game yet, and it runs like a mutant on a mission. Across my 22-hour playthrough on the base PS5 (disc edition), the game held a steady 60fps in its default “Performance” mode, complete with ray-traced reflections throughout all four unique areas.
The game looks sharp, even on my 1080p TV, and I could see every pore on Logan’s face during close-up shots. Thanks to the PS5’s SSD, getting back into the bloody action took no longer than 2 seconds. Mission replays and Nightmare Challenges loaded as quickly as Wolverine unsheathes his claws, so the performance definitely doesn’t end up with the game’s woes.
However, I did run into one hilarious bug where Logan glitched out of the map while I opened Photo Mode to capture a shot of the Animated Suit. I’d hardly call it a performance issue. The blood and gore looked great on the base PS5, and I hope Insomniac brings the game’s detailed suit damage to Marvel’s Spider-Man 3.
Verdict: Bub, Even Your Healing Factor Can’t Fix This One
Marvel’s Wolverine isn’t a bad egg in Insomniac’s basket full of good eggs. It’s more of a cracked one. The developers still cooked a dish with it, but it fails to be as delicious as their previous web-filled offerings. The combat feels fluid and crunchy, Liam McIntyre and Krizia Bajos deliver phenomenal performances as Logan and Jean, the set pieces dazzle, and the game looks stunning on a base PS5.
However, the ambitious scale of the story, which is clearly a setup for the X-Men game, limited exploration opportunities within the gorgeous locations, and the egregious use of white paint and cloth, despite the mission design being linear, bog it down significantly. I had a good time with it, and I reckon most will, but maybe not at the premium $70 price point.
If you’re a fan of the character and want a brutal, visceral 15–20-hour standard action experience with excellent combat that feels surprisingly reminiscent of 2000s PC gaming, Marvel’s Wolverine will be right up your alley.
But if you’re looking for something that builds upon what Insomniac accomplished with Spider-Man, you might want to slice this one off your wishlist for now and wait for a sale. Wolverine has the adamantium skeleton of an incredible game; however, what we got is ultimately just “good”.

There is pride and honour in Newcastle's agonising NRL grand final defeat
In the end, the final mountain proved too high for Newcastle to climb even if they got a good, long look at the summit.
The Knights gave that mountain everything they had and then a little bit more. Until the very end of their 19-18 loss to the Roosters, they never stopped fighting for their miracle.
It was perhaps the cruellest fate of all, to come so far, to do so much, to play so proud and strong, only to fall short by the narrowest margin possible, to come so close to defying the odds one last time.
- Report: Roosters beat Knights by one point in classic NRL grand final
- Quick hits: Ponga lights up the grand final as DCE seals the premiership
- Clive Churchill Medal: Tedesco wins best on ground
- Jai Arrow Tribute: Amy Shark leads grand final tribute
It is easy, when you’re not of a Novocastrian persuasion, to say they lost no admirers, or that they did themselves proud.
Such words are of cold comfort in the quiet void of defeat, and truth doesn’t always cut through the pain.
But it is still important to say it, because there is still honour to be had, and they earned that with their effort and their toughness and their ability to save at least half a dozen tries.
When Kalyn Ponga went the length of the field midway through the first half, completing a play where he started out making a try-saving tackle on Billy Smith in one corner and finished scoring in the other, running about as far as a person can on a rugby league field, it felt like the moment that would last forever from this match.
The gut-busting effort to cover so much ground in the first place, the long journey towards the very heart of the Newcastle fans who had turned Stadium Australia into a little piece of the Hunter and the fact that the Knights had, yet again, scored from a thousand miles out gave a feeling that maybe this really was destiny.
Those tries from the ends of the Earth have been Newcastle’s hammer of the gods through this finals run, but in the second half the Roosters gave them no Earth to run from because the Tricolours were as inevitable as the tide through the middle of the field.
They tried to starve the Knights to death and just about did it.
Newcastle had six tackles inside the opposition all night compared to 51 for the Roosters as the newly minted premiers went direct and they did it hard and often.
It was a game plan made for Clive Churchill Medal winner James Tedesco as he put up a run metres total that may as well have been the distance back to Newcastle itself.
But he was not alone. Naufahu Whyte showed why he is a man of iron and Spencer Leniu ran like he didn’t care what happened to him next.
They bent the Knights up like pretzels, so much so that the underdogs could have started charging rent inside their own 20. But Newcastle would not break.
The tries they did concede came from one of those Mark Nawaqanitawase efforts that only he could do, a Billy Smith barge-over that came after three try-saving efforts in as many plays beforehand and a wicked bounce off the posts that fell just right for Tedesco to fire a ball out for Nawqanitawase’s second.
The Knights barely kept it together when they held up Lindsay Collins and stopped Robert Toia from going in, but they did.
They were hanging on by a thread, but they used that thread to haul themselves back into it.
They were rewarded for their courage under fire when they wound up for their last big punch, because it landed true. Greg Marzhew’s late try was just about the only chance they had in the entire second half.
By rights, they shouldn’t have been near. But by rights they shouldn’t have been here at all. Defeat was in the air but they refused to breathe until the siren.
This time, almost 30 years after their first premiership, the Darren Albert moment did not come for them. There are no premiership heroes but that doesn’t mean there aren’t heroes still.
Francis Manuleleua, in just his 15th NRL game, was magnificent in defeat, scoring a try in the first half after running a line that was a piece of rugby league art.
He and backrow partner Jermaine McEwan call themselves “The Bruise Crew” and they’ll have as many as they dished out while prop Cody Hopwood made 46 tackles which is more than his age (20) and his number of NRL appearances (18) combined.
Ponga was their best and not just for his try. His defence was stellar; he threw himself into collisions and refused to give up on anything.
The captain – and he is the captain now, when once he was just the bloke who led them onto the field – was close to tears at the end of the match.
His people left the ground in the horrible daze that comes only when the greatest prize has been ripped from your hands, but they could not have asked for more from their team.
The Knights could have played better – a couple of passes were loose and some of their work under the high ball wasn’t great — but it is difficult to imagine a way they could have fought harder.
They cannot take a premiership trophy home, but they can take plenty of hope.
The future might feel like it doesn’t matter now but between the young forwards, the return of Dylan Brown, Trey Mooney, Jacob Saifiti and Phoenix Crossland combined with Newcastle, it makes it very unlikely they’ll have to wait another 25 years for another shot.
But you never know. Each chance at a premiership can be the last.
That’s why it’s important, if they were fated to go down, that they did it like this, why men of steel and coal had to leave a little piece of themselves out there.
Their city will be proud of them. Their people will be proud of them.
There is little glory in defeat, but after a game like that, there is no shame either.

A court in Shopian on Tuesday sentenced a man to life imprisonment for the murder of a person in 2019, observing that the case did not fall within the “rarest of rare” category warranting the death penalty.
Principal Sessions Judge Shopian Mehmood Ahmed Chowdhary awarded life imprisonment and a fine of Rs 1 lakh to Bilal Ahmad Seh, who was convicted under Section 302 of the Ranbir Penal Code (RPC).
The court said the convict had been in custody since his arrest on April 21, 2019, and had spent nearly seven years in custody during the trial.
The case, registered as FIR No. 19/2019 at Police Station Zainapora, initially involved charges under Sections 302, 307, 147, 148, 506, 109, 341 and 34 of the RPC.
While deciding the quantum of sentence, the court considered the mitigating and aggravating circumstances and referred to the Supreme Court’s guidelines on awarding the death penalty.
The court noted that the case was based on four eyewitnesses as well as circumstantial evidence. It also took into account that the convict was a first-time offender, was a farmer by profession and had been supporting his family.
The court observed that there were no aggravating circumstances of such an exceptional nature as to warrant capital punishment.
“Life imprisonment is the appropriate punishment to be awarded to the convict for commission of murder of the deceased,” the court said.
The court also noted that other accused named in the case, including the convict’s brother and two sisters, had been acquitted, while proceedings against another accused had abated following his death. A juvenile accused in the case is facing separate proceedings before the Juvenile Justice Board, according to the case record.
Since the sentence is one of life imprisonment, the court directed that the case file and judgment be submitted to the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh for confirmation of the sentence as required under law.
The convict was directed to be sent to Special Jail Pulwama to undergo the sentence. The court also informed him of his right to appeal against the judgment and sentence before the High Court within 15 days.

Hurricane Polo is barreling towards the Baja California region of Mexico, the latest system in a Pacific hurricane season that has been notably active in recent months. On 22 September, a measurement of 892 millibars was registered for Hurricane Polo, making it the second-most intense hurricane on record in the east Pacific. It is fuelled by exceptionally warm waters across the Pacific Ocean, providing favourable conditions for the system to maintain its considerable strength.
Polo is expected to turn towards the west-north-west, before taking a more north-westerly trajectory on Saturday. It has maximum sustained winds of around 150mph, with even stronger gusts occurring within the most intense parts of the hurricane. Hurricane-force winds extend outward for approximately 40 miles from the centre, while tropical storm-force winds reach as far as 125 miles. These powerful winds, combined with torrential rainfall and dangerous seas, could have significant impacts. Although some fluctuations in intensity are possible over the coming days, Polo is expected to remain powerful as it tracks north-westwards.
In India, a deep 988-millibar low-pressure system – a tropical storm in this case – is centred along the east coast, bringing widespread and potentially disruptive weather conditions to Odisha and surrounding areas. The system is producing heavy rainfall across the region, with the latest forecast models suggesting totals could exceed 200mm in some locations over a 24-hour period. Rainfall rates are expected to be particularly intense at times, with hourly totals potentially exceeding 30mm in the heaviest downpours. Such intense rainfall could cause significant surface water and localised flooding, particularly in low-lying areas and places with poor drainage. Strong and gusty winds are also affecting coastal parts of Odisha. Winds are forecast to reach around 50-60mph, creating hazardous conditions in exposed areas and potentially causing disruption to travel, infrastructure and power supplies. Authorities have closed numerous schools across the affected districts for safety reasons.
Meanwhile, in Iberia, the relentless heat of summer is extending into meteorological autumn, with temperatures rising into the high 30s celsius on 23 September. Alvega, in Portugal, recorded a maximum temperature of 41.7C, smashing many July records from previous decades.

Desmond targeted by Celtic fan protest at Alfred Dunhill
- Published
Celtic's largest shareholder Dermot Desmond was targeted in a protest at the Alfred Dunhill Links golf tournament in St Andrews as tennis balls were thrown towards him.
Tennis balls with pictures of the 76-year-old's face scored out were thrown on to the green of the 15th hole of the pro-am competition, with images showing Desmond having to be escorted off the course by security.
The Celtic Fans Collective have since released a statement, along with footage and images of the incident.
It read: "Dermot Desmond has essentially been allowed to run Celtic Football Club whilst using his wealth to hide from supporters and accountability. Fans took the chance today to send a message that this arrangement cannot continue."
Desmond is the largest individual shareholder of the Scottish Premiership club but has been criticised in recent seasons for the club's lack of progress in Europe and underwhelming transfer business.
In the wake of Brendan Rodgers' resignation at the beginning of last season, Desmond blamed the former manager for much of the problems that marred the beginning of the 2025-26 campaign.
Then at Celtic's annual general meeting last November, which had to be abandoned due to fan unrest, Desmond's son Ross read out a statement on his behalf.
He began by defending his father, a "lifelong and passionate" Celtic supporter, and vowed that the board would not be "bullied by aggressive and irrational" criticism.
The Irishman defended then chairman Peter Lawwell and chief executive Michael Nicholson, claiming attempts to "dehumanise and vilify them are shameful".
Desmond went on to criticise a section of fans over a recent incident that led to the Green Brigade ultras group being banned and added: "Those people are bullies."

A popular national footwear brand recently published a collaborative Instagram post with a fraternity, despite two former members being recently accused of disseminating nonconsensual intimate images of a fellow college student.
On September 25, HEYDUDE, a viral shoe brand that was acquired by Crocs in 2022, posted a photo on its Instagram account promoting shoes that appeared to be UF versions of the brand’s popular “Wally” loafer, a lightweight slip-on sneaker with a foam insert.
“@heydude called, @thetachiflorida answered,” the caption read, alongside photos of Theta Chi members clowning around and wearing orange-and-blue sneakers. The brand also posted a video on its TikTok account outside of the Florida fraternity house with the caption “wtf is any shoe besides a HEYDUDE?”
The post led to backlash in the comments section, with many questioning why the brand would choose to work with the fraternity. “#CancelHeyDude,” one person wrote. Another chimed in: “I would boycott if I wore fucking ugly shoes but I don’t so I can’t.”
As WIRED previously reported, two former members of the UF chapter of Theta Chi, Kamran Ahmed and Brendan Pitfield, allegedly used anonymous burner accounts with the handles "Steve 'SC’ Cumfull" and "Arnie_Grape16" to disseminate a nonconsensual intimate video of Maddie Kowalski, then a 19-year-old UF student. One of the "Steve 'SC' Cumfull" posts on X identified Kowalski by her full name and sorority affiliation.
According to affidavits from the Gainesville Police Department, the posts accumulated thousands of views. Kowalski’s name went viral on X, causing her “widespread public humiliation and significant emotional distress,” according to the affidavit. Ahmed and Pitfield are currently being charged with sexual cyberharassment, a first-degree misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in jail and a $1,000 fine. Kowalski is also suing both men for financial damages in Florida Northern District Court. Through their attorneys, Pitfield (who has entered a plea of not guilty) and Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Though no other Theta Chi members have been charged, a screengrab of Instagram comments from an account linked to Ahmed appears to show fellow members referencing his alleged burner name. Some comments also appear to reference a cryptocurrency in Kowalski’s name, that the police affidavit alleges Ahmed promoted on X. When reached for comment, Theta Chi CEO Michael Mayer previously told WIRED that the alleged behavior described in the affidavit is “reprehensible” and “completely contrary to Theta Chi’s ideals.”
The charges against Pitfield and Ahmed, as well as WIRED’s reporting on the case, sparked an outcry on the UF campus. On September 15, a group of students advertised a protest outside the Theta Chi fraternity house, circulating a flier demanding that the chapter be removed from the UF campus. “They need to be held accountable,” the flier reads.
On YikYak, the anonymous campus forum, there have also been calls to “boycott” or “nuke” Theta Chi, according to screengrabs reviewed by WIRED. Some anonymous YikYak posts appeared to suggest that the September 15 protest was broken up by campus police outside of Theta Chi: “Cops nuked the theta chi protest good job UF,” one reads. “Typical.” Blake Trauschke, the assistant director of public affairs for UF, tells WIRED that while “there were calls and social media posts for a protest,” she was on site and “none emerged.” She clarified that, as standard UF practice, university police were present “to ensure the safety and security of all.”
Founded in 1856, Theta Chi has established more than 246 chapters at colleges and universities across the country, and it has more than 250,000 initiated members nationwide, according to the organization’s website. At UF specifically, Theta Chi has 190 active members, according to the UF Interfraternity Council.
When asked about the post with HEYDUDE, a representative for Theta Chi tells WIRED Ahmed and Pitfield are no longer members of Theta Chi Fraternity. “If it is determined through the legal process that the defendants are guilty of the alleged behavior described in the complaints, Theta Chi will support the maximum allowable penalty under the law and the permanent expulsion of the student offenders from the University of Florida,” the spokesperson says.
In mid-September, the Cornell Sun published the names of seven Cornell University students who a former student alleged gang-raped her in 2024 at a Chi Phi frat house; In September, the Jane Doe filed civil cases against them. The revelation has sparked widespread criticism of frat culture on social media. The content creator and activist @bluraybeyond, who has also posted about the Kowalski case, made a Reel calling out HEYDUDE for posting with UF Theta Chi, writing in a caption “@heydude what the actual heck is your problem #maddiekowalski.” “HEYDUDE is sending the same message we're seeing out of Cornell and the DA's office: Survivor experiences [are] unimportant to us,” she tells WIRED. She believes the company “has chosen to reward sexual [exploitation] with a lack of accountability and free PR swag.”
After seeing the collab post with HEYDUDE, Kowalski tells WIRED she and her mother emailed the company to ask why they had decided to work with the UF chapter. She says they did not hear back.
In a statement to WIRED, a HEYDUDE spokesperson says the company “has no affiliation, sponsorship, or ongoing partnership” with UF Theta Chi, and that the post was part of a larger “HEYDUDE Tailgate Tour” visiting various locations, including frat and sorority houses, across the country.
“We were unaware of the allegations made against” members of the UF Theta Chi chapter “when the tour was planned,” the spokesperson says. “Our company does not support this alleged behavior and takes allegations such as these very seriously. We will re-evaluate future stops for the remainder of the tour.”
As of Friday morning, the post was still up.

A STAT analysis of National Institutes of Health spending shows that in the 2026 fiscal year, which ended Wednesday, the agency continued reducing grant awards involving health disparities, race, and ethnicity but made little progress toward other Trump administration priorities, including disbursing funds more evenly across the country and expanding support for early-career scientists.
While the agency, like last year, spent its entire external grants budget of roughly $34 billion after a slow start, the manner in which it did so is sowing deep uncertainty among researchers. In a survey and interviews, they said delays in the grant review process are slowing down the pace of their work, and making it difficult for them to propose and conduct the sort of innovative, impactful science that the NIH exists to support.
Overall, the agency funded around 58,000 projects, a slight drop from the 61,000 awarded during the 2025 fiscal year and well below the roughly 63,700 grants awarded annually in the years before the second Trump administration. Though this number may increase somewhat in the coming weeks because of reporting lags in the NIH grants database, the smaller number of grants potentially resulted from the White House’s push to fully fund more multiyear grants in advance, which meant that there was less funding on hand to issue new awards.

Poor diet, sedentary habits, and prolonged screen use are contributing to metabolic disorders among young people at increasingly younger ages, said Challa Suresh, Scientist ‘G’ and Director Grade, Head of the Cell Biology Division, AcSIR Coordinator at the ICMR-National Institute of Nutrition, at an oration organised by Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research recently.
Delivering the Prof. S.P. Thyagarajan Endowment Oration on ‘The Modern Lifestyle Paradox: Why are Young People Developing Metabolic Disorder Earlier?’, Prof. Suresh stressed the importance of nutritious food and healthier lifestyle habits in preventing lifestyle-related illnesses.
He advised young people to choose wholesome, nutrient-rich foods, and limit processed and packaged foods, which he linked to rising obesity. He also called for reducing screen time, noting that prolonged use of digital devices encourage sedentary behaviour and affect memory and overall well-being.
The event was attended by university officials, academicians, clinicians, researchers, and students.

Reliance Industries Executive Director Anant Ambani has called for a new approach to farming in Andhra Pradesh, saying young people need better skills, technology and entrepreneurial opportunities if agriculture is to become a career they actively choose. Speaking at the foundation stone-laying ceremony for the Rayalaseema Global Horticulture Hub and Indian School of Agriculture (ISA) in Madanapalle on Friday, Ambani said many young people were moving away from farming because of uncertain incomes and limited opportunities. “Too many young people leave farming because incomes are uncertain and opportunities seem limited. Let us give them the skills, technology and enterprise to build successful futures in their own villages,” he said. The event was attended by Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman, Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan and state minister Nara Lokesh. The horticulture hub is part of a wider initiative aimed at developing Rayalaseema’s agricultural economy. Ambani said Reliance Industries would establish and manage the Indian School of Agriculture, which he described as an institution that could help make farming a profession that young Indians pursue with pride. The proposed school is expected to focus on modern agricultural practices while combining technology with the experience and traditional knowledge of Indian farmers. Artificial intelligence, drones, robotics and cloud computing could all have practical applications, Ambani said. He gave the example of AI systems that could alert farmers to pest attacks before they spread, drones that could assess crop health and guide the use of water and nutrients, and robotics that could reduce physically demanding farm work and crop losses. The broader horticulture project is planned across 10 districts, with development structured through 201 clusters covering 303 mandals and thousands of villages. The initiative is being implemented in phases and has an estimated investment of ₹1 lakh crore. Ambani said Reliance Jio would work with the Indian School of Agriculture to take training modules to farmers in Indian languages through interactive virtual classrooms in villages. The idea, he said, is to take agricultural education beyond the campus and directly into farming communities. Educated rural youth could also work as digitally enabled extension workers, helping farmers put the lessons into practice. He pointed to Reliance’s Jio Krishi platform and said the company had developed products intended to support farmers. Ambani also spoke about price intelligence, saying technology could help farmers determine when and where to sell their produce. Water management was another focus. Cloud-based advice and technology, he said, could help farmers work towards the government’s ‘Per Drop More Crop’ objective, while greenhouse technology could allow cultivation to continue through more of the year. Ambani also linked his agricultural vision to animal welfare, describing himself as a “pashu sevak”, or someone dedicated to serving animals. “Pashu seva bhi prabhu seva hai,” he said, stressing his belief in technology-driven animal husbandry. He referred to Vantara in Jamnagar, the animal welfare and conservation initiative associated with the Reliance Foundation, and said work had begun towards what he described as a global university for wildlife and veterinary sciences. His comments placed animal welfare alongside farming and clean energy as parts of the wider vision he outlined in Andhra Pradesh. Ambani also announced that Reliance Industries plans to invest ₹1 lakh crore in Andhra Pradesh to establish compressed biogas (CBG) plants. According to PTI reporting, the investment is expected to create more than three lakh jobs and generate nearly ₹60,000 crore in revenue for the state over the coming decades. This ₹1 lakh crore commitment is separate from the ₹1 lakh crore estimated investment attached to the Rayalaseema Global Horticulture Hub. Ambani said the CBG projects would help connect agriculture with energy production, while creating another potential source of income and employment in rural areas. Ambani also made a personal appeal to the people of the state, asking them to consider him a “son of Andhra” and guide him on how he could contribute to its development. “Today, I request you to treat me as a son of Andhra and direct me as to what I can contribute to your beautiful state. Nannu Andhra bidde ga bhavinchandi,” he said. He added that the foundation stone ceremony was about more than construction, saying the projects were intended to lay the groundwork for stronger villages, rural enterprise and improved livelihoods for farmers. The Rayalaseema initiative is being positioned by the Andhra Pradesh government as a major push to expand horticulture through irrigation, technology, processing and market infrastructure. The project is expected to promote crops including mango, banana, tomato and pomegranate across the region. New Delhi, Sep 23: The Congress on Wednesday alleged that for the Modi government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform but an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, as well as a tool for stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation.
The opposition party's assertion comes after former Bombay High Court judge Justice R C Chavan resigned from the Maharashtra government's panel to prepare a draft for implementing the Uniform Civil Code (UCC), citing serious reservations over its decision to restrict public feedback on crucial social issues to a "Yes/No" format.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh said the resignation of a former high court judge from the Maharashtra government's committee to draft a UCC for the state raises larger questions, apart from his several concerns on the functioning of this committee.
Posting his statement on X, Ramesh said, "A retired High Court judge has shown courage to resign from a committee set up by the Maharashtra government to prepare a uniform civil code for the state. Here is our statement on the non-uniform 'Uniform' Civil Codes (UCC) the HM is trying to bulldoze through in every state."
"Did the Constituent Assembly ever imagine a situation in which every state would enact its own separate version of a UCC? The answer is a resounding no," Ramesh said.
Did the architects of our Constitution led by Dr B.R. Ambedkar ever conceive states competing with one another to have different UCCs according to the political machinations and calculations of one political party, he asked.
"Again, the answer is a resounding no," Ramesh added.
He pointed out that on June 17, 2016, the Modi government referred the question of the UCC to the 21st Law Commission of India for detailed examination.
"After extensive research, the Commission published its Consultation Paper on Reform of Family Law on August 31, 2018. Its conclusion appearing in paragraph 1.15 on page 7 of the Consultation Paper was clear: 'The formulation of a Uniform Civil Code is neither necessary nor desirable at this stage'. Instead it recommended addressing nor discrimination within individual family laws while preserving India's legal and cultural diversity," Ramesh said.
The Modi government has chosen to disregard the findings of the very Commission it tasked with examining the issue because the facts, as usual, did not align with its political agenda, the Congress leader said.
Over the last three years, one BJP-ruled State after another bulldozed through its own version of a UCC, Ramesh said.
The UCC came into effect in Uttarakhand from January 27, 2025. Subsequently the Gujarat Assembly passed the UCC Bill on March 24, 2026, the Assam Assembly on May 27, 2026 and the Madhya Pradesh Assembly on July 21, 2026," he pointed out.
Ramesh said these State-level UCCs, never envisaged in the Constitution, are not uniform.
"They contain different provisions, different penalties, different procedures and significant exemptions. Contrary to claims, the Uttarakhand UCC, the only one in force, continues with a number of patriarchal traditions and is creating many problems for perfectly law-abiding residents of the state," Ramesh argued.
Union Home Minister Amit Shah has made a typically bombastic announcement that a UCC will be implemented in all NDA-ruled States before the 2029 Lok Sabha election, he said.
Evidently other NDA parties have lost their voices and are being silenced by the BJP, the Congress general secretary said.
"For the Modi Government, the UCC is not an instrument of considered legal reform to be implemented after the widest possible consultations and public debate and with the broadest possible consensus. It is, in reality, an instrument of division, disruption and diversion, a tool for harassment and intimidation, stoking prejudices and keeping society in a state of permanent polarisation," Ramesh said.
Later, asked about the statement, he said, "The UCC bulldozer is to permanently polarise society."
In a letter to the panel chairperson Justice Ranjana Desai (retd), former Bombay High Court judge Chavan criticised the committee's approach, stating that reducing complex societal questions, such as delayed marriages, perversions, infertility, and rising matrimonial disputes, to binary options undermined the primary purpose of consensus-building.
The former judge said he had misunderstood that the committee aimed to gather views of the people of Maharashtra and to generate a consensus to remedy the issues of late marriages, infertility, unstable marriages, time-consuming dispute resolution mechanism and so on.
"Now that the misunderstanding is removed, I realise that the aim is to just provide an opportunity to people who may care, to share their responses, in a 'yes or no' format to the questions posed so that analysis of data becomes easy," the letter said.
In July, the state government set up a seven-member committee headed by retired Supreme Court Justice Ranjana Desai to draft a framework for implementing the UCC, which seeks to establish equal laws across religions on issues about marriage, divorce, and property.
Justice Chavan, a former high court judge, resigned from the panel on September 19.
The Congress' statement also comes days after Shah said the BJP-led NDA governments in 21 states will introduce UCC before 2029. The next Lok Sabha polls are scheduled for 2029.

Sinfield completes final ultramarathon challenge
- Published
Sir Kevin Sinfield has completed his latest endurance challenge raising money for motor neurone disease (MND) causes in memory of his friend and teammate Rob Burrow, who died in 2024.
Sinfield completed seven ultramarathons in seven days, crossing the finish line at Old Trafford Stadium in Manchester ahead of the Super League Grand Final.
The fundraiser and his team have raised more than £13m for the MND community since his first annual challenge in 2020.
Speaking to the crowd, Sinfield said: "The rugby league community has got right behind the MND community and Rob would be so proud to see how you've supported and cared, and showed your love for a community that really needs us."
Sinfield began his final ultramarathon challenge in Hull on September 27 and visited all 12 Super League clubs along the way.
The 7 in 7: The Grand Finale week ended at Old Trafford earlier where he brought out the trophy ahead of the game between Warrington Wolves and Wakefield Trinity.
Along the way he was surprised by royals, including The Prince and Princess of Wales and the Princess Royal, as well as famous names from the sporting world such as former England football manager Sir Gareth Southgate and Leeds boxer Josh Warrington.
Each day was split into 7km, hour-long blocks with an additional extra mile for members of the MND community to join.
Funds raised by the challenge will go towards the work of the MND Association, Leeds Hospitals Charity, My Name5 Doddie Foundation, Darby Rimmer Foundation, MND Scotland and the Irish MND Association.
Sinfield, 45, who played his entire professional career with Leeds Rhinos, is one of the most successful players in Super League history.
He and Burrow met at the Leeds Rhinos academy aged 14 and 12. They went on to win seven titles together with Leeds Rhinos.
Burrow's wife, Lindsey Burrow, told BBC Radio 4's PM that her late husband "would have been incredibly proud" of his friend.
"It's bittersweet that Rob's not here today to see Kevin finish his final challenge but Rob will be with us in spirit and it's just testimony to Kevin that he's so humbled to do this not just for Rob but for the whole MND community," Lindsey said.
"It's just incredible. I am in complete awe of the efforts of Kevin and his team over the last seven days, and not just over the last seven days but over the last seven years," she added.
Sinfield's son, Jack Sinfield, lined up in the Wakefield side seeking to clinch their first top-flight title since 1968.

A decade ago, actor Deepika Padukone said in an ad campaign: ‘My body, My choice.’ But, in reality, when it comes to older people, society often wrests that agency from them. Last week, as the world observed both International Day of Older Persons (October 1) and Gandhi Jayanti (October 2), Mumbai-based Sumira Roy’s documentary film Bhangaar (Obsolete), raised the question of dignity in death and the right to die for the elderly.
The yet-to-release Marathi film, which won the National Film Award for Best Non-Feature Film last month, was screened by the Kriti Film Club in Delhi NCR.
Bhangaar trains the lens on Narayan and Iravati Lavate, an octogenarian Maharashtrian childless couple, who petitioned for active euthanasia in 2018. Iravati succumbed to cancer in 2023, Narayan lives in an old-age home. His eyesight and memory, too, have deserted him. After the news of the National Award came in, Roy wanted to share the moment with Narayan. She rang up Prakash Joshi, the brother of Iravati, who also appears in the film. Joshi told her that due to Narayan’s present old-age health and impediments there of, nothing would register with man.
While Nilesh Maniyar and Shonali Bose’s documentary A Fly on the Wall (2024) is also on the same subject and travels with Chika Kapadia to Switzerland for his last days, Roy’s documentary shows how only privilege can afford that right.
Monisha Advani, Bhangaar’s producer and partner, Emmay Entertainment, calls the film personal, “My late mother was a Maharashtrian and while growing up, the frugality of my maternal grandparents’ lives somewhere was mirrored in the Lavates. Sumira has given me the opportunity, in a private way, to pay tribute to my familial pedagogy."
Excerpts from an interview with director Roy:
You are from an advertising background; how, when and why did you transition into filmmaking and documentary films at that?
Since I’ve been a student, I’ve been passionate about films and documentary films and had even sat for the FTII entrance examination. But the women in my family were against me going to Pune and feared the casting couch in the film industry. Years later, when I went to Japan for work, I did a postgraduate course in Japanese cinema, theatre and painting. I was just hooked on when I saw [films by Yasujirō] Ozu and all the greats there. So, I thought, there’s a roundabout way to do films through advertising films. There’s a great amount of discipline in ad films; you shoot minimally and you have only 30-40 seconds to tell your story. Ad films [at Ogilvy and JWT] also gave me a lot of exposure to a lot of things that you need in documentaries. For instance, understanding human behaviour. And then, in documentaries, I learnt how to listen… to people’s stories. I went on foreign location shoots and for post-production. All that’s helped me now. In 2011, I left advertising and started two agencies, mainly for production. I was a little bit jaded and cynical, trying to do these falsehoods to make people buy things they didn’t need.
Did the Central Board of Film Certification raise any objections in Bhangaar?
Only to the title. The censor board didn’t like the word bhangaar [obsolete] and called it insulting. I had to keep going back to explain to them that the word is what Narayan uses [in life and in the film]. It’s his, not mine. After some time, they agreed but asked me to carry a disclaimer in Marathi at the start of the film that this is the character’s interpretation of the title. That was fine by me.
There seems to be a thematic continuity between your documentaries Last DaysLast Shot (2017) and Bhangaar. Tell us about the earlier film.
I have an idea, and then I make a film. I don’t just go and make documentaries, because I’m not an activist or an investigative filmmaker. As Narayan says in the film [Bhangaar], the day you’re born is the beginning of death. He echoes the Myth of Sisyphus when he says there’s no purpose to life; it’s absurd. I am drawn to existentialism, and like diving into the interior of minds.
For my earlier film, I was interested in exploring the philosophy of moksha and nirvana. I went to Banaras [Hindu] University, and walked around in the gullies and ghats. People would pop out from the woods to say, ‘Come listen to my poem.’ There, I found a Bengali poet-artist who had gone to Japan and become famous. He returned to Varanasi with his Japanese wife [they ran the Kumiko Guest House]. By the time I shot him, he looked like Rabindranath Tagore. He was about 80 or 81. He told me his idea of moksha: to dissolve the ego. Then I met a 26-year-old Dom in Harishchandra Ghat cremation ground, who [told me he] hardly got a chance to light the fire, and couldn’t make money with it. So, he bought a camera and started shooting the relatives of the dead. He said from his experience that a good person’s corpse burns faster than a sinner’s.
What drew you to Iravati and Narayan Lavate’s story?
It’s a personal reason. My long-widowed mother was quite active in life. She’d drive, have a social life, her body and mind intact. A year before she passed away, she started saying, ‘I want to die with dignity.’ I was a documentary filmmaker, but I never listened to her nor asked her what she meant. I was petrified of her dying. [After] she passed away, I was stricken with grief and regret. I came across the Lavates’ story in Mid-Day; they asked for the right to die together with dignity. That struck me, and I went to meet them in their 12x12 room in a Mumbai chawl, to get closure for what I hadn’t done with my mother. They taught me so much about Marathi literature and theatre. Narayan looked like Picasso to me. He knew the Constitution by heart. I asked, how could they want to die. He said, ‘It’s time to go.’
They had this fixed spiel they would rattle to the media/news channels. They would do the same during our initial days of shoot. I just told them not to look at the camera and go about their days. I had to be a fly on the wall and filmed them over four years. Afterwards, they forgot there’s a camera. My DOP is brilliant because it was a boot camp for her, with no lights, no space to set up the camera. The aerial shot of them playing cards was shot from atop a washing machine.
In India, the elderly population is growing rapidly even as the birth rate declines. What did your research throw up about ageing and caregiving?
The elderly are growing three times faster than the population of the youth. Palliative care exists only for the rich. There’s no geriatric care and no focus on what is going to happen to the elderly population. All of us are in some stage of caregiving. We are either watching our parents or grandparents.
Gandhi spoke of self-rule. Swaraj is not just political self-rule but also the rule/autonomy over oneself. Does that idea of self-determination versus duty get complicated when it comes to an older person’s choice to die?
Loss of personhood and loss of autonomy, which older people fear, is exactly why they [Irawati and Narayan] asked for it [active euthanasia]. We do not connect with our families. Our conversations revolve around whether they have taken their medicines, if the oxygen tank is running low, if the nurse administered the injection. That’s our only conversation with them. The elderly feel like they are [outdated] machines. We have moved away from joint families to nuclear families. As a society, we have forgotten how to respect someone who has lived longer than expected. We keep talking about Gen Z and loneliness, but loneliness is far worse among the older generations. We hardly talk about it. Even our films don’t.
We’ve read about the Aruna Shanbaug case. This year, the Supreme Court gave its landmark judgment permitting passive euthanasia for Harish Rana who was in a vegetative state for over 13 years. What has been the impact of the Lavates’ petition?
Narayan and Iravati are the pioneers of this, at least in our country, or in South Asia. The courts are getting more and more petitions since. The press doesn’t cover many of these.
Bhangaar (Obsolete) screens on October 1 at the India Habitat Centre, Delhi, and on October 4 at Museo Camera, Gurugram at 4.30 pm.

Each rare disease affects very few people. However, there are around 8,000 rare diseases, and they cumulatively affect hundreds of millions of people. In India, 1,004 rare genetic disorders have been reported so far.
It used to be that because the number of patients for a rare-disease drug was very small, so the pharmaceutical industry’s interest in developing such drugs was limited. Therefore they were called orphan drugs.
In order to overcome this hesitancy, many governments have incentivised companies to develop orphan drugs. Examples include the Orphan Drug Act, which the U.S. passed in 1983 to provide tax incentives, seven years of market exclusivity for the first approved product for a given condition, grants, regulatory fee waivers, etc.That is, it reduced the costs of developing the drugs and enabled companies to make a good profit.
This allowed companies to diversify into rare-disease drugs. Before the passage of the Orphan Drug Act, only 38 relevant drugs had been approved in the U.S. But after that, by 2022, there had been 1,122 approvals. Subsequently, several countries and regions, including Japan, Australia, and the European Union had approved similar legislation encouraging pharmaceutical companies to develop and manufacture orphan drugs.
Because of the small market, companies tend to set very high prices for these medications, and it is not unusual for a rare disease patient to find that a year’s worth of the drug costs around $100,000 (Rs 1 crore) or more. This puts the medication out of reach for virtually all patients around the world unless a health insurance scheme or government health service covers it. Samples of such high-priced pharmaceuticals are described in the table.
Two challenges
Although the Government of India supports rare disease patients with up to a total of Rs 50 lakh for their treatment, this is often insufficient to cover the necessary costs even for a year, and patients may have to resort to crowdfunding to raise the required capital.
For example, in mid-2025, Rs 9 crore was raised through crowdfunding to pay for gene therapy for a 16-month-old child in Kolkata. In fact, almost 4,000 children are listed on a Government of India crowdfunding platform, with the cumulative annual cost of treatment for these patients amounting to over Rs 9,000 crore.
Many drugs for rare diseases have been developed, but they cater to only about 5% of rare diseases and associated conditions. Therefore, most patients lack suitable drugs, even those available at high cost.
Two key challenges in developing new orphan drugs are identifying a patient cohort for conducting clinical trials and determining endpoints in these trials. Once a drug is approved, undertaking small-scale manufacturing and distribution that is affordable and of high-quality are other major challenges.
In this article, the authors present here a possible solution to these issues. These solutions touch on how foreign companies that tend to develop novel drugs can work with India both for clinical trials and manufacturing.
Trials for new drugs
With an overall population exceeding 1.4 billion, India has a large number of patients with any given condition. And due to high rates of endogamy in certain social groups, the prevalence of a particular rare disease is even higher than might be expected based on its prevalence elsewhere.
For example, research has shown that in particular ethnic groups, the prevalence of beta-thalassemia in India can be 10.5% whereas, per a 2023 review, the prevalence in India’s general population is 3.7%. Indian patients have also become increasingly organised in recent years, with a proliferation of patient advocacy groups focusing on specific diseases.
On the research front, for example, one longitudinal study has been tracking a group of 70 people with a rare condition called GNE myopathy. Patient groups pertaining to Rett syndrome have a registry of more than 400 patients. The gene pool of the Indian diaspora also has unique mutations, often across different ethnicities.
In all, there is a large number of rare disease patients, which should help in finding a suitable patient cohort for trials. However, patients from India are not usually participants in international trials for orphan drugs.Therefore, there is considerable scope to increase their involvement in such trials. The government could foster the collaboration of foreign companies and local organisations, as it does in the area of chip manufacturing. It also could invite multinational drug companies to set up drug-development centres vis-à-vis rare diseases in India, in collaboration with patient groups.
If Indian patients are important participants in developing such drugs, they are also likely to be more interested in accessing the resulting drugs than in any monetary compensation. Put another way, Indian patients may be willing to help drug development but only if they see themselves as beneficiaries of the approved drugs.
Overpriced drugs that they cannot access serve no local purpose. To this end, the authors propose that India decide on the price of drugs sold within the country or in the Global South. The company developing the drug can be free to set prices in the rest of the world.
The authors say this with reference to the concept of benefit-sharing. Recently, country representatives and medical experts discussed this concept in the context of the Pandemic Agreement of the World Health Organization (WHO). The idea is that in the event of a pandemic, countries will rapidly share information about pathogens, including their genetic information, with the rest of the world. That way, pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies can develop diagnostics, drugs, and vaccines as early as possible. The catch is such products must be shared across countries, fairly and equitably.
Notably, U.S. and Chinese companies are locked in a charged race to develop drugs for rare diseases. Chinese companies will usually have access to enough patients, and also to low-cost manufacturing. Likewise, companies from the Western nations may find it worthwhile to explore opportunities of collaboration in India.
Manufacturing in India
India has been called the “pharmacy of the world” due to its production of small molecule generics, which fill 47% of the prescriptions for generics in the U.S. India also has the largest number of manufacturing sites approved by U.S. regulators outside the U.S.
Indian firms also manufacture and export biosimilars to the U.S. and the European Union and supply 15% of all biosimilars sold in the U.S. Of late, facilities in the country have been producing a relatively novel therapy personalised to each patient for particular cancers, called CAR-T, to international standards.
In effect, India can manufacture various categories of high-quality drugs at low cost. Local manufacturers are also ready to do this for small volumes, whereas manufacturers in Western nations are often unwilling to do so.
After understanding how foreign companies could develop and manufacture orphan drugs in India, we can consider how existing orphan drugs that have been approved abroad can be produced in India.
Under Rule 101 of the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019, the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO) has specified six countries — including the U.S. and the U.K.; if one of these countries approves a drug, the drug need not have a new clinical trial conducted in India before its maker seeking the Indian regulator’s approval.
This provision can be a major incentive to manufacture and market certain generic drugs in India. However, this policy can benefit from greater transparency, including guidance documents to help drug developers and sponsors file applications to the regulator. Regulatory agencies abroad routinely develop such documents to ease the applications process.
As a rule, the approval of such drugs should be based on bioequivalence, i.e. their behaviour in the body should be the same as that of the original drug; safety and toxicity studies; and the drug’s effectiveness once it is on the market.
Such a pathway will require appropriate safeguards for quality, safety, a system that looks out for adverse events after the drug is on the market (i.e. pharmacovigilance), and manufacturing standards — but it will also considerably reduce the need for duplicate paperwork.
What the state can do
We also have an opportunity to take advantage of India’s expertise in generic drugs to create a global orphan drug manufacturing industry. The government should draft policy that reduces the financial barriers to producing such drugs locally. A useful model could be developed along the lines of the production-linked incentive schemes for manufacturing. That is, companies investing in the manufacture of selected orphan drugs could receive incentives linked to production, investment, exports, and patient access.
The financial incentives could include tax incentives for investing in orphan drug manufacturing and production-linked incentives for approved orphan drugs. Other kinds of support could include support for technology transfer and process development in collaboration with a national laboratory, advanced market commitments (AMCs) by the government, committing to buy a certain output at a certain price point, and distributing it through the Centres of Excellence on Rare Diseases, the Central Government Health Scheme, and the Pradhan Mantri Bhartiya Jan Aushadhi Kendras. Manufacturers could also benefit from predictable demand during the early stages of production, and incentives for exporting to low- and middle-income countries.
The overall objective should not simply be to subsidise companies. Instead, the government should de-risk the initial investment enough to make orphan drug manufacturing commercially viable.
With a streamlined regulatory pathway, appropriate financial incentives, and government procurement, India could build a globally competitive rare-disease pharmaceutical sector.
Taken together, India has already shown the world how to make drugs affordable. The next challenge is to show the world how to make rare-disease drugs accessible.
Gayatri Saberwal, Rakesh Mishra, and Alok Bhattacharya are with the Tata Institute for Genetics and Society. Bhattacharya is also with ‘World Without GNE Myopathy’.

BJP President Nagenthran condemns intimidation of journalist by TVK cadres
BJP State president Nainar Nagenthran alleged a journalist’s phone was taken and videos forcibly deleted after he filmed Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam functionaries at Dharapuram in Tiruppur district
Published - October 04, 2026 03:42 pm IST - Chennai
BJP state president Nainar Nagenthran said the journalist was threatened and his mobile phone was taken away after he recorded visuals of party functionaries falling at the feet of Mr. Anand.
| Photo Credit: Bashkaran N
BJP State president Nainar Nagenthran on Sunday (October 4, 2026) condemned the intimidation of a journalist by Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) cadres at Dharapuram in Tiruppur district, after he shot visuals of some of them reportedly falling at the feet of Minister and TVK general secretary N. Anand.
In a social media post, Mr. Nagenthran said the journalist was threatened and his mobile phone was taken away after he recorded visuals of party functionaries falling at the feet of Mr. Anand. The BJP leader further alleged that the videos were forcibly deleted from the device, calling it an attack on the fourth pillar of democracy.
Describing the incident as an attack on press freedom, Mr. Nagenthran said it reflected growing intolerance towards the media. He also criticised the police, alleging the incident took place in their presence, but that they failed to intervene.

LeT’s Moosa used honey to treat bullet wounds while hiding in J&K forests
NEW DELHI: Lashkar-e-Taiba (LeT) commander Mohammad Asif, alias Hashim Moosa, used pure honey to treat bullet wounds while hiding in the forests of Jammu and Kashmir, news agency PTI reported citing officials on Sunday.Moosa, described by officials as one of the masterminds of the 2025 Pahalgam terror attack and the LeT’s chief operational commander in the region, was killed by the Army in a high-altitude operation in Yousmarg, Budgam, earlier this week. He was also believed to be a former commando of Pakistan army’s Special Services Group (SSG).
Unable to access medical care because of the security cordon, Moosa allegedly applied honey to his wounds.Officials said photographs of his honey-treated injuries were recovered from Yasir’s phone after he was killed in Yousmarg in September.The images were reportedly sent to handlers in Pakistan, who instructed that pure honey be arranged to aid Moosa’s recovery.Officials said Moosa was injured during an encounter in the Dorimal-Gambhir Moghla area of Rajouri during 'Operation Sheruwali'.The operation lasted more than 45 days as security forces searched for Moosa and his associate Yasir, who were hiding in the Poonch-Rajouri forests.
