Lawrence Rothman has a lot of nerve, starting an album with a song called “The Meaning,” and then daring to ask some of the questions inherent in the big picture created by those two words — like, if not what is the meaning of life, then what is the meaning of music? (Of course, for a lot of musicians and music lovers, those two questions might as well be synonymous.) But thoughtfulness and intent are never far away from Rothman’s music, or at least hasn’t been since they made a shift about five years ago toward recording in Nashville and feeling the embrace of the Americana community, as opposed to drifting through a series of rock ‘n’ roll bands and personas in L.A. for a lot of years prior.
“The Meaning” kicks off Rothman’s new album, “Here Lives Love/Sawdust to Stardust,” which they consider the completion of a trilogy of Americana-rooted albums that tell the story of the singer’s life and career to date. (Rothman suggests the music being formulated for the next album actually has more of a jazz flavor, though they’re convinced that belongs as much in Americana as the acoustic singer/songwriter material being emphasized at present.)
Popular on Variety
During the recent AmericanaFest in Nashville, Variety sat down to talk with Rothman not just about wrapping up the fruitful trilogy with “Here Lives Love/Sawdust to Stardust” but about a rich and growing side career producing other artists, including Amanda Shires‘ 2025 confessional album “Nobody’s Girl” (and “Take It Like a Man” before it), Maggie Rose‘s vivacious “Half Moon” and Tift Merritt‘s comeback, “Sugar.” When Rothman begins the new album asking the most core question of them all, “Why am I breathing?,” any of these albums — the ones produced for others, and their own new one — offers a substantial and worthy enough answer.
To ask first about your production work: You work with a lot of great singer-songwriters, and there’s a lot of versatility in the types of sounds you get with different people. No one would mistake an Amanda Shires record for the Maggie Rose album you just had come out.
I don’t know if it’s the Gemini in me, but I’ve loved so many different types of music. my entire life. So to produce and to be able to add sounds, textures and treatments to things that are in a new style every month — because I produce something once a month — helps keep me alive, really, and eep my inspiration up. Amanda Shires makes poetic songs that are just these heartbreaking stories, done in a way that’s so classy, and like Leonard Cohen. It is such a great thing to immerse myself in, because I love sad music, and she definitely makes some beautifully sad songs. You can do that for a while and you’re in that zone, and then it’s great to be able to pop out and do something like Maggie Rose, where it’s more of a celebratory thing of being a mother and this new stage of her life, where it’s about a weird youthfulness in the energy a family gives back to you. T hat record feels very celebratory, and very different than the Tiff Merritt record I made earlier in the year, which was more of a look at the life of an artist, much like myself — what I’ve gone through and what she went through, in a heavy lyrical mode.
I’m a little Method when I produce. I have to feel like I’m in the band. As a sensitive artist yourself, when you’re with all these musicians and you’re getting Method with them, you can lose yourself in it and start to feel a bit like you’re taking on everybody’s trauma. So it’s nice to be able to go amongst these groups of musicians that I work with who telling their truths and spilling their drama and their sadness. They’re all such great people that when you leave those sessions, it’s almost like you’ve been acting in a film, crying and singing and laughing with them, and then at the end of it, you can walk away like yourself again. And I feel like all those artists that I work with, when they’re done, it’s like a clean reset. They got it out of them. I got it out of myself. It’s like a little bit of a demon that you dance with, when you’re producing things.
How do you make yourself “part of the band”? Is that literally through playing an instrument as part of the sessions?
Like I said, I like to be immersive with it, and I don’t want to feel like I’m the producer behind the glass. I stand in the recording room, not the control room, when I’m producing. If a singer’s singing, I’m right next to them. Sometimes I’ll take my shirt off and dance. I’ll do whatever it takes to get it to have an energy. Because there’s something so clinical, almost like a doctor, about being behind a glass, and they’re in the distance — it just feels odd to me. So I’ve never been one to not just immerse myself physically in the room. If I’m not playing something, I’m tapping something or just getting people to get going.
You’ve talked with liking having women’s voices on your own albums…
I like to frame my voice. My voice is so low that a woman’s texture, or that range, always complements my voice well. So for this record, I have Amanda and Jillian Jacqueline and Katie Pruitt singing on some song, and I got to sing with Sarah Klang (as a duet on “A Fire Test”).
The artists we were just talking about you producing recently — Amanda, Maggie, Tift — are all women. Not that that would be solely your focus, but do you find you gravitate toward women artists more than others?
Yeah, I don’t look at it like that at all. I have to just love the music. And I’m not doing producing to become a millionaire of any sort. I’m doing it because I want to help this singer express what they’re doing in a way that feels like, are we pushing the envelope in some direction that’s forward? And with Americana music, funny enough, I think it’s the most forward-thinking music of any genre right now — because you can be R&B, you can be rock ‘n’ roll, singer-songwriter, folk, you can even be a little bit jazz, and it’s all accepted in the community of Americana. And I think the term Americana is being reinvented as different than what it started as. and now it’s the place for people who want to take all the styles that have sort of, I guess, begun in America or become more mainstream through American culture, and mashing them up to be something that’s uniquely its own.
I think some of the freshest and most exciting music I’ve heard in the last five years has come out of the Americana quote-unquote “scene.” So I find myself working and producing a lot of artists that are under that umbrella. But to me, they’re also all, like, either a rock ‘n’ roll artist or someone like Maggie Rose, who is like soul meets singer-songwriter. So when you’re asking me about, is it women, or… For me, I think right now it’s that it has to resonate in a way that’s pushing genre forward. And if we’re gonna still use use those genre terms like Americana, pop and alt rock, Americana is the place where I feel like you can kind of be anything. I wouldn’t be shocked if somebody put out a space-dance-country-folk record. You can kind of be anything in it and you’re welcomed into the party, as long as the thing that ties it together is the music’s played by real people. There’s great lyrics, whether it’s storytelling or more abstract. And I’m not anti-AI, but I feel like gives the identity to Americana music is that humans created it all. It’s the human touch music.
You have come to feel very comfortable in Americana, though it’s not at all where you started. And with your new album being pretty acoustic, you’re pretty in the pocket with that at the moment.
Yeah, the last three albums, I’ve pretty much focused on that, and that’s been the community that’s welcomed me, so it’s the one I want to identify myself with and support. But if I want to go make a jazz record for the next one, I’m gonna go make it. If it’s called jazz or Americana, I don’t really care. It’s come up a lot that it’s been hard to label what I do, and that’s fine with me. I love Beck, and Beck’s hard to label as well. David Bowie, I don’t even know what the label of that music would be, you know?. He started as a folk artist, and then was a rocker, and then was a pop star, and then was kind of an abstraction star.
You met and talked with David Bowie, and he had an impact on your thinking about things,, right?
I met David Bowie early on when I was starting my solo career. I’d disbanded my band with my brothers called Living Things that we were doing for 13 years, and I was exhausted. I’d met David Bowie, and I had a song that I had just written called “Montauk Fling,” and I showed it to him. I said, “Hey, I think I’m starting this new chapter of my musical existence, and what do you think of this?” Because it was very different from what I’d done before. And he listened to it, and gave me some great advice. He was just like, “The chorus that you’re singing about there, and the verses, do you mean it?” And I’m like, “Well, yeah!” And he’s like, “But what’s the meaning of it?” So I had to explain it to him. And he’s like, “Well, I don’t think you hit the meaning of it. You need to be more direct.” And so I went back in and rewrote that chorus, and I was very direct. The chorus (ended up being) “Why do you want to fuck like strangers?” I got right to the meaning of what I was trying to say. But that was a really interesting exercise from such an icon, because I had never really looked at David Bowie’s lyrics as I do Leonard Cohen’s per se.
At that point he was about to do “Blackstar,” and when you listen to that record, it’s very much him, autobiographical. He’s about to die. And so I guess he was at a point of what is the meaning of all of what we’re doing in art? — and he was examining it in his own self with “Blackstar.” And I wrote that down in my journal at the time: “David Bowie says, ‘What’s the meaning of all of this?'” It led me to start writing this song called “Glory,” which was on my album “Good Morning America.” A lot of people responded well to it, so when I got to this new record, I wanted to keep exploring what Bowie had said with that. I started the record with the song “The Meaning,” because it’s like, what is the meaning of me putting out music, or any of us putting out music? It’s very ego-driven. As a musician, you’re out there playing rock star — or you’re not, and that’s also playing rock star. If it’s all performance, what is the meaning of doing any of it? With him, I felt like I got to a result of, like, the meaning of doing any of it is just to tell some kind of solid story that somebody can understand, that when they’re going through it, they can go, “That’s pulling me through this hard time.”
For Bowie with “Blackstar,” obviously that was cathartic to write about death because he was dying. With “The Meaning,” I wrote about, why am I putting this album out right now? Why am I doing this music? I’m doing it because it’s my primal scream. It’s my therapy.
You are calling this album, “Here Lies Love/Sawdust to Stardust,” the conclusion to a triology, which began for you with 2021’s “Good Morning, America” and had its middle part with 2024’s “The Plow That Broke the Plains,” which we previously discussed for Variety. Why do you think of them as a trilogy?
Henry Miller is one of my favorite writers of all time, and his his trilogy called “Sexus, Plexus and Nexus” was in my psyche my whole life. I thought, “One day I want to make a record that has the feeling of that, as far as telling a story across three pieces of work.” So when I went into the first record, “Good Morning America,” that was the clean slate. I said to myself, “I’m gonna do this trilogy now, starting with the South,” and it brought me to Nashville. I knew that I wanted to get back to letting songs and lyrics be the forefront of what I was doing as an artist; less so, production, because I had been doing records where I felt the production was kind of the centerpiece. I had gotten to a stage in my life where storytelling and the lyrics and presenting things that were the true me. At the beginning of my career, I was nine different people. I used prosthetics and I had nine different names and I performed different concerts as different alters, as I called them. I did that for seven years and it kind of just overtook my whole lifestyle. So at the top of that 2021 record, I wanted to get back to “this is what I’m going through” on the page with some chords behind it.
So the start of the trilogy was with that idea, and I connected with Lucinda Williams, who has been a huge influence on my life on every level. On that record, she sang with me on a song called “Decent Man,” and that brought me to Nashville. I’d come here as a kid to record, I fell back in love with the city and the scene, and then that record just sort of dictated where I was gonna go. I started writing more songs from that record that appeared on the last record, “The Plow That Broke the Plains,” and then a few of those songs I wrote during that period have appeared now on this one. I brought back some of the same collaborators throughout the three records. Katie Pruitt is on the first one, and now she’s on the last one with me. Amanda Shires is on all three. And Jason Isbell is on the last one and the new one. We wrote a song called “Nothing Like Shakespeare” together in the same three hours that we wrote a song off my last record called “Poster Child.”
Both of those songs, “Nothing Like Shakespeare” and “Poster Child,” sort of tell my origin story. “Poster Child” tells the story of what I went through as an artist at a young age, being signed at eight different major labels and getting dropped and getting signed again, and them sort of using my story as fodder for press and things like that, and how I felt like I got a little bit taken advantage of. “Nothing Like Shakespeare” is how I got to L.A. to get that first record deal. I lived with this girl who was the first love of my life, and we broke up when we got to L.A. In the lyric, I say, “I took the bus, she took the house,” because that’s what literally happened. I got a new record deal with a band with my brothers, and I’ll never forget the bus pulling up at our house, and I came out with everything I had, and it was done.
So, that’s the backstory with the trilogy situation. I hope one day people have the attention span to sit with it and listen from song one, which was “Thrash the West” on that first record in 2021, to the final song on this record, which is “Sawdust to Stardust.” Because basically that is the opening and the ending of this sort of filmic record that I’ve made that tells my complete adulthood story of the trials and tribulations I went through and how I got into music.
Is it a cathartic story, overall?
You know, it’s been a painful experience being in music, I’m not gonna lie. But it’s something that I can’t live without. Every time through the years that I’ve gone “I give up,” the next morning I wake up and I’m at the piano or guitar. My wife laughs at me about it because I give up, like, once a year. But I can’t get away from it. I’ve been on stage playing music since I was 8 years old; got my first record deal at 16. And it has more to do with the act of creation than it has to do with the fame or the fortune. I always say to my wife, “You can’t have a little hallelujah without a little hell.”
I’ve been on this journey a long time, and I’ve never gotten famous, and that’s never been my goal. There’s a lot of expectations you get from family members and things like that of like, “Why don’t I see you on late night TV?” Or “Why aren’t you over here on the radio?” That’s part of what I call the stress pool of making art, is the expectations of your audience, of your family, of your friends. For me, art’s always been about the act of creation. I don’t really care about who likes it or who doesn’t. There’s many people who only like my first album that I did, which was very indie pop, and all this newer singer-songwriter stuff, they don’t like. I lost probably thousands and thousands of fans, but I don’t care. It’s not why I’ve gotten into this. … When you’re in the mercy seat as a musician, and there’s all this expectation, regardless if you’re famous or not famous, but you always have a fan base. And I just find I have to stay true to myself, and with that brings a lot of hell, you know?
I don’t think I can really write stories about other people. Unless it’s a friend of mine and I’m observing it, it has to be something connected to me. Those types of writers that can just kind of observe from afar and write about it, that to me is more like work, and I can do that for other people, because I write a lot for other people. But for me, when I’m writing my own songs, if there’s not some weight behind it that’s resonant with my real life, I feel like it’s empty words. So it’ll always be autobiographical, I think. But hopefully, next time, I’m thinking it’s gonna be happy. Maybe I’ll have my Bobby McFerrin moment, you know?
Going back to the song “The Meaning,” a press release said you were donating proceeds to the Trevor Project. Why that cause?
I’m doing a portion of my whole album for it, but for that one song, I’m giving the full. If let’s say it got synced in a movie or something — which is hopefully what will happen; Madi Diaz and I originally wrote it for a movie that got shelved — I’m giving the full fee to the Trevor Project. You know, growing up being torn apart to pieces daily, it’s part of why I moved to L.A., because it was a little bit more acceptable to just be yourself. So I feel like I want to support what they’re doing as much as I possibly can. I’m not a rich person, but, I do put out art, and I can afford to help in the way that I can help, which is through my art, basically. And I’ve had a lot of people reach out to me since (the song went online). It’s ticking the box where somebody will listen to it, they’re having a bad day, and it’s lifting them. So I felt like that’s an appropriate song for that cause, because a lot of those kids are really going through it, and the song mirrors that there’s hope, you know? I went through it, and I’m still here. And I’m glad I did. I found meaning in my existence of why I was a little bit different growing up than everybody else. That created who I am today, which is completely unique. Back in the day, people picking on my physical appearance used to kill me. Now I take all that and I just put it in a song. So that’s the meaning of me being a little bit odder than everybody else.
You look like a rock star now, but if that’s how you looked growing up, there are reasons to understand why that might not have been the popular thing. Missouri is not the rock star milieu.
It was a lot of shit. You know, my mom was always the type of person where it’s like, “Be you. You’re an individual. Be yourself.” And I could wear a dress; I could wear a cowboy hat and no shirt with cut-off jean shorts if I wanted. She didn’t give a shit. I could put makeup on, do whatever I wanted to do, so I was always super eccentric. Back then, the word everybody would use was “androgynous.” That was how I was defined in the ’90s growing up, is like, “Oh, that’s the androgynous kid.” Growing up in Missouri, and you get a lot of heat for being not an athlete or at least dressing like an athlete.
To ask about another song on the new album, “Worn Out Woman” — was that inspired by anyone in particular?
I’m glad you brought up that one. Nobody’s asked about that, and that’s one of my favorite ones. It’s about my wife (Floria Sigismondi, known as the writer-director of “The Runaways” and dozens of music videos going back to the early ’90s). She’s a director and photographer, and she’s been doing it professionally for about 35 years, and is highly successful at it. She actually grew up in a time when there were no women directors, and came to work with people from Bowie to Rihanna. As time went on, I could tell that the weight of misogyny in the business of film was hitting her hard. and one night she was in the process of making her upcoming movie and a lot of stuff was being thrown at her. Her mother was dying. I sat at the piano and started to come up with that, and I kept it in my back pocket. I got together with a great songwriter called Amy Wadge (known as the co-author of Ed Sheeran’s “Thinking Out Loud”), who came over to my house the next week. She was like, “Let me hear it,” and afterward, she was like, “I’m gonna cry. That’s me.” And so I said, “Well, let’s write that. Let’s finish that.”
Amy’s got a record coming out, too, and she’s about the same age as my wife. She was telling me the parallel story of how she’s been the head of the family, or the light bearer, and that’s the same with my wife. My wife grew up with her sister and her parents, and she was like the parent. And that, mixed with being a woman director in Hollywood, is intense. She ironically directed three episodes of “The Handmaid’s Tale.” And she did this thing for Sigur Rós where it was like gas masks and art sort of become reality. She was like, “I don’t know about that song. I don’t want that to become my reality, (that) I’m worn out.” I’m like, “No, no! We’re just doing the the primal scream. We’re just screaming out the bad vibes on it and now it’s gone. Now you’re not worn out…” I told her, “I think a lot of other women will feel similar and see themselves in it.” It’s a testimony.
About another new song, “A Word’s a Weapon” — was that prompted by contemporary discourse?
It’s a saying that I’ve said my whole life, actually. I would just be like, your words are weapons and they go cut through me like a knife. I don’t know why it never dawned on me to write it in a song. But the political state that we’re in right now is so loaded and so huge and so even sometimes even beyond my comprehension. The one thing I know for sure, especially in the United States of America, is that people can hurt each other, like on steroids, 10 times more, by the things that they say than actually pushing them down the stairs. It’s really hard sometimes to wash off what somebody said to you, because it cuts harder than a punch or a fall or even getting stabbed. It’s just something that really psychologically changes you. And the way Americans speak to each other is so rancid and vile. I’n this country, I think everybody just needs to wash their mouths off with soap and pick up some books and just relearn how to talk to one another.

President Donald Trump’s new assistant press secretary — a former reporter for Real America's Voice — once posed for a photo with a rifle while wearing a "f*** Joe Biden" T-shirt and was a fan of slain conservative influencer Charlie Kirk.
Beni Rae Harmony, 24, announced on Friday that she will join Trump's White House press team as the new assistant press secretary. Anti-MAGA accounts on Instagram quickly found the photo of Harmony in her anti-Biden shirt, according to The Daily Beast.
The photo was posted by former Republican Virginia congressional candidate Jarome Bell in 2021. The post includes the caption "My campaign Public Affairs Director @beniraeharmony is a beast. This is how we roll."
Harmony's Instagram account liked the post. Bell ran for Congress in 2022 in Virginia Beach.
Harmony will join the White House's communications team following a staff shakeup that included the departure of former Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt in August.
"It's been an honor to report, travel, and cover this historic administration as Senior White House Correspondent for Real America's Voice. My goal has always been to ask questions that matter to real Americans and make sure their voices are heard," Harmony wrote in a post announcing her hiring. "I'm incredibly grateful to President Trump for this opportunity and his trust."
Harmony formerly worked for the far-right broadcaster Real America's Voice, which always airs Steve Bannon's weekday show, The Charlie Kirk Show, and Ted Nugent's Spirit Campfire.
She said she joined the broadcaster after she was suspended from her previous place of employment, WICS-ABC20 in Springfield, Illinois, allegedly for sharing an unprompted on-air tribute to Kirk following his 2025 assassination.
Harmony defended her decision to air the memorial, calling it "non-partisan."
She previously worked at Kirk's Turning Point USA conservative youth organization in 2020 and 2021. Harmony said she considered Kirk a "mentor."
Her LinkedIn profile says she also interned for Arizona Republican Congressman Paul Gosar and former Florida Congressman Matt Gaetz.
Harmony may have caught Trump's eye during a trip to Ireland last month, where she was present as a reporter on Air Force One.
Anna Kelly, the White House principal deputy press secretary, confirmed Harmony's new role in a statement.
“Beni Rae Harmony has been a trusted voice for the MAGA movement as a White House correspondent,” Kelly said. “She will be an outstanding addition to President Trump’s communications team as an assistant press secretary. We look forward to having her on board.”

Swyer syndrome is a rare condition in which a person is born with XY chromosomes, the combination usually associated with males, but their reproductive organs develop along a typically female pattern. The person typically has female external anatomy and a uterus and fallopian tubes.
The condition often goes unnoticed during childhood and comes to light during adolescence, when puberty does not progress normally or menstruation does not begin. It can also be diagnosed later during investigations for infertility. Here’s all you need to know about Swyer syndrome.
What is Swyer syndrome?
Swyer syndrome is a rare difference of sex development, medically known as 46,XY complete gonadal dysgenesis. According to the US’ Genetic and Rare Diseases Information Center, a person with the condition has a 46,XY chromosome pattern, but the gonads do not develop into functioning testes. Instead, they remain as small, non-functioning structures called “streak gonads”. The person generally develops female external genitalia, while the uterus and fallopian tubes are usually present. The condition is estimated to occur in about one in 80,000 people,
Swyer syndrome results from disruption of the genetic pathway involved in testicular development during early embryonic development. The SRY gene, located on the Y chromosome, plays an important role in initiating this process. However, an SRY mutation is not found in every person with Swyer syndrome.
What are the symptoms?
Swyer syndrome may not be apparent during childhood and often comes to light during adolescence, when puberty does not progress normally. One of the most characteristic signs is primary amenorrhoea, meaning that menstruation does not begin.
Delayed or incomplete development of secondary sexual characteristics can also prompt investigation. Because the streak gonads do not produce sufficient sex hormones, spontaneous breast development may be limited. The condition can sometimes remain undiagnosed even when a person reaches adulthood.
How is Swyer syndrome diagnosed?
Diagnosis usually involves looking at the person’s chromosomes, hormone levels and reproductive anatomy. Karyotyping, a test that examines the number and structure of chromosomes, typically shows a 46,XY pattern in Swyer syndrome. Blood tests generally show evidence of gonadal failure, including low levels of sex hormones and elevated levels of hormones such as follicle-stimulating hormone and luteinising hormone. Ultrasound or MRI can be used to examine the uterus and the gonads.
Genetic testing can be used to investigate the underlying cause, including variants in SRY and other genes involved in gonadal development. However, not finding an SRY mutation does not exclude Swyer syndrome. In some patients, even more extensive genetic testing may not identify the precise molecular cause.
Can Swyer syndrome be treated?
There is currently no treatment that can change the 46,XY chromosome pattern or turn the streak gonads into functioning ovaries. However, the effects of Swyer syndrome can be effectively managed. Hormone replacement therapy, usually involving oestrogen and subsequently an appropriate progestogen regimen when indicated, is used to induce and maintain puberty, support development of secondary sexual characteristics and protect bone health.
The streak gonads also need to be assessed because they carry an increased risk of gonadoblastoma, a type of germ-cell tumour. Decisions about gonadectomy and its timing are now generally individualised according to the underlying diagnosis and tumour risk.
Fertility is another important consideration. Because the streak gonads cannot produce eggs, people with Swyer syndrome cannot conceive using their own eggs. However, if the uterus is present and sufficiently developed, pregnancy can be possible through IVF using a donated egg or embryo. Research shows that patients with Swyer syndrome can have successful pregnancies following endometrial preparation with hormones and IVF using donated eggs. Following pregnancy and delivery, continued hormone replacement is important for maintaining bone health.
In other words, Swyer syndrome itself cannot currently be reversed, but its effects can be managed. Hormone replacement can address the absence of normal gonadal hormones, removal of the streak gonads can reduce the risk of tumours, and assisted reproductive techniques can make pregnancy possible for some patients.

Co-pilot in FlyDubai incident is identified as Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami
The co-pilot suspected of stabbing the captain on an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight has been identified as an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami
CAIRO -- The co-pilot suspected of stabbing the captain of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight before passengers and others stopped the attack is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami, three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and Western diplomat, said on Saturday.
All spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.
The Gulf diplomat said investigations are underway to establish whether he acted as a “lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups.”
The co-pilot, who officials said nearly crashed the sharply plummeting flight with 182 people aboard, was barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a person familiar with the matter said.
The co-pilot was then hired by the United Arab Emirates-based airline FlyDubai, the person said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation. It was not immediately clear to what extent he was vetted when he was hired. Oman’s barring of him was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
How the co-pilot managed to be working in the cockpit on Wednesday morning is a central question for investigators.
Israel says has it has long-standing agreements with foreign carriers to keep pilots from flying into the country if they are citizens of nations that don’t maintain diplomatic relations with Israel. Israel and Oman do not have formal diplomatic relations.
There was no immediate comment from FlyDubai, the UAE government or Oman Air. Oman’s government has said nothing publicly in response to repeated questions since the incident.
UAE senior diplomatic adviser Anwar Gargash on Friday called the attack a “dangerous terrorist act” in a post on X. The incident is a test for the UAE government, which has earned a reputation for effective measures against extremist activities but has also bristled in the past over criticism of security lapses.
Little else was immediately known about the co-pilot’s background. His Instagram account was active until the day of the flight and then deleted.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radicalization,” but provided no evidence.
The captain, who was badly wounded, has said he used his remaining energy while being stabbed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing people who had noticed alarmingly unusual sounds to come in, tackle the co-pilot and stabilize the plane. It made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Investigators have not publicly identified the object used to stab the captain or said whether it was carried onto the plane or came from inside the aircraft.
Both the captain and co-pilot were later taken to the UAE as it leads the investigation. Officials have said a number of countries including Israel are participating.
___
Mednick reported from Tel Aviv, Israel. AP Washington bureau chief Anna Johnson contributed to this report from Washington.

Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
- Published
The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar.
Capt Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia.
The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tubak City, north-western Saudi Arabia, where he remains in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh.
Writing on X, Netanyahu said Capt Machchhar "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster".
What do we know about Capt Machchhar?
Capt Machchhar joined Flydubai in 2022 - he was an experienced pilot by then, having worked at Indian airline SpiceJet since 2011.
He has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".
Last year, Capt Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.
Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work with his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]," he added.
Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.
"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.
He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.
"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.
At the time of the conversation, Capt Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had had to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues causing delays.
He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."
Indian social media has been awash with praise for Capt Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.
What happened on the Flydubai flight?
Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.
The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.
Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.
Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.
At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.
Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.
Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.
But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.
He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".
The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-eastern Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.
The stabbed pilot, who is in a stable condition according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia, was later identified as Capt Machchhar.
Modi and Trump praise Capt Machchhar
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.
"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.
Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".
Speaking to reporters at the White House, US President Donald Trump said that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.
"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

A marine biologist says the smell of a whale carcass recently removed from the Clarence River will attract sharks.
The carcass has been taken out to sea a day after it was spotted on a sandbar near Iluka on the Mid North Coast.
What's next?
The marine biologist says people should wait about a week before entering the water.
A marine biologist says sharks are likely to be attracted to a New South Wales sandbar where a dead whale was left for more than a day.
Crown Lands worked to remove the carcass from the Clarence River west of Iluka on the Mid North Coast. It was taken out to sea on Sunday afternoon.
Volunteer whale rescue organisation ORRCA was notified about the whale at 1:30pm on Saturday.
An ORRCA spokesperson said there were concerns that the juvenile humpback may have been stranded, but volunteers found it deceased.
The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development released a warning on Shark Smart social media accounts stating that increased shark activity had been reported.
Macquarie University marine biologist Culum Brown said the smell of the carcass would linger.
"If it's been there for that long it will already be leaching all sorts of good smells into the river and the surrounds, and the sharks will certainly be able to smell that for a long way," he said.
"I would be making sure that nobody was swimming in the river or the adjacent beaches.
"My advice would be to stay out of the water for the next week or so, which is not what people want to hear on the long weekend."
Dr Brown said he was surprised that the whale had travelled 11 kilometres up the river.
"That doesn't happen every day," he said.
"To get that far up a river is very strange, it makes me wonder if perhaps a mother and calf did come into the mouth and perhaps the mother turned away and the baby kept going."
Footage of the deceased whale was recorded by Brooms Head photographer Amiria Takarangi.
She said filming the animal it was unsettling.
"It felt wrong, honestly. But I reminded myself why I do this — to show compassion, to understand, and to share whatever knowledge I can gather," Ms Takarangi said.

India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
Kumar has become a highly contentious figure after a report in the Indian Express newspaper alleged irregularities and internal concerns about a process to revise and “purify” India’s electoral register, called the Special Intensive Revision (SIR).
SIR, which was overseen by Kumar, has resulted in tens of millions of people being deleted from the electoral register. Large numbers are challenging their removal.
Opposition politicians and civil society groups have alleged SIR is part of a widespread manipulation of India’s electoral system to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
The CJP began as online satire but grew into a powerful manifestation of youth power and an unexpected challenge to the Narendra Modi government. There were protests for weeks in the heart of Delhi and the education minister was eventually pressured into resigning in July. In the aftermath, the group declared it would remain active as a “pressure group” to hold the government to account on issues of education and democracy.
Last week, after the revelations about the election commission, the CJP’s founder, Abhijeet Dipke, announced that if Kumar did not resign over the controversy, the “Cockroaches” would resume their agitation until he stepped down. Dipke said the Mumbai protest would kick off a nationwide movement, with more protests planned in Delhi, Goa, Kolkata and Bengaluru.
The authorities denied permission for the group to hold their protest at Mumbai’s Shivaji park but Dipke had vowed to go ahead regardless. “We are fighting against those in power,” he said, at a press conference. “We all remember Mahatma Gandhi, who fought against the Britishers. Did the British ever permit him to agitate?”
Hundreds of people assembled in Mumbai on Friday afternoon, amid a heavy police presence, including many young people who said they were there to fight for India’s democracy.
“Voting is the most basic right of any citizen, but because of the actions of Kumar and the election commission, that right is under attack,” said Deesha, 22, a student activist. “So many millions of people have lost their votes and aren’t even recognised as citizens of India any more. This attack on our democracy must stop. The first important step is to get Gyanesh Kumar to resign, and then SIR must be reversed.”
Janvi Upadhyay, 18, said that the Cockroach movement had awoken the young people of India “and if they think they can just come and take away votes and cheat the elections, we will show them just how wrong they are”.
“We already forced the education minister to resign. Gyanesh Kumar should be very worried right now because he is definitely next,” she said.
The election commission has denied wrongdoing in the SIR but in a move that appeared aimed at easing tensions, officials were directed to expedite the process to register newly eligible voters and those who claimed to have been wrongly omitted from electoral rolls.
Anger at Kumar and the election commission also erupted in Delhi on Friday, even as the police took draconian measures to try and stop people from protesting. Thousands of police were deployed to the Jantar Mantar protest site in Delhi – which was the epicentre of the last Cockroach agitation in July – a dozen metro stations in the surrounding area were closed and an internet shutdown was imposed.
Hundreds of those who turned out to Jantar Mantar were immediately forced into police buses. The mass detentions of at least 700 people, including civil society leaders and opposition politicians, prompted outrage, with protesters leaning out of the bus windows to accuse police officers of depriving them of their fundamental democratic rights.
Opposition parties said they would also start a nationwide protest movement to demand Kumar’s resignation. All opposition lawmakers plan to march to the election commission office in Delhi next week.

Spotlight on new coaches as road to Afcon 2027 begins
- Published
Just eight months on from the final of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) - and with the world still waiting to find out the ultimate destination of the title - the road to the 2027 tournament begins in earnest.
The 48 sides still in contention will play two rounds of qualifying in this extended international window, which gets under way on Thursday.
Two more matches follow in November, with the groups reaching their denouement with the final two fixtures in March.
The top two in nine of the 12 groups will progress to the 24-team finals in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda.
Preparations for the tournament in East Africa may be lagging behind but, with the three hosts all guaranteed qualification, there is only one spot on offer in their respective groups. That means a second-placed finish may potentially not be enough.
Several managerial changes have occurred since the last Afcon in Morocco and this year's Fifa World Cup, while several star players have hung up their boots. Here's what to keep an eye on in the first two rounds of action.
- Senegal appeal date set after Afcon win overturned 
  - Published24 July
Big names in the dugout
Among several coaching changes, two in particular have caught the eye.
Herve Renard, the only man to win Afcon with two different nations, has returned to the Ivory Coast job some 11 years after leading the West Africans to the title.
The 57-year-old Frenchman starts his second stint with the Elephants at home against Ghana on Thursday in what is the standout match in the first round of fixtures.
In the opposing dugout, the experienced Carlos Queiroz is back at the helm after leading the Black Stars to the last 32 at the World Cup. However, Tottenham's Mohammed Kudus is among a number of players to withdraw from his squad.
Patrick Vieira is another high-profile arrival, as the 1998 World Cup champion with France takes charge of Senegal, the country of his birth.
The former Arsenal midfielder, 50, describes the role as "an absolute dream" yet he will begin with two away games against Mozambique and Ethiopia because Dakar is getting ready to host the 2026 Youth Olympics.
- Africa prepares for historic Olympic moment at Dakar 2026 
  - Published23 July
Other new arrivals
Cape Verde were one of the great stories of the 2026 World Cup, pushing Argentina all the way in the last 32 before the debutants lost 3-2 after extra time.
Long-serving coach Bubista has since resigned from the Blue Sharks hotseat, with his former assistant Humberto Bettencourt stepping up.
He will begin his reign in Mali on Friday before hosting Rwanda on Tuesday.
Algeria, Tunisia and South Africa have also changed coaches since the World Cup.
The Tunisians have turned to former Esperance and Renaissance Berkane boss Moin Chaaban as they aim to move on from their disastrous World Cup campaign which saw Sabri Lamouchi dismissed after one game and Renard fail to orchestrate a revival.
Pitso Mosimane has been reappointed by South Africa some 14 years on from his last spell in charge - which saw Bafana Bafana miss out on the 2012 Afcon - and Brahim Hemdani has taken over Algeria after Vladmir Petkovic's departure.
Meanwhile, Afcon legend Claude Le Roy has returned at the age of 78 after signing on for a second stint with Congo-Brazzaville.
The Red Devils have not appeared at the finals since 2015, while Frenchman Le Roy is aiming to coach at a record-extending 10th edition of the finals.
Burkina Faso have turned to ex-Comoros boss Amir Abdou and, after a stint with Libya, 2021 Afcon-winning coach Aliou Cisse has his first competitive matches in charge of Angola.
The former Senegal boss starts with a tough away assignment in Egypt.
An era ends
Some big-name players have called time on their international careers since the World Cup, with several of them former Afcon winners.
Senegal are looking for a new number one after Edouard Mendy hung up his goalkeeping gloves.
The 34-year-old helped the Teranga Lions become champions at the 2021 and 2025 tournaments - even if the latter title is still disputed at the Court of Arbitration for Sport.
Wing wizard Riyad Mahrez, who captained Algeria to the trophy in 2019, has quit international duty while Ivory Coast will have to cope without midfielders Seko Fofana and Jean-Michael Seri.
Ellyes Skhiri has also called time on his international career and will not be involved as Tunisia aim to reach a record-extending 18th consecutive Afcon.
Meanwhile, Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang has stepped back from Gabon duty, saying he felt "humiliated" by his treatment after their exit at the previous tournament.
The 37-year-old was excluded from the national team set-up after their group-stage exit. That sanction was later lifted, but Aubameyang ruled himself out of Sebastien Migne's Panthers squad despite his fine start to the season with Deportivo La Coruna.
Return of the Red Sea Camels
Elsewhere, Eritrea are back in the group stage of Afcon qualifiers - for the first time since the build-up to the 2008 edition - after seeing off Eswatini 4-1 on aggregate in the preliminary round in March.
Chad, Djibouti, Mauritius, Sao Tome and Principe and Seychelles are the other five nations already eliminated.
However, seven Ertirea players absconded after the away leg of their tie which was held in South Africa.
Occurrences of Eritrean sportsmen and women failing to return home to what is a one-party state and a highly militarised society has long been an issue, and was part of the reason for the East Africans withdrawing from qualifying for both the 2023 Afcon and 2026 World Cup.
Yet the Red Sea Camels, who have been drawn alongside Kenya, South Africa and Guinea in Group D, are now largely relying on talent drawn from the diaspora.
Just three home-based players have been named in the squad for their opening two fixtures, which see them take on the tournament co-hosts in Nairobi on Saturday before a 'home' game against Bafana Bafana in Cairo on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, Somalia have reached the group stage of qualifying for the first ever time but face a very tricky draw alongside Ivory Coast, Ghana and The Gambia.
The Ocean Stars are ranked 53rd on the continent but, like Eritrea, can at least dream of reaching Afcon as the tournament returns to East Africa for the first time since 1976.

How ‘Israel’s 9/11’ was averted after midair stabbing as co-pilot’s motive remains a mystery
Passengers on Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv have been celebrated as heroes for preventing disaster. Maira Butt looks at how it all unfolded

When the first reports about a diverted flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv came through on Wednesday, it appeared to have been caused by a tussle between two pilots.
Early claims even suggested one was Russian and the other Ukrainian.
But, in the age of social media, the true chaos aboard the FlyDubai Flight FZ1073 quickly came to light. Footage and images sent from the plane by blood-covered passengers showed them overpowering the co-pilot, who it later emerged was an Omani national.
The plane, a Boeing 737 MAX aircraft, was carrying over 170 people from Dubai to Tel Aviv when it plunged more than 17,000ft in two minutes as the fight broke out. An emergency alert was sent out and the plane changed course towards Jordan, eventually landing in Saudi Arabia.
Aviation experts told the BBC that the rapid descent led to damage pictured on the plane’s rudder adding that the incident could easily have led to the plane breaking up in mid-air.
Captain Smit Machchhar, an Indian national, was identified as the victim of the attack, while his arrested co-pilot was identified as Hamam al-Hammami on Saturday by sources cited in CNN.
The motive for the incident is still being determined but Netanyahu’s administration suggested early on that it was a suspected terror attack.
‘Blood everywhere’
A six-year-old on her way to the toilet accompanied by her mother, was the first to raise the alarm when the pair heard shouting coming from the cockpit, prompting cabin crew to rush to the scene. What they saw was a blood-spattered scene.
“There was blood all over the cockpit and very, very sharp fighting moves,” Nina Manes’ mother, Tali Manes told Israel’s Channel 12.
“I screamed, ‘He’s stabbing the pilot, he’s stabbing the pilot, come help!’ People looked at me and didn’t understand.”
Her husband Tzvika Manes said: “The shrieks of my daughters when the plane nose-dived [are still with me]. They said, ‘Dad we don’t want to die.’ [Their cries] were the triggers that caused me to run inside the cockpit.”
One passenger recorded the ordeal on his phone and later shared the footage to social media. With blood dripping down his face, he declared that the passengers had “subdued the terrorists”. “Whoever is hearing me, we need help,” he added.
On Saturday, UAE prosecutors said Cpt Machchhar had been attacked by a “crash axe”, a tool kept in the cockpit in case of emergencies, bypassing stringent security protocols.
Yaniv Hayun, a 50-year-old owner of a sewage plumbing company, was travelling with his wife and two daughters when the incident took place.
In his blood-spattered t-shirt, he was hailed as a hero by Netanyahu who personally thanked him for helping to subdue the attacker and to prevent the plane from crashing.
Along with Tzvika Manes and Asaf Rajuan, he broke into the cockpit to stop the attacker. By mimicking gestures he says he’d see on television, Hayun “grabbed the controls and started pulling back the handles”. He said he’d learned the techniques from watching Air Crash Investigation.
He said it took 20 to 25 minutes to fully subdue and bind the pilot and they used cords from headphones linked to the plane’s entertainment system.
Hayun was helped by a dentist, Dr Shota Musayev, who administered “life-saving medical treatment” to Cpt Machchhar, including treating him for severe wounds to his head and cuts to his fingers. He helped to successfully stop the bleeding and to stabilise his blood pressure before emergency surgery.
All five are expected to receive Israel’s Presidential Award for Civilian Heroism, president Isaac Herzog said on Thursday.
Both pilots have been transferred to the UAE for further investigations and for medical treatment.
‘Suicidal and indoctrinated’
Netanyahu told Fox News that the attacker was “suicidal” and called out to the crew: “kill me, kill me!” after he was subdued.
“It’s clear he was suicidal, that’s not a question,” he added. The Israeli leader said that he had undergone a “Islamist radical indoctrination” and promised to reveal whether he had connections to Iran in the coming days.
The prime minister said those onboard managed to “prevent a 9/11 disaster, because that's what it looks like was happening”, claiming that the intent may have been to crash the plane.
A regional official familiar with the FlyDubai investigation told the Associated Press that investigators in Saudi Arabia were working with authorities from the UAE, US, Oman and Israel, and that “all possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into”.
“Nothing is ruled out for now”, the official said.
Al-Hammami was banned from flying last year over concerns that he had radical ideological views, according to Saudi state media.
Two Israeli security officials said that the co-pilot was probably acting alone, according to their initial assessments.
He was arrested by Saudi security forces after the plane landed in Tabuk, northwest Saudi Arabia, and was being questioned by investigators.
On Saturday, the UAE prosecutor general said that al-Hammami had attempted to carry out a “terrorist” attack, according to the country’s state news agency WAM.
Investigations are ongoing to determine the circumstances of the incident, the motives and any related connections, as well as to examine physical and digital evidence, he added.
Netanyahu said: “It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane … The Islamist tendencies, that radicalisation that are found in his background, I think that’s a pretty good clue.”
Warnings and questions over security
Opposition leader Yair Lapid said on Wednesday that politicians had been warned in a national security briefing the night before that Israel’s enemies could attack in the run up to the country’s elections due to take place on 27 October.
A ban on pilots from states without formal relations to Israel was not enforced appropriately, according to a report cited by the Times of Israel.
Under the law, pilots from nations including Oman, which does not have formal ties with Israel, were banned from flying but airlines and security agencies did not enforce the rule.
Furthermore, Israel’s security agency, Shin Bet, had raised concerns about flights from the UAE for months before the incident.
Shin Bet director David Zini had reportedly clashed with Israeli airlines over restrictions on flights to the UAE, reasoning that security measures at Emirati airports were insufficient, according to Israel’s N12 News.
Israeli authorities were concerned with possible missile attacks or attacks at an airport, the outlet reported on Thursday. A scenario like Wednesday’s hijacking attempt was “not raised in any discussion”, they said.

A rumor spread in late September 2026 that CNN television host Anderson Cooper built a free hospital for homeless people. According to the claim, the journalist opened the Anderson Cooper Homestead Medical Center in New York, complete with 250 beds, 120 apartments and a range of additional services — all at zero cost to patients.
Snopes readers searched our website and emailed us about the claim, with one reader asking, "Did Anderson Cooper build a free hospital for homeless people in New York?"
Several Facebook users shared the rumor. The posts generally featured the same image allegedly showing Cooper cutting a ribbon in front of a building with a sign reading, "Anderson Cooper Medical Center."
(Jeannette Piña via Facebook)
According to the posts, Cooper said of the hospital, "This is the legacy I want to leave behind." The facility allegedly cost $142 million, with the Anderson Cooper Foundation raising all funds from anonymous donors over an 18-month period — complete with no public fanfare or announcements until opening.
In short, the rumor is false. No evidence suggests Cooper opened a free hospital for homeless people. The claim is nothing more than "AI slop," spam-type content generated using artificial intelligence tools that has, in recent years, deluged social media with untrue stories, as well as fake images and videos, usually featuring public figures.
CNN spokesperson Shimrit Sheetrit said via email that the rumor is false.
Researching the claim
Searches of Bing, DuckDuckGo, Google and Yahoo uncovered no news media outlets reporting that Cooper opened a hospital. Even if a famous person secretly raised funds to open a hospital without publicity, news organizations would at some point publish articles about the facility's existence. Officials would eventually launch a website or use other online means to alert homeless people of the project and its offerings. No such information has been published or shared.
The story in the posts is inconsistent with the AI-generated images accompanying it. For example, the text in one post refers to the hospital as "Anderson Cooper Homestead Medical Center," while the image features a sign reading, "Anderson Cooper Medical Center." A different post (archived) contains other fake images of Cooper wearing completely different clothes at the supposed opening, with the different facility name, "The Anderson Cooper Center." The posts also say there was "no ribbon" and "no fanfare" at the supposed opening, despite the images containing both a ribbon and a crowd.
This claim possibly originated from a post on a Facebook page called The Silver Voice, which links to an external website hosting an advertisement-filled article. That website's domain name appears to be at least partially in Vietnamese, a language that often appears alongside "AI slop" website content, as Snopes has previously reported.
The heartwarming subject matter about Cooper's purported grand act of kindness resembles glurge, which Dictionary.com defines as "stories, often sent by email, that are supposed to be true and uplifting, but which are often fabricated and sentimental." Creators of such content capitalize on social media users' willingness to believe and share the made-up stories, profiting from advertising revenue on external websites to which the posts link. (Snopes has also previously reported on this business strategy.)
AI-generated content and similar rumors
A scan of the Facebook posts' text with AI detection tool Pangram displays the results, "We believe that this entire text is AI," and, "100% of this text is AI." A scan of one of the post's images returns the same result.
Snopes doesn't depend solely on AI detection tools, which vary in reliability, and instead considers the tools' results as one of several data points toward judging an image's authenticity. With Pangram, we bear in mind the platform's strong performance in third-party and internal evaluations, as well as some criticisms of the tool.
Reporters at fact-checking website Lead Stories previously reported on many other celebrities being named in similar "AI slop" stories about them opening free hospitals for homeless people.
Snopes also previously addressed a false claim that first lady Melania Trump and her son, Barron Trump, opened a hospital for homeless people, and a similar rumor about late-night host Stephen Colbert and his wife, Evelyn McGee-Colbert. The latter also features an AI-generated image that resembles the fake photo of Cooper.
For further reading, we previously reported about numerous fabricated stories that circulated online following the deadly Texas flash floods in July 2025, as well as how those false accounts show signs of originating in Southeast Asia.

Indian proposal for Ukraine truce ‘most comprehensive’, says Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha
Sybiha said similar proposals have been made by Turkey and Egypt, which proposed a truce in the Black Sea to restore grain exports from Ukraine.
Ukraine has received ceasefire proposals from four countries, including one from India that is the “most comprehensive”, Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha has said.
The other proposals were from Turkey, Egypt and the US, and Ukraine is ready for various options for a truce with Russia, Sybiha told reporters in Kyiv on Friday, according to a report by European Pravda.
Also read: Ukraine attacks major Russian refinery and oil pipeline hub with drones in Samara region
Ukraine is ready to consider different ceasefire formats, including along the front lines, but only if the truce covers attacks on energy and port infrastructure and the situation in the Black Sea, he said.
‘India’s proposal most comprehensive'
“We have four proposals. The most comprehensive is India’s proposal. We are ready for an energy and Black Sea truce, but only in this combination,” Sybiha said. “This [should be] a complete energy truce, a stop to attacks on all energy facilities, including port infrastructure.”
Sybiha said similar proposals have been made by Turkey and Egypt, which proposed a truce in the Black Sea to restore grain exports from Ukraine.
The fourth proposal by the US insists that Ukraine and Russia agree on an energy truce, he said. The US proposal was discussed during a meeting between President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump.
Also read: Russia-Ukraine tensions rising? Putin warns of using ‘all types of weapons’ if Kaliningrad attacked
“In general, we believe a truce could be one of the results of a meeting between President Zelensky and [Russian President Vladimir] Putin. We are ready for different formats of a truce, including an unconditional one along the line of contact,” Sybiha said.
Sybiha did not provide further details and it could not immediately be ascertained when India had made the proposal. There was no comment on the matter from Indian officials.
India's emphasis on ending the war
The Indian side has emphasised that it remains in touch with Russia and Ukraine and is ready to assist in ending the war, which New Delhi has repeatedly said has impacted food, fuel and fertiliser security, especially for the Global South.
While addressing the annual meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow on Thursday, Putin said Prime Minister Narendra Modi consistently raises the question of ending the conflict in Ukraine every time they meet. “He takes a keen interest in the matter and has excellent ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable…solutions. In this sense, [Modi] certainly maintains a neutral position while remaining committed to seeing the conflict end,” Putin said.
“We are also grateful to the Prime Minister for his ideas – I will not go into details now – and for his commitment to resolving this conflict, among others, peacefully and as quickly as possible,” he said.
Modi met Putin on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Kyrgyzstan in August and called for a shift from endless war to the end of war. The Ukraine conflict figured again in a meeting between Modi and Putin ahead of the Brics Summit in New Delhi last month. Modi last met Zelensky on the margins of the G7 Summit in France in June.
External affairs minister S Jaishankar travelled to Kyiv in early September, days after the meeting between Modi and Putin in Kyrgyzstan, and emphasised that the conflict cannot be resolved on the battlefield and that India stands ready to help in all efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

People who have a Medicare Advantage plan — and wind up needing care and prescriptions next year — are in for a rude awakening.
Medicare Advantage insurers are raising out-of-pocket costs for enrollees, drastically cutting money for dental work and other benefits, and eliminating plans that have broad networks of hospitals and doctors, according to federal data released this week and analyzed by STAT and several investment firms. That could result in more shock for older adults, like discovering their doctor is no longer accepted by their plan, if they don’t shop carefully during Medicare’s annual enrollment period for 2027 plans, which starts Oct. 15.
Big companies like UnitedHealth Group, Humana, and others are chasing higher profits by pruning benefits, after investors grew dissatisfied with margins that were smaller than the insurers had promised. The changes in plans even come even after the industry won a payment increase and delayed reforms from the Trump administration in April.
