I clawed my way to the top but need a break - Azpilicueta
- Published
Cesar Azpilicueta was an all-encompassing leader for Chelsea - and, now retired, he reflects on how his passion for education and attention to detail helped him build a career at the highest level.
One story sums it up. Before Chelsea's Champions League final victory in 2021, Azpilicueta could not take his customary pre-match nap and opted to study instead.
He says his work towards an MBA in business management from the Berlin School of Business and Innovation took his mind off the pressure and noise on the streets of Porto.
Later that day, he lifted the Champions League trophy after captaining Chelsea to victory against Manchester City.
Azpilicueta told BBC Sport: "When I was a kid my parents pushed me to get good grades and finish school.
"I wasn't a professional footballer until I was 17, in my last year of school. Education was always important. When Covid-19 arrived, we had more time.
"I found some courses but I didn't start because I thought it was the end of my career. It was more that I wanted to learn, improve myself and do it in another language.
"It wasn't because I thought it was my last year as a footballer, but it did help me navigate the final years of my career, become a better person and a better footballer."
Azpilicueta, 37, was speaking at Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, where he joked he did not feel "entirely comfortable", while collecting a diploma in global football sport directorship through the PFA Business School, adding to qualifications that also include a diploma from Harvard Business School.
Now retired from playing after spending last season at Sevilla, he replied "maybe" when asked whether he could become a sporting director one day, but says football has left him in need of a post-career break.
Now at a "different stage of life", he cannot even contemplate playing football with friends for fun because it would trigger his competitive instincts.
"It was time to stop playing football because, even though I could probably still play, I didn't have the energy to commit myself fully for an entire season," he reflected.
"At the moment I have another commitment, which is my family. I want to play some golf and enjoy life.
"For 20 years I was constantly travelling, playing and preparing for seasons. This summer looked completely different."
After beginning at boyhood club Osasuna, Azpilicueta joined Marseille, where he learned French. However, it was his move to Chelsea in 2012 that proved transformative.
'Chelsea made me who I am'
Completing his latest course highlights Azpilicueta's thirst for knowledge and a desire for constant self-improvement.
It was something he learned at Chelsea, where he arrived as a relatively low-profile £7m signing in a dressing room full of established leaders such as John Terry, Frank Lampard and Petr Cech, alongside star names including Fernando Torres, Eden Hazard and Ashley Cole.
He explained: "I started as a right winger, moved to France, then moved to Chelsea. I wasn't a star signing. I had to find my way. Left-back, wing-back, centre-back in a back three.
"It was about consistency. I had to work hard to stay fit, adapt to different managers and different positions.
"When you arrive at Chelsea, you feel the ambition straight away. Every three days you have to win. Every game and every trophy matters.
"That culture pushed me to the maximum and, especially when I left Chelsea, I felt that I had given everything I had for the club."
Azpilicueta explained how his education away from the pitch helped him develop into a leader at Stamford Bridge.
It gave him the confidence to represent Premier League players during the Covid-19 pandemic, while also helping to organise initiatives and keep the club moving forward after owner Roman Abramovich was sanctioned following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
His defining moment came in that 2021 Champions League final victory.
There is little doubt that, having succeeded Terry and then Gary Cahill as captain, Azpilicueta ranks among Chelsea's greatest leaders. Yet he revealed that, since leaving the club in 2023, he has not returned to Stamford Bridge.
He was among dozens of players to leave after Chelsea changed ownership from Abramovich to the current American-led consortium in 2022.
"I left Chelsea, but Chelsea will always stay in my heart," he said. "I follow every game and I hope the club comes back to where it belongs.
"There are some very strong teams around and football sometimes needs a bit of time. You need connections, people playing together and understanding each other.
"At a big club like Chelsea, the demands are high. But I think that's normal. It should be demanding and ambitious because, speaking as a Chelsea fan, you always want to see the club winning trophies.
"I have confidence that [manager] Xabi [Alonso], the staff and the players will do good work. Hopefully they can bring a lot of happiness to the fans."
He has been following Chelsea's latest captain Reece James, who he believes will grow into a better leader, since over-30 players Jordan Henderson, Danny Welbeck and Emiliano Martinez joined over the summer.
When it is suggested that he might return to Stamford Bridge in some capacity to be marked by a warm reception from supporters, Azpilicueta responds modestly: "I don't know about that.
"I will come back one day. I won't be putting on my boots, though."

The Supreme Court faces another term jam-packed with controversy
The U.S. Supreme Court formally opens a new term on Monday, with big test cases on religion, bans on semi-automatic weapons, climate change, immigration and — waiting in the wings — election law cases.
It used to be that the first Monday in October marked the beginning of a new Supreme Court term. And that's still true, technically. But for all practical purposes, the formerly quiet summer months after the court finishes its opinions in all argued cases no longer exists.
Indeed, as Georgetown University law professor Stephen Vladeck observes, the number of emergency appeals has ballooned during the Trump administration, while at the same time, fully briefed and argued cases have dropped precipitously over the years.
"So now we have twice as many full court rulings on emergency applications as we have on the merits docket," Vladeck observes, adding, "That is a very new phenomenon."
The difference is that decisions on the emergency docket are rendered quickly, with little briefing, no oral arguments, and ultimately little or no explanation of the ruling. In contrast, a decision on the merits is typically worked on for months after full briefing and lengthy oral arguments.
Of late, the court seems to be making an effort to offer some limited explanations of its emergency docket rulings, but lower court judges, both liberal and conservative, complain that isn't enough to provide them with adequate guidance. And the Trump administration often takes what used to be the rare step of getting to the Supreme Court by leapfrogging over lower appellate courts that the administration views as hostile.
With that backdrop, here are the cases the court will be hearing in the coming weeks:
Climate change
The opening case, to be argued Monday, tests whether state and local governments can sue energy companies for allegedly deceiving the public about the damaging effects of fossil fuels.
"The theory is that the energy company defendants deceived the public for many years," says Deepak Gupta, who teaches at Harvard Law School and practices law in Washington, D.C. What the companies were telling the public for years, he says, is "the opposite of what the company's own scientists knew, and the local cost of that deception."
That said, however, most court observers see the case as an uphill battle for environmentalists.
Religion
Perhaps the biggest case of the term so far, in terms of ripple effects, involves religion, a subject on which the court's conservative super majority has dramatically changed its legal doctrine. Indeed for the better part of a century, the Supreme Court emphasized the First Amendment's separation of church and state, with the free exercise of religion playing an important — but secondary — role. Since President Trump's appointment of three new justices, however, things have changed.
"It's literally the opposite of what the law was not that long ago, and it's just a complete shift," observes Michigan State University law professor Frank Ravitch.
The court may, in fact, be on the verge of requiring taxpayers to fund religious schools that refuse to admit LGBTQ students and parents. Last term the justices deadlocked on the issue in a separate case after Justice Amy Coney Barrett recused herself because of a conflict. The 4-4 tie vote automatically left in place an Oklahoma Supreme Court decision that barred overtly religious charter schools from from being funded by the taxpayers. But this year the issue is back in a case from Colorado. The case centers on a state law that provides universal preschool programs that are open to all students, regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation or gender identity.
St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colo., wants the state funding guaranteed in the state's universal pre-k law. But it doesn't want to admit LGBTQ students or students with gay or trans parents. The parish maintains such admissions would violate church's right to the free exercise of religion. The state counters that funding the church school would violate the state's anti-discrimination law.
The court's conservative majority has, in multiple cases, ruled in favor of religious exemptions from generally applicable laws. Until now, however, the court has never said that religious schools are entitled to full taxpayer funding. But given the current court's views, and with Justice Barrett participating in the Colorado case, taxpayers could well end up having to fund religious schools in Colorado and elsewhere.
Bans on semi-automatic weapons
In December the court will hear a case testing whether state and local governments violate the Second Amendment right to bear arms when they ban semi-automatic weapons, like the AR-15.
Former Solicitor General Don Verrilli Jr., articulates two different ways to look at the question.
On the one hand the AR-15 "can deliver upwards of 100 bullets per minute" without any enhancements, and 500 bullets per minute with various enhancements. On the other hand, he notes that millions of Americans own AR-15s, "and it would be quite disruptive to suggest all these Americans ... would be dispossessed of their weapons."
Lawyer Erin Murphy, who has litigated lots of cases on behalf of gun owners, says the "single most important question is who gets to decide what guns you have," and he argues it makes no sense to say, "You've got this right against the government, but the government decides which arms you can get."
Immigration
The Trump administration has repeatedly taken positions in immigration cases that no other administration has adopted. Most recently, the court announced it would hear arguments and decide a case testing whether the Department of Homeland Security may deport migrants to so-called "third countries," when their countries of origin refuse to accept them. Since Trump began his second term, his administration has deported thousands of people to third world countries where they have no connections, may not speak the language, have often been jailed and allegedly subject to torture. The court has twice blocked lower court decisions that prevented the third country policy, and now the justices have said they will hear arguments about the policy in December.
In a second immigration case, the issue is the Trump administration's policy of detaining undocumented immigrants without a bond hearing, regardless of how long they have been in the U.S.
Possible cases: The 10 commandments and much more
There are many more cases waiting in the wings that the justices may take up. Among them is a case that seeks to reverse a nearly half-century-old Supreme Court precedent; it bars public schools from posting the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms. Now, however, Texas, Arkansas, Louisiana and Alabama have passed laws that conflict with the Supreme Court's 1980 ruling, and the lower courts are split on the question. That split all but guarantees the the Supreme Court will revisit the question.
Another case that could to make it to the court this term tests whether states can regulate Kalshi, the $40 billion prediction market behemoth that has sports fans betting on everything from the next pitch to the point spread or at the other end of the spectrum, betting on the outcome of Supreme Court cases.
And then there are cases that the Trump administration has slow-walked for close to two years, after quickly losing in the lower courts. Prime examples are the administration's attempt to deny medical research grants to Harvard University, and other attempts to deny security clearances to law firms, as well as seeking money damages from law firms Trump views as hostile. Earlier this year the Justice Department told a federal court in Washington that it was dropping the law firm cases. But the next day it went back to court to reverse course.
"They don't want to take up cases that they're going to lose, but on the other hand, they have a boss who wants everything taken up there [to the Supreme Court]," says Stanford University law professor Pam Karlan.
Georgetown's professor Vladeck adds that in his view, "The real story of the upcoming term hasn't been written yet because what we're going to look back on as the biggest cases of the term … are not on the docket yet."
Elections
More immediately, the probability is that like it or not the justices will be drawn into the election. The Trump administration has sought to influence elections in numerous ways, and it's unclear what efforts the administration might take going forward.
Democrats have a battalion of lawyers lined up to deal with problems on the ground — whether it's moving polling places at the last minute or having federal agents stationed near polling places. But if there are serious voting problems, they will likely end up at the Supreme Court's door — on the emergency docket.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Expansive red flags raised by two Election Commissioners within the poll panel over the Special Intensive Revision of voters list triggered a massive political storm on Wednesday, with the Opposition accusing CEC Gyanesh Kumar of indulging in "one-man autocracy" and demanding his removal.
Officials said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of voters' list.
The reactions poured in after a report in The Indian Express revealed that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Congress general secretary in-charge communications Jairam Ramesh shared the screenshot of the media report on X.
Ramesh said that on behalf of the party, his colleague Abhishek Singhvi will be speaking in detail to the media on the sensational revelations made in the leading national newspaper on the way "the CEC has destroyed the credibility and integrity of the Election Commission of India".
Congress general secretary in-charge organisation K C Venugopal said there is no doubt remaining that Kumar has no right to remain in office.
"How the hell can one man, acting on His Master's orders, strike off names at whim? How can he sideline fellow Constitutional officers to only take blatantly illegal steps that put our democracy in danger?" he said.
"The right to vote is an essential Constitutional power given to every citizen, the fundamental bedrock of our democracy. If it is to be taken away, due process must be followed with utmost probity," he said.
"Today, when we are staring at crores of genuine voters being excluded and a similar number of bogus voters being added to the rolls, it is clear that Gyanesh Kumar was the Chief Architect of the nationwide 'Vote Chori' exercise, with the the Modi top brass pulling the strings," he alleged.
"We demand Gyanesh Kumar's immediate removal and a Supreme Court-monitored impartial investigation to expose the rot that has destroyed the ECI's credibility," Venugopal said.
If Kumar remains in office, the people of India will come forward and make sure that our democracy is not destroyed by a mere bureaucrat, he added.
Congress' media and publicity department head Pawan Khera lashed out at Kumar, saying he is "planted" and being "protected" by the BJP to hollow out the Election Commission of India from within.
"It was already known that things were not exactly well within the ECI. But just how messy, dysfunctional and, frankly, disturbing things had become is laid bare by this brilliant expose by @IndianExpress," he said on X.
Kumar has to be the single most sold-out bureaucrat of the Modi era who has disenfranchised crores of Indians, and he must face the law, he alleged.
Congress MP Manish Tewari also reacted to the media report, saying that if the ostensible facts as reported are correct then it seems to suggest that there is an "invisible hand" running the Election Commission.
"If rules were not allegedly followed and decisions were taken that were not unanimous or by majority then all the decisions of @ECISVEEP are per -se arbitrary and capricious if not completely illegal," Tewari said on X.
"This is perhaps a fit case for serious considering an impeachment proceeding but more importantly the fundamental question is as to how will the credibility of @ECISVEEP be ever resurrected," he said.
Rajya Sabha MP Kapil Sibal demanded Kumar's suspension and filing of an FIR to probe who is behind his actions.
Former chief election commissioner O P Rawat said changes to the statutory voter registration Form 6 are "absolutely wrong and illegal", while describing revelations of differences within the Election Commission as "very serious" and "unfortunate".
CPI(M) MP John Brittas said this is no longer an Election Commission, it is a "one-man autocracy" under CEC Kumar.
"Two Election Commissioners have formally objected 14 times in 10 months. They branded the addition of new voters and mass deletion 'unauthorised and illegal'. They recorded objections to secret deletions, restorations, and form 6 changes that harass young first-time voters - all while being kept in the dark," he said.
This is the open subversion of the EC and our democracy too, Brittas said.
"Parliament must immediately start the process for the removal of the CEC. We had in fact submitted a notice for removal on 24th April, 2026 as per the constitutional stipulations - solid grounds and around 70 members signing( 50 in the stipulated number)," he said.
The Constitution provides this power for precisely such moments of institutional capture and subversion, he said.
"The Supreme Court must annul the entire SIR process without delay. When two of the three Commissioners put on record that the exercise is illegal and destructive of the electoral roll's integrity, judicial silence becomes complicity," Brittas said.
What Kumar is doing is the death knell of a democratic nation, he said.
"Remove the CEC. Strike down the SIR. Or accept that free and fair elections in India are already being buried," the CPI(M) MP said.
Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut also cited the media report, and said "A-Gyanesh Kumar will go to jail! He will have to go! His masters will flee the country and run away!"
TMC Rajya Sabha leader Derek O'Brien said on X, "Five months ago, 60+ Rajya Sabha MPs (50 needed) wrote to Chairman RS moving Motion to remove CEC Gyanesh Kumar. After big news break today that two Election Commissioners objected to many of CEC's actions, it's time to bring out the RS Motion today. Impeach CEC to save democracy".

Milt Windler, one of the four leaders of Mission Control who in 1970 directed the round-the-clock efforts to bring the Apollo 13 astronauts back to Earth safely, has died at the age of 94.
Windler died on Thursday, surrounded by his loving family, according to a brief notice posted online.
Named a NASA flight director in 1968 after working on recovery operations during the Mercury and Gemini programs, Windler also led a shift of flight controllers for the Apollo 8 first circumlunar flight and Apollo 10 lunar landing dress rehearsal, as well as the second, third and fourth moon landings — Apollo 12, Apollo 14 and Apollo 15. He then served as a flight director for all three crewed missions to the United States’ first space station, Skylab.
“Apollo was such a rapid pace that I don’t think people had the chance to think about it very much. It has only become more clear to me later on that we were making history,” said Windler in a 2006 oral history interview for the University of North Texas. “You’d do a mission and then you’d immediately turn around and get ready for another mission.”
“It was not [a] time for reflection,” Windler said.
Maroon Flight
Each flight director chose a team name (at first colors). As the seventh person to be appointed to the position — and one of the first two to be selected from outside of the flight operations team — Windler became “Maroon Flight.”
On his first mission at the flight director’s console, Windler was assigned to the third shift, putting him at the head of the operations control room when it was time to send the first humans beyond Earth orbit. The trans-lunar injection, or TLI, burn placed Apollo 8 crew members Frank Borman, Bill Anders and Jim Lovell on a trajectory to advance the United States ahead of the Soviet Union by becoming the first nation to orbit people around the moon.
Realizing this, Windler, working with his wife, Betty, and other flight controllers’ spouses, secretly prepared a batch of small red and blue flannel banners, each with the numeral “1” in white at their center. He planned to distribute the flags to the members of his Maroon team to wave at TLI as a not-so-subtle message to their space race adversaries.
“However, it was decided that this display was inappropriate, especially since the mission was only half over,” wrote Windler in a 2020 letter accompanying one of the flags that had since been acquired by a collector. “Consequently, the flags were never displayed during the mission and American flags were used at the time of a successful landing on Earth.”
Later, Windler and all of his colleagues in Mission Control were provided with a dramatic reminder about why you do not celebrate until the crew has stepped onto their recovery ship. For Apollo 13, Windler was named lead flight director.
“What that meant was you did the ascent — the liftoff from Earth, I should say, the launch — and you did the lunar surface activity,” he told the UNT interviewer. “But then, of course, after we lifted off from the Earth, when we got more toward the moon, why, the whole mission changed.”
Flight director Milt Windler, Maroon Flight (at left) looks on as the director of flight crew operations Deke Slayton displays a makeshift “mail box” as devised to adapt square command module carbon dioxide scrubbers with the round receptacles in the lunar module on board the crippled Apollo 13 spacecraft in April 1970.
Credit:
NASA
Flight director Milt Windler, Maroon Flight (at left) looks on as the director of flight crew operations Deke Slayton displays a makeshift “mail box” as devised to adapt square command module carbon dioxide scrubbers with the round receptacles in the lunar module on board the crippled Apollo 13 spacecraft in April 1970.
Credit:
NASA
An explosion tore through the Apollo 13 service module, crippling the spacecraft and venting the crew’s oxygen supply into space.
Instead of overseeing the third time humans had walked on the moon, Windler — together with Gold Flight, Gerry Griffin — polled the flight controllers in the room to develop three options for when, where and how long to fire the lunar module’s engine to put the Apollo 13 spacecraft on a path back to Earth.
It would not be the last time Windler was involved in re-planning a mission already underway, but not because something had gone awry. As flight director during the Skylab missions, the challenge was working with emerging scientific events.
“We had to come up with a system that would allow us to plan in real time and accommodate the science people. If something interesting happened on the sun, which it did several times, then we needed to be able to schedule the ATM [Apollo Telescope Mount] work,” he said in 2006.
“We invented a way of flight planning in real time, or cycles,” said Windler, where one day the science people talked about what they wanted to do, and the ‘Science Czar’ got with them and said, ‘All right, then, we need these particular objectives for tomorrow.’”
After the Skylab missions ended, Windler went to work on the space shuttle and the development of the remote manipulator system or “Canadarm,” the winged orbiters’ robotic arm contributed to the program by Canada. He then retired from NASA and joined private industry to work on what would become the International Space Station, consulting on the operations aspect of the orbiting laboratory, and later, as modules were produced, on some of the verification procedures.
‘Pay more attention’
Born on Jan. 10, 1932 in Hampton, Virginia, Milton Windler graduated from Virginia Tech (Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University) in 1954 with a degree in aeronautical engineering. He joined the U.S. Air Force’s Reserve Officers’ Training Corps (ROTC) while still in school and then worked for the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics (NACA), NASA’s predecessor, before serving in the Air Force for four years.
Windler rejoined NACA at Langley Research Center in Virginia and was there for its transition to becoming a NASA facility. He relocated to Houston, Texas, just as the Manned Spacecraft Center (today, Johnson Space Center) was being established.
Milt Windler stands with fellow flight directors Glynn Lunney, Gene Kranz and Gerry Griffin for President Richard Nixon’s presentation of the Presidential Medal of Freedom to NASA’s Apollo 13 mission operations team on April 18, 1970.
Credit:
NASA
Milt Windler stands with fellow flight directors Glynn Lunney, Gene Kranz and Gerry Griffin for President Richard Nixon’s presentation of the Presidential Medal of Freedom to NASA’s Apollo 13 mission operations team on April 18, 1970.
Credit:
NASA
As a member of Mission Control during the Apollo 13 mission, Windler and his fellow flight directors and controllers were awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom by then-President Richard Nixon in 1970. Windler was also honored with NASA’s Exceptional Service Medal.
Milton and Betty (née Selby) Windler had three children and eight grandchildren. A memorial service will take place in the coming weeks at the family’s former church in Friendswood, Texas.
“If I did it again, I’d probably try to do something more about trying to pay more attention,” said Windler. “Apollo was — well, all of [the missions] were … bang-bang-bang. You couldn’t enjoy, really, in a way you couldn’t savor it, like maybe it would have been better to have done.”
Robert Pearlman is a space historian, journalist and the founder and editor of collectSPACE, a daily news publication and online community focused on where space exploration intersects with pop culture. He is also a contributing writer for Space.com and co-author of "Space Stations: The Art, Science, and Reality of Working in Space” published by Smithsonian Books in 2018. He is on the leadership board for For All Moonkind and is a member of the American Astronautical Society's history committee.

OpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.
The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.
On Friday evening, OpenAI revealed agents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.
It is the sixth government website in Australia to be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announced OpenAI’s agents had hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.
The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.
In a blog post this week the company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.
OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.
“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.
“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”
The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.
AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.
As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.
OpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.
Organisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.
“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.
OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.
The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertake a stocktake of legacy technology to reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.
Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.

Bowie seizing Scotland shot after World Cup disappointment
- Published
Sometimes, the solution to a problem can be hiding in plain sight.
On 19 May, Steve Clarke assembled his collection of players to embark on a World Cup journey.
Despite featuring and scoring for a Hellas Verona side heading for relegation from Serie A, and with a perennial problem of strikers not firing regularly for Scotland, Kieron Bowie was overlooked.
Given the loyalty Clarke showed to those who had served him so well, it was not a huge surprise. Neither was the impotence of the national team in the USA as they conjured up just one John McGinn goal.
"I received a message from him saying that I'm not in the squad but these things happen and it's just about how you bounce back from it to be honest," said Bowie.
"I scored goals in a struggling Verona team and that was as much as I could do. I was happy with where I was at and I was happy with how I'd played.
"I just spent a lot of time at home with my family and then a little golf holiday to Portugal for a week and that was all I did."
Bowie may have been cursing his luck again on Tuesday when his first international start was reduced to a mere 13 minutes following Jack Hendry's red card in the Hampden loss to Switzerland.
The landscape now looks very different.
The former Raith Rovers and Hibernian forward was one of the main Scotland heroes in Skopje after sending a deliciously whipped finish into the net in the 2-0 win over North Macedonia.
Playing in a new 3-4-1-2, Bowie started the game up top with Oli McBurnie in an ultra-attacking line up set out by Sebastien Pocognoli.
Throughout the game, his stats stacked up. The most shots with seven, the most on target with four, most shots in the box with five and the most touches in the opposition box with 11.
"You play all your life to represent a country and to score a goal is just an unbelievable feeling," said the 24-year-old Fifer.
"This manager's come in and he's put a lot of trust in me.
"I think the style that he wants to play definitely plays into my strengths. I think you've seen today a lot of times running them in behind and just showing strength against occupying defenders is one of the main things.
"It's a process but I think everyone's enjoying that process and it's a bit of a change."
The word "process" has been used so many times by the Scotland head coach and his players in recent days it's probably the new team motto.
But there is truth in it.
Pocognoli is trying to implement a radically different system to his predecessor. Not only that, it's a different mindset. All while trying to embed a clutch of new players.
It's early days for the Belgian, his group, and, of course, Bowie. But the man on loan at Sassuolo believes things are clicking, and it's an opportunity for him to make his mark.
"It's a lot longer international break," he explained. "We spend a lot more time together so it's good for him to get his message across and his ideas. Also, we play more games so we have to train a little bit less of course.
"I think for me it's a fresh start with a new coach and different ideas.
"He said to me 'you don't need to prove yourself, just go and do what I know you can do' and I feel like I'm just doing that."
Bowie, who made his Rovers debut at 16, added: "I think people, obviously Scottish fans, have the same idea of how I was when I was at Hibs and that's all they can remember.
"But I feel like since I moved to Serie A, it's a different league, different challenge and I'm getting more experience at a higher level.
"So, yeah, I feel like I've definitely kicked into another gear and I feel like I'm showing that."

On the eve of Chinese president Xi Jinping’s state visit to Cairo last month, the city authorities were busy removing a 66-metre-long mural from the esteemed guest’s line of sight.
Depicting the Pharaoh Tutankhamun and Queen Nefertiti, the painting was among 40 murals commissioned to beautify the city for Xi’s arrival and was painted by volunteer youth group Rasmet Basma, in Tahrir Square.
But it drew a furious reaction for depicting the two historical figures with dark skin – angering those Egyptians who saw it as reviving Afrocentric claims about the Pharaohs’ origins. The artwork vanished under fresh paint just hours before Xi landed.
Now, Ahmed Moussa, the 22-year-old founder of Rasmet Basma, has admitted it was asked by the Cairo governorate to paint over its work, which had been prepared in just five days in late August.
The team used the AI programme ChatGPT to generate the designs, which volunteers then painted on to the wall.
Moussa said Cairo’s deputy governor and the head of the district had visited the site throughout the process and were impressed by the murals – until controversy began to build on social media.
“We used a golden-bronze tone that cast a kind of shadow on the faces at night, so they appeared dark-skinned,” Moussa said.
“We acknowledge our mistake in not consulting specialists in archaeology and art.”
Afrocentrism is a political movement asserting that ancient Egyptian civilisation was black African in origin and population.
One user asked whether anyone involved had “even seen what Nefertiti actually looked like”, while others accused Afrocentric groups of appropriating the images to claim Egyptians endorsed their theories.
Zahi Hawass, Egypt’s former antiquities minister, said the volunteers should not have been allowed to paint a city site as significant as Tahrir Square without expert oversight, and that the public outrage was justified.
“Claims linking ancient Egyptian civilisation to sub-Saharan Africa are nonsense,” Hawass said.
“Temple carvings from the late period show Egyptian kings depicted alongside captives from parts of Africa, Libya, Syria and Palestine, with the king himself not shown as dark-skinned,” he said.
This is just the latest episode in a long-running debate over the complexion of ancient Egyptians. In 2023, a Netflix documentary provoked discussion after casting a dark-skinned actor as Cleopatra, and a similar dispute flared in June 2024 after a guide reportedly gave an Afrocentric perspective of Egyptian history in Cairo’s Egyptian Museum.
Monica Hanna, an Egyptologist at the American University in Cairo, labelled Afrocentric claims “pseudoscience”. She said Egyptian society had always been ethnically diverse, from Nubian communities in the south to Mediterranean populations in the north.
“Egyptians were never one skin colour,” she said. “We are not snow-white, or the colour of cream.”
Walid Mahmoud, an AI researcher and expert in African anthropology, said AI tools such as ChatGPT reflected whatever information was most widely shared online, rather than what was factually accurate.
They were built by companies in the US and Europe, he said, and the content they generated could shape how those audiences saw themselves.
“That’s why we should never simply accept what it produces, especially when it comes to cultural identity and heritage,” Mahmoud said.
Mostafa Eissa, an art critic, said AI should remain a tool, never a decision-maker in its own right.
“I favour using technology without abandoning the human element within the artist,” he said, warning that letting such tools substitute an artist’s own skill risked emptying a work of its originality.

- The claim that male students who were accused of raping a female student at Cornell University were fired from their jobs or expelled from Cornell is still under investigation.
- Snopes readers asked us to determine what happened to each of the seven accused, including whether the university penalized them or their employers fired them.
- A spokesperson for Cornell said via email that the university issued suspensions for some students and expelled others but did not specify which students received which penalties. Cornell did not respond to our specific questions about each student.
- Using the university database, social media posts, a lawyer's statements and college news reporting, Snopes was able to determine that at least one of the accused was still a student on campus. Three others were alumni at the time of the September 2026 lawsuit, while the remainder have an undetermined status at the university.
- Snopes has also reached out to most of the accused students using emails from the college database. We will update this report if we get more information.
In September 2026, a lawsuit brought against Cornell University and seven of its male students alleged the men drugged and raped a 20-year-old female student in October 2024. The story spread online along with claims that the accused students faced little or no consequences, though some allegedly lost their jobs or were expelled.
As Snopes previously reported, the lawsuit named seven male students as defendants: Matthew Ingalls, Johnathan Newell, Winston Lee, Gillio Lopes, Diego Sarabia, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar. According to the lawsuit — filed on behalf of the plaintiff, identified only as Jane Doe, on Sept. 14 — the drugging and multiple assaults occurred the night of Oct. 19, 2024, into the early hours of Oct. 20 at the Xi chapter of the Chi Phi fraternity.
According to Doe's lawsuit, Cornell temporarily suspended the accused students on Nov. 8, 2024, (Page 29) but they were given the opportunity to mitigate their conduct by writing an essay to the university. Cornell has denied that the students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure.
Posts on X, Facebook and Instagram claimed two of the accused students, Sarabia and Ingalls, lost their jobs at Wells Fargo and Data Annotation Tech, respectively. Jane Doe's attorney also reportedly claimed two of the students were expelled from the university, without naming them.
Snopes emailed a spokesperson for Cornell University to determine the enrollment status of each of the accused students. The university declined to respond to specific questions about the accused, directing us to its official statement. The statement says that students were expelled and/or suspended but would not identify which students:
Temporary suspensions and other restrictive measures were issued when the conduct was reported. Chi Phi, Xi Chapter was closed in 2024 and remains barred from campus. Following the university's Title IX investigation, sanctions including expulsions and suspensions were issued by a hearing panel comprising trained faculty and staff. Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students, and the university is therefore unable to make a public statement regarding any other disciplinary response.
Below we break down everything we know about the education and employment status of each of the seven accused students. We will update this story as we learn more.
Diego Sarabia
Student newspaper The Cornell Daily Sun and Cornell's online directory say Sarabia is an alumnus from the class of 2025. 
Gossip outlet TMZ reported, citing anonymous sources, that Sarabia is no longer employed at a Wells Fargo bank branch in Charlotte, North Carolina. It was not possible to independently verify this ourselves. According to the report, Sarabia had worked at the branch since 2022. Wells Fargo has not publicly commented on the story as of this writing.
Snopes has contacted several Wells Fargo representatives to learn more about Sarabia's role, employment status and the circumstances around his alleged termination. The company has not responded to our queries.
Snopes has also reached out to Sarabia through an email address in the student directory.
Matthew Ingalls
On Sept. 30, Data Annotation Tech responded to the claim that it had employed one of the accused. The company, which hires independent contractors to train artificial intelligence models, said on Instagram (archived) that one of the accused was blocked from its platform in May 2024, long before the lawsuit.
According to its Instagram post, which does not name Ingalls, the claim that the company employed one of the accused is "incorrect." It continues, "He has had no access to our platform or our company at any point since then."
We contacted Data Annotation Tech to learn more about whether Ingalls, specifically, had ever been a contractor or employee there.
The Daily Sun reported that Ingalls was a member of the class of 2027. Cornell's online database initially listed Ingalls as a student but his college affiliation as "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
Snopes has reached out to Ingalls through an email address in the student directory.
Gillio Lopes
The Daily Sun reported that Lopes was a member of the class of 2027 and was still listed in the directory as a student in the College of Arts and Sciences. Snopes was unable to confirm the directory listing.
Footage shared online purported to show a woman confronting Lopes on Cornell's campus in late September 2026. Lopes' lawyer confirmed the veracity of the footage to TMZ, saying:
What has emerged today only reinforces how dangerous it is to rush to judgment. The contemporaneous texts and other evidence now being reported show a far more complicated and evolving factual picture than the one initially presented to the public.
[…]
Due process exists for precisely this reason. Publicity is not evidence. Repetition is not proof. An accusation cannot be allowed to become its own proof. He is entitled to have the evidence tested through the legal process—not by headlines, social media, or people confronting him in public or threatening his family.
Snopes has reached out to Lopes' lawyer, Andrew Miltenberg, to learn more.
Winston Lee
The Daily Sun reported that Lee was a member of the class of 2027 and was still listed in the directory as a student in the College of Arts and Sciences.
Some social media users claimed (archived) Lee was still on campus and had changed his name to Jay Lee. As of this writing, Snopes was unable to independently verify this claim.
Snopes was unable to determine Lee's status via the student directory or to find contact information for him.
Scott Kretzschmar
The Daily Sun reported that Kretzschmar is an alumnus from the class of 2026. When Snopes first looked at the student directory, it listed him as a student, but his college affiliation was "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
Snopes has reached out to Kretzschmar through an email address in the student directory.
Johnathan Newell
The Daily Sun reported that Newell was a member of the class of 2027. When Snopes first looked at the student directory, it listed a "Jonathan Newell" (with a different spelling) as a student, but his college affiliation was "not applicable." When Snopes went back to the directory on Oct. 2, there was no record of a Johnathan or Jonathan Newell.
Snopes has reached out to Newell through an email address in the student directory.
Scott Norris
The Daily Sun reported that Norris is an alumnus from the class of 2026. Cornell's online database initially listed him as a student but his college affiliation as "not applicable." When Snopes returned to the directory on Oct. 2, his name had been removed.
Snopes has reached out to Norris through an email address in the student directory.

A car has crashed into a crowd of people in Newcastle injuring several as fans waited to farewell the Knights team bus before the NRL grand final.
New South Wales police said that emergency services were called to Newcastle Link Road at the Transfield Drive roundabout in Wallsend about 9.30am on Saturday after reports a vehicle struck multiple people in a crowd.
The driver was arrested at the scene.
“Several people have been injured and are currently receiving treatment at the scene,” police said.
The Newcastle Link Road was closed in both directions, leading to the diversion of the Knights grand final procession.
The club confirmed in an Instagram post that it had changed its route, apologising to fans who may have missed farewelling the team but saying “public safety is our priority”.
Police appealed for fans to leave the area.
“Police acknowledge many loyal supporters may have missed the opportunity to see the team and show their support.
“Members of the public are asked to safely disperse from the area and keep roadways clear to assist emergency services and traffic management efforts.
“Police thank the community for their patience, cooperation and assistance.”
The NSW premier, Chris Minns, said his thoughts were with the families and friends of those injured.
“It’s heartbreaking to see fans who were sending off their grand final team involved in such a terrible incident,” he said. 
“We’ve seen how this grand final has brought Newcastle together, and I hope the whole community remains united as we continue to respond.”
NSW ambulance service has also been contacted for comment.

NRLW grand final quick hits: Sydney Roosters complete 101-year first to defeat Brisbane Broncos
The 2026 Sydney Roosters NRLW side has cemented its legacy with a crushing grand final win over the Brisbane Broncos.
Twelve months on from a heartbreaking loss to the women from Brisbane, the Roosters not only won the premiership, but did something no other top-flight rugby league team has achieved in Australia for more than a century.
Here are the quick hits from Sydney's NRLW grand final win over Brisbane.
1. Origin wingers make uncharacteristic errors
It doesn't matter how much experience you have, every player feels some sort of pressure on grand final day.
And the pressure of a grand final was on display in the opening minutes, with a pair of State of Origin representatives making uncharacteristic errors.
Sydney Roosters winger Jayme Fressard had a proper shocker to begin the grand final, failing to gather the opening kick-off and nudging it into touch.
As the ball came to the NSW State of Origin rep, she tried to trap it with her foot but kicked the footy over the sideline.
The Roosters were able to defend their goal-line and then it was a Broncos Origin rep to have a shocker.
It was Fressard's opposing winger, Julia Robinson, who dropped the ball stone cold in her own half, which gifted the Roosters a golden chance to open the scoring.
Unlike the Broncos, the Roosters were able to score when winger Brydie Parker fielded a great cross-field kick from five-eighth Jocelyn Kelleher and touched down in the corner.
2. Tarryn Aiken takes over in 7-minute blitz
The Roosters were dominating the grand final in the first half, as multiple errors from Brisbane kept them under immense pressure.
But Brisbane's goal-line defence was one aspect of their game that was withstanding the impressive Roosters.
That was until Sydney halfback Tarryn Aiken, who missed last year's decider due to an ACL injury, produced three moments of brilliance in a 7-minute stretch that led to a trio of tries for the Roosters.
First Aiken grubbered for herself and when the ball bounced off the arm of Brisbane winger Kerri Johnson, the Sydney halfback caught the ricochet and scored the game's second try.
Four minutes later, Aiken was setting up the third try of the match. The halfback lined up at lock in an attacking scrum 10 metres from Brisbane's goal-line. Aiken passed from the base of the scrum to the left, wrapped around and retook the footy, then gave a perfect short pass to captain Isabelle Kelly who charged over.
The Roosters then charged down the field again and when a sixth tackle play looked to be coming unstuck, it was Aiken again who produced a great kick which Brisbane's Deleni Paitai fumbled, and the Tricolours regathered and Fressard scored in the corner.
3. Brigginshaw on report in her farewell game
The trailblazing career of Ali Brigginshaw, someone who has been instrumental in the growth of women's rugby league, came to an end with an NRLW grand final.
But the legendary Broncos, Maroos and Jillaroo might have considered herself lucky not to have been sin-binned in her farewell game.
With the Roosters on top, Brigginshaw was desperate not to let Aiken put in an attacking cross-field kick.
Aiken did, which led to a try, but Brigginshaw's low dive resulted in her clattering into the planted leg of Aiken.
A hit under the knee led to Aiken landing hard on her back and could have easily resulted in Brigginshaw being sent for a 10-minute break on the sideline.
But referee Belinda Sharpe decided that putting Brigginshaw on report was the only action necessary, which really is academic considering this was her farewell outing.
4. Dally M medallist pulls off one of season's best tackles
Down 26-0 early in the second half, Brisbane's misery looked destined to continue when the Roosters were about to cross over for what would have been their seventh try of the grand final.
A high bomb from the Roosters was allowed to bounce, the ball took a wicked turn and landed in the arms of Brydie Parker, and a brilliant flick pass on the inside looked set to end with Jessica Sergis scoring in the corner.
But Brisbane's captain and fullback Tamika Upton, the Dally M medalist this season, produced a try-saving tackle as good as any seen this season.
The Brisbane number one screamed across in cover and was able to twist her body in the tackle and make sure she was under the ball as Sergis fell to the line.
With Upton around her like a snake, Sergis was unable to get her arm free and ground the ball. It didn't change the outcome, but it was another example of why Upton is the best player in the competition.
5. Roosters complete first perfect season in 101 years
The Roosters came into Sunday's decider with plenty of confidence.
They had won 30 of their previous 31 NRLW matches. There only loss was last year's grand final, to the Broncos, denying them an undefeated season.
But the Tricolours regrouped in 2026, won every match on their way to the decider, then exacted revenge with a commanding win to complete the perfect season.
The Sydney Roosters became the first men's or women's side in top grade rugby league to go the entire season without suffering a loss since the 1959 ST George Dragons.
That Dragons team recorded 17 wins, and one draw, on their way to a fourth consecutive premiership, in a dominant era of 11 straight titles.
But the 2026 Roosters NRLW side had no draws, just 13 wins from 13 matches. The last team to win every match in a season was South Sydney, way back in 1925.

Eradicating Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection early could become an important strategy for preventing gastric cancer, Nobel laureate and gastroenterologist Dr. Barry Marshall said, stressing the need for wider testing, appropriate treatment and confirmation that the infection has been cleared.
Dr. Marshall, who shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robin Warren for their discovery of H. pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease, said the bacterium should no longer be regarded only as a cause of ulcers.
“H. pylori is much more than an ulcer organism. If the infection persists for many years, it can cause chronic inflammation in the stomach and increase the risk of gastric cancer. That gives us an opportunity because this is a potentially preventable cause of cancer," Dr. Marshall told PTI.
Dr. Marshall was in India to attend the World Congress of Gastroenterology (WCOG 2026) in the national capital.
Held in India for the first time, the four-day event, which concluded on October 3, brought together around 3,000 delegates from 61 countries to discuss the changing global burden of gastrointestinal and liver diseases, including H. pylori infection, gastric cancer prevention, early diagnosis and treatment.
His comments come amid renewed global focus on population-based H. pylori "screen-and-treat" programmes for gastric cancer prevention.
The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) working group has recommended such programmes in populations where the benefits are expected to outweigh potential harms.
Dr. Marshall said the priority should be to identify infected individuals and ensure they receive effective eradication therapy.
"If we can find the infection before there has been extensive damage to the stomach, we have a much better chance of preventing the chain of events that can eventually lead to cancer," he said.
However, rising antibiotic resistance is emerging as a major challenge to this approach, he highlighted.
A 2026 review in Gastroenterology noted that increasing antimicrobial resistance is threatening the success of established H. pylori treatment regimens, while concerns also remain about the effects of repeated antibiotic exposure on the microbiome.
"We cannot simply keep giving the same antibiotics and expect the same results. Resistance varies between countries and even between regions, so treatment needs to take local resistance patterns into account," Dr. Marshall said.
The IARC guidance similarly emphasises antibiotic stewardship, treatment based on local resistance patterns and follow-up testing to determine whether eradication has been successful.
Dr. Marshall said India, where H. pylori infection is common, has an important role to play in generating evidence on local bacterial strains and antibiotic resistance.
"India has a very large population with H. pylori, so it is an important setting for research. We need to understand which strains are circulating, what antibiotics are still effective and how we can make testing and treatment accessible," he said.
According to the IARC guidance, Indian recommendations have included bismuth-containing quadruple therapy in areas with high clarithromycin resistance, highlighting the importance of regional resistance patterns in treatment decisions.
Dr. Marshall also stressed that successful treatment should not be assumed simply because symptoms improve.
"Treating the patient is only half the job. We should confirm that the bacterium has actually been eradicated. Otherwise, the patient may continue to carry the infection and remain at risk," he said.
He said non-invasive testing could make detection easier and help expand screening.
Dr. Marshall has also invented PYtest, a C14 urea breath test that provides a 15-minute, non-invasive and quantitative method for detecting current H. pylori infection using a breath sample from the patient.
The patient-friendly test could help Indian doctors detect active H. pylori infection through a quick diagnostic procedure.
PYtest is available in India through Pylorium Diagnostics, part of Trimed Australia, founded by Dr. Marshall and headed by Bhanu Rahoni in India.
The need for prevention has gained urgency as gastric cancer remains a major global health burden, with the highest incidence concentrated in several Asian regions.

'I don't even know if my parents are alive' - the war heroes jailed 25 years ago
- Published
Hanna Petros Solomon breaks down in tears as she recalls how she and her siblings effectively became orphans 25 years ago when their father was arrested in Eritrea and jailed without trial. Their mother was subsequently detained - and no-one has heard from either of them - or of them - since.
"He had a towel on his shoulders like a sportsman," she tells the BBC about the last time she saw her father when she was 10 years old, and he had gone out for a jog.
"He used to work out every morning."
Her parents met when they both fought in the long liberation war that saw Eritrea gain independence from Ethiopia in 1993.
Her father Petros Solomon had been one of the senior leaders during the war and is regarded by many as a national hero for his critical role.
After independence, he had served as defence minister, then foreign minister and had been heading the fisheries ministry when his troubles began.
That was in May 2001 when he and 14 other high-profile politicians signed an open letter to President Isaias Afewerki calling for the implementation of a constitution that was ratified after independence and demanding national elections. They became known as the G-15.
Isaias, the leader of the Eritrean People's Liberation Front (EPLF) which had fought against Ethiopia, did not take the criticism well.
Unbeknown to Hanna, her father had been dismissed as a minister, though he still went out early to get some exercise each day.
It was not until a few days after 9/11 - when the world was distracted by the al-Qaeda attacks on the US - that the country was to discover the full extent of Isais's displeasure in what became a watershed moment in Eritrea's history.
In the early hours of 18 September, the security forces positioned themselves outside the homes of 11 senior government officials in the capital, Asmara, on the president's orders.
Petros was picked up by security agents as he left in his tracksuit.
The family had no idea what had happened to him. Hanna and her three siblings went to stay with their paternal grandmother as their mother, Aster Yohannes, was away studying in the US.
It was only some days after Petros had disappeared that things became clearer, says Hanna about the painful memories.
"My classmates told me that my father sold out his country.
"That is when I understood how serious the situation was, and how people framed my dad and his colleagues who fought for the independence of their country. I was hurt."
In the US, Aster was shell-shocked by what had happened - and was in a very bad way. She asked government officials if they could issue the children with passports - but they refused, telling her to come home.
After agonising about the situation for two years and reportedly receiving assurances from government officials, she packed her bags to return.
Hanna and her siblings desperately wanted her back - but they were also worried.
"I told her on the phone: 'What if they arrest you?'" Hanna remembers.
"She insisted nothing would happen to her, saying: 'I haven't done anything wrong, and am only coming to raise my children.'"
Hanna says she learned later that President Isaias himself had promised Aster that she would be safe. But while the family waited at Asmara International Airport on 11 December 2003, she failed to emerge through arrivals with the other passengers.
Their hopes began to wilt along with the flowers they had brought: "It was a long, long wait. Eventually we gave up and went back home.
"First we called to the US, friends and relatives told us they saw her off at the airport."
Then ominously an official called from the airport asking Aster to collect her luggage. That is when they realised she had arrived in the country but would not be coming home.
All pleas and requests for information fell on deaf ears in the months that followed. Instead Hanna's grandmother was warned by authorities to stop inquiring.
The family later heard that Aster was being held in the infamous jail known as Karshelli in the heart of Asmara.
Hanna's father is believed to be detained, with the others arrested on 18 and 19 September 2001, in the remote, hostile and highly secretive prison known as Ela-Ero, located in eastern lowlands north-east of Asmara. Accused of treason, none of them has ever been brought to trial or allowed to see their relatives.
At around the same time, the government also shut down all the fledgling independent newspapers and detained their editors and journalists - also believed to be imprisoned in Ela-Ero.
The Eritrean government - including its embassy in the UK - has not responded to the BBC's request for comment regarding the whereabouts of the prisoners or whether or not they are alive.
Hanna, like many thousands of young Eritreans fleeing conscription and in search of better opportunities, left the country - travelling secretively over the border without a passport.
Now 35 years old, she is married and lives in the US, working as a trauma specialist - but still feels traumatised herself by how she lost her parents.
As she stares at old pictures of her parents, she worries her memories will fade of the happy times before their arrest - the laughter, the family gatherings, the birthday parties: "My dad always wanted to gather people in the house, they were good days."
She also hankers after her mother's "unmatched" egg and potato sandwiches.
On trips down to the coast when her father was the minister of fisheries, Hanna remembers him organising singing competitions in the car: "He would ask us to sing one by one and whoever won would get a present."
One of his favourite songs included the lyrics: "I had a sweater, a blue sweater, that my sister took" - which reminded him of his sister who was also a freedom fighter and had been killed during the war.
She also has memories of her mother loving music - playing and singing hits by Abba, Dolly Parton and Whitney Houston.
Until her father's arrest, Hanna remembers September as being full of hope with its three big Orthodox Christian festivals, including the Geez New Year. Now the month brings her no joy.
Ibrahim Sherifo knows exactly how she feels. Both his parents, who were senior members of the ruling People's Front for Democracy and Justice (PFDJ), were among the G-15 people arrested 25 years ago.
He was 13 years old at the time
"For me 18 September 2001 is a dark day, but not only for me, it is a dark day for Eritrea and its people, because it is the day when law and democracy was detained," he tells the BBC.
He is now 38 and living in exile in the Netherlands, where he was granted asylum, and is pursuing an MA in political science - following in his father's footsteps.
His dad Mahmoud Ahmed Sherifo was the local government minister and de facto deputy president before his detention.
Ibrahim was with his mother, Aster Fissehatsion, staying with her sister when he remembers security agents knocking on the door early in the morning and taking her away in her pyjamas.
Worried about his father, Ibrahim immediately ran to his nearby house but was told he had already been picked up when he had gone out for exercise.
Both Hanna and Ibrahim say they are forever grateful to the friends and family who offered them care and supported them as they grew up without their parents, despite the risks.
They are also proud of what their parents stood for and daring to call for reforms.
"They had conscience and couldn't observe idly while what they fought for what had been hijacked by Isaias and his coterie," says Ibrahim.
"As a family, we should be informed whether they are alive or not," he adds, accusing the government of wanting to erase all memory of the political prisoners.
Hanna also wants the plight of the many others whose relatives have disappeared over the years to be heard too.
Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down"
Human rights groups, including the UN, consider the G-15 prisoners of conscience and have been calling for their release.
President Isaias, now 80, has still not implemented the country's first constitution - approved in 1997 - and remains in power without ever holding an election.
Hanna recalls that on the eve of her father's disappearance, she had a "bad feeling" - and had crept into his bed and tied his legs to her own with string while he slept.
"In the morning he woke up to find he was tied up and to release himself he pulled my legs and I woke up. I begged him not to leave but he assured me that he would return [after his run]."
Describing the years of sorrow since, she says it is like living in the deep sea.
"Sometimes it is calm and you can float, but other times the sorrow comes back to you like a wave and drowns you deep down.
"Sometimes you lose hope and you are out of breath."
Asked what she would say if she could get a message to her parents, she replies: "Don't worry about us.
"Like you survived the struggle through sheer steadfastness, we hope you can pull through this too and return to us."

David Robinson used to write the safety reports that accompanied every major model release at OpenAI. This week, he resigned from his position and is now speaking out in an editorial in The Atlantic.
An OpenAI safety employee has quit and is sounding the alarm
David Robinson used to write safety reports at OpenAI and now says its culture is ‘broken’
It’s understandable if you’re feeling a bit cynical about everyone suddenly coming out of the woodwork to warn about how dangerous the thing they helped build is. They did, after all, make this mess. But that doesn’t mean we should discount their warnings.
Robinson says that the culture in industry is fundamentally broken. That this is a deeper issue than simply slapping a few new rules or regulations on how we handle training models. Silicon Valley has operated with “extreme confidence” and “perpetual sprints,” he says, building bigger and better models with “unimpeded optimism” that ignores or underestimates potential problems.
He says the time has come for AI companies to develop a sense of humility and look outside the insular, move-fast-and-break-things world of the tech industry. Specifically, he says AI needs nuclear-level safeguards:
Given today’s risks, frontier labs need to run like nuclear power plants or busy airports, with layers of redundancy and careful, time-consuming planning, so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster.
Robinson is just the latest in a growing parade of researchers and safety workers who have left their positions at prominent AI firms. Jacob Coxon seems to have kicked off the exodus by quitting Anthropic and then publicly saying AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade.” He was followed by Robert O’Callahan, Bilal Chughtai, and Josh Engels at Google DeepMind, as well as Joe Benton at Anthropic.

New Delhi: With Cuba facing a severe food security crisis, Cuban Ambassador to India Juan Carlos Marsán Aguilera has proposed joint food production in Cuba, under which the country would provide land for Indian companies to grow rice, beans and sugarcane, with the produce also exported to other markets.
Cubans are bearing the consequences of the US tightening its blockade of the country, Aguilera said in an interview, adding that oil supplies from Venezuela and Mexico have stopped, with no other country able to sell to Cuba. He said that while the infant mortality rate in Cuba before the US sanctions was 4 per 100 new births, it has exponentially increased to 10 per 100 new births, with people dying in the absence of proper medication and medical equipment amid the US sanctions.
“In the case of Cuba, in food production, if we don't have the financial capacity to buy all that we require from India, why don't we go for co-production? We offer the land in Cuba, and Indian companies can go to Cuba and produce in Cuba. We are talking about rice, beans, and sugarcane. We offer to Indian companies this possibility, go and produce there, and we can focus on export,” Aguilera said.
US President Donald Trump passed an executive order in January 2026 stating that “the situation with respect to Cuba constitutes an unusual and extraordinary threat,” declaring it a national emergency and imposing additional tariffs on any country that “directly or indirectly sells or otherwise provides any oil to Cuba.” Trump has called Cuba an “absolute failed state” and declared that “freedom will be coming to Cuba”, in his 22 September speech at the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.
India and Cuba share traditionally warm and friendly relations, dating back to India being among the first countries to recognize the Cuban government after the 1959 revolution and establishment of diplomatic relations in 1960. Bilateral trade between India and Cuba rose 31% to $24.31 million in 2025-26 from $18.46 million a year earlier, according to data from the ministry of commerce and industry.
Aguilera said that Cuba is working very hard as a country to overcome this situation and is contacting companies across the world, including India, to participate in the Cuban economy that is undergoing an energy transition.
“We were more than 80% dependent on oil and fuel that we should import from abroad. And we are now more determined in order to be self-sufficient in energy. And the way for Cuba is renewable resources. We cannot depend anymore on oil, gas, or from abroad. Solar will be the main, I can say, source that we can use in Cuba. But also wind energy, hydro energy, and new energies, hydrogen and many others that India also has a new experience. So, we would like to connect more with India in this sector. We are opening this sector for foreign investments in our country,” said Aguilera.
India and the Community of Latin American and Caribbean states (CELAC) countries, comprising 33 countries, recorded a trade value of $50 billion in 2025-26, according to a ministry of external affairs statement. India’s total trade with Latin America and the Caribbean region, comprising 43 countries, stood at $39.19 billion in 2024-25, according to the ministry of commerce and industry.
“Nowadays, we are producing 20%—21% of the demand for the total energy in Cuba through renewable resources, mainly solar. And we have the target by 2030 to reach 30%,” he added.
Cuba is a member of the International Solar Alliance (ISA), co-founded by India and France. Mint reported in August 2021 about India’s strategy of showcasing its green energy credentials abroad has gained traction, with state-run NTPC Ltd securing the project management consultancy (PMC) contract for setting up 900 megawatt (MW) solar projects under the aegis of the ISA
“The problem is that they are strengthening this policy of blockade towards my country, imposing a collective punishment on our population. The people are suffering the consequences of this policy of blockade, sanctions. Blockade to oil supply to a country. How can you accept this? An island that depends on import of the fuel, the oil that is required for their normal functioning, to supply electricity to the population,” Aguilera said.
With a population of 10.94 million in 2025, Cuba consumed approximately 117,295 barrels of oil per day in 2024 and 15.81 TWh of electricity, according to World Bank and U.S. Energy Information Administration-linked energy data.
Experts say given India's track record, it’s a natural choice.
“India and Cuba are charting a new, long bilateral diplomatic relationship to collaborate on several emerging areas including energy. This would give a fresh impetus to the long-standing relationship between India and Cuba existing since the last several decades. The renewed thrust on energy is viewed in the context of the 'oil blockade' by the US leading to prolonged supply scarcity of electricity in Cuba,” said Gopal Sarangi, associate professor at TERI School of Advanced Studies.
Sarangi also said that given India's track record of renewable energy technology development, such a collaborative approach would open up new avenues for both the countries.
The latest high-level Indian visit to Cuba was that of minister of state (MoS) for external affairs Pabitra Margherita in November last year.
“India could contribute not only through extension of technology support, but also through capacity building and institutional support to accelerate the energy transition in Cuba,” Sarangi said. “However, India's engagement requires careful crafting of diplomatic, financial and geopolitical architecture given the current economic and geopolitical tension encountered by Cuba. If structured well, this cooperation could augur well for India’s Global South diplomacy.”
