‘Make in India’ cannot mean manufacturing a dictator, says Uddhav Thackeray
NEW DELHI: Shiv Sena (UBT) chief Uddhav Thackeray and Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray on Sunday led a joint protest march in Mumbai against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, with participants demanding the cancellation of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Maharashtra.Addressing the gathering after the march, Uddhav Thackeray accused the government of attempting to create a dictatorship under the slogan of “Make in India”.“I think you will also remember that when Modi ji first became Prime Minister, he gave the slogan, “Make in India.” Remember? We accept that. But if, under “Make in India,” you are also going to manufacture a dictator in our country, then we have gathered here today to bury that dictatorship and put an end to it. Everything else under Make in India is fine. But if, in the name of Make in India, you are going to create a dictatorship, then consider that we have buried your dictatorship...”Speaking ahead of the protest, Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut said the demonstration was a collective response to what he alleged were attempts to undermine democratic institutions, electoral processes and the constitutional rights of citizens.
“This protest is against the Hitler-rule prevailing in the country, hijacking elections, keeping the Election Commission and the Supreme Court in one's pocket, running a dictatorship, stealing votes, stealing elections, and poaching MPs and MLAs. This is a revolt against all that, much like the one in 1857,” he told reporters.
Thackeray questioned the appointment process of Election Commissioners.“I have a question mark over the appointment of the Election Commissioners. The Election Commission should be appointed through an election. Earlier, there was a committee comprising the Chief Justice of India, the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition. They (the central government) removed the Chief Justice from this committee. In place of the Chief Justice, they appointed a minister chosen by the Prime Minister. That minister is Amit Shah. There are hearings after hearings in the courts, but there is no accountability.”Thackeray also questioned how Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar was appointed and alleged that powers related to citizenship rights were being exercised through the Election Commission.“The first question is: How was Gyanesh Kumar appointed? Does the Home Ministry have the power to cancel a person's citizenship rights? They are using that power through Gyanesh Kumar, and that is why we do not want Gyanesh Kumar. Earlier, it was 'India Against Corruption', and now it is 'India Against Vote Chors'... The BJP does not know how to run a government... The way you are running the government is not governance; it is revenge...”The march, dubbed the Virat Garjana Morcha (Grand Roar March), began at Metro Cinema and proceeded towards the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation headquarters in south Mumbai. State leaders of the Congress and the Sharad Pawar-led NCP (SP) also participated in the protest.
The protesters demanded the removal or resignation of Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the SIR exercise.Party flags were not allowed during the march, with participants and supporters asked to carry only the national tricolour.

Everything ixigo has done since it started off in 2007 can be called a stepping stone to get to where it is today. It was always one step after another rather than a leap to become a full stack OTA. After building itself as a flight meta-search platform for nearly eight years since inception, i.e. helping consumers compare fares and travel options, ixigo gradually moved towards a marketplace model by adding pieces gradually. For the first few years, no actual booking took place on ixigo, but instead it earned a small commission when customers booked flight tickets through its price comparison tool. It later expanded into train and bus ticketing, and only in 2019, actually launched its own air ticketing platform, allowing users to book directly on its platform and making ixigo the merchant of record. That shift changed more than just where the transaction happened. It opened up new ways for ixigo to monetise every booking through commissions, convenience and service fees, value-added services, ancillaries and advertising. Over time, the company has also added hotels to its offering, while its multi-brand strategy has brought ConfirmTkt and AbhiBus into the fold. The acquisition route has helped ixigo build depth across trains and buses while retaining separate brands and apps for different traveller use cases. Today, ixigo operates in a crowded OTA market alongside MakeMyTrip, EaseMyTrip, Yatra and Cleartrip, while also competing with specialised platforms and direct travel-booking channels. The business is also exposed to the seasonality of travel demand as well as increasing geopolitical tensions — meaning booking volumes, revenue and operating performance can vary across periods. Yet, the company has built considerable scale. In Q1 FY27, ixigo’s GTV grew 19% YoY to ₹5,524 Cr, while revenue from operations rose 13% to ₹357 Cr and contribution margin increased 13% to ₹145 Cr. However, adjusted EBITDA declined 7% YoY to ₹29 Cr, as ixigo continued to invest in newer areas including hotels, AI and brand building. That gap is central to ixigo’s current money map — contribution is growing, but part of the operating leverage generated by the mature businesses is being redeployed into its various segments. Here is how ixigo’s travel engine works, and where the money comes from. From Search To Revenue ixigo’s travel business does not begin with a ticket purchase. It begins with a traveller looking for information. Train schedules, PNR status, flight information, bus availability and other travel utilities bring users onto ixigo’s platforms, creating an opportunity to convert that engagement into bookings. The company has built this model across trains, flights, buses and hotels, with its portfolio spanning the ixigo app, train-focused ConfirmTkt and bus-focused AbhiBus, alongside its flight and hotel offerings. Having wide coverage is particularly useful when individual travel categories face disruptions. The scale of that funnel is visible in its user base. In Q1 FY27, ixigo had 8.5 Cr monthly active users, while its apps saw 3.27 Cr downloads during the quarter. Once a user is in the booking funnel after comparisons and filtering, ixigo has several ways to monetise that transaction, depending on the category. For flights, ixigo earns commissions or incentives from airlines and other travel partners based on the bookings it generates, while convenience fees are charged to the traveller. In buses, ixigo gets access to available seats and routes through operators and aggregators, and earns commissions and convenience fees on bookings. Hotels add another commission-led stream, with the company building direct relationships with properties. For trains, ixigo earns through agent service charges, VAS and advertising, along with payment-related revenue. Notably, ixigo does not disclose a standard commission percentage for every airline, bus operator or other travel supplier. Instead, the company reports the combined economics through its segment revenue, gross take rate and contribution margin. This means the ₹100 paid by a traveller does not translate into ₹100 of ixigo revenue. A portion flows to the underlying travel supplier, while ixigo earns commissions, and other fees. At the consolidated level, ixigo groups its operating revenue into ticketing revenue, advertising revenue and other operating revenue. Ticketing remains the dominant pool and we will break down the other revenue segments later in the article. In FY26, of the ₹1,228 Cr revenue from operations, ₹1,129 Cr came from ticketing, ₹65.3 Cr from advertising and ₹33.5 Cr from other operating revenue. But ticketing revenue is not the same as the value of tickets sold. GTV captures the total value of transactions flowing through the platform, while ixigo earns only a portion of that value through commissions, fees and other services. In Q1 FY27, its GTV reached an all-time quarterly high of ₹5,524 Cr (up 19% YoY) and revenue from operations of ₹356.75 Cr (up 13% YoY). Take rate and contribution margin matter more than GTV alone because of the nature of the business. Contribution margin stood at ₹144.94 Cr in Q1 FY27, up 13% YoY, with the contribution margin at 40.6% versus 40.5% a year earlier. Ixigo defines contribution margin as net ticketing revenue plus other operating revenue less direct expenses. Among its verticals, hotel bookings is perhaps the least mature segment. On the other hand, in recent earnings calls, ixigo believes maturity in trains, flights and buses is generating operating leverage, and the company is reinvesting that leverage into hotels, AI and brand/marketing. Trains, Flights Or Buses: What Drives ixigo? The economics of ixigo’s three mature segments are naturally quite different, even though all three ultimately monetise bookings through commissions, fees, VAS and other services. In Q1 FY27, buses generated the highest contribution margin, while flights generated the highest GTV. Flights had a GTV of ₹2,341.84 Cr on 29 Lakh passenger segments. Revenue stood at ₹104.56 Cr, while contribution margin was ₹41.04 Cr, translating into a 39% contribution margin. Its gross take rate was 8.41%. Gross take rate shows how much gross ticketing revenue ixigo earns for every ₹100 of GTV processed. For instance, a 10% gross take rate means ixigo earns ₹10 in gross ticketing revenue for every ₹100 worth of bookings made on its platform. Meanwhile, trains generated ₹2,138.86 Cr in GTV, on a passenger segment of 2.44 Cr. Revenue grew 9% to ₹141.04 Cr, while contribution margin jumped 29% YoY to ₹52.74 Cr, taking the margin to 37%. Its gross take rate stood at 6.54%. The bus business is where the economics stand out. Bus GTV grew 39% to ₹947.43 Cr, while passenger segments rose 33% to 89 Lakh. Revenue grew 34% to ₹102.55 Cr, but contribution margin grew 28% to ₹54.22 Cr, giving buses a 53% contribution margin and making it the largest contributor to group contribution margin at 37%. Its gross take rate was 11.76%. The numbers show why GTV does not tell the full story. Flights had the highest GTV in Q1, but buses generated a larger contribution margin at half the GTV. After Q1, CEO Aloke Bajpai said, “The big opportunity lies in categories like buses and hotels, where penetration remains low despite higher take rates and contribution margins.“ One way to boost contribution margins is value-added services (VAS), ancillaries and advertising to its in Q1 core ticketing revenue. These include air ticketing addons such as ixigo Assured, Assured Flex, Trip Guarantee and Price Lock, along with seat selection, meals and other extras. The platform reported an ancillary attachment rate of 31%, meaning ancillary products were attached to roughly three out of every 10 transactions. Advertising is another way ixigo monetises its traffic without requiring another ticket purchase. Brands and travel partners can use its apps and websites to reach travellers through advertising and other promotional placements. Advertising contributed ₹65.33 Cr to ixigo’s ₹1,228 Cr operating revenue in FY26. The Cost Of Running ixigo’s Travel Machine Travel is a fickle business because even a booking doesn’t guarantee revenue. Customers change plans and sometimes market conditions result in mass cancellations. Like all other platforms, ixigo has to accommodate these cancellations and account for potential refunds every time a customer books. For every direct booking, the company still spends on technology, employees, advertising, partner support and distribution. And that’s if the booking does not end with a refund. On an annual basis, in FY26, advertising and sales promotion was the largest cost centre at ₹324.46 Cr, up 48% YoY. Customer refunds and cancellation costs stood at ₹260.61 Cr, up 44%, while partner support costs increased 40% to ₹142.76 Cr. Payment gateway charges rose 22% to ₹70.50 Cr, and distribution costs increased 32% to ₹39.15 Cr. The rise in refunds was partly due to the growing volume of revenue from value-added services, where ixigo had to bear the cost of refunds or modifications for all cancellations. Meanwhile, partner support costs increased with higher train bookings and newer offerings. Payment gateway and distribution costs moved up with a surge in transaction volumes and activity across distribution partners. Brand marketing is one area where the spending can move sharply between quarters. Responding to a question on the sequential jump in advertising spend, CEO Bajpai said the company’s brand marketing is “very seasonal”, with Q1 typically seeing higher spends. This year, ConfirmTkt’s IPL activity and higher marketing by AbhiBus also contributed to the increase. It is to be noted that these expense buckets are common across all the categories ixigo operates in. However, the direct cost burden differs across the three mature businesses. Buses generate a higher contribution margin despite operating at a much smaller scale than flights. While flights retain a lower share of revenue after direct expenses despite processing the highest GTV. The Next Leg Of ixigo’s Growth The reinvestment of operating leverage is now centred around three areas: hotels, AI and brand building. While the first two are intended to create new growth and efficiency engines, brand spending is aimed at strengthening customer acquisition across ixigo’s portfolio. Hotels are the biggest new business being built out. ixigo said it has more than 10,000 direct hotel partnerships across nearly 700 towns, while around 90% of its hotel bookings come from its existing user base. The strategy is to use the company’s large train, bus and flight user base to build hotel demand, rather than acquiring every hotel customer from scratch. The company is also expanding the supply side through direct hotel relationships and its acquisition of Brevistay. ixigo expects this combination of captive demand and direct supply to improve the economics of the hotel business over time. But even after all these years, ixigo is clear that hotels will have a longer gestation period; the business is likely to remain an investment drag before it reaches operating leverage. During the Q1 earnings call, Bajpai said, “Hotels will have a longer gestation period than our other categories. We are currently a small player in a large market, but over the next four to five years, our ambition is to become the number one discovery and booking platform for India’s mid-market and budget hotels. That ambition will require investment, patience and disciplined execution. We intend to bring all three.” As a result of being in the investment phase, hotels and other undisclosed businesses reported a negative contribution margin of ₹3.06 Cr in Q1 FY27, compared with a positive ₹1.86 Cr in the year-ago quarter. The second pillar is AI. ixigo is building ixigo NEXT, an AI-native platform aimed at changing how users search, plan and book travel, while also using AI internally to improve productivity. The company has invested upfront in engineering talent, AI infrastructure, model development and its own small language models. Some of these costs are one-time, while token and inference costs will rise with usage. As Inc42 reported in May this year. ixigo rebuilt its consumer app around an AI-native architecture instead of layering a chatbot on top of its existing interface. The company believes AI agents will eventually handle everything from flight bookings and refunds to check-ins and itinerary planning. “Our long-term roadmap includes AI agents that can autonomously check users in for flights, send boarding passes, call hotels to reconfirm bookings or even speak to airlines on behalf of customers,” Bajpai told us in an earlier interaction. Management expects the investment payoff to come through higher productivity rather than simply lower technology spending. It is tracking metrics such as output per employee, cost per task, cost per customer interaction, speed of product development and incremental revenue generated through AI software and tools for travel providers, hotels and fleet operators. For instance, the company recently launched busGDS.ai, an AI-first operating system and global distribution platform for bus operators along with its AI-first hotel platform HELLO (Hotel Extranet for Listing, Loading and Operations) to help hotel and accommodation partners manage their property listings, pricing, and daily operations. Bajpai’s recent words after the Q1 results that ixigo’s ambition is to become the leading hotel discovery point over the next four to five years indicate that ixigo is taking the slower lane even after all these years. The company is not simply trying to maximise margins from mature verticals, but using that growing leverage to comprehensively cover the travel horizontal while also building an AI and software moat.

Srinagar, Sep 22: National Conference MLA from the Baramulla constituency, Javid Hassan Baigh, on Tuesday said tourism was not solely dependent on the scenic beauty of the destination but was deeply tied to the prevailing situation of the place as well.
Talking to Greater Kashmir outside the Assembly complex, MLA Baramulla cited the example of Gulmarg, which witnessed no visitors during the period of conflict.
"Tourism is not only related to beauty, it is also related to the situation. Gulmarg is a beautiful place, but during tense situation no one visited the place. You should not link tourism to beauty," MLA Baigh told Greater Kashmir.
He said tourism is a culture that needs to be developed through a gradual process.
"I will share details of several projects for Baramulla once they materialise. When many such projects will come for Baramulla, I will share them with you. You will get an idea of where our government is and how many projects have come to Baramulla," he said.
Talking about the developmental challenges in his constituency, MLA Baramulla said Baramulla's problems are inherited, with land scarcity being the foremost hurdle.
"The problem in Baramulla is that we have inherited from the past. For example, we do not have acute scarcity of land," he said.
He said the expansion and decongestion of Sopore, a project worth Rs 500 to 1,000 crore, was under discussion.
"CM Omar Abdullah (sahab) called me and asked to identify 200 acres of land so that we can decongest Baramulla. I met the Commissioner Secretary of Urban Development. But the issue is that land is not available," he added.
"I do not have land for a hockey ground in Baramulla. Do you have any land in Baramulla? The whole land in Baramulla is either with defence or the government offices. So, how can we decongest Baramulla? you tell me," he said.
He also pushed back against the perception that Baramulla alone had been left behind, saying, it wrong to say that only Baramulla is backward.
"Not only Baramulla, but everyone in Kashmir has seen an unexpected situation over the last 35 years," he said.
He, however, said that people of Baramulla will soon receive the good news with regard to the developmental projects.

Over the past four months, Amber Retzloff, a critical care nurse in Florida, requested to work 50 specific 12-hour shifts. But over half the time, she says her hospital’s Palantir-powered scheduling software assigned her to different shifts, often putting her on back-to-back-to-back days and leaving her mentally drained. Retzloff doesn’t expect to always get the slots she wants, but by her count the tool does a far worse job honoring her preferences than managers did when they assigned shifts by hand.
Retzloff’s experience mirrors that of other nurses across HCA Healthcare, the largest hospital chain in the US. Since 2023, HCA has rolled out an AI scheduling tool it co-developed with Palantir called Timpani at roughly 130 of its 190 locations. Retzloff’s hospital adopted it nearly two years ago.
“No one is happy with Timpani,” says Retzloff, echoing what five nurses at other locations reported in interviews with WIRED. “Everyone complains all the time.” Other purported HCA workers have expressed similar gripes about the tool on platforms like Reddit.
The nurses who spoke with WIRED allege that Timpani has potentially harmed patients by causing care teams to be understaffed, imbalanced, and exhausted. Operating with minimal oversight, they say the tool routinely schedules too few nurses or not enough experienced veterans during shifts, particularly on Sundays. It also frequently ignores nurses’ stated preferences for spacing out shifts, working nights and weekends, or taking specific days off.
As a result, nurses say they are being forced to waste more time trying to trade shifts or appeal their schedules than prior to the arrival of the software. They also believe colleagues are increasingly calling out, using paid or unpaid time to skip assignments, though doing so more than a few times annually puts them at risk of termination.
Retzloff, 34, a National Nurses United labor union leader with a decade of bedside experience, recalls recent shifts where all four of her colleagues were junior. Because she was the only senior nurse working, Retzloff says she had to delay care for the sickest patients to guide the novices through milder cases.
HCA is “letting AI dictate,” Retzloff says. “We are overriding clinical judgment and the human-to-human piece of health care with an app.”
Previously, managers handled scheduling manually and generally consulted nurses well in advance when overriding requests. With Timpani, nurses report needing to make alternative arrangements on shorter notice and an increase in temporary reassignments to different teams. “I can’t remember any issues before,” says a non-union nurse in Texas who asked to remain anonymous out of fear of retaliation from HCA. “Everything came out on time.”
Harlow Sumerford, an HCA spokesperson, says that nursing leaders, not Timpani, make final scheduling decisions. Assertions that the tool “is designed to reduce staffing at the expense of patient care” are misrepresentative, he adds.
HCA’s goal is “to have the right caregivers, with the right skills and experience, available to meet the needs of our patients while also considering our colleagues’ scheduling preferences,” Sumerford says, noting that the company is continuing to improve Timpani based on nurses’ feedback.
“Being Kicked”
On average, Timpani schedules nurses for 1 percent of their requested days off, or what are known as red days, according to HCA. Lee Barker, an HCA nurse in Missouri, says while that number might appear relatively low, getting scheduled on red days was previously unheard of at their facility.
But less than a year after management introduced Timpani, Barker says now essentially every nurse has been assigned to work on a day they were supposed to be off. Barker delayed a long-planned doctor’s appointment for a chronic condition after struggling to trade an assigned red day. “It feels like we’re being kicked while we’re already down,” Barker says.
Complaints about Timpani have prompted HCA management to make minor updates to the software, but problems still persist, according to nurses across the US. Leaders of National Nurses United, the labor union representing about 10,000 of HCA’s 100,000 nurses, says the company has rejected their requests for information about the technology.
Some purported details emerged in July when a former HCA data science manager, Angelique Russell, sued the company for allegedly firing her in retaliation for raising concerns about Timpani. She accused HCA of routinely deleting data the tool uses to create schedules, which prevented auditing how well it worked and she claimed may have violated several healthcare laws. (HCA has yet to formally respond in court, and Russell declined to comment.)
Timpani was built on Palantir Foundry, a software platform for storing and analyzing different data from across a company’s operations. Named after the beat-keeping musical instrument, it uses algorithmic forecasts of patient volumes and staffing needs to automatically build nursing schedules. When Timpani launched in 2023, HCA’s top innovation executive Michael Schlosser told WIRED it would save time and money, as well as eliminate favoritism in assigning shifts.
Schlosser said in a paper this past July that Timpani has drastically reduced the number of hours managers spend on scheduling each month, lowered reliance on costly contract nurses to fill shifts, and increased retention. “The efficiency comes from AI generating stronger initial schedules,” he wrote, adding that over 98 percent “include a mix of skill and experiences.”
HCA’s responsible AI policy emphasizes protecting individuals from “physical” or “emotional” harms, and executives have said they spoke to nurses and took an empathetic approach in developing Timpani. In marketing materials, the company features nurses praising the tool for being easy to use and saving them time. Yet other HCA nurses say they feel ignored and disrespected, and they are not the only health care workers who have raised concerns about Palantir’s push into their industry.
Rayus Radiology, a large US imaging chain, began receiving complaints about scheduling errors earlier this year after it introduced a tool also built on Palantir Foundry, according to internal documents viewed by WIRED. The software is designed to populate scheduling fields from doctors’ orders. But in a number of cases, it linked the requests to the wrong patient profiles, listed tests or scans that didn’t match the orders, or made up personal details about patients. Schedulers who work at Rayus suspect that non-standard forms, illegible handwriting, and insufficient human review contributed to the issues.
Rayus spokesperson Kit Crancer says “the broad characterizations” do not fairly reflect its “processes, safeguards, or commitment to safe, accurate, and timely patient care.” He adds that Rayus uses technology “to support, not replace, appropriate human judgment and oversight.”
A Palantir spokesperson declined to comment using their name, but the company has described its software as merely presenting information in a more helpful manner and emphasized that customers are responsible for the data, policies, and decisionmaking.
Palantir Anxiety
Palantir’s sales have nearly doubled recently to almost $2 billion per quarter, as organizations seek its help analyzing data and automating tasks. Soaring costs and staffing shortages have made health care providers especially eager customers. Cleveland Clinic credited Palantir software with boosting patient capacity by forecasting ER discharges and replacing manual coordination.
But Palantir has also received pushback from civil rights activists over its defense and immigration work, as well as the stated political views of cofounders Peter Thiel and Alex Karp. In the UK, Palantir landed a $440 million contract with the National Health Service to try to cut appointment wait times, but nurses and activists have demanded it be canceled over privacy and security concerns.
At HCA, some nurses also want Palantir gone. While studies show AI-based scheduling holds promise, nurses say Timpani has become a source of anxiety. “Everyone checks immediately and every month you hear, ‘Man, why did it schedule me like that?’” Barker says.
Initially, some local managers could edit Timpani’s schedules. Now, nurses must flag problematic shifts to a centralized team at HCA headquarters in Nashville, which reviews appeals without direct communication or room for explanation, according to nurses. If denied, they try to swap shifts, but the chances of success are about only 50 percent, Barker and Retzloff claim.
Barker, who is a National Nurses United leader at an HCA psychiatric center, claims several colleagues quit over Timpani and that workplace injuries have climbed in the first 12 months with the tool. The center’s union of about 500 nurses filed a grievance over the software, arguing HCA is failing to sufficiently honor scheduling preferences. The matter is likely headed to arbitration.
In Timpani’s early days, HCA’s Schlosser acknowledged health care workers can be slow to adopt tech “because they have people’s lives in their hands.” But he envisioned a future where frontline nurses actively pushed for more tools: “Then it’ll be fun.” Three years later, some nurses see little reason to rejoice.

Joker persona helps Cong 'feel the fear' in opponents
- Published
Before Wang Cong faces off with her opponents, she dyes her hair green, paints her face white and draws a bright red grin from cheek to cheek.
Fans may assume Cong is paying tribute to Batman's notorious arch-enemy the Joker, but the Chinese fighter says her persona is rooted in the joker playing card that inspired the comic-book villain.
The 34-year-old, who is on a four-fight win streak, says she can "feel the fear" in her opponents when she wears the face paint.
On Saturday at UFC 332 in Salt Lake City, Cong will be hoping she can invoke the same emotions in Brazilian Natalia Silva, when the pair fight for the vacant flyweight world title.
"It means the most powerful card, so I want to be the most powerful," Cong tells BBC Sport.
"When I have paint on I feel crazy. It makes me perform better, it inspires me. There's not much different between paint and no paint, this is my true personality."
Cong has bewildered opponents at weigh-ins while wearing the face paint, and says she even adopts the Joker alias when using social media messaging back home in China.
She tossed an imaginary coin and pretended to shoot a gun before her fight against Gabriella Fernandes in 2024, while in July she bizarrely gifted Tracy Cortez a pack of fake eyelashes before the pair's flyweight encounter.
Cong laughs as she reveals Silva can expect a "surprise" of her own before their fight at the Delta Centre, although she then turns serious as she pays tribute to her opponent.
Silva, 29, enters the contest on a 14-fight win streak across different promotions and is the favourite to capture the vacant title after Valentina Shevchenko was forced to vacate the belt last month through injury.
"She's an incredible fighter, an eight-fight win streak in UFC, beaten three former champions, she has amazing footwork, distance control and kicks," adds Cong.
Silva, who is number one in the UFC's flyweight rankings, was set to face Shevchenko for the belt before the bout was cancelled, so was expected to challenge for the vacant title.
Some fans were surprised that sixth-ranked Cong was chosen for the title fight however, and she admits she felt the same way.
"To be honest I was a little bit surprised but if you see the rankings, the girls ranked higher than me have either a fight booked or they have just fought," said Cong.
"I'm on a four-win streak so that makes sense."
The fight represents the first women's main event in the UFC since Mackenzie Dern beat Amanda Ribas is January 2025.
The last time two women headlined one of the UFC's flagship numbered events was when Amanda Nunes defeated in June 2023.
Cong says it's "meaningful" to be flying the flag for women's MMA after a period of under representation in the UFC, and is excited for the opportunities her success could create in China.
If Cong wins, she will become only the second Chinese UFC champion after former strawweight title holder Zhang Weili.
"MMA is my final transition in my combat sports career. I think my success will encourage more athletes to be brave and try mixed martial arts in China," said Cong.
The event has received criticism from some fans on social media, who instead called for the main event to feature fighters such as Jiri Prochazka, Ciryl Gane and Alex Pereira.
When asked if Cong has a message for her critics, she was concise in her response.
"I've got nothing to say right now. After my fight I think they will shut up," she said.

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu, Deputy Chief Minister K. Pawan Kalyan and YSRCP president Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy were among the leaders who paid tribute to veteran filmmaker Singeetham Srinivasa Rao. One of Indian cinema’s most innovative and versatile directors, he died on Saturday (October 3, 2026).
Mr. Naidu said the director, who was born in Udayagiri in Nellore district, had been a guiding light for the film industry, and his experiments on screen had won the appreciation of audiences. He would remain in the hearts of film lovers, the Chief Minister said.
Mr. Pawan Kalyan said Mr. Singeetham had enriched Indian cinema with a wide variety of films. He recalled the director’s experiments and creativity in films such as Pushpaka Vimanam, Vichitra Sodarulu, Mayuri, Aditya 369 and Michael Madana Kamaraju, and the popularity of songs in films such as America Ammayi and Pantulamma. His continued passion for cinema even in his 90s reflected his dedication to the art, Mr. Pawan Kalyan said.
Education and IT Minister Nara Lokesh described the director’s death as an irreparable loss to the film industry. Recalling his association with the Nandamuri family, he said the director had worked with his grandfather, actor N.T. Rama Rao, and had given the industry several memorable films. He particularly recalled Aditya 369 and Bhairava Dweepam, which he described as gems in the career of his uncle Nandamuri Balakrishna.
Cinematography Minister Kandula Durgesh said Mr. Singeetham had left his mark on Indian cinema through films with unconventional themes. He recalled how Pushpaka Vimanam, a silent comedy made during the talkie era, created a nationwide sensation, and Aditya 369 introduced the concept of time travel to Telugu cinema through science fiction. His use of lens techniques to create the dwarf character in Vichitra Sodarulu, at a time when modern computer graphics were unavailable, demonstrated his technical ingenuity, Mr. Durgesh said.
Mr. Jagan Mohan Reddy described Mr. Singeetham as a multifaceted personality who made his mark as a director, screenwriter, producer, music director and actor. His experimental films, innovative storytelling and use of new technology raised the stature of Indian cinema, he said.
Actor Nandamuri Balakrishna termed the filmmaker’s death a “great loss for Indian cinema” and recalled their collaboration on Aditya 369, Bhairava Dweepam and Sri Krishnarjuna Vijayam. He said Mr. Singeetham had shared a special bond with the Nandamuri family, having worked as an assistant to director K.V. Reddy and later as an associate on several of N.T. Rama Rao’s films.

Online retailers that don't support digital wallets are losing Gen Z customers
A study suggests younger people are more likely to walk away if their preferred payment option isn't supported.
Gen Z, the generation widely considered to be digital natives, is particularly choosy when it comes to online purchasing, a new study has found. Online shoppers frequently browse sites, fill their carts and head to checkout — only to abandon the purchase if their preferred digital wallet is not available for check out, according to a recent study from global data and analytics platform PYMNTS Intelligence. And this phenomenon is particularly pronounced in the Gen Z demographic.
More than one-third (36 percent) of Gen Z shoppers abandoned a cart in the last 30 days because they couldn't pay the way they wanted, 1.7 times the overall average, followed closely by millennials at 31 percent. Collectively, 40 million consumers in those two age groups walked away from intended purchases in a single month, the study found, resulting in massive profit losses for online retailers. These cart-abandonment rates are significantly lower for Gen X, with only 15 percent walking away from purchases, and baby boomers and seniors, at only 8.3 percent. With Gen Z's spending power expected to grow to $12 trillion by 2030, retailers risk missing out on a major demographic if they fail to expand online payment options.
Digital wallets are on the rise
Digital wallets like Apple Pay and Google Pay are becoming increasingly common for both online and in-store purchases. Digital wallets were used in 40 percent of online purchases in 2025 and 17 percent of in-store spending, according to a study from payment technology firm Global Payments.
Meanwhile, the PYMNTS study found 87 million consumers, or one-third of US shoppers, had used a digital wallet online in the prior 30 days. Despite Gen Z's well-documented proclivities for analog life, the demographic remains the most likely to use digital wallets, at 47 percent, followed by millennials at 44 percent
These digital natives are driving a global shift to digital wallets, particularly in the US, where $4.1 trillion of total spending is expected to take place via digital wallet by 2030 — a 64 percent increase from 2025. With Gen Z increasingly reaching for their digital wallets, companies that don't adapt risk being left behind, as the group's behavior is a harbinger for future consumer trends.
What payment services does Gen Z prefer?
Financial precarity, unsurprisingly, has major effects on how people spend: the PYMNTS study found that when their preferred method was missing, 29 percent of consumers living paycheck to paycheck who struggle to pay bills abandoned a cart. The rate is nearly three times that for consumers who do not live paycheck to paycheck, at 11 percent.
This issue is particularly pronounced for Gen Z, which has a current unemployment rate of 8.3 percent — double the national average. Even young people who are employed struggle with cost of living in the US, with 42 percent of Gen Z living paycheck to paycheck.
With many young people facing financial pressure, preference for Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) services supported by online wallets are on the rise. Such short-term financing options let users make a down payment and then split the remaining balance into several subsequent payments.
The PYMNTS study found 17.7 million customers abandoned a purchase in the last 30 days because PayPal wasn't available, and 11.1 million of those cited the lack of PayPal Pay Later as a specific reason for failing to purchase. PayPal Pay Later was more popular than other leading BNPL services, with 20% of consumers preferring the service to Klarna at 12.4 percent.
Gen Z walks away; retailers lose out
The bottom line is that missing digital wallet options mean losing out on profit: 33 percent of digital wallet users overall said they would have delayed a purchase, switched merchants or skipped it if their wallet hadn't been accepted, the PYMNTS study said. That number is much higher for Gen Z, with nearly half of the age group stating they would have changed merchants or abandoned the transaction.
Overall, 21 percent of consumers in the US had abandoned an online purchase in the 30 days before being surveyed by PYMNTS, 47 percent of whom wanted to use a digital wallet. That's 26.3 million customers lost, the study notes.
"Checkout is the last handoff in a relay, and a missing payment option can drop the baton just before the finish," the PYMNTS study said. "Every unsupported payment method is a potential lost sale, and the younger your customer base, the higher the risk."

A hot tip to battle performance anxiety? 'Pretend flush' a mistake down the toilet
Never miss a story or episode from Life Kit. Sign up for our weekly newsletter to get our journalism delivered directly to your inbox.
In 2012, psychologist Cindra Kamphoff was running a marathon. Then at Mile 22, her self-doubt started to kick in. She remembers telling herself, "This is dumb. Why am I doing this?"
Life Kit
Beat performance anxiety with these quick tips
But Kamphoff, who works with top athletes on how to overcome performance anxiety — including from the Minnesota Vikings and USA Track & Field — was prepared. She had written positive phrases on her arm that she could read when she needed a boost during the race: "I'm strong, I'm fast, I'm fit, I'm ready."
This is just one of many techniques that Kamphoff shares in The Confidence Habit: 7 Core Practices to Transform Self-Doubt to Self-Belief, published in September. The book offers creative ways to manage fear and negativity — like pretend-flushing your mistakes down the toilet — before, during and after a high-stakes task.
These tools can be applied to any situation, whether it's a race, work presentation or a job interview. The goal is for people to "be their best in the moments that matter most to them," she says.
Kamphoff, who has a PhD in sport and performance psychology, shares four tools you can try today.
Move on quickly with "learn, burn, return"
Maybe you fumble the ball in a big game or forget the lines in your school play and can't stop thinking about it afterward.
If you make a mistake during a high-stakes moment, Kamphoff says it's important to move on quickly.
She suggests a tool she calls "learn, burn, return" to build back your confidence and keep your goals in reach. Try this if you fumble mid-performance, or as a way to reflect after the event.
Learn: Ask yourself, what did you learn? Use this prompt: Next time, I will _____.
Burn: Think of a motion or a cue you can use to remind yourself to move on quickly. Kamphoff says you can snap your fingers, say "that fast" or "you might literally pretend to flush a toilet."
She taught the toilet flush move to former Minnesota Vikings player Adam Thielen, who used it after he fumbled during a playoff game in 2020. He then went on to catch a 43-yard pass over his head that helped the Vikings win the game.
Using the same motion or phrase every time you "burn" helps your brain strengthen new neural pathways when it comes to moving through anxiety, she says.
Return: Now it's time to build yourself back up. Remind yourself, "you got this, you're doing the best that you can," says Kamphoff.
Speak to yourself powerfully
How you talk to yourself matters, Kamphoff says. According to the American Psychological Association, self-affirmations, even in small doses, can have lasting effects on our self-esteem.
When Kamphoff wrote positive messages on her arm to motivate her during her marathon, they worked because she was giving her brain evidence that she could be successful.
As Kamphoff repeated these phrases during her race, her pace picked up. She ended up not only winning the race in her division, but running her last four miles the fastest out of any part of the marathon.
To make what Kamphoff calls a "power phrase," choose a statement that starts with I will, I can or I am. Then ask yourself, How am I at my best? What does that look like? What does that feel like?"
Kamphoff chose phrases that reminded her of her love for running — and that she had trained for hundreds of miles to run the race.
Set gold, silver and bronze goals
Instead of focusing on one perfect outcome, set a range of goals for yourself. Kamphoff recommends creating a "gold, silver and bronze goal," she says.
Let's say you're running the mile in track. Your bronze goal might be running a time you're generally happy with, your silver goal might be to run a personal best, and your gold goal might be to win the race.
This can help decrease anxiety and increase confidence by removing the pressure of one ideal performance and shifting focus to the present moment. Especially because "an outcome is something you can't control," she says.
Fact-check your self-doubt
If you're feeling overcome with negative thoughts right before a job interview or a big test, ask yourself three questions:
- Is that thought true?
- Is that thought serving you?
- What would be a more empowering statement? 
This method is similar to other frameworks, like acceptance commitment therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy. It can pause negative thoughts and help you get back to the present moment.
For example, if you walk into a job interview thinking, "If I don't ace this, I'll never get another job," this exercise can challenge that thought. And it can help you find a more positive, grounded alternative: "Even if I don't get this job, I know I'm capable of success and that there are better opportunities for me."
Remember, she says. Confidence is a choice you get to make.
"You get to decide in the moment, are you going to be confident?" she says. "Many times the action of confidence comes before the feeling, and it's a skill."

Keralam orders probe against CEC Gyanesh Kumar over 2006 road project case
The allegations arose at the time following the death by suicide of Malaysian civil engineer Lee See Been, who was associated with the project
Keralam home minister Ramesh Chennithala on Sunday ordered a Vigilance and Anti-Corruption Bureau (VACB) inquiry against chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in a 2006 case of alleged irregularities in a road construction project when the Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer was then secretary of the state public works department.
Chennithala said the probe was ordered based on a complaint filed by Malayankeezhu Venugopal, a Congress leader and member of the state unit executive.
The investigation will be a continuation of a preliminary VACB inquiry which was conducted in 2006 against Kumar and which fizzled out after the IAS officer left the state on a central deputation to Delhi that year.
The home minister said the decision to order the inquiry was taken following legal counsel and consultations with chief minister VD Satheesan.
The inquiry will probe corruption and bribery allegations in connection with the upgradation of MC Road under the Kerala State Transport Project (KSTP) by the PATI-BEL consortium. Kumar was then the Public Works Department (PWD) secretary who oversaw the project.
The allegations arose at the time following the death by suicide of Malaysian civil engineer Lee See Been, who was associated with the project, in Kuala Lumpur, said the minister.
“Two suicide notes were written by Been, one to his superior at work and one to his wife. Gyanesh Kumar was named in one of the suicide notes,” said Chennithala.

Venugopal alleged that there were repeated delays to the road modernisation project which had propelled PATI-BEL to write complaints to then State government.
“Been, who was the project manager then, had come to the State several times to meet top PWD officials urging them to clear his bills on time. He was under tremendous pressure from the sub-contractors. The treatment meted out to him by then PWD officials was extremely bad and he died by suicide in Kuala Lumpur. Kumar was among the PWD officials who were named in the suicide note,” said Venugopal.
The home minister said a preliminary probe was ordered under then Left Democratic Front (LDF) government of VS Achuthanandan in 2006 and saw Kumar being shunted off the PWD department.
“Shortly after, he earned a deputation to Delhi and left Keralam. He never came back to the state and the probe fizzled out,” said Chennithala.
TM Thomas Isaac, CPI(M) leader and finance minister during the 2006-11 LDF Government, welcomed the vigilance probe and said the country needed to know what happened in 2006.
“The case files of the 2006 vigilance probe should be with the department. They must be examined. As far as I know, PATI-BEL did not want to continue with the project at the time and was fearful of the company’s name being maligned by a corruption probe. But today, the circumstances are different and people can come forward with any evidence they have,” the former minister said.
The inquiry against Kumar comes as he faces growing allegations of taking unilateral decisions within the Election Commission. Opposition parties and outfits, including political pressure group Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) staged protests demanding his resignation from the post.

Christa Pike donated her last meal to homeless before botched execution
Christa Pike’s defense team warned a judge that a lethal injection was a bad idea due to her small veins and blood disorder

Just before the state of Tennessee botched her execution and left her unconscious and on a ventilator, it offered Christa Pike a last meal.
She turned it down, asking instead that the money that was to be spent on her be used to buy pizza for homeless people in downtown Nashville, according to The New York Times.
Pike was to be executed on Wednesday at 10 a.m. By the end of the day, she would survive two lethal injection attempts, end up in the hospital, and force Tennessee to enact its second moratorium on executions in the last five years, according to the paper.
Pike, as of Oct. 3, was unconscious, intubated, and on a ventilator at a Nashville-area hospital following the failed execution.
The 50-year-old woman's execution had been a point of contention and concern for both her legal team and anti-death penalty advocates in the weeks before the incident.
She had been convicted and sentenced to death for torturing and murdering her classmate, Colleen Slemmer, when she was 18 years old. Pike has admitted that she was without remorse when she was convicted, but has grown over the years to regret the life she took.
Her defense team argued during the trial that Pike was a victim of extreme trauma and sexual abuse, and that the weight of those factors on her actions was not considered during her trial and sentencing.
The family of the victim told the NYT that Pike deserves “swift justice.”
Pike received a short-lived stay of execution just 90 minutes before she was scheduled to die on Wednesday. A federal appeals court issued the stay, saying it needed more time to consider new arguments in her case.
Later, just after 5:45 p.m., the U.S. Supreme Court lifted the stay, clearing the path for the execution.
The Department of Corrections has insisted it followed its lethal injection procedures to the letter. Randy Spivey, Pike's attorney, claims otherwise.
He told the NYT that state protocol says the process should take 10 minutes, but it instead took an hour.
“I counted at least seven needles used in her left arm alone, one of which appeared to be bent when it was pulled from her arm after an unsuccessful attempt,” he said.
He told the paper that the legal team had warned the state that a lethal injection was a bad idea, noting that Pike has small veins and a blood disorder.
Spivey said Pike was even trying to help the executioner find viable injection spots.
“Over and over again she said, ‘Please try up on my shoulder higher, please try here, please try here,’” Spivey told the paper.
The state ultimately failed to execute Pike and instead left her unconscious and critically ill.
Despite the current moratorium on executions, there may be future attempts to kill Pike. Gubernatorial front-runner Sen. Marsha Blackburn said, if elected, she would try again to execute Pike, according to the NYT.
Whether the state can try again may be determined by the state of Pike’s mind when — or if — she recovers. The Supreme Court has previously ruled that a prisoner sentenced to die must have the cognitive abilities to possess a “rational understanding” of why they’re being executed.
Pike’s lawyers have asked Gov. Bill Lee to allow her to live out the rest of her life in prison. He has ordered an investigation to determine what went wrong during the execution.

New Delhi: Centre wants the land currently used by Air Force Golf Course on Lok Kalyan Marg to be returned to ministry of housing and urban affairs (MoHUA). This has been communicated to the entities concerned, an official said.
This comes at a time when Land and Development Office under MoHUA has expedited the process to get back land parcels in this location close to the PM's official residence, which were earlier given on lease or were encroached, including those occupied by Delhi Race Club, Indian Polo Association and Delhi Gymkhana Club.
No official details were available about the purpose of getting back the land parcel. Sources said this is part of the govt's larger scheme of things for the efficient use of prime land parcels for public purposes.
Earlier, in 2017, L&DO had slapped notices for the eviction of five properties, including the Air Force Sports Complex, Jaipur Polo Ground and Old Willingdon Camp. But no further action was taken.
L&DO evicted the Delhi Race Club from its 53-acre premises on Lok Kalyan Marg in Aug, citing that the land was required for an unspecified "public purpose".
Similarly, it evicted the Indian Polo Association from Jaipur Polo Ground in the vicinity for a larger public purpose, public governance and defence infrastructure projects.
It has also initiated eviction proceedings against the Delhi Gymkhana Club to get back 27 acres of prime land and has cited the urgent need for defence infrastructure, public security and governance-related public-interest projects. The matter is before the Delhi High Court.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have been photographed together in Britain for the first time since returning to the UK with their children in August, choosing a low-key pub lunch in the Cotswolds for their latest public appearance. The Duke and Duchess of Sussex were seen holding hands as they arrived at The Falkland Arms in Great Tew, Oxfordshire, on Thursday, 1 October. Photographs published by The Sun showed the couple dressed casually as they walked towards the pub, with both wearing sunglasses. The outing was notable because, although Harry and Meghan have each made appearances in Britain since their return, they had not previously been photographed together in public. PEOPLE reported that the couple's family returned to England in late August, with their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, beginning school in the UK. The family continues to maintain its home in Montecito, California, while the location of their UK residence has been kept private. For the pub visit, Meghan wore a black jumper with dark trousers and white trainers. Harry was seen in jeans, a jacket and a Santa Barbara Fire Department baseball cap, a detail that offered a reminder of the couple's continuing connection to their California home. According to The Sun, Meghan ordered gluten-free beer-battered haddock and chips with mushy peas and tartare sauce, while Harry had chicken, ham and leek pie with seasonal vegetables, mashed potatoes and gravy. A source at the pub told The Sun that the couple were treated in the same way as other customers. “When they visited, Harry and Meghan just acted like locals,” the source said, adding that visitors to the pub are treated alike regardless of who they are. The choice of a local pub also offered a markedly different setting from some of Harry's recent appearances in Britain. Since the family's return, he has attended charity and public events, including the WellChild Awards and a London gala supporting Ukraine. Meghan, meanwhile, has largely stayed out of the public spotlight while the family adjusts to life in Britain. She has continued working on her lifestyle brand, As Ever, while also sharing occasional glimpses of the family's life in the UK. The couple's return to Britain has not been without complications. Their children's schooling became a particular concern after photographers were reportedly seen around the perimeter of their school. PEOPLE reported that two men were observed by school staff and private security monitoring the school grounds. One was later identified by police as an international photographer working for a European press agency. The Sussexes' spokesperson described the incident as an unacceptable intrusion into the children's privacy. The children subsequently changed schools shortly after starting the new term, with the couple's spokesperson saying the decision followed discussions with their security team about the practicalities of their arrangements. Against that backdrop, Harry and Meghan's quiet pub outing provides one of the clearest public glimpses yet of their return to everyday life in Britain. Predictions that Taylor Swift would make a cameo on “Saturday Night Live” with host Dakota Johnson came to fruition when the duo appeared together in the opening monologue.

Then the subject returned to Johnson’s dating life. For example, a Facebook page called The Local Situation posted the claim alongside an image purportedly showing the 83-year-old budding "tomato" gardener with his alleged gold medal cannabis plant (screenshotted). The caption says the man is from Ulladulla, a coastal town in southeast New South Wales.
"Panellist Marjorie Budd said the panel was so taken by its lush foliage and rich aroma that nobody asked where the tomatoes were," the post adds.
The rumor spread elsewhere on Facebook (screenshotted).
Snopes readers searched our website to determine whether the story was rooted in truth or just blowing smoke.
In short, the claim is labeled as satire. The Local Situation Facebook page was the first to post the rumor. The account's content is dedicated to fake stories based in Australia.
"Real local issues with a satirical edge," the page's account description reads (archived).
The person behind The Local Situation said in an email to Snopes that the story was satire and had no connection to any real stories.
"I regularly do Cannabis related satirical posts to raise awareness for medical cannabis driving rights and cannabis legalisation in Australia," said the account owner.
Growing and consuming cannabis for recreational purposes is illegal in New South Wales and in most of Australia.
The image in The Local Situation's post was also generated using artificial intelligence, according to OpenAI's detector tool, which checks for an invisible AI watermark known as SynthID. (OpenAI is the company behind ChatGPT; its detection tool can only tell if the image was created using the company's own AI software.) The Local Situation also confirmed that the image was created using AI.
(OpenAI)
Other indicators the image is AI-generated include distorted faces in the background and unreadable text on name tags and labels.
Pangram, which is considered a leading AI text detection tool, determined that 100% of the text in the original post was also AI-generated. (Despite Pangram's comparative reliability, it is worth noting these tools are still fallible.)
If this story were true, reputable local news media outlets would likely have reported on it. Searches using Google, DuckDuckGo and 
These searches did, however, find several Australian news stories about men who were busted or arrested on charges of growing cannabis, who either claimed they were growing tomatoes or were actually reportedly growing tomatoes near the cannabis plants.
Snopes has debunked similar fictional rumors, such as a claim that Canada faced a major donut shortage shortly after the country legalized recreational marijuana use.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates
- Published
Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict.
On Thursday, Ethiopia announced it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security.
Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.
Meanwhile, a pro-government militia says it has seized the town of Milazat, which is just 20km (12 miles) south-east of Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, where the main anti-government group is based.
The BBC has not been able to verify this claim.
The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters.
It follows a sharp deterioration in relations between the neighbours, with Ethiopia accusing Eritrea of supporting a new rebel alliance – an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied.
Eritrea described the decision to expel its ambassador as "astounding".
"Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia," its foreign ministry said, warning of "negative corollaries" from the decision.
The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian federal forces battle fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.
Ethiopia has also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, giving him 48 hours to leave the country, according to state media. The government has not publicly given a reason for the decision.
Egypt responded by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period, according to the state-affiliated Al Qahera News.
Relations between Ethiopia and Egypt have been strained for years, largely over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a huge hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile.
Egypt, which relies heavily on the Nile for its water supplies, has long expressed concern about the dam's potential impact on its share of the river's water.
- How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia 
  - Published17 hours ago
- WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces? 
  - Published4 days ago
The cutting of ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea mark a dramatic reversal from 2018, when Abiy restored relations with Asmara after two decades of hostility, prompting joyous scenes as the border reopened and families separated for years were reunited.
The rapprochement helped earn the Ethiopian prime minister the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019.
The latest hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people had died during that two-year conflict.
Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.
A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines.
The BBC has not independently verified the allegation.
The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and the internet and phone lines have been cut, making it difficult to get reliable information from the region. It is not clear who was responsible for cutting communications.
In a rare response to the BBC before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel denied that it was involved in the fighting in Tigray, which borders his country.
He told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia.
The two countries were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.
But relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea.
Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993.
Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports.
Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards Mekelle, the regional capital. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting.
The TPLF has also been fighting in neighbouring Afar, which lies along Ethiopia's crucial transport corridor to Djibouti and the sea. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to have fled their homes there.
Both the Ethiopian government and the TPLF accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding to a federal offensive and drone strikes, while Addis Ababa says Tigrayan fighters launched attacks after taking control of federally administered airports in Tigray.
The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region.
The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said drone activity and air strikes were putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk, while insecurity and road closures were restricting humanitarian movements.
The UN has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

Whittaker survives late scare to hold on for points win
- Published
British light-heavyweight Ben Whittaker survived a dramatic late onslaught from Conor Wallace to move a step closer to a world-title shot with a points victory in Birmingham.
The 29-year-old controlled much of the contest with his trademark showboating and superior boxing skill at the Utilita Arena before Wallace came roaring back in the championship rounds.
The Northern Irishman rocked Whittaker in the 10th and came close to a remarkable turnaround in the 12th, with the home fighter forced to hold on until the final bell.
The judges scored it 117-111, 116-112 and 115-113 as Whittaker became mandatory challenger for the IBF world title.
"It was too easy and I took my eye off the ball a little bit. He caught me with a good shot but that's boxing," Whittaker said.
"When it got a bit too easy I was playing too much and doing silly antics."
The Olympic silver medallist extended his unbeaten professional record to 13 wins and one draw and is now mandatory challenger for IBF champion Dmitry Bivol, who also holds the WBA 'super' and WBO belts and is expected to face Liverpool's Callum Smith in December.
Wallace, 30, suffered the second defeat of his 19-fight career and called for an immediate rematch.
"If he wants to run it back and get a beat down again he can. If not, we'll move on," Whittaker responded.
Showboating Whittaker clings on in Birmingham
Whittaker made an extravagant entrance, accompanied by a live string ensemble playing WWE star The Undertaker's theme before switching to "Icon" by Karen.
Despite being from nearby West Bromwich, Whittaker was greeted by as many jeers as cheers from the roughly 5,000 fans inside the arena.
The fight came alive in the third when Whittaker briefly staggered Wallace with a shot that skimmed his forehead.
Wallace's travelling support made themselves heard, only to be drowned out by an airhorn smuggled into the arena as Whittaker found his rhythm
Among those in attendance were former UFC champion Leon Edwards and American Cassondra Gainey, who travelled nearly 4,000 miles from North Carolina after Whittaker's social-media videos helped lift her spirits during cancer treatment.
Wallace offered a warning of what was to come when he landed a heavy left in the sixth.
"Stay focused. Just because you're comfortable, don't get lazy," trainer Andy Lee told Whittaker, who regained control before an almost disastrous 10th round.
Wallace hurt him with a thudding southpaw left before Whittaker walked on to a huge shot and looked in serious trouble.
Whittaker briefly got some respite when Wallace was warned for punching on the break, but he continued pushing forward as a major upset suddenly felt possible.
Whittaker hit the canvas three times in the final round, none ruled knockdowns, as Wallace threw everything at a visibly tiring opponent.
By the end, Whittaker had done enough to win - but not without giving Wallace and his support reason to wonder what might have happened with a little more time.
"I only have myself to blame," he said. "I feel like I've got the best support in the world. This felt like my home show tonight even though it's in Birmingham."
Promoter Eddie Hearn welcomed the possibility of a rematch: "We know Ben is in the position to fight the winner of Bivol-Smith but it's likely that won't be until next summer, so he needs to fight in the interim."
Kamara wins debut, British-title success for Fawaz & Uddin
On a strong undercard showcasing domestic talent, there was British-title success for Walsall's Hamza Uddin and Londoner Bilal Fawaz.
Nigeria-born Fawaz, who is fighting for a British passport, stopped Eithan James in the eighth round to retain his British and Commonwealth light-middleweight titles.
Fawaz – who earned a £5,000 stoppage bonus offered to him by promoter Hearn earlier in the night - called out IBF world champion Josh Kelly and Conor Benn after his win.
"It doesn't matter who is in front of me, with the capacity of what we are trying to achieve, no one can stop us except if they are at world level," Fawaz told BBC Radio 5 Live.
Unbeaten Uddin, 23, dominated Sean Bruce, dropping him twice in the fifth with punishing body and head shots for an eighth straight win.
Uddin closed the show in the eighth with a heavy right. Bruce rose at the count of nine before the referee stepped in.
Given star billing in the chief support on his professional debut, standout amateur Odel Kamara, 22, dominated Thodoris Ritzakis, dropping the Greek in the first before a somewhat premature third-round stoppage.
"Liverpool has a star. Britain has got a star. This kid is going all the way," Hearn said of the debutant.

Cornell president ‘deeply disturbed’ by alleged gang rape, pledges transparency
Cornell University’s president has called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 “deeply disturbing”

Cornell's president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 “deeply disturbing” Saturday, said it would weigh on the university for years to come and pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school’s handling of the case.
In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.
“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.”
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent review of Cornell's handling of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said the school's Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul’s decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.
“I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say,” Kotlikoff said. “We don’t have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves.”
Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell’s response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.
During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell’s response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.
Hochul, asked at a news conference Friday whether she believed Kotlikoff should resign over the university’s handling of the case, declined to take a position, saying she did not yet have enough information.
Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough, saying that has led to distrust. While citing “real legal and privacy limits” on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.
He also committed Cornell’s support to legislative efforts to change New York’s sexual assault laws.
The case has renewed scrutiny of a state law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman’s original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.
Critics have long sought to close what they call the “voluntary intoxication loophole,” which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.
Kotlikoff also called for a “serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life,” saying Cornell would engage students, alumni and others in examining how to preserve the benefits of Greek life while strengthening accountability and transparency.
“Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others or for speaking up when someone may be at risk,” he said.

Digger is poised to be one of the biggest box-office flops of the year
Tom Cruise-led Warner Bros. film is projected to rake in a disappointing opening weekend
Despite a major star's return to dramatic acting, a two-time best director winner at the Oscars and enough publicity to rival the moon landing, Digger looks set to become one of the biggest box-office disasters of the year.
According to Variety, the dark comedy from director Alejandro G. Iñárritu and starring Tom Cruise saw its costs balloon from an original budget of $125 million US to $160-180 million — putting a break-even return around $350 million US when including its marketing spend. (Warner Bros. pushed back on this, telling Variety their actual break-even point is around $300 million US).
It earned only $1.2 million US in previews. And according to the Hollywood Reporter, Warner predicts the film will only earn $12-15 million US domestically this weekend: a dismal opening for the studio in a year already littered with poor performers. Following their films The Bride!, Supergirl, The End of Oak Street and Practical Magic 2 all releasing to apparent losses, that string of failures will possibly be capped by one of Warner Bros.'s biggest flops of the decade.
A bizarre story about an oil tycoon tasked with saving the world from a catastrophe his drilling caused, Digger was always a risk. The R-rated black comedy opted to skip the festival circuit entirely — instead operating on the hopes that strong word of mouth and big-name buzz would convince audiences to get off the couch and head to theatres.
The strategy of avoiding early critical negativity and gunning straight for Cruise fans made a sort of sense: it represents the actor's first non-franchise film since 2017's Barry Seal biopic American Made.
And it is directed by Iñárritu: the auteur whose Birdman won best picture and director at the Oscars, while the following year's The Revenant snagged Leonardo DiCaprio his long-awaited best actor award along with another director win for Iñárritu. But as its earliest critical responses started to release last month, a wave of negative press threatened to sink those chances.
It has been called "the worst movie of Tom Cruise's career" by the Boston Globe, "a metafictional morass" from RogerEbert.com and "a lumbering white elephant of a movie that it almost makes you sorry for everyone involved" by the New York Times. In response to the negative reviews, the film's producers released an ad positioning Cruise's character cursing out critics.
But largely, even critics who loved the film — such as this writer — widely predicted that Digger would be too experimental and odd to ever hope to recoup its budget.
That puts Warner Bros. in a potentially difficult position; after a strong, awards-leading 2025 (including hits like Sinners, Weapons and One Battle After Another) their 2026 slate only offers modest success. Wuthering Heights, Lee Cronin's The Mummy and Evil Dead Burn did pull off positive numbers, though not a single Warner movie has earned above $100 million US domestically this year.
At the most extreme estimates, Digger's failure could put it into the arena with 2026's other big flops: Melania, which earned roughly $16 million US off a reported $40 million budget, and the Anthony Mackie-led Desert Warrior, which made less than $1 million US off its reported $150 million US budget, is still the biggest failure of the year.
- REVIEW Tom Cruise is fantastic in Digger. You might hate it
- Ridley Scott's The Dog Stars bombs at the box office. Here's what that tells us about what audiences want
Digger could still prove valuable for Warner Bros. Despite its dismal expected performance, there is still speculation on whether Cruise could be pushed to Academy Awards success in the end. And given Cruise films' strong brand recognition, it could prove to be popular on streaming.
But the failure comes as the last release before Warner Bros. is fully acquired by Paramount on Tuesday. Digger's failure also came the same weekend as the Hollywood Reporter suggested that Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy — Warner's famously director-friendly film chiefs — would not continue with the company after the merger.
Digger taking bold, thematic risks — and being rewarded with such poor box office returns — could bode poorly for the new conglomerate's artistic choices.
