What's the difference between battery capacity and battery life?
A large battery doesn't necessarily last for a super-long time.
When comparing the batteries of different devices or analyzing how well your own device performs, you'll often see two terms: "battery capacity" and "battery life." While these go hand-in-hand, they are different metrics. Knowing the difference helps you estimate battery performance and be aware of when you need to replace your battery. This applies to smartphones, portable battery packs, laptops and similar.
Battery capacity measures the maximum amount of energy a battery can store; it's expressed in milliampere hours (mAh) for small devices like phones and power banks, or watt hours (Wh) for larger devices like laptops. Battery life is how long the device can last before it requires recharging, typically measured in hours.
A third metric, battery health, is closely related to capacity. Health is expressed as a percentage of your battery capacity when it was brand-new. This is tied to how many cycles your battery has gone through: one cycle occurs every time your battery goes from 100 percent to zero percent charge (these don't have to be all at once).
For example, starting with the Google Pixel 8a, Pixel devices are rated to retain up to 80 percent battery capacity for 1,000 full charge cycles. So if you add 100 percent charge to your device daily, you may need a battery replacement in about 2.5 years.
While these battery metrics are all related, there are other factors to consider alongside them.
Battery capacity versus battery life
The higher the battery capacity of a device, the more energy it can store, which theoretically increases its run duration per charge (i.e. battery life). So a phone with a 5,000mAh battery should, on paper, last longer than one with a 4,200mAh battery. Similarly, in theory, the capacity of a power bank should indicate how many times it will charge your phone.
For example, an iPhone 18 Pro (US model) has a battery capacity of 4,288mAh, meaning that a 10,000mAh power bank could theoretically charge it a little more than two full times. However, charging isn't perfectly efficient; you'll usually see a 20 to 30 percent loss with normal charging. Fast charging and wireless charging generate more heat and thus have even higher loss percentages.
When it comes to real-world battery life, many factors like this are at play. You need to consider how quickly the device consumes energy and how efficient the battery is. If you're using a laptop with a large battery capacity to play modern games at high graphic settings, its battery will likely deplete faster than one with a lesser battery capacity used only for word processing.
Elements like screen size matter; an iPad has a bigger battery than an iPhone, along with a much larger screen that uses more energy. Temperature also impacts battery life; you've likely noticed your phone battery draining more quickly when taking photos outside on a hot summer day. OS and hardware efficiency plays a part too, which is why Apple silicon MacBooks last so much longer than older Intel models.
Battery life can never be a perfect measurement, since you don't use your devices exactly the same way each day. Because of this, companies often provide battery life numbers based on hours of playing video files, with Apple adding a "typical battery life" number for some of its newer devices.
And as batteries age, their capacity decreases. This is why knowing your battery health is important; after 1,000 charge cycles, that "100 percent" battery life icon doesn't mean what it did when you got your device.
Making the most of your batteries
No matter its battery capacity, you can extend battery life by adjusting how you use your device. Keep the device updated to the latest OS, lower the screen brightness, shut down background activities you don't need, and check which apps are draining your battery most. For long-term battery health, try to keep the battery between 20 and 80 percent as much as possible, rather than waiting until it completely depletes and charging up to 100 percent.
A battery will chemically age over time no matter what you do. Once the battery is at 80 percent capacity, it's a warning sign that you should replace it. On many smartphones, you can check battery health percentage in the Settings menu under the Battery section. Yours might even send a warning notification when the battery is significantly degraded. But with normal use, it should last a long time. My iPhone 17 Pro, for example, is still at 94 percent battery health after 316 full charge cycles over the last year I've had it.
Some of the latest devices are switching to silicon-carbon batteries that can pack larger battery capacities into smaller spaces, so you don't have to deal with a heavier or thicker device to enjoy long battery life. But it could be a while before these are mainstream.

North Macedonia vs Scotland. UEFA Nations League Group B1.

North Macedonia 0-2 Scotland: Sebastien Pocognoli earns first win as captain Andy Robertson hits 100 caps
Match report as Scotland beat North Macedonia; Kieron Bowie opened the scoring with his first international goal; John McGinn doubled the lead from the spot after an earlier penalty decision was overturned; Scotland ended the match 10 men after Scott McKenna's straight red card
Saturday 3 October 2026 22:00, UK
Sebastien Pocognoli secured his first Scotland win at the third time of asking as captain Andy Robertson became just the second player to reach 100 caps.
The head coach insisted there was no extra pressure after drawing a blank in their opening two Nations League games, but he and the players silenced some critics with a strong performance in Skopje despite a second red card inside a week as they beat North Macedonia 2-0.
Robertson missed two brilliant chances before Kieron Bowie - hooked after Jack Hendry's early sending off against Switzerland in midweek - smashed the ball into the bottom corner to earn his first international goal and Scotland's first in over 420 minutes.
Play was stopped by a dog running onto the pitch before Scotland continued to dominate with Bowie, Robertson and Ben Gannon-Doak going close before the break.
Scotland were awarded a penalty when Gannon-Doak went down in the box after half-time, only for the referee to overturn his decision after being called to the monitor.
VAR did then award the visitors a penalty soon after. Rangers striker Bojan Miovski was judged to have stopped Bowie's rebound with his arm after Scott McKenna hit the post.
Questions had been asked about John McGinn's Scotland future but the Aston Villa skipper sent the 'keeper the wrong way to double their lead. It was his 27th goal for his country.
But with the visitors looking comfortable, it was a repeat of Hendry's red on Tuesday as McKenna was sent packing late on for his last-man challenge on Agon Elezi.
Scotland host Solvenia at Hampden Park on Tuesday night in the final Nations League match of this extended international break.

Guests arriving at Disneyland Paris over the busy autumn period have been met with an unwelcome message: the parks are full. Both Disneyland Park and Disney Adventure World reached capacity on Saturday, 3 October, according to a report by Inside the Magic, with the resort’s official availability calendar showing no registration availability for guests holding undated admission. This means visitors who hoped to make a more spontaneous trip may find themselves unable to enter. The situation is particularly significant for people travelling to the resort without a dated ticket or confirmed reservation. Disneyland Paris does not publish a live figure for the number of visitors inside its parks, so there is no official public headcount for the day. However, capacity restrictions were in effect, and access for some categories of guests was no longer available. Inside the Magic also reported that both parks had been full during September, suggesting that the latest restriction is part of a wider period of heavy demand rather than an isolated occurrence. Disneyland Paris itself has been warning visitors that its parks are full on many dates because of high demand. According to the resort’s official guidance, guests with dated tickets can enter on the specified date, subject to the conditions attached to their admission. Those holding undated tickets, Annual Passes or Disneyland Passes must register their visit in advance, with admission dependent on availability. The resort also makes clear that tickets are not sold at the park entrances. That distinction is important because having a ticket does not necessarily mean that every visitor can simply arrive at the gates and enter. For certain ticket types, registration is required before the visit, and Disney says availability depends on park capacity. Disneyland Paris explains that its maximum capacity is based on the number of visitors the parks can accommodate while maintaining satisfactory conditions. The threshold can vary depending on factors including the attractions available and the parks’ operating hours. The latest capacity pressure comes as Disneyland Paris enters one of its busiest seasonal periods. The Disney Halloween Festival began on 26 September and is scheduled to continue through 1 November. The resort has introduced seasonal decorations, Disney Villains, special character appearances and the return of Mickey’s Halloween Celebration at Disneyland Park. Disney Fanatic previously reported that the parks reached capacity on the opening day of the Halloween Festival, with visitors encountering signs warning that the parks were full unless they had the required ticket and reservation. The resort is also operating with a significantly changed second park this year. The former Walt Disney Studios Park has been transformed into Disney Adventure World, with the new World of Frozen forming one of its major attractions. The combination of new experiences and seasonal entertainment has made advance planning increasingly important for visitors, particularly those travelling from outside the Paris region. For families who have already arranged hotels, trains and other parts of a holiday around a Disneyland Paris visit, discovering that park access is unavailable only after reaching the entrance can be especially disruptive. The resort’s advice is therefore straightforward: visitors should check availability before travelling and make sure they have the correct dated admission or registration required for their ticket. The recent capacity restrictions do not mean every ticket holder has been turned away. Disneyland Paris’ own rules distinguish between different forms of admission, and guests with valid dated tickets or qualifying hotel packages can have different entry conditions. For visitors planning an autumn trip, however, the message from the resort’s recent warnings is clear: checking park availability is now an essential part of the visit, rather than something to leave until arrival. Russia has struck another major bridge in Kyiv as the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, arrived in the capital in a show of support for Ukraine.
A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, marking the fourth consecutive day that Russia has targeted bridges used by thousands of residents commuting between the city’s two banks. Video footage showed cars driving across the bridge as the drone plunged into the roadway and exploded in a burst of fire. Two people were injured in the strike, said Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko.
The attack came shortly after Merz arrived in the city on an unannounced visit intended to underline Germany’s backing of Ukraine as the country enters one of the most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Germany has become Ukraine’s biggest provider of military aid since Merz entered office in May 2025, surpassing the US as American support has declined.
Kyiv has come under near-constant attack from Russia’s new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, as an intensifying strike campaign increasingly disrupts everyday life in the capital and threatens to leave the city without power this winter.
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, told Merz that people in Kyiv were suffering “terrible nights and days” from the relentless attacks, and called Ukraine’s Russian adversaries “absolute barbarians”.
“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” said Merz, adding as he arrived that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.
Russia had already damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly struck its Southern Bridge. Although the crossings remain standing, repeated attacks and the threat of further strikes have prompted the city’s authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of the city’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, causing temporary closures and large traffic jams.
The attacks form part of a broader Russian campaign against civilian and industrial infrastructure inside Ukraine. In recent weeks, strikes have hit logistics hubs, railway lines, datacentres, medical storage facilities and steel plants, alongside a sustained assault on the country’s energy system that is expected to intensify over the winter.
Russia’s foreign ministry on Saturday warned foreign nationals and diplomatic staff against remaining in or travelling to Ukraine.
“Responsibility for any possible adverse consequences lies entirely with those who choose to disregard this warning,” the ministry said.
A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.
In Moscow, some pro-war commentators noted with glee that the Russian strikes had continued despite Merz’s arrival. “Russia used to pause strikes on Kyiv during visits by European politicians. Not any more,” wrote Sergei Markov, a prominent pro-war commentator.
The trip is Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been among Kyiv’s most outspoken supporters in Europe and a leading voice warning about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other nations.
Last month, Germany formally accused Moscow of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a key logistics hub for western military aid to Ukraine. But Merz is also facing growing discontent at home over his support for Ukraine, as his approval ratings fall.
Germany’s far left and far right are sceptical of support for Ukraine and want Berlin to scale back aid. The pressure has intensified as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made big electoral gains.
“Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis,” Alice Weidel, the AfD’s co-leader, wrote in a social media post.

Imagine spending a decade trying to solve one of mathematics’ hardest problems. You finally make progress only to see an AI model produce a possible solution in a matter of days. This is what happened to Tristan Buckmaster, a 41-year-old Australian mathematician at New York University who has spent years studying the mathematics of how fluids move and behave. At the core of the issue are the Navier–Stokes equations, a set of mathematical equations developed in the 19th century to describe how fluids move. Engineers and scientists use them to model everything from airflow around aircraft to weather systems. But mathematicians still aren't sure whether these equations always hold, or could break down and produce an infinite or otherwise impossible result. Solving this is one of seven Millennium Prize Problems. According to OpenAI, it asked an unreleased AI model to work on the problem on September 1. Four days later, the model produced a possible proof. This is exactly where the controversy starts. Buckmaster and his collaborator Levent Alpöge had put drafts of their unpublished research into OpenAI’s coding tool, Codex. Buckmaster was concerned that OpenAI’s AI may have drawn on his unpublished work, but he had no way to prove that it had. While OpenAI denied that the mathematician's work influenced the system, it acknowledged that data from users’ interactions with its products may, depending on the settings, be used to improve its models. The entire episode is especially concerning for researchers, engineers and academicians, who routinely put unpublished papers, code, designs and ideas into AI tools. And if AI models are using the research work, how can researchers safely use AI without exposing work that is not yet public? Does India have rules to answer this question? Let's find out... In Indian Labs Draft AI Rulebook As AI seeps into all walks of life, all kinds of workplaces are utilising it, and research and academia are no exception. One of the significant examples is Google Deepmind’s AlphaFold, an AI system that predicts the 3D structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences with high accuracy. This also helped Demis Hassabis and John Jumper of Google DeepMind win the 2024 Nobel Prize. This system has been utilised by over 3.3 Mn researchers worldwide to accelerate breakthroughs in biology, medicine, and disease research. In fact, research intelligence firm Wiley found that the overall usage of AI tools surged from 57% in 2024 to 84% in 2025, including specific use for research and publication tasks, which grew significantly to 62% from 45%. Indian academicians and researchers are also relying on AI at varying degrees. For instance, professor Arindama Singh, head of the department of mathematics at IIT Madras, uses AI for literature review and idea generation. However, he added that his approach to AI usage is cautionary, a practice he has been following even before the OpenAI-Buckmaster case blew up. “We do not give our complete solutions to AI for checking; we rather suggest an idea to check. We do not ask AI to check a new method in its entirety, or any patentable idea,” said Singh. Singh is not alone in drawing that line, and institutions are now trying to formalise what individual researchers have been doing by instinct. At IIIT Hyderabad, the caution extends to which models get used. The institute has no institutional AI subscription. It has compute of its own — smaller open-weight models running on campus servers, with individual projects maintaining their own GPU clusters. Those are what researchers are encouraged to use when the data is sensitive. The reasoning is jurisdictional as much as technical. According to Sandeep Kumar Shukla, professor and institution director, the problem with a frontier model is that the user controls nothing behind it. That thinking is now being written down. IIIT Hyderabad constituted a committee in May to frame an institutional AI policy, covering how much AI is permissible for students in homework and lab work, and for research scholars and faculty. Deemed university MAHE, Bengaluru Campus, is at a similar stage. Mangalampalli Surya Sudheer, assistant director of research told Inc42 it is developing institutional guidelines for the responsible and ethical use of AI, including the secure handling of unpublished research. As of now, researchers are expected to rely on broader principles of research integrity and confidentiality. Where Indian Law Leaves Researchers India's one serious attempt at a rulebook for AI training was not written with researchers in mind. For instance, in 2025, the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade formed a committee to examine where generative AI meets copyright. Its working paper, released that December, proposed a hybrid licensing framework: AI developers would get an automatic right to train on any lawfully accessed copyrighted work, rights holders could not refuse, and creators would be paid a share of revenue instead. A second part on AI outputs is still expected. None of it is law yet. The framework treats the harm as financial. Creators lose money, so creators get paid. That works for a publisher or a musician. It works poorly for a scientist. "DPIIT’s proposed compulsory royalty model doesn't work here because money is not the only main harm for researchers," said Mishi Choudhary of SFLC.in, a legal services organisation that brings together lawyers, policy analysts, students, and technologists to protect freedom in the digital world. Lose priority on a result and you lose the credit, the citation, and sometimes the career step that follows. Choudhary's rule is a list of what should never go in: "unpublished manuscripts, proofs, source code, datasets, grant proposals, theses under embargo, patent sensitive material or confidential peer review material," unless the terms clearly prohibit training use. That last condition is where the legal exposure sits. "The real issue isn't whether you typed your idea into an AI tool, it is what the tool does with it," says Gunjan Paharia, managing partner at Zeus IP Advocates LLP. Her advice to researchers and founders comes down to five steps: Protect Your Idea First: File a provisional patent application before sharing a patentable idea with an AI tool. Read AI Tool’s Terms: Don’t rely only on what the product’s marketing says. Check whether your data can be used for training, whether humans can review it, and how long the company retains it. Where possible, use enterprise or API plans that explicitly prohibit training and data retention. Ask For Stronger Safeguards: If you are working with an AI provider, seek clear commitments on no training, no human review, data deletion timelines, breach notifications and applicable jurisdiction. Keep Sensitive Work Out Of AI Tools: Use AI for lower-risk tasks such as literature searches, translation, formatting and early drafts. Keep unpublished findings, core ideas, patent-sensitive material and confidential data offline. Keep A Clear Record Of Your Work: Maintain dated notebooks, version histories and other records that can establish when you developed an idea. Institutions should also have clear AI-use policies that researchers formally acknowledge. "Work that never should have gone outside your four walls cannot be fixed with careful process later," Paharia said. According to Shukla of IIIT Hyderabad, “There is no technological method for stopping them from looking at your uploaded information.” For researchers, the lesson from the Buckmaster episode is that AI comes with questions around confidentiality, ownership and credit. Indian institutions are beginning to address these concerns, but formal policies and legal protections are still evolving. Until clearer rules emerge, researchers are largely left to protect their own work by limiting what they share. At a time when AI is being touted as man's closest companion for everything, including research, the real question is: do we really understand the stakes here?

Senior Judicial Officer, Yash Paul Bourney was sworn in as the Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh at a solemn ceremony held in the Chief Justice’s Court at the Srinagar Wing of the High Court on Tuesday.
Dr. Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh, administered the oath of office to Justice Yash Paul Bourney.
The Warrant of Appointment was read out by M. K. Sharma, Registrar General, High Court of J&K and Ladakh, who also conducted the proceedings of the ceremony.
The ceremony was graced by Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Justice Mohd. Akram Chowdhary, Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal, Justice Rajesh Sekhri, Justice Mohd. Yousuf Wani and Justice Sanjay Parihar. Justice Sanjeev Kumar, Justice Sindhu Sharma, Justice Sanjay Dhar, Justice Rahul Bharti, Justice Moksha Khajuria Kazmi and Justice Shahzad Azeem joined the ceremony through virtual mode from Jammu wing of the High Court.
The family members, close relatives and friends of Justice Yash Paul Bourney were also present on the occasion, lending special significance to the ceremony.
Among other dignitaries present were Mir Syed Latif, Judicial Member (HOD) of the Central Administrative Tribunal, Srinagar Bench, Shaleen Kabra, Additional Chief Secretary, M.K. Sinha, ADGP CID, Achal Sethi, Commissioner Secretary Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs; Divisional Commissioner, Kashmir, IGP Kashmir, IGP Security, Senior Advocates; Executive Members of the Kashmir Advocates’ Association and the J&K High Court Bar Association, Jammu; Law Officers; Judicial Officers; and officers of the High Court Registry.
The Ministry of Law and Justice, Government of India, issued the notification appointing Justice Yash Paul Bourney as the Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh on September 19, 2026.
Born on August 25, 1967, Justice Yash Paul Bourney hails from village Dadwara, Bhaddu, Billawar, District Kathua. During his distinguished judicial career, he has held several important judicial and administrative assignments. He served as Principal District & Sessions Judge at Leh, Baramulla, Udhampur and Jammu, besides serving as Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Srinagar and Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, Jammu.
Justice Bourney also served in key institutional positions as Member Secretary, J&K Legal Services Authority; Registrar Vigilance, High Court of J&K and Ladakh; and Director, J&K Judicial Academy.
After serving as Principal District & Sessions Judge, Jammu, Justice Bourney was appointed on deputation as Member, J&K Special Tribunal, Jammu. He was serving in the said capacity immediately prior to his elevation as a Judge of the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh.

Pakistan summons Indian envoy to lodge 'strong protest' over alleged killing of 2 men near Punjab border
Pakistan's foreign ministry said it categorically ‘rejects any attempt to mischaracterize’ the two men killed along the border as “infiltrators".
Pakistan on Saturday said its foreign ministry summoned Indian Chargé d’Affaires to lodge protest over the alleged killing of two Pakistani men by Border Security Force (BSF) personnel in the Bedian Sector along the International Border on October 2, 2026.
BSF troops on Friday shot dead two suspected Pakistani intruders along the international border in Punjab's Tarn Taran district, officials said, news agency PTI reported.
Pakistan alleged that the BSF personnel ‘resorted to unprovoked lethal force against unarmed civilians.' “Such use of force was wholly unjustified and grossly disproportionate, resulting in the tragic loss of two precious lives. Pakistan categorically rejects any attempt to mischaracterize the deceased as ‘infiltrators’," Pakistan foreign ministry said in a statement.
Pakistan described the killings as a ‘violation of fundamental human rights, including the right to life’.
It further said the Indian side was called upon to conduct and ‘immediate, transparent and credible’ probe into the incident. It also sought disciplinary and legal action against those responsible.
“India was further urged to ensure respect for fundamental human rights and international law, strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements and established border procedures, exercise maximum restraint in dealing with such situations, and take effective measures to prevent the recurrence of such incidents,” the statement issued by Pakistan's foreign ministry said.
‘Two men provoked Indian troops’
The firing incident reportedly took place at around noon on Friday along the border in Punjab where the two countries share a 553-km long border.
Tarn Taran Deputy Superintendent of Police (Bhikiwind) Atul Soni said three intruders were advancing towards the Indian side, but one later returned to Pakistan. The two others continued moving towards the Indian side despite warnings from BSF troops to turn back, Soni was quoted as saying.
According to a BSF sentry, the two men were also provoking the troops and saying they wanted to enter Indian territory, he was quoted as saying. The BSF subsequently opened fire, killing the two men, Soni said, adding that senior BSF officers visited the spot.
Pakistan says the three men were ‘unarmed’
Pakistani state media Radio Pakistan on Friday reported that two ‘unarmed civilians’ were killed by India's BSF personnel near the border in Kasur, a border city in Pakistan's Punjab province. The incident took place when three men of Ladhar village had come a few steps ahead of a border pillar, the report added, citing locals. Two of the three men were reportedly killed, while another one sustained injuries after the BSF opened fire. The deceased have been identified as Azmat Rasool and Mohsin Jutt.
Radio Pakistan further claimed that none of the three men had attempted to cross the border fence, while adding that the ‘incident constitutes a violation of the border agreement and the standard operating procedures governing the Pakistan-India international border’.

Grand Theft Auto 6 brings several new mechanics to the franchise, including dual protagonists, a unique wanted system, an honor profile, changes to how cash is handled, and much more. With so many new features, GTA 6 has introduced new icons to help players keep track of them. So, here is a rundown of all GTA 6 UI and HUD icons to help you understand the meaning of every new symbol you encounter in the game.
Meaning of All GTA 6 Icons
GTA 6 releases on November 19, 2026, but we already got a detailed look at the gameplay with the Netflix Extended Look. Though it did not reveal every small or new mechanic Rockstar has baked into the game, it revealed a lot for us to go by.
Check out the complete list of symbols and icons you will see on the GTA 6 UI and HUD, along with their respective explanations.
| GTA 6 Icons | Description | 
|---|---|
| BUCKME | Shows cash stored inside the BUCKME bank account. Funds in the bank account are safe. | 
| Cash Wallet | Shows cash you have on you in person, and it can be up to $20,000. This money is at risk if you are on an active mission and can be lost if you get arrested or die in action. | 
| Health | GTA 6 health icon, paired with the health bar. | 
| Stamina | Affects your strength, and it’s paired with the stamina bar. Stamina is depleted when you sprint, cycle, or perform other physical GTA 6 activities. | 
| Oxygen | Oxygen tank capacity in GTA 6, paired with the oxygen bar. It only appears when you go underwater with a scuba tank. Decreases based on how long you stay submerged. | 
| Focus | This focus icon is paired with the focus bar in GTA 6. It offers heightened awareness and precision, giving you the ability to scan surroundings, find weak points, and slow down time to shoot enemies. | 
| Relationship Status | Represents the relationship status between Jason and Lucia. | 
| Good Deeds | Notifies when committing a good deed, like petting a dog. Affects your GTA 6 Criminal Profile positively. | 
| Neutral Deed | Criminal Profile is not yet updated or is in unknown status. Also, possibly notifies when committing a neutral act that doesn’t affect the Criminal Profile. | 
| Violent Deed | Notifies when committing a violent act or being evil, for the Violent Criminal Profile state. | 
| Psycho Deed | Notifies when acting like a Psycho, like punching a random person for no reason and adds negatively to the Criminal Profile. | 
| Wanted Star Level | GTA 6 Wanted System star. The more stars you have, the higher the wanted level. | 
| CCTV Profiling | The player’s criminal act has been seen or recorded by a surveillance camera. | 
| Weapon Profiling | The player’s GTA 6 weapon used in an act of crime has been identified. | 
| Couple Profiling | The police know that a couple is responsible for the crime. Read about the dual protagonists in GTA 6 and their Bonnie-and-Clyde dynamics here. | 
| Appearance Marker | The police know when either Jason or Lucia is responsible for the crime. | 
| Clothing Profiling | The player’s clothing worn during an act of crime has been identified. | 
| Vehicle Profiling | The player’s GTA 6 vehicle used during an act of crime has been identified. | 
These are most of the GTA 6 UI and HUD icons that have been revealed so far. All these icons were showcased in the GTA 6 Netflix Extended Look, and we will update this guide as more information comes out. Do you think we missed out on any icons? Let us know in the comments section below.

On 25 September 2026, several opposition parties, including the Congress, held protests across the country demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, while the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) had separately demanded his resignation and appealed to Gen Z to join its proposed agitation. In Delhi, police detained protesters, including Neha Bora, who had reached Jantar Mantar. The protests followed a report by The Indian Express that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had filed at least 14 written objections over the previous 10 months concerning the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and other Election Commission decisions (here, here, and here).
In this context, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Gen-Z protesters taking to the streets of Delhi in September 2026, demanding the removal of EVMs and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Gen-Z protesters in Delhi in September 2026 demanding the removal of EVMs and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar.
Fact: The viral video is not from the September 2026 protests. It shows a protest against EVMs held at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi, on 31 January 2024, organised by 22 organisations and addressed by Bharat Mukti Morcha president Waman Meshram. Gyanesh Kumar was appointed as an Election Commissioner only on 15 March 2024 and was not part of the Election Commission during the January 2024 protest. He later took charge as the 26th Chief Election Commissioner of India on 19 February 2025. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to several social media posts (here, here, and here) (archived) from late January and early February 2024 featuring the same visuals. According to these posts, the visuals are from a protest against EVMs, led by Waman Meshram, with a large march to the Election Commission office scheduled for 31 January 2024 at Jantar Mantar, New Delhi.
Taking clues from these posts, we used relevant keywords and found (here, here, and here) that 22 organisations, including the Bharat Mukti Morcha, Rashtriya Kisan Morcha, and Bahujan Mukti Party, held a protest against Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) at Jantar Mantar on 31 January 2024. The protest was addressed by Waman Meshram, the national president of the Bharat Mukti Morcha.
We also found a Facebook post by Waman Meshram featuring pictures from the protest held at Jantar Mantar on 31 January 2024, showing a similar location as seen in the viral video.
We also found a video uploaded on Waman Meshram’s YouTube channel on the same day, featuring visuals from the same event and showing a similar crowd and location to those seen in the viral video.
PIB Fact Check also debunked the claim, stating that the video is old and dates back to January 2024.
It is important to note that Rajiv Kumar was the Chief Election Commissioner from 15 May 2022 to 18 February 2025. Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu joined the Election Commission as Election Commissioners on 15 March 2024. At the time of the 31 January 2024 protest, Gyanesh Kumar was not an Election Commissioner. He completed his tenure in government service on 31 January 2024 and was subsequently appointed as an Election Commissioner on 15 March 2024. Gyanesh Kumar later took charge as the 26th Chief Election Commissioner of India on 19 February 2025.
To sum up, a 2024 video of a protest against EVMs in Delhi is shared as a September 2026 protest demanding Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.

This is Crepe, a delicate young girl who’s just 1½ years old and weighs only 3 kilograms.
She only recently came to ARK, along with three of her siblings, when her owner moved to a no-pet apartment. And, in the beginning, little Crepe was very good at doing imitations of a rock. Perhaps she thought that if she could just stay still enough, everything would return to what she’d known before.
Now, however, Crepe is beginning to realize that this new world isn’t so bad after all. She is more adventurous and has started to explore her environs, limited as they are. She’ll come out for pats when she notices that the humans bear gifts of food.
Crepe has also discovered toys and how they bring out her joy and her kitten side.
We’d love Crepe to find a new home, preferably along with one of her siblings, which would surely help her quickly gain confidence in her new home.

Ganesh 'visarjan' over, Gyanesh Kumar 'visarjan' remains: Prakash Raj
"Ganesh visarjan is over in Karnataka, Andhra and entire India. Now, Gyanesh Kumar visarjan remains," he told reporters here.
Criticising the SIR process, actor and activist Prakash Raj on Saturday said the 'visarjan' (immersion) of Ganesha idols as part of Ganesh Chaturthi festivities is over and that the 'visarjan' of CEC Gyanesh Kumar remains.
Referring to media reports that 38 lakh appeals from voters (for inclusion) who were removed from the electoral rolls are pending before the tribunals in West Bengal and that it may take 10-12 years to decide them, he asked whether the huge number of applicants should wait that long.
"Ganesh visarjan is over in Karnataka, Andhra and entire India. Now, Gyanesh Kumar visarjan remains," he told reporters here.
Deep Dive
SIR was stated to be a cleaning-up process when it began, but it has been found to be a deleting process, not an inclusive one, he alleged.
Elections are not numbers but citizens of the country who are alive, he said.
He said he took a 10-day tour of different districts to meet people and he was told that their names were "deleted" just because they were not at home when a Booth Level Officer (BLO) visited.
Daily wage workers who have gone elsewhere for work have been removed from the electoral rolls, he alleged.
He also asked whether Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who conducts 'Mann ki Baat', had explained the SIR process in advance.
"Our demand is that SIR has to be stalled and scrapped," Raj said.
Meanwhile, Telangana BJP chief spokesperson N V Subhash slammed Raj for his "insulting" remarks against the Chief Election Commissioner who heads a Constitutional body.
"He (Prakash Raj) may be entitled to criticise the Election Commission, but comparing the CEC to an idol immersion crosses the line from political criticism to disrespect for a Constitutional institution. Democracy demands debate, not derision," Subhash said in a statement.
If Raj has objections to the SIR process, he can place the facts and evidence before the appropriate forum instead of resorting to "provocative street rhetoric," he said.
Meanwhile, a protest was organised here on Saturday by Telangana People's Front, Cockroach Janta Party and other organisations demanding the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, scrapping SIR exercise and repeal CEC Act 2023.
The protesters displayed posters with messages such as "Gyanesh, It's Done Bro!", "Gyanesh Kumar Must Resign", "Save Democracy," among others.

The team behind the award-winning film NAZA, which details the Israeli military’s targeting policies in Gaza and its alleged acceptance of high numbers of civilian deaths, have revealed they spoke to more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.
The disclosure came in response to an Israel Defense Forces statement seeking to discredit the documentary.
In its response, which the IDF said was based on statements made by the film-makers and a review made by a representative who had attended a viewing, the Israeli military claimed there were “substantial errors” in the film and that it had relied on interviews with two dozen intelligence and other troops who had only a partial picture of the target approval process.
At the centre of the IDF’s rebuttal was its often repeated claim that its rules of engagement explicitly distinguish between militants and civilians and prohibit deliberately targeting civilians, while requiring commanders to take steps to minimise civilian harm, claims that have long been challenged over the years by critics.
While acknowledging that it used AI to help recommend potential targets in Gaza, the IDF also said final decisions made on strikes, and the risk of civilian casualties, were signed off by officers.
The IDF also denied that it had approved, planned or carried out an attack anticipating 500 civilian casualties in pursuit of a single Hamas target.
The IDF statement follows previous efforts by Israeli politicians to dismiss NAZA – a military acronym euphemistically used by Israeli intelligence to indicate the number of civilians that it expects will be killed in an airstrike – which have accompanied death threats against the film’s directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, and calls by the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, for them to be stripped of their Israeli citizenship.
It also echoed previous complaints by some Israeli critics – including journalists – that the film’s military sources were anonymised, despite the fact that source protection in media investigations is commonplace and regarded by much of the media as an ethical requirement.
“The film NAZA presents a distorted, misleading, and unrealistic picture of the IDF’s target planning and strike processes. The film’s narrative is based on fundamental factual errors stemming from a skewed and manipulative portrayal,” the statement added.
Responding to the IDF statement, the Guardian, which produced the film, disclosed further details of how the team had verified the allegations which involved scores of interviews with those with knowledge of IDF targeting and authorisation processes.
A spokesperson said: “The IDF’s attempt to portray the 24 participants in NAZA as junior-ranking officers involved only in the early stages of the targeting process is false.
“They include officers and soldiers who were involved in multiple stages of the targeting process in Gaza, including intelligence, operations and the final authorisation process.
“The process of assessing the credibility of the testimonies was rigorous. It included leaked classified documents, detailed verification of specific strikes and corroboration via a wider pool of confidential journalistic sources who did not appear on camera in the film.
“Over the past three years we have together interviewed more than 100 sources familiar with IDF systems used in the war in Gaza, including senior-ranking commanders directly involved in the authorisation of strikes.
“The Guardian stands fully behind the film, which builds on three years of detailed reporting by the Guardian and our partners. Several highly respected news organisations have subsequently confirmed the IDF’s use of AI-driven systems in the Gaza offensive and the loosening of safeguards to protect civilians, including the New York Times, Washington Post and Associated Press.”
While Netanyahu has claimed that Israeli military safeguards have led to one of the lowest civilian-combatant ratios in modern warfare, that has been challenged by the IDF’s own leaked casualty assessments, by the UN’s commission of inquiry in 2024 and research by NGOs including Action on Armed Violence.

New Delhi: Jio Platforms is likely to list by October end at an enterprise valuation of USD 143–146 billion, or above Rs 12 lakh crore, sources tracking the development told PTI.
The digital services company could raise around USD 3.8 billion through its initial public offering. Jio Platforms did not respond to an email seeking comment.
IPO timeline takes shape
The company has completed overseas roadshows and is expected to file its final IPO papers with SEBI in the week starting October 12, according to banking and other sources.
Akash Ambani and Isha Ambani led investor meetings in the US, UK, Dubai, Hong Kong and Singapore. An Indian roadshow is expected after the red herring prospectus is filed.
Sources said the anchor investor round could begin before Dussehra, with the public offer opening after the festival but before October 23.
SEBI issued its final observations on August 28, following the filing of draft papers in June.
Fresh shares on offer
The draft prospectus outlines an issue of up to 27 crore fresh equity shares, representing about 2.9 percent of the equity base after the issue.
Reliance Industries owns around 66.4 per cent of Jio Platforms, while Meta and Google together hold about 17.7 percent.
The offering would mark the Reliance group's first IPO since 2008 and the first public offer of a consumer business within the conglomerate.
Digital business expands
Jio Platforms houses Reliance's digital operations, including telecom, cloud, artificial intelligence and enterprise network services.
Its telecom arm serves 50.6 crore mobile customers. Jio had 26.85 crore 5G customers as of June 2026 and about 1.5 crore fixed wireless access subscribers.
For FY26, profit after tax increased 15 per cent to Rs 30,053 crore, while annual revenue rose 14.5 per cent to Rs 1,46,885 crore.
Nuvama Research expects Reliance Jio's profit after tax to grow at a compounded annual rate of 18 per cent between FY26 and FY30.

The British invasion of the mid-1960s was a multi-pronged attack, an assault led above all by The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, and The Who. Their seismic impact on American and world culture has been well documented. But of the leaders of those three mega-bands, perhaps the most mysterious remains Pete Townshend, The Who’s songwriter and enigmatic eminence, thrashing chords and smashing guitars while Roger Daltry handled lead vocals.
His sheer brilliance and rock innovation is captured in the documentary Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes, which held its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival. It’s directed by Frank Marshall (The Bee Gees: How Can You Mend a Broken Heart) and Nigel Sinclair (producer, Billy Preston: That’s the Way God Planned It). Despite the enormity of The Who’s success – the rock operas Tommy and Quadrophenia, songs “Won’t Get Fooled Again,” “My Generation,” “Love Reign O’er Me” and so many others – somehow the band’s primary creative engine can remain obscured.
“A lot of people, when we say, ‘Oh, Pete wrote all the songs,’ they go, ‘What?’ They don’t understand because Pete’s also very quiet,” Marshall says in an interview at his home in Telluride. “He’s not the front man. Roger’s the front man… So, I do feel he’s underappreciated.”
Watch on Deadline
Key to understanding Townshend, as the film explores, is his background as an artist. He studied at Ealing Art College as a teenager and absorbed lessons from a teacher there, Roy Ascott, who propounded theories of technology and consciousness that would deeply influence Townshend. An exercise at Ealing in “auto-destruction,” where students smashed up pianos or other musical instruments, would lead to Townshend’s signature move with The Who, destroying his guitar at the end of performances.
“Actually, I have one of those smashed guitars, which I had a guitar builder lay out in an exposed frame like a skeleton,” Sinclair tells us. Smashing instruments “became a habit in shows. Obviously, in that club on Goldhawk Road, [Townshend] didn’t intend to do anything. His guitar went up into the ceiling and broke through cheap, old fashioned kind of stuff — with asbestos in those days. And it crumbled on Pete — the guitar and the neck was tipped over. So, he just threw it on the ground and smashed it. That was the first time. And the audience and Roger and the other [band members] are genuinely thinking, ‘What is he doing?’ And then [Keith] Moon, who only takes him about half a millisecond to tack, immediately started smashing his drum kit.”
More than mere theatrics, the frenetic smashing of instruments and The Who’s music itself, written by Townshend, channeled the sense of rage, frustration and angst felt by so many young British people in that post-war period of crumbled empire and dwindling opportunity.
“We see it in that first [Who] song, ‘Can’t Explain,’ when somebody said to him, ‘You’re expressing what we all feel and that connection,’” Marshall comments. “And he didn’t even know, but he was, as an artist, taking what was happening and channeling it into a song.”
Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes contains remarkable archive footage of the band in private moments and on stage, material unseen for decades. Archival producers Kate Griffiths and Catalina Curbishley were key to unearthing it.
“The Who had actually put all of their assets in frozen storage back in the ’80s. It’s in this house, in somebody’s back garden,” says producer Cassidy Hartmann. “Our team actually went in there and sorted through everything and found this material and we were able to transfer it. And once we saw it, of course we were astounded at what was there because it’s like the dream of every documentary filmmaker to find something like this that no one’s ever seen.”
“The treasure chest,” Marshall says.
Townshend was born in West London in May 1945, just days before Germany’s surrender, to musical parents – his father a professional saxophonist and his mother a singer. His parents’ marriage was a rocky one and as a small boy, Pete was sent to live with his maternal grandmother, a woman he would later describe as “clinically insane.” That devastating experience would unconsciously inform Tommy, the rock opera about a “deaf, dumb, and blind kid” who becomes a pinball wizard.
“A big part of our approach to the film was surrounding this idea of Pete as two people, as this divided person,” Hartmann observes. “And I think the trauma speaks to that. He says, ‘I divided then back when I was a kid and became this introverted, imaginative writer person.’ And then of course he also becomes this rock star on stage. And I think a big part of the tension in the film that we were interested in was that contradiction between those two sides of himself and his struggle to kind of reconcile those.”
Pete Townshend: Behind Blue Eyes screens Saturday and Sunday at the Hamptons International Film Festival in New York. It also screens Sunday on the other side of the country – at the Mill Valley Film Festival in Northern California. “Behind Blue Eyes,” of course, is one of Townshend’s greatest compositions, a song at times plaintive and reflective, at other moments ferocious in its anger. That, and “Going Mobile,” “Baba O’Riley,” and “Won’t Get Fooled Again” were written for Lifehouse, a kind of futuristic rock opera Townshend created after Tommy. It was his single most ambitious project (which is saying something) but never came to fruition, for reasons explored in the film. Lifehouse remains the great white whale of Townshend’s career, and a narrative thread throughout the documentary.
“The engine for us was once we realized that he wants to feature this abandoned project, Lifehouse — which is quite hard to understand and of course collapsed for a number of reasons over the years — but it’s incredibly important to him,” Sinclair says. “It’s an itch that he never stops scratching… Frank said we needed to actually explore Pete as a person because what’s interesting about Lifehouse is it’s so important to him. That’s what drives [the film].”
Distribution plans for the documentary are pending. Given the track record of Marshall, Sinclair (Wilder, David Frost Vs.) and Hartmann (The Apollo, Lilith Fair: Building a Mystery), optimism on that front seems warranted. Marshall, a five-time Oscar nominee and six-time Primetime Emmy nominee is one of the top producers in motion picture history. At Telluride, the film became a hot ticket, generating interest from festival-goers including a certain Oscar-winning director, who had his own film in the festival, Ink.
“Danny Boyle was over there saying, ‘I’ve got to see the Townshend film,’” Sinclair reports. “So I spoke to him and said, ‘If you can’t see here, I’ll send you a link.’ So we’re feeling pretty good about getting it placed.”
Hartmann was born after the height of The Who’s success. “I learned a lot on this project. I developed a deep affection for Pete especially. And I did see an opportunity to introduce the band to a younger generation,” she notes. “I thought that there was an opportunity there for that to connect with a bigger audience than just The Who fan base. There was something relatable and universal in Pete’s story for anyone who’s a creative person trying to do something in the world.”

Blazing triple-digit heat bears down on Braves-Dodgers NLDS opener in Los Angeles
The Los Angeles Dodgers are hosting the Atlanta Braves in what is forecast to be the hottest postseason game at Dodger Stadium since 2017

The Los Angeles Dodgers are hosting the Atlanta Braves in what is forecast to be the hottest postseason game at Dodger Stadium since 2017.
Shade was at a premium on Saturday for Game 1 of the National League Division Series, which began at 1 p.m. local time. The game-time temperature of 100 degrees was forecast to reach 101 degrees Fahrenheit (38 degrees Celsius), about 20 degrees warmer than the average for early October.
The highest game-time temperature ever recorded at Dodger Stadium is 103 degrees (39 degrees Celsius) twice. The first time was Oct. 24, 2017, for Game 1 of the World Series against Houston. It was equaled on Sept. 8, 2024, for a regular-season game against Cleveland.
The Braves seemingly were unfazed by the blazing sun, cloudless skies and rising thermometer while taking pre-game batting practice. The two-time defending World Series champion Dodgers? They stayed inside.
“Remember, we're from Atlanta,” Braves manager Walt Weiss said before the game. “It's not that big of a factor.”
Braves center fielder Lane Thomas added, "I feel like this is a little cooler 98 than Atlanta.”
Some of their fans agreed.
“It's hot, but it's not bad,” said Helen Greene of Valdosta, Georgia, who was sitting in the sun nine rows behind the visiting dugout with her long hair arrayed under a Braves cap. “In Atlanta, my hair would have been up by now.”
Greene and her husband, Chad, were hydrating with water.
“I'll have beer later,” she said, smiling.
Tickets for Game 1 were still available early Saturday. The lowest get-in price ranged from $56 to $61, depending on the secondary marketplace.
Fans still gathered in the outfield pavilions in hopes of catching a stray ball off the Braves' bats pre-game. But other seating areas were mostly empty 90 minutes before first pitch.
Christopher Hernández of Long Beach and his girlfriend sat in the sun behind the Dodgers dugout with giveaway towels covering their heads.
“We play sports and we know how it feels to be in the heat and we know how to beat the heat, too,” he said, showing off a blue plastic bottle with a fan attached to spritz water. “It's not as bad as people think it is.”
Dodgers manager Dave Roberts planned to keep an eye on his pitchers and catcher Will Smith, who wears a mask and padding behind the plate.
“It’s the same conditions for both teams,” the manager said, “and you’ve got to just stay hydrated and manage it.”
Braves reliever Brent Suter graduated from Harvard in 2012, having majored in environmental science and public policy.
“In the back of my mind, I’m like 100 degrees in October in L.A., that’s definitely not normal,” he said before the game. “Obviously super El Niño is a big thing to do with that. It’s going to be a challenge for both sides to stay hydrated, especially the position players.”
Short heat spells in October are normal for Los Angeles, but the prolonged extreme heat warning — forecast to last at least a week — is keeping temperatures 10 to 15 degrees above normal. The average high in Los Angeles in early October is 81 degrees (27 degrees Celsius).
“Just making sure everyone is hydrated and staying loose and getting electrolytes in us,” Suter said.
Emergency medical teams were in their usual spots around the stadium, staying alert for anticipated cases of heatstroke, dehydration, excessive sweating caused by heat exposure, and the more typical drunkenness.
The Dodgers encouraged fans to wear hats and sunscreen. They were allowed to bring in non-alcoholic drinks of one liter or less in factory-sealed plastic bottles. Empty refillable water bottles were also allowed. Bottle filling stations and water fountains are scattered around the stadium.

BANIHAL, Sept 22: Two police personnel were found unconscious under suspicious circumstances inside a car at Ziarat Morh in Sana area of Batote tehsil of Ramban district on Tuesday evening, police sources said.

‘Balanced and acceptable’: labour chief defends helper wage rise amid criticism
Chris Sun says the 2.35 per cent increase to HK$5,220 reflects Hong Kong’s stronger economy, but unions and employers’ groups remain unsatisfied
Hong Kong’s stronger economic performance over the past year is the reason for raising the monthly minimum wage for foreign domestic helpers, the labour minister has said amid disappointment from both unions and employers’ groups.
Defending the government’s decision to raise the monthly minimum wage by 2.35 per cent to HK$5,220 (US$665), Secretary for Labour and Welfare Chris Sun Yuk-han said the government sought to keep the annual adjustment mechanism “balanced and acceptable”.
Speaking after a radio programme on Saturday, Sun said: “If you look back, the average annual increase has been between 2 per cent and 2.5 per cent for many years.”

India is likely to have a much older population later this century, as the country’s age structure is beginning to shift and fertility has fallen “below replacement,” Moody’s Ratings said on Tuesday (September 29, 2026).
Moody’s said population growth has long been a tailwind for economic growth and creditworthiness, but falling fertility is now changing that picture.
Fewer workers will limit productive capacity, while fewer households and consumers will weaken demand. As a result, countries will have to rely more on productivity to sustain growth.
Moody’s said the global fertility rate had declined from 4.9 children per woman in 1950 to about 2.2 today, only slightly above the replacement rate of 2.1.
“What makes this episode particularly significant is that many of the world’s largest economies are ageing at the same time. In fact, more than 70% of the world’s population now lives in countries with fertility rates at or below replacement level,” Moody’s said in a report on global demographics.
It said fertility rates across much of Latin America were now comparable to those of Europe and Japan, while several East Asian countries had some of the lowest fertility rates ever recorded.
Japan has the most top-heavy population structure, with nearly 30% of its population over 65 and about 11% under 15.
South Korea is close behind, while China is moving rapidly in the same direction. Emerging markets, including Brazil, India, Thailand and Türkiye, are also progressing along the same path.
“Although India’s population remains relatively young, fertility has already fallen below replacement and the country’s age structure is beginning to shift, setting the stage for a much older population later this century,” Moody’s said.
Declining fertility ultimately reshapes age structures as well as population growth, it said. Countries experiencing the steepest fertility declines today will also age most rapidly in the coming decades.
