No one expected an American pope. Here's the inside story of how 'Bob' became Pope Leo
NPR's Daniel Burke and Scott Detrow covered the 2025 conclave that elected Pope Leo XIV. The following excerpt is adapted from their new biography of Pope Leo, American Pope, out Tuesday.
In the days immediately following Pope Francis' death, messages from friends poured into Cardinal Robert Prevost's phone.
Father Ramiro Castillo Castro, who had studied under Prevost in the 1990s, was among those who sent condolences. "Thank you, Ramiro," Prevost responded. "We have to pray a lot. Big hug."
"Polly and I send our love and prayers for you in these momentous days," wrote John Snider, a Lutheran pastor with whom Prevost had spent a summer in Minneapolis debating theology and learning how to minister to the sick and dying before they were both ordained.
Now, decades later, Snider was winding down his career, and Prevost was about to participate in a conclave to elect the next pope. "As I near retirement, 3 weeks, you are taking on such intense responsibility," he wrote. "God is with you!"
"Everything is in God's hands," responded Prevost, thanking the Sniders for their friendship through the years.
John Barry, Prevost's friend dating back to high school, was overcome by the news of Francis' death. "I know you were close to him and I'm sorry for your personal loss. The world has lost a great man. You also lost a friend," he wrote.
He offered his prayers and then turned to something that Prevost's friends around the world — in Illinois, in Peru, in Rome and elsewhere — were thinking.
"Okay, now Bob please don't get upset with me, but I believe what [their mutual friend] Jeanette first said — that you could possibly be the next pope. (Of course, you're too humble to entertain such thoughts.) I realize it's not a job a person would want, but in my heart I know you would make a great pope. You've obviously got the brains for the job. But your compassion, your kind heart, and your holiness are what really elevate you in my eyes. You're the best man I know. And this may or may not be a silly question, but if you do become pope, can I still email you?"
Amid the flurry of activity in Rome, Prevost found the time to quickly write back.
"I just leave everything in the Lord's hands," he responded. "Francis' passing is a true loss ... it will take time to process. ... Thank you for your prayers!"
"Since I really don't think there will be a need to change addresses," he added at the end, "you can still write. … Just tell your dad that you call me by the right name!" (This was a reference to a running joke between the two of them about how upset Barry's father was that his son called his high-ranking cardinal friend "Bob.")
For all his friends' intuition, Prevost was not one of the cardinals initially focused on as a "papabile," a papal contender (the phrase literally means "pope-able" in Italian).
There were many reasons for that. Most prominent: Prevost was American.
An American had never been pope, and the prevailing conventional wisdom was that one never would be elected. The country already had too much influence over world events, some argued.
The political situation in the United States may have made the prospect of an American pope seem even more unlikely. President Trump had returned to power and had spent the first months of 2025 asserting his "America First" agenda on the world through brute force. And just as cardinals arrived in Rome in the wake of Francis' death, Trump posted an AI-generated image on social media depicting himself as the next pope, offending the cardinals and Catholics around the world.
So no one expected an American pope, certainly not in that moment.
"We're talking about a country that has political, economic, military power in the world," Chicago's archbishop, Cardinal Blase Cupich, said in an interview with the Chicago Sun-Times, "and so I think it's a stretch to say that it's prudent to go ahead and have someone who is from that country. … I'm not going to handicap anybody in terms of their chances. But I think that'd be a stretch."
Prevost read the article.
"Cupich said they aren't going to elect an American," he told his friend Father John Merkelis after the interview. "I'm sleeping well at night."
Merkelis relayed Prevost's sentiment to their old friend and mentor Sister Thérèse DelGenio, who had worked with both of them as they learned to minister to addicts in Calumet City, Ill., in the late 1970s.
"Oops," DelGenio responded. "He forgot about the Holy Spirit."
"I had never met the man"
Over the course of the next week, cardinals from around the world descended on Rome to mourn Francis and begin the process of electing the next pope.
That included the most high-profile cardinal in the U.S., New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan. One of the few voting cardinals who had also participated in the 2013 conclave, Dolan reveled in his seniority, even as he batted aside questions about his electability.
"I've got a better chance at batting cleanup for the Yankees than I do being pope," he joked to a reporter at the airport.
Dolan was an ally of Trump's. He had prayed at both of the president's inaugurations and served as a member of the White House's Religious Liberty Commission. As the church's leading representative in the media capital of the world for more than a decade, he was far more visible than his colleagues. And, as a jovial extrovert, he prided himself on knowing many, if not most, of the cardinals in the conclave.
And yet, as he flew to Rome, Robert Prevost was not on his radar at all.
But when he landed, he was bombarded by other cardinals who immediately began asking about his fellow American. What was he like? What were his interests? His temperament? Dolan was taken aback.
"I said, 'Who?'
"I didn't even think of him as an American," Dolan explained. "I mean, the little bit I knew about him was good — I had heard good things about him. But I had never met the man."
When the questions kept coming, Dolan realized he had to change that fact — and fast. He saw Prevost at a gathering of cardinals. Unlike many others, he noticed, Prevost was not working the room or approaching others to greet them. It wasn't aloofness that drove that behavior, though. Dolan thought it might just be shyness. He approached Prevost with an outstretched hand. "Robert, my name is Tim Dolan. I don't think I met you before."
The movie Conclave drives up excitement for the real thing
Starting the day after Francis died, the cardinals began assembling daily in an auditorium off St. Peter's Square. Sitting in a steep lecture hall, wearing laminated name tags over their black cassocks and red sashes, they held General Congregation meetings that often stretched on for hours, during which they would discuss the state of the church, the priorities its next leader would have to face, and what sort of qualities they wanted to see in him.
"On some days, it was a little disorganized," Cardinal Joseph Tobin, of New Jersey, admitted. "They said it was kind of like listening to an argument in an Italian barbershop while watching an episode of The Sopranos." Whenever order was eventually restored, Tobin said, the sessions would gravitate to the same big questions: "What does the church need? What does the world need? What are we hoping for, what are we dreaming about?"
Outside the walls of Vatican City, Rome was abuzz with excitement. Thousands of reporters from all over the world had poured into the city to cover the conclave. Every morning, crowds of journalists and religious pilgrims would swarm as soon as they saw a man in a red skullcap and black cassock walk into St. Peter's Square. The reporters would ask questions about the latest intrigue, while the pilgrims would ask for prayers and blessings. Some cardinals would stop — more often for the prayer requests than the questions — but others would keep walking.
The 2024 movie Conclave, which had been nominated for Best Picture at the recent Academy Awards, also drove up interest in the proceedings. The sumptuously shot adaptation of Robert Harris' novel was a political thriller about the selection of a new pope as the church is at a moral and political crossroads. It depicted cardinals whipping vote counts and debating campaign strategies as they smoked cigarettes in stairwells and glided through the ornate halls of the Vatican.
Many of the real-life cardinals insisted they hadn't watched the film, but Prevost had. He had talked about it with his brothers. His high school friends had asked him about it, too. They'd all, Prevost included, jokingly tried to match up each movie character with his real-life inspiration. It was all in good fun, but Prevost insisted to them he wasn't a Conclave character. Harris had written the book in 2016, he pointed out, before Prevost had been made a cardinal.
"If it does happen, let it be OK"
As the meetings went on, more cardinals began to seriously consider Prevost.
He was a close ally of Francis and committed to many of Francis' top priorities: making decisions through the more communal approach known in the church as synodality, standing up for immigrants and speaking up on the environment. He had spent years as a missionary and was arguably as closely tied to South America and Peru as he was to the United States. "The least-American American" was a phrase that suddenly began to pop up in news articles, attributed to various cardinals.
Prevost was also becoming increasingly attractive to some of the cardinals who wanted stylistic changes from the Francis era. Dolan was among them. As much as he praised Francis' heart and pastoral energy, Dolan and others hoped for something different from their next leader. "Non-flashy. Reliable. Not impetuous, not unscripted," he explained. "Just sort of measured, circumspect. Calm. There's not going to be any bombshells. You know, you're not going to have to wake up in the morning and say, 'How are we going to answer the questions about this statement?'"
Dolan began doing more homework on the quiet American. At one point, he asked a colleague, one who had worked closely with Prevost, for insight.
"He runs a good meeting," came the reply.
"Well, that sure is Irish praise," Dolan thought. "Is that all you can say about it?" But then, the answer's meaning settled more deeply. "I thought, maybe he meant that he knows what he's doing," Dolan later recalled. "He's got an agenda, he's ordered, he's got certain goals in mind."
Dolan had been a public face of the American church for two decades. But sitting in the General Congregation meetings, he began to consider that the first American pontiff might be a radically different kind of figure. During one of the meetings' many coffee breaks, he brought an espresso to an older cardinal, one who was too old to vote
in the conclave. They sat there together in the auditorium sipping their drinks.
"So, who do you think?" Dolan asked.
The older cardinal looked down toward a group of their peers at the front of the room. He pointed at Prevost.
Toward the end of their 12 meetings, the cardinals continued to talk through the qualities they wanted from the next pope. They wanted someone to continue the fight against sexual abuse in the church. To fix the Vatican's disorganized finances. To continue Francis' push to reform the Vatican bureaucracy, the Curia. To work for peace throughout the world. They also wanted someone who, like Francis, prioritized the environment and the need to fully address climate change.
As he heard all this, Peruvian Cardinal Pedro Barreto laughed. The 81-year-old Jesuit was too old to vote in the coming conclave, but he could suddenly see how it would play out. Abuse? Prevost had headed the Peruvian bishops' council to address it. Economic reform? He had played a leading role in working to address church finances in Peru, as well. Fixing the Curia? He'd been in Rome two years — enough time to learn the ropes, but not enough time to become an entrenched member himself. He kept going down the list of priorities.
"Check, check, check, check, check," Barreto said to himself. His friend Robert could become pope — if the cardinals could get over the fact he was an American.
Cardinal Joseph Tobin was coming around to the idea, too. He had known Bob, as he called him, for three decades. They had worked together in Rome, when Prevost ran the Augustinians and Tobin headed his order, the Redemptorists, and then again in Peru.
One night, Tobin, Prevost and several other cardinals gathered together to pray and share dinner. As the evening wrapped up, Tobin took his friend aside.
"I think you may be asked," he said. "So all I'm doing is praying for you."
Prevost didn't debate Tobin or try to dissuade him. He simply thanked him for his prayers. He knew he had no control over his destiny.
Forty years earlier, as a student in Rome, he had voiced a similar feeling in a letter to his friends John and Polly Snider as he waited for his next assignment. It might have been in Rome, he said, or the U.S. It might have been in Peru. He just didn't know. But he had trusted God at that moment, as he had at every other juncture in his life.
As the May 7 start to the conclave approached, he faced a similar crossroads. He had started, in recent years, to fantasize about retirement. Now there was a realistic possibility he'd head the church, and in the process become one of the most famous and influential people in the world. As daunting as that was, he was determined to, as always, give himself over to God's will.
"I took a deep breath," he later said. "I said, "Here we go, Lord. You're in charge. You lead the way.'"
In New Lenox, Ill., John Prevost was praying, too.
Like his brother, John had at first dismissed the idea of an American being elected to the papacy. But as he'd heard the reports and debates, doubts had begun to creep in.
After a Mass at St. Jude, the priest, Father John Merkelis, had approached him to say that his brother currently had the same odds that Jorge Bergoglio had faced going into the 2013 conclave. Merkelis took it as a sign. He joked to John that he had briefly considered pointing him out in the pews that night and telling the congregation they were joined by the brother of the future pope.
"Don't you dare," John Prevost quickly responded. He didn't want that kind of attention. He didn't want his brother to become pope, either. That would mean an end to his brother's visits home, an end to his life as he currently knew it.
He prayed that night for it not to happen. "Then I said, 'Well, if it does happen, let it be OK." Then, as his prayers continued, another shift. "Not my will," he said, "but, what's good for the church."
The day before the conclave began, Robert Prevost went to the Augustinian General Curia, as he often did, to pray and eat with about a dozen fellow Augustinians. He talked with Father Alejandro Moral Antón, the man who'd succeeded him as the order's prior general. They then prayed together to the Holy Spirit, asking it to accompany Prevost and the other 132 electors as they entered the Sistine Chapel the next day.
When the prayer was done, Moral Antón turned to Prevost and told him he was always welcome to return to the Augustinian community for meals, Mass and prayer, no matter what color he happened to be wearing.

Farage 'not being listened to' on safety threats, deputy says after terror plot charge
Nigel Farage's security concerns have been ignored, according to his deputy, Richard Tice
LONDON -- Anti-immigration Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage was ignored when he complained of threats to his safety, his deputy said Saturday after the man accused of killing former British politician Ann Widdecombe was charged with plotting a terror attack against Farage.
Richard Tice said Farage had discussed the risks to his security many times over the years and the charge amounts to a wake-up call.
“What’s particularly upsetting for those of us in and around him is sometimes he’s not being believed, not being listened to,” Tice told the BBC.
Joshua Kerry, 28, was charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, including against Farage, the Crown Prosecution Service said Friday.
Authorities did not release additional information about the charge, but counterterrorism police in August said they had reopened a probe into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage's south London home.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood expressed sympathy for Farage and his family.
"I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning," Mahmood said on X. “Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all."
Mahmood said she would work to strengthen protections for politicians after Parliament returns from recess on Oct. 12.
Kerry was previously charged with murder in the July 8 beating death of Widdecombe, who was found dead in her house in an isolated southwest England village.
Widdecombe, 78, was a spokesperson for the Reform Party after a long career as a Conservative member of Parliament and government minister known for her blunt-spoken, socially conservative views opposing abortion and the expansion of LGBTQ+ rights.
She later found fame as a contestant on the reality television shows “Strictly Come Dancing” and “Celebrity Big Brother” and returned to politics.
Widdecombe's killing renewed concerns over the security for politicians, which had been tightened in the past decade after the murders of two prominent MPs. Labour lawmaker Jo Cox was shot and stabbed in 2016 by a far-right extremist, and Conservative David Amess was stabbed in 2021 by an attacker inspired by the Islamic State group.
Tice said the party had a series of high-level meetings with the government about security and that authorities had shifted their approach to treat threats more seriously.
Kerry is due to appear Wednesday in Westminster Magistrates' Court on the new charge.

Opponents of Anthropic's Dario Amodei are circulating a highly negative brief about him to the White House ahead of an important dinner with President Trump, per an Axios review of the document.
Why it matters: No company wants to be on Trump's bad side — and a Sunday night dinner between the president and Amodei could be what thaws relations after a year of tension.
Behind the scenes: The brief, which is not an internal White House document, casts Amodei as having "a long record of attacking Trump" and having "deep Democratic ties."
It notes the company's falling out earlier this year with the Pentagon as a "clear example of Dario showing he doesn't trust President Trump."
The brief is intended for Trump's eyes and is likely to get in front of him, according to a source familiar with the internal workings of the White House. Its origin is unclear.
It even reads in "Trump Talk," a name the president gives to his style of posting: "Dario claimed that AI would eliminate half of all entry-level white collar jobs as soon as this year. WRONG!"
Between the lines: The brief's creators are appealing to a president who prizes loyalty and puts a premium on praise.
Amodei's failure to communicate properly with the Trump administration has previously cost the company.
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Yes, but: Trump has also been laser-focused on winning the AI race and Anthropic is one of the few companies on the frontier of the technology.
Anthropic is also valued at hundreds of billions of dollars and has plans to go public soon, making it even harder for the White House to ignore.
"The WH is trying to get everyone seated at the table," one source told Axios.
The bottom line: Anthropic and the White House both have something to gain from Sunday night's dinner, so long as Amodei's critics don't get there first.

This little-known app lets you display song lyrics on Apple CarPlay
You can host your own episode of Carpool Karaoke with the Dynamic Lyrics widget.
Few things are more irritating than driving around with people who sing songs without knowing the lyrics. Thanks to Apple CarPlay's that never has to be the case on long road trips or short errand runs. The best part? James Corden doesn't have to be along for the ride; all you need is an up-to-date iPhone, some passengers, and, most importantly, the little-known Dynamic Lyrics app.
As one of many third-party apps that are compatible with CarPlay, this one displays time-synced lyrics on your infotainment system after you connect your preferred streaming service, making it seamless for Apple Music or Spotify users.
That said, like with any CarPlay feature, we'd never recommend taking your eyes off the road to enjoy it, but it's a great choice for keeping passengers entertained for hours on end. So if you want to celebrate The Blueprint's 25th anniversary while riding in the HOV lane, you can get the whole car to rap along to any track. Or, you can enjoy translated lyrics when listening to songs in other languages, which comes in handy for singing along to tracks you love but don't fully understand.
However, there is a catch: it costs $9.99 to enable this feature permanently. So before downloading it, make sure you're willing to pay the one-time price when you open the app, and that your device is updated to iOS 26 so you can enable it on CarPlay.
How to add the Dynamic Lyrics widget
Once you confirm your phone is updated, start by downloading the Dynamic Lyrics app in the App Store. When you open up the app, it'll prompt you to connect your streaming service of choice; whether Apple Music or Spotify, simply allow access to get started.
While the process is a breeze for Apple Music and Spotify users, the latter will have to authorize the app using either a Default or Custom method. While Default authorization only takes a tap, you'll likely need to re-authorize time and time again; on the other hand, Custom authorization will take a couple of extra minutes to set up and requires a Spotify Client ID more time to set up, but the Dynamic Lyrics app walks users through it to simplify things.
As shown above, the premium version of Dynamic Lyrics lets you toggle between different themes and customize the CarPlay widget to your liking. Some of the options include different colored backgrounds, including white, black and a gradient that changes based on the album cover, as well as a pair of cover styles: vinyl or picture, the latter displaying the full album cover.
After you've made your picks in the app itself, head over to Settings > General > CarPlay, select your car and tap the Widgets menu under Customize. Once you press Add Widget, you'll see three options; you'll want to select one of the two titled Lyrics widget. Once you add it, these will appear in your widget stack as small squares, but can be enlarged by pressing for a bigger view of the lyrics.

How both parties have changed since 2024
The 2026 midterms will test Republican disillusionment with Trump — and Democrats’ new appetite for a fight.
Depending on your political appetite and your geographic location, you absolutely do not need me to remind you of the upcoming midterm elections. But for those of you unencumbered by an unhealthy attachment to political news, and unassaulted by the onslaught of ever-more-brazen political ads, consider this your official notice that the midterms are approaching. Fast.
In less than six weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices. The stakes are arguably unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical norms and limits.
So starting this evening, I’m partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s Midterms, Actually team for five weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the 2026 midterms. Together with outside experts, we’ll break down one issue each week and suggest further reading and races to watch in November.
Up first, and without further ado: the profound shift that both parties have experienced since the 2024 election. These are not your mother’s Democrats. Or Republicans.
Go a little deeper
To kick this series off, I asked Astead to imagine a hypothetical world in which he hadn’t followed politics since 2024. (An outlandish counterfactual: Astead is acutely plugged into politics.) But in this alternate universe, I asked, what would surprise him most about 2026?
Easy, he said. The GOP’s disillusionment with President Donald Trump, who remade the party in his image.
Let’s put some numbers on that phenomenon, to start. Trump’s approval rating has dipped to record lows, even among Republicans. According to an NBC poll conducted in mid-September, just four in 10 Republicans strongly approve of Trump’s performance, down 11 percentage points from the spring.
Republicans have soured on Trump over his handling of the economy and attacks on Iran, which violated his promise to keep America out of foreign wars. Trump’s delayed release of the Epstein files also fueled distrust in his base by exposing his own ties to the dreaded “elite insiders.”
In response, some Republican candidates have worked to distance themselves from Trump, even defying him in campaign ads. But it’s unclear whether that tactic will win over disillusioned or disengaged Republicans. If enough stay home, Astead said — especially with Democrats eager to vote — Democrats could flip the House and/or Senate and make Trump’s last years in office far more difficult.
And speaking of Democrats…they’re also undergoing a major transformation after their 2024 presidential defeat. That loss disproved their previous theory of Trump-era politics: namely, that Trump’s rise was an aberration that competence, decency, and normalcy would eventually overcome.
By contrast, today’s Democrats want a party that “fights,” Astead told me. “The open question is who they’re fighting: The oligarchy? Big Tech? The Billionaire/Epstein class? Trump’s Republican Party?”
Democrats face ideological questions, too. Since 2024, voters have lost trust in the establishment and in party leaders’ ability to pick the best candidates; left-wing candidates have thrived in that vacuum. It’s pretty wild, when you think about it, that a Muslim democratic socialist in New York ranks among America’s most popular Democrats.
For both parties, then, November 3 is a test of their respective visions for America. Not just between the parties — as in, Republicans vs. Democrats — but within them, as well. That, in turn, will help determine the rest of Trump’s presidency…and the 2028 presidential election.
But it’s only October 1. Let’s not get ahead of ourselves.
➨ Races to watch: Michigan’s Senate race, where progressive Democrat Abdul El-Sayed faces Republican Mike Rogers; Florida’s 27th District, where Republican María Elvira Salazar publicly broke with Trump; and the Nebraska, Idaho, and South Dakota’s Senate races, where independent candidates will test both sides’ exhaustion with the two-party system.

The Echo Dot Max is an elegant redesign of Amazon’s orb-shaped smart speaker, with high-quality knit fabric, a flat face, a new LED ring, and touch controls. It’s the first Echo Dot with Amazon’s improved two-way speaker system and support for its new AI-powered assistant, Alexa Plus, which is enabled out of the box.
Amazon Echo Dot (Fifth-Gen)
Amazon’s Echo Dot is an affordable way to add a smart speaker to your space. The small, powerful speaker offers surprisingly robust sound, and it’s great for controlling smart home devices, including those compatible with Matter. The Dot also offers faster response times than its predecessor, and it can act as an extender for an Eero Wi-Fi system. Read our review.
Amazon Echo Show 11 (2025)
The Echo Show 11 features an 11-inch screen and 1080p resolution. It includes Alexa Plus and can be used as a smart home hub with support Thread, Matter, and Zigbee smart home protocols. Read our review.
Amazon Echo Show 15
The new year is the perfect time to reset your routines and get organized, and the Echo Show 15 is a great tool for doing just that. Designed to function as a shared household hub, it keeps calendars, schedules, reminders, to-do lists, and notes visible at a glance, making it easier to keep on top of things. As an Alexa-enabled smart display, you can also add events by voice and control compatible smart home devices.
Eero Pro 6E tri-band router
Eero’s Pro 6E mesh router is the Amazon-owned company’s last-gen model. It supports the 6GHz Wi-Fi band with speeds of up to 1.3Gbps and covers up to 2,000 square feet with one unit. Wired speeds can go up to 2.5Gbps. Read our review.
Samsung 32-inch Movingstyle smart display
Similar to LG’s rollable StanbyME display, the Movingstyle Essential is a 32-inch 4K display on a base that’s height-adjustable (and supports swiveling, pivoting and tilting). Unlike LG’s model, though, this one has no built-in battery.
Dreame X50 Ultra
With high suction power, an improved brush system, and the ability to scale thresholds up to 6cm, the X50 Ultra stands out as a great robot vacuum and mop hybrid.

In Summary
- Xiaomi released a number of power banks in the Indian market recently.
- The most eye-catching of the new power banks is the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank, which is the successor to the Ultra Slim power bank launched last year.
- The UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is the slimmest power bank in its class – it is a mere 6 mm thin, and less than 100 grams in weight. It also comes with a super premium design, with a metal build and a fiberglass wireless charging area.
- It has a premium design and feel, but the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank comes with a stiff price tag of Rs 5,999, which many might find outrageous for a 5000 mAh power bank. But it could be perfect for many others!
Power banks and “beauty” are seldom used in the same sentence. They are notorious for being bulky, heavy, and brick-like. Even the ones that can be slapped on the back of your phone and attached magnetically often feel uncomfortable to use along with a smartphone. Unless one is using the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank.
Xiaomi pleasantly surprised us all with a super thin power bank last year, the Xiaomi Ultra Slim power bank, which was so slim and compact that many of us had mistaken it for a card holder. It, however, lacked wireless charging, so it could not be stuck onto the back of a phone. The UltraThin power bank fixes this shortcoming. It comes with a 5,000 mAh battery with up to 15W wireless charging support, and 22.5W charging support (up from 20W on the Ultra Slim). While these numbers are nothing to rave about, it is the design and build of the power bank that are showstoppers. But can its lightweight make up for its rather heavy price tag of Rs. 5,999? Let’s find out:
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Design and Appearance: A treat to hold and carry!
It is difficult to think that anything out of the ordinary can be done with the design of power banks, given just how simple and functional the devices are, but Xiaomi has managed to make the design of the UltraThin power bank its biggest USP. As the name suggests, the power bank is truly “ultra thin.” In fact, at 6mm, it is almost half as thin as the Ultra Slim power bank that impressed us last year, and is the thinnest power bank we have used to date.
The power bank is quite compact as well. It is 98.5 mm tall, 71.5 mm wide, and weighs just 98 grams, which means that it will not only easily fit on the back of any phone out there, but will add only about as much weight as a routine phone case. Even though the Xiaomi UltraThin powerbank is quite sleek, it still feels very sturdy. The body is made of an aluminum alloy shell, giving it that reassuring solid feel, and the wireless charging side comes with fiberglass.
The power bank is available in three different colors – Graphite black, Glacier Silver, and Radiant Orange. While we received the black color option, we think all three colors look very good – the bright orange is the exact shade of the iPhone 17 Pro series’ orange and will basically blend with your iPhone 17 Pro or Pro Max (Apple seems to have stepped away from the shade in its latest iPhones, though).
Our unit came with a matte finish, and the back has a small “Mi” logo in a glossy contrast. The thin sides curve softly around the edges, while the front (which is the part that connects wirelessly to your phone) has a huge circular mark to highlight wireless charging connectivity, along with some information. All the sides are bare except the base, which has a small power button, a USB Type-C port for charging, and four tiny LED lights highlighting the amount of charge in the power bank.
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic power bank is a treat to both hold and carry. It exudes premiumness, and its thin form factor makes it easy to carry around, regardless of whether you hold it in your hand, carry it in your trouser pocket, or in your bag. Or even on your phone. It was so thin and light that we actually used it as a bookmark from time to time.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Specs and Hardware: Decent, rather than exceptional
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is more about style and convenience than specs. It comes with decent enough specs, but nothing that will make people sit up in surprise. The power bank comes with a 5,000 mAh battery, which is a touch more than the UltraSlim, which had a 4900 mAh battery. Xiaomi has used an advanced silicon carbon battery instead of the usual lithium-ion one, which allows more mAhs to be packed in a much smaller form factor.
In terms of charging speed, the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank offers up to 15W wireless charging support and 22.5W wired charging support (up from 20W on the UltraSlim). That sounds brisk enough, but this 15W wireless charging speed is only delivered with the Xiaomi 17 series. For other smartphones that come with wireless charging support, you will get 7.5W charging speed, including the iPhones (MagSafe is supported, but the charging speed remains slow).
Xiaomi has added a number of safety features in the power bank as well. The brand says there are ten layers of safety protection on the device, including foreign object detection, overcurrent, short circuits, overvoltage, overcharging, overdischarging, and over-discharging, amongst other safety features.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Performance: Super convenient, but not super fast
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank’s spec sheet means that it cannot fully charge most modern smartphones from 0-100 percent – while it has a capacity of 5000 mAh, its rated capacity is lower (3000 mAh), as in most power banks. As a result, it was able to take our iPhone 17 (which comes with a 3692 mAh battery) from 20 percent to nearly full only once. And as its wireless charging speed for iPhones is fairly sluggish, it took comfortably over an hour. And it took even longer to charge our Pixel 10 Pro XL. That said, thanks to its slim size and light weight, you can just stick it to the back of your phone and forget it.
If you need relatively faster charging, you can connect your phone to the power bank with a Type-C cable and enjoy 22.5W wired charging speed, which is pretty much three times the 7.5W wireless charging speed with non-Xiaomi 17 series phones, and does get the phone charged much faster in comparison. However, if your phone comes with a relatively big battery (and many phones these days are comfortably above 5000 mAh), the power bank might only be able to get them up to 40 or 50 percent charged before needing charging assistance itself.
While you can use the power bank to charge two devices at once – wired and wirelessly – that compromises speed and its charging capacity a fair bit, as both get divided. The power bank also gets fairly warm while charging a phone wirelessly, which can make the temperature of the phone attached rise too. Our iPhone 17 often got very warm while charging.
The magnetic hold of the power bank is very strong. It latched on very easily to our iPhone and did not budge when we kept the pair of them in our pocket or bags, or even while using the phone. This is by far the most comfortable and convenient power bank to use with a phone – you hardly feel its weight.
Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank Review Verdict: Pricey, premium and a convenience contender
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank comes with a very steep price tag of Rs 5999. You can get power banks with way more mAh, more ports, and much faster charging speeds at a lower price from Xiaomi itself. Other brands also have their version of slim power banks at far lower prices – Boat has the Magnacharge at Rs 1,599 and URBN the One Premium MagSafe at Rs 1,999. However, none of them brings the sleek form factor and the premium build that the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank offers, nor the long-term assurance that the brand offers. In fact, its only real competitor would perhaps be Samsung’s Galaxy Magnetic Wireless battery pack, which comes with a similar capacity and 15W wireless charging, but is bulkier and not exactly super affordable at about Rs 4,900.
If you are in the market for a power bank with more mAh in capacity and more Ws in charging speed, and what’s more, want both for a small price tag, the Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank is not for you. However, if you are someone who wants to invest in an ultra-portable, very premium power bank which can simply give your smartphone a power-packed nudge without adding too much bulk to your gadget life, or even to your device itself, the Xiaomi UltraThin Powerbank might be perfect for you. Yes, it is expensive, but it brings with it terrific design, ease of use, and convenience, which is likely to be coveted by many premium phone users, especially those who use iPhones and Pixels!
The Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank’s style is its substance. And it is substantially stylish. Yes, it does have a big price tag, but then, convenience can also be a powerful feature of a power bank.
Buy Xiaomi UltraThin Magnetic Power Bank

- Impressively thin
- Very portable (phone can be used easily even when attached to it)
- Premium metallic build
- Good magnetic connectivity
- Expensive
- Small capacity
- Only charges the Xiaomi 17 Series at 15W wirelessly (others at 7.5W)
- Gets warm

US becoming a lonelier power by choice, says Jaishankar at Munich meet
Jaishankar said at the Munich Security Conference that the US has deliberately become a lonelier power and that China's rise is reshaping the world. He said emerging and middle powers are responding through de-risking, diversification and flexible partnerships.
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar has described the United States as having “deliberately become a lonelier power”, saying a radical repositioning of Washington and the rise of China are reshaping the global landscape.
Speaking at the 62nd Munich Security Conference, Jaishankar said the international order was being defined by sharp US-China competition, growing self-reliance among emerging and middle powers and a push to diversify partnerships and reduce risks.
“No one in the room would disagree with the fact that the landscape today is primarily marked by a radical repositioning of the United States,” Jaishankar said.
He described the repositioning as “a posture of choice” and said the US had “deliberately become a lonelier power”.
CHINA’S RISE ANOTHER KEY FEATURE
Jaishankar said the second major feature of the current international landscape was the rise of China.
He pointed to China's economic strength, saying it accounts for about one-third of global manufacturing and that its economic capabilities are translating into political influence.
“China, which sees itself as a unique country that is in a way both its self-perception, in many ways, also the reality,” Jaishankar said.
He said the world was witnessing “very sharp competition” between the US and China, with the rivalry extending beyond the two countries.
“That competition today, not limited to these two countries, has led to a weaponisation of any leverage that any country has,” he said.
At the same time, Jaishankar said this competition coexists with the “complexity of interdependence”.
MIDDLE POWERS SEEK MORE SELF-RELIANCE
Jaishankar said emerging and middle powers were becoming increasingly aware of their own interests and were seeking greater self-reliance.
“What unites the emerging and middle powers, differentiated as they may be, is a growing self-awareness of their interest,” he said.
“All of them, in a way, are becoming more self-reliant. It's a term, ‘Atmanirbhar’, very much in vogue in India as well,” he added.
According to Jaishankar, these countries are increasingly assessing what they can bring to the table when they participate in discussions and negotiations.
He said most emerging and middle powers are now focused on diversification and de-risking, extending beyond their economies and security concerns.
“They are developing agenda-based cooperation,” he said.
‘IDENTITY OF VIEWS’ NO LONGER NECESSARY
Jaishankar said emerging and middle powers were also working towards more resilient supply chains and developing new arrangements.
He argued that countries no longer need complete agreement on every issue to work together.
“The operating principle for emerging and middle powers should be, and perhaps is already, a reasonable degree of convergence,” he said.
“The days when you have to have an identity of views or a very strong congruence of interest, I think that's too high a bar today,” he added.
Jaishankar said countries could work together if they had enough common ground.
“If you have enough touch points, that is good enough for countries to work together,” he said.
He added that through “de-risking, diversifying, and hedging”, a new global architecture was slowly taking shape.
QUAD, BRICS AMONG NEW COOPERATIVE ARRANGEMENTS
Jaishankar said emerging and middle powers could cooperate with each other while also maintaining ties with both the US and China, provided they did not have direct clashes of interest.
He cited several examples of such cooperation, including the Quad.
On connectivity, he pointed to the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor, the International North-South Transport Corridor and the Northern Sea Route.
Jaishankar also cited BRICS as an example of countries coming together because their collective voice can be stronger than that of individual countries.
“BRICS is an example of various parties who feel that their collective voice is much stronger than the individual ones,” he said.
He also referred to the International Solar Alliance and the Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure, both initiatives led by India.
‘TODAY’S EVOLVING GLOBAL ORDER’
Jaishankar said countries were increasingly coming together when their interests required cooperation, even when they were not among the world's leading powers.
“They come together where their interests require them to do so: they find working arrangements, develop an agenda, develop organisations, develop habits of cooperation,” he said.
He described this as part of the world’s “evolving global order”, shaped by countries seeking flexibility, resilience and partnerships based on areas of common interest.

Rows of hardware and car-part shops line Garstin Bastion Road, with faded signs crammed together above their shutters. By day, the street is one of Old Delhi’s busiest commercial thoroughfares. But as dusk falls, GB Road, as it is known locally, transforms into one of the city’s most notorious red-light districts.
An estimated 2,800 sex workers live and work in brothels that occupy the upper floors of the dilapidated buildings, their entrances tucked behind narrow stairways and unmarked doors. Women sit on plastic stools beneath the stairways, calling out to men passing on the street, while others watch from windows above, their eyes following the movement below before customers are directed upstairs.
The challenges the women of GB Road face are numerous and well documented – from health risks to abuse, debt to poor sanitation. Now they face a new struggle: India’s controversial electoral reform process. The Election Commission’s special intensive revision, or SIR, is a nationwide exercise in which electoral rolls have shrunk by more than 58 million voters across the 13 states covered in the first two of three main phases. In Delhi, covered in the third phase, the scale of exclusion is the highest recorded as a percentage: 4.76 million names – 33% of the city’s previous electorate – do not appear on the city’s draft roll published on 31 August.
The government says SIR is meant to “purify” the electoral rolls by removing ineligible voters, including alleged undocumented migrants, but critics have accused Narendra Modi’s government of using it to target minority voters and reshape electoral rolls in ways that could benefit his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP).
On GB Road, the proportion of those excluded is even higher. Data shared by officials overseeing about 1,300 voters in the area show that about 650 were sex workers on the previous electoral roll. Of these, at least 500 have either been marked as “shifted”, meaning they have moved home or location, or have been unable to establish their eligibility because of missing documentation – more than three-quarters of the sex workers on the local roll.
One of them is 36-year-old Beauty*, who has lived on GB Road for more than two decades. She got her first voter ID in 2008. At the time, the address where she lived and worked as a sex worker and verification by a government official called a booth-level officer (BLO) were enough to put her on the electoral roll. She voted in previous elections.
But under the new rules, voters had to establish eligibility by proving their link to the relevant previous electoral roll or by producing prescribed documents such as a passport, birth or education certificate – a paper trail Beauty struggled to reconstruct. Trafficked at 16 and brought to the brothels of GB Road, she has no contact with her family. She does have an Aadhaar card, India’s biometric identity document used widely to establish identity and access government services, with her GB Road address. But Aadhaar is not proof of citizenship and does not, by itself, establish eligibility to vote under the SIR process.
She tried to get a copy of her matriculation certificate, which is evidence of schooling, from the village in Rajasthan where she grew up. One of her regular customers of the past 10 years – a man she refers to as her husband, agreed to help track down the old record but failed.
“If I had the papers to show my father’s birth certificate, or even my own matriculation certificate, then I could prove who I am,” she says. “But how can I go back to my village to ask for these things when my trafficking has brought so much shame to my family that they no longer accept me?”
Now Beauty has lost hope – and, for now, her vote. Her name was left out of Delhi’s recent draft electoral roll. For her, the voter ID had meant more than a piece of identification. Sex workers, she says, are accustomed to being treated as immoral, degraded and less worthy than others.
“We all shit. That is what makes us equal as human beings. Voting is the same in the realm of rights. When I stand in that queue, nobody is more or less than me. It reminds me that whatever people think about my work, I am still equal to everyone else.”
Beauty is not alone in struggling to prove her eligibility. The SIR requirements have exposed the precarious paper trails of women across GB Road, a roughly 1.5km stretch running between two of Delhi’s historic landmarks, Ajmeri Gate and Lahori Gate.
Of the nine sex workers interviewed for this story, none had successfully completed the SIR process: six said they had never received the enumeration form distributed by BLOs to verify voters’ details and collect information for the electoral-roll revision, while the remaining three were unable to meet the documentation requirements.
According to Kiran Deshmukh, a sex worker and coordinator at the National Network of Sex Workers (NNSW), many have spent years, even decades, in Delhi but possess few documents establishing their family histories or links to earlier electoral rolls. “Some were trafficked as children and lost contact with their families; others never attended school or have moved between rooms and brothels without leaving a stable documentary trail,” says Deshmukh. “It is impossible in such circumstances to prove such rigid eligibility requirements under SIR.”
The process is so cumbersome that even people who are literate and have institutional and organisational support can struggle to establish their eligibility. “The process of receiving the enumeration form, knowing when you have not received it, reaching out, then trying to create a paper trail is so daunting that the entire burden of proving your eligibility is placed on the citizen to protect their own constitutional right,” says Deshmukh.
Sagrika Rajora, a researcher and member of Voter Adhikar Manch, a citizens’ collective, argues that the burden falls particularly heavily on people whose lives do not fit neatly into the categories used by the verification process. “To identify people of such marginality is a tedious task. These categories of ‘shifted’ become an easy way forward for booth-level officers, when finding people on the ground is already time-consuming.”
BLOs are often drawn from occupations such as auxiliary nurses or health workers, adding electoral duties to already demanding jobs. Some have raised concerns about the workload and unrealistic timelines of the exercise. Yet, Rajora says, there has been little effort to streamline the process to ensure that “no eligible citizen is left out”, the aim outlined by the Delhi chief electoral officer, Ashok Kumar.
“There is so much discretion vested in one BLO. Even if you leave citizenship aside and talk only about voter rights, the entire process of delivering and collecting these forms depends on that one person. There are no grounds for entrusting one person with such a huge responsibility without any accountability at all,” Rajora says.
“It is not surprising that sex workers are among those being excluded. When people have lives that are so complex and mobile, you are going to be untraceable, absent from the system. These are the people for whom such a verification system is simply not designed to work.”
The gaps also cause problems for workers’ children when they reach adulthood. “Children may not possess documents establishing parentage in the manner expected for verification. Some are raised by relatives, guardians or members of the community, while others grow up in institutional care, making conventional family records difficult to establish,” says Deshmukh.
For 23-year-old Dinesh*, whose mother was a sex worker, the problem is not abstract. His mother died three years ago, but she never had a birth certificate. Without one, obtaining her death certificate became nearly impossible, leaving Dinesh with little documentation through which to establish his maternal lineage.
When Dinesh submitted his enumeration form, he relied on his matriculation certificate as proof of his identity. But the booth-level officer pointed out that it did not have his father’s name. “If my mother gave birth to me, why do I need a man’s name on any official certificate?” he asks.
Dinesh says his name is missing from the draft electoral roll. He is still unsure why, but suspects the absence of his father’s name may have been a factor.
The NNSW has written to the chief electoral officer seeking special measures to ensure that sex workers and their children are not excluded from the SIR. But the joint chief electoral officer, Balram Meena, told The Hindu there was no separate process for sex workers. “If their mapping can’t be done and there are no documents either, their names will be removed as per the process.”
The fear of losing the vote is not only about voting rights. In West Bengal, where the SIR has already been completed, the BJP government has used lists of voters deleted during the exercise to scrutinise eligibility for welfare schemes. The BJP chief minister, Suvendu Adhikari, says welfare programmes will continue under a “transparent process”, but adds: “No deceased person, illegal infiltrator, or non-Indian individual will be allowed to avail benefits meant for citizens of the state.” The government has excluded about 3 million beneficiaries from its new Annapurna Bhandar welfare for women scheme, using SIR deletion data in its verification process.
In Delhi, the next stage of the SIR process – issuing notices to those whose eligibility or previous electoral-roll details could not be established or matched, and dealing with claims and objections – has now begun and will continue until 29 October. Those excluded from the draft roll can challenge their omission. But Dinesh says he does not intend to.
After years of being asked to produce documents that his family never had, he is unsure what more he can submit to prove that he exists.
“Even if my mother were alive today, I don’t think that would be enough to prove anything. She never had the documents they are asking for. So how am I supposed to get those documents now, especially after her death?”
* Names have been changed. Workers and residents did not permit any photography during the Guardian’s visit

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'
- Published
"I witness men hitting women all the time," says Kgomotso Mathekga, 30. "Especially when they are both drunk."
"I once had an argument with my girlfriend," he admits, "and I grabbed and slapped her."
Mathekga is speaking frankly during a gathering of men aimed at helping reduce the high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
The meeting is held in a narrow street in a Johannesburg informal settlement known as Organic Market. It is a maze of corrugated metal shacks and unpaved roads, close to Alexandra township.
"Now I feel pain," Mathekga continues. "We broke up and I no longer see my child. I feel like I've contributed to the problems in South Africa, instead of being the gentleman that I know I am."
At a nearby tavern, a group of men have pulled their chairs into a circle in the dust.
At the centre stands Itumeleng Stephen Tamaga, known locally as Bra Steve.
He raises his fist.
"We are men!" he shouts.
The group clap and cheers. Some sip bottled beer.
"Listen guys," Bra Steve says. "We must stand together to fight against gender-based violence and femicide."
Bra Steve is the local organiser of Father A Nation, a non-profit that works with men and boys to promote positive masculinity and help end violence against women.
The group's meeting comes as South Africa grapples with renewed anger over renewed cases of femicide and violence against women.
The discovery of the bodies of 12 women over three months, in the city of Ekurhuleni, near Johannesburg has reignited questions about the scale of what many people see as being a crisis of violence against women.
South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa has acknowledged that his government has not done enough and announced measures he hopes can make women feel safer.
The country has one of the highest murder rates in the world, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
In that period, according to the South African Human Rights Commission, 569 women were killed, an average of six a day, and 1,052 others survived attempted murder.
A report in 2022 by the Human Sciences Research Council found that more than 35% of South African women experienced physical or sexual violence, many from their own intimate partners.
For Bra Steve, part of the solution to the crisis is helping men to understand the issue and take responsibility for their actions.
"We are a lost generation," he says. "We must restore dignity to the men around here."
Amongst the group of men outside the tavern is Zizipho Mtwesi, the project co-ordinator of Father A Nation.
Reflecting on recent weeks, he says more should be done.
The latest measures announced by Ramaphosa, including better street lighting and a review of unsolved cases, are too little, he says, and too late.
"When I think about all of these recent murders in Johannesburg, I get angry. Why do we have to wait for this to happen for us to act?"
He looks around and gestures at the meeting. "We are trying to reach men before things like these murders happen again."
Craig Wilkinson is the founder of the group. "We get men to talk, to process their feelings," he explains.
"And as they do, this healing takes place. And the second phase is teaching and training positive masculinity.
"We ultimately hope that this will eliminate the scourge of gender-based violence."
He stands up, moving into the centre of the group, calling out to the men.
"You as a man are a powerful force for good," he tells them. "You choose what kind of man you want to be. Women need to be safe."
Father A Nation operates across South Africa, teaching healthy masculinity and running training programmes across dozens of schools and colleges.
Mystery surrounds the spate of murders which has sparked South Africa's latest moment of soul-searching about the safety of its women.
Police have not ruled out potential links between some of the Ekurhuleni deaths but have not said they are investigating a serial killer. Suspects in some of the cases have appeared in court.
But the spate of deaths has sparked new concerns and in Organic Market some women are more fearful than ever.
Outside a nearby shack Linkie listens with interest as she cleans clothes in a large metal bucket.
"We are not safe when we are outside our place," she says.
"We are afraid when we see a car behind us when we walk. We feel afraid. We feel scared. What if this guy's going to kidnap me or do something to me?"
It is a feeling shared by many women here. In the local hair salon, sporting a mane of thick pink braids, is Providence Maseko.
She comes to the door to speak to Bra Steve.
"Safety here is very bad," she says, "Maybe you are the serial killer. How do I know who to trust?"
Bra Steve laughs. "We must talk about these things," he urges. "Come to our meetings and we can learn to trust each other."
Maseko tells me that she now takes an e-hailing taxi everywhere in the hope that it is safer.
Back at the tavern, the men's meeting is wrapping up.
"As we try to stop gender-based violence," says Zizipho, "each and every man needs to know that they need to play a part in this.
"And if they wouldn't allow these things to happen to their own daughters or own mothers, they mustn't allow it to be done to someone else's daughter, which is their wives or their girlfriends."
Mathekga is impressed with what he has heard.
"I would love them to keep on practising what we have learned, because we no longer have role models," he says. "Our fathers and our uncles, they are there in prison. We must now become role models and help make this country better."

Hong Kong’s IPO haul more than doubles to HK$388b in first 9 months: Paul Chan
Finance chief says amount raised already surpassed whole of 2025, while HKIC’s CEO says over 30 portfolio firms set to list in city later this year
Funds raised through initial public offerings in Hong Kong more than doubled year on year to over HK$388 billion (US$49.4 billion) in the first nine months of 2026, already surpassing the total amount for the whole of last year, according to Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po.
Adding to the positive outlook, Clara Chan Ka-chai, CEO of the government-owned Hong Kong Investment Corporation (HKIC), noted on Sunday that more than 30 of its portfolio firms were preparing to apply for Hong Kong listings this year.
Paul Chan also revealed in his weekly blog that the average daily turnover on Hong Kong’s stock market from January to September stood at HK$272.9 billion, representing 6.4 per cent year-on-year growth.
“The yields of long-term US bonds have risen to a 24-year high, which has heightened investor concerns over global economic prospects and inevitably dampened recent sentiment in the Hong Kong stock market,” he said.

In the Oct. 3 cold open on “Saturday Night Live,” Andrew Dismukes and Ashley Padilla play Republican strategists who have their work cut out for them building buzz for their party.

‘Brain fog’ is used to describe a feeling of mental slowness, difficulty concentrating, finding words, remembering information or processing things as quickly as before. But it is not a medical diagnosis, and persistent cognitive difficulties should not automatically be attributed to brain fog.
What brain fog feels like
Brain fog is a subjective description of changes in cognitive functioning. People may feel that their thinking has become slower or more effortful, that they cannot concentrate on a task, lose their train of thought, struggle to find words or read something without absorbing the information.
“Brain fog is basically a subjective feeling that you are cognitively slow, that you are mentally slow, that you are not able to do your daily activities as quickly or as deftly as before,” says Srividhya S., associate consultant, department of neurology, Rela Hospital, Chennai.
It is different from the occasional forgetfulness that occurs when a person is tired, distracted or stressed. Forgetting where the keys were kept or briefly forgetting a name, for instance, does not by itself indicate a cognitive disorder. Tiredness is also not the same as brain fog. Fatigue is primarily a feeling of reduced physical or mental energy, while brain fog refers more specifically to difficulties with attention, memory, processing or mental clarity.
T. Swathi, consultant, neurology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai, says people with brain fog are often aware that they are not functioning as efficiently as before. This also distinguishes it from some memory disorders, where relatives may be the first to notice changes such as repeated questions, difficulty managing regular tasks or getting lost in familiar places.
Health factors
The causes of brain fog can be varied, and more than one factor may be involved. Poor or inadequate sleep is a common contributor. Sleep apnoea can also disrupt sleep repeatedly without the person being aware of it.
Stress, anxiety and depression can affect attention and processing speed. Other possible contributors include thyroid disorders, diabetes, anaemia and nutritional deficiencies such as vitamin B12 and folate. Migraine and hormonal changes, including those during pregnancy, the postpartum period and menopause, can also be associated with cognitive symptoms.
Medicines should also be considered. Sedatives, some sleeping medicines, antihistamines, anticholinergic medicines and some anti-seizure drugs can affect alertness or cognitive function. Alcohol and dehydration may add to the symptoms.
“Brain fog has several possible causes and can be due to more than one,” says Arulselvan V.L., senior consultant in neurology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. “It is crucial to not think that all brain fog is neurological.”
Cognitive difficulties can also occur during or after infections. A recent systematic review of 47 studies involving more than 25,000 people with long COVID estimated the pooled prevalence of brain fog at 30%. However, various studies use different definitions and assessment methods. There is so far no comparable prevalence estimate because brain fog is a symptom description and not a defined medical diagnosis.
When tests are needed
There is no fixed duration after which every case of brain fog requires investigation. Persistence, progression and its effect on daily functioning are important.
Doctors advise evaluation when symptoms continue despite adequate sleep and lifestyle measures, recur frequently or gradually worsen. Repeatedly forgetting important information, struggling with previously familiar tasks, difficulty following conversations or unusual changes in work performance are also reasons to consult a doctor.
Symptoms lasting for several weeks without an obvious explanation, particularly when they affect work, studies or relationships, should be assessed. New symptoms such as persistent fatigue, weight changes, breathlessness, tingling, low mood or excessive daytime sleepiness can provide additional clues.
Evaluation usually begins with a detailed history. . A neurological examination may then be performed.
Depending on the history and examination, doctors may check blood counts, blood sugar, electrolytes, thyroid function, kidney and liver function and nutritional markers such as vitamin B12.
A brief cognitive assessment may be useful when there are concerns about memory, attention or language. Brain imaging such as an MRI is also not routinely required for uncomplicated brain fog. It may be considered when symptoms are progressive, the neurological examination is abnormal or there are other features suggesting a structural or neurological cause. A sleep study or EEG may be considered in selected cases.
Certain symptoms, however, require prompt attention rather than being attributed to brain fog. Sudden difficulty speaking, facial drooping, weakness or numbness on one side, sudden problems with vision or balance, seizures, fainting or severe confusion can indicate an acute neurological problem such as stroke. A sudden, severe or unusual headache also requires urgent assessment.

- The Miami Heat will rebrand as Vice City for its November 18 game against the Milwaukee Bucks, celebrating the GTA 6 launch.
- The event will feature an exclusive Vice City-themed uniform, a custom court, and special game-night activities at the Kaseya Center.
- GTA 6 x Miami Heat collaboration also includes exclusive Vice City merchandise, with more items expected to be revealed later.
The Miami Heat is taking a trip to Vice City ahead of the GTA 6 launch. The NBA team will rebrand as Vice City for its November 18 game against the Milwaukee Bucks, with a new themed uniform, a custom court, and special game-night activities planned.
Dubbed A Night in Vice City on the official NBA website, the event will take place at the Kaseya Center. This exclusive match will happen one day before GTA 6 releases on November 19. The game is scheduled to tip off at 7 PM ET, televised on ESPN nationally and on Local 10 in South Florida. The Heat says the event will include a never-before-seen court design and a completely reimagined uniform.
The Heat will play under the Vice City name for this one night, turning its home game into a celebration of Rockstar’s upcoming game. The team has confirmed that the special hardwood will be built for Vice City, while the new uniform will be designed specifically for the event. Neither design has been fully revealed yet.
GTA 6 and Miami Heat Partnership Reveals Exclusive Merch
The collaboration also extends beyond the single basketball game itself. The Miami Heat Store has launched a Vice City-themed merchandise collection featuring shirts and other apparel inspired by GTA 6’s fictional take on Miami.
The merch is closer to the game’s theme than the GTA 6 collector’s box. Especially the classic ‘Vice City’ neon signature, ‘CALL 1-999-VICECITY’ T-shirts, and more are part of the offering. The official site also reveals more merch is on the way.
The event follows the appearance of Vice City branding at the Kaseya Center. The arena was lit up with a “Welcome to Vice City” sign to promote the collaboration. We have already seen the Vice City sign being set up last month.
The tickets for the one-time exclusive GTA 6 x Miami Heat are already up for grabs via Ticketmaster. Are you getting the exclusive Vice City merch from the GTA 6 Miami Heat partnership? Let us know in the comments.

In the 53rd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu, Zubeda Hamid, Senior Assistant Editor, and Athira Elssa Johnson, Senior Reporter, discuss medicine pricing, drug safety and dengue surveillance.
The episode examines the Supreme Court’s concerns over the difference between the supply price and maximum retail price of essential cancer medicines. In one instance, the court was told that a cancer drug with a price to retailer of about ₹2,700 carried a maximum retail price of ₹27,000. The Bench described the difference as “broad daylight dacoity”.
The discussion also covers the court’s concerns about hospitals requiring patients to buy medicines from their own pharmacies, its suggestion of a uniform 16% margin and questions around generic prescriptions and the implementation of the Drugs (Prices Control) Order.
The episode also covers the risks of indiscriminate painkiller and antibiotic use, including kidney disease and antimicrobial resistance. While prolonged or inappropriate use of painkillers can cause kidney-related complications, unnecessary or incorrect antibiotic use can make infections harder to treat. The discussion highlights the importance of appropriate prescribing and responsible medicine use.
The final segment focuses on a Dengue Early Warning System being developed by researchers at the Institute of Advanced Virology in Keralam. The system combines disease surveillance data with rainfall, temperature and humidity to generate weekly, district-level forecasts using machine learning.
Trained on six years of data, from March 2020 to February 2026, the system aims to help health authorities anticipate increases in dengue transmission. If validated, the forecasts could support earlier surveillance, mosquito-control measures, healthcare preparedness and public alerts. The system is still under development and evaluation.
The episode ends with a fun fact about dengue mosquito eggs, which can remain dormant for months in dry conditions and hatch when water becomes available. Even seemingly dry containers can harbour eggs that may contribute to future mosquito populations.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

In 2016, the American Academy of Pediatrics issued a policy statement urging doctors to offer medications for opioid use disorder to adolescent and young adult patients who needed them.
New national data show that more young people with an opioid use disorder diagnosis did start receiving addiction medications like buprenorphine and methadone, but the increase was small. And the number of young people who stayed on medication for six months — already quite low — may have actually decreased.
“There have been some real positive changes, and then there have been some really catastrophic changes,” said Scott Hadland, the chief of adolescent and young adult medicine at Mass General Brigham for Children.
Hadland’s latest paper, published Friday in JAMA Network Open, offers a national perspective on the continuity of addiction care among young people. Researchers analyzed Medicaid enrollment and insurance claims for people ages 13 to 25 who were diagnosed with an opioid use disorder between 2016 and 2023. Out of nearly 230,000 young people over that period, about half initiated treatment by seeing a clinician, and about a third had at least two appointments in the first month. Of those youth engaged in care, about 1 in 6 received some medication. But just 1 in 32 continued with medication for six months.
As with the general population, overdose deaths skyrocketed among young people beginning around 2019 and into the early 2020s. For those age 19 and under, poisonings including overdose rose to the third-leading cause of death.
“I have had patients die as recently as this past month here in Massachusetts, from overdose,” Hadland said. “And so the stakes here are really, really high.”
Medications for opioid use disorder, specifically buprenorphine and methadone, are highly effective treatments that are also relatively cheap and easy to deliver. Yet adults often struggle to get these medications, and for minors, it can be nearly impossible. Federal law requires minors to have two documented “failed” attempts at recovery without medication before they can start methadone, and even then, many of the specialized clinics that provide it won’t accept minors. Buprenorphine is easier for doctors to prescribe, but recent research shows that few residential treatment facilities for adolescents actually offer it.
“Once you turn 18, a whole bigger field of people are open to helping you,” said Sivabalaji Kaliamurthy, a child and adolescent psychiatrist who treats addiction. “And it’s just a number if you think about it.”
In Hadland’s study, fewer than 10 minors received methadone over the entire period — a number so low that researchers had to suppress the specific number and categorize it as “not defined” to protect people’s privacy.
While there are dozens of studies showing the safety and effectiveness of these medications, very few focus specifically on young people. That means doctors don’t have a definitive answer for families when asked how long their child might need to stay on the medications, or what the long-term effects might be. Still, existing research and clinical experience are clear that the longer someone is on the medication, the better they do.
Kids often don’t want to hear that, Kaliamurthy said, and families can be apprehensive about such an open commitment. On top of that, young people also face the same structural barriers that hamper adult care: For example, the study found that Black young people and other racially minoritized groups had worse attrition through the stages of care than their white peers.
Kaliamurthy found the number of young people initiating treatment after diagnosis to be promising, but he and others agreed that more work needs to be done to prevent attrition over time.
“It doesn’t matter how good the treatment we have actually is if we haven’t created a clinical environment that is appealing, safe, compassionate, and nonjudgmental,” said Sarah Bagley, an internist and pediatrician at Boston Medical Center who provides addiction treatment to adolescents. “That engagement piece is everything, because without it, nothing.”
For Bagley, it’s important to continue advocating and doing research around young people as a distinct population. “Because it is different taking care of young people compared to adults,” she said. They have different systems organizing their lives, like school and parents.
Primary care physicians and pediatricians who have longstanding relationships with patients and families need to feel comfortable prescribing buprenorphine, addiction doctors said. And over time, interest from generalists in understanding and treating opioid use disorder does appear to have increased, Bagley said.
Hadland sees it, too. Where he used to feel like he was pitching his pediatric colleagues and professional organizations on the importance of understanding addiction treatment, now there appears to be active demand for such knowledge. On the day the study was published, he traveled to the AAP’s annual conference, where he’ll give a plenary talk on the big stage about addiction and the potency of the drug supply. To him, that signals a cultural shift that will, hopefully, equip more doctors to help young people struggling with addiction. Because currently, he said, the pediatric workforce is not keeping up.

China’s hospital ships project a different kind of naval power in Africa
A surgery performed or a child delivered safely aboard a PLA medical vessel can leave memories long after the ship has departed
When the Auspicious Ark entered Dakar, Senegal, on September 25, the scene looked closer to a public health mission than a naval deployment. Senegalese people and members of the Chinese community were waiting at the port as the vessel arrived for the first visit by a Chinese naval hospital ship to Senegal.
The contrast was already visible in Mauritania, the ship’s previous stop. During its seven-day stay in Nouakchott, a woman with a high-risk pregnancy sought help and gave birth aboard the vessel. That evening, the ophthalmology team completed its first cataract operation of the visit. The ship handled more than 1,600 patient visits in a single day.

The objective of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, is not merely to punish persons found guilty of corrupt practices, but also to ensure that the fruits of such corrupt conduct do not remain available for enjoyment or disposal by those who acquired them through illegal means, the Madurai Bench of the Madras High Court has said.
Justice B. Pugalendhi said attachment of properties acquired through corrupt means, or through wealth disproportionate to known sources of income, was an important component of such a mechanism, and that corruption and corrupt practices had to be treated more seriously than any other offence.
Mandatory attachment and confiscation were essential to combat the vice of corruption, which had affected every part of society, the Court said.
The Court said it was of the view that necessary amendments had to be carried out in the Prevention of Corruption Act, and that the attachment of properties believed to have been obtained through corrupt means, and through wealth disproportionate to known sources of income, had to be made mandatory.
Only if such strong and deterrent measures were prescribed under the Act, the Court said, could the government effectively undertake the attachment of properties and instil fear in the minds of officials who enjoyed properties obtained through corrupt means.
Otherwise, these provisions would merely remain on paper, without any deterrent effect, the Court said, hoping that the government would take the initiative and introduce suitable amendments to the Prevention of Corruption Act.
