Kerala Health Minister K. Muraleedharan on Saturday (October 3, 2026) denied reports of a shortage of medicines in government hospitals and alleged that pharmaceutical companies were behind claims highlighting such a crisis.
Speaking to reporters, Mr. Muraleedharan described the reports as a “media creation” and maintained that adequate stocks were available in government hospitals.
“There is no crisis at all. There is sufficient stock of medicines. If needed, you can ask the Superintendent or anyone whether there is medicine stock or not,” he said.
He alleged that some pharmaceutical companies were attempting to create an impression of a shortage and accused sections of the media of highlighting their claims.
“Some pharmaceutical company representatives have come out with sticks and swords. And to highlight that, some big and small TV media people have also stepped out,” he said.
Reiterating that medicines were available in sufficient quantities at government hospitals, Mr. Muraleedharan said he would not be intimidated by such allegations.
“There is adequate stock of medicine. Furthermore, if any pharma company people come out brandishing sticks and swords, I am not someone who gets scared seeing that. That is all,” he said.
On the spread of infectious diseases, Mr. Muraleedharan said the number of cases reported so far was lower than during the corresponding period last year.
“Compared to last year, that many cases have not been reported. So far, infectious diseases haven’t been reported in such numbers,” he said.
On the proposed All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) in Kerala, the Minister rejected Union Minister Suresh Gopi’s allegation that the State government was not cooperating with the Centre.
He said Mr. Gopi was unaware of the facts and that the Principal Secretary of the Health Department had already submitted a report to the Centre on the matter.
“If he asks for it, I can show him a copy. Then why unnecessarily blame the State Government?” Mr. Muraleedharan said.
He said Mr. Gopi was keen on establishing AIIMS at a particular location.
“However, we don’t have any such preferences. Our only demand is that Kerala should get an AIIMS,” he said.
On cases of alleged medical negligence, Mr. Muraleedharan said the Health Department had not received any direct complaints.
“If we receive a complaint about anything, we will investigate it. There is no doubt about that,” he said.
Sabarimala preparations
Mr. Muraleedharan, who also holds the Devaswom portfolio, said preparations for the upcoming Sabarimala pilgrimage season were progressing.
A meeting chaired by Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan would be held at Pampa on October 17 to review the arrangements, he said.
“The government is providing full support to the Travancore Devaswom Board. Therefore, what we expect is that things can be conducted without any issues,” he said.
The Sabarimala pilgrimage season begins on November 17.

A decade ago, the biggest demographic concern gripping the globe was population overgrowth. Cut to 2026, and the demographic worry has shifted to the other end of the spectrum: declining birth rates. In developed economies such as Germany and Japan, fertility rates have fallen well below the replacement rate of 2.1 births per woman. The demographic imbalance is resulting in a growing shortage of workers to support the ageing population. Such countries are increasingly looking overseas, particularly to talent pools in parts of South and Southeast Asia, to fill blue-collar jobs. Plugging this supply-demand mismatch is the opportunity that upGrad cofounder Mayank Kumar is betting on. While helming the upskilling giant, Kumar felt that the local blue-collar ecosystem remained “under-penetrated and under-represented”. But the domestic opportunity was harder to monetise, as workers in these segments were less willing to pay large amounts for training. Kumar found this gap especially stark in the nursing profession when he travelled to Germany and visited nursing homes. This pushed him towards building a system that could train workers in one country and move them into jobs in another. To realise his new idea, he joined forces with Ayush Mathur, a former colleague, to incorporate BorderPlus. Founded in 2025, BorderPlus is building what it calls a vertically integrated talent mobility platform that trains workers, matches them with overseas employers, and then handles everything from language and skills training to visas, documentation and relocation. Kumar focuses on sourcing and developing talent, while Mathur works on building demand among overseas employers. Backed by Owl Ventures, CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti and OYO founder Ritesh Agarwal, the founders raised $7 Mn last year within a month of its launch. But how does BorderPlus play the cross-border mobility game? Controlling The Talent Pipeline BorderPlus wants to control the entire journey of moving a skilled worker overseas, including sourcing, training, employer interviews, placement and visa processing. For placements in Germany, its model starts with sourcing candidates through direct applications and college partnerships. After multiple rounds of screening, they enter language and finishing-school programmes before being introduced to overseas employers. Once selected, BorderPlus handles documentation, qualification recognition, visas and relocation. This allows BorderPlus to monetise beyond recruitment. Candidates initially pay ₹10,000 for the first month of the programme and, after clearing the subsequent screening, another ₹1.9 Lakh. However, Kumar says that the startup derives the bulk of its revenue from successful placements. Recruiters pay BorderPlus around €8,000-€12,000 (₹8.7 Lakh to ₹13 Lakh) per successful placement, equivalent to roughly three months of the candidate's salary. The startup then uses this revenue to cover expenses related to visas, examinations, documentation, translations and flights. The structure helps fund a recruitment cycle that typically lasts eight to 15 months. Kumar says upfront collections cover a large portion of the company's working-capital requirements, while the business generates a gross margin of around 70% per candidate. The economics also give BorderPlus an incentive to be selective. Only 30-40% of applicants are accepted into its full-time finishing schools, according to Kumar. He says this is because the business makes most of its money when a candidate is successfully placed, rather than simply enrolled. With an examination pass rate of more than 90% for its selected candidates, the startup is betting that hospitals and recruiters will return to the platform if it can consistently deliver language-ready and qualified candidates. Moving Beyond Germany BorderPlus is now moving beyond its core market, Germany, and has recently begun expanding into the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) and Japan. However, around 90-95% of its business still comes from Germany, according to Kumar. The startup claims that it has built a network of 80-90 hospitals and care homes in Germany, giving it a direct employer base. It also operates eight finishing school locations across India, the Philippines and Brazil with more than 50 physical trainers. Around 70% of its candidates are from India, while the remaining 30% come from markets such as the Philippines, Brazil and North Africa. Women also make up roughly 70–75% of the candidate pool. On the employer side, it has completed around five acquisitions in Germany to gain access to existing hospital and care-home relationships, with two more acquisitions underway. The startup is also looking to expand its physical presence in Germany, where it currently has offices in Düsseldorf and Frankfurt. The startup is also looking to go beyond its current three markets. It plans to roll out its services across English-speaking markets such as the US, UK, Australia, New Zealand and Canada. Nevertheless, Kumar expects Germany to still account for around 70% of the business next year, with Japan and the Middle East making up the remainder. Once those markets are established, BorderPlus plans to foray into the English-speaking markets. It also plans to extend its employee mobility network beyond healthcare to other areas like hospitality, kindergarten teaching, retail and last-mile delivery, manufacturing and construction, and logistics and trucking. BorderPlus has already started working on hospitality. Meanwhile, Kumar says one or two additional sectors could be tested in the near term, with a more concerted push planned for the next financial year. But the startup does not intend to stop at merely expanding its footprint. Leveraging AI For Revenue Extraction Beyond geographic and sectoral expansion, BorderPlus is also trying to build a second layer to its business through NursePlus, an AI platform designed to support nurses after they move to overseas markets. While the startup’s core business is still talent placement, Kumar sees NursePlus as a way to extend the relationship beyond the point of recruitment. NursePlus has three components: Learn, Ask and Do. Learn uses conversational simulations to help nurses practise local languages, cultural nuances and 1,000 hours of clinical scenarios before they arrive in their destination country. Ask is an AI assistant trained on local medical literature, compliance requirements, insurance guidelines and hospital protocols. Do focuses on documentation, allowing nurses to have their responses transcribed, translated and formatted for electronic health records. Kumar claims this can save nurses anywhere between 15 minutes and an hour on certain documentation tasks. Unlike the placement business, NursePlus follows a B2B subscription model, with hospitals and other employers paying for the software once the nurses have joined them. BorderPlus had around 100-150 subscribers in August, with pricing at roughly €30 per month. This allows BorderPlus to also have recurring revenue streams from the same worker after they have entered the workforce. Kumar believes AI could eventually contribute 5-30% of the startup’s revenue, while accounting for a considerably larger share of EBITDA because of the software's scalability. The same infrastructure could be adapted across countries and professions by changing the underlying language, regulatory and workplace context. This fits into BorderPlus' larger ambition to build a repeatable talent-mobility infrastructure rather than a Germany-focused nursing recruitment business. The Scale-Up Challenge Kumar expects the startup’s revenue to at least triple in the current financial year, adding that BorderPlus could achieve $10 Mn in annualised revenue run rate by the last quarter of the current financial year. On the operating side, BorderPlus is targeting around 1,000 placements across Germany, Japan and the Middle East in FY27, including 700-800 in Germany. Despite its grand plans, it is yet to be seen whether BorderPlus’ talent-mobility model can scale into a venture-sized business. For BorderPlus, the biggest test will be whether it can replicate its Germany playbook without any hitch. Revenue concentration also remains a risk as Germany still contributes 90-95% of the business, while the newer Japan and GCC corridors are only beginning to scale. The startup is also exposed to the usual risks of cross-border hiring, including immigration and visa policies, shifting attitudes towards migrant workers and recruitment cycles that can stretch for 15 months. At the same time, expanding physical training infrastructure across new source markets and professions could make the model operationally heavier. BorderPlus’ answer is diversification, technology and deeper employer relationships. But the jury is still out on whether BorderPlus can turn its Germany-focused nursing recruitment business into a repeatable global talent powerhouse.

Eight organisations from different parts of the world have come together to form the Global Alliance for Diabetic Foot Survival and Limb Preservation. This was announced at the Diabetic Foot Society of India’s (DFSI) national conference held in Bengaluru on Friday, October 2, 2026. The founding organisations also signed a joint declaration calling for diabetic foot ulceration to be recognised as a global public health priority.
The eight organisations are the DFSI, King’s College London, the International Association of Diabetic Foot Surgeons, D-Foot International, the Pan African Diabetic Foot Study Group, the American Limb Preservation Society, the International Federation of Podiatrists and the Podiatric Surgeons’ Society.
A 2023 review cited in the alliance proposal estimated that about 18.6 million people worldwide are affected by diabetic foot ulceration annually. It reported a five-year mortality of about 30% following a diabetic foot ulcer and over 70% following a major amputation.
The proposed alliance will focus on research, workforce training, comparable data collection and advocacy with the World Health Organization and national governments to secure greater policy recognition of diabetic foot disease.
The proposed framework also emphasises the involvement of people living with diabetes, those who have experienced foot ulcers and people living with amputation or disability in decision-making and programme design. It envisages regional demonstration programmes, a common measurement framework and an annual report on progress.
The DFSI Scientific Committee is proposed as the alliance’s interim secretariat, with a governing council representing the founding organisations overseeing strategy, finances and activities. The members are expected to meet within 30 days to discuss governance, collaboration, resource mobilisation and implementation.

Co-pilot in FlyDubai attack is identified, and other Mideast developments
The co-pilot suspected in this week’s FlyDubai attack has been identified as an Omani national
The co-pilot suspected in this week's FlyDubai attack has been identified as an Omani national. Meanwhile, a hospital in Gaza says Israeli strikes have killed five people, including four women.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Full coverage is available here.
The co-pilot suspected of stabbing the captain of an Israel-bound FlyDubai flight before passengers and others stopped the attack is an Omani national named Hamam al-Hammami, three people with knowledge of the situation, including a Gulf and a Western diplomat, said.
All spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media. The Gulf diplomat said investigations are underway to establish whether he acted as a “lone wolf or has any connection with any extremist groups.”
The United Arab Emirates said the co-pilot attacked the captain with the cockpit’s crash axe and tried to take control of the plane in a “terrorist attack.”
The co-pilot, who officials said nearly crashed the sharply plummeting flight with 182 people aboard, was barred from flying by Oman over concerns he had adopted extremist views, a separate person familiar with the matter said, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss the ongoing investigation.
- By Samy Magdy, Sam Mednick, Anna Johnson
Israeli strikes overnight in Gaza killed five people, according to al-Shifa Hospital, where the casualties were taken. Four women were among the dead. A mother and daughter among them were Christians, a minority in Gaza, the hospital said,
A large fire burned at the site, where the strikes tore a gaping hole in the ground floor of a multistory building. The hospital said people were still reported missing beneath the debris.
Israel's military did not immediately comment, saying it was checking for information.
Israeli strikes have killed at least 1,439 Palestinians in Gaza since a ceasefire was reached with the Hamas militant group nearly a year ago, according to the territory’s Health Ministry. Its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not give a breakdown of civilians and militants.
Israel says it is targeting Hamas and other militants who pose a threat, and in response to ceasefire violations, including occasional attacks.

A five-km walkathon to raise awareness on cardiovascular health, importance of physical activity, and preventive care was held in Chennai on Sunday to mark the upcoming World Heart Day. The ‘SIMS Rhythm of Life’ walkathon was flagged off from the hospital premises in Vadapalani by Raju Sivasamy, vice-president, SIMS Hospital, along with K. 'It's a nightmare.' Former refugee, professor on Trump's new Medicaid policy
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Mustafa Rfat has been getting frantic phone calls recently from refugees with disabilities. As of Oct. 1, refugees are losing access to Medicaid across the country because of H.R. 1, the Trump administration's major budget bill Republicans passed last summer.
"I spent these past two weeks just talking with so many of them, literally just terrorized by the reality that their children with disabilities are losing coverage," he says. "For example, a father is a refugee with disabilities, with two kids with disabilities, and he's just confused how he's going to get the medication."
Rfat is a professor of social work at the University of Nebraska at Omaha, and his research focuses on refugees with disabilities, an experience he knows firsthand.
When he arrived in the U.S. as a refugee from Iraq in 2011, the chronic condition that affects his spine was severe. "I was in a very bad situation," he says. "I couldn't walk. I was in so much pain. I missed my medications for a long time. I didn't see a doctor. So it was a very, very difficult and vulnerable situation."
As he moved from Alabama to Illinois to West Virginia trying to find housing and continue his education, Medicaid was a lifeline, Rfat says. "I had to climb this big mountain of acclimating into the culture here, learning English, dealing with the traumas of the war, the loss of family members, the challenges that I faced, being alone with a disability," he says.
"I was determined and in this determination, Medicaid was the big factor that made my dreams come true." In fact, he says one of the specialists who treated him wrote his first reference to apply for college. He has since become a U.S. citizen with a family, a doctorate, and a job as a professor.
Now, he's trying to help refugees with disabilities facing the challenges of navigating life in the U.S. without that lifeline. As of Oct. 1, refugees are among the groups that will lose Medicaid coverage.
Hundreds of thousands will lose coverage
Only a small portion of legal immigrants have been eligible to enroll in Medicaid, including refugees and asylum seekers. Because of the changes to "Alien Medicaid Eligibility" in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Republicans passed last summer, an even smaller subset now have access. An estimated 280,000 people will lose Medicaid in October, according to an analysis by KFF Health News.
That includes immigrants admitted to the U.S. on humanitarian grounds who are waiting to be approved for a green card, explains Ben D'Avanzo, senior strategist at the National Immigration Law Center.
"The people who are losing Medicaid and CHIP [the Children's Health Insurance Program] are among some of the most vulnerable immigrants — people who have experienced violence in their own homes or on their journey, who may have physical and mental conditions, who are fleeing persecution and war," he says. "These are people who we have long, in the United States, welcomed, and populations who have had very strong, historic bipartisan support."
Rfat points out that refugees are more likely to have serious health conditions than other groups. "More than one third of them have at least one type of disability — this is what the research tells us," he explains. In refugee camps and during war access to doctors and medication is difficult, and simple conditions can become serious and complex.
That was his own experience with an inflammatory condition called ankylosing spondylitis. "By the time I arrived in the U.S., a lot of doctors told me, 'You are one of the worst cases that we are seeing,'" he says. "And that is the case for a lot of refugees that come here."
In a statement to NPR, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services wrote that they are enacting the law passed by Congress working with states to accurately implement the policy. They did not respond to a follow up question about the effect of the policy on refugees with disabilities.
"Once these changes take place, these groups of immigrants will be left with very few options for affordable, comprehensive coverage," says Drishti Pillai, director of immigrant health policy at the nonpartisan health research organization KFF.
"They could still buy full price coverage from ACA marketplaces, but that is often unaffordable," Pillai says. "Employer-sponsored coverage is also an option, but many immigrants, especially those who are on Medicaid, don't work in jobs that don't offer employer-sponsored coverage, such as jobs in construction, agriculture, food service."
She says a few states are creating their own coverage options for these groups, but many have tight budgets and are facing even bigger Medicaid cuts in January. Most states have also opted in to allow Medicaid to continue to cover pregnant women and children who would otherwise be losing coverage.
D'Avanzo points out that the categories of people losing coverage now will eventually become green card holders who are eligible for Medicaid.
"So these are people who are going to put off preventative care, who are not going to treat their chronic conditions, who are going to forgo important medication," he says. "And then when they are Medicaid eligible again in the future, once they've received their green card, they're going to be needing much more specialized care and much more costly care."
Hope for change
Mustafa Rfat is headed to his alma mater Washington University in St. Louis, Missouri this weekend to meet with a few dozen refugees with disabilities and share some of his recent research. He says the loss of Medicaid and food benefits will hang over the event.
"It's a nightmare for the community," he says. He hopes Congress will reverse course.
He's decided to devote part of the event to teaching about civic engagement. "To understand the importance of voting when they become citizens, to understand the importance of being aware of the policies, being aware of who their representatives are, how to communicate with their representatives," he says.
"These are new Americans," he adds. "These people are going nowhere. By making their health and well-being worse, it's not going to benefit anyone."

Reversing a downward trend over the past two months, monthly electric two-wheeler (E2W) registrations bounced back in September. As per Vahan data, total E2W sales for the month of September stood at 2.07 Lakh units, up 12.2% month-on-month increase from 1.84 Lakh units registered in August. Important to note that Inc42 had reported 1.72 lakh E2W registrations for August based on the data available on August 31, while the latest Vahan data puts the month at 1.84 lakh units, a 7% upward revision. From a year-on-year (YoY) lens, September’s total registration almost doubled 1.05 Lakh units registered in September 2025. The top three traditional OEMs — TVS Motor, Bajaj and Hero MotoCorp — together accounted for around 61% of September registrations, with all three recording month-on-month growth. In contrast, new-age players such as Ola Electric, Ather and BGauss saw more mixed performance. While Ather’s registrations rose 4.9%, Ola declined 3.5% and BGauss was broadly flat. The September rebound also comes against a broader strengthening of India’s electric mobility market. As per reports, total EV registrations rose 64.6% YoY to 3.15 Lakh units in the month. In this, E2Ws accounted for the bulk of this growth. The growth could partly reflect the build-up to the festive season, when automakers and dealers typically step up inventory and promotional activity. Established two-wheeler manufacturers are also expanding their EV portfolios and distribution reach, making electric scooters more accessible to mainstream buyers. This shift towards mass-market products could further support volumes as manufacturers target buyers beyond the early-adopter segment with more affordable models and wider retail networks. While Ather launched its ₹99,999 scooter, Konarc, in late August, Ola Electric launched the S1Z scooter, priced at ₹79,999, around the same time. Incumbents Maintain Lead E2W market leader TVS Motor led the charge in September as well, with its market share now at 26%. The original equipment manufacturer (OEM) recorded 53,989 E2W registrations in September, an almost 10% MoM increase from 49,284 units recorded in the month prior. After capturing over a quarter of the Indian E2W market, TVS Motors has now embarked on an international expansion effort which includes establishing and expanding presence in countries like Nepal, Kenya, Sri Lanka and now, Indonesia, where it is planning to set up a manufacturing facility. With its current monthly manufacturing capacity at 40,000-45,000 units currently, it plans to raise that to 50,000-plus units in three to four months. Meanwhile, Bajaj Auto is hot on the trail, strengthening its position further in September with 48,383 registrations recorded in September, a 17% jump from 41,341 units recorded in August. Its total market share now stands at 23.4%. The OEM is on track to launch an electric motorbike in the coming months, and is meanwhile expanding its market position through its portfolio spanning premium to mass-market offerings. HeroMotocorp, while failing to re-enter the top three ranking, saw registrations soar 27% in September to 24,306 units. The OEM is nevertheless planning to launch its own electric motorcycle in 2027 alongside new e-scooter variants, while doubling down on manufacturing. Ather, Ola Lose Market Share In comparison to larger OEMs, Ather Energy saw tepid growth in September, with registrations inching up 5% MoM to 30,479 units from 29,068 in August. Its market share, meanwhile, fell 110 basis points to 14.7% during the month. Important to highlight that Ather’s overall sales have now crossed the 8 Lakh mark, making it the fourth OEM in the country to achieve the milestone. It expects sales momentum to accelerate as its newly launched affordable scooter Konarc picks up, and could make up for half of its sales within two years. Meanwhile, Ola Electric continued its downward trajectory in terms of registrations, which dipped 3.5% MoM to 13,449 units in September. The September decline comes as Ola attempts to rebuild its distribution network through dealer-led stores, targeting a network of more than 500 outlets, while also pushing cheaper products and its in-house Bharat Cells. E-scooter maker E-Sprinto recorded a blockbuster 16X MoM increase in registrations during the month to 1,997 units.The OEM is planning to substantially increase its presence on Indian roads in coming months, buoyed by plans to launch an affordable family scooter with a claimed range of 130 km on a single charge. Meanwhile, electric motorbike maker Oben also recovered substantially in September, registering 1,417 units in September, a 120% MoM surge from 642 units in August. On the other hand, its rival electric bike maker Ultraviolette saw registrations dip over 12% MoM to 536 units. The startup raised $85 Mn in equity funding during the month as it plans to shore up manufacturing and enter new markets in US, Latin America, and Southeast Asia. Besides Ultraviolette, River raised $120 Mn in August to expand its manufacturing as well. The e-scooter maker saw its registrations increase 6.4% to 5,549 units. Simple, which raised $180 Mn earlier this week, saw its registrations dip 19% MoM to 1,351 units in September. It plans to focus on a new manufacturing facility, higher production, an expanded distribution and service network, and the next generation of products. The startup recently launched the Simple Wave, an affordable family scooter series starting at ₹1.10 Lakh.

Network 10 to disappear in parts of SA, NSW's Riverina, after no deal made
In short:
Audiences in Mount Gambier and the Riverland in SA, and Griffith in NSW, will lose terrestrial Network 10 channels on Friday.
Network 10 and license holders WIN failed to come to a new agreement after months of negotiating.
What's next?
WIN says it will be "challenging to maintain services", due to the economics of regional broadcasting.
Viewers in parts of regional South Australia, and parts of the Riverina in New South Wales, will lose access to Network 10's terrestrial channels, after the network and license holder, WIN Network, failed to reach an agreement.
WIN has announced it will stop broadcasting 10, 10 Drama and 10 Comedy in the Mount Gambier, Riverland, Griffith and Murrumbidgee Irrigation Area, with the final broadcasts to be on Friday, October 9.
The network had flagged its agreement with Network 10 would expire in July, and that the channels would be pulled.
However, local audiences were given a three-month reprieve, with Network 10 saying it would provide its feed "free of charge" to WIN while the parties worked on a deal that has not eventuated.
High costs of regional TV
In a statement, a WIN Network spokesperson said providing Network 10 services to the impacted markets was "no longer viable".
"This is a business decision that reflects the realities of regional broadcasting," they said.
"Regional markets carry high transmission and infrastructure costs, while digital disruption continues to erode audiences and advertising revenue.
"These economics will continue to make it challenging to maintain services across regional Australia.
"WIN recognises this will be disappointing for viewers and thanks them for their understanding."
The move follows a similar loss of Seven Network channels to the same markets, after Seven and WIN failed to reach an agreement before Seven's deal expired last year.
The channels were eventually restored after a multi-day shutdown that saw the channels replaced with red screens advising they were "no longer available".
Country audiences missing out
A Network 10 spokesperson said audiences could continue to access the network's channels online and via its app.
"WIN holds the broadcast licences in the Riverland, Mount Gambier and Griffith regions and although Network 10 has worked closely with WIN to explore options to maintain local access to its content, WIN has advised that continuing to operate them is no longer commercially viable," they said.
"Network 10 remains committed to serving regional Australian audiences."
It is not the first time a regional market has lost Network 10 channels due to the financial challenges of regional broadcasting.
In 2024, audiences in Mildura, Victoria, lost their Network 10 channels when Mildura Digital Television (MDT), which carried 10's signal to the market, was closed by co-owners Seven and WIN.
The networks said "it did not make commercial sense" to keep MDT going, as it had been unprofitable throughout its existence.
Federal Communications Minister Anika Wells has been contacted for comment.

Long-awaited outback hospital reaches practical completion amid another cost blowout
In short:
Construction of the new Laverton Hospital in WA's northern Goldfields has reached practical completion.
The new eight-bed hospital cost $67.6 million after a $37.5 million tender was awarded last year.
What's next?
The hospital is set to open its doors to patients for the first time this week.
WA's Health Minister Meredith Hammat has defended the cost of a new eight-bed outback hospital, which has reached practical completion at a cost of $67.6 million, or more than three times the original budget from 2015.
Construction of the new Laverton Hospital began last year to replace the aging facility, which was built in 1973 for the northern Goldfields community, about 950 kilometres north-east of Perth.
WA Premier Roger Cook and Ms Hammat flew into Laverton on Sunday to announce practical completion of the new hospital, which includes a 24-hour, telehealth-equipped emergency department.
The hospital also has flexible care beds, specialist facilities for visiting clinicians as well as outpatient services for community health, mental health, and space for an onsite private GP clinic.
When pressed on the cost of the build, Ms Hammat said it reflected the reality of delivering major infrastructure in remote locations.
"What we see with all our health infrastructure projects, particularly in regional Western Australia, is that it's always challenging to deliver them," she said.
"But we are absolutely committed to deliver the health services and the health infrastructure that people need.
"A look at the old Laverton Hospital confirms the reality that this facility is incredibly needed for the community, and we've taken the opportunity to co-locate services like community health, child health, as well as a GP service."
Long road to new hospital
The Shire of Laverton has been lobbying for a hospital redevelopment for more than a decade.
The former Liberal-National government promised a $19.5 million redevelopment of Laverton Hospital in 2015, before funding was cut by WA Labor when it came to power in 2017.
Mr Cook, who was minister for health in 2017, said the new Laverton Hospital would open its doors to patients from Wednesday.
"I'm a previous health minister and this project has been on the books for a long time," he said.
"It's with a sense of deep relief but great pride that we're now in a position to welcome patients here."
After years of delays, the state government announced in February 2025, on the eve of the March election that year, that ADCO Constructions had won the tender to build the new hospital at a cost of $37.5 million.
Minister for Health Infrastructure John Carey confirmed in October last year those costs had blown out to $63.6 million.
The final cost of $67.6 million includes a federal government contribution of $16.8 million towards the project.
Hospital vital for Outback Way
Shire of Laverton president Pat Hill said the new hospital would be vital in emergencies due to the projected increase in traffic once the Outback Way was sealed.
The Outback Way stretches 2,719km through central Australia, from Laverton in Western Australia's northern Goldfields to Winton in Queensland, and it is hoped the final stretch can be sealed by 2032.
"It's been on the cards for over 15 years … I know they've had challenges but it's completed and it's a beautiful, first class facility," he said.
"With the development of the Outback Way and more people coming through these isolated, remote communities, and also the mining interests around Laverton, we've got over 7,500 people working fly-in, fly-out, so it's great to see governments working to put infrastructure into these remote areas."
Mr Hill has been chairman of the Outback Highway Development Commission since 1997 and is set to attend its annual general meeting in Alice Springs on Tuesday.
Kalgoorlie MLA Ali Kent echoed Mr Hill's sentiments on the hospital's importance due to the Outback Way.
"Laverton is in the middle of the desert, it's a long way from the Perth CBD and to have a hospital of this standard delivered here … it's been a difficult journey because we were putting tenders out and couldn't get builders that could do it," she said.
"When the Outback Way goes through, this hospital is going to become even more important."

‘A fruit cuts the knife’, the title of my new film.
Director-producer Nag Ashwin shared a screenshot of this single-line message he had received from veteran filmmaker Singeetham Srinivasa Rao on September 5, 2026, on social media soon after the news of the legendary filmmaker’s passing.
At 94, Rao lived and breathed cinema well into his final days, writing stories meant for the large screen.
In June 2026, with the Telugu musical fantasy drama Sing Geetham, Rao showed yet again why it matters to break free from the mould. He did it all through his career, spanning more than 70 years, giving us iconic and memorable films across languages — Raaja Paarvai, Bhairava Dweepam, Aditya 369, Apoorva Sagotharargal, Mayuri, Michael Madana Kama Rajan, and Pushpak — to name just a few.
His films cut across languages and genres. He showed us that science fiction could be fun; he made generations of filmmakers and audiences wonder how he and the team pulled off the Appu act of Kamal Haasan (he plays a dwarf), way before the widespread use of visual effects. Imagination and technique were all that it took.
Filmmaking as a puzzle
Speaking to this journalist before his 2013 Telugu film Welcome Obama, Rao had said, “I like my films to be like a puzzle, which I can solve while making. Films that have a set format with four songs and a few comedy scenes have never interested me.” He had shot Welcome Obama in film format, when the industry was swiftly moving towards digital. “We purchased raw stock and shot in Eastman Color, which no one does these days,” Rao had stated. “This is a film in which skin textures and colours needed to look real. None of the actors was allowed to wear makeup,” he had added.
In the 1980s, Rao did not hesitate to narrate a relatable story through the silent film, Pushpak. The courage that he had to think and act differently is evident in his simple retort, “Why not?” when he was asked by Suhasini Mani Ratnam about why he wanted to make Pushpak as a silent film. He was speaking during the four-part ‘Apoorva Singeetham’ conversation series (available on YouTube) by Raaj Kamal International to honour his contribution to cinema.
It was the same conviction with which he conceived the idea for Sing Geetham nearly 40 years ago. The story takes the audience into a fictional village, Kuberapuram, which resembles a dystopian setting after human greed tampers with its ecological balance. When the last-surviving tree in the village is under threat, things no longer remain the same.
Rao wanted it to be a musical, with the dialogues being sung. Several producers were reluctant until Nag Ashwin, and sisters Swapna and Priyanka Dutt of Vyjayanthi Films backed his vision.
During the making of Sing Geetham, Rao suffered a temporary health setback. But his zest for life and cinema remained undiminished. He interacted with the young team of co-writers and assistant directors, led by co-director Sankalp Gora, who executed his vision.
Sing Geetham arrived in theatres after the dull summer during which Telugu cinema nearly drew a blank at the box office. The musical was a fresh breath of air, with Devi Sri Prasad’s score as its backbone. At 94, Singeetham Srinivasa Rao had managed to bring out the child in many a viewer.
Rao has consistently inspired generations of filmmakers. In his early years, he worked as an assistant director to KV Reddy on the sets of Maya Bazar.
The drama in ‘Mahanati’
Rao was consulted when Nag Ashwin decided to make Mahanati, the biopic of actor Savitri. During an interaction, Nag Ashwin told this journalist on how Rao’s inputs helped heighten the drama in a key scene through which he recreated an episode from Maya Bazar: “I was aware that we were trying to recreate a piece of Telugu cinema history. I was more worried about KV Reddy’s ghost visiting the sets and throwing something at me if things didn’t go well.”
The idea for the drama in that sequence, with Savitri having to shed precisely three drops of tears from her left eye, came from Rao. When Nag Ashwin narrated the portion he was trying to recreate, Rao stated that it was flat and could do with some drama. The scene was rewritten such that a young Rao (played by Tharun Bhascker) breaks the bottle of glycerine by mistake and Savitri has no choice but to internalise the character and deliver what is required.
The inspiration
Several younger filmmakers in Telugu cinema have often recalled the influence Rao’s films have had on their work. Take the case of Hanu-Man director Prasanth Varma. Prior to his debut film, Awe, he had looked up to Rao and even consulted him. He was struck by how Rao explored diverse genres, and tried to follow that path. Rao had advised Prasanth to follow his heart rather than wait endlessly for stars.
Writer-director Vivek Athreya described Rao as “the Indian Steven Spielberg for my generation”. Director Mohana Krishna Indraganti had pointed out that some of the humour in his films was subconsciously influenced by Rao’s films, particularly Michael Madana Kama Rajan.
While the drama, in the emotional and comedy sequences in Rao’s films, emerges from the writing, he had a keen eye for detail. Director Venkatesh Maha pointed out the chorus in the song ‘Madhurame Sudhaganam’ in the Telugu film Brundavanam, where the singers’ voices mimicked how the sound moved from left to right in stereos of the 1980s and 90s.
For Rao, it was a joy to be a part of cinema. During the 2013 interview, he told this journalist, “When I am making a film, I feel like I am on a holiday. I inherited my sense of humour from my father and my sense of music from my mother. If someone quarrels with me, rather than get angry, I observe their facial expressions and body language. I find this humorous.”
Rest in peace, sir. Your cinema will continue to inspire.

Horse racing can be an unusually dangerous profession for both the jockey and the horse: Riding a half-ton animal at nearly 40 miles per hour means your fate depends on the health and performance of both athletes. How to improve your laptop's webcam quality
It's not hard for your laptop camera to look bad, but you can fix it.
You've probably wondered why the webcam on your laptop looks so bad. It's hard to point to a single reason, since factors like ambient light can have a major impact on how a camera's image looks.
Though in many cases, this is an inherent hardware issue. Laptop manufacturers have to fit a camera into an ultra-thin lid — we're talking about millimeters in thickness. Large camera sensors, like the ones found in smartphones, won't fit on a laptop lid, and smaller sensors capture less light. The result is an image that might look blurry, grainy or washed.
The good news is that there are a few tricks to help improve your webcam's image. Some of them are as simple as changing a few settings on your laptop, while others may require you to adjust the lighting in your room. While they can take a bit of effort, they're cheaper than spending money on a new external webcam.
Lighting matters a lot
Before getting into the settings, start by cleaning your webcam. The camera on most laptops is in a spot your fingers touch every time you open the lid. Fingerprints can make the image blurry, so wiping down your webcam before a video call is always a good idea. A microfiber cloth is usually enough for cleaning — using household cleaning products can damage your screen.
Lighting is arguably more important than any software settings. Poor lighting conditions ruin the image, even if you have a good webcam. Most laptop webcams have trouble handling contrast between light and shadow, which is why you should never film yourself with a bright light behind you.
Try facing a window instead of having it at your back. Having a table lamp or an LED light in front of you can help, too. The Elgato Key Light and the Logitech Litra Glow are two of the most popular options for streaming lights.
If you can't afford an external light or don't have room for one, your computer screen can double as a light. Macs have a feature called Edge Light, which works like a ring light on your screen. This feature has been available since macOS 26.2 and works any Apple silicon Mac. Windows lacks a feature like this by default, but third-party apps like LightON or Edge Light for Windows can do the same job.
Changing a few webcam settings might help
While it can't overcome a low-quality webcam or bad lighting, software can still help improve your webcam's image. On Windows 11 PCs, open Settings and go to Bluetooth & Devices. Click Cameras and select your webcam. Depending on your webcam, you'll have the option to change levels like brightness and saturation. Play around to pick the settings that look best in your room, and they'll become the new default in any app that uses your webcam. Some cameras also offer Video HDR in this menu, which helps balance the contrast between the darkest and brightest areas of the picture.
Some graphics cards also have their own tools for enhancing webcam image quality. NVIDIA Broadcast uses GeForce RTX cards to improve your video with features like noise removal and eye contact correction. A similar tool called Camo is worth a look if you don't have an NVIDIA card.
Mac users don't have this range of options available when using the built-in webcam, but you can try using Studio Light. Just click the green camera icon in the Menu Bar (it only appears when the camera is in use) and look for Studio Light. The Edge Light feature mentioned above is there, too.
If you rely on your webcam a lot and none of these tips have helped, buying a good external webcam might be your best option. You can use a high-end camera as a webcam or use your iPhone as a Mac webcam, too.

The cost of borrowing money is moving unrelentingly higher, with profound implications for savers, borrowers and the U.S. government's fiscal outlook.
The big picture: The bond market moves over the last few weeks have pushed most risk-free interest rates north of 5%.
Barring a rapid reversal, expect pain to come in interest-sensitive sectors like housing, new stress on federal government finances and greater risks of financial disruption.
It is better news for savers, who have taken paper losses on existing bonds in recent weeks but can now deploy cash safely with the best prospective returns seen in decades.
Zoom out: It is clearer than ever that the era of cheap borrowing and abundant capital that lasted from 2008 to 2021 is well and truly over.
Every individual looking to take a home mortgage or car loan is in competition with the voracious capital needs of the AI giants and the U.S. government.
While the Federal Reserve has gotten out of the business of forecasting its next moves, it is now looking out of position. Its leaders increasingly believe that it has set its policy rates too low to control inflation amid a growth boom, and are now looking to adjust course, which means last week's rate hike won't be the last.
Rate hikes may not deter much AI investment or government borrowing, which leaves all other interest-sensitive sectors to bear the brunt of bringing the economy into better balance.
Zoom in: The surge in rates has been driven for the most part by a rise in real yields — implying a stronger growth outlook, not an outburst in expected inflation.
Investors can now buy a 30-year inflation-protected Treasury security that pays 3.26%, the highest since 2002. This time five years ago, that number was negative.
The forward earnings yield of the S&P 500 is about 5%. With the 30-year nominal Treasury bond yielding around 5.5%, bonds look more attractive relative to stocks than they have in ages.
State of play: The recent surge in longer-term rates is poised to push 30-year fixed-rate mortgages to near 8%. Mortgage News Daily on Thursday clocked the 30-year rate at 7.45%, or 7.55% for jumbo loans.
Mortgage rates got that high briefly in the fall of 2023, but the last time they were above that level on a sustained basis was in 2000.
Over time, the housing market can find a balance. But in the near term, surges in rates just mean pain as the market freezes up.
People can't afford to buy houses with 7.5%+ rates, and sellers don't want to cut their prices, so there is a standstill, as witnessed in the fall of 2023, until either rates fall or prices adjust.
The intrigue: Higher rates, if sustained, will make America's fiscal situation considerably thornier.
The U.S. government's debt service costs were already projected to reach new highs in the coming years — but that burden will be much worse if the rate surge of the last few weeks is sustained.
By the numbers: In projections that the Congressional Budget Office produced last February, net interest costs are already at $1 trillion this year and on track to reach $2 trillion by 2035, meaning that much of federal spending is needed just to service old bills.
But those projections assumed 10-year Treasury yields were in the ballpark of 4.3%. They're now nearly a full percentage point higher than that.
In startling numbers that CBO released this week, in a scenario in which interest rates were 1 percentage point higher than its baseline, debt held by the public would grow to 222% of GDP in 2056, 47 percentage points higher than the baseline.
Reality check: Higher interest rates don't flow through to government debt service costs immediately. Longer-term bonds gradually mature over time.
So a reversal in rates would help the fiscal arithmetic (at least so long as it wasn't caused by a recession or productivity slump).
The bottom line: If the 5% world is here to stay, it commands a rethinking of the U.S. government's tax and spending policies, the price of assets, and more generally what we consider normal in an era of steep global demand for capital.

Indian spacetech startups TakeMe2Space, SatLeo Labs, and EON Space Labs sent AI computing and Earth observation technologies into orbit aboard SpaceX’s Falcon 9 today. The Transporter-18 rideshare mission lifted off from California, carrying TakeMe2Space’s MOI-1A satellite with EON Space Labs’ MIRA imaging system onboard. SatLeo Labs’ TAPAS-1 thermal-imaging payload flew on Dhruva Space’s LEAP-2 satellite. Hyderabad-based TakeMe2Space’s MOI-1A is designed to process Earth observation data in orbit using AI, allowing customers to receive insights without downloading large volumes of raw imagery. Ahmedabad-based SatLeo’s TAPAS-1 is designed to capture land-surface temperature data, while Hyderabad-based EON’s MIRA captures imagery across multiple spectral bands. TakeMe2Space’s Bet On Computing In-Orbit MOI-1A is a 14-kg satellite with onboard computing capacity of 117 trillion operations per second (TOPS), 2 TB of storage, and a nine-band multispectral imager. Customers can deploy AI models directly on the satellite to analyse imagery in orbit, instead of downloading it to a ground station for processing. This can reduce the volume of data that needs to be downloaded by a factor of 1,000, TakeMe2Space founder and CEO Ronak Kumar Samantray told Inc42. The satellite identifies objects or patterns in imagery and sends back the results. He explained that a 2,000-km stretch of synthetic-aperture radar (SAR) imagery could generate around 300 GB of data. If an AI model is instead used to identify specific objects or patterns in orbit, the resulting output could shrink to only a few kilobytes. The startup’s first-generation satellites are designed around inference rather than AI model training. TakeMe2Space has signed up 23 customers for its in-orbit inference services. Around 80% are outside India, according to Samantray. These include international geospatial companies, while Indian educational institutions are using the infrastructure as an orbital research laboratory. The use cases currently span agriculture, defence, supply chain intelligence, mining and insurance. Building A Six-Satellite Constellation MOI-1A follows TakeMe2Space’s 2024 technology demonstrator, which validated onboard AI inference and data processing. The startup subsequently lost MOI-1 during the unsuccessful PSLV-C62 mission earlier this year. Samantray said the broad satellite architecture remains similar, but individual subsystems have undergone multiple development cycles since the earlier mission. The startup expects to make MOI-1A commercially available shortly after reaching orbit. It plans to launch its other Gen-1 satellite, MOI-1B, in November aboard ISRO’s SSLV. That satellite will carry a black-and-white imager primarily intended for object detection. TakeMe2Space then plans to launch larger spacecraft as it builds a six-satellite constellation. Its Gen-2 satellites will have roughly 10X the capacity of the Gen-1 spacecraft, according to Samantray, with around 100 TB of storage per satellite and significantly greater computing capacity. The startup also plans to introduce laser-based links between satellites, allowing them to exchange data without routing it through ground stations. For instance, one satellite could pass processed data to another with a better connection to a ground station for transmission to Earth. Two Gen-2 satellites, MOI-2 and MOI-3, are planned for launch in 2027, most likely aboard Indian launch vehicles. Samantray said the startup has not booked these launches yet because he expects Indian launch services to operate more regularly by then. The startup has secured a slot aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 mission in late 2028 for MOI-4 and MOI-5, which would complete the constellation, he added. Samantray expects each Gen-2 satellite to generate around $1 Mn in annual revenue. The startup is targeting about $6 Mn in annual recurring revenue from its in-orbit computing business by 2028. It is also designing Gen-3 satellites in the 1,500-kg class with around 25 kW of power, with a potential launch around 2029, he said. SatLeo, EON Expand Imaging Capabilities SatLeo Labs’ TAPAS-1, which the startup describes as India’s first dedicated commercial thermal payload, uses thermal infrared sensing to capture temperature information. Potential applications include urban heat mapping, crop-stress monitoring, disaster monitoring, and infrastructure surveillance. The payload flew aboard Dhruva Space’s LEAP-2 satellite, which also carries a star tracker from France’s Sodern. The mission will test TAPAS-1’s sensing, calibration, and processing capabilities in orbit. EON Space Labs’ MIRA, meanwhile, is a compact multispectral imaging system weighing 502 grams. Integrated with MOI-1A, it is designed to capture Earth observation imagery for applications spanning agriculture, mining, marine monitoring, supply chains, and insurance. Together, the missions bring specialised imaging and onboard data processing into focus as India’s spacetech startups work towards commercialising their technologies. IN-SPACe chairman Pawan Goenka called the launch a “big day for India's private space sector”, saying it showed the “range and ambition” of India's private space ecosystem.

SpaceX's Crew Dragon "Grace" spacecraft stacked atop its trunk section during preparations for the Crew-13 mission at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida.
Credit:

A four-person crew rocketed into orbit Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, heading for a six-month expedition on the International Space Station.
Riding a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft, the four crew members departed from Space Launch Complex-40 at Cape Canaveral at 11:10 am EDT (15:10 UTC) Thursday. Nine minutes later, they were in orbit to begin closing in on the space station for docking Thursday evening.
The launch was delayed from mid-September to replace a balky valve in the Dragon spacecraft’s propulsion system, a task that involved cutting into a propellant line inside the ship to swap out a faulty component.
Jessica Watkins, a 38-year-old geologist turned astronaut, leads the four-person crew sent into orbit Thursday, becoming the first Black woman to command a spacecraft. Watkins is the only veteran astronaut on the mission—designated Crew-13—after spending 170 days in orbit on a long-duration spaceflight in 2022.
Pilot Luke Delaney, a Marine Corps veteran, was seated next to Watkins for the Dragon spacecraft’s ascent into orbit. Two international crew members rounded out the Crew-13 team: Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, a former pilot in the Royal Canadian Air Force, and Sergey Teteryatnikov, a Russian cosmonaut who served as a naval engineer before his selection to the Roscosmos Cosmonaut Corps in 2021.
Kutryk and his wife Heather are expecting their third child later this year. It’s rare, but astronauts have been off the planet for their child’s birth before. Most recently, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, set to command the Artemis III mission next year, was flying aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 2009 when his wife gave birth to their daughter, Abigail Mae, in Houston.
“Leaving these three (plus one on the way) is the hardest thing I’ve ever done. But that has always been the nature of exploration,” Kutryk wrote on X.
Watkins and her crewmates were on course to reach the International Space Station (ISS) about eight hours after launch, the fastest-ever launch-to-docking transit to the ISS by a US spacecraft.
NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, commander of the Crew-13 mission, arrives at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of launch.
Credit:
NASA/Kim Shiflett
NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins, commander of the Crew-13 mission, arrives at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of launch.
Credit:
NASA/Kim Shiflett
“What an epic ride. What an epic ride it was,” Delaney radioed mission control soon after reaching orbit. “Today, we proudly continue the streak of humans living and working in orbit, building on the legacies of yesterday to pave the way for the future of space exploration.”
The ISS has been permanently staffed since 2000, with crews flying to and from the orbiting outpost on NASA’s Space Shuttles, Russian Soyuz spacecraft, and most recently, SpaceX’s Crew Dragon. NASA and its international partners plan to keep the space station operating through at least 2030. SpaceX’s plans to retire the Crew Dragon vehicle around 2030 have prompted NASA to work more closely with Boeing to bring its troubled Starliner crew capsule into service.
Honing their craft
Thursday’s flight was the 13th crew rotation mission launched by SpaceX under a multibillion-dollar contract with NASA, and SpaceX’s 21st human spaceflight overall, including test flights and fully commercial missions.
The company’s success with the Crew Dragon spacecraft restored the country’s ability to launch astronauts into orbit after a nine-year gap following the Space Shuttle retirement in 2011, ending NASA’s sole reliance on Russia for crew transportation. NASA’s other commercial crew provider, Boeing, has repeatedly stumbled on a series of test flights with its Starliner spacecraft.
SpaceX’s plans to retire Crew Dragon and the Falcon 9 rocket mean the fleets are now well beyond halfway through their operational life. SpaceX has nine more Crew Dragon flights in its backlog, including three additional crew missions to the ISS that NASA recently secured in a $946 million contract extension, bringing NASA’s total contract for 17 SpaceX crew missions to $5.92 billion.
That figure is a drop in the bucket next to SpaceX’s projected revenues from its ever-growing Starlink broadband service, the Starship/Super Heavy rocket, and orbital data centers. SpaceX, now a publicly traded company, is prioritizing its most lucrative lines of business, and flights to the ISS aren’t among them.
Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk poses for a photo with his wife, Heather, and children after walking out from the Neil Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of his launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Credit:
Paul Hennesy/Anadolu via Getty Images
Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk poses for a photo with his wife, Heather, and children after walking out from the Neil Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at Kennedy Space Center, Florida, ahead of his launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.
Credit:
Paul Hennesy/Anadolu via Getty Images
Bill Gerstenmaier, SpaceX’s vice president of build and flight reliability, declined to say in a prelaunch press conference Wednesday if there is a “hard cutoff” for when the company will no longer offer Crew Dragon flights to NASA. The recent contract extension may be the last.
“We were just awarded Crew flights 15, 16, and 17, so I think our real focus is to make sure we get the most out of those flights,” Gerstenmaier said. “So we’re working really super hard to make sure that our vehicles are ready, things are ready to go fly, and we’ll keep moving forward.”
Notably, SpaceX is winding down Crew Dragon and Falcon 9 at the top of their game. Gerstenmaier pointed to the valve replacement inside the Crew Dragon spacecraft for the Crew-13 mission as evidence of SpaceX’s commitment to fulfilling its contract with NASA.
NASA announced a postponement for the Crew-13 launch in late August to give ground teams time to resolve an oxidizer leak inside Dragon’s propulsion system detected during launch preparations at Cape Canaveral. SpaceX traced the leak to a valve. The spacecraft was already loaded with nitrogen tetroxide, or NTO, the volatile, toxic oxidizer used by Dragon’s control thrusters in combination with hydrazine fuel.
Teams devised an unprecedented bit of spaceship surgery to replace the valve without draining the propellant and disassembling the spacecraft, steps that would have triggered a much longer delay. The fix involved cutting into the propellant line, removing and replacing the valve, then welding the line together again. It was the first time SpaceX has performed such a repair with a fully assembled Dragon spacecraft loaded with propellant.
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft lifts off on the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.
Credit:
NASA/John Kraus
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket carrying the company’s Dragon spacecraft lifts off on the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station.
Credit:
NASA/John Kraus
“By cutting it out, we physically went in and actually cut the valve out of the line,” Gerstenmaier said. “It was welded in place, and then we actually re-welded a new valve in place.”
Engineers are testing the bad valve to diagnose the cause of the leak, but NASA officials were pleased with the fix. No leaks were detected during final preparations for launch Thursday, and Dragon’s propulsion system appeared to be functioning well after arriving in orbit.
“We looked at the plans, all of the data coming out of that, the welds, the leak, everything looks great,” said Dana Weigel, NASA’s program manager for the International Space Station. [We’re] really happy with how that repair was done.”
SpaceX’s preference to cut out the valve in place, rather than take a longer stand-down, kept the Crew-13 mission on track to arrive at the space station in time to replace Crew-12, which will return to Earth in mid-October after eight months in orbit.
The Crew Dragon spacecraft was inside SpaceX’s fueling and hazardous processing facility, known as Area 59, at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, not at the company’s usual maintenance hangar a few miles away.
“I actually went down and looked at the vehicle itself, got in the clean room, and took a look to see where they actually had to cut the valve out,” Gerstenmaier said. “There was not a lot of room, but there was good access up on the platform. I think the unique aspect of this was the location where it was being done.
“We also did it with oxidizer onboard the vehicle, and the oxidizer tank was full, so we made sure that was all clear,” Gerstenmaier said. “We had to get special permission from the [Space Force’s Eastern] Range to do these activities, to do ‘hot work’ with NTO, with nitrogen tetroxide on the vehicle.”
Stephen Clark is a space reporter at Ars Technica, covering private space companies and the world’s space agencies. Stephen writes about the nexus of technology, science, policy, and business on and off the planet.

Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
- Published
Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.
Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.
"That's just risk management," Carney said.
Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.
In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.
"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.
Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.
But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.
In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.
Why it is unlikely to happen
A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.
"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.
Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.
They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.
The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.
Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.
Not always the best of friends
After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.
But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.
"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.
Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.
Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.
In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.
Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.
Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.
It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.
They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.
A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.
"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."
What a US invasion could look like
Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.
He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.
"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.
Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.
So what would it be like if it happened?
The first phase of a war could be quite short.
According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week
Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.
Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.
The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.
The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.
He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.
Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.
An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.
Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.
"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.
"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."
Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.
But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.
"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.
Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

World Contraception Day on September 26 offers an opportunity to look closely at a part of family planning that receives very little attention: contraception for men. The key question here is why the range of methods available to men and women remains so different.
Women today have options including oral pills, injectables, implants, intrauterine devices and permanent sterilisation, though access and affordability to safe and reliable contraception in our country continues to remain a major challenge. For men, the practical choices are still largely limited to condoms for reversible contraception and vasectomy for permanent contraception. Male and female reproduction are governed by the same broad hormonal axis, yet the biology, anatomy and mechanics of preventing conception create very different problems. Understanding those differences helps explain why a male equivalent of the pill has remained elusive.

Brazilians will vote in a highly polarized presidential race on Sunday. Here’s what to know
Millions of Brazilians are voting in an election featuring two main rivals: President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Millions of Brazilians will vote Sunday in an election dominated by two rivals: incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of ex-leader Jair Bolsonaro who Lula defeated four years ago.
Twelve candidates are on the presidential ballot, but only Lula and Bolsonaro are thought to have a real chance of becoming Brazil’s next head of state. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the top 2 will advance to a runoff on Oct. 25.
Lula, who at 80 is one of the world’s oldest heads of state, is running in his seventh presidential election. Bolsonaro, 45, is competing in his first and seeking to return his family name to power after his father governed Brazil from 2019 through 2022.
The two represent opposite sides of the political spectrum, with conflicting visions on issues ranging from how to tackle organized crime to the relationship Latin America's biggest country should have with the Trump administration.
Here’s what to know about Brazil’s election.
Brazil holds general elections every four years, and voting is mandatory. Those who fail to cast a ballot without justification face a small fine.
On Sunday, Brazilians will choose a president, state and federal representatives as well as governors and some senators. Elections for mayors and city councilors are also held every four years, but in different years.
Almost 160 million eligible voters will use electronic voting machines to punch in the digits corresponding to their candidates, preparing number-heavy lists.
Brazilian authorities adopted electronic voting machines in the 1990s to combat fraud. In earlier local elections, ballot boxes were stuffed or stolen, and paper ballots were routinely falsified, according to Brazil’s electoral authority. The country held no direct presidential elections between 1960 and 1989, a period that included military rule from 1964 to 1985.
Now, results are reported mere hours after polls close.
In the lead-up to the 2022 vote, Jair Bolsonaro repeatedly cast unfounded doubts on Brazil’s electronic voting system. No significant fraud has ever been detected.
Lula, who got his start as a union worker and has a missing pinky finger following an accident in a factory when he was 19, has at times inspired cult-like devotion. He spent more than a year in prison on corruption convictions that were later annulled before winning a third nonconsecutive term in 2022.
Former U.S. President Barack Obama once called him “the world's most popular politician.” But during his current term, Lula's approval ratings fell as low as 24%, one of his lowest levels. Voters' concerns about crime and the cost of living could hurt him at the ballot box. He has promised to ensure Brazilians are the ones to benefit from the country's rare minerals and resources, protect the Amazon rainforest and continue his flagship welfare program Bolsa Familia.
With former President Jair Bolsonaro barred from running as he serves a 27-year-long sentence for a coup attempt, his eldest son has largely embraced his father's ultra-conservative agenda, while at times trying to strike a more moderate communication style to attract centrist voters.
His hardline security policies have been a pillar of his campaign, and polls show these proposals are popular among Brazilians. The senator has pledged to fight the country's criminal groups by building El Salvador-style megaprisons, following the Trump administration's lead by designating transnational gangs terrorist organizations and reducing the age to be tried as an adult to 16.
Deforestation in the Amazon rainforest, which plays a vital role in stopping climate change, hit a record high under former President Bolsonaro. His son has also denied human-caused climate change and only committed to stopping illegal deforestation.
Sen. Bolsonaro's admission of accepting millions of dollars from disgraced banker Daniel Vorcaro to produce a film on his father's life has cast a shadow over his campaign. He is under investigation for corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in connection with the case.
Lula has repeatedly warned the U.S. not to meddle in Brazil's elections. The Trump administration did not respond to a request for comment on whether it is seeking to interfere in the vote.
Last year, Washington imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing — among other reasons — the trial of Jair Bolsonaro, a Trump ally. Earlier this year, the U.S. imposed a new round of tariffs, citing unfair trade practices despite running a U.S. surplus, and classified Brazil’s biggest drug-trafficking groups as foreign terrorist organizations shortly after a visit to the White House from Sen. Bolsonaro. Lula opposed both moves.
A victory by Sen. Bolsonaro would add Brazil to a list of Latin American countries — including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica and Peru — that have elected Trump-friendly governments in recent years.
Lula has made defending Brazilian sovereignty a major campaign issue. In the days before the election, his team launched a Portuguese version of the Bad Bunny song, “Lo que le pasó a Hawaii,” which invokes the U.S. colonization of Hawaii as a cautionary tale.
