The setting for perhaps the country’s biggest exercise in public debate was quintessential rural India: fields of green paddy, a pond, a temple. On a normal day, as dusk falls in the village of Ajgara, in Uttar Pradesh, people gather beside the pond to chat about the price of crops, the weather, or the theft of a goat.
But for more than a month, metaphysics and ethical dilemmas replaced the usual topics. Is it permissible to use deceit to defeat an evil enemy? Is a lie justified to save a life? What is the nature of reality?
The debating tournament was the brainchild of Abhishek Pandey, district magistrate of Pratapgarh district in Uttar Pradesh. When he took up the post two years ago, he knew the area was rich in archaeological treasures connected to the ancient Indian epic, the Mahabharata.
Throughout the text, Yudhishthira, one of the central characters, debates the nature of human existence. In Ajgara he answers a string of philosophical questions to save the lives of his four brothers.
Pandey, 35, like most Indians, grew up on this story and was proud of the intellectual depth of the dialogues. When he attended Oxford University on a fellowship, he admired the debating society, which has a 200-year-long history. But India’s tradition of sophisticated public debate is much older, going back more than 3,000 years.
Pandey started to question why the tradition had not survived. “Indians have celebrated certain traditions for centuries,” Pandey says. “Why have we ceased to celebrate the legacy of debate and questioning?” Was it possible to revive this noble tradition, particularly when it was a vital component of a democracy?
He decided that the annual fair held in Ajgara in September would be a good time to stage the event. In the run-up to the fair, Pandey and his team arranged 1,500 debates across the district.
Age and education were no bar. The youngest participant was a 10-year-old schoolboy, the oldest an 80-year-old farmer. In debating for and against a motion, participants were judged on reasoning and moral clarity.
The overwhelming public response dumbfounded Pandey. Thousands of people participated in multiple rounds, and were whittled down to eight finalists – two women and six men.
While villagers milled around, enjoying the food, watching folk theatre, buying local crafts and taking a ride on a ferris wheel, a silence descended inside the debating tent.
The finale of the Great Ajgara Debate 2026 on 17 September lasted about six hours.
One topic was women’s rights. A finalist, Vivek Singh, argued that women might have equality on paper but society’s expectations of them impeded the exercise of these rights.
Another, Prajjwal Shukla, 24, argued that the real question was not what role society assigned to women but who had the authority to make those choices. Whether a woman chose a career, household responsibilities, or both, should be her choice and hers alone, he said.
“What amazed me the most was not the intellectual quality of the debates (which was great), but the atmosphere. Everyone listened respectfully, patiently, without interrupting. No one got personal. People sat for hours,” says Pandey.
Marx’s adage that history repeats itself, first as tragedy and then as farce, is a perfect description of how debate in India has descended from the sublime to the farcical.
In television studio debates everyone shouts at the same time. No one can finish a point. Personal abuse and gibes fly while the anchor whips them into ever greater frenzies.
Sadhana Dwivedi, one of the two women to progress into the last round of the Great Ajgara Debate, despises this new format.
“People need to learn to listen, to understand there may be value in another person’s point of view,” she says. “In a democracy, it is crucial for all opinions to be aired so that we can get to the truth.”
The turnout was a good demonstration of the thesis posited in economist Amartya Sen’s book The Argumentative Indian that India had a rich tradition of questioning authority and entertaining heterodoxy.
It is only in recent years that dissent has been suppressed, notably by the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party, which values conformity.
“It’s ironic, because the BJP wants to recreate a Hindu state but is not even acquainted with the traditions of ancient Hindu civilisation, such as that of debate and being open to different ideas,” says author and commentator Parsa Venkateshwar Rao Jnr.
At the end of the tournament, the eight finalists were garlanded and driven around in an open-top car to much cheering, feted as “intellectual heroes”. The winner was Shukla, who is preparing to sit exams to enter the civil service.
“I can’t believe I am the winner of a debate that took place at the exact same spot as in the Mahabharata all those centuries ago. I participated just because I wanted to hear other people’s thoughts,” he says.
Pandey is still processing the public enthusiasm. “My deputy asked me if we should get some police deployment because the turnout everywhere was so big, but I laughed and said no. That would be a sad affair.”
He hopes to spread the event across other Indian states and perhaps nationwide. “We have to inculcate a culture of debate. It’s the hallmark of a democracy.”
Meanwhile, he has planted his flag. The inscription on the stone slab he has installed at the site reads: “The Great Ajgara Debate. First Debate 3152 BC: Yudhishthira. Second Debate 2026: Prajjwal Shukla.”

66% of Hong Kong’s 8-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, experts warn
Association finds 67 per cent of grade-one pupils already have insufficient hyperopic reserve, urging parents to start eye checks at age three
More than 60 per cent of Hong Kong’s eight-year-olds could be short-sighted by 2028, optometrists have predicted, citing a shrinking “hyperopic reserve” that normally helps delay nearsightedness.
The Hong Kong Association of Private Practice Optometrists released the findings on Sunday from a screening of more than 3,500 pupils at eight primary schools conducted between November and May, urging parents to begin comprehensive eye checks when children turned three.
The association found that 67 per cent of six-year-olds had less hyperopic reserve than the recommended standard of 0.75 dioptres (75 degrees), while 24 per cent were already short-sighted.

A video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with claims that it allegedly shows the Chief of the Army Staff, General Dhiraj Seth, dancing with Supreet Sapra, described as the wife of an Army major. The video features a purported CNN headline stating, “Indian Army Chief Dhiraj Seth Spotted Dancing with Army Major’s wife Supreet Sapra,” giving the impression that CNN published the video. Let’s verify the truth behind the video in this article.
Claim: The video shows Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major.
Fact: The video has been digitally manipulated to make it appear as though Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth is dancing with Supreet Sapra. CNN has not published any report or headline matching the one shown in the viral video. The original video, shared in March 2026, features a different man and woman dancing at a gathering. Supreet Sapra has also clarified that she is not an Army major’s wife and that the woman shown in the viral video is AI-generated. The Indian Army’s fact-check wing has also confirmed that the video is digitally manipulated. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
To verify the claim, we conducted a Google search using relevant keywords but found no credible reports carrying the viral footage on CNN’s official website or any report or headline matching the one circulating with the video.
Upon closely reviewing the viral video, we noticed several inconsistencies. Though the man and woman appear to be dancing while holding glasses, the liquid inside them does not move or splash naturally as they dance. In one frame, the man’s ear and cheek area also appear smudged, while the faces of people in the background appear heavily blurred. The man’s face remains almost completely frozen with a wide smile throughout the video, further raising signs of AI manipulation.
We then ran the video through multiple AI detection tools, including DetectVideo AI and Meta AI’s verification platform. Both assessed the clip as likely AI-generated and detected AI signatures in the video.
The viral video contains an inset photograph showing a woman with a different man wearing a defence uniform. To learn more about the photograph, we conducted a reverse image search, which led us to an Instagram post (archived) by @sufimeranaam, dated 22 February 2026, featuring the same image. Newschecker contacted the account user regarding the viral video. She identified herself as Supreet Sapra and said, “I am Supreet Sapra, but I am not a major’s wife. My husband retired four years ago. The woman in the video is AI-generated, so apart from the name, everything is misinformation.”
Further investigation led us to an Instagram post (archived) by Rhythm Gupta, shared on 11 March 2026, with the caption, “Always dancing weirdly.” The video features a man and a woman dancing at a gathering. Their dance movements, the way they hold their glasses, and the song playing in the background are the same as those in the viral video. Although the background differs in colour and certain visual details, the overall setting and arrangement of elements are similar, and the movements of people around the dancing pair also closely resemble. This indicates that the viral video was likely manipulated using the earlier footage to make it appear as though the Army Staff chief was dancing with an Army major’s wife. Comparison of screengrabs from the viral clip and the Instagram video can be seen below.
The Indian Army’s fact-checking wing also clarified in an X post (archived) on 29 September 2026 that the viral video is digitally manipulated and fake.
To sum up, this viral video of Chief of the Army Staff General Dhiraj Seth dancing with Supreet Sapra, the wife of an Army major, is AI-manipulated.

South African white genocide does not exist, new ambassador to US tells BBC
- Published
South Africa's new ambassador to Washington has a personal reason to challenge Donald Trump's assertion that there is a genocide against white Afrikaners - he is "a born Afrikaner" himself.
"Is he talking about us?", Roelf Meyer remembers thinking, when he first heard President Trump say it.
His response to the US president's claim is blunt.
The notion of a mass attack on the white Afrikaner minority in South Africa does not exist, he told the BBC, adding that his identity gave him the legitimacy to say so.
Meyer was one of the chief mediators to end white-minority rule known as apartheid in South Africa in the 1990s. He was appointed ambassador to the US in April, after diplomatic relations between the US and South Africa plummeted.
In an interview with the BBC, Meyer said the facts about violence in South Africa had been misrepresented and he never got a clear answer about where this "misdirection of information" was coming from.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
Since last year, nearly 13,000 refugees were admitted to the United States and all but three were South African.
Among them was Lielie, the name she uses publicly, who moved with her family to Texas from South Africa, where they had lived on her stepfather's farm, growing macadamia nuts and bananas.
Despite walls around the house, an electric fence, and eight bull terriers, she said she felt "fear the whole time" and that on three occasions she saw people entering her property.
"Nothing was stolen, we weren't harmed, but there are friends of my husband, people that lived around us, they were brutally attacked," she said.
She said since moving to the US under the Trump administration's refugee pathway her life had changed, she felt safer walking around, and "my kids can actually play outside".
The Trump administration is planning to admit up to 17,500 additional white Afrikaners as refugees over the next 12 months, according to a notice sent to Congress on Tuesday.
In a statement to the BBC, a White House spokeswoman said: "President Trump has provided a lifeline for Afrikaners, who are being raped, maimed, killed and driven off their property across South Africa.
"While the South African government and many in the media have brushed off the horrific lived experiences of this community, the Trump administration continues to process applications for refugee status because the president has a humanitarian heart."
SJ Du Venage, who lives on South Africa's west coast, has been trying to move to the US under the new scheme.
Du Venage is a council member of the Freedom Front Plus, a right-wing Afrikaner party, and argues that there is a "political drive towards killing white people, and killing the farmers on the farms".
"There's absolutely an agenda to wipe us out here," he says.
- Race policies or Israel - what's really driving Trump's fury with South Africa? 
  - Published23 February 2025
- Is there a genocide of white South Africans as Trump claims? 
  - Published2 June 2025
- Do Afrikaners want to take Trump up on his South African refugee offer? 
  - Published15 May 2025
An Afrikaner lobby group is holding a vigil on Saturday with thousands of white crosses on Washington's National Mall to commemorate what it says are victims of "farm attacks".
Claims of genocide against white South Africans have been discredited by every political party in the country, including by those representing Afrikaners.
"I'm an Afrikaner from South Africa myself," Ambassador Meyer said, "and I can say that I've never experienced something of that kind."
Meyer said he would like to have a conversation with Trump about the reality of the situation, saying that as a "born Afrikaner", he has the "legitimacy" to speak about the subject.
The ambassador helped negotiate an end to apartheid on behalf of the National Party, which was responsible for it, with now-president Cyril Ramaphosa also a key negotiator for the African National Congress party.
He said the "trust" between the two men was one reason President Ramaphosa appointed him to help mend US-South Africa relations, as well as "the fact he also saw the value of me being an Afrikaner".
"But I'm not here to represent the Afrikaner only," Meyer says.
Last week, the Trump administration announced visa restrictions for those South Africans who it said were responsible for "race-based discrimination" against white people. It also warned of further punitive actions if South African leaders did not address the issue.
Police data shows the majority of victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black. Farm violence, often motivated by robberies, is an issue but represents a smaller number of homicides in the country.
While no politician disputes that crime is a problem in South Africa, many experts say this does not qualify as "persecution".
Larry Bartlett, the former director of the US Refugee Assistance Programme, said it could even be "unlawful" to appropriate a programme defined in law for people who "really have no chance to go home".
He said white people who were unlikely to qualify as refugee in law were taking scarce opportunities meant for those fleeing war or ethnic cleansing.
The programme has its critics among Afrikaners in South Africa too.
"Why single out the white Afrikaner to say this group qualifies to flee to the US? This country suffers gender-based violence. Why not single out women?" Rudi Swanepoel, a pastor from Johannesburg told the BBC.
Swanepoel thinks it is not persecution but a "loss of privilege" that is causing some Afrikaners to feel aggrieved.
"To use the metaphor of a cake, 30, 40 years ago the white people of South Africa controlled the cake," he says. "Since democracy came, the obvious reality was we had to now start sharing that cake and those privileges."
Alongside "rural safety", the Trump administration has raised other concerns about South Africa, including targets for companies to increase non-white employment and a law allowing the state, in exceptional circumstances, to expropriate land without compensation. These are aimed at redressing historic racial inequality.
Meyer wants Trump's executive order against South Africa, which underpins the refugee pathway, revoked.
He said South Africa had never prevented people from leaving and had addressed all the US concerns, stressing that the land expropriation law is awaiting a court judgement.
"South Africa has challenges with the prevention of crime and with the combatting of crime," he said.
But he added: "It's a problem all around. It's not rural. It's not farm attacks only. If you look at the total picture, the huge levels of crime in the black townships of South Africa are the biggest concern, proportionally, far more than anything else."
He said he would encourage the US to help South Africa with resources on combatting crime, including by providing equipment to speed up reaction times.
Meyer also has a message for Afrikaners protesting against "farm attacks" by laying white crosses in Washington.
"It doesn't help us to raise a voice outside, if we are not committed to doing something inside the country," he says.

Senior Election Commission officials led by Deputy Election Commissioners will start visiting the five poll-bound States from this week to oversee election preparedness at the field level.
Functionaries said this week teams from the EC will visit Goa, followed by Uttarakhand next week. The EC officials will also visit Punjab and then Manipur in coming weeks.
There is no word yet on when EC officials will visit Uttar Pradesh.
Usually, the "full Commission" comprising the Chief Election Commissioner and fellow Commissioners visits poll-bound states ahead of announcement of election schedule.
While the term of the 403-member Uttar Pradesh assembly ends on May 22 next year, the terms of 60-member Manipur, 40-member Goa, 117-member Punjab and 70-member Uttarakhand assembly end on different dates in March, 2027.
Provisions of The Representation of the People Act, 1950 allows EC to hold polls "earlier than six months before the term expires".
As part of poll preparation, Uttar Pradesh and Goa have initiated 'first-level checks' (FLCs) on electronic voting machines and paper trail units to be used in polling.
During FLCs, electronic voting machines and paper trail machines are checked for mechanical flaws by engineers of BEL and ECIL, the two PSUs that manufacture the two equipment. Faulty machines are returned to the manufacturers for repair or replacement.
A mock poll is also held to check the two machines in the presence of representatives of political parties.
The FLCs are an important part of the poll preparedness.
The EC issues a calendar which states have to follow and these checks are part of the schedule. During FLC, any data from previous elections remaining on the control units and ballot units is completely cleared.
Once a unit passes all diagnostic tests, it is marked as "FLC OK" and sealed with a specialised pink paper seal to prevent any unauthorised access before the next stages of election preparation.
At least one ballot unit, one control unit and one paper trail machine make for an EVM.

Temperamental traits and adverse experiences during childhood may together offer clues to vulnerability to major psychiatric disorders, a transdiagnostic study by researchers at NIMHANS has found.
The study, published recently in the Journal of Affective Disorders, examined 1,162 adults, including 532 people with psychiatric disorders, 457 unaffected first-degree relatives (FDRs) and 173 healthy controls. The participants were drawn from 393 multiplex families - families in which multiple members had been diagnosed with psychiatric disorders - involving schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and alcohol use disorder (AUD).
The researchers examined four broad dimensions of adult temperament - negative affectivity, extraversion/surgency, effortful control and orienting sensitivity - along with adverse childhood experiences (ACEs).
“Our findings suggest that temperament does not map onto psychiatric disorders in a simple, one-to-one manner. Rather, different combinations of temperamental characteristics are associated with different disorders, and some of these characteristics are also seen among unaffected family members,” said Srinivas Balachander, corresponding author and one of the lead researchers of the study.
Temperament shared within families
Using data from the erstwhile Accelerator programme for Discovery in Brain disorders using Stem cells (ADBS) project, (funded by the Department of Biotechnology and Pratiksha Trust), now known as the Rohini Nilekani Centre for Brain and Mind, at NIMHANS, the researchers found evidence of familial sharing across all four temperamental domains.
This was observed despite considerable variation in the psychiatric diagnoses within the same families. The finding is of interest because temperament is known to have a substantial heritable component, although the study did not directly establish that the temperamental characteristics observed were caused by specific genetic variants.
“In our study, considering the significant within-family heterogeneity in terms of different diagnoses, there was still a significant degree of shared temperament,” Dr. Balachander said.
Among affected participants, schizophrenia and bipolar disorder were associated with lower extraversion/surgency and orienting sensitivity. OCD was associated with higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity, along with lower effortful control and extraversion/surgency. Participants with AUD showed higher negative affectivity and orienting sensitivity and lower effortful control.
Some of these patterns were also observed among unaffected first-degree relatives. Relatives of people with schizophrenia showed lower extraversion/surgency, while relatives of people with OCD showed higher negative affectivity and lower effortful control.
“These findings are particularly interesting because some temperamental characteristics were evident even in individuals who did not have the disorder but belonged to families carrying a higher degree of familial risk,” Dr. Balachander said.
Childhood adversity and alcohol use disorder
The researchers also examined whether adverse childhood experiences altered the relationship between temperament and psychiatric disorders.
The clearest evidence for an interaction between temperament and childhood adversity emerged in alcohol use disorder. The overall ACE score was significantly associated with AUD, and interactions between childhood adversity and two temperamental domains - extraversion/surgency and effortful control - were also observed.
“Childhood adversity appears to add another layer to the relationship between temperament and psychiatric vulnerability. In our study, the evidence for this interaction was particularly apparent in alcohol use disorder, rather than uniformly across all four disorders,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers, however, cautioned against interpreting the findings as evidence that a particular temperament or childhood experience causes a psychiatric disorder.
The study was cross-sectional, meaning that the assessments were made at one point in time. The adult temperament measures were self-reported and could be influenced by current illness, treatment, illness duration or an individual’s perception of their own past Reports of childhood adversity may also be affected by recall and measurement biases.
Testing the findings
To examine whether the findings extended beyond the genetically enriched family sample, the researchers tested their statistical model using an independent community-based cohort from the Consortium for Vulnerability to Externalizing Disorders and Addiction (c-VEDA).
The analysis included 2,485 adults aged 18 to 23 years for whom the relevant temperament, ACE and psychiatric assessments were available.
The model showed an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.822 for alcohol use disorder, 0.742 for bipolar disorder and 0.752 for OCD. Its performance for schizophrenia was close to chance level, with an AUC of 0.526.
“The external validation gives us some indication that the associations identified in the family-based sample may extend to community populations for some disorders. However, the findings for schizophrenia did not replicate well, which is an important limitation and needs further investigation,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said the findings point to the need for prospective studies that follow unaffected family members over time. Such studies could help determine whether particular temperamental characteristics precede the onset of psychiatric illness or are partly consequences of illness and its treatment.
“Temperament and childhood adversity may eventually become useful components of broader risk assessment frameworks, but we need prospective longitudinal evidence before we can say that they have predictive or preventive value,” Dr. Balachander said.
The researchers said that studying temperament alongside childhood adversity could eventually provide a more nuanced understanding of psychiatric vulnerability than considering family history alone. However, they stressed that the present findings do not establish that these measures can predict who will develop a psychiatric disorder.
The researchers said continued longitudinal follow-up of the cohort would be important to establish whether the observed temperamental patterns have value in identifying individuals at increased risk before the emergence of clinically significant symptoms.

When the government officials arrived in Tarluvada last year, they came with abundant promises.
Google, one of the world’s richest and most powerful tech companies, would soon be bringing a “golden opportunity” to this tiny village in south India: a $15bn AI datacentre.
The project, being built in the Indian state of Andhra Pradesh, is set to be Google’s largest “hyperscale” AI datacentre outside the US and would, officials said, make the village of Tarluvada into a world-famous tech hub. Jobs, usually scarce in this impoverished community, would become bountiful, real estate prices would soar and compensation for any land would be generous.
Few in the village – which sits on a dusty unpaved road and is surrounded by farms and forest – had even heard of AI or knew what a datacentre was. Yet it did not take long for local jubilation over Google’s arrival to turn to suspicion.
Just as protests have erupted globally over AI datacentres – from California and Texas to Scotland and Australia – communities in Andhra Pradesh, too have been gathering in opposition to the project, fearing that the people will end up bearing a crippling environmental and economic cost.
“We have learned that America does not want the problems of datacentres and so now Google is bringing them here,” said Tarluvada’s village head, BRB Naidu, who admitted he was torn about whether the datacentre would bring prosperity or ruin to their community. “Many in the village are very worried. But the government has refused to answer our questions.”
Pointing up to the nearby hillside – where bulldozers recently stripped the land bare of trees to ready it for Google’s mega AI campus – Naidu adds: “The work just continues every day.”
The state government, which is allied with Indian prime minister Narendra Modi’s party, have been accused of trying to obfuscate the true scale of the vast AI hub being built in Andhra Pradesh, to push the project through at lightening speed and avoid more stringent environmental scrutiny. Google has partnered with the Adani Group, one of India’s largest and most politically powerful conglomerates with a reputation for getting approvals through quickly, to build the project.
Publicly it was announced as a 1GW project – already a larger energy requirement than most AI datacentres. In its response to the Guardian, Google referred to it only as an unspecific “gigawatt scale AI hub”, that was “comparable to other projects”.
But state environmental clearances reveal that permission has been granted for it to be more than double that size – 2.51GW; the power equivalent of two large nuclear reactors at full output. Over a year, it amounts to upwards of 30% of the current energy consumption of the whole of Andhra Pradesh, a state home to more than 55 million people.
Activists fear that meeting the datacentre’s vast energy demands will lead to seismic environmental consequences for the region, including driving up fossil fuel emissions. While Google has pledged to help generate “new, clean energy” to power its AI hub, currently 75% of the country’s electricity grid is run on coal.
The state government argues AI datacentres will be essential to India’s growth and long-term digital competitiveness. According to the government of India’s Economic Survey 2025–26, India generated nearly 20% of the world’s data but hosts only about 3% of global datacentres.
But locals and activists say that building one of the world’s largest AI datacentres in a region of India already struggling with issues over extreme heat, water, land, forests, power shortages and environmental regulation comes at a heavy cost.
Google’s project will in fact encompass three separate datacentres around the state capital of Vizakhapatnam. One other site nearby to Taluvada is a few metres from reserve forest, a drinking water reservoir and a wildlife sanctuary home to endangered species such as leopards.
Despite the AI datacentre’s expansive footprint, the state government issued environmental clearances to Google in just nine days, with no public consultation.
Three petitions challenging the state’s quick approval of the project have now been filed to India’s National Green Tribunal (NGT), the country’s top environmental court. The petitions allege that government’s assessment of the risks to the environment and water supplies were “grossly inadequate, scientifically unrealistic, and misleading”. A public litigation has also been filed in the Andhra Pradesh high court.
“This datacentre will be unprecedented in scale but there was no public hearing and no substantial evaluation of the ecological damage or the economic cost for local communities,” said VS Krishna, an activist with Human Rights Forum, the organisation which filed the NGT cases.
Krishna alleged that their campaign to protest against the datacentre had been met with a deliberate silencing, including videos and social media pages being taken down. The government did not respond to this allegation.
“We just have to look at the protests happening across the world to understand how environmentally catastrophic this will be,” Krishna added.
In Tarluvada, temperatures regularly soar to about 45C during the summer and there are concerns the datacentres – documented emitters of heat – could make this even worse. The mass deforestation required for the project – more than 100 acres, could drive up temperatures even more. In response to the Guardian, Google said the project would have “no expected impact” on the local community.
The strain on water supplies in this already water-stressed area has also been a cause of concern. In similarly water-stressed cities in the US, datacentres have been accused of exacerbating drought while polluting the water supply. Google said this project would use air-cooling instead of water, and would therefore have no impact on local drinking water supplies.
Venkat Surynarayana, 40, a farmer in Tarluvada, said that when officials had initially come to measure land for the datacentre “they never mentioned anything about risks of pollution or water or heat, they didn’t even tell us what the project was.
“We are sick with worry since we learned about the problems a datacentre can bring. This area can not afford to be any hotter. What if this makes our land dry and worthless? What will happen to my crops and my livelihood?”
Surynarayana claimed attempts to get answers from the local administration had been met with police threats and protesters such as himself had been routinely detained. “When we raised our voices, they ignore us and then they shut us down,” he said. “But if this is not stopped, it could be the end of Tarluvada.”
For the state government of Andhra Pradesh, the deal struck with Google to build this vast datacentre on its turf is a source of enormous pride, part of a wider policy to make the state into India’s most advanced and affluent tech hub. “Artificial intelligence is becoming foundational infrastructure for the global economy,” said Sribharat Mathukumilli, a local MP with the ruling state government, who rejected the environmental concerns.
The subsidies and incentives they offered to Google, from decades-long tax breaks and discounted land to access to cheap electricity and water, are estimated to amount to 220bn rupees ($2.2bn) over 20 years.
“Our objective is not simply to host a datacentre, but to create an AI and digital ecosystem,” said Mathukumilli. Late last year, the state granted permission for another 1GW AI datacentre, to be built by Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries.
Google insisted the design choices of its AI datacentre have been tailored to local conditions and that it had “engaged deeply” with local communities, claiming it would generate thousands of jobs around Vizakhapatnam.
But swathes of villagers in Tarluvada allege they were forced to give up land for the project against their will, and say they have not been given all they were promised in return.
“No one will tell us the truth about this project,” said T Applaraju, 40, who was one of the 520 local families in Tarluvada who recently had land taken back that the government had allocated to him 20 years ago. He claims he was given no notice that his land was to be taken until April this year, when security guards working for the Adani Group erected fences and blocked locals from entering the plots they had farmed for years.
“They took land that we thought belonged to us, it’s a big shock,” he said. “Why are Google building this here and not in America?”
The state government claims no lands were forcibly taken and that it gave “generous compensation” to those who were eligible. The Adani group says that all necessary legal approvals were given. But many of the 47 farmers from the impoverished Dalit community who were compensated for their land are also unhappy.
One farmer, P Venkat Rao, alleged he was pressured by the government into giving up his only acre of land against his will. He received $40,000 in compensation, but said the government’s promise to give them a replacement piece of land and one job per family had not materialised. Without land to farm, Rao described the compensation as “worthless”.
“I am a farmer, without my land I am nothing,” he added. “They have taken my livelihood and broken their promises.”

It was true that there was a spike in registration of Slovenian domain names in May and June, followed by a separate spike shortly before the executive order in September. A claim that U.S. President Donald Trump signed an executive order changing the term "artificial intelligence" to "super intelligence" in order to profit from the sale of domain names with the top-level domain ".si" circulated in late September 2026.  
People on social media platforms shared the rumor, with some claiming that an "investigation shows that in the past 60 days insiders bought thousands of .si domain names. They've profited hundreds of millions of dollars so far."
The ".si" domain is for the country of Slovenia — also the home country of first lady Melania Trump, a detail that appeared to help fuel the rumor — and is typically used for businesses operating from that country.
The rumor suggested that Trump tipped off associates so that they could purchase Slovenian domains, sit on them, and then resell at a high markup to companies or individuals looking to expand their web presence to the ".si" top-level domain, a practice called domain squatting.
The claim circulated following Trump's Sept. 29, 2026, signing of an executive order demanding that any reference to "artificial intelligence" be instead called "super intelligence" within the U.S. government's executive branch.
Trump and tech leaders also signed an accord in an effort to assuage fears over AI, which Snopes previously reported featured a misspelling of "United States." Polls have shown that AI is increasingly unpopular and critics called the move an attempted "rebrand" of AI.
Prior to the official documents, Trump had previously posted about "super intelligence" on his Truth Social social media page on Sept. 19.
It was true that there was a spike in registration of Slovenian domain names months before the executive order, but Snopes could not independently verify claims that Trump or his associates either financially benefited from the domain purchases or knew about the "super intelligence" executive order ahead of time.
The claim originated with a thread on X by independent journalist Adam Cochran.
Cochran cited the 
Register.si's website called the ".si" domain "an internationally recognized top-level domain that represents Slovenia and is the first choice of address on the Internet for all individuals and organizations related to Slovenia."
A post on Register.si's website explained the organization does not directly register domains, but rather works "through approximately 90 domestic and foreign registrars."
The same post indicated that there had been a spike in registrations and specifically mentioned Trump's "super intelligence" announcement as a possible cause, stating his social media post and resulting "discussion quickly attracted the attention of the public and the technology community, including speculation about the impact of the potential new abbreviation on the Slovenian national domain .si."
A graph depicting the number of daily ".si" domain registrations shared by Register.si indicated a jump from fewer than 1,000 registrations on Sept. 20 — one day after Trump posted about "super intelligence" on Truth Social — to over 4,000 on Sept. 23.
(Register.si)
More broadly, a monthly graph with a range of July 2025 to September 2026 showed a sharp rise from fewer than 2,500 registrations a month to more than 10,000 in September 2026. The graph also showed a spike in May and June 2026, both around 5,000.
(Register.si)
The spikes in May and June appeared to be Cochran's main evidence that connected the purchases to "Trump's inner circle." While it is possible Trump tipped off associates about the coming change and that they were the individuals who bought up .si domains, a theory is not proof. Snopes can only offer a rating after independently verifying primary evidence; therefore, we have left this claim unrated.
Further, "super intelligence" as a term predated Trump's use of it.
We reached out to Cochran asking him to share his evidence for independent review, as well as Register.si to ask about any other explanations for the spike in May and June. We will update this article if we get a response. We also reached out to the White House press office for comment and have not heard back, as of this writing.
Domain squatting, also called cybersquatting, is nothing new.
Typically, it involves parties purchasing a domain that could be confused with an established brand or company, or even a common misspelling or typo of the company's name. Once the new owner has control of the domain, they can then sell it to the company at a higher price than a typical fresh registration.
The World Intellectual Property Organization, a United Nations agency that aims to "protect and promote" intellectual property "across borders and acting as a forum for addressing cutting-edge IP issues," reported its highest caseload of domain disputes to date in 2025 with over 6,200.
Register.si's website stated that their price "is the same for all registrars and amounts to EUR 10," but that "the final price for domain holders depends on the policy of the individual registrar and Register.si has no influence on it," according to a Google translation.
The organization said that speculation about potential earnings for the country of Slovenia because of the increased interest in their domain "have no real basis" and they advised "holders of trademarks, slogans, companies, ... who do not yet have a domain under .si to register it as soon as possible."

Srinagar, Sept 23: PDP president Mehbooba Mufti on Wednesday warned that India could “resemble a banana republic” if electoral rolls continue to be altered according to the wishes of the ruling BJP, while praising two Election Commissioners for raising objections to decisions taken by the poll panel.
Speaking about reports that two Election Commissioners had raised objections on several occasions to decisions and positions taken by the Election Commission, Mufti said their dissent was important for the health of Indian democracy.
“Today they are trying to subvert the very fundamental of Indian democracy, which is the electoral process, by, you know, fudging the electoral rolls, which the two Election Commissioners have pointed out,” she said.
She said India and Pakistan, which she described as “sibling states”, appeared to be competing with each other in ways that harmed their own people and institutions.
“I feel that our both the sibling states, India and Pakistan, they are trying to undo each other, competing with each other — who can damage their people the most, who can damage their country the most,” Mufti said.
Referring to India’s description of itself as the world’s largest democracy, she said the country’s electoral process was central to that democratic identity.
“Our country India, which is seen as the largest democracy in the world and which our Prime Minister proudly talks about, ‘mother of democracy’, whenever he is abroad,” she said.
“But if it continues to be like this, you know, where electoral rolls — deletion and addition — happens at BJP’s will, then there are dangers that at some point of time our country, which is the largest democracy in the world, is going to resemble a banana republic.”
Mufti also contrasted the situation in India with developments in Pakistan, particularly the detention of the sisters of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan.
“At the same time, look at Pakistan, which goes around the world as a peacemaker, as mediator of peace, is crushing dissent within its country with an iron hand,” she said.
“Look at — I mean, detaining Imran Khan’s sisters, who are unarmed, who are protesting very peacefully, them detaining just because they are trying to stand up for their brother. What does it speak?”
She said the detention of women protesters was at odds with Pakistan’s international image.
“You are going around the world as a peacemaker and, in your home, inside your house, women who have no weapons in their hands, you are detaining them,” she said.
Mufti said the “only silver lining” she could see was that India still had officials willing to question those in power.
“The only silver lining I can see is that in India we still have people like the two Election Commissioners who have the courage and integrity to question the people in power,” she said.
She contrasted this with Pakistan, saying there were no comparable voices within the establishment willing to question what she described as the “arbitrary detention” of Imran Khan’s sisters.
“It’s a very, very sorry state of affairs,” she said.
Mufti also referred to the deletion of voters from draft electoral rolls, saying the scale of the changes made the independence of Election Commission officials particularly important.
“If we do not have people like the two Election Commissioners, I don’t want to take their name at this point of time. I don’t know what trouble they are going to go through,” she said.
“They will be ED raids now, Income Tax raids now. What will happen to them?”
She concluded by reiterating her warning about the consequences of continued changes to electoral rolls.
“But if we continue like this, I mean, there will be a time when we are going to resemble a banana republic. There will be no democracy,” Mufti said.

United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) has said they would go ahead with the three-day nationwide strike beginning September 28, as a conciliation meeting before the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner on Tuesday remained inconclusive.
The conciliation meeting was held a day after the Finance Ministry appealed to bank employees to refrain from resorting to strikes and resolve their remaining demands through dialogue.
UFBU, which claims to represent 90 per cent of the banking workforce, is primarily seeking 5-day banking among other demands.
The strike, if it materialises, may impact banking services for five days as the weekend before September 28 is a holiday. It would coincide with the half-yearly closing of the banking sector.
“Responding to the appeal made by the Department of Financial Services (DFS), Indian Banks’ Association (IBA), Bank managements to defer the strike, we informed them that if there is any concrete and positive development towards implementation of our demand for introduction of 5 days banking, UFBU will consider the same,” UFBU said in a statement after the meeting with the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner.
Otherwise, it said, UFBU will be constrained to go ahead with the proposed strike on September 28, 29 and 30.
Representatives of the DFS, Ministry of Finance, informed that the Government has been taking many initiatives for the welfare of the bank employees and the issue of 5-day Banking is also under consideration as they have to take into account the views of many other stakeholders before any decision is taken, it said.
Hence, it said, they requested the UFBU to defer the strike and continue the dialogue. Bank unions under UFBU had gone on nationwide strike on September 11 over their demand.
UFBU’s other demands include an update and improvement of pension, a uniform dearness allowance formula for all pensioners and an option for employees covered under the National Pension System (NPS) to switch to the old pension scheme (OPS).
Many public sector banks have started issuing advisories to their customers to use digital channels such as Mobile Banking, ATM, Internet Banking, BC Point and UPI for banking needs if the strike materialises.
The proposed 3-day strike period also coincides with the half-yearly closing of banks on September 30, a date of particular significance for reconciliation, provisioning and treasury and market operations.
A disruption of this nature, combined with the preceding weekend, would result in an effective five-day closure of banking services at a particularly sensitive point in the financial calendar - causing considerable inconvenience to customers, businesses, Government transactions and international banking operations.
Strikes cause disruption in banking services that inconvenience the public, impact the business of the banks, and ultimately harm the interests of bank employees and there is no fruitful outcome that is achieved through strikes, the finance ministry had said on Monday.
The government assured that it remains committed to the welfare and well-being of bank employees and to addressing their genuine concerns through constructive engagement.

One argument that often comes up about climate change is that fossil fuels are good because they powered economic growth that has left most people better off overall. And, to an extent, that has been true, but it’s also an extremely limited perspective.
It’s pretty obvious now that the growth they powered has come with very high costs that we’ve only recently started to pay, in the form of damages and disruptions from extreme weather events. With things like sea level rise expected to continue for centuries even if we hit net zero, it’s difficult to estimate how expensive that growth will eventually be.
But that perspective is also limited: We now have better ways to power our growth—ways that are less environmentally damaging now and won’t leave our descendants with a carbon debt that will be difficult to manage.
Open or closed?
In 2013, I was introduced to a metaphor about changing the relationship between economic growth and fossil fuel use: opening scissors. For decades, GDP growth and carbon emissions were locked together like the two blades of a closed pair of scissors. The idea was that we needed to open them: continue GDP growth (ideally in ways that improved citizens’ lives), but disconnect it from carbon emissions.
At the time, Sweden provided an example of this. In 1996, its carbon emissions began a gradual decline that has continued to the present, with total emissions down by a third from its recent peak in 1996 and more than half from its maximum levels in 1970. But its GDP continued growing. At the time, the data only went as far as 2011, but the World Bank now shows its GDP as having more than doubled since 1996.
In 2013, it was possible to question whether the Swedish example really represented a long-term transition. But with 30 years of data, it is now very clear that Sweden had opened the scissors.
A larger question was whether its example was applicable elsewhere. Sweden was fortunate to have lots of hydropower and an established base of nuclear reactors. And its economy, while substantial, isn’t as diversified as that of some larger countries. Like, for example, the United States.

Gaza Friendly: the French label turning consumer choices into Palestine solidarity
Among the many apps available on the Play Store, one stands out thanks to its heart‑shaped icon featuring a Palestinian flag: “Gaza Friendly”.
Created in June 2025, the label certifies shopkeepers involved in the boycott of products originating from the occupied Palestinian territories and marketed by companies supporting Israel’s settlement expansion.
To date, the app and its associated website list 80 businesses in France, mainly butchers, restaurants, bakeries, caterers, tea rooms and food distributors.
The list is updated regularly, and the app features an interactive map allowing consumers to locate certified shops near their homes.
The app, which has been downloaded more than 500 times so far, was created by Pierre-Amael Noailly Charny, a paediatrician of Tunisian origin from Lyon, in east-central France, along with a small group of friends.

Noailly Charny explains that shopkeepers who join Gaza Friendly can express their commitment to the Palestinian cause in a concrete way.
‘This label gives people outraged by the genocide in Gaza the possibility to turn their consumption into a lever for justice and solidarity’
- Pierre-Amael Noailly Charny, founder of Gaza Friendly
“The existence of this label gives people outraged by the genocide in Gaza the possibility to turn their consumption into a lever for justice and solidarity,” Noailly Charny told Middle East Eye.
The label draws inspiration from the Boycott, Divestment, Sanctions (BDS) movement, an international campaign launched in 2005 by Palestinian civil society to encourage consumers and institutions to refuse to buy Israeli products or goods originating from Israeli settlements, which are illegal under international law.
“Boycott works because refusing certain products cuts off resources from the oppression,” Gaza Friendly argues on its homepage, with the ambition of building a strong network of certified shopkeepers to give greater visibility to the boycott campaign.
‘My business is doing better’
To be certified, shopkeepers must comply with a three‑point charter: no Coca‑Cola Company beverages, no PepsiCo beverages, and no fresh products imported from Israeli settlements.
For Noailly Charny, boycotting Coca‑Cola and PepsiCo is a peaceful tool with strong symbolic impact, given their documented involvement in the illegal occupation of Palestinian territories.
In 2025, BDS revealed that Coca‑Cola operates a regional distribution centre and refrigerated warehouses in the settlement of Atarot in the West Bank, while PepsiCo is targeted for investments and subsidiaries linked to Israel.
‘The idea appealed to me, especially since some customers had already blamed me for selling Coca‑Cola’
- Akli, Gaza Friendly‑certified shopkeeper
Although PepsiCo maintains it does not support Israel politically or militarily, activists argue that its ownership of Israeli brands SodaStream and Sabra, along with its operations in the country, amount to indirect support for the Israeli state. Coca‑Cola, for its part, insists that it does not endorse any country, government or policy, but has not addressed the allegations concerning the Atarot facility.
Both companies declined to respond to MEE’s request for comment.
“Even before Gaza Friendly existed, some shopkeepers had already taken the initiative to stop selling Coca‑Cola and Pepsi products. We therefore chose to put them in the spotlight and list them to set an example and encourage others to join,” Noailly Charny said.
Aid Boucherie Halal in Creteil, near Paris, is one of the latest certified businesses. Its name appeared on the Gaza Friendly list on 4 September. Akli, the owner, says he heard about the label through an acquaintance.
“The idea appealed to me, especially since some customers had already blamed me for selling Coca‑Cola. Personally, I didn’t know the company had interests in Israel,” he told MEE.
Akli says he has always been supportive of Palestinians but didn’t know how to express that support.
“Now I don’t sell Coca-Cola or Pepsi, and my business is doing just as well - actually, even better,” he said, noting a slight increase in customer numbers.
Solidarity brands
In addition to listing shopkeepers, Gaza Friendly provides them with visual materials such as posters and stickers to improve visibility. It also offers a non‑exhaustive list of alternative products, particularly beverages, to replace brands targeted by the boycott.
Some of these drinks come from companies committed to Palestine. This is the case for Pales Drinks, a Belgian brand of sodas created in 2024 by young entrepreneur Abdelhakim Tarnach, which donates 10 percent of its profits to humanitarian actions in Palestine.
The same year saw the launch of Palestine Cola, a soft drink marketed by Safad Food AB, a company founded by entrepreneurs of Palestinian origin based in Malmo, Sweden.
Here too, part of the profits from the sale of cans - decorated with an olive tree and wrapped in a keffiyeh pattern - funds emergency aid projects in Palestine such as clothing, tents and food assistance.
In France, Palestine Cola is mainly distributed by Jebalia, an online retailer promoting alternative, ethical and solidarity‑based consumption. On its Instagram page, each purchase is presented as an act of support for humanitarian causes.
Since July, Jebalia has been listed among Gaza Friendly‑certified businesses. Its owner Sofiane Slimani proudly embraces his commitment to Palestine.
“We’ve reached a point where boycotting products linked to Israeli settlement activity is no longer enough. We need to offer alternatives,” he told MEE.
Jebalia claims to have sold 100,000 cans of soda in 2025, its founding year. Beyond social media, the company uses other communication channels to make itself known.
‘We’ve reached a point where boycotting products linked to Israeli settlement activity is no longer enough. We need to offer alternatives’
- Sofiane Slimani, Gaza Friendly‑certified retailer
It was present at the latest edition of the Annual Gathering of Muslims of France in Le Bourget last April and regularly partners with engaged businesses to offer its drinks at solidarity events, such as the charity football tournament Salam Cup held a few months ago in Bobigny, near Paris.
During this event supporting Palestine, Jebalia products were sold by Inda Coffee, a French coffee shop and matcha bar supporting aid initiatives for Gaza.
Although involved in the boycott campaign, Inda Coffee is not yet certified by Gaza Friendly. According to Noailly Charny, many shopkeepers still don’t know the label exists - hence the need, he insists, for more publicity.
“We’re trying to reach influencers who work in the food sector,” the paediatrician said. In Lyon, AmarFood, a content creator specialising in gastronomy and halal, alcohol‑free restaurants in Lyon and the Paris region, often promotes Gaza Friendly in his videos.
More recently, another videographer shared a story in which he explained the concept at length.
Beyond France, Gaza Friendly aims to expand internationally. Shopkeepers from around 15 countries are already members of the label, which has no equivalent anywhere else in the world.

Kuku Technologies Limited, parent company of audio OTT platform Kuku FM and microdrama app Kuku TV, swung into the black in the fiscal year FY26, reporting a net profit of ₹182.7 Cr against a net loss of ₹152.6 Cr incurred in FY25. The company’s profitability came on the back of a notable uptick in its top line performance. The IPO-bound startup, which filed its confidential DRHP with the SEBI earlier this year, saw its operating revenue for the fiscal year zoom more than sixfold to ₹1,484.2 Cr in FY26 from ₹241.6 Cr in the previous fiscal. Including other income of ₹26.2 Cr, total income for the fiscal stood at ₹1,510.4 Cr. Subscriptions remained the overwhelming source of Kuku Technologies' revenue during FY26. The company generated ₹1,475.4 Cr from subscriptions, accounting for more than 99% of its operating revenue. This was followed by ₹6.9 Cr from pay-per-piece (PPV) content purchases, while advertising brought in the remainder ₹1.9 Cr. India continued to account for the vast majority of its business, contributing ₹1,463.6 Cr, or roughly 99% of operating revenue. International markets contributed ₹20.5 Cr during the year. The profitability was also charged by a deferred tax credit of ₹98.2 Cr and a tax expense of ₹4 Cr. Excluding that, the profit for the year stood at ₹88.6 Cr. At the operating level, Kuku Technologies swung to an EBITDA profit of ₹82.9 Cr in FY26 from an EBITDA loss of ₹159.8 Cr in FY25. Kuku Turns Profitable Ahead Of IPO The company, which operates audio OTT platform Kuku FM, microdrama app Kuku TV, among others, has swung to the black ahead of going public. Earlier in September, the markets regulator Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) approved the proposed listing of Kuku Technologies. Kuku filed its confidential DRHP with the SEBI in June. As per sources, the IPO’s size could be in the range of ₹2,500-3,500 Cr ($261-366 Mn) and could potentially value it at ₹15,000 Cr (about $1.8 Bn). The IPO will consist of a fresh issue of shares as well as an offer-for-sale component. Kuku plans to deploy the capital to upgrade its tech, AI infrastructure, content production and fuel geographic expansion. As of now, the startup’s content library spans more than 20,000 titles across seven languages and multiple genres including drama, finance, and well-being. It claims to have more than 1 Cr listeners and creators on its platform and 400 Mn app downloads across its portfolio. Kuku has raised over $156 Mn to date from the likes of Fundamentum Partnership, Krafton, Vertex Ventures, IFC, 3one4 Capital, among others. Its most recent $85 Mn Series C funding round, in October 2025, was led by Granite Asia. Magnifying Kuku FM’s Spending Total expenses for the fiscal year surged 3.5X to ₹1,421.8 Cr in the year under review from ₹411 Cr in FY25. Here is a breakdown of where the startup spent a major share of its expenses: Marketing And Advertisement Expenses: Constituting 77.7% of the overall expenses, Kuku FM spent ₹1,105.1 Cr on marketing and advertising in FY26. This is a near 4X jump compared with around ₹284.8 Cr spent on marketing in FY25. Operational Costs: Spending under this head rose 11X to ₹96.3 Cr in the year under review from ₹8.7 Cr in the previous fiscal. Employee Benefit Expenses: Employee-related expenses grew at a much slower pace, increasing about 24% to ₹74.1 Cr in FY26 from ₹59.9 Cr in FY25.

A sharp mind, a quirky sense of humour, a young heart and a perennial desire to experiment with his movies defined Singeetham Srinivasa Rao. As he departs at 94, he leaves behind a body of work that has a sense of permanence.
Having found an ally in Kamal Haasan, Singeetham discovered a sense of freedom, especially in the Tamil industry. A hero being visually challenged was never the template for films, but the duo smirked at such notions through the 1981 flick Raaja Paarvai. For many fans the song Andhi mazhai from this lovely film, remains a ear-worm.
A celluloid venture without dialogues? Bring it on, said Singeetham and along with Kamal, dished out Pesum Padam, also called Pushpak, Pushpaka Vimana and Pushpaka Vimanam. The 1987 silent film had different titles across languages, just for the fans to connect.
The film, extensively shot in Bengaluru, proved that the right visuals, actors and background score could mask the absence of the uttered word. And can ice be used as a weapon of murder? Apparently it works, as evident in one crazy scene.
Siblings split at birth and then finding their way back together is a trope as old as the hills. Singeetham gave it a twist by making one brother a dwarf, who is also consumed with a sense of extracting revenge. The result was Aboorva Sagodharargal in 1989.
With Kamal dishing out a bravura performance, the film was a blockbuster. And if you want to figure out black humour, just watch the song Vaazha veikum kadhalukku jai in which Kamal and Gautami are prancing on a truck, oblivious to a dead body in their midst.
Even as Telugu and Kannada outings kept Singeetham busy, he dipped into Tamil often and in 1990, along with Kamal, helmed Michael Madana Kama Rajan. The story of quadruplets growing up in different homes and speaking Tamil dialects ranging from Palghat to Madras, remains a classic. “You know what I mean?,” is a dialogue that even today evokes laughter while a fish went missing in sambar!
In 1994, Singeetham directed Magalir Mattum, headlined by Urvashi, Revathi, Rohini and Nasser. Produced by Kamal, the story of how three women form a sisterhood and strike back against their lecherous boss, stays relevant. And veteran Nagesh as the corpse, was a hoot.
Singeetham also dished out Chinna Vathiyar with Prabhu and Khushbu in the lead in 1995. After their 1998 reunion for Kaathala Kaathala, a laugh-riot, Singeetham and Kamal joined hands in 2005 for Mumbai Express. A black-comedy centred around a kidnapping and some bumbling men, worked for some, did not work for another section, and yet it had its moments.
It was also fitting that Kamal did a retrospective on Singeetham, reliving their films together and getting inputs from his other collaborators. Those videos on YouTube are an essential watch for all cinephiles. Singeetham will be remembered for his boundless energy, one that also helped him direct Sing Geetham, well into his nineties.

NRL Grand Final: Daly Cherry-Evans kicks crucial drop goal as Sydney Roosters hold on by one point to break Newcastle Knights hearts
Dual-code international winger Mark Nawaqanitawase scored two tries as the Sydney Roosters edged the Newcastle Knights 19-18 in the National Rugby League final on Sunday, securing the foundation club a 16th title
Sunday 4 October 2026 12:35, UK
Hull FC-bound Daly Cherry-Evans kicked the crucial drop goal as the Sydney Roosters held on by one point to break Newcastle Knights hearts in a dramatic NRL Grand Final.
The Roosters overturned a 12-point deficit to deny Newcastle a fairytale ending to their Cinderella season and claim a 16th premiership after a thrilling Grand Final in Sydney.
Inspirational captain, James Tedesco, and a show-stopping performance from Mark Nawaqanitawase, who could represent Australia at both the league and union World Cups over the next 12 months, handed the Red White and Bluesters their first title since 2019.

Cherry-Evans, who was playing 15 years after his first premiership medallion, said. "I didn't do anything. I'm so grateful. Thank you so much for the support. It's been an amazing journey. I'm so lucky.
"I had so much belief in this club, the players, the coach. This is what it's all about. And we did it. And I'm so, so proud to be here, and I just can't wait to go see my family."
The underdog Knights stormed into a 12-0 lead with Francis Manuleleua opening the scoring before Kalyn Ponga scored a classic Grand Final try by running the length of the field to touch down and send Newcastle fans wild at a sold-out Accor Stadium.
Nawaqanitawase, playing the final game of his two-year stint at the Roosters before his return to rugby union, cut the deficit after superb footwork and then Billy Smith showed strength and composure to pile over and level the scores.
Sam Walker converted a penalty after a defensive infringement to put Sydney ahead and then Nawaqanitawase, nicknamed 'Marky Mark' flew into the corner to put his side 18-12 ahead.
Cherry-Evans, the oldest Grand Finalist in history, used all his experience to nudge over a simple field goal to extend his side's lead beyond a converted try.
And it proved a vital score with Greg Marzhew breaking a couple of tackles to roll over for Newcastle with Sandon Smith converting brilliantly from the touchline. But the 'Chooks', one of the two clubs remaining from the first season of what became the NRL in 1908, held on, to secure their fourth title under long-term coach Trent Robinson.
"Credit to the Knights, they fought for 80 minutes there," said Nawaqanitawase, after lifting the Provan-Summons Trophy.
"This is going to last me a lifetime, it's sad to go but I love everyone here, I love all the boys, and let's celebrate this win, far out."
The Knight headed into the match just a day after CEO Peter Parr expressed his deep concern after a vehicle drove into a crowd of people supporting the NRL team on Saturday, as they prepared for their Grand Final.
Police said 10 people were injured in the incident in Wallsend, New South Wales, including several children, while the 18-year-old man driving the vehicle was arrested.
Two of the injured, a five-year-old girl and a 67-year-old man, are in critical condition, and the other eight are in stable condition at a hospital, according to New South Wales Police.

The past fortnight has brought several developments around Apple in India. The iPhone 18 Pro and Apple’s foldable iPhone Duo began shipping, putting the company’s latest hardware in focus. But another development has drawn attention: Apple Pay, a service the company has been talking about bringing to India for more than a decade, is finally here. Apple launched the service in India on September 30, 2026, allowing users to pay at physical stores, within apps and on websites using an iPhone, iPad or Apple Watch. In 2016, then CEO Tim Cook during his visit to India said that Apple was looking at bringing Apple Pay to India, and had even met the then ICICI Bank CEO Chanda Kochhar to understand the bank’s views on mobile payments. Ten years later, Apple Pay is finally here, but the payments landscape has changed considerably. The Unified Payments Interface (UPI) processed 24.51 Bn transactions worth ₹29.82 Lakh Cr in August 2026, as per the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI). The question is whether Apple can find room in a market where consumers already have several ways to pay. Narrower Than The US Version Apple Pay allows users to add eligible cards to Apple Wallet and authenticate payments through Face ID, Touch ID or their device passcode. At physical stores, they can tap their devices against compatible contactless terminals. Online, they can pay without repeatedly entering card details. The India offering is narrower than the service available in the US, where customers can use cards from a wider range of participating banks and issuers. US users can also access Apple Cash for person-to-person money transfers, subject to eligibility. Apple has not announced a comparable service for India. At launch, Apple Pay supports eligible Axis Bank-issued Visa and Mastercard credit cards. RuPay cards and cards from other banks are not supported under the initial rollout. This limits the number of consumers who can use the service, even among iPhone owners. Tarun Pathak of Counterpoint Research said Apple’s entry is late from both a global launch and competition standpoint, but pointed to regulatory requirements and the relatively small size of India’s installed iPhone base as possible reasons for the delay. “Clearance of regulatory and technical roadblocks allowed Apple to hold its standard global architecture when it comes to Apple Pay experience built around NFC card tokenisation, plus the native Apple ecosystem leveraging the security of Face ID, Touch ID, and Apple Watch integration for fast NFC tap-to-pay at POS terminals,” Pathak said. Apple’s approach keeps the payment experience tied to its own devices and security architecture. However, the restricted bank rollout means the company will need to expand its partnerships before the service can reach a wider customer base. UPI Poses A Challenge For Apple Pay UPI’s dominance presents a different challenge for Apple Pay. Unlike markets where card-based payment plays a larger role, India has built a digital payment ecosystem around direct bank-to-bank transfers, with consumers using apps such as PhonePe and Google Pay for everyday transactions. According to the Reserve Bank of India’s Payment System Report, December 2025, UPI accounted for 85.5% of digital transaction volume. This figure underlines how firmly UPI is embedded in India’s payment ecosystem, leaving Apple Pay to build adoption in a market where consumers already have an established way to pay. Apple Pay’s launch in India does not support UPI integration. Its initial use case is therefore centred on consumers who own compatible Apple devices and hold eligible credit cards. With Apple Pay, the company is offering contactless payments, but Apple will need to give users a reason to choose card-based payment through its devices when UPI is already widely available. The availability of tap-to-pay alone may not be enough to change consumer habits. Samsung Wallet already offers NFC-based payments on compatible Galaxy devices, alongside other wallet features. Despite Samsung supporting UPI payments, it has hardly made a dent. An industry insider who has worked in fintech told Inc42 that the service is unlikely to make a major difference to the sector in its current form. “Apple Pay launch is only restricted to Axis Bank, with no UPI integration. Even today Android users are around 90% of the mobile phone users. Apple Pay is just allowing you to save the card and pay via NFC,” the insider said. The insider also pointed to existing options for Android users, saying popular apps such as Phonepe have integrated card-based payment features for Visa and Mastercard users. The source expects some Apple users to adopt the service for high ticket purchases but does not see it as a threat to the fintech industry. The insider also questioned whether Apple would enter UPI, citing NPCI’s transaction data storage requirements and Apple’s policies of not storing transaction details. Can Apple Pay Drive Card Payments? Apple Pay’s entry could give a push to credit card transactions, particularly among iPhone users who prefer using cards for higher value purchases. Amrish Rau, MD and CEO of Pine Labs, had anticipated the service’s India entry before its launch, arguing that it could shift some transactions towards cards as credit card payments and UPI continue to grow. “We do believe Apple Pay will enter the market before the end of this year. What that is going to do is flip and create a spread in terms of how payment transactions will happen. More and more payment transactions will go back to credit cards, as credit cards plus UPI continue to grow in the market,” Rau said during the company’s Q1FY27 earnings discussion. Data from the Reserve Bank of India’s Payment System Report, December 2025 points to the growth in credit card spending. Credit card spending rose to ₹23.2 Lakh Cr in calendar year 2025, up from ₹8.9 Lakh Cr in 2021. Private banks also strengthened their position in the segment, accounting for 71.1% of outstanding credit cards. Debit card usage, meanwhile, has moved in the opposite direction. Transaction volumes fell 67% between CY2021 and CY2025, as consumers increasingly shifted to UPI for everyday payments. The divergence matters for Apple Pay. While UPI has become a common choice for routine transfers and purchases, credit cards continue to serve consumers looking for credit, rewards and payment flexibility. Apple pay could make card payments more convenient by allowing users to tap their devices at compatible terminals instead of carrying a physical card. However, growth in credit card spending does not automatically translate into demand for Apple Pay. Besides, its reach will also depend on how many consumers are willing to change their existing payment habits. For Apple, the immediate opportunity may be to increase the frequency with which existing users pay by card through its devices. Whether that translates into a meaningful shift in India’s payment mix will depend on wider bank support, merchant acceptance and consumer adoption. A proposed redesign of the federal government’s annual health survey would result in significant undercounting of Americans with intellectual and developmental disabilities, according to advocates for the vulnerable population.
The National Health Interview Survey has historically undercounted people with disabilities, but the changes are a “head-scratcher,” said Katy Neas, CEO of The Arc, an advocacy group. “If we don’t have the government as a trusted source of data, asking questions about real people and what their real experiences are, we’re never going to get better [health outcomes],” she said.
The proposed changes, and its expected impact, runs counter to health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s stated goals of reducing the burden of chronic disease. Adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities face significantly higher rates of chronic conditions such as heart disease, diabetes, and obesity.
In August, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s National Center for Health Statistics proposed an overhaul of the National Health Interview Survey, which has been collecting a broad range of Americans’ health data for researchers and policymakers to make use of since 1957. The overhaul would remove several disability-related questions, even though more than a quarter of Americans have one.
A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services declined to answer questions about why questions tracking certain disabilities were struck from the redesign, but indicated that the changes were driven by a push to lower the cost of data collection.
“It just feels like there’s one hit after another [from the Trump administration] and this particular hit would make it so that we know less about who is disabled in America and what their experiences are, and therefore we don’t have to worry about providing programs or supports for them,” said Jean Hall, disability scholar and professor emerita at the University of Kansas.
With this redesign, roughly 25,000 households will receive a mailed questionnaire — a slight drop from past surveys — with separate questionnaires for children and adults. The adult questionnaire saw the greatest changes. The proposed changes include reducing 482 questions to 150 questions, striking questions about hearing aids, fatigue, cognition, and even mobility supports like wheelchairs and scooters.
The questions used in the survey primarily capture functional disabilities, such as how well a person sees, hears, or walks. Some researchers suggest that past surveys already undercounted people who are deaf or blind or use wheelchairs. But the data gap was particularly glaring for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, potentially missing 75% of the population, according to a recent paper co-authored by CDC statisticians.
“You’re making us choose between bad and worse,” said Scott Landes, a sociology professor at Syracuse University.
Getting better health outcomes data is critical for this population. Although many people in the disability community face serious health disparities, people with a “self-care disability” — meaning they have difficulty dressing themselves or bathing themselves, as people with intellectual and developmental disabilities often do — had the highest mortality rates, according to a 2024 study using National Health Interview Survey data that Landes authored.
“It feels as if our government doesn’t care about the well-being of disabled people, doesn’t care about the well-being of folks with some of the worst health outcomes,” said Landes, who has multiple disabilities, including low vision. “It seems like we would want more information, not less.”
It seems that CDC staff are aware that these changes will impact the agency’s ability to track the disability community.
In 2025, Stephen Blumberg, the director of the CDC division that oversees the survey, published a memo outlining the redesign. In a footnote, he wrote, “It does not provide the desired depth of information on specific topics (e.g., health insurance, functioning and disability, chronic conditions, injury) that are specifically named in our authorizing legislation … and that has been a feature of the questionnaire since 2019.”
Some people in the disability community see this survey redesign as the latest indignity from a Trump administration that has repeatedly targeted disabled people’s health and wellbeing, including laying off scores of federal employees with disabilities or rolling back protections that prioritized people with disabilities living in their communities.
“Data collection isn’t that sexy, but it’s absolutely essential for decision-making, right?” said Neas, of The Arc. “If we don’t have [real information], how are we supposed to make a decision that could either help or not help somebody?”
