The city around it has changed dramatically, but the story of Fort Catholic Girls’ School in Visakhapatnam has unfolded across the decades. Even before the city had its steel plant or naval base, the school witnessed generations of students pass through its classrooms. Today, as the school celebrates its 175th anniversary, its history offers a glimpse into how education for girls in Visakhapatnam has evolved.
“Celebrating 175 years is not something to be taken lightly,” says Sr. Fathima Mary, principal of the school. “It is a significant milestone.” She shares that the jubilee year runs from March 1, 2026, to March 1, 2027, and that the celebrations were formally opened on August 5, as the early months fell in the summer holidays and the examination season. The closing ceremony is planned for January 2027, she adds.
The school’s history began when a small party of sisters from France established a primary school for girls near St. Ann’s Cathedral at Fort area in the Old Town in 1852, which was then described as a little fishing village.
Rich legacy
The school in its jubilee note traces its lineage back to 1650, when Father Jean Pierre Médaille founded the Congregation of the Sisters of St. Joseph at Le Puy in France, dedicated to humble service, particularly the education of the young and the care of those in need. The link to this coast was Father Sebastian Neyret of the Missionaries of St. Francis de Sales (MSFS), who later became a bishop and reached Visakhapatnam in 1846.
He appealed to Mother Aloysia, Superior General of the Sisters of St. Joseph of Annecy, to send sisters to India. The first party of four sisters set out on February 24, 1849, and, after a turbulent journey at sea, arrived at Yanam in Puducherry on December 5.
A second group of six, led by Mother St. John Boissart, sailed from France on June 30, 1851. Yanam was their intended destination, but they landed at Visakhapatnam on December 9, 1851. The school’s history documents this halt as a significant turning point.
The sisters, who were warmly welcomed by Bishop Neyret, met with sights of poverty, illiteracy, and the plight of orphaned children on their arrival. In March 1852, the MSFS entrusted the historic Fort House, near St. Ann’s Cathedral, to them, and it became their first convent in the city. Soon afterwards, they opened the first Catholic primary school for girls at Fort, with an orphanage attached.
Despite limited resources, the effort won the community’s confidence. The school received government recognition in 1856, and in 1884 Father John Mary Clerc acquired a larger building to house the rising numbers.
The years that followed brought several changes. The school received recognition up to Class 7 in 1987, and for Classes 8 to 10 in the following year. The management then decided that the school should follow the Indian Certificate of Secondary Education (ICSE) syllabus.
An inspection was held in April 1992, and the school was affiliated with the Council for the Indian School Certificate Examinations, New Delhi, on October 23, 1996. The first batch had written the examination in 1995 as private candidates.
Unbreakable bonds
“We were the first ICSE batch,” says P. Anuradha Padmavathi, who has been associated with the school for 40 years, first as a student and then as a teacher. She came to the school with her brother, P. Ramchandra Rao, a retired physical training master of the school. Today, she is the head examination coordinator for Visakhapatnam and has served on the ICSE syllabus panel. “It is nothing but a gift from my school,” she says.
For former students, the school holds a more personal significance. Matilda Francis, who joined Class 2 from Waltair Convent and completed her schooling in 1973, says the school was “like a home”. The annual concert and Sports Day, she recalls, carried great warmth. “With about 20 girls in a classroom, the teachers knew each pupil individually. They were very strict, but also caring and loving,” she says.
The day began with moral science, taught as the first period, followed by home science—cooking in the classroom: cakes, gulab jamun and biscuits, she reminisces. “The school’s motto was no labour, no gain,” she adds.
Ms. Francis fondly speaks of a school that did not turn away children for want of means. Girls who could not afford the prescribed uniform were admitted anyway and told to come in whatever appropriate clothing they could manage—a half-sari or a salwar kameez.
The school drew pupils from everywhere, including Sindhis, Punjabis, and Malayalis, and people of different communities. “No girl stopped at the sixth or seventh standard to sit at home,” she says, adding that she and her classmates went on to study at St. Joseph’s College.
Dr. R. Parvathi, a retired Professor of Physiology at Andhra Medical College, studied at the school in the late 1960s. She remembers a town that fell silent at twilight, a large playground across the road where drill was taught, and bougainvillea bushes on either side of the gate against the compound wall. Toffees were sold at a corner of the verandah. “For 10 paise, six toffees! What a deal! They were nothing short of ambrosia in taste,” she writes in the school’s jubilee note. The school, she adds, was “a mini-India, with Anglo-Indian, Malayali, Tamil, Bengali, Gujarati, Sindhi, and Telugu girls.”
For June Gallyot, now the District Sports Development Officer, who joined in the first standard and passed out in 1984–85, sports were an integral part of her school life. She recalls that the school encouraged athletics, hockey, basketball, and handball, and many students went on to compete at the national level.
Gallyot says she played in the under-14 nationals while in fifth standard, as well as in the under-16 school nationals, the sub-junior nationals, and the junior nationals. While still at school, she represented Andhra Pradesh in hockey at the junior national level. She names Cecilia, Sylvia Adams, Judy Fernandes, Lovelyn Bothwick, and Helen Cruze among the hockey players, and recalls Bernadetta and Anita as national-level athletes and Lynette Adams as a basketball player. “The school was a very nurturing ground for sports,” she adds.
She also credits her teachers and says, “Principal Sr. Teresita, though strict, backed the girls’ sporting ambitions, and Mr. Govind, the physical education teacher, helped build the programme.” She recalls that her biology teacher, Linda Hefference, told her, “I strongly believe you can also excel in your studies,” and then proudly adds that she took the science stream and finished in the first class.
For many, the connection to the school continues long after they have left the institution. Begum Iqbal, a member of the 1973 batch and now an advisor at Siva Sivani High School in Marripalem, lists honesty, punctuality, respect for elders, and service among the lessons that have stayed with her.
The Batch of 1977, in a collective tribute written for the jubilee, says that the foundation of who they are today “was laid within the nurturing walls of our school” and credits it with teaching them “how to become better human beings.”
Ms. Padmavathi recalls that years ago, aspirants queued at 4 a.m. for admission forms. New schools now stand on almost every street, yet the school has kept up its strength and its values, with particular stress on discipline, she says. Moral Science still has its place: the timetable reserves periods for it and for catechism, something she calls rare today.
Going strong
Beyond the memories of individuals, the school has also brought together its former students through alumnae groups to stay connected with their alma mater. The FCGS Alumnae Group began in June with the principal’s help and was formally inaugurated on August 5.
Nearly 1,900 former students have been brought together, the principal says, and Ms. Padmavathi adds that two WhatsApp groups spanning the 1950s to 2000 have been created, where members are sharing articles about their classrooms and the city as it was. These will become souvenirs for the closing ceremony, and a magazine is also being planned, she says.
The school has planned a series of celebrations to mark the milestone. After the launch of the celebrations on August 5, a poor-feeding programme was organised on August 19, and the Inter-School Fancy Drill Competition followed on September 19, with city schools and a few from the Araku region taking part. “An Evening with the Alumnae” is set for December 19, and a “Marathon Run for Education” is planned for the same month. Inter-school elocution and other competitions are to follow.
Sr. Mary Daniel, the vice-principal, who first served at the school from 2011 to 2014 and returned in 2025, calls it the first school in India established by the Sisters of St. Joseph, and says the community is “continuing with the same spirit that was entrusted to us by our pioneers”.
The school describes itself as a family “where knowledge is enriched by values, discipline is tempered with compassion, and every student is encouraged to discover her God-given potential”. It has 1,275 students from LKG to Class 10 and 42 teaching and non-teaching staff.

Nagoya – The Olympic Council of Asia (OCA) said on Sunday that a near 20% jump in revenue, strong viewership figures and a slew of world records proved the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games were a success, despite logistical problems plaguing the multisport showpiece.
The number of participants ballooned to 17,000 following a flurry of late entries — around 2,000 more than projected.
With no dedicated Athletes’ Village, participants were housed in a mix of hotels, container-style living units and a cruise ship.
Satoshi Murate, secretary general of the organizing committee, apologized after the unexpected increase strained accommodation and transport networks, prompting complaints from athletes and team officials over cramped rooms and small beds.
However, OCA Director General Husain Al-Musallam pointed to the 54 world, 11 junior world and 89 continental records set at the Games as evidence of effective organization.
“This achievement does not come without the best environment,” the Kuwaiti, who is also president of World Aquatics, told reporters at a news conference on the final day of the Games.
“The athletes cannot perform if they don’t have transportation. The athletes cannot perform if they don’t have good healthcare. The athletes cannot perform if they don’t eat food. Number talks, it’s evidence. We are here to present you the evidence.”
He added that at a time when the Games must be sustainable and financially viable, the Aichi-Nagoya model was one worth copying.
“We are happy to see that there is no big financial burden in the organizing committee, and there is no white elephant staying in Nagoya or any place.”
The revenue increase, measured against the Games in Hangzhou three years ago, came mainly from digital growth and stronger viewership figures, with India’s hockey and cricket matches against Pakistan drawing large TV audiences, OCA officials said.
Al-Musallam also said the Games had provided a moment of unity during a time of geopolitical turmoil.
“When you look to the news, conflict everywhere — in Asia, outside Asia,” he said. “Economic problems everywhere. But look at Asia, how united we are in sport.”
Tayyab Ikram, chairman of the Games Coordination Committee, acknowledged the logistical problems but said they had overcome them by working together.
“There is no Games without challenges,“ said Ikram, who also heads the International Hockey Federation. “In future, we would like to see more sustainable solution, more improvement and innovation ... but without compromising on the athletes’ conditions.”

Good morning. Shocking news of a cockpit stabbing. Graphic footage of bloodied crew members. Mid-air testimony from terrified passengers.
This was the tenor of the heart-in-mouth reporting as the horrifying events unfolded onboard flight FZ 1073 to Tel Aviv: the early morning budget flight that plummeted 17,000ft in under two minutes before the courageous intervention of passengers and crew averted an apparent hijacking, potentially saving the lives of not just the 170+ passengers and crew on board, but many more.
This morning, speculation and conflicting reports are continuing to emerge about this dramatic incident in the sky above the most geopolitically sensitive region in the world.
So how does the Guardian report a swiftly developing story engulfed in misinformation, as accurately and responsibility as possible? I spoke to the reporters, bloggers and editors involved to find out. But first, this morning’s headlines.
Five big stories
- UK politics | Ministers are working up sweeping plans for welfare changes including scrapping a key disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.
- Northern Ireland | Talks aimed at resolving the Drumcree parade dispute have broken up without agreement, with Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant describing the situation as being between a “rock and a hard place”.
- US news | Tennessee’s governor has suspended all executions in the state and ordered an independent inquiry after a botched attempt to put a condemned inmate to death on Wednesday night.
- AI | When prompted, AI chat bots will edit images to remove the hijabs from Muslim women, a violation of one of the world’s most common and visible expressions of faith.
- Europe news | A fast-growing protest by high-school students over long hours, teacher shortages and decaying facilities has escalated into “urban violence”, the French government has warned.
In depth: ‘It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening’
International leaders have rushed to praise Smit Machchhar, the captain of flight FZ 1073. Bleeding heavily from multiple stab wounds, he somehow managed to release his cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to gain entry and overpower his co-pilot turned assailant, an Omani national, who had attacked Machchhar in an apparent attempt to crash the plane. Other crew members were able to stabilise the flight and, just before 11am local time on Wednesday, the Boeing 737 Max made a safe emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. All 174 passengers on board escaped serious injury.
Yesterday, as internationally coordinated investigations continued, the attacker’s motives remained unknown. Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu told Fox News it was “too early to say” if there was any Iranian involvement, while claiming the co-pilot had previously undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was suicidal. Other senior Israeli figures have been more vehement, with ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, describing the incident as a “terror attack”. Two Israeli security sources later told Reuters that they had not yet found Iranian involvement.
Saudi investigators detained the co-pilot upon landing and are cooperating with the United Arab Emirates, the US, Oman and Israel to determine his reasons and potential affiliations. William Christou, a Beirut-based reporter with the Guardian, tells me: “They’re examining whether it’s a terror attack, whether it had any previous planning or prior direction, and if it could be a lone wolf attacker, who was perhaps motivated by anti-Israel hate, but wasn’t necessarily linked to any larger organisation or state.”
‘The story changed moment to moment’
William began drafting his initial report as soon as he woke up to news alerts about a potential hijacking. The Israeli government originally minimised the incident, describing it as a fight between pilots, while another early report suggested the plane had to land because of a fight between Ukrainian and Russian co-pilots.
“I was sifting through so much misinformation,” he says. “The story changed very quickly, and moment to moment.”
Back in the UK, Oliver Holmes was looking at flight trackers. Now based at Guardian HQ, Oliver has reported extensively across the Middle East. What I didn’t know until we spoke is that he once trained as a pilot, which has left him with an enduring interest in aerospace and aviation.
Flight tracking websites have transformed how we report in-air incidents, he tells me. “Before any government has made an announcement, these platforms can tell you something seriously wrong has happened.”
Flight tracking website Flightradar24 recorded the aircraft rapidly descending from its cruising altitude of about 34,000ft to 17,000ft in less than two minutes, just as it reached to the Saudi-Jordanian border. Oliver suggests that investigators will look at whether this sudden and ferocious plunge was why the plane eventually landed with part of its tail missing.
Oliver sent what he could interpret from the tracking data to his international desk editors, who asked him to work on a tick-tock piece – not, for once, a reference to social media, but an old-school print term for an article that sets out the hour-by-hour narrative of an unfolding news story.
“It was very, very tricky to untangle what was happening,” says Oliver. Eventually there came a flood of footage purporting to show images from inside the plane – but was it real? Each clip that the Guardian incorporated into our reporting had to be verified, particularly given the potential for AI-generated fakes. (The Guardian’s head of photography Fiona Shields is fascinating here on how we assess AI images.)
‘Netanyahu was trying to present himself as Mr. Security’
But this wasn’t just an aviation disaster. “It was taking place in this hugely sensitive geopolitical situation,” says Oliver. “The plane landed in Saudi Arabia which does not officially have diplomatic relations with Israel.”
The budget airline itself, flydubai, had by now suspended all its flights to and from Israel, but warned against “premature speculation” while multiple governments, and Israeli officials in particular, were doing just that.
This incident has occurred at a moment of extreme instability across the region, with the strait of Hormuz still closed as a result of the US-Israel assault on Iran and the resurgence of conflict in Yemen. It is also weeks ahead of knife-edge Israeli elections, with polls showing Netanyahu’s current coalition unlikely to meet the threshold needed to form a government but no clear path to power for his rivals.
Just days ago, Netanyahu warned Israel faced an unspecified attack risk during the election period – an assertion greeted with cynicism by political opponents. The Israeli military subsequently confirmed they had no specific intelligence of an anticipated attack. “Most people interpreted that as Netanyahu trying to stir up his base by presenting himself as Mr. Security,” says William.
Nevertheless, Netanyahu’s supporters consider him vindicated. On Thursday, William tells me, the Israeli foreign ministry started briefing diplomats that the flydubai incident was an attempt to drive a further wedge between the UAE and Israel, a relationship already strained after leaks suggesting Netanyahu was personally alerted to the 7 October attacks by the UAE president a week before it took place, something the president has denounced as “an absolute lie”.
‘These stories can be incredibly powerful’
It’s a challenging time to report a story like this, says Taz Ali, who led our live blog which covered the incident unfolding in real-time on Wednesday. “Readers are making connections with what’s happening in the Middle East in general, and you’re trying to answer their questions, first with very scant detail and later with a deluge of information, much of which is proved to be inaccurate.”
Taz, who has a decade of experience in reporting on global events, knows the human drama of a potential hijacking immediately grabs reader’s attention. “Often those stories can be incredibly powerful, involve emergency landings, and sometimes they end in great tragedies”. And with the recent 25th anniversary of 9/11, the incident had an even deeper resonance. “Especially with the anniversary happening so recently, those memories would have been so raw in people’s minds when they came to this story.”

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Eleven-year-old Bodhana Sivanandan has become the youngest ever ‘woman grandmaster’ at the Chess Olympiad in Uzbekistan – while playing on a car booster seat so she could reach the board.
Sivanandan, who lives in Harrow, was taught to play by her father when she was five. Within a year, she was beating him and by eight she had beaten the former British champion Peter Lee. If she reaches a rating of 2,500 in the next 11 months, she will become the world’s youngest ever outright grandmaster.
She fits her chess career around school, but takes everything in her stride. “Now that I’m in secondary school there might be more homework,” she says, “but I should be able to manage”. Her ultimate ambition, she says, is simply to be the best chess player in the world.

Every week, Mint’s Plain Facts section highlights key data releases and announcements to watch in the week ahead. Over the next few days, the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) rate decision, quarterly results from Tata Consultancy Services Ltd (TCS), US trade data, the Nobel Prize announcements and World Mental Health Day will be in focus.
The central bank's Monetary Policy Committee is expected to raise repo rate, which would be the first increase since February 2023, as higher energy prices and the war in West Asia revive inflationary pressures. Tata Consultancy Services will report its September-quarter (Q2) results, kicking off the earnings season for India’s large IT firms. Investors will watch whether big deal wins are finally translating into revenue growth. The US will release its monthly trade data amid a widening deficit, with the full effects of fresh tariffs yet to emerge.
It is also Nobel Prize week, with research on GLP-1 therapies for diabetes and obesity among the possible contenders. In addition, India will observe World Mental Health Day and release its National Mental Health Survey report after a nine-year gap, amid growing mental health concerns among young people.
Policy pivot
The RBI is widely expected to raise the repo rate by 25 basis points to 5.50% on 7 October, its first hike since February 2023. This would mark a reversal from the August meeting, when the MPC held the rate at 5.25% and retained its neutral stance.
Since then, higher crude prices have added to inflation risks, with retail inflation rising to 4.82% in August from 4.45% in July. At the same time, a higher-than-expected GDP growth of 7.8% in April-June has reduced the case for supporting demand through lower rates. The US Federal Reserve’s rate hikes have also added to the case for tighter policy in India by increasing the risk of capital outflows and pressure on the rupee if Indian rates fall behind.
Against this backdrop, most economists expect another 25-basis-point hike in December, taking the repo rate to 5.75% by year-end. Barclays expects two such hikes, saying upward revisions to growth and inflation forecasts “offer a solid backdrop to commence a monetary tightening cycle”.
TCS Q2 results
Tata Consultancy Services will report its September-quarter (Q2) results on 8 October, kicking off the earnings season for India’s large IT firms. The results come as the sector faces weak client spending and pressure from artificial intelligence (AI)-led productivity gains.
TCS’s Q1 revenue growth was only 0.4% sequentially in constant-currency terms, even as its $9.5 billion total contract value included an $800 million AI-led deal with SKF. That followed $12 billion in total contract value (TCV) in the March quarter, among its highest quarterly levels. The disconnect between large deal wins and modest revenue growth will be closely watched by investors, particularly after the Nifty IT index fell 11% in September.
TCS is also undergoing a broader reorganization, having created five new business groups in July as it seeks to adapt its operations to AI-driven changes in client demand. Its Q2 commentary will therefore offer clues on whether large contracts are translating into revenue, how quickly AI business is scaling and whether client spending is improving. Brokerages expect another muted quarter for large IT firms, making management’s outlook a key focus.
Trade watch
The US trade data due on 6 October will offer a detailed look at how trade flows are evolving after more than a year of tariff changes. The country-wise numbers will be key, as the US trade deficit has narrowed sharply with China even as it has widened with several other major suppliers.
In the latest monthly data, the US deficit with China has remained well below early-2025 levels, while deficits with Mexico, Vietnam and Taiwan have grown substantially. Vietnam overtook China in the monthly trade surplus with the US earlier this year, while Mexico has also recorded some of its largest deficits in recent months.
The numbers come as Washington continues to recalibrate tariffs. In July, the US imposed additional 10% or 12.5% duties on goods from 60 economies under new Section 301 measures. At the same time, the US and China agreed last week to reduce tariffs on about $30 billion of goods each, excluding semiconductors. The country-wise data will therefore be important for tracking whether the large US-China trade imbalance remains compressed and how much trade is being accounted for by other major suppliers.
Nobel buzz
Nobel Prize 2026 week kicks off on Monday with the medicine award, setting off a week of announcements that will draw attention to some of the year’s most consequential research and ideas.
Speculation is already building around possible winners, with research on GLP-1 therapies for diabetes and obesity, new gene-editing methods, quantum electronics and optical imaging among the areas attracting attention. In economics, work on monetary policy and digital markets is also in the conversation.
The Nobel committees, however, keep nominations under wraps, leaving only informed speculation about who could make the cut. An analysis of the winners data shows nearly 41% of all Nobel laureates since 1901 have been from the US, although its dominance varies sharply across categories.
American recipients account for 73.7% of economics prizes, 49.4% of medicine, 44.8% of physics and 43.7% of chemistry. In literature and peace, the shares are much lower at 12.2% and 16.1%, respectively. Since 1901, the US has had 415 Nobel laureates, compared with 124 from the UK, 82 from Germany and 67 from France. India has had five.
Minds in distress
World Mental Health Day will be observed on 10 October, drawing attention to mental health as a growing concern, particularly among young people.
Sapien Labs’ 2025 global survey of more than 1 million people across 89 countries found that 41% of those aged 18–34 were distressed or struggling with their mental health, compared with 12% of those aged 55 and above.
India shows a similar age gap. Among Indians aged 18–34 years, 43% reported being distressed or struggling, compared with 12% of those aged 55 and above. Their Mental Health Quotient (MHQ) scores were 33 and 96, respectively.
India ranked eighth among G20 countries and 18th among 89 countries on the share of 18–34-year-olds reporting distress or struggling. Its ranking on the MHQ score for this age group fell 10 places, from 51st in 2024 to 61st in 2025. India is also set to release its National Mental Health Survey report on 10 October, nine years after the first survey in 2015–16. This year’s World Mental Health Day theme is Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change.

Seventy years ago last summer, a group of scientists met at Dartmouth College to discuss a wild idea—that machines might one day be capable of human-like thought processes. One of those scientists, John McCarthy, had suggested a name for the new field: artificial intelligence. It stuck. When you search Google Scholar for “artificial intelligence,” approximately 7,420,000 results appear. The term is utterly ubiquitous. Everyone understands it. Even for people who despise AI, the least of their worries is what we call it.
Well, not everyone. Somehow, President Donald J. Trump developed a distaste for the term, and when he doesn’t like something, he feels free to issue an edict against it. In a September 23 speech at the United Nations, he hinted that he might want to do away with the term “artificial intelligence.” His rant seemed like bluster, even for someone with a penchant for renaming gulfs, lakes, and centers for the arts. Renaming an entire field of study and America’s most pivotal industry? This week, at a White House lunch with top AI leaders, he actually pulled the trigger with an executive order declaring that “artificial intelligence” was now a verboten coinage. Instead, the government will call it “Super Intelligence.” Clearly the president expects the private sector to follow suit.
To their shame, the lords of AI meekly acquiesced. From this point on, they will presumably be known as the lords of SI.
One can’t help but see this as the ultimate presidential flex—for all the executives’ trillions of dollars and all their actual intelligence, the alpha in the room was the guy with the orange skin. Changing a name might seem like a minor matter compared to the enormity of constraining a potentially catastrophic technology. But to this crowd, artificial intelligence is much more than a bunch of letters strung together. It’s their foundation. Their identity. When they were kids reading science fiction books under the covers, the term ignited their imaginations.They built or transformed their companies in service of AI, and it's just about all they’ve talked about for the past four years.
Yet when the president used his lunch soiree to win their approval for his wacky idea to undo 70 years of history, apparently not a single person in the room expressed an objection. Not Jeff Bezos, Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Greg Brockman, Alex Karp, or Elon Musk.
Jacob Weisberg, author of the recent book Profiles in Cowardice: A Study of Collaboration in the Trump Era, views the episode as a classic Trump loyalty test, meant to assess if otherwise powerful people will demean themselves to curry the president’s favor and avoid his wrath. If you pass the loyalty test, you fail the backbone test. “The only way to resist this kind of thing is by acting collectively,” says Weisberg. “If all of those guys had just said, ‘We'll agree to the terms of the self-regulation, but we don't accept [the name change], what would he have done?”
Instead, because of the lamb-like silence of the billionaires, Trump could claim that those leaders actively blessed his idea. When a reporter in the post-lunch press gaggle mentioned AI agents, he corrected her, saying, “The name has been changed by the biggest, the, smartest, the greatest people anywhere in the world.” Really?
Even using the magic of, uh, superintelligent systems like ChatGPT or Gemini, I could not find a single instance of any one of those great people previously politicking that the term artificial intelligence should be put to rest. Satya Nadella did once say that he would have preferred that AI had been called “different intelligence,” but that hasn’t dissuaded him from repeatedly using the term. And while it’s true that Mark Zuckerberg recently established a Superintelligence Lab, his company persistently pushes a product called Meta AI to its billions of users and sells what it calls AI glasses.
I asked Google, Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, and xAI whether they were going to change instances of AI in their product names, research papers, and communications. My query to the latter two was whether they were going to change their company names to get in sync with the presidential order. As I write this, none of them have gotten back to me.
My bet is that they will do the minimum to avoid presidential ire, while trying to run out the clock until the next administration puts this bizarre idea out of its misery. It’s been suggested that the executives actually welcome a rebranding of what has become a toxic term. I’m skeptical of that, especially since the president’s mandated replacement, “super intelligence,” is a hell of a lot scarier than the original term.
From a scientific perspective the change also makes no sense. No less an expert than Nick Bostrom, the philosopher who popularized the term superintelligence in an eponymous book, seems baffled by the idea. Superintelligence, he explained to me in an email, “refers specifically to systems that greatly surpass all the best human brains. ‘AI’ has referred to a much broader category of systems, which includes, for example, email spam filters, spell checkers, simple navigation systems, early LLMs, and the chess engines of the ’70s that didn’t yet match the best human chess players. It seems awkward to refer to these as ‘superintelligent.’”
So what is the president’s reason for demanding the change, besides because he can? In his UN speech, he said he didn’t like the term because “the word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence fake. And it is not fake.” What is fake, he said after the White House lunch, is the term “artificial intelligence.” “It’s a fake word, it’s not good, an inappropriate term.” You don’t need to be a psychologist to see how this impulse might be associated with his decision to bounce CNN, Politico, and MSNow from the White House, because he perceives their news as “fake.”
Still, the leap that equates artificial with fake doesn’t track. In 1956, McCarthy used it to distinguish between human intelligence and the machine version of intelligence. The problem isn’t that the term leads people to regard AI’s output as fake—in fact, it’s so real that we human beings often can’t tell whether we’re dealing with an AI model or a human. Mandating that the distinction be explicit, with watermarks and labels, should be one element of the AI regulation that the White House seems allergic to.
As Weisberg notes, it’s very much in character for Trump to make a crazy edict like this one. What’s disturbing is the glaring lack of character from the executives who didn’t push back. They left with the prize of self-regulation instead of strict oversight, but not with their dignity.
But failure to defend the freedom to refer to artificial intelligence as artificial intelligence (as California governor Gavin Newsom decreed in his own Trump-trolling executive order) casts doubt on even that agreement. Making voluntary standards effective requires considerable fortitude, as prioritizing safety can be at odds with financial and competitive factors. Yet we are being asked to trust these supposedly independent corporate giants who nodded like bobbleheads while a technologically unschooled crank-in-chief demanded they abandon the term at the center of their lives and livelihoods. Inappropriate, and fake.

Many of Netflix’s biggest critically acclaimed hits have been the products of its multiyear production deals with noted directors like David Fincher and Shawn Levy. In the past few weeks, though, the streamer has brought some of those partnerships to an end in a way that feels indicative of a larger strategic shift. With rival studios Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery on the verge of a megamerger that will reshape the entertainment landscape, Netflix is clearly thinking about how it can continue to hold its own in the ongoing streaming wars. But as the company charts its path forward, its plan to court subscribers might not put so much emphasis on big-name moviemakers.
Netflix is pivoting away from prestige
A series of high-profile director exits makes it seem like the streamer is rethinking its strategy for success.
On Thursday, Netflix shared that its production deal with David Fincher is coming to an end after six years. First announced in 2020, the partnership — which was originally scheduled to last for four years — gave Netflix the exclusive streaming rights to Fincher’s then-upcoming projects like his Herman J. Mankiewicz biographical drama, Mank. With Fincher having previously executive produced original series for Netflix like House of Cards and Mindhunter, the deal seemed to be a sign of Netflix having faith in his ability to keep audiences riveted.
At the time, Fincher joked that Mank’s critical reception and box office performance before it began streaming would determine what kinds of projects Netflix would let him make. Critics generally praised the film and it was ultimately nominated for 10 Academy Awards — two of which it won. But during Mank’s three-week theatrical run, it only made around $100,000 against a $25 million budget, and once it hit Netflix, it only managed to spend a single day on the streamer’s list of its top 10 most-watched movies (in last place). Though Fincher’s next project for Netflix — 2023’s The Killer — debuted at No. 1 on the chart, the project’s $452,000 box office gross against a $175 million budget made it another financial dud. And with The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth set to show in theaters for two weeks before it hits Netflix on December 23rd, the film could be another example of Fincher delivering a movie that isn’t exactly a huge monetary win for the streamer.
Fincher’s track record with Netflix is somewhat similar to director Shawn Levy’s. After almost a decade of working exclusively with the streamer on projects including Stranger Things, The Adam Project, and Shadow and Bone, Levy announced last month that he had signed a new overall production deal with Disney. Levy — whose directing career began with a number of Disney Channel series — framed his decision to leave Netflix as a kind of homecoming. But it was hard not to see his jumping ship as having been prompted by the way Stranger Things’ final season left audiences and critics disappointed.
The same was true when Stranger Things co-creators Matt and Ross Duffer announced last August 2025 that they were leaving Netflix for a four-year TV / film production deal with Paramount. The brothers could still have a hand in future Stranger Things projects, and their next series — The Boroughs — debuted on Netflix this past May to respectable numbers. But just one month after its release, The Boroughs was canceled.
In a recent interview with The Hollywood Reporter, Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said that Levy’s and the Duffer Brothers’ departures were driven by the filmmakers’ desire to spend more time working on feature-length projects. Levy’s Star Wars: Starfighter is slated to premiere next May, and the Duffers’ untitled Paramount film will debut sometime in 2028. Though Sarandos framed the filmmakers’ exits in a positive light, they’re part of a larger trend that makes it seem like Netflix is moving on from its era of signing filmmakers to lengthy deals. The company has also parted ways with Marriage Story writer-director Noah Baumbach, whose other Netflix projects, like White Noise and Jay Kelly, failed to make much of a splash.
Netflix is still banking on some directors being a major draw. The streamer’s production deal with Guillermo del Toro is ongoing, and it is treating the first of Greta Gerwig’s upcoming Narnia films as a proper event that will spend seven weeks in theaters before it begins streaming. And while Rian Johnson is taking a break after fulfilling the obligations of his $450 million deal to produce two Knives Out sequels, he could very well come back to Netflix with a plan to make more.
Going forward, it seems like Netflix’s main game plan is to put an increased focus on producing lower-budget series, live events, and sports programming. The company obviously isn’t giving up on movies — Gerwig will direct another Narnia feature and there’s a KPop Demon Hunters sequel on the way — but episodic content has been shown to be much more effective at keeping subscribers coming back.
This is why we’ve recently seen Netflix hyping up strange reality shows like Squid Game: The Challenge, Wonka’s The Golden Ticket, and The New Stanford Prison Experiment. None of those shows exactly come across as must-see TV like the horror series Mike Flanagan produced for Netflix before Amazon poached him in 2022. But that may not matter to Netflix as long as people are watching. After years of spending millions of dollars to produce movies that did not always result in consistent subscriber growth, Netflix appears to be entering a period of making more conservative bets. That might make the service feel a little less premium than it has in the past, but it could help it live to fight another day.

In a major push to make legal services more accessible, transparent and citizen-friendly, Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo today launched the ‘e-Nyaya Sarathi’ web portal and mobile application, providing citizens a unified digital gateway to legal information, judicial resources and government legal services.
The event was attended by senior officers including ACS PWD; Principal Secretary, Home; Principal Secretary, Culture Department; Registrar General, High Court of J&K and Ladakh; Sr. AAG Mohsin Qadri; Member Secretary, J&K State Legal Services Authority; Commissioner Secretary, H&UDD; Commissioner Secretary, Social Welfare; Commissioner Secretary, Science & Technology; Commissioner Secretary, Law; Secretary, RDD; Secretary, Legislative Assembly and other officers of the Department of Law, Justice & Parliamentary Affairs. Members of the technical development team also attended the launch event.
Developed by the Department of Law, Justice & Parliamentary Affairs, the platform brings multiple legal services under one roof, enabling citizens to access essential legal information and services anytime and from anywhere. The initiative seeks to simplify the public’s interaction with the legal system and replace conventional bureaucratic hurdles with a more transparent and digitally accessible service delivery mechanism.
Speaking at the launch, the Chief Secretary described the initiative as a significant step towards citizen-centric digital governance, emphasising that legal services should be accessible, reliable and easy to navigate. He said that e-Nyaya Sarathi would help bridge the gap between citizens and legal institutions by bringing critical legal resources directly to their fingertips.
Giving details about the platform, Commissioner Secretary, Law, Achal Sethi, revealed that the portal offers a range of services, including legal aid and pro-bono assistance, a central repository of Acts, Rules, Judgments and Government Notifications, in addition to facilities like ‘Search Your Case’ and ‘Find My Court’ and dedicated modules for Women & Child Development and Advocate Related Matters.
Adding a technology-driven dimension to the initiative, the platform also features an AI-powered chatbot to guide users through legal queries and assist them in navigating various services available on the portal. The integrated framework is aimed at making access to legal information simpler and more responsive, particularly for citizens seeking quick and reliable information.
Moreover, it was also apprised that the e-Nyaya Sarathi portal is now available at www.enyayasarathi.jk.gov.in, while its mobile application can be downloaded from the Google Play Store and Apple App Store.

More than one billion people globally have experienced traumatic dental injuries, making it a significant yet often overlooked public health concern with potentially long-term consequences for oral health and quality of life, AIIMS experts said.
Observed annually on September 21, Global Dental and Oral Trauma Day is supported by the Indian Society of Dental Traumatology to raise awareness about prevention, timely management and equitable access to care for traumatic dental injuries.
A study published in the Dental Traumatology journal in 2018 reported that more than one billion living people worldwide have experienced traumatic dental injuries (TDI).
Researchers highlighted that TDI represents a neglected condition of substantial global burden, noting that, if included among the world’s most frequent acute and chronic diseases and injuries, it could rank fifth in terms of prevalence.
"Dental trauma can happen anytime, anywhere and to anyone. It can have both immediate and long-term consequences. It is not simply a broken or displaced tooth. For many patients, a traumatic injury can initiate a lifelong cycle of treatment, follow-up and rehabilitation," said Ajay Logani, professor of endodontics at the Centre for Dental Education and Research (CDER), AIIMS Delhi.
Dr. Logani stressed the emphasis has to shift from treating trauma only after it occurs to preventing injuries. The public should also know what to do immediately after an accident, he said.
Falls, road traffic accidents, sports injuries, domestic violence and everyday accidents are among the common causes of dental trauma.
Children are particularly vulnerable to dental trauma, and the first few minutes after an injury can be critical, Nitesh Tewari, professor of paediatric dentistry at CDER, AIIMS Delhi said.
"For a child, a traumatic injury can affect not only the tooth but also facial development, appearance, psychological trauma and quality of life. Parents should know that dental trauma requires timely assessment and should not be dismissed as 'just a broken tooth'," said Dr. Tewari.
Experts said awareness about immediate first aid remains inadequate, despite the fact that the response in the first few minutes can influence the outcome of an injured tooth.
"The first person to handle a dental injury may be a parent, school teacher, sports coach, or even a bystander. A few simple fact -- what to do with an injured tooth, what not to do, how to transport it and where to seek care -- can potentially make a lifelong difference," said Sidhartha Sharma, associate professor of endodontics, CDER, AIIMS, Delhi.
Dental trauma education therefore needs to move beyond dental clinics and into schools, sports facilities, emergency services and the community, Dr. Sharma underlined.
"Teachers, coaches and parents should be equipped with basic information on recognising serious injuries and taking appropriate immediate steps. This can help reduce avoidable complications and improve the chances of preserving an injured tooth," he stated.
Dr. Tewari said prevention should include safer sports practices, use of appropriate protective equipment, road safety measures and greater awareness of risks in children and young people.
Experts stressed that dental trauma should not be viewed merely as a cosmetic problem, as injuries can have long-term consequences for oral health, function, appearance and quality of life.
The observance carries a message extending beyond the dental profession: prevent injuries where possible, know the correct first-aid response when trauma occurs, and ensure timely access to evidence-based care.

What does FDM stand for in 3D printing and how does it work?
FDM printers are incredibly common.
3D printers are all the rage, with professionals and hobbyists alike deploying the technology to print everything from razor parts to entire homes. Fused Deposition Modeling (FDM) is one of the most popular types of printing technologies and is ideal for those looking to break into the world of 3D creations. FDM printers build three-dimensional objects through layers of thermoplastic filaments that fuse together to form a cohesive object.
FDM prints often begin with a computer-aided design file, or CAD, that is translated into instructions your printer can understand. Next, the printer funnels spools of filament through a heated nozzle. The printer then layers this melted filament upon the build plate according to the CAD's designated pathways. Once that initial layer is complete, the printer will lay the next layer atop the model. The process continues in this way for hours or even days, depending on the printer used, the print settings, and the model size and complexity.
FDM printers are compatible with a variety of non-resin print materials. One of the most popular filaments is polylactic acid (PLA), an inexpensive biodegradable polymer plastic that has become a favorite of 3D printing fans for its ability to be printed at low temperatures, making it ideal for beginners. Another option is PETG, or polyethylene terephthalate glycol, a durable plastic often used in water bottles and praised for its glossy surface and print accuracy. If you are searching for a tough, sturdy material to use with your FDM printer, acrylonitrile butadiene styrene (ABS) is a great option. For higher-quality prints, you can opt for thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU) or nylon filament. You can also use wood and metal filaments as well as high-density polyethylene (HDPE) and polyethylene co-trimethylene terephthalate (PETT). These possibilities make FDM printers fairly flexible, providing a range of color and material options. Some materials call for high temperatures that most beginner printers can't accommodate, and others require special nozzles or proper ventilation to eliminate fumes. So if you're hoping to print in a specific material, make sure your printer and space can handle it safely.
Pros and cons of FDM printers
FDM printers provide a quick turnaround, often taking anywhere from minutes to a few hours to finish a small print. The speed of the printing process makes them popular for prototyping, allowing engineers and other users to quickly and efficiently test and rework their designs. Moreover, the ability to use cheaper filaments helps make FDM prints fairly inexpensive. Add low equipment costs and minimal maintenance, and FDM printers are ideal for those looking for budget proof-of-concept or parts production.
But FDM printers have their limits. For one thing, FDM models are low resolution, meaning it is more difficult for them to produce the finer details of a print. Due to the relative thickness of each layer, FDM prints struggle to produce prints with small, intricate parts. As such, Apple probably won't use an FDM printer to make your next phone or watch — it opts for precise, industrial-grade printers that can print titanium. Warping is another common issue with FDM printers, as the filament often cools at different rates, causing uneven pressure to warp your designs. Because these printers lay down layers horizontally, FDM prints are also prone to breaking when facing acute pressure on the z-axis and shouldn't be relied on to make strong, sturdy pieces. A common FDM printing technique known as infilling, in which the model's interior prints with lower density to save time and filament, also makes them prone to breaking.
Good beginner FDM printers are affordable, reliable and somewhat low maintenance. However, if you want to create sturdy, precise structures, you may need to invest in a higher-end printer from a highly-regarded brand like Prusa Research, Bambu Lab or Ultimaker. For ultimate precision, consider stereolithography (SLA) and digital light processing (DLP) printers, which deploy light to cure layers of resin, creating models with fine details and smooth surfaces. Selective laser sintering, or SLS, deploys lasers to fuse nylon powders together and is ideal for creating sturdy, support-free structures. Multi Jet Fusion (MJF), direct metal laser sintering and selective laser melting are other worthy options, depending on your intended use case and materials.

‘We will not stop’: Students’ blunt message as school protests spread across France
More than 5,000 people have been arrested across the country this week as student demonstrations about overcrowded classrooms and school conditions turned violent. Jessie Williams reports

This week France has been rocked by nationwide student protests that turned violent, with thousands arrested, more than 100 schools damaged and dozens of teachers injured.
By midday on Friday, the ministry of national education announced that 564 schools have been affected. Dramatic pictures show fires in the streets, barricaded entrance gates and youths clashing with riot police. At least four hundred high schools, roughly one in 10, were closed due to the unrest.
The protests began last week over frustrations about school conditions with peaceful blockades of secondary schools around Paris.
They soon morphed into wider discontent with the government and spread across the country, after France's main union for secondary school students called for a nationwide blockade. University students and other supporters also joined the demonstrations.
French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told TF1 TV on Friday that police had arrested a total of around 5,000 people, most of them teenagers, since Monday.
Justice Minister Darmanin had earlier told RTL radio that parents of those damaging property should pay reparations.
So far 65 school staff have been injured, including 40 headteachers, and there has been significant damage to facilities, with classes now taking place remotely, French education minister Édouard Geffray told French media on Friday. More than 300 police officers have also been injured in the chaos.
Students claim there has also been police violence against the protestors, with officers in riot gear using batons and tear gas.
In Tours, a city in central France, a 16-year-old student was injured on Wednesday outside his secondary school after being hit in the eye with an LBD-40 – Lanceur de Balles de Défense or Defence Ball Launcher. The controversial riot gun used by French police has caused severe injuries at previous protests.
A 19-year-old university student in Tours and member of the student union Fédération Syndicale Étudiante, Martin, has been taking part in the demonstrations over the last few days. He told The Independent the injured boy was in a “critical state” and that he could be blind for the rest of his life.
“The police have shown an extreme brutality, hitting students and using excessive amounts of tear gas,” Martin (not his real name) said.
“Apparently high-schoolers are too young to be listened to but old enough to be repressed.
“The situation shows how the government is scared of the movement, they're struggling to contain the anger of the youth and the working class. Despite their best efforts to scare us we will not stop.”
Another student, aged 14, lost multiple teeth and suffered severe facial injuries in Val-d’Oise after being hit in the jaw by a tear gas grenade launcher. His mother told French newspaper Le Parisien that his mouth had been “torn apart”.
French authorities have opened multiple investigations to examine the accusations of police violence.
Amnesty International said the reports of secondary school students being assaulted are “extremely alarming”.
“Many are minors, children. They must be protected, not beaten with batons,” the human rights organisation posted on X on Thursday evening.
“Let's be clear: since the beginning of the blockades, there have also been acts of violence on the part of certain protesters. They are not acceptable. But even in these situations, including in the event of an arrest, the use of force must remain proportionate.”
The mayor of Tours, Emmanuel Denis, appealed for calm on Thursday and said the student movement’s demands are “legitimate”. He also said he was going to meet with their representatives on Friday.
Some parents also support the protests. Vincent Martin joined his daughter outside Helene Boucher high school, in Paris, saying students were ‘fundamentally right to demand ... better learning conditions”.
The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, the student union which orchestrated the blockades, said they want authorities to address the “shortage of teachers and staff, dilapidated high schools, overcrowded classrooms, and overloaded schedules.”
Martin said that one particular policy university students are protesting against is a new measure which will see the end of university fee waivers for non-European students.
“The end goal [of the government] is to the increase the fees for all students, because of the lack of budget for universities. The recent governments have been putting less and less money in public services such as schools and universities and hospitals while investing in the army and big companies,” he said.
Another university student in Tours, 21 year-old Vinnie, said that they are watching their universities “fall apart in real time” due to unrelenting budget cuts.
“What the government should do is very simple,” he said. “Unlock funding. Every year money is being pulled from every public service imaginable, every year everyone in public service is asked to do more with less.”
The education minister claimed on Friday that the student protest movement had been “hijacked” and that teachers had told him that “the people in front of me were not my students.”
A number of schools have been set on fire over the last few days, including the Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes in the west of the country, while staff at Victor Hugo high school in the southern city of Marseille were splashed with petrol as protesters reportedly filled containers.
French Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin has said there is an “active and violent minority” taking part in the protests.
"We're not entirely sure that they are even high school students themselves," he told France's RTL radio.
"We have gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance. When people target buses and set schools on fire, it is no longer simply a protest issue," he added.
Vinnie says that as with every protest movement there are some casseurs or vandals who try to cause destruction, which the students do not want.
“I have personally witnessed on the first day of the protests a small group of young men who were not students bring cardboard to the front of a blocked high school to light it up.”
“They don't all have the same motivation, some just want to destroy, some think it really is the only way to protest even when the protesters most involved disagree and some are actually opponents of the movements with goals of destabilising it,” he added.
Martin said that he has seen people who aren’t students join the movement “because what we're asking for is much larger than just about universities”.
“We're calling for a large movement uniting high-schoolers, students and workers, because we must stay strong together, especially against police violence and repression.”
He said that they have seen solidarity across all generations, notably from the former gilets jaunes protestors. He said he was looking forward to 17 October, when there is a large demonstration planned by the ‘yellow vest’ group.
Before that there is another big student protest planned for Tuesday 6 October. “In the mean time, we'll keep protesting in the university and beyond,” he added.
The demonstrations come at a tense time for the country as next year’s presidential election approaches.
The French prime minister and far-right politicians, like Marine Le Pen, presidential candidate for National Rally, have blamed the hard left for igniting the protests, particularly La France Insoumise (LFI) party.
LFI leader and presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has attended some of the demonstrations, said he was in favour of non-violent protests, but argued that blaming the left would not solve the issues behind the demonstrations.

Editor’s note, October 4, 8 am ET: We’re bringing you some of our best-loved Your Mileage May Vary columns while Sigal Samuel is on parental leave. The one below was originally published last year.
When does trying to have a healthier baby become eugenics-y?
New genetic testing offers us the chance to create superbabies. It can come with unintended consequences.
This unconventional advice column offers you a unique framework for thinking through moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism: the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. Submit your own question here.
My partner and I did IVF recently and luckily we ended up with several embryos. One of those will be implanted in me so I hopefully get pregnant. But which one?
My fertility clinic is encouraging me to do PGT-A testing, which would screen for things like Down syndrome and would also let me see the sex of each embryo so I could potentially choose whichever I want. (And to be honest, I really want a girl!) I’m also hearing about these new companies that can test embryos for all kinds of things — like how smart the kid might be, how tall they’ll get, and whether they’ll have a lower chance of getting breast cancer, diabetes, mental illness, stuff like that.
I don’t know how to feel about any of this. On the one hand, it feels weirdly eugenics-y to do so much tinkering with embryos, and I can’t help feeling a little pressured into overmedicalizing everything with these expensive tests. But then again, if I could do something to make my baby healthier and happier, don’t I kind of have to do everything in my power? What does a parent owe their child?
Dear Expecting,
This is such an exciting — and also confusing — time. You’re about to have your first kid, and that comes with all sorts of fears and insecurities and hopes and dreams. You want to do the right thing — no, the best thing! — for your child. It’s a beautiful impulse. Unfortunately, it makes it easy for companies to prey on you.
So let me walk you through what these companies can and can’t really provide. After we talk about the science, we can talk about the ethics.
The simpler test you mentioned, PGT-A, has been around since the 1990s. It can indeed screen for conditions like Down syndrome and let you see the sex of each embryo. Mind you, that doesn’t predict what gender your child will ultimately end up identifying with — more on that soon.
The newer testing you mentioned is called polygenic testing. The conditions it screens for are complex ones, influenced by thousands of genes. We’re talking about everything from breast cancer to depression. Some companies even offer screenings not for disease prevention, but for genetic enhancement — so you can select for a taller kid or a kid with higher IQ.
Polygenic testing companies claim to predict each embryo’s risk for each condition, and the potential reduction of risk you’ll get if you choose one embryo over another. As the statistical geneticist Sasha Gusev explains, it’s very, very easy to be misled by this claim. If the company claims to lower absolute risk of Type 2 diabetes by 12 percent, you might think this means, “The chance of my kid ever developing diabetes just went down by 12 percent — great!” But really what it means is that, all else equal, a kid who would’ve developed diabetes is likely now at the high end of pre-diabetes instead, or just develops diabetes a few years later. The same holds true for other conditions, like breast cancer. Sure, if your kid is going to develop diabetes or breast cancer, you’d rather they develop it later — but it’s not the bill of perfect health customers might imagine.
“Typical risk reduction estimates tend to exploit statistical assumptions to overstate their benefits and lead to confusion,” Gusev writes.

It’s also important to note that there’s a difference between a physical disease like cancer, which is straightforwardly and universally negative, and a complex mental health condition like depression. For one thing, polygenic scores don’t perform as well in psychiatry, as the psychologist Eric Turkheimer notes. Plus, most mental health conditions come in mild to moderate to severe forms, and it’s not clear that we should want to get rid of mild or moderate manifestations.
“Sure, it would be nice if no one ever got depressed, but what would that actually mean?” Turkheimer writes. “People are going to be sad, and the most modern models of psychiatric disorders view most of them as extremes on continuous dimensions of normal behavior. I don’t think we want some kind of genetic version of Soma.”
To give a personal example: I have generalized anxiety with some obsessive tendencies. Is that a major pain in the butt sometimes? You bet. But if I could wave a magic wand and get rid of it, would I? No. In my experience, this trait is linked to another trait I deeply value: my creativity. The same thing that propels me down rabbit holes of worry also propels me down rabbit holes of getting super curious about some topic, researching it into the wee hours of the morning, and then writing a novel or children’s book about it.
That brings me to one other scientific issue: pleiotropy. It’s a fancy term for a simple truth, which is that genes can have an effect on more than one trait. When it comes to behavioral polygenic testing, we actually know very little about which genes cause what — a gene that’s correlated with depression or anxiety may also be correlated with a bunch of other things. So, if everyone were to start selecting embryos to try to protect their kids from depression or anxiety, what would happen? We don’t know!
Pleiotropy is a scientific issue, but it’s also a moral issue, because in trying to protect your kid from a negative outcome, you could also be accidentally barring them from a positive one.
And that’s just the tip of the moral iceberg.
Another issue is the potential psychological harm that can result from commodifying our kids — treating them like consumer objects with selectable parts. Let’s say you use polygenic testing to try to select for high IQ. Even if the company’s predictor is right 80 percent of the time, that means it’s wrong 20 percent of the time. What happens if it’s wrong about your kid, and they end up with a low IQ instead of a high one? How will your kid feel? Unless you hide the truth from them, they’ll know that they are not what you wanted, that they failed to live up to the vision you went out of your way to chase.
The same goes for sex selection via good old PGT-A. I know you really want a girl. But what would happen if you select for a girl, and then your child grows up and turns out to be trans? They may feel an extra sense that they’re letting you down by not conforming to the gender expectations you had for them.
Then there are the ethical questions around unequal access. Polygenic testing isn’t cheap. (One company, Orchid, charges $2,500 per screened embryo. Test 10 embryos and that’ll cost you $25,000.) So, at least in the short term, that raises the specter of entrenching a caste system, where the gap between rich and poor expands dramatically as the rich get smarter and stronger.
Technologies tend to get cheaper over time, so maybe everyone will ultimately be able to afford polygenic testing. But that raises another problem: implicit coercion. If more and more of us make ourselves smarter and stronger, we may create a society in which everyone feels pressure to alter their child’s biology — even if they don’t want to. To refuse embryo selection would mean to put a child at a huge professional disadvantage, or to face moral condemnation for making “suboptimal” kids when optimization is possible. Society may no longer offer health insurance benefits or accommodations for kids with disabilities (or even non-enhanced IQ), reasoning that “it was the parents’ choice.”
Some philosophers, like Julian Savalescu, already argue that parents have a “moral obligation to create children with the best chance of the best life.” Polygenic testing companies love that argument; Orchid founder Noor Siddiqui tells parents that “the responsible decision” is to “protect their children” from disease, using language like, “What if you could have stopped it...but chose not to?” And we generally live in a culture that’s obsessed with optimization.
So it’s no wonder that you find yourself asking, “If I could do something to make my baby healthier and happier, don’t I kind of have to do everything in my power?”
It’s a view that will be very appealing to utilitarians, who believe the right action is the action that maximizes well-being or happiness. But maximizing principles can be dangerous. If we’re laser-focused on maximizing one value, however noble it may be, that can lead us to overlook a host of other important values. Think about diversity, for example; polygenic testing could lead to a less diverse world.
And it’s not even clear how to maximize well-being given that each embryo will have some downsides: How would you choose between one embryo with a slightly elevated risk for schizophrenia, another with a moderately elevated risk for cancer, and a third with a high risk for Alzheimer’s? You’d have to decide how to rank the importance of each condition, which would require a dizzying bit of moral math: How much weight do you put on the longevity associated with each condition, how much on patient-reported quality of life for each condition, and how much on your own ability to cope with each — and society’s ability (which will change over the years)? Plus, even if the screening does end up optimizing life for your individual child, it could have negative effects on the population level, for the reasons we covered above.
As the Nobel laureate Herbert Simon pointed out, many problems contain way more variables and way too much uncertainty for maximizing along a single axis to be feasible or even desirable. So it often makes sense to just go with an option that’s “good enough.” He coined the term “satisficing” — a portmanteau of “satisfying” and “sufficing” — to describe opting for this good enough choice.
What would satisficing look like in the context of embryos? If there’s a very serious condition that runs in your family — like Tay-Sachs or the BRCA mutation that markedly increases cancer risk — then I do think there’s a strong case for screening for that. These conditions are debilitating and can lead to early death. Nobody wants them. Genetic testing that lets us prevent them is an awesome gift.
Then there are conditions that can include suffering, like autism, but can also be very compatible with a happy life. Mental health conditions in particular are heavily socially constructed — a lot of the associated suffering comes about because society constructs a certain biological reality as a problem and doesn’t support the people who have it. In these cases, if you want to give your child a “good enough” or even “optimized” life, remember that you don’t have to achieve that by biological means; working to change the social environment can be just as important, and it doesn’t carry the societal risks associated with polygenic testing.
Ultimately, when considering what counts as a “good enough” life, each parent will draw the line in a slightly different place. And there’s a part of that that can’t be boiled down to objective facts about disease, because this is also about how well-resourced the parent feels — emotionally, socially, and financially — to deal with a certain condition. What feels manageable to one parent may feel crushingly hard to another.
So, I can’t tell you exactly which screenings to do and which to forgo. What I do want to tell you is to resist being bullied or shamed by others, especially those with a profit incentive to push you in a certain direction.
As the epidemiologist Abby Lippman has noted, genetic testing is supposed to offer parents more choice, but it too often has the opposite effect. When someone like Orchid’s Siddiqui says about a disease, “What if you could have stopped it...but chose not to?” — well, that language preys on parents’ worst fears and insecurities. It holds parents hostage while pretending to be giving them more autonomy.
You are nobody’s hostage. You are a moral agent free to look at the many different relevant factors, weigh them all in the balance, and then make the choice that works well enough for your family.
Bonus: What I’m reading
- Silicon Valley is obsessed with IQ, so it’s no surprise that tech execs there are using polygenic testing in hopes of creating supersmart babies. This article shows the kind of mental pretzels customers get into when trying to figure out whether to select the embryo with the highest predicted IQ or that with the lowest risk of disorders. One couple asks: “How much additional risk of ADHD cancels out against 10 extra IQ points?”
- Rereading “The Last Children of Down Syndrome,” Sarah Zhang’s 2020 Atlantic feature on prenatal testing, it struck me that when people think “prenatal testing,” Down syndrome is often the first condition that comes to mind, even though it’s not the most severe or straightforwardly negative (it’s compatible with a happy life). It’s just that Down syndrome was easy to test for, so we started testing for it early. I wonder if that built up the condition as a bogeyman in the expectant parent’s imagination — if the fact that we could screen for it shaped the public’s perception of Down syndrome as something that should be screened for and potentially screened out.
- One trait that many people assume we should select for is a great memory. But I highly recommend the short story “Funes the Memorious” by Jorge Luis Borges. It’s a reminder that having too good a memory is not always a benefit.

Humphries to face Price in World Grand Prix final

World number two Luke Humphries secured his place in the World Grand Prix final with a 5-3 victory over James Wade.
Humphries averaged 96.92 and threw 10 180s as he reached the final for the fourth successive time.
The 31-year-old Englishman will face Welshman Gerwyn Price on Sunday evening in Leicester after he beat Nathan Aspinall in the other semi-final.
"I've got to do it again because there's so many major finals I've let slip. Gezzy [Price] is playing well but if I play like that again, it's going to be a cracking game and I hope it is," Humphries told Sky Sports.
"To make four Grand Prix finals on the trot is super special. It's history for myself and I'm proud of that but unless I pick that trophy up, unfortunately that history doesn't mean anything."
Humphries, who won this title in 2023 but has lost in the past two finals, took the opening set of the semi-final but Wade produced a brilliant 141 checkout en route to drawing level.
The pair exchanged the next two sets before Humphries took control of the contest to move 4-2 ahead.
Wade refused to go quietly and pulled one back to keep the match alive but Humphries held his nerve in the eighth set to seal victory on double top.
In the other semi-final, Price beat a spirited Aspinall 5-2.
The Welshman took a three-set lead as Aspinall struggled to reproduce the form that had seen him average 105.15 in his quarter-final win over Ryan Joyce.
Aspinall briefly rallied and produced a superb 132 checkout - the highest of the match - to get a set on the board.
The 35-year-old then threatened to turn the match around when he reduced the deficit to one set at 3-2.
However, Price regained his composure and closed out the next two sets without reply to secure his place in the final.
Price said he was "frustrated" by Aspinall's antics during the match as he interacted with a partisan crowd at the Mattioli Arena.
"I'm glad to come through the game. Nathan was complaining about the crowd, but they were on his side," Price said.
"He's performing a little bit on stage. I'm great friends with Nathan, but take it on the chin sometimes when you're losing."

Zimbabwe tycoon Wicknell Chivayo and wife killed in helicopter crash
- Published
Prominent Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife have been killed in a helicopter crash that left six people dead, his family have confirmed.
The helicopter came down in the Marondera rural area, about 70km (43 miles) east of the capital, Harare, on Wednesday evening. Police said all six people on board died.
Family spokesperson Herbert Chivayo confirmed the deaths of the businessman and his wife Lucy Muteke to state broadcaster ZBC, saying the family was devastated by the tragedy.
Chivayo was known for his lavish lifestyle, close ties to some African presidents and lucrative government contracts that had repeatedly attracted scrutiny.
He had denied allegations of wrongdoing linked to his business dealings.
Police spokesperson Commissioner Paul Nyathi said the aircraft crashed at about 17:00 local time (15:00 GMT) and had six occupants, but authorities did not immediately identify all those on board. Two of the six were pilots, according to government officials.
ZBC reported that the group was travelling from Gandami in Chikomba, where Chivayo and his wife were building a rural home, when the helicopter crashed at Kudenga Farm about 40 minutes after take-off.
"We are at a loss for words after the tragic news," the family spokesperson, told the ZBC.
The cause of the crash was not immediately known, and police said investigations were under way. Emergency services were sent to the scene on Wednesday evening.

At least 17, mostly Catholic pilgrims, killed in crash on highway in Kenya
A road crash in Kenya has killed seventeen people, most of them pilgrims heading to a prayer site
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Seventeen people, most of them pilgrims on the way to a prayer site, were killed in a road crash Saturday involving multiple vehicles on the highway to the Kenyan coastal city of Mombasa.
The incident in the Salama area happened after midnight when a truck driver tried and failed to overtake another truck. That caused a collision with vehicles including a van carrying pilgrims, according to local police.
The driver and 16 passengers, most of them women, in that van died at the scene, police said.
The pilgrims were going to a prayer site in Nakuru County, west of the Kenyan capital of Nairobi, said Martin Kivuva, Archbishop of the Catholic Archdiocese of Mombasa.
The primate said in a statement that he and others were “saddened with lots of grief” over the deaths. “Let us pray for the repose of their souls as we pray for their families,” he said.
Road accidents are a problem across Africa. The accidents often are blamed on poorly maintained vehicles, excess speed and poor road conditions.

The LAFC said the commission has been formed in response to growing concerns raised by citizens regarding the "design, implementation, and consequences" of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral roll undertaken by the Election Commission of India.
