The Jammu and Kashmir Agriculture Production Department has received a proposal seeking transfer of more than 1,500 kanals of its land at Allowpora in Shopian to SKUAST-K for establishing a Centre of Excellence, with the proposal subsequently forwarded to the University for examination.
The issue was raised by MLA Shopian Shabir Ahmad Kullay through an Un-Starred Question in the Legislative Assembly, asking whether the government had received a proposal for utilisation/transfer of more than 1,100 kanals of land belonging to the Allowpora Seed Farm to SKUAST-K for establishment of a Centre of Excellence in Horticulture, including production of quality planting material, seed multiplication and seed development.
In its written reply, the Agriculture Production Department said it had received a D.O. communication from Kullay dated July 24, 2026, regarding the transfer of more than 1,500 kanals of Agriculture Department land at Allowpora to SKUAST-K for establishment of a Centre of Excellence for production of quality planting material.
“The proposal was received in the Agriculture Production Department and was forwarded to SKUAST-K for examination,” said the department.
According to the reply, SKUAST-K, in its communication dated August 19, 2026, proposed establishment of a Centre of Excellence for certified disease-free planting material, elite clonal rootstock multiplication and breeder/foundation seed production, besides diploma and short-term certificate courses, demonstration orchards, mother blocks, polyhouses and farmer-training facilities.
SKUAST-K has also proposed developing Allowpora as a regional scientific and skill hub for horticulture in South Kashmir, according to the reply.
However, in response to a separate question on whether a substantial portion of the farm was lying vacant or underutilised, the department said the 64.885-hectare farm was largely being utilised.
Of the total area, 58.90 hectares are presently being utilised for seed multiplication activities involving maize, oats, pulses, potato and floriculture seedlings, it said.
The department further said 20 hectares had been identified for establishment of a Saffron Corm Nursery, for which Rs 4.03 crore had been approved by the Government of India under PM-RKVY.
A Centre of Excellence for Precision Farming is also being established under the Capex Budget/SASCI scheme during the current financial year, with an allocation of Rs 4.96 crore, the reply said.
“In view of the above, it is not a fact that a substantial portion of the Seed Multiplication Farm, Allowpora is lying vacant or underutilized,” the department stated.
On whether the land would subsequently be transferred to SKUAST-K, the department said that since the land was already being utilised for various ongoing departmental activities, including seed multiplication, establishment of a Saffron Corm Nursery and a Centre of Excellence for Precision Farming, “transfer of the Allowpora Seed Farm land to SKUAST-K for the proposed purpose is not under consideration.”

The Best E-Readers That Aren’t a Kindle
Featured in this article
There are no fewer than 10 e-readers in my house at any given time, and I wouldn't have it any other way.
While nothing replaces the feel of a physical book, I usually reach for one of my e-readers as part of my nighttime routine. To me, these tablets are the easiest way to read because they grant immediate access to whatever is in my TBR pile at a given time. Whether it's a library book through the Libby app or a series I'm buying up because I can't wait any longer for a copy to be available, whatever I want to read, I can access it immediately on my e-reader.
It’s also convenient that e-readers (short for “ebook readers”) can store thousands of books at a time. These slim devices use E Ink screens to give text a paperlike appearance. They’re also designed to strain your eyes less than other digital devices, like your phone or computer screen.
And while many strongly associate Kindle with e-reader, you don't have to turn to Amazon for the best device. In fact, my all-around favorite isn't a Kindle at all, and there are plenty of other models to shop from that let you steer clear of the tech behemoth and its recent price increases. These are all my favorite e-readers that won't require you to support Amazon to enjoy the experience.
Updated October 2026: I've moved all Kindle recommendations (and details about the newly announced Kindles) out of our top picks to focus entirely on non-Amazon e-readers. There are also new sections for what I'm testing next and e-reader accessories compatible with my picks.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Comparing Our Favorite E-Readers
| Model | Display | Resolution | Color? | Storage | Weight | Battery Life and Charging | 
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Kobo Libra Colour | 7 inches, adjustable front light | 300 ppi, black-and-white; 150 ppi, color | Yes | 32 GB | 7.03 ounces | Up to 40 days, USB-C charging | 
| Kobo Clara Colour | 6 inches, auto-adjusting warm light | 300 ppi, black-and-white; 150 ppi, color | Yes | 16 GB | 6 ounces | Up to 42 days, USB-C charging | 
| Boox Go 6 (Gen II) | 6 inches, adjustable warm light | 300 ppi | No | 32 GB | 5.6 ounces | Unspecified battery life, USB-C charging | 
| Xteink X4 Pro | 4.3 inches, adjustable warm light | 219 ppi | No | 16 GB | 2.5 ounces | Unspecified battery life, USB-C charging | 
Honorable Mentions
Below, find a few more e-readers I like but don't necessarily love as much as my top picks.
Boox Go 7 ($270) and Boox Go Color 7 ($290): Boox is known for its wide range of e-paper tablets, including the Boox Go 6 (Gen II) I recommend above. If you're looking for something a little larger with a similar Android-based experience, the Go 7 and Go Color 7 are both solid choices. There are page-turner buttons, and it's a nice square shape that's easy to hold and use. If you, like me, don't use color features a ton, it's worth saving the extra money on the black-and-white model. Regardless, it's great that the price difference between the two models isn't steep.
Boox Palma 2 for $250: This is a fun, pocket-sized device, with fingerprint recognition, a faster CPU, and a newer version of Android than previous models. Former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So loved using it with the Kindle app, but she wishes it cost less. Boox recently announced the Palma 3 is coming out (though it doesn't have a confirmed launch date) which explains why it's been unavailable for so long. The Palma 3 is next on my testing list, but if you want a similar device you can purchase now, the Boox Palma 2 Pro ($400) is available with a higher price tag, but color screen.
Nook GlowLight 4 Plus for $200: The 4 Plus is the only waterproof Nook in the lineup, and it has the biggest screen at 7.8 inches, along with 32 GB of storage. It also has physical page-turn buttons and a headphone jack for listening to audiobooks (you can also connect wireless earbuds via Bluetooth). Unfortunately, it was often slower than my Kindle and tended to freeze. While the large library has cheap and even free ebooks, it's not as good of a selection as Kindle Unlimited. The process of getting a book from the library on a Nook is also frustrating. You'll need to download either Adobe Digital Editions or Android File Transfer before physically connecting the device to your computer and then transferring the files.
Nook 9-inch Lenovo Tablet for $150: If you mainly read cookbooks or other color-intensive materials, and you want a dedicated reader, you might want to consider this affordable tablet from Nook and Lenovo, which has the Nook app built in. It's a tablet rather than an e-paper device like the rest of the gadgets in this guide, so you'll lose the E Ink screen and the distraction-free nature of an e-reader. You can at least turn off notifications while in certain apps, which I recommend doing for the Nook app. It uses Android 13 OS, and it's not built for heavy work, like video or photo editing.
Xteink X4 for $69 and X3 for $69: These are similar to the Xteink X4 Pro above when it comes to the app and basic capabilities, but you'll lose out on the touchscreen, home button, and front light. Instead, there are more buttons, providing a Tamagotchi-like experience as you tap them to go back and forth between menus and pages of your reading material. The X3 is super small, with just a 3.7-inch screen that fits on the back of my iPhone 16 Pro, and it has stronger magnets to put itself into place. But the standard X4 is more comfortable to read on than the X3 since it's larger (and won't require quite as many page turns, though it'll still need a lot) with a 4.3-inch screen, like the X4 Pro above.
What I’m Testing Next
There have been several new e-readers announced, mainly new models from Boox like the Palma 3 and Picco, that I'll be reading my latest books on this fall, which will include R.F. Kuang's Babel and the latest ACOTAR book, along with an alarmingly long list of suspended holds in my Libby app that I really need to work on. Here's what I'll be testing next:
Boox Palma 3 for $320: Boox's popular Palma devices are made to be mobile e-paper screens, and are a popular choice as a smaller e-reader. The new Palma 3 has been announced after months of the Palma 2 being out of stock, and it promises a 6.13-inch screen, dual-tone front light, a rear camera, dual microphones, and a customizable smart button. There's no timeline yet for its launch, but I'm hoping we see it available before the end of the year.
Boox Picco for $100: This miniature e-reader will have a tiny 3.97-inch screen and be Boox's smallest e-reader to date. The Boox Picco isn't the smallest e-reader ever—Xteink still holds that crown—but promises a different experience to Boox's other e-readers and e-paper devices by focusing on Boox's new Tiles app and productivity tools. Boox says it's the first of its Tiles ecosystem, so I'm keeping an eye out for more launches within that line. The Picco is currently available for preorder and is due to ship in October.
Boox Note Mini C for $550: When Boox announced the Palma 3, it also announced its new e-paper tablet, the Boox Note Air6 C, and a miniaturized version, the Boox Note Mini C. The Mini C has a smaller 8.52-inch screen that's more ideal for reading than the larger tablet, and I'm curious how it compares to both the Palma 3 and the Boox Go line.
The 2026 Kindles: Amazon has announced new versions of all three of its main e-readers, with a 2026 version of Kindle ($150), Kindle Paperwhite ($200), and Kindle Colorsoft ($290) coming out this fall, plus a Kids version ($180+) of each of these new models. There are now aluminum-backed versions of all three, though the Paperwhite and Colorsoft have it as part of the higher-end Signature Edition that comes with a few more features. I'll be testing and will add my top pick to this guide for reference, but this guide will focus more on non-Kindle e-readers going forward.
What If I Want a Kindle?
Maybe you've read this guide and decided a Kindle is best for you. That's fine! Kindle is my longest-used ecosystem and it's plenty convenient, especially if you already have ebooks purchased through Amazon. While I have an entire guide dedicated to shopping for a Kindle, here's a quick overview of my top picks (and other models you might spot).
Also, Kindle does have new versions of the base Kindle, Kindle Paperwhite, Kindle Colorsoft, and its Kids versions of each model coming out. You might want to wait and see if you prefer the newest versions to these, and I'll be testing them soon to see how they compare to past Kindles and other e-readers. Kindle also raised the prices of most of its e-readers at the end of August, and the new models match that pricing.
Kindle Colorsoft Signature for $320 and Kindle Colorsoft ($290): The Kindle Colorsoft Signature is Amazon's first Kindle with a color screen. I do like the Colorsoft if you read books with illustrations or heavily annotate your e-books, but the Kobo devices I recommend can do the same thing for cheaper.
Kindle Scribe (3rd Gen, 2025) for $500 and Kindle Scribe Colorsoft for $630: The latest Kindle Scribe arrived in December 2025 with a color version. It also has a new exterior design that does away with the single thicker side and standardizes bezels and frames across all sizes, and a lot of AI features. The older Kindle Scribe (2nd Gen) is still my preferred option if you want a Kindle e-reader that doubles as a digital notebook.
Kindle Scribe Without Front Light for $430: This is the third and final installment of Amazon's latest generation of Kindle Scribes. It's similar to the third-gen Kindle Scribe above, but it removes the front light and wireless charging. If you want a cheaper Kindle Scribe, I still prefer the second-generation model, though you'll lose out on AI reading features and the ability to connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive.
Great E-Reader Accessories
Looking to jazz up your new e-reader? Here are some of my favorite accessories to pair with my favorite non-Kindle e-readers. It's a tougher buy to find—since Kindles are so popular, most cases and accessories are made with those models in mind, but there are options out there for the rest of the e-reader world, too. Here's what I've tested and liked for my e-readers.
FAQs
How Do You Get Ebooks?
Ebooks can be cheap, but as with regular books, the cost can add up if you're a big reader. To keep costs low, take advantage of your library card and check out ebooks instantly from the comfort of your home. We have a detailed guide that explains How to Get Free Kindle Books With Your Library Card, but the short version is that most libraries distribute books via OverDrive. You can access these books a few ways: through Kindle or directly from OverDrive with a Kobo, or you can download the Libby app. These ebooks are automatically removed from your device and returned to the library when they're due.
Each e-reader's own book service varies in quality. My favorite is Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month, which includes millions of titles, including audiobooks and magazines. Amazon's Prime Reading also offers a handful of free books every month, which is good to know if you already have a Prime account. You can even lend books to friends and family for a short while (or have them share a book with you). For more details on each option, check out our guide to the Best Ebook Subscription Services here.
What File Formats Do E-Readers Support?
The most widely used format is EPUB, which works natively with all the e-readers in this guide except for Kindle—technically. You can still upload EPUB files to your Kindle, but you'll have to use the “Send to Kindle” feature (through Amazon, your email, or the Kindle app) to convert it to Amazon's proprietary format called AZW. (Newer Kindles support AZW3 and KFX, specifically). Other formats that will work with these e-readers include PDF, TXT, HTML, DOC, and DOCX.
Can I Install Apps on an E-Reader?
Kindle, Kobo, and Nook all use proprietary operating systems that don't allow you to install third-party apps. The Boox, on the other hand, runs Android (mainly Android 11 and newer). That means you can use it to download any apps available in the Google Play Store or side-load apps from your computer.
Do You Need an E-Reader? What About a Phone or Tablet?
You don't have to buy a separate device to read ebooks. Smartphones and tablets are perfect for this purpose. You can use Amazon's Kindle app to read ebooks (iOS, Android) and download OverDrive's Libby app (iOS, Android) for library-book access. However, the E Ink screens found in e-readers are just nicer to look at. I also like that these devices are one-trick ponies; there are no distracting notifications or social media feeds ripe for doomscrolling.
If you'd still rather have one smart device you can use for reading and other purposes, take a look at our Best Tablets and Best iPads guides for recommendations.
What About a Digital Notebook?
I've tried just about every digital notebook on the market; these devices are designed for handwritten notes on an E Ink screen. E-readers with that capability usually still prioritize reading, though there are plenty of models I like that can do both. The Kobo Libra Colour is my favorite option for annotating books, and it can double as a small digital notebook. If you want a larger option, check out my full guide to every digital notebook I've tested.
How Do I Test E-Readers?
The most important step I take when testing e-readers is to read on them! I spend hours reading books acquired in a variety of formats, including books I purchased directly from each brand's store, downloaded from local libraries via OverDrive/Libby, and PDFs acquired for free from God knows where.
In the process, I evaluate battery life, brightness, performance lag, screen responsiveness, and text sharpness. I check for extra tools, like whether the tablet in question accommodates accessories like a stylus. I also note features like waterproofing, annotation capability, and access to exclusive subscription services.

'Enough is enough': Women protest after string of murders near Johannesburg
Runners gathered in South Africa to pay tribute to Elizabeth Moselakgomo after her body was found east of Johannesburg.
She is one of nine women found in the Kempton Park area, since July.
The jogger, known as "Tsontso", went missing during a routine run.
Runners organised an event in city of Centurion to honour her and defend women's right to run freely.
"This is for her - we just want to live and go running and come back home without having to think that it may be one of us", said Nonhle Mpohlo.
In Cape Town, people gathered in a vigil to honour the victims and called on the government to act.
The police have since set up a task team to investigate the murders and have urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone "particularly in isolated areas".

The ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a powerful 2-in-1 Windows tablet for creators, with a sharp 3K OLED display, strong Snapdragon X2 Elite performance, excellent battery life, and full desktop apps. However, its high price, weak touch experience, and some ARM app limits hold it back.
People still debate why the tablet category exists. Some people believe they can replace laptops, while others see them as glorified smartphones with bigger screens.
I agree with both statements, as tablets are extremely portable. They are thinner, lighter, and easy to carry anywhere, and they can also convert into a laptop on the go, with the added advantage of a stylus for note-taking, sketching, or even marking up PDF files. Not to mention, they’re also great for watching movies and other entertainment.
But they are extremely limited in software capabilities despite hardware that can run fully native desktop applications. But Apple’s software limitations are also a deal-breaker for many. On the other hand, it runs the full Windows 11 OS on tablets without limitations. But it isn’t optimized for tablets.
For most people, or for creative work, the iPad is the first choice. But I recently got a chance to review the ASUS ProArt PZ14, which is a 2-in-1, tablet-first Windows device designed for creative work that is portable and offers an excellent OLED screen, solid performance, solid battery life, and is capable of running fully native applications, and comes with a keyboard and a pen out of the box for all your creative work and note-taking. I have been using the ASUS ProArt PZ14 for the past two weeks. In this detailed review, you will find out whether the ASUS ProArt PZ14 breaks tradition by doing things differently. Or is it just another tablet in the debate? Let’s find out.
Table of Contents
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Design and Build: Lightweight and practical, but the design is an acquired taste
ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a tablet-first Windows PC. The keyboard detaches completely from the tablet, and all components, including the processor, sit on the back of the display.
As a result, it carries all the weight. ASUS includes a magnetic case in the box that you can attach to the back of the tablet to use as a stand and to hold the ASUS Pen 3.0. I wouldn’t recommend attaching it without the case because, while you’re holding the tablet, the magnets are not strong, and it can easily fall off, which it did. But hopefully, thanks to the build, it survived accidental falls.
Thanks to the matte finish, the back of the tablet isn’t a fingerprint magnet either, but stains are visible if you look at it a certain way, and they wipe off easily with any standard cloth.
An ASUS design choice on the back can be a hit or a miss depending on your perception. Right off the bat, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 doesn’t look like a tablet. It felt like a very niche tablet designed for a specific purpose. It has a single rear camera. Thankfully, there is no bump, and it comes with a lot of stickers, which indicates it is more than just a tablet.
You get ProArt branding at the top in the center. Overall, the fit and finish are solid, but the looks can be hit or miss based on your perception. I wish it looked more like a tablet.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with dual speakers, with one on each side The power button is on the top in landscape and on the right in portrait, which is convenient for landscape use but less convenient in portrait.
And you can find the volume-down and volume-up keys on the right as well, making it easy to control with your right hand. The SD Express 7.0 card reader and two USB4 Type-C ports are on the left side.
The look changes entirely from the front. It comes with a 14-inch 3K OLED display with a 144Hz refresh rate and minimal bezels, similar to the iPad Pro, but wider overall. At the top, you get an 8MP IR front camera with no privacy shutter.
The tablet weighs just 790 grams, making it lightweight and easy to use, but the larger display is hard to hold for long periods when using it as a tablet. The tablet has rounded corners on the back, which make it easy to hold for long periods, and the textured finish on the front half provides better grip. The matte finish makes it less slippery.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 also has an IP52 rating. ASUS officially claims that it is tested to MIL-STD-810Hstandards . So you have the military standard, but don’t drop-test it like other laptops.
When I first held the ASUS ProArt PZ14, the back finish felt like plastic. However, ASUS claims the chassis uses an aluminum alloy. The sides feel very solid.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Display: A gorgeous 3K OLED made for creators
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 display is one of the best-looking, and if there is one reason to choose this tablet, it’s this display. Whether you are a business user, a graphic designer, or someone who wants to casually watch movies and play games, it delivers a great viewing experience.
The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with a 14-inch 3K OLED display. It comes with a 144Hz refresh rate for a smooth experience. The 14-inch display is a sweet spot. On your desk and used with the keyboard, it is a sweet spot and a perfect middle ground between the 13.6-inch and 15-inch laptops, but it feels very large in hand when you hold it and use it as a tablet.
The OLED display is one of the best I have seen on a tablet, matching premium, high-quality displays with 100% DCI-P3 color gamut and PANTONE validation. The blacks look deeper, and colors are represented very accurately, making it a good choice for designers and photographers who want to edit images accurately. The touch response is also fast, but Windows is the one to blame. It makes interactions less convenient, which I will cover more in the OS section.
The display also supports a stylus. ASUS includes the ASUS Pen 3.0 out of the box. Writing and drawing on the display feels faster and more fluid. But because of the glass finish, it feels slippery while taking notes. You can apply a matte-finish screen protector for a better typing and note-taking experience on this tablet. After the iPad Pro, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 provided the best note-taking experience, even better than the Apple Pencil in some cases.
ASUS, being extra generous, added the pencil-scribble sound while taking notes. Well, thank you, ASUS, for looking at those tiny details to enhance the user experience. But it sounds so artificial.
Next, this 16:10 aspect ratio is perfect for watching content. I watched three episodes of Better Call Saul (season 4) on Netflix, and the experience was better on the ASUS ProArt PZ14 than on my iPad Pro.
With 3K resolution and 243 pixels per inch, it is also one of the sharper displays. It looks sharp even when you zoom in on minor editing details.
However, if you often read web pages, blogs, or docs on this tablet, while it looks fine when using it in laptop mode, as soon as you pick it up and use it as a tablet, you are holding a massive tablet, and 16:10 feels very wide when you put it close to your eyes, which means you need to move your head to read the text. Also, portrait mode isn’t appealing either, with that 14-inch massive screen making it hard to read and scroll. With this large form factor, using it with a single hand is almost impossible. You can try if you want.
Overall, the display is one of the ASUS ProArt PZ14’s biggest strengths. Whether you’re watching content, editing, or designing, everything looks incredible on this massive screen.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Keyboard and Trackpad: Laptop-like typing, but better suited for a desk
ASUS also provides a keyboard out of the box. Unlike with the iPads, which you need to buy separately and are also expensive. Fortunately, the typing experience is as good as on thin-and-light laptops. However, if you’re used to mechanical keyboards or longer key travel, you might find it hard to type at first, but you can eventually get used to it.
Also, there are a few things that you need to know: the keyboard completely detaches from the tablet, which means it doesn’t have a hinge that holds the display and keyboard together. A small magnetic attachment on the bottom of the tablet connects to the keyboard.
You can just hover the tablet over the keyboard, and it attaches magnetically. However, the magnet isn’t as strong, so it can also detach easily. And since there is no strong hinge holding the keyboard and tablet together, you cannot place it on your lap and type on uneven surfaces, where the tablet takes the full weight and could tip back.
Fortunately, ASUS also included a full touchpad, and again, it’s almost like using the touchpad on a regular thin-and-light laptop. The speakers are very loud. They have rich sound. There is no headphone jack.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Specs and Performance: Snapdragon X2 Elite delivers plenty of power
Under the hood, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 runs on the Snapdragon X2 Elite X2E-88-100 processor. My variant has 32GB of LPDDR5X RAM and a 1TB M.2 NVMe PCIe 4.0 SSD. That’s a large configuration by current standards.
Qualcomm is trying too hard to become a name for its PC processors after it conquered Android phones. The processor offers very solid performance. Tasks feel faster, and it compares with some of the best in the industry right now, including the Intel Core Ultra 7 series and Ryzen AI Max+, among others. In comparison, in Geekbench single- and multicore scores, Snapdragon X2 Elite has produced very good numbers.
You can see the benchmarks of the ASUS ProART PZ14 from third-party testers.
The tablet also offers a dedicated performance mode that provides extra power when needed. This results in smooth day-to-day performance; whether it’s opening apps, touch interactions, gaming, or uploading files, everything feels smoother on this tablet
The built-in SD Express 7.0 card reader delivers strong sequential read and write rates, including 730 MB/s sequential read speeds. So if you are a creator who copies videos and files to and from the tablet, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 won’t consume your time.
However, while the processor is solid in CPU performance, the GPU is still weaker on Snapdragon processors, and the same is true of the Snapdragon X2 Elite. It comes with an integrated Qualcomm Adreno GPU. That performs decently; however, it’s not as good as Radeon or Intel Arc GPUs.
Because of this, it might not excel at higher-end applications or even gaming. It can offer decent performance, but not top-tier.
While the GPU might not be the most powerful, the NPU performance is significantly better. The Snapdragon X2 Elite includes a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU rated up to 80 TOPS. This lets you offload a few AI tasks locally for better performance. For instance, if you are a creator, you can run AI models locally.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 also comes with a fan. Under load, the tablet tends to get a bit warmer, and the fan kicks in.
Overall performance is impressive for such a thin and light device. Daily use, such as browsing the web, watching movies and shows, and running a few high-end software applications, feels faster and handles every task without breaking a sweat.
Moreover, while compatibility with popular ARM apps on Windows has improved over the years since Qualcomm announced Snapdragon X Elite, some older programs and plug-ins still aren’t natively compatible with Windows on ARM, and some run via x86 emulation.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Battery Life: Easily lasts an entire workday
The battery life is incredible on this tablet, and Windows on ARM has already proved it. The ASUS ProArt PZ14 comes with a 75Wh four-cell lithium-ion battery. ASUS also offers a 68W USB-C charger in the box.
Even in performance and non-performance modes, battery life stays consistent. On average, I got around 12 to 14 hours of battery life with light to medium use and about 10-11 hours with heavy use, including gaming. With light use, just using the browser, I even got two days of battery life.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Windows 11 Experience: Full desktop software, but a poor tablet interface
Now let’s address the elephant in the room: Windows 11. I would say having Windows 11 is both the biggest strength and also the biggest weakness of this tablet. The ASUS ProArt PZ14 ships with Windows 11 or Windows 11 Pro out of the box, depending on the configuration. My unit comes with Windows 11 Home.
No matter which version you are on, Windows 11 isn’t optimized for the touch interface. In Windows 11 touch mode, it feels like a desktop and has very small buttons, menus, and toolbars.
If you primarily want to use the ASUS ProArt PZ14 as a tablet, and you’re used to iPad Pro-type interaction, you will definitely find it hard to use day-to-day. Fortunately, using the pen minimizes this. However, if you primarily use your hands, keep that in mind.
Also, this tablet has a core Windows problem. The biggest problem is the annoying Windows updates. They are still an issue even after Microsoft promised to reduce those interruptions. Unfortunately, I haven’t been able to set up the tablet from scratch because it’s a pre-owned unit, and someone else has already set it up for me, so I was saved from dealing with lengthy setup processes.
Another big limitation of Windows running on ARM is limited app support. While app support has improved significantly since I first reviewed the Snapdragon X Elite laptop, most popular applications are now natively available on Windows on ARM, but a few legacy applications still use Prism emulation, which affects performance and misses core features. However, if you mainly want to use it as a creator tablet, most creator apps are natively available on Windows, and a few games are also natively supported on Windows on ARM.
But the biggest advantage is that, since it runs on Windows, you can run full desktop-level software without any limitations. You can multitask with multiple windows. If you want better multitasking and portability at the same time, this is something you should get.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Ports and Connectivity: USB4 and SD Express are useful, but some ports are missing
Despite its tablet form factor, ASUS has included decent port support on the ASUS ProArt PZ14. It comes with two USB 4.0 Gen 3 Type-C ports that support up to 40 Gbps, which can be used to connect external SSDs, docks, and even an external monitor.
It also includes an SD Express 7.0 card reader, which is excellent for transferring video and photos from your cameras. There’s no HDMI port, which I miss, but you can easily work around it with external peripherals. The camera quality is also good, much better than the webcam quality on other ASUS laptops I have tested. The rear camera is also decent in good lighting, which you can use to scan documents quickly. The tablet also supports Wi-Fi 7 or Bluetooth 6.0.
ASUS ProArt PZ14 Verdict: A powerful Windows tablet for creators on the go
So, that is everything that you need to know about ASUS ProArt PZ14. With its excellent display, tablet-first design, portability, battery life, and solid performance, it is a great pick for anyone who wants a powerful tablet on the go.
The 3K OLED display also makes it a great option for entertainment whenever you want to watch content or even play games. Overall, the ASUS ProArt PZ14 is a great option for a creator-first experience and for anyone who values portability and wants an all-in-one tablet that can replace a conventional laptop and a tablet at home. However, the tablet costs Rs 2,69,990 for 32GB LPDDR5X RAM. It is expensive.

Illinois catering business ordered to shut down after high school football team got sick before homecoming
The unlicensed caterer served a taco bar with fajita chicken, seasoned taco beef, cheese, flour taco shells, cheesy pepper beans, cilantro corn rice and pico de gallo or salsa

Illinois health officials shut down an unlicensed, home-based caterer after a high school football team dinner sickened at least 45 people and forced the school to postpone its homecoming game.
The Rock Island High School football team’s Sept. 24 dinner was held around 5:30 p.m. in the school cafeteria, where about 75 players, coaches and parents were served a taco bar catered by Sunshine and Spice. The Moline-based home operation is about 10 minutes from Rock Island, local health officials confirmed to KWQC.
The menu included fajita chicken, seasoned taco beef, cheese, flour taco shells, cheesy pepper beans, cilantro corn rice and pico de gallo or salsa.
By about 11 p.m., 23 players, five coaches and three parents were experiencing vomiting and diarrhea, football team trainer Kyle Hoffmann reported to Rock Island City Health Inspector Andy Swartz the following afternoon, the news outlet reports.
At least 45 people total eventually reported illness. None required hospitalization, though one player saw a doctor. Most recovered within 24 hours.
The high school postponed its homecoming game until all affected players had been symptom-free for at least 24 hours, as advised by the Rock Island County Health Department and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, per KWQC.
During the investigation, Swartz met with Sunshine and Spice owner Joshua Harris and found that the home-based catering operation was not licensed or food-safety certified. Swartz ordered the business to stop operating immediately and gave Harris information on how to obtain the required licenses, according to the news outlet.
Harris told Swartz that the meal’s ingredients were purchased from Walmart in Moline, Spotted Apron in Geneseo and farmers markets in Davenport and Coal Valley.
Harris said in a statement to KWQC that Sunshine and Spice was sorry for what happened and denied intentionally providing unsafe food.
“First, Sunshine and Spice wants to sincerely apologize and send even more prayers to anyone affected by last week's Rock Island Football Team Meal. We provided a taco bar-style potluck before the team was dismissed to prepare for their Homecoming Game,” Harris said.
He further explained how he prepared the food.
“All of the food purchased from Walmart on Wednesday Night was fully cooked (beef, chicken, rice). We put all of the leftovers in plastic bags provided by the team parents for anyone to take home. We have cooked for numerous parents of the team/school in the past and have no reason EVER to provide a sub-standard meal or purposely attempt any tampering shenanigans.”
Harris continued, “We are saddened by this whole situation. We have been working side by side with the Rock Island County Health Department and Rock Island City/County Law Enforcement Agencies to be a part of their continuing investigations. Again, we want to extend our deepest apologies and continued prayers to those affected.”
Health officials said the investigation remains ongoing and that leftover food from the dinner was seized for testing.
Swartz worked with county health officials and the Illinois Department of Public Health to survey people who became sick. According to the results, obtained by KWQC, the most commonly consumed items were cilantro corn rice, fajita chicken, cheese and flour taco shells:
- 92 percent consumed cilantro corn rice
- 88 percent consumed fajita chicken
- 88 percent consumed cheese
- 88 percent consumed flour taco shells
- 83 percent consumed seasoned taco beef
- 58 percent consumed cheesy pepper beans
- 58 percent consumed pico/salsa
Rock Island lost their Friday game to East Moline United Football, making their 2026 record 0-7.

Ali Brigginshaw's NRLW career ends in defeat but her legend will be eternal
As the merciless Roosters ran away with the NRLW grand final it was hard to think of a less fitting end for a career as legendary as Ali Brigginshaw's.
The 36-year old and the rest of the Broncos were helpless to stop a Tricolour massacre that ended 30-6 as the Roosters earned a manner of vengeance for last year's grand final defeat to complete a perfect season.
It was over by half-time because Brisbane did not pick up their guns, let alone fire a shot.
They completed just three sets in the entire first half as they drowned under a sea of Roosters points.
From the 15th minute to the 34th minute they only touched the ball to kick it off, drop it or be driven back into the in-goal.
For almost 20 minutes they did not play the ball once, with the Roosters running in six straight tries and between the 15th and 39th minutes they did not complete a set.
All of the weapons that have made Brigginshaw great — her skill, her guile, her cunning and class as a playmaker, which she has carried through her 17 years at the top of women's rugby league — were blunted before she even got a chance to use them.
She did manage to sneak through for a line-break in the second half, a 35 minutes of football that felt like it only happened because it had to happen so we could get to the end, as she held up a pass before hitting a gap with exquisite timing, but had no support.
In the end, her last day was destroyed by a monster of a team who are without question the best NRLW side ever assembled.
They are the culmination of a transformation in women's rugby league that Brigginshaw herself helped bring about through a career that stretches all the way back to the primordial days of women's rugby league.
When she started playing for Queensland and Australia in 2009 her Broncos teammate Reegan Hicks was three years old.
Club football was ad hoc, pathways barely existed and the NRL may as well have been a different universe. For the committed few who kept the women's game going it was day-to-day as much as it was hand-to-mouth.
Interstate matches were not played under the State of Origin banner and were held at suburban grounds in front of tiny crowds.
A World Cup final was the only game that could get on television and even then, only if the network was feeling generous.
Footage of those days leading up to the first NRLW season in 2018 is grainy and hard to find. Even basic details of matches — things like team lists, scorers and attendances — aren't always easy to track down.
In a very literal sense of the word, it's almost prehistoric.
Today it's a new world, a world Brigginshaw helped create as the premiere footballer and one of the biggest stars of the transitional era and into the early NRLW years.
For proof, look no further than the words of Julia Robinson, who has played with Brigginshaw ever since that first Broncos season.
“She’s a true leader, on and off the field, she’s the heart of the Broncos, she’s going to be this legacy that carries on for generations," Robinson told ABC Sport.
“She’s going to be missed, missed by the team, missed by everyone but she’ll still be around and make a big impact on the rugby league community.”
“I’m so grateful I had the opportunity to play with Ali, she’s one of the greats.”
Brigginshaw was a pioneer and a trail blazer, who set a new mark and standard for others to aspire to and acted as a legend for an entire game to believe in.
To see the Tricolours complete their perfect season is to see the end product of that belief. Today's players are bigger, faster, stronger and more skilful.
They play together for longer and the improvements to the sport are plain to see. They are better athletes and better footballers and so many of the best of them play at the Roosters.
John Strange's side are the culmination of almost a decade of progress, the ultimate example of what's possible when a club with some serious muscle decides to really invest in a women's program.
As Brigginshaw proved what was possible for the women's game in terms of star power and sheer class, the Roosters prove what is possible when those attributes are taken to their very limit.
Now they are what Brigginshaw was — a star for the entire league to sail by, and they are filled with players who can trace their lineage to the retiring Bronco.
In a cruel irony, without Brigginshaw there might be no Tarryn Aiken, who was named the Karyn Murphy medallist with a brilliant display at halfback for the Roosters or Jocelyn Kelleher, Brigginshaw's opposite number, who tortured Brisbane with her kicking game.
Closer to home might be no Tamika Upton, who succeeded Brigginshaw as the world's best player but just could not get into the game for the Broncos until she set up a late try, or Jesse Southwell, who scored that try and is so clearly an evolution of an archetype that Brigginshaw pioneered — not an athlete, but a pure footballer.
She is one of the players who entered the NRLW having played league all their lives, unlike Brigginshaw who had to stop when she was 12 because there were no more teams to play on and that's just one change Brigginshaw has born witness too.
Origin matches are ratings gold and attracts crowds that dwarf what they were even five years ago, the NRLW has been born and expanded twice over and the product and support is edging towards the point where a standalone grand final doesn't just feel possible, it feels like a logical step for a game that continues to grow.
Brigginshaw helped raise that profile as a mainstay in Brisbane's early premierships and a Queensland regular. She was not just a star, she was the star.
She didn't just adapt to the new world, she brought it to heel as she became a legend and now retires as an icon — if they were to rename the women's Dally M after a modern player, the Ali B certainly has a fine ring to it.
When you are a player of that stature, to whom greatness has been a constant companion for years and who remained a threat right to the end — even at 36, Brisbane did not win a game this year without Brigginshaw — a grand final massacre is no way for a career to end.
She has given the game so much but the game could not give her the perfect ending.
But as she prepares for the rest of her life, Brigginshaw leaves the game as a figure that sits astride two eras, who helped bring her game to life and make it bigger than anyone in the old days could have dreamed.
There is still progress to be made and in retirement Brigginshaw will not stop pushing for it.
She believes in a brighter future and she knows one is possible, because she has already built one. We are living in it right now.

Drone maker ideaForge Technology has received a GST demand and penalty order totalling ₹109.2 Cr over alleged tax underpayment on drone sales. The order comprises a tax demand of ₹54.6 Cr and an equal penalty. In an exchange filing, ideaForge said it received the order from the Additional Commissioner of CGST and Central Excise, Belapur, yesterday. It covers the period between January 2022 and March 2024. The tax authority alleged that ideaForge incorrectly paid GST at 5%, resulting in a shortfall of 13 percentage points. ideaForge said it had submitted its response to the show cause-cum-demand notice. It also pointed out that the government clarified in 2025 that the GST rate applicable to drones is 5%. The company said it would appeal the order after consulting its tax advisers and expects a favourable outcome. It does not anticipate any immediate material impact on its financials, operations, or other activities while the matter remains unresolved. The tax dispute comes after ideaForge reported a net loss of ₹2.3 Cr in Q1 FY27, compared with a net profit of ₹61 Cr in Q4 FY26. However, the loss narrowed over 90% from ₹23.5 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Its operating revenue rose to ₹68.6 Cr from ₹12.8 Cr during the same period, although it declined 51% sequentially from ₹141 Cr. ideaForge started FY27 with an order book of more than ₹300 Cr and added to its growth pipeline during the June quarter. The company raised ₹500 Cr through a QIP in July, with domestic and international institutional investors participating in the issue. It also received a government LoI for financial assistance of up to ₹151 Cr under the RDI Scheme to develop YETI, its middle-mile logistics platform. Shares of ideaForge ended yesterday’s trading session 0.13% higher at ₹734.30 apiece on the BSE. With the GST notice, ideaForge has joined other new-age tech companies facing tax demands. In June, Zomato and Blinkit parent Eternal received a ₹9.63 Cr GST demand from Andhra Pradesh authorities over alleged short payment of output tax, with interest and penalty also applicable. The same month, coworking company Awfis received a GST show cause notice involving about ₹7.1 Cr over alleged discrepancies in its FY23 filings.

OpenClaw creator Peter Steinberger took an unusual route to get attention for an Android app review delay: he asked publicly on X whether he knew anyone at Google who could help. The person who responded was Google CEO Sundar Pichai. "Do I know anyone at Google who could help? We're now over a week in review limbo for OpenClaw's Android app," Steinberger wrote on X. Pichai responded directly to the post, writing, "Ack, will follow up." The exchange quickly caught the attention of social media users, with Pichai’s response drawing 2.1 million views and 10,000 likes, according to the figures cited in the post. Steinberger later returned with an update, confirming that the new version had gone live. "And the new update is live - thanks so much!" he wrote. The brief exchange between the OpenClaw creator and the Google CEO triggered a wave of reactions on X, with users joking about the unusual customer-support escalation. "This needs to be shown in the Customer Support handbooks," one user commented. Another wrote, "Monster himself came for the support !" "Looks like you have the best person in the company to help out, but here if you need anything," a third user commented. A fourth user summed up the exchange by writing, "peter: “do i know anyone at google” sundar:," Another user brought in the wider AI industry context, writing, “I wish people at Anthropic were that responsive.” In November 2025, Peter Steinberger began building OpenClaw, an open-source personal AI agent designed to address limitations he saw in existing AI assistants, Time reported. Within nine months, the project grew to a 10-person team, with its GitHub repository crossing 387,000 stars and 81,000 forks. OpenClaw connects AI assistants with tools and messaging services, allowing agents to act through everyday chat apps. In July, OpenClaw announced plans to become an independent nonprofit foundation. In August 2026, he made it to the list of Time Most Influential People in AI. OpenClaw is an open-source AI assistant designed to act as a proactive personal agent. It can connect AI models with users’ local files and messaging platforms, including WhatsApp and Discord, to automate tasks. The project has become one of the more prominent open-source AI agent projects. GitHub described OpenClaw in August as the fastest-growing project in its history, with approximately 388,000 stars and 81,000 forks at the time. Steinberger, who created OpenClaw, joined OpenAI in February. OpenAI said the project would remain open source and move under a foundation that the company would continue to support. The Android app is now available on Google Play, according to OpenClaw’s documentation. It functions as a companion node that connects to an OpenClaw Gateway. For now, however, it was the brief interaction between Steinberger and Pichai—not the app itself—that became the social-media story. 'I reduced my running because of urine leaks' – Commonwealth finalist Korir
- Published
Naomi Korir's career on the track reached a high point in August when she finished fifth in the final of the mile at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
But things could have been very different for the Kenyan middle-distance runner.
The 28-year-old was born with fistula, a medical condition in which abnormal openings develop between organs and can lead to uncontrolled leakage of urine or faeces.
While Korir loved athletics as a child, it initially forced her to rethink any plans to be a runner.
"I played most of the sports activities: football, netball, athletics, even rugby," she said.
"But it was difficult because [of] the training, and the urine is flowing continuously. It's bad.
"I reduced my running to shorter distances to reduce the leaking.
"I began doing 100m hurdles."
Despite the challenges, Korir's love of sport also offered a form of escape and belonging.
"I could do it because I loved it," she explained.
"Because most of the people could avoid me, I did a lot of activities just to pass time and not to feel that I'm excluded."
Three surgeries and a second chance
The charity Doctors Without Borders estimates that 500,000 women live with fistula globally.
Some develop a fistula after childbirth while for others, like Korir, it is congenital.
Access to good obstetrics, or to simple surgery, means that the condition has all but disappeared in some countries, but it remains a problem in sub-Saharan Africa, where high quality medical care can be hard to access.
Korir was born with genitourinary tract fistula - an opening between bladder and vagina which caused her urine leakage.
Surgery was required, but her first two operations failed to solve the problem.
In August 2013, a third operation finally brought relief for the then 13-year-old.
The procedure was carried out in her home town Eldoret by the Gynocare Hospital, which specialises in fistula, obstetrics and reproductive health.
"It's a difficult condition to live with every day," Gynocare director Caroline Mabeya told BBC Sport Africa when discussing the stigma and isolation women with the condition suffer.
"They are ostracised in the society. That's the psychological torture that they face with the fistula."
The hospital has treated patients from across East Africa since opening its doors in 2011. Its work extends beyond surgery, with a post-operation programme designed to help women rebuild their confidence.
"We offer free treatment for these women at Gynocare because most of them are very poor," Mabeya explained.
"When they come into the facility, they are crushed, they have low esteem. So, there's a huge amount of effort that is put in to make them at least be strong enough to be reintegrated and get back into the community."
'A champion in sport'
For Korir, successful surgery offered a second chance, both on the track and in the classroom.
As well as allowing her to run properly again, she continued her education through Gynocare's Beyond Fistula programme.
"I have a family in GynoCare, a fistula home," she said.
"That is where I schooled after my surgery until I finished my secondary level."
In 2019, Korir began competing professionally and two years later was part of the Kenyan duo which claimed a silver medal in the 2x2x400m mixed relay alongside her partner Ferguson Rotich at the World Relays in Poland.
A year later she went one better, bagging gold as part of Kenya's 4x400m relay team at the African Championships in Mauritius.
The mile at this year's Commonwealth Games was her first appearance in major global final.
"I'm giving hope to young women maybe who have lost hope," she said of her achievements.
"They need to come back again in living and enjoying life."
Mabeya says Korir's transformation makes her a powerful example to the women currently receiving support at Gynocare.
"She makes them realise that you can actually pull yourself out of these struggles and still make it in life and succeed.
"Naomi actually is one of those patients that inspires us to continue working very hard, because we struggle with this condition and these women. The work is not easy."
As a young girl, Korir sang in church and played the keyboard, convinced that music was a more likely career than athletics.
"But now I'm in different career and I'm so happy," she beamed.
And with the World Championships in Beijing next year and the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, Korir believes there is another chapter to write.
"I know I'm a champion in life, because conquering fistula alone is being a champion.
"Now I'm looking forward to be a champion in sport."

The Telangana State Government is consistently lagging behind in achieving the revenue receipts projected in the budget estimates as could be seen from the figures released by the Reserve Bank of India.
The RBI, in its report related to recommendations on increasing the Ways and Means Advances limit for States, has taken into account revenue receipts of the three consecutive financial years 2022-25. Telangana registered revenue receipts of ₹1.59 lakh crore in 2022-23, ₹1.69 lakh crore in 2023-24 and ₹1.67 lakh crore in 2024-25. The figures for the three years are much lower than the quantum presented in the budget estimates of the three fiscal years.
For instance, the State Government projected revenue receipts of ₹1.93 lakh crore in the budget estimates of 2022-23, whereas the realisation was ₹1.59 lakh crore, ₹ 34,000 crore less than the estimates. In 2023-24, the projected revenue receipts were ₹2.16 lakh crore as against the actuals of ₹1.69 lakh crore, and the same was the case in 2024-25 when the State reported receipts of ₹1.67 lakh crore against the projected ₹2.21 lakh crore. This clearly indicates that the revenue collections are frequently lagging behind the initial budget projections.
An overview of the budget estimates reveals that revenue receipts under a few heads have been much less than anticipated leading to the mismatch between the projections and actuals. This is clearly illustrated by the budget estimates and actuals of Grants-in-Aid & Contributions (payments made as assistance, donations, or contributions to support operational or capital expenditures and used to bridge resource gaps and address regional disparities in a multi-tiered governance framework).
The State Government has projected receipts in the form of grants-in-aid and contributions at ₹41,002 crore in 2022-23, and the actual realisation was just ₹13,179 crore. The same was the case in 2023-24, when the actuals were ₹9,934 crore against the estimates of ₹41,259 crore and in 2024-25 ₹7,913 crore was realised against the projected ₹21,636 crore.
Non-tax revenues are another head where revenue receipts continue to be much lower than the estimates, leading to a mismatch between estimates and actuals. Non-tax revenue during 2022-23 was ₹23,608 crore, against the ₹35,208 crore estimate, and the situation repeated over the next two financial years, although the difference was much lower.

A purported Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping (here & here) claims that the Rajasthan High Court has given a judgment that provides for six months of imprisonment and a ₹50,000 fine for any candidate who fails to secure at least 100 votes in the Sarpanch elections. Let us verify the authenticity of the claim made in this post.
Claim: A Dainik Jagran newspaper clipping claims the Rajasthan High Court has ordered a six-month jail term and a ₹50,000 fine for Sarpanch candidates securing under 100 votes.
Fact: The viral newspaper clipping is an AI-generated fake image. The Rajasthan High Court has given no such judgment, Dainik Jagran published no such report, and Indian electoral laws contain no provision imposing jail time or fines for low vote counts. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
First, an initial search confirmed that the Rajasthan High Court has not issued any such judgment regarding low vote counts in Panchayat elections. Additionally, we found no news reports published by Dainik Jagran corroborating this matter. Moreover, no such law, Court order, or judicial mandate exists under the Election Commission of India or Indian electoral statutes (such as the Representation of the People Act, 1951) penalising candidates with imprisonment or fines purely for receiving a low vote count. Under current election rules, the only major consequence for a poor electoral performance is the forfeiture of the security deposit, which applies if an unelected candidate fails to secure more than one-sixth of the valid votes polled.
Further, we ran the viral newspaper clipping through the OpenAI content detection tool, which confirmed that the clipping is an AI-generated image created using OpenAI tools. Earlier, we debunked a similarly fabricated clipping that falsely claimed a woman gave birth to puppies in the United States.
To sum it up, the viral newspaper clipping is a fabricated AI-generated image, and there is no legal provision or court order mandating jail time or fines for securing low votes in a Sarpanch election.

Mark Carney for Nobel Peace Prize? Probably not, but his name's out there
Carney at one point was a favourite to win on the predictions market
If relations between Canada the U.S. are cool now, the temperature could plummet if Prime Minister Mark Carney were to win the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize this year.
"[Donald] Trump will be unhappy whoever gets the Nobel," Nelson Wiseman, professor emeritus at the University of Toronto, told The Associated Press. "If Carney got it, it would make relations with Canada rockier than they are."
Carney's name has been mentioned as a possible recipient of the prestigous prize, an award Trump has made no secret he wants to win.
On Oct. 9, the Norwegian Nobel Committee will announce the winner of the annual Peace Prize in Oslo.
Last year, the award went to Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado. Machado presented Trump with her medal at the White House in January. Although Trump accepted it, the Nobel Committee stressed that the prize itself remains hers.
Trump has repeatedly said he has ended eight wars, but experts say his invasion of Iran and attack on Venezuela make him an unlikely recipient this year.
Prizes in other categories will also be awarded that week, with several Canadians being discussed as possible recipients.
The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million US), whether awarded to an individual, small group of laureates or an organization. The deadline for nominations was Jan. 31. After months of discussions and evaluations, the committee votes in October.
Nobel Peace Prize (Oct. 9)
Earlier this week, traders on the U.S.-based prediction market Kalshi put Carney's chances of winning at 14 per cent. His odds later fell.
"I don't think his chances are great," Haakon Gjerløw, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, told CBC News.
His organization releases an annual list of potential candidates for the prize. Gjerløw said the Nobel laureate has to meet three broad criteria to win: international co-operation, disarmament and the promotion of peace.
"So it's whoever did the most for these three criteria over the past year," he said.
He said Carney's name has likely been floated because of his resistance to Trump, along with the prime minister's efforts to strengthen ties with Europe — both seen as signs of international co-operation.
But Gjerløw pointed to other possible candidates, including the International Space Station.
"It would be a symbol of what we can achieve when we are able to co-operate as humanity," he said.
Gjerløw's other candidates include Mykola Kuleba and Save the Children, Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, the Committee to Protect Journalists, and the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court.
Nobel Prize for physiology or medicine (Oct. 5.)
When The Scientist magazine asked its readers to suggest potential Nobel Prize winners in science, Canadian researcher Dr. Daniel Drucker was among the names put forward.
The endocrinologist won a 2025 Breakthrough Prize in Life Sciences for discovering the GLP-1 hormone used in diabetes and obesity medications — including Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro — that have changed the lives of millions of people around the world.
Prediction market Kalshi has also listed Drucker as one of the top contenders to win.
Nobel Prize for Literature (Oct. 8)
Another Canadian being discussed is poet and essayist Anne Carson, who has frequently been mentioned as a strong Nobel contender. Carson is a two-time winner of the Griffin Poetry Prize, and author of Autobiography of Red, Antigonick and Red Doc>.
However, one of Canada's most famous authors, Margaret Atwood, is also a contender according to Kalshi, but at lower odds. The Handmaid's Tale author has won two Booker prizes, and for years her name has been mentioned as a possible candidate for the Nobel Prize.
The last Canadian to win in this category was Alice Munro in 2013.

Tamil Nadu is recording around 200 cases of dengue a day. Fresh cases are being reported in places including Chennai and its neighbouring districts and cities such as Coimbatore and Madurai.
Officials of the Directorate of Public Health (DPH) and Preventive Medicine said the caseload remained steady and was not at outbreak proportions. A. Somasundaram, Director of Public Health and Preventive Medicine, said cases had not risen exponentially, with the numbers remaining broadly steady. “We are seeing nearly 200 cases a day. The numbers are not doubling or tripling, which usually happens in an outbreak. Right now, there is a static trend in the number of dengue cases, and we are expecting the cases to decline soon,” he said.
Cases are being reported across cities including the Chennai belt (Tiruvallur and Kancheepuram), Coimbatore, and Madurai. This could partly be due to a “natural bias” with these areas having more hospitals and testing facilities, Dr. Somasundaram said.
“We have specifically instructed staff to increase the number of tests for dengue for better surveillance and patient management. This is so we don’t miss a case, and when samples are tested, we can identify pockets of cases or clusters, which are likely to bring about an outbreak,” he said. There are over 4,500 government and private laboratories in the State, he added.
Surveillance measures to identify Aedes mosquito breeding pools are continuing, but the number of pools detected has started to decline as a result of source reduction measures. The mosquito density is slowly coming down, the official said. About 25,000 Domestic Breeding Checkers (DBC) have been engaged across the State, with 20 persons covering one block.
Dr. Somasundaram said while preventive measures had been intensified, they had been holding daily monitoring meetings with District Health Officers via video conferencing. “We are analysing the case trend, whether increase or decrease or static, and number of laboratory tests conducted. We are also monitoring fever triaging, patient management, and discharge policy. Patients are being categorised as having mild, moderate, or severe symptoms and treated appropriately. Right now, the severity of infections is less. Fogging operations and source reduction measures, along with work taken up by DBCs, are being supervised. We are also looking at creating awareness among the public,” he said.
With October and November being crucial months, he said, there could be intermittent or heavy rain and people should ensure that their household environment is clean. “Avoid storing water unnecessarily. If you have too, keep containers closed properly,” he added.

The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.
The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When Ars Technica talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project, but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.
Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyper scaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo, Microsoft, and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.
Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.
Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store, but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy.

Q: I get headaches whenever I use my phone or computer for a long time. Are screens damaging my brain?
A: Screens are not known to damage the brain simply through use, but prolonged use can cause eye strain, dry eyes, blurred vision, neck and shoulder tension and headaches. Poor posture, glare and inadequate breaks can worsen symptoms. Follow the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes, look about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Adjust brightness, reduce glare and blink regularly. Frequent or severe headaches, especially without screen use, need medical evaluation.
Q: Is every headache a migraine?
A: No. Headaches can result from stress, tension, dehydration, poor sleep, eye strain, infections, sinus problems, stomach problems or migraine. Migraine may cause throbbing pain, nausea and sensitivity to light or sound, though symptoms vary. A new, unusually severe or rapidly worsening headache, especially with weakness, confusion, fainting, seizures, vision changes, fever or difficulty speaking, needs urgent medical attention.
Q: I have a headache, so I take a painkiller immediately. Is that okay?
A: Occasional appropriate use may be fine for some people, but frequent painkiller use can cause medication-overuse headaches and, depending on the medicine, stomach, kidney or liver problems. If you regularly need painkillers for headaches, find the cause rather than repeatedly treating the symptom.
Q: Do I really need a flu shot if I usually get only a mild flu?
A: Influenza can be mild but can also cause serious illness, especially in high-risk people. Flu vaccination reduces the risk of influenza and its complications, though it does not prevent every cold or respiratory virus. Because influenza viruses change, seasonal vaccination is recommended for many people according to individual risk. Ask your doctor if it is appropriate for you, particularly if you have chronic diseases, are pregnant or belong to another recommended group.
Q: Can the flu shot give me influenza?
A: No. Injectable flu vaccines do not contain live influenza virus capable of causing influenza. Soreness, tiredness or a mild fever can occur briefly after vaccination and usually reflect an immune response. You can also catch another respiratory virus around the same time. Remember that protection takes time to develop.
Q: My eyes burn after looking at my phone for hours. Do I need “screen glasses”?
A: Not necessarily. Digital eye strain can cause burning, dryness, temporary blurred vision and headaches because we blink less while concentrating. Take regular breaks, blink consciously, reduce glare and keep the screen at a comfortable distance. Prescription glasses may help if you have an underlying vision problem. Blue-light glasses are not a magic solution. Persistent pain or significant vision changes need an eye examination.
Q: Does using a phone in the dark permanently damage eyesight?
A: Ordinary phone use in a dark room has not been shown to permanently damage eyesight, although the bright screen against a dark background can cause strain, dryness or headaches. Keep some ambient light on and adjust screen brightness. Persistent blurred or double vision, eye pain or headaches should not simply be blamed on the phone.
Q: I use my phone until I fall asleep. Does it really affect sleep?
A: It does. Screen use keeps the brain engaged, while light from screens can affect the body’s sleep-wake rhythm. Messages, videos and social media can be particularly stimulating. Keep the phone away from the bed, choose quieter activities before sleep and maintain a regular bedtime. Persistent sleep problems need further evaluation.
Q: Can sitting in front of a screen all day cause neck and back pain?
A: Yes. Prolonged sitting and poor posture can cause neck, shoulder and back pain, while looking down at a phone can add neck strain. Change position regularly, keep the screen at a comfortable height, support your back and move around during the day. Exercise and strengthening can help. Persistent pain, numbness, weakness or pain spreading into an arm or leg should be assessed.
Q: I feel dizzy and get a headache after spending hours on my phone. Is it because of radiation?
A: There is no good evidence that ordinary mobile-phone use causes headaches or dizziness through the radiation emitted by phones. However, prolonged use can indirectly contribute through eye strain, poor posture, dehydration, lack of sleep and inactivity. Look at the whole pattern and take regular breaks. If headaches or dizziness keep returning, particularly without screen use, consult your doctor.
Q: Are “sugar-free” foods healthy?
A: No. “Sugar-free” does not mean nutritious. Sugar-free biscuits, chocolates and snacks may still be high in calories, refined flour, saturated fat or salt. Some contain sugar alcohols or other sweeteners that can cause gas, bloating or diarrhoea when consumed in excess. They may also keep our preference for very sweet foods alive. Sugar-free is a label, not a health certificate. Always check the complete nutrition label.
Q: Are zero-sugar drinks harmless?
A: Not necessarily. They can be a better choice than sugary drinks if you are trying to reduce sugar and calories, but they are not automatically healthy. Some sweeteners can cause gas, bloating, abdominal cramps or diarrhoea, particularly in people with sensitive digestion or IBS. If a particular drink repeatedly causes bowel discomfort, stop it and see whether symptoms improve. Zero sugar does not mean zero consequences.
Public Advisory: Not every health problem needs a tablet—and not every health myth deserves to be believed. From WhatsApp remedies and “natural” cures to advice from friends and relatives, health information can easily become distorted. Before starting, stopping or changing a treatment, ask the doctor—not the WhatsApp group.
NOTE: These responses are for general awareness and do not replace professional medical advice. Older adults often have multiple illnesses and medicines, so individual medical advice should be taken from a qualified healthcare professional.

An explosive and newly partially unsealed court filing alleges that the US Department of Homeland Security built up dossiers on ICE observers—including their photos, license plate numbers, and other information—and stored them in a system called the Investigative Case Management database, which was built by Palantir.
Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
A spokesperson for DHS calls the case “meritless” and says that “the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS.”
Plaintiffs allege in the filing, which is heavily based on documents produced by the government and depositions of DHS agents, that agents had a practice of intimidating protesters and observers. They did this, the filing says, by doing drive-bys of the observers’ homes and, in the case of at least one observer, requiring that she be referred to secondary inspection any time she tries to cross the border until at least January 2027.
"The government is treating people who exercise their First Amendment rights and seek to hold it accountable as criminal suspects, and that's what we're asking the court to stop,” says JoAnna Suriani, an attorney at Protect Democracy who is representing ICE observers in the case.
The filing focuses on agents’ conduct during “Operation Catch of the Day,” an immigration enforcement surge in Maine this past January. It is part of a proposed class action brought in federal court in Maine by four observers: Elinor Hilton, Colleen Fagan, Polyxenia Pantos, and Carlyn Williams. It was filed under seal in September, and a redacted version was made public Friday.
In particular, it describes how one DHS agent, referred to as “Agent J.C.” in the filing, used the Investigative Case Management (ICM) database, which the government describes as the case management system the ICE component Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) uses to document its investigations, to flag observers.
According to the filings, J.C. created ICM records on at least six observers; the government puts the number of people at eight. He labeled two people he filmed at a Home Depot parking lot with “Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor,” according to the filing, and sent photos of them and others to a US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) officer so he could run a facial recognition search on them using an app called Mobile Query.
On January 20, Pantos briefly watched and photographed an arrest in Portland, Maine, standing a few car lengths away beside their spouse's car. Hours later, per the filing, J.C. ran the car's plate and pulled a report on the owner—Williams—from Accurint, a LexisNexis database for law enforcement, which listed her address, phone numbers, and cohabitants. J.C. then allegedly circulated her photo to his team, asking, “Was this the protestor.” Another agent, per the filing, replied that it didn’t match the woman he had dealt with at the scene; J.C. then told colleagues he was "adding them in ICM now."
According to the legal filing, that afternoon, J.C. called Williams on her cell phone, identifying himself only as "the Department of Homeland Security." According to Williams, he told her she "should encourage" her spouse, Pantos, "not to do anything like that in the future because people who are doing things like that might get added to a domestic terrorism watchlist." J.C. testified in a deposition that he warned Williams she would be arrested if she “continue[d] to do this.” Government attorneys asserted in a court filing that he denied referencing a “domestic terrorism watchlist.”
According to documents produced by the government, Williams’ ICM record says that she was the registered owner of a vehicle used to “interrupt ICE arrests” and that her driver’s license photo matched a video of "aggressive woman [who] interject[ed] herself into an arrest." According to a 2016 DHS privacy assessment, ICM automatically shares the subject records agents create with CBP’s TECS system, where they act as "lookout records" for screening travelers at the border.
ICM is the system used by HSI agents to create and track case files. ICE awarded Palantir the contract to build ICM in 2014, and the system is built on the company’s Gotham software, which ICE says was customized specifically for operational needs. In 2022, ICE awarded Palantir a new five-year ICM support contract initially valued at up to about $96 million. In 2025, the agency added nearly $30 million to that contract to develop a new platform called “ImmigrationOS.”
Todd Lyons, the former acting director of ICE, wrote in an April letter to Rep. Maxwell Frost, the Florida Democrat, that ICE “does not maintain any kind of database of U.S. citizens protesting ICE activities.” He also said DHS isn’t keeping a “separate, standalone database” of people it hasn’t arrested or detained.
The government’s motion to dismiss argues that these were isolated incidents and that DHS policy prohibits this conduct. It says J.C. made records on people he believed were “potential threats to law enforcement” and “did not attempt to nominate any individuals to the terrorist watchlist.”
Attorneys for the observers say that DHS’s efforts have had a chilling effect on their First Amendment rights. According to the motion, Pantos stopped all ICE observation work after J.C.’s phone call to Williams, who briefly continued to observe ICE activity and then stopped all together too.
The observers are asking the court to order that Williams’ records be archived, to bar DHS from using the information it collected about the plaintiffs against them, and to prohibit agents in Maine from threatening observers with watchlists or following them to their homes.
