The story so far
The groundwater resources of Kerala have been under severe stress due to changes in rainfall pattern following climate change, high population density as well the fact that approximately 62% of the population relies on groundwater from an estimated 6.5 million open wells for their domestic needs. The State’s fragmented wastewater management system and the unscientific construction of septic tanks and pit latrines at homes close to shallow and open wells have resulted in persistent faecal contamination of ground water in the State, which has been documented by several studies.
A 2024 study in the Journal of Environmental Management reported that 7.4% of the State’s population could be making do with poor quality of groundwater and estimated that 0.59 million people in 252 local self government bodies in the State could be continuously exposing themselves to health risks from consuming ground water from wells which may not be chlorinated regularly.
And the latest report on E.coli contamination comes from Pala, where a water quality assessment conducted in flood-affected areas along the Meenachil river detected E. coli bacteria in 67% of the samples, raising concerns over the safety of drinking water sources in and around Pala.
Researchers attributed the spike in bacterial contamination to the recent floods, which may have allowed contaminated surface water to enter water sources.
How is contamination taking place?
It is a dangerous combination of high population density, unplanned urbanisation with hundreds of septic tanks and wells sitting close to each other in small plots and the State’s natural hydrogeological features that allow surface pollutants to reach the water table quickly. In recent years, unpredictable and heavy rainfall has been adding to the State’s woes, as oversaturation of the soil and the overflow of drainage systems can quickly allow pollution and microbial contamination to infiltrate ground water.
Environmental scientists explain that groundwater is drawn mostly from shallow, unconfined aquifers, which are recharged directly by rainfall and surface infiltration. In most areas the local water table might be sitting just below the level of the river bed and it naturally leaks water downwards to recharge the underlying unconfined aquifers. If rivers are polluted, then all groundwater resources in the surrounding area would also be carrying the same pollutant.
What is the extent of groundwater contamination in Keralam?
A community-level GIS study of 449 households in an urban area of Thiruvananthapuram in 2018 had reported that most of the wells were in an intermediate-high contamination risk state, with more than 77% of wells having a septic tank within 7.5 m radius. Coliform contamination was prevalent in 73% of wells, and the groundwater was predominantly acidic with a mean of 5.4, rendering it unfit for drinking.
This picture could be true for the rest of the State also. Because of the State’s unique geography and highly dispersed, continuous rural-urban settlement pattern, just about 5-6% of major urban zones are connected to a centralised pipe-based sewerage network system. The State’s sanitation strategy relies heavily on onsite sanitation systems, with individual household septic tanks and soak pits for sewage disposal.
Unscientific construction of these household sanitation systems has rendered much of the groundwater resources unsafe for human consumption, unless properly treated.
What are the health impacts?
Safe drinking water is one of the crucial social determinants of health. It is thus unfortunate that a State which has made enviable strides in developing its public health sector has paid little attention to ensuring that people have access to safe drinking water. While people in urban areas have to a large extent, access to treated water supply, in many rural areas of the State serviced by local small water supply schemes, water distribution lines often run close to sewerage lines and even small breaks in the pipelines can lead to the contamination of drinking water
Recurrent outbreaks of water-borne diseases like Hepatitis A, Shigellosis and norovirus outbreaks have been the bane of the State in recent years, especially in the northern districts of the State, indicating the scale and impact of groundwater contamination. Hepatitis A in particular has been taking a heavy toll on the State since the last three years, with significant mortality and in many instances, leaving people with severe morbidities
Epidemiological studies conducted by the ICMR and Health department into amoebic meningoencephalitis, which has emerged as a significant public health problem in Keralam in recent times, has traced the infection to the use of non-chlorinated well water which has high concentration of E.coli, in which free-living amoeba thrive
What is the sewerage infrastructure status?
To modernise sewerage infrastructure, the State is executing projects under the AMRUT 2.0 Mission, a Central initiative aimed at ensuring universal access to safe water and reliable sewerage connections across urban areas. The CAG’s 2025 report stated that at the closure of the AMRUT Mission (Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation), Kerala’s overall achievement was just 11.25% and only 0.13% households got sewerage connections.
Keralam’s geography, population density, lack of vast tracts of uninhabited land means that many proposed treatment plants end up being close to residential areas, which triggered huge public protests. Such protests led to the cancellation of multiple approved septage treatment plant projects in many parts of the State. There are also reports about the State’s financial crunch affecting project payments leading to delays in implementation

Here’s a fun history lesson for you. Don’t worry, we’ll make it quick! In 1966, nearly 51,000 people died on US highways. The overwhelming evidence suggested that many lives could have been saved with modern seat belts, which by then had been around for several years. The automotive industry responded by rallying together, and, in a triumph of self-regulation, voluntarily put the safety feature in every new vehicle that rolled off the line.
Kidding! Of course they didn’t do that. In the fall of 1966, Congress established the Department of Transportation and then passed the National Traffic and Motor Vehicle Safety Act as well as the Highway Safety Act, giving the federal government sweeping new authority to set safety standards. By 1968, seat belts were required in every new car. Despite a massive increase in highway traffic in the last 60 years, far fewer fatalities happen on the road today.
I was thinking about this while watching various AI CEOs huddle around US president Donald Trump on Tuesday, congratulating themselves and each other on having signed an AI safety accord. My colleague Maddy Varner wrote about the specific stipulations here, but the short version is that it’s largely up to the AI labs to keep themselves in check.
Or, as Trump put it even more succinctly in the Oval Office on Wednesday: “They’re gonna police, and they’re gonna police each other, and they’re gonna self-police, they’re gonna police themselves. It’s going to work out very well.”
So this is the current state of AI safety regulation. On one side are the AI executives, employees, and tech luminaries, who are all saying that there need to be clear, thoughtful, tactical rules introduced to avoid potential disaster. (Bill Gates, for instance, has been on a media blitz playing Cassandra about an AI apocalypse.) On the other side is Trump’s magical thinking that if you say something enough times, it must be true.
That’s not to say any of this is simple or easy. The question of how to properly “pace the frontier,” as some of those same executives like to say, remains open. Even if all of the major AI labs were to agree to a slowdown, there’s no good way to keep them to their word, and China would likely continue on its own path regardless. The US economy is increasingly propped up on the AI industry, which itself has become an ouroboros of financing deals and circular investments; any meaningful crackdown risks major instability that reaches well beyond Silicon Valley.
The automotive industry is also admittedly an imperfect analogy for all kinds of reasons. There’s no seat belt equivalent for AI, no straightforward solution that can demonstrably reduce risk overnight. (It also took decades for the majority of states to pass laws mandating that people actually wear them.) The potential harms are less certain and less quantifiable. AI doomers will tell you the technology could result in human extinction in a decade; skeptics argue that’s sci-fi marketing malarkey.
We’ve talked about various AI risk scenarios before, but no one can say for certain what’s going to happen next. If you’re looking for data points to calculate your own personal p(doom), I’d point to a recent CNN report about how the US military supposedly nearly boarded a Chinese ship in part because a false AI-generated report said it was carrying nuclear materials. What, if anything, does the AI accord accomplish to prevent similar incidents from happening in the future? Unclear.
The correct answer to all this uncertainty surely isn’t “I guess we’ll find out.” But that’s exactly what self-regulation encourages. To its credit, OpenAI has delayed and even canceled the release of its most advanced models over security concerns. But not before they went on various, extensive hacking sprees, new details about which are still trickling out at a steady pace.
In an interview with TIME published on Thursday, Trump suggested that the Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation were sufficient “guardrails” for the artificial intelligence industry. Are they? It’s far from clear if AI companies can even be held legally responsible when their models go rogue. And it’s not like AI agents themselves are being served subpoenas.
The truth is, no one knows how to solve for AI safety right now. It’s going to take massive amounts of coordination, resources, and regulatory authority to develop the right framework and enforce it, which is exactly the kind of thing governments are designed to provide. Instead of even attempting to work through any of that, the Trump administration is getting out of the way and telling everyone to step on the gas. Don’t bother buckling up.

Tony Gilroy blasted the “tragic” nature of the Paramount-Warner Bros. merger at the world premiere of his new film, “Behemoth!” Produced on a $36 million budget, “Behemoth!” is representative of the mid-budget, adult-oriented drama that once sustained Hollywood’s theatrical business — and allowed filmmakers like Gilroy to make a name for themselves in the industry. He fears the impending merger (which David Ellison just announced would place both of the historic movie studios under a company named Skydance) threatens to dismantle the very “healthy and beautiful business” he has worked in for over three decades.
	“People say the movie business is in trouble,” Gilroy told Variety Friday night at Alice Tully Hall. “You go around, you stand anywhere you want, what do people talk about? Did you see this? Did you see that? What episode are you on? The business is solid, and to destroy the architecture that made it so in the name of venture capital, it’s tragic.”
Starring Pedro Pascal as a gifted cellist re-immersing himself in the world of Hollywood film scoring, “Behemoth!” marks Gilroy’s first major project since completing his work on the Emmy-winning series “Andor.” It was also selected as the centerpiece of the 64th New York Film Festival, following James Gray’s star-studded opening-night film “Paper Tiger” and preceding Ava DuVernay’s closing-night documentary “14th.” While introducing his new film, Gilroy praised the festival’s lineup as a bright spot amid an increasingly turbulent Hollywood landscape.
Popular on Variety
	“Thank you for making [the festival] so elegant and glamorous, and for surrounding us with so many amazing films,” Gilroy told the crowd. “The way this is curated this year, this is a freakin’ lineup! Holy sh*t. And everybody knows it. When so many things go to shit in Hollywood, this is like a thank you. Thank you for letting us bring our soufflé to your groovy party.”
Gilroy also thanked Matt Greenfield and his partners at Searchlight Pictures, the indie studio owned by the Walt Disney Company, which also produced “Andor.”

Skydance has tentatively set Tuesday, Oct. 6, to close the merger, which will consolidate Hollywood’s traditional Big Five studios (Disney, Universal, Sony, Warner Bros. and Paramount) under just four corporate owners. While Ellison has maintained that Paramount and Warner Bros. will retain their separate studio identities under Skydance, industry figures — including “Behemoth!” producer Sanne Wohlenberg — fear the consolidation will make the “possibilities for a filmmaker alarmingly limited.”
“God, it’s certainly turbulent and uncertain times, isn’t it? It never seems to get any easier,” Wohlenberg said. “I do think you have to take a deep breath and keep believing that things will be circular and come back. When you look at history, there have been many, many bad times. Sadly, we are steering into one, which will make the competitive nature of the industry and possibilities for a filmmaker alarmingly limited. And it shouldn’t be like that. I think we will survive it and I hope for better times.”

UK-Iranian dual national arrested over RAF Fairford released on bail
- Published
A UK-Iranian dual national arrested on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts in connection with an incident at RAF Fairford has been released on bail.
The 25-year-old man was arrested in the London borough of Westminster on Thursday. Searches of two properties in the same area have now finished.
A major incident was declared and dozens of homes were evacuated after police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase in Gloucestershire last weekend.
Five other men in their twenties were arrested and were subsequently released on police bail. All five were UK nationals from London.
The investigation into the circumstances surrounding the events are continuing, police said.
Last weekend, the five men aged between 23 and 25 were arrested in the early hours of the morning after vehicles were reported to be travelling towards the base operated by the US Air Force (USAF), sparking a major security incident.
The BBC understands that one of the men had dialled 999 himself, about an hour before a local farmer alerted police to a "large group" of masked men near the vehicles.
They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and later on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act, before being released on bail on Monday in what police called an "investigative decision" that was "grounded in experience and strategy".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a Cobra meeting that afternoon in response. He later said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident, but did not provide any more details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement. The Iranian embassy in London said on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" what it called "unfounded and malicious speculations" linking Iran to the incident.
RAF Fairford has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.
In recent months, US bombers have taken off from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
Late on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told a TV show that it was clear a "foreign actor" had been involved in events over the weekend.
Without providing evidence or giving further details, he told Fox News network's "Hannity" programme: "What happened, what almost happened, what could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation. It's one that clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor."
Speaking earlier at the Oval Office, US President Donald Trump said he would not have let the five men arrested out on bail, and that he was "surprised" they had been released.
"We know everything about them, we would not have released them," he said, adding that the UK had worked with the US "very closely" on this.

Srinagar has an estimated 64,416 stray dogs, according to a scientific survey conducted by the Srinagar Municipal Corporation (SMC) in 2023, the Government stated today. It said nearly one-fourth of the dogs in Srinagar, that is 15,266 stray dogs, were sterilised between June 2023 and September 2025.
The figures have been provided by the Housing & Urban Development Department (H&UDD) in a written reply to a starred question raised by MLA Zadibal Tanvir Sadiq. According to the reply, the 2023 survey carried out by SMC used the Lincoln-Petersen Formula to estimate the stray dog population within SMC limits. The Animal Welfare Board of India has recognised it as a scientific survey and it found approximately 64,416 in Srinagar.
The government has stated in the reply to the question of the legislator that from June 2023 to September 2025, SMC sterilised 15,266 stray dogs and immunised 15,725 dogs. The surgeries and vaccinations were carried out at Animal Birth Control (ABC) centres at Tengpora and Shuhama.
The government also said dog-bite cases in J&K were being recorded and monitored through the State Surveillance Officer under the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP). The IDSP operates under the Directorate of Health Services, Kashmir.
It has also said that SMC currently has ABC centres at Tengpora Bypass and Shuhama in SKUAST. Together, these facilities have a combined kennel capacity of 121.
An additional ABC centre at Ahal Chatterhama is also coming up, with the kennel capacity of 60. The three centres will have an aggregate kennel capacity of 181, once the third one is ready, according to the government.
The department said ABC/ARV programmes are also being implemented in Jammu. The Jammu Municipal Corporation (JMC) has sterilized 50,000 dogs since 2014.
“However, keeping in view the scale and geographical spread of the stray dog population in the urban areas of the Union Territory, the existing infrastructure and operational capacity require further augmentation and strengthening to ensure wider, effective and sustained coverage,” the reply states while acknowledging gaps in efforts to control stray dog population.
It listed its strengthening efforts as: the expansion of ABC centres, strengthening veterinary manpower and dog-catching facilities, augmentation of holding/isolation and post-operative facilities, expansion of sterilisation and ARV coverage, scientific identification and record-keeping of sterilised/vaccinated dogs, regulation of designated feeding points, improved solid-waste management and intensified public awareness.
The government has said that veterinary surgeons/doctors have been deputed to municipal corporations and urban local bodies to for helping in ABC/ARV programme.

America's $28B hemp THC industry is under threat from a looming ban
Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in the hemp law he championed

Inside a commercial kitchen near Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns pours a blue-green substance into gridded moulds to create a flagship product for his business: high-strength THC gummies containing the main psychoactive component found in marijuana.
He could soon be forced to close the operation. The United States’ multibillion-dollar market for intoxicating hemp items — spanning THC-infused seltzers stocked by Target stores to smokable cannabis flower — faces potential shutdown after Congress voted to plug a federal loophole that permitted the trade to expand.
Industry lobbyists and several lawmakers are working to rescue the sector. A short-term federal spending bill signed by President Donald Trump last month pushed back the implementation date of the "hemp THC ban" from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, granting Congress additional time to consider regulating the products rather than an outright prohibition.
“It’s such a weird spot to be in,” said Hohns. “You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.”
Marijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. “Rope, not dope” was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp.
To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill.
But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole. Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high.
Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country, including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana’s THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned.
The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal.
Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products.
McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history.
The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn’t take effect for a year.
The ban “threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,” according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market.
The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds.
The owners of Kentucky’s Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that’s what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said.
“If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it’s gone,” Zipperle said.
They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year.
The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable.
Hohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what's available in states that have.
“When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry,” Hohns said. “No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope.”
That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business.
Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin' Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production. Co-founder Matt Swanson took himself off the payroll on Thursday.
“There’s just so much uncertainty,” Swanson said. “I'm actively looking for employment.”
Among those who have come to the defense of the hemp industry are alcohol retailers, including Total Wine & More. Sales of cannabis seltzers have helped offset falling alcohol sales.
Opponents include people who say the products are dangerous.
“I have sympathy for people losing their jobs, but I also have sympathy for the many, many more people whose lives are affected by this,” said Kevin Sabet, CEO of Smart Approaches to Marijuana.
The regulated legal marijuana industry, which sees hemp THC as unfair competition, also supports the ban. Cory Harris, a lobbyist for state-legal cannabis operators, suggested that dire predictions about its effect on the intoxicating hemp industry are overstated.
While the ban would end interstate sales of products like THC seltzers and gummies, some could find a home in legal in-state markets, he said. It's possible THC drinks could be sold at stores in the states where they were produced. States like North Carolina could adopt legal hemp programs.
“If you go from having virtually no rules to suddenly having an awful lot of rules, that’s a buzzkill,” Harris said. “Welcome to our world. But if you establish your whole business within a legally questionable loophole, that’s just sort of the risk you take.”

Mumbai: Nationalist Congress Party (SP) chief Sharad Pawar on Sunday reacted to the protest organised in Mumbai by the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) and Shiv Sena (UBT) against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged voter list irregularities, asserting that the demand is not limited to Mumbai.
Pawar calls for political parties to come together
Speaking to reporters, Pawar said that the demand for action against the Election Commission of India, led by Gyanesh Kumar, was not limited to Mumbai, but was also being raised in Pune, Nagpur and other parts of the state.
“The state government is going through the SIR process. When all concerned political parties come together to find a solution to this issue and take a decision regarding those who have committed irregularities, we will stand with them and extend our support,” Pawar added.
Thackeray-led protest draws crowd
A massive crowd was seen at the Garjana Morcha protest led by Raj and Uddhav Thackeray near the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation headquarters. Several protesters were seen holding the Tricolour and posters targeting Gyanesh Kumar while raising slogans against him.
Visuals from the protest show demonstrators supporting the Thackeray brothers in their demands against Gyanesh Kumar and calling for his resignation.
The morcha began from Metro Cinema in South Mumbai and proceeded towards the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC) headquarters. State leaders of the Congress and the Sharad Pawar-led NCP (SP) also participated in the protest.
Raj Thackeray raises vote concerns
Raj Thackeray demanded that the entire SIR process conducted in Maharashtra should be cancelled, electronic voting machines should be discontinued and that the elections should be conducted using ballot papers.
“I had said that elections should be boycotted... There is definitely something wrong with the voting process. Elections cannot be conducted in this manner. What I said at that time is now being understood by everyone. How did they get a complete majority in the Assembly elections?” Raj added.
The MNS chief questioned how the total number of voters increased by 40 lakh to 60 lakh between the 2024 Lok Sabha election and the Maharashtra Assembly election held later that year.
Uddhav Thackeray, meanwhile, asserted that the reason for the protest was that the fight against 'Vote Chori' did not belong to any single party, individual, caste or religion. He said that the protest was a fight of the entire country to save their freedoms.
“I remember, and you might remember too, that when Modi ji became Prime Minister for the first time, he made an announcement: ‘Make in India.’ Remember? We agreed with that. But if a dictator is being made in our country under ‘Make in India,’ then today we are standing here to crush and throw that dictator out of this country,” Uddhav added while addressing the crowd.
The 'Garjana Morcha' marks a significant escalation in the opposition's campaign against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, with calls for his resignation.

‘I don’t know what the rules are’: NIH grant decisions stymie scientists
What’s the current climate for research funded by the National Institutes of Health? In the words of one researcher, “not as terrible as last year” — though “it’s not like I understand what’s going on.”
A new STAT analysis breaks down how the NIH awarded $34 billion in grant money to universities in fiscal year 2026. Funding went to 58,000 projects this year, compared to the historical average of 63,700 in the years before the second Trump administration, and the agency further reduced the number of awards for research tied to health disparities, race, and ethnicity. The analysis also includes a survey of about 50 NIH-funded researchers, who say that delays in the grant review process are slowing down the pace of their work. How big is Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak?
News of a fifth measles death in Pennsylvania underscores a longstanding issue about the disease. The full scope of the outbreak — in the state and in the country — isn’t known or even knowable.
Only confirmed cases are reported. As of Wednesday that total was 943 in Pennsylvania, about a quarter of the 2026 national total. About 20% of infected people end up needing hospital care and some other portion will see a doctor. But some will never come to the attention of public health.
That’s especially true in a place like Pennsylvania, where a number of counties have large numbers of Amish people. (It was true, too, in last year’s outbreak in Mennonite colonies in Texas.) People in these communities don’t interact much with the wider world. Measles vaccination rates are low, families are large, and people may not seek care unless the illness becomes severe.
At some point, researchers will come up with modeling estimates that may give us a better idea of how big this outbreak actually is. But for now, we’re just seeing a portion of the iceberg. “It is much worse than is being claimed,” says Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “I think we don’t know how bad.” — Helen Branswell
Protecting marathon runners amid climate change
Heat stroke is a growing risk for marathon runners amid global climate change. Collecting data from the medical tents on race courses where runners seek care is the best way to help event organizers prepare for and avoid inevitable crises, writes Vibhu Krishna in a new First Opinion.
Krishna, an avid runner and senior resident physician at UC San Francisco, explains how better data on the patients who come to medical tents can help ensure that care providers have all the ice, cold water immersion tubs, and other supplies they need. Compiling and sharing data from large races can also help event organizers assess whether changes like earlier start times or alternate dates help reduce the number of people who get sick or hurt. New numbers point to ‘crisis’ in disability care
People with disabilities are struggling to find caregivers — and when they do, they’re more likely to experience problems with the quality of their care.
The grim findings come from a survey of 524 disability care providers published Wednesday by ANCOR, an advocacy group for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities.
The report revealed that 85% of providers in the United States experienced moderate or severe staffing challenges in the past year and 55% have had to turn away people in need of care due to inadequate staffing. Care quality is down, while reportable incidents are up.
It’s unlikely these numbers will improve. States have already started slashing caregivers’ pay and other critical disability services in anticipation of Medicaid cuts that will roll out next year. — O. Rose Broderick

Delay in induction of new fighter jets hurting IAF, says Air Chief
Singh said the IAF could finalise the MRFA contract by the end of the financial year.
The delay in inducting new fighter jets is hurting the Indian Air Force, and the country needs to produce up to 40 aircraft a year to plug capability gaps and build long-term combat strength, IAF chief Air Chief Marshal AP Singh said on Saturday.
He said the IAF is counting on the timely induction of the LCA Mk-1A, new multi-role fighter aircraft (MRFA) and additional Sukhoi-30MKIs to shore up its fighter fleet and keep the number of its combat squadrons from falling below 30, while underscoring the need to deploy fifth-generation aircraft too.
“There is some extra delay this time, and there is no doubt that it is going to hurt us,” Singh said at his annual media briefing ahead of the 94th IAF Day on October 8. “We need to induct two fighter squadrons every year. That means anything between 36 and 40 aircraft should be produced and inducted into the IAF for us to stop going down from the current 30 fighter squadrons and start improving towards the target of 42. Actually, we need even more than that.”

Singh said the IAF could finalise the MRFA contract by the end of the financial year. It refers to the proposed purchase of 114 Rafale fighter jets from France to sharpen the IAF’s combat edge at a cost of roughly ₹3.25 lakh crore.
“Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) is talking about producing 20 LCA Mk-1As every year. If the MRFA deal goes through, we will get about 12 aircraft per year from that contract. That makes the number around 32. We also have a contract for 12 Su-30 aircraft. Let’s say if six come in one year and six come in another year, so we will be in the region of 35-40 aircraft per year. We are hoping that these things will happen and then we will be able to achieve the pace of growth that we have set for ourselves,” the IAF chief said.
Also Read | IAF chief AP Singh takes sortie in F-15EX Eagle during US visit
Under the MRFA model being considered, the Rafales will be made in India by French plane maker Dassault Aviation and a local partner. France is expected to supply 20 Rafale jets in fly-away condition while the remaining will be made in India under the government-to-government deal.
The LCA Mk-1A is finally nearing induction after missing several deadlines. Both the IAF and HAL are confident that induction will start by year-end. It will replace the IAF’s workhorse MiG-21s, which retired last year after more than six decades of service. The IAF has placed two orders for 180 Mk-1A fighter jets worth a combined ₹1.1 lakh crore. The first contract for 83 aircraft was signed in February 2021, followed by a second one for 97 fighters in September 2025. The deliveries, likely to begin in December, are under the first contract.
The first Mk-1A aircraft, ordered in 2021, was due for delivery in March 2024. That deadline was missed due to a combination of factors, including US firm GE Aerospace’s inability to supply the F404-IN20 engines on time and delays in securing key certifications.

Mumbai Police file FIR against 500 unidentified persons, organisers over CJP's Shivaji Park protest
Mumbai Police registered FIR against organisers, 400-500 unidentified persons for Cockroach Janta Party's protest held at Shivaji Park on Friday.
Mumbai Police registered an FIR against organisers, 400-500 unidentified persons for Cockroach Janta Party's protest held at Shivaji Park on Friday. No arrests have been made as police carry out investigation.
Filed on the complaint of a resident of the Shivaji Park, the case has been registered for unlawful assembly, wilful disobedience of lawful order issued by public servant, and other offences. The case has been filed under sections 189 and 223 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), read with sections 37(1)(3) and 135 of the Maharashtra Police (MP) Act.
The Cockroach Janta Party, led by founder Abhijeet Dipke, held a massive protest at Shivaji Park on October 2, seeking the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar for alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.
Mumbai Police had denied permission for holding the protest at Shivaji Park, citing concerns over noise pollution, traffic congestion and disruption to vehicular movement in the area. Responding to the refusal, Dipke had given the call for 'Jail Bharo Andolan’, asking protesters to gather at the venue.
Earlier on Friday, resident Siddhi Deolekar, who is also an advocate, lodged a complaint at Shivaji Park Police Station against Cockroach Janata Party activists Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, Saurav Das, and Ratna Singh for gathering at the Shivaji Park despite being denied police permission.
"This is not 'peaceful protest'. This is an attempt to defy the law under the cover of a political protest," Deolekar said.

I had that one last fight left in me: Braveheart pilot
Mumbai, Indian pilot Smit Machchhar, being hailed as a hero for foiling an attempt by his co-pilot to crash an Israel-bound flydubai flight, has said he did not want to go down without a fight and so put in all he had to open the cockpit door from the inside.
"It began as a normal flight. The co-pilot wanted to pray, which a lot of locals do and which is not out of the ordinary. While he was praying, out of respect, I was just looking at the front and not at the back," Machchhar told Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call on Saturday.
"Suddenly, after I think I would say about four or five minutes, there was a big blow to the back of my head. My first thought was that there was a catastrophic damage to the aircraft and something is not right," he said.

"But then the blows kept coming one after the other. And that's when I realized that it's not the aircraft, it's the other guy who was in the cockpit with me."
Machchhar said he tried to stop the co-pilot, but because of the initial blows, his vision was blurred.
"At that point the next thought, the next feeling that I had was that the aircraft was sharply going down. My memory is still in bits and pieces right now. But this is what I remember out of that time.
"I did try and manage to open the door once but I think he shut it back closed. At this point I remember I was lying down on the cockpit floor and I felt the aircraft and the whooshing sound and people screaming.
"I had that one last fight left in me. Call it personal or call it for the people, but I thought that if I don't do it, I am going to die. And that is when I pushed against everything. I gave everything that I had and just went for the door and opened the door. And thankfully, people were waiting to pounce back, took over the control," he said.
The cockpit door has a twist from the inside, the pilot said.
"From the outside, it can only be opened with a code. My colleagues from outside were trying to punch in the code but the guy was not allowing to open the code," he said.
"The only way to open the door was to reach the knob to twist it open. It was a short quick twist but once I had my hands on the knob, I guess I twisted it and opened it," Machchhar said.
An Omani citizen, Hamam al-Hammami, has been identified in media reports as the co-pilot who attacked Machchhar with a crash axe, an emergency tool normally kept in the cockpit.

Venus is shrouded in a veil of mystery. The yellowish “lower haze” at the bottom of its atmosphere was discovered by the Venera and Pioneer Venus probes in the 1970s. These spacecraft were some of the first to successfully send images of the planet back to Earth, but the haze they saw went unexplained for decades. Now the mystery Venus was keeping has been unveiled.
What nobody knew then was that the haze is an accumulation of particles from meteorites. “Shooting stars” that burn up in the atmosphere leave behind cosmic dust particles, and after sulfuric acid interacts with these particles, it leaves behind a haze. Planetary scientist Hiroki Karyu and his research team at Tohoku University in Sendai City, Japan, finally figured out how the haze formed using a microphysical model. This type of model involves microphysics—the micro-scale processes that create clouds and precipitation on Earth and other bodies.
“The continuous influx of cosmic dust is sufficient to sustain this lower haze layer with the particle size distribution observed by the entry probes,” Karyu said in a study published in Nature Astronomy. “These haze particles of cosmic origin act as efficient condensation nuclei, promoting cloud formation in the main cloud deck even far from their initial source.”
Hazed and confused
Previous speculation suggested the haze formed from volcanic ash. Venus is known as the most volcanically active planet in our Solar System, with signs of volcanism first observed by the Magellan spacecraft in the early 1990s. Recent studies discovered the planet is more volcanically active than previously thought, but the researchers found that ash belched out by Venusian volcanoes is not the source of haze particles.
Surface dust was also ruled out. Karyu found that even if there were much larger influxes of volcanic or surface dust on Venus, the particles would still not be able to interact with the atmosphere’s sulfur in the right way to form the haze.

For startups, it’s a relatively new but increasingly critical rite of passage, one that not only signals coming of age but also creates pathways for investor exits and wealth creation. Inside The Dalal Street Startup Ride Indian startups had gained a reputation for being “loss making” by prioritising growth at all costs and market share over immediate profitability. The trend of putting scale ahead of the bottom line was at its peak amid the funding boom of 2020-22. While prioritising growth is not wrong for startups, especially at early stages, the start of funding winter in 2022 gave a reality check to the Indian startup ecosystem. Subsequently, startups started pushing for profitability. Giving further wings to the aggressive profitability push was the ambition to list on the exchanges. While new-age tech companies look to turn profitable before filing their draft IPO papers, those that cross the line manage to stay in the green, data shows. About 60 of the 73 new-age tech companies are currently profitable. In terms of profits, Groww now leads the pack of new-age tech companies, posting a net profit of ₹2,083 Cr in FY26. Prominent internet companies Paytm and Eternal trail Groww in terms of profitability, raking in profits of ₹553 Cr and ₹366 Cr in FY26, respectively. It is pertinent to mention that these companies have been listed on the bourses for years now, with Info Edge making its public market debut in 2006. While these companies trace their origin back to the 90s, a large majority of the new-age tech stocks under Inc42's purview are about a decade old. From a broad perspective, Inc42 data reflects that the median time taken for a startup to get listed on the bourses is 11 years. While listing for 18-year-old ixigo and 19-year-old Fino Payments Bank came relatively much later, ArisInfra's IPO materialised within four years of its operations. Meanwhile, the new-age tech companies that have made their public market debuts this year generally turned profitable right before their public market debuts. For instance, eyewear major Lenskart reported a net profit of around ₹297 Cr , a significant turnaround from a ₹10 Cr loss in FY24. The company maintained profitability in FY26, raking in a PAT of ₹494 Cr in the fiscal. Urban Company also reported its first consolidated net profit of approximately ₹240 Cr for FY25, it returned to the red in FY26. For the full year FY26, the company reported a net loss of ₹234.8 Cr against a net profit of ₹239.8 Cr in previous year despite seeing a revenue growth of 36% YoY to ₹1,555.5 Cr Sectors Driving India’s Startup IPO Boom The startup sectors producing the most number of listed companies is proportional to the private funding trends witnessed in the Indian startup ecosystem. The three most funded sectors, fintech, ecommerce and enterprise tech, also house the highest number listed startups. The dominance of the fintech and ecommerce sectors on the bourses is expected to continue as the likes of PhonePe, Zepto and OYO would soon be making their public market debuts. Delhi NCR Home To Highest Number Of Listed Startups While Bengaluru continues to be the startup capital of India, Delhi and its neighbouring cities Gurugram and Noida account for the most number of listed new-age tech companies. Dubai Crown Prince and UAE Deputy Prime Minister Hamdan bin Mohammed has praised Indian flydubai pilot Captain Smit Machchhar for his courage, saying he had demonstrated the “highest degrees of courage, responsibility, and care for human life.”
Hamdan shared a photograph from his visit to Smit Machchhar, who is receiving treatment in hospital, and said the UAE leadership extends its “appreciation and praise” to the pilot.
In a post on X, Hamdan said Smit Machchhar had become part of the UAE’s national story and praised his contribution in protecting lives.
Quick answers to key questions
On September 30, during flydubai Flight FZ1073, Captain Smit Machchhar was seriously injured by his co-pilot in an alleged attack that resulted in a rapid descent of the aircraft before emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Captain Machchhar is being praised for his remarkable courage and quick thinking during the cockpit attack, which allowed crew members and passengers to intervene and avert a potential disaster.
Despite sustaining serious injuries, Machchhar managed to unlock the cockpit door, enabling crew and passengers to subdue the co-pilot and ultimately make an emergency landing.
Captain Machchhar has received praise from various public figures, including Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Bollywood stars like Shah Rukh Khan and Salman Khan, acknowledging his bravery.
As of the latest updates, Captain Machchhar is under medical care and is recovering well, with the Indian Embassy confirming they are in contact with his family and supporting his recovery.
“We are proud that he is part of our team… part of the story of our nation” Hamdan wrote, adding that Machchhar was also part of the UAE’s “human experience”.
He concluded the message by describing the UAE as a “a nation of compassion… a nation of peace… and a nation of life.”
Smit Machchhar was seriously injured during an alleged attack inside the cockpit of a flydubai flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
Despite his injuries, the pilot was able to respond during the confrontation, while crew members and passengers intervened. The aircraft subsequently made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.
Machchhar remains under medical care as authorities investigate the circumstances surrounding the incident.
The Indian Embassy in the UAE said Machchhar remains under medical care and is recovering well.
“Indian braveheart Capt. Smit remains under excellent medical care & is recovering well,” the embassy said on X, adding that it remains in contact with his family and local authorities.
Machchhar was initially treated in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, before being transferred to Abu Dhabi for further treatment.
The incident took place on September 30 aboard flydubai flight FZ1073, a Boeing 737 MAX 8 carrying 170 passengers from Dubai to Tel Aviv.. The aircraft was forced to make an emergency landing in Tabuk after a violent confrontation inside the cockpit.
According to UAE Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, the co-pilot attacked Machchhar with a crash axe and attempted to take control of the aircraft. The UAE has described the incident as an attempted “terrorist act”. Investigators are continuing to establish the circumstances and motive.
Despite his injuries, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door. Passengers and crew then intervened and subdued the co-pilot, while two off-duty pilots helped operate the aircraft before it landed safely in Tabuk. The plane reportedly lost more than 16,000 feet during the incident.
The co-pilot has been identified by multiple reports as Hamam al-Hammami, an Omani national. He had previously been grounded in Oman amid concerns over alleged extremist views.
Investigations involving UAE and Saudi authorities are continuing, with authorities examining the circumstances and possible motive behind the cockpit attack.

Ethernet cables can do more than just improve home internet
They can also transmit power, video and audio.
Ethernet cables are probably one of the least exciting tech accessories you own. But you may not realize they can do more than just connect devices to your router. They can also carry video, audio and power. However, just because they can do that doesn't necessarily mean they're the best option.
Long-distance video
HDMI usually connects two devices that are relatively close together, but some people's setups need video to travel over longer distances. This is one area where the same cables you use for Ethernet (category cables) could find a second use.
Ethernet cables won't do that on their own. For this setup, you'll need to buy HDMI extenders to pair with your Cat5e, Cat6 or similar cables. Those adapters put a transmitter at one end and a receiver at the other, while using the cable as the connection between them. That lets you send video much farther than you typically could with an HDMI cable.
Despite the familiar cable, this isn't actually Ethernet networking. (AV over IP, on the other hand, does use your local network to transmit audio and video.) Here, the category cable is simply carrying the signal between two extenders. It could be handy if you already have an unused cable in your walls or you need to reach something distant, like a projector.
Still, it isn't necessarily the best solution even for those cases. Active optical HDMI can also handle long distances, and some cables support formats like 4K at 120Hz that many extenders don't. Think of category cables as a potentially useful option for some niche setups, rather than a go-to solution.
Replace audio cables
These same category cables can also carry multiple channels of analog audio. With the right adapters, a single cable can carry several channels. For example, a studio could use it to connect microphones in one room to recording gear in another without pulling a bunch of individual cables through a wall.
For most setups, standard XLR cables are easier and pretty cheap. But if the wiring is already there, category cable can be a clever way to replace several cable runs with one. Some setups also need shielded cable, especially if the microphones get power through the connection.
PoE
Speaking of power, Power over Ethernet (PoE) is where category cables can find a second life that's more than just a clever gear hack. PoE lets one Ethernet cable carry both data and power. It's especially handy for security cameras, Wi-Fi access points and other devices that aren't near an outlet.
For example, a camera on your porch could use one Ethernet cable for both power and its network connection. Or you could run it to a Wi-Fi access point on your ceiling. The cable just needs to lead back to an accessory that provides PoE, like a compatible switch or injector.
Unlike the other uses, PoE isn't just an oddball option, it's a truly useful standard. However, you still need to make sure your equipment supports it and provides enough power for the device.

West Indies coach Daren Sammy, on the eve of the third and final ODI against India, said that a win against the world’s top-ranked side would give his team the much-needed confidence at a time when the players brace for pay cuts back home.
On Saturday, Shai Hope made his coach’s wish come true, leading from the front with an inspirational unbeaten 162 (143b, 17x4, 3x6) to guide his side to a five-wicket win and salvage pride by avoiding a whitewash at the Maharaja Yadavindra Singh International Cricket Stadium.
Chasing 352, Hope, opening the batting, scored his second century on the bounce as the Caribbean outfit hunted down the target with 10 balls to spare.
IND vs WI, 3rd ODI - As it happened
Hope set the tone in the PowerPlay with exquisitely timed shots through covers, down the ground, and off the pads. The skipper, along with Amir Jangoo (67, 56b, 5x4, 1x6), the other centurion from the second ODI in Guwahati, stitched together a 109-run stand for the second wicket off just 99 deliveries. The Indian bowlers looked flat and struggled to create chances in dewy conditions. However, against the run of play, Jangoo was run out when his partner sent him back. Keemo Paul chipped in, scoring a quickfire 44 (35b, 5x4). Once Paul departed, Hope dug deep despite battling fatigue. With the asking rate climbing above 11, Hope swatted Kuldeep for a six and a four in the 46th over. He followed it up with a brace of boundaries off Gurnoor Brar and Anshul Kamboj and, in the process, brought up his 150 as well.
Earlier, India posted 351 for seven, riding on K.L. Rahul’s well-paced unbeaten 129 (87b, 10x4, 6x6).
Electing to bat, the Men in Blue were rocked early in the third over when Jayden Seales struck twice. He had Gill caught down the leg-side and cleaned up Virat Kohli with an in-dipper that uprooted the middle-stump.
Rohit Sharma (92, 85b, 10x4, 3x6) and Ruturaj Gaikwad (57, 69b, 1x4, 4x6) steadied the innings with a 137-run stand. The former started cautiously against a disciplined opening burst from Seales and Matthew Forde before shifting gears.
After Rohit’s departure, Rahul took charge. The latter hit boundaries through conventional strokes, the best being the straight drive off Seales. During his knock, Rahul surpassed 10,000 international runs. At the back end of the innings, he showcased his repertoire and brought up his ninth ODI ton in style, pulling Seales over fine-leg for a maximum.
However, on this day, Hope did spring eternal for West Indies.

North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, a day after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.
Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches across the Korean peninsula.
The missile test might be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.

Turning artificial intelligence research into real-world tools isn’t always straightforward, despite the remarkable progress in recent years ranging from self-driving cars to large language models. Systems that perform well in controlled lab settings often fall short when deployed in homes, in hospitals or on city streets.
Vision-based systems, for example, hold promise for improving safety, monitoring health and aiding rehabilitation. For example, a camera-based system could help a clinician assess a patient’s gait or rehabilitation progress.
In the future, an assistive robot in an older adult’s home might need to recognise when the person is struggling to stand or reaching for an object. But a major challenge is ensuring these robots perform reliably beyond the lab, particularly in messy, unpredictable or low-visibility conditions.
As a computer scientist who studies AI systems designed to understand human behavior – especially through visual cues like body movements and interactions with objects – I see three main challenges to taking AI from the lab to the real world: generalisation, human behavior and resources.
Challenge 1: The generalisation gap
Most AI vision systems are trained on well-lit, high-quality images, often from curated sources like motion capture studios or daytime recordings. But when these systems are deployed in real-world settings, such as in a dimly lit home, hospital room or nighttime street, they often struggle. This is not because the technology is flawed, but because the data used to train it cannot fully represent the enormous variability of the real world.
Take human pose estimation, for example. This task involves detecting key points on a person’s body, such as joints, to understand how they’re moving. The result resembles a digital skeleton that represents the positions of a person’s arms, legs and other body parts. Pose estimation has been studied for health and rehabilitation applications, including measuring a person’s gait, monitoring rehabilitation exercises and assessing movement patterns associated with the risk of falling. In well-lit environments, modern AI models do this with impressive accuracy. But in low or uneven lighting, performance can drop sharply. That’s because the model has learned from clean, consistent data and isn’t prepared to generalise to tougher conditions.
Would collecting more nighttime training data solve the problem? More labeled data would certainly help, but collecting it is especially difficult. When a person’s joints are hard to see in an image, they are also hard for a human annotator to label accurately. Low light can also obscure visual information rather than simply make an image darker, and nighttime conditions vary with cameras, shadows, glare and other sources of noise. Collecting and manually labeling examples that cover all these conditions is therefore difficult and expensive.
We’ve been working to close this gap by developing AI systems that perform better in low-light scenarios. One method we use is unsupervised domain adaptation, where a model trained on well-lit, labeled data is adapted to handle low-light settings, without needing manual body-joint labels for the low-light images. This helps bridge the “domain gap” between clean training data and the messier world where these systems are actually used.
In our 2026 study on low-light human pose estimation, we generated realistic low-light training images and designed the system to balance uncertain visual evidence with its learned knowledge of human body structure. The method substantially improved performance on two low-light benchmarks, although the broader challenge is far from solved.
Challenge 2: Human behavior
Another major hurdle is the sheer variety of human behaviors, especially when people interact with objects. In computer vision, this is known as human-object interaction detection. Teaching an AI system to recognise actions like cutting a tomato or passing a basketball requires not just object detection, but an understanding of context and intent.
The real challenge is scale. The number of objects is large, and the ways humans interact with them are even greater. You can sit on a chair, carry it, drag it or stack it. Each is a distinct interaction. A cup might be used for drinking, washing, pouring or handing something to another person. An assistive robot would need to distinguish among these actions to respond appropriately. It’s simply not feasible to collect and label data for every possible combination.
In my research, we study how an AI system can detect interactions it has never seen during training. Researchers call this a generalisation-to-unseen-classes problem, and it’s a key challenge for building models that don’t just memorise patterns, but can adapt to new situations. Our work has explored how foundation models can help recognise previously unseen interactions. In a more recent study, we used large vision-language models, models that combine computer vision and natural language processing, to identify the parts of an object that support particular actions, without training the system on labeled examples for that specific task. This matters in areas like assistive robotics and safety monitoring, where AI needs to respond intelligently to behaviors it wasn’t specifically trained on.
This challenge is different from the low-light problem. In low-light pose estimation, the system is trying to recognise a familiar type of movement under unfamiliar environmental conditions. In human-object interaction detection, the action-and-object combination itself may be new. Both are generalisation problems, but they require different solutions.
Challenge 3: The resource gap
Even when researchers know how to make models more robust, applying those improvements isn’t always easy, especially in academic or smaller research settings. Today’s most powerful AI systems depend on massive computational resources in the form of data centers that contain huge numbers of specialised computer chips.
These are often too expensive for university labs or public-sector researchers, and the computing power needed to train leading models has continued to rise. According to the 2026 AI Index Report, the technology industry produced more than 90% of the notable AI models introduced in 2025.
At the same time, a model developed using large computing clusters may ultimately need to operate in a clinic, school, robot or home device, which means running on much smaller hardware. Such systems may also need to respond quickly without continuously sending sensitive data to the cloud. This mismatch creates a widening gap between what’s possible in theory and what’s practical in deployment. Bridging that gap requires not just better models, but more efficient algorithms and open-source tools that broaden access to advanced AI.
Why it matters
These challenges aren’t just academic. They affect how and whether AI tools can be trusted in the real world. Imagine a fall-detection system that fails at night, a workplace safety monitor that misses a crucial action or a robot that misunderstands what a person is doing because it’s never seen that exact interaction before. These aren’t just minor bugs – they’re breakdowns in trust, usability and sometimes even safety.
AI systems are being deployed in homes, hospitals, factories, vehicles and other everyday environments. If they can’t adapt to different environments or recognise new human behaviors, their usefulness becomes limited and their risks amplified. That’s why researchers are increasingly focusing not just on accuracy in ideal conditions, but on robustness, generalisation and real-world readiness.
Looking ahead: Closing the gap
Closing the gap between lab-trained AI models and messy, unpredictable real-world environments won’t happen overnight, but it’s possible. In my research, we’ve explored techniques like using augmented data to simulate challenging conditions and help models adapt. We’ve also worked on enabling AI systems to better generalise to new, unseen situations by using knowledge from foundation models to distinguish unfamiliar interactions from similar ones encountered during training.
Ultimately, I believe that making AI systems more reliable in everyday settings is a challenge worth solving, not just to improve gadgets and apps, but because AI has the potential to support human well-being, whether that means safer streets, smarter healthcare or more secure homes.
Bo Wang, assistant professor of Computer and Information Science, University of Mississippi

In September 2026, a rumor (archived) circulated online that water levels in Wyoming's Yellowstone Lake dropped 11 feet between Sept. 26 and 27.
For example, a Facebook user wrote on Sept. 29:
YELLOWSTONE NATIONAL PARK - Scientists are investigating after portions of Yellowstone Lake reportedly dropped nearly 11 feet overnight when an unknown underground channel opened beneath the lake bed.
Rangers first noticed the change Sunday morning after several docks were found sitting completely above the waterline. Geologists believe shifting rock beneath the lake may have opened a previously sealed underground passage, allowing millions of gallons of water to drain into Yellowstone's extensive subterranean geological system.
The rumor also spread on X and Threads (archived, archived).
The rumor originated from the Facebook page Casper Planet, which described its content as satire. The page's About section read, "Snews that doesn't matter directly to your Snews feed. Did we say this is satire? Well it is, names/locations are made up."
In addition to Casper Planet's own declaration of the satirical nature of its content, we found no reporting from reputable sources on Google, Yahoo or DuckDuckGo (archived, archived, archived) that supported the Facebook page's claim about Yellowstone or cited the "geologist Dr. Aaron Keller" who featured in Casper Planet's post.
The image that Casper Planet used to illustrate the satirical story was fake. The highly regarded Pangram artificial intelligence detection tool found the image to be "fully AI." Open AI's Verify scanner found that someone had generated the image using Open AI's tools.
Though Casper Planet did note on its page that its content was satire, it did not say so on the actual post. Shares of Casper Planet's posts on X and Threads contained no indications (aside from the nature of the content) that the story was satire.
The United States Geological Survey's water level readings from the Yellowstone River at its inlet into Lake Yellowstone did not show an 11-foot drop in water levels between Sept. 26 and 27. The USGS found that water levels between 9 a.m. on Sept. 26 and 9 a.m. on Sept. 27 varied by inches, not feet.
Snopes has previously investigated other satire claims shared by Casper Planet, including whether an ancient city appeared under Wyoming's Horse Peak Mountain or whether Wyoming wolves mauled a Colorado man who tried to join their pack.
Since the effectiveness of satire is subjective, we use "originated as satire" or "labeled satire" ratings based on creators' description of their work. It's your call on whether you agree.

BUNIA, Congo — Congo’s Ebola outbreak has killed more than 4,000 people, authorities said, as they struggle to contain what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history.
The latest figures released by the Health Ministry on Thursday showed that 4,018 people have died among 8,300 cases recorded since the outbreak was declared in eastern Congo on May 15.
Some health workers, meanwhile, gathered at the epicenter in Ituri Province to demand payment for wages owed them. The protesters, who included surveillance team members, waved placards saying, “No money, no data!” and “No payment for months.”
Some of the workers haven’t been paid for August and September, said Biongi Beiza, one of the protesters in Bunia, Ituri’s capital. “There is no explanation from the administration,” he said.
Congolese authorities did not immediately address the issue. Front-line workers have gone on strike several times since the outbreak began, further hampering efforts to contain the disease.
A senior U.N. official said an Ebola-hit displacement camp housing a transit center for infected patients was burned by soldiers earlier this week as they were looking for weapons in Kigonze, on the outskirts of Bunia, forcing 19,000 people in the camp to flee.
Creating such transit and treatment centers has been a struggle, requiring money and staff, all of which are in short supply, said Julien Harneis, the U.N. senior Ebola coordinator. “When we lose a center, that means we lose capacity, we lose investment, and we have to start again. And above all, it means that people do not get access to the care that they really need,” Harneis said.
Infected aid worker evacuated to the Netherlands
An aid worker with Médecins Sans Frontières, known in English as Doctors Without Borders, was infected with Ebola while working in Congo, the group said in a statement.
The worker arrived in the Netherlands late Thursday on a special medical flight and was transferred to a high-level isolation unit, the Leiden University Medical Center said in a statement.
“The human cost of this crisis is unprecedented in the DRC, with communities facing the largest Ebola disease outbreak ever recorded in the country,” MSF said.
At least 50 health workers have died after contracting the virus.
Mobile labs are helping detect cases quickly
One way local authorities have tried to contain the outbreak is through mobile laboratories. In Butembo, an Associated Press journalist watched a medical team operating one such lab near an Ebola treatment center on Thursday.
Test results that used to take 72 hours can now be obtained in six hours with the mobile labs, said Lota Kalubi, a doctor at the treatment center.
The labs have also made it easier to get to locations usually difficult to reach, said Michel Ngimba with the National Institute of Biomedical Research in Butembo. “So we can go, if today we have an emergency, for example, in Katwa, we can start up the vehicle, and we can move the lab to Katwa,” said Ngimba.
Insecurity and community resistance are hampering containment efforts
The World Health Organization has recently raised the alarm about the virus’ rapid spread into new health zones, stretching limited resources. The current outbreak is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, which killed 11,000 people, WHO has said.
The number of newly confirmed cases is falling, but that could be attributed to insecurity and challenges in getting communities to cooperate in some of the hot spots, Africa CDC said on Thursday. While the spread of the disease has slowed in some areas, it has accelerated in others.
Confirmed cases fell from around 850 cases and 470 deaths a week in mid-July to an average of 490 cases and 230 deaths in September.
A Congolese politician was beaten to death earlier this week in one of the emerging hot spots after defending government measures to deal with the outbreak, highlighting tensions and mistrust in communities.
Authorities last month launched a village-centered approach that involved working with local leaders to educate people about the virus, but those efforts face resistance from residents who dismiss Ebola as a hoax. There is also deep distrust in the country’s government for reasons including how it’s managed past Ebola outbreaks and chronic corruption.
— Dieudonne Dirole and Ope Adetayo
Adetayo reported from Lagos, Nigeria. Sebastien Kitsa Musayi in Butembo, Congo, Chinedu Asadu in Abuja, Nigeria, and Mike Corder in the Netherlands contributed.

Sliding student scores spark fresh calls to revisit how we're teaching math
Vast research on how kids learn not always translating into classrooms, professor says
Earlier this week, Kendra Corbett stood at a blackboard breaking down an addition question for her Grade 3s, laying out step by step how to determine the answer and occasionally testing out suggestions her students called out.
A little later, she split her class into groups. Some youngsters played math games while others worked on an assignment using base ten blocks — manipulating the small plastic cubes, bars and squares (denoting units of one, 10 and 100, respectively). Corbett settled in with a handful of kids for a focused lesson on ordering numbers from least to greatest. All the activities allowed for practice learning three-digit numbers.
"We assume kids come in knowing what numbers actually mean. If they can count to 10, that doesn't necessarily mean they understand what 10 represents," said Corbett, a teacher in Upper Grand District School Board in Orangeville, Ont., some 60 kilometres northwest of Toronto.
"If they don't have the foundation of knowing what numbers actually mean and understanding of magnitude, then they're really going to struggle later on."
Knowledge and understanding of math rests on building blocks that students usually start developing in primary school. But with recent international and provincial assessments warning about sluggish and waning math skills among Canadian students — a slide that pre-dates the pandemic — some experts say we should revisit how we teach math and pay numeracy the same attention literacy has received in recent years.
What worries Canadian mathematician John Mighton are the changes happening over time, specifically the growth in students who are slipping to lower levels — where some can only handle basic math or are considered below functional numeracy — and the wider impact of that trend.
"That's a real threat to our country, to our economy, even to our political system. How can you think your way through problems that involve risk or probabilities or science if you can't do the simplest math?" said Mighton.
"It's a tragedy that we think math is not as important as it as and that we're not doing something about it."
Back in 2002, Mighton founded JUMP Math, an education charity that's grown to work with students and teachers in K-8 schools across Canada and abroad.
Teaching novices a new concept takes a different approach than teaching those already fluent in a topic, he says, yet much math instruction of the past 20 years has treated kids like experts before they're ready.
"From day one, you're given a lot of rich problems … highly contextualized, lots of complexity, lots of language. People don't feel they're really giving kids math unless they're doing that kind of problem," Mighton said.
"We mistake the end where we want to get kids to — we want them to be great chess players, great problem solvers — with the means to get them there," he said.
"Guide kids more, scaffold more, give more practice, build foundational knowledge, so the kids can become experts …When you do that, kids become much better problem-solvers."
Building a solid foundation and then strong reasoning and problem-solving skills are especially important amid the rise of artificial intelligence, he says.
"It's a dangerous idea that kids are just going to be able to deal with all the challenges that are coming from AI … if they don't have any domain-specific knowledge, particularly in mathematics.
"You're going to be so easily fooled and misled and you'll make disastrous decisions if you don't understand the math."
Not a return to rote learning
As with the recent shift toward more explicit, structured and phonics-led literacy teaching, there's a growing call for more systematic, teacher-led, direct instruction in math.
That doesn't mean rote learning, Mighton says, but does mean relying on evidence-based practices. He encourages teachers to use screenings, for instance, and regular low-stakes assessments to help them to make adjustments that propel students' progression.
There's a wealth of research about how children learn — on their attention spans, their ability to absorb information, barriers to that, and more — yet that research doesn't always translate into classrooms nor into the training that aspiring and working teachers receive, says neuroscientist Daniel Ansari, a professor of psychology and education at Western University in London, Ont.
He also advocates breaking up math learning into multiple, simplified steps, because it helps developing minds more readily pick up information.
"Sometimes teaching can assume that children start out as experts and they are required immediately to focus on their understanding, explaining their answers. And these sorts of things can overwhelm their cognitive systems and thereby prevent information making its way into long-term memory," he said.
Ansari says educators can absolutely strike a "balance between explicit instruction and letting children discover things working by themselves," but adds teachers must keep in mind what's developmentally appropriate and what learners are ready for.
Take timed practice — a.k.a. those "mad minute" sheets with rows of addition, subtraction, multiplication or division questions to be answered as quickly as possible — as an example.
Introduced too early, it overwhelms cognitive capacity, Ansari says. But once students have some time to learn and a bit of practice, "mad minutes serve as a way of increasing and deepening their fluency — and then it can also become something really fun."

Rather than touting a "back to basics" mentality, Ansari instead suggests we consider "how can we improve things further, pick some things that we maybe discarded too early? Keep some things we're doing right now, but reassess some others."
Back in Orangeville, Upper Grand K-12 math lead Ashley Kozak has overseen a multi-pronged plan to improve early math learning. It includes central math facilitators, creating new teaching resources, employing an early math screener and, for the schools with the greatest need, sending in support teachers to deliver focused tutoring.
Updated math training for Grade 1 and Grade 3 teachers and principals has also boosted educator confidence, Kozak says, adding the board saw improvement in its latest EQAO results.
While she loves seeing kids' "a-ha" moments when visiting math classes, she says it's even better seeing students confidently approach the next questions.
"It's more than memorization. It's about problem-solving. It's about making those connections," she said. "Seeing that ... makes me feel like 'OK, we got this. We can do it.'"
