The security alert issued by MI5 regarding a Chinese state-owned conglomerate accused of conducting espionage in the UK reveals the extent to which British intelligence remains concerned about Beijing’s influence, and risks casting a shadow over UK-China cooperation at a time when the bilateral relationship is enjoying a revival.
The UK’s domestic security service on Wednesday warned researchers and academics to cease work with the China Academy of General Technology (CAGT), an organisation MI5 described as a “significant threat”.
The CAGT, which is also known as the China General Technology Research Institute, is accused of paying UK academics working in sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence and cybersecurity for “research that directly improves MSS technical capability for espionage”. The MSS is China’s Ministry of State Security, its intelligence agency.
China’s approach to intelligence gathering involves hoovering up vast amounts of data, often from unsuspecting individuals who believe they are participating in normal research or consultancy work.
This year the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre warned businesses about Beijing-backed attempts to hack into everyday devices such as wifi routers.
Last year, MI5 issued another China-related security alert, warning parliamentarians about approaches from two LinkedIn profiles thought to be linked to Chinese intelligence.
Wednesday’s alert said academic institutions or researchers should be aware of the 2023 National Security Act, which makes it an offence to engage in conduct that is likely to materially assist a foreign intelligence agency. The warning is likely to send a chill through the UK’s cash-strapped higher education institutions, which have for years turned to China for funding and collaboration opportunities.
The UK is one of the leading countries to partner with China’s higher education sector. In May, China’s education ministry announced 219 new transnational education partnerships, with more than a fifth of the approvals being with British universities. That puts the UK at the top of the list of partner countries, ahead of Russia, France and Italy.
Chinese students are also the largest group of non-EU international students in the UK, generating about £600m a year for the higher education sector.
There has been growing concern in the UK that partnerships with China pose a risk to national security. The 2023 Intelligence and Security Committee report on China said UK academic institutions “provide a rich feeding ground for China to achieve both political influence and economic advantage” and flagged the risk of China “directing or stealing UK academic research”.
In this case, MI5 said that more than 100 academics linked to the UK had contributed to projects funded by the MSS via the front company. The areas of interest were AI, cybersecurity and steganography, the embedding of hidden data in pictures online.
Sam Goodman, the senior policy director at the China Strategic Risks Institute, said UK academics were “between a rock and a hard place” when trying to navigate areas of advanced interest that could be of interest to Chinese intelligence. “There is a lack of a coherent steer from government on something like AI. It isn’t particularly clear on AI at this juncture what levels of collaboration we can have with the Chinese,” Goodman said.
Analysts say the UK should do more to highlight which areas are of potentially dual-use interest to Chinese intelligence and provide more guidance to universities and academics.
“It’s all very well issuing these warnings,” says Charles Parton, a senior fellow at the Royal United Services Institute. “Actually far more important, surely, is a consideration of which technologies can be cooperated with China, and which can’t.” He said naming specific Chinese companies as a risk would not help UK researchers to do due diligence on every potential partnership. “The Chinese are not stupid. If they want to hide the origin of someone, they’ll do it,” Parton said.
Meia Nouwens, a senior fellow at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said more clarity was needed on the UK side to help guide researchers working in sensitive fields.
Nouwens said: “A problem has been that in the past there hasn’t been a great deal of discussion of what areas of research constitute a national security risk. Without understanding the limits are of what the UK seeks to protect, it is impossible to have a conversation about managing risk.”
The MI5 alert specifically accused the CAGT of being a front for China’s intelligence. But any research institution in China is ultimately controlled by the Chinese Communist party. “Research institutes that are conducting research on areas of strategic interest for China such as technology will have oversight from the party-state,” Nouwens notes.
That does not mean any collaboration with Chinese educational institutions is inherently dangerous, but it does mean UK academics working in sensitive fields will feel increasingly uneasy about working with a country that has financially underpinned the UK’s higher education sector for decades.

) India is among the top countries with 90% of the world's chewing tobacco-related health burden, and South Asia is the "epicentre" of chewing tobacco, according to new research published in The Lancet Global Health journal.
Researchers estimated that chewing tobacco contributed to 251,000 deaths globally in 2023 -- there were 241 million chewing tobacco users globally, with use peaking among individuals 60 to 64 years old, they said.
The analysis, part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) and covering 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, distinguishes the burden of chewing tobacco from that of other forms of smokeless tobacco, the team said.
"Chewing tobacco is not a uniform public health problem, and our findings show that a relatively small number of countries bear an overwhelming share of its health burden," lead author Gabriela Gil, research scientist at Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME), University of Washington, US, said.
"Understanding how patterns of use differ within these populations is critical to designing more effective prevention and tobacco control strategies," Gil said.
The researchers said despite decades of progress in tobacco control, the global prevalence of chewing tobacco use has remained relatively unchanged. Stroke and lip and oral cavity cancer were found to comprise much of the health loss attributable to chewing tobacco use globally.
South Asia had the highest concentration of chewing tobacco use, with 14.6% of people aged 15 years and above chewing tobacco products in 2023.
The region accounted for 2,10,000 chewing tobacco-related deaths -- about 84% of the global total, the study estimated.
However, more than 90% of chewing tobacco-related deaths and disability burden among men was found to occur in 10 countries, including India, Bangladesh, China, Pakistan and the US.
Among women, more than 90% of the burden was concentrated in countries, including India, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Indonesia, Myanmar and China.
The researchers said the figures reflect total deaths and disability, meaning countries with larger populations may account for a greater share of the burden even if their rates are not the highest.
Patterns of chewing tobacco use also varied substantially by age and sex.
"These findings show why chewing tobacco control cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach," senior author Emmanuela Gakidou, professor in the department of health metrics sciences at IHME, said.
"Prevention and cessation strategies need to reflect how patterns of use differ by country, age, and sex, as well as the cultural and social factors that shape tobacco use in each setting," Gakidou said. PTI KRS

Though I have treated thousands of patients since, Nov. 6, 2022 — the day of a record hot New York City Marathon — still weighs on me. Around the three-and-a-half-hour mark of the race, the finish-line medical tent filled. Inside, I was volunteering as a medical provider and an amateur runner, assigned to a row of cots in the moderate-severity zone. The unseasonably climbing temperatures were taking a visible toll on athletes of all levels.
A volunteer wheeled into my zone a middle-aged man — I’ll call him John — who had collapsed at the finish line. I asked him his name; he answered without hesitation.
“Can you tell me where we are, John?” I asked. His eyes roved the tent’s plastic ceiling.
“Nick’s house,” he said. His skin was flushed.
John’s oral temperature read 107 degrees. He had been mistriaged. I grabbed a senior physician from the critical care area: “We need to upgrade this patient immediately. Heat stroke.”
We quickly moved John, cut off his soaked singlet, and began cooling him with our last bags of ice. The tent’s only cold-water immersion tub was already occupied by a young woman I recognized from club running in Central Park. Likewise overheated, she was deliriously swatting at the attending physician. To worsen matters, the tent’s only electrolyte analyzer was backlogged and every vital-signs monitor was in use. We rationed monitors based on who would benefit most.
In the middle of Manhattan, flanked by some of the nation’s best hospitals, we were practicing resource-limited field medicine.
Thankfully, no one died that day. Credit is owed to thousands of volunteers who sacrificed 12 hours of their Sunday, some sprinting to bodegas for more ice.
But goodwill is not a safety system. Even now, each time I am an event physician, I think about John — his mistriage, the dearth of supplies, the mere minutes that could have cost his life. The question that bothers me most: Why weren’t we adequately prepared?
It is tempting to dismiss stories like this as niche, but as endurance event popularity and global temperatures rise, these scenes are increasingly predictable. That same year at the hot, humid Brooklyn Half Marathon, 16 participants were taken to the hospital. Yes, these events are voluntary, and runners, one could argue, ought to understand their individual risk. Heat acclimation, pacing, and hydration are participant responsibility. I don’t disagree. But when an event swells to the size of a city — the New York City Marathon had nearly 60,000 finishers last year — climate risk is no longer solely a personal matter. It is a public health matter with the ability to strain local systems.
Of note, several races already are adapting to rising temperatures: adding warning flags, moving start times earlier, shifting dates, canceling outright. Decades ago, Grandma’s Marathon, held in Minnesota every June, actually quantified and shared the impact of their strategies to reduce runner morbidity. After it added a half-marathon option and an earlier start time, aid tent utilization dropped. Twin Cities Marathon reported similar information, though without detailed analysis of risk reduction methods. At the elite level, the International Olympic Committee formed a working group on heat risk ahead of Tokyo 2020, where heat illness accounted for 96% of marathon and race walk medical tent admissions. Those games became the first in Summer Olympic history to publish invaluable epidemiologic data such as diagnoses, core temperatures, and minutes-to-cool, which continue to inform Olympic planning.
This March, due to heat risk, the Los Angeles Marathon controversially allowed runners to collect marathon finisher’s medals at the 18-mile mark. Nearly 1,000 runners took this option, and the race charted 652 incidents of injury or illness. We know LA Marathon’s numbers only because they shared them. Many don’t — and incidence data alone models neither climate-related medical sequelae nor the efficacy of mitigation measures. Consequently, we are left with questions rather than lessons learned. Were these illnesses and injuries because of the 18-mile option, or despite it? How were aid needs affected?
Shortly after the LA Marathon, the contiguous United States experienced its hottest summer ever recorded. Several states hosting large fall marathons have high chances of above-average temperatures, including New York, Pennsylvania, and California. On top of long-term climate change, this year’s El Niño (recently deemed “super status”) may exacerbate extreme heat and humidity. Though these predictions exist weeks ahead of events, their impact on preparedness is nebulous.
The answer to “Why weren’t we adequately prepared?”may be simple: The data that could have prepared us was not adequately used. Goodwill is not a safety system — but evidence could be.
To run safe, large-scale events in a warming climate, organizers should use a shared evidence base that allows them to predict race-specific resource needs and evaluate safety interventions. Every major race generates a veritable treasure trove of data — chip times, pace decay, did-not-finish rates — all tied to tens of thousands of runners’ basic demographic information, all cross-referenceable with real-time, publicly available climate conditions.
Critically, medical data are missing.
Medical operations at many major races are contracted to third parties, and there is no shared standard for what gets recorded, how, or by whom. Even municipal special-event permits rarely explicitly require medical data collection as a condition of approval. At one event, a contractor may run a sophisticated, proprietary digital system. Another may rely on paper forms and one veteran’s instincts. What could be a living, cumulative evidence base — one that gets smarter every race — is instead fragmented and opaque, if it exists at all. Furthermore, smaller, less-resourced events — which comprise the majority of U.S. races — are left without objective best practices from leading events.
It doesn’t have to work this way. If, with participant permission, the New York City Marathon analyzed and reported de-identified tent encounter data against variables such as climate, its organizers could predict, rather than guess, event resource needs. Other races would learn what to capture and how to protocolize it. If all World Marathon Majors —popular global races including the NYC Marathon with over 300,000 runners collectively last year — followed suit, the standard for data-driven planning in the entire sport would shift.
Potentially lifesaving and cost-saving decisions to shorten courses, redistribute staff, streamline, or expand resources could come from quantified inputs, in conjunction with prior experience. Somewhere in that data is the next John, along with the ice, monitor, and tub that should be ready to receive him. As a physician, I am afraid of losing a patient to a condition we know how to prevent. As a runner, I don’t want to lose a friend. The finish line should mark the end of a race, not a life.
Vibhu Krishna, M.D., M.P.H., is a senior resident physician in the Division of Occupational, Environmental & Climate Medicine at UCSF. She is an avid runner with a background in emergency medicine, event medicine, and public health consulting.

Anyone with ovaries who lives long enough will experience menopause. While menopause is a natural transition in midlife, it can strongly affect a person’s quality of life and their current and future risk of heart disease, osteoporosis and other issues. So you might think that whether someone is experiencing or has gone through menopause would be noted in their medical records.
But when we and our colleagues examined the electronic medical records of almost 240,000 women, only 12% included mention of menopause, even though more than half the women reported separately that they were experiencing this transition. Our findings, published in the journal Menopause, reveal a major gap in how clinicians capture basic information about women’s health.
The menopausal women we examined are from a broader group of 400,000 who participated in the All of Us Research Program, a nationwide study run by the National Institutes of Health to compile a wide range of health data from at least 1 million Americans. We looked at how information about menopause was included in electronic health records and how this information differed by demographics, such as age, education, race and income.
Because study participants filled out health surveys upon enrolling, we could track discrepancies between their own reports of menopause and what was in their medical records. Age at menopause and symptoms, such as hot flashes or sleep disturbances, were also largely missing from the medical records and survey.
Missing links
Many aspects of menopause, and the diversity in women’s experiences with it, remain poorly understood.
For example, when menopause begins, as well as how disruptive its symptoms are, can vary greatly. Some women experience extreme hot flashes, sleep disruptions and brain fog, while others do not. One woman may go through natural menopause at age 45, and another at 54. Both ages would be considered normal, but that timing can affect current and future health in distinct ways.
Electronic medical records offer an unmatched opportunity to investigate these knowledge gaps, enabling researchers to study the experience of hundreds of thousands or even millions of people using routinely collected data.
Such large-scale studies may shed light on how menopause symptoms change over time and who is more likely to experience them; how markers of heart disease, bone health or mental health track with menopause; how social determinants of health, such as ethnicity and access to healthcare, affect someone’s lived experience of menopause; and countless other unanswered questions.
Closing the data gap
Our study is not the first to point out how inconsistently menopause status and symptoms are recorded in healthcare settings and electronic health records. But it systematically highlights the enormity of the gap, showing that menopause is often not even recorded at all.
It’s not clear why menopause is so rarely documented in electronic health records. It may be because menopause is not a disease, so it does not generally occur to clinicians to note it as a diagnostic code. It may feel obvious or irrelevant to diagnose or measure. It’s possible that patients themselves often don’t bring it up unless their symptoms are severe. Healthcare providers routinely ask middle-aged patients about their reproductive health – for example, when they had their last menstrual period – but this information rarely ends up getting documented in the electronic health record.
As we see it, not capturing this information is a colossal missed opportunity to drive vital research and improve personalized healthcare. Our team is developing a short, simple questionnaire about menopause status and symptoms for patients to fill out as they check in for medical appointments. These responses could then be added to their medical records for use by both their healthcare team and researchers. We are also developing a computer-based approach to infer menopause-related information from other data in a woman’s health record or genetics.
Finally, we are exploring the All of Us dataset to identify systematic differences – for example, in patients’ cultural background or income level, specific health system practices, urban versus rural settings – that might be linked with whether menopause data gets recorded in medical records. These associations can point to targeted ways to encourage its collection.
It’s impossible to research, and treat, what’s not measured. Capturing the menopause transition is an essential step to improving healthcare for women in midlife.
Audrey Hendricks, University of Colorado Anschutz and Nanette Santoro, University of Colorado Anschutz

Restaurant named after Xi Jinping attacked by Chinese nationals in South Korea
- Published
A restaurant in South Korea named after Chinese leader Xi Jinping has been vandalised by a group of Chinese nationals who fled home right after the attack, police say.
Surveillance footage from the restaurant in Seongnam, a city south of Seoul, shows four masked men storming the premises in the early hours of 24 September, smashing furniture and spraying lacquer.
The restaurant's owner told local media he picked the name Xi Jinping because he "wanted it to be the best Chinese restaurant [in South Korea]". He added that "There was no political intent".
The restaurant has been running for eight years but only began getting demands for a name change over the past year, The Chosun Daily reported.
The owner said that in August last year, when news broke that Xi would be attending the Asia Pacific Economic Co-operation Summit in South Korea, he received dozens of phone calls relating to these demands. Some people even offered money, he said.
"People claiming to run businesses in China proposed large sums if we changed the name," he told The Chosun Daily. "They were persistent."
In April this year, someone filed a complaint with South Korea's Ministry of Intellectual Property regarding a dish on the restaurant's menu called Xi Jinping Special Rice, but the ministry eventually closed the case, finding no issues.
The owner said last week's attack was the largest one he's experienced over the past year, telling local media the property damage amounted to about 15 million won ($11,100; £8,400).
Xi Jinping restaurant closed for five days following the attack and reopened on Tuesday. The owner says his team is now considering a new name for the eatery.
Police on Tuesday said the four suspects were Chinese men between the ages of 20 and 40. After the attack they are believed to have fled to Shanghai and Yantai, a city in China's Shandong province.
Police say they are planning to request red notices from Interpol for the four men. These are not arrest warrants, but rather requests to police around the world to detain someone pending extradition.
Xi Jinping restaurant serves a wide range of Chinese dishes, although its menu also includes some South Korean offerings, according to screenshots shared online. Google reviewers have given it an average score of four out of five stars.

Riot police clash with students as education protests rage in France
- Published
Riot police have clashed with protesters as thousands of students demonstrating over education standards disrupted more than 700 schools in France on Friday.
Fires have burned in the streets as high school pupils and others objected to a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms and run-down buildings.
The protests began last week in Paris and have spread across the country, with cities including Montpellier, Nantes and Marseille affected.
French justice minister Gerald Darmanin said things had "gone from high-school student demonstrations to a public order disturbance".
- School protests send shivers down French government's spine 
  - Published4 hours ago
On Friday, a 17-year-old was arrested on suspicion of attempted homicide after protests in Belfort, north-eastern France, where a police officer was targeted.
At least 65 staff members have been injured in the unrest, the education ministry said.
In the Paris suburb of Pantin police charged at protesters and made arrests after projectiles where thrown at officers.
Meanwhile, in Strasbourg tear gas was deployed as police feared conditions would become more hostile, according to the Reuters news agency.
Rubbish bins have also been set on fire in Rennes and Paris.
"As far as we're concerned, we've won - our school is closed this morning," Lola, a 16-year-old protester, told the AFP news agency on Friday.
She said police actions had made things worse.
"It makes us even angrier - the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us," she added.
Police published pictures of some of the items they had seized from demonstrators, including petrol bombs, an axe and so-called mortar fireworks.
"Significant damage" had been done to school facilities, the education ministry said, after attacks on school gates, entrances and fences.
Nelson Mandela high school in Nantes suffered more than €2m (£1.7m) damage, according to the regional government, after fire destroyed its glass entrance and some areas inside the school.
The blockades and protests started last week before spreading to hundreds of schools across the country.
Students say school hours are too long, classrooms too hot and too many members of staff are off work.
It comes at a crucial time for French President Emmanuel Macron, six months before next year's presidential election.
Budget cuts planned, which will impact on education funding, have infuriated the young protesters.
French Education Minister Édouard Geffray said on Friday that the movement had been hijacked by non-students.
He told French broadcaster BFMTV that teachers had said "the people in front of me were not my students".
Parents have also been worried that their children have become caught up in a wave of violence and unrest.
At the Claude Monet school in southern Paris, 53-year-old Anya was looking for her son.
"We banned him from coming. I hope he isn't here, but he did leave the house," she told AFP. "We're afraid the situation might escalate."
Darmanin, the justice minister, said prosecutors had been asked to hold parents liable for damage caused by their children and "pay for repairs".
He said since the start of the movement, about 2,000 people - most of whom were children - had been taken into custody.
Many French unions have given their support to the protesting students.
Education union SNEP-FSU, public services union SNUEP-FSU and Solidaires have all called for members to support them.
Solidaires Trade Union Federation said in a statement: "Let's not let them fire on our children.
"Secondary school pupils have the freedom of assembly, association and demonstration."

From Beckham to Bale - ranking the best British exports this century
- Published
Gazza's baggy Roman shellsuit, John Charles plundering black-and-white goals in Turin, King Kev's floodlit perm dazzling Volksparkstadion terraces, Glenn Hoddle's minuscule Monegasque shorts.
They were all trailblazers and trendsetters, their tales relayed through continental dispatches and espresso-fuelled Saturday morning showreels.
Yet what was once an exotic European escapade for Britain's star footballers is now a well-trodden pilgrimage, as an increasing number of players eye opportunities further afield.
Eight of England's most recent World Cup squad are currently playing abroad - from Munich to Madrid, and Milan to the Middle East - while Scotland have even more overseas, predominantly in Serie A.
So while we acknowledge and applaud the groundwork put in by those early jetsetters, this week we're looking at the best British exports since the turn of the century.
I've ranked my top 10 below - you can have you say in the comments, too.
10. Kieran Trippier - Atletico Madrid
Kieran Trippier was seemingly deemed surplus to requirements at Tottenham after the north London outfit's Champions League final defeat by Liverpool in 2019, but the defender managed to renew his career under Diego Simeone in Spain.
The right-back became Atletico Madrid's first English player in almost a century, and then helped Los Rojiblancos win only their second La Liga title since the turn of the millennium, breaking the Barcelona and Real Madrid stranglehold.
It was the first trophy of his career, and Trippier returned to the Premier League after his Spanish sabbatical renewed, refreshed and ready to enjoy a successful spell at Newcastle.
9. Fikayo Tomori - AC Milan
John Charles, three-times winner; Jimmy Greaves, with Milan in 1961-62; and Gerry Hitchens, with Inter the following season, were the only British players to clinch a Scudetto before Juventus' Aaron Ramsey ended a wait that stretched back more than half a century in 2020.
Ramsey's Turin expedition, though, was inconsistent and expensive, and while Ashley Young then helped Inter win a first title in 11 years, his San Siro stay lasted only 18 months.
So the Scudetto winner we're plumping for here is Milan stalwart Fikayo Tomori.
The England defender lifted the prize in 2021-22, earning a spot in the Serie A team of the season on the way. And, despite ups and downs under various bosses since, the 28-year-old is now into his seventh season with the European giants. A quietly impressive feat.
8. Jadon Sancho - Borussia Dortmund
Jadon Sancho's career may not have continued on the trajectory many expected when he departed Germany in a £73m move for Old Trafford, four years after initially leaving Manchester, but his time at Dortmund was an undoubted success.
It was brave, as a 17-year-old, to reject Manchester City and move to a new country, but the young winger was vindicated with rapid progress at Dortmund.
In his second season, Sancho scored 12 goals and added 18 assists in 34 Bundesliga games, the following term he netted 17 times.
In fact, by the time Sancho left Dortmund aged 21 he'd scored 50 goals and made 64 assists across 137 games in all competitions, winning a German Cup and finishing runner-up in both the European Golden Boy prize and the Kopa Trophy for the world's best young player.
More than that, he helped establish a pathway for young British prospects to grow and develop abroad that many have followed since.
7. David Beckham - Real Madrid, LA Galaxy, AC Milan & PSG
It was tempting to include Bradley Wright-Philips, a man who followed a half-season stint at League One Brentford with a move to New York Red Bulls, winning a pair of Golden Boots, three Supporters' Shields and netting more than 100 goals during his time in the Big Apple.
But if we're talking Major League Soccer impact then there's only one winner. David Beckham swapped the Galactico comforts of Real Madrid, where he spent four seasons and collected a sole La Liga crown, for a Hollywood welcome at LA Galaxy.
Beckham's presence was at times questioned, especially when spending loan spells in Milan, but the England captain and global superstar brought a huge amount of eyeballs and allure to the American game. He left with silverware, too, twice winning both the MLS Cup and Supporters' Shield.
There was room for a five-month stay in Paris before the midfielder hung up his iconic Preds, winning Ligue 1 and waving an emotional goodbye in 2013.
6. Scott McTominay - Napoli
Maybe it's the tomatoes. Scott McTominay wouldn't touch one back in Manchester, but since moving to southern Italy he boasts the glow of a man loving both the local Neapolitan cuisine and his football.
The Lancaster-born Scot has undergone a slick transformation. Few would have expected him to veer from United squad player to cult hero mentioned in the same breath as Napoli's greatest adopted son, Diego Maradona.
But McTominay, with a little help from compatriot Billy Gilmour, has thrived in the football-obsessed maze that is Naples, firing the club to only a fourth Scudetto in history with 12 goals from midfield during his debut Serie A season.
It landed him the league's MVP award.
Finishing runners-up last term, McTominay has already etched his name in Napoli folklore, with more goals - and tomatoes - likely to follow.
5. Owen Hargreaves - Bayern Munich
Owen Hargreaves is something of an anomaly. You could argue he shouldn't count as an export given he was born and raised in Canada, before moving to Bayern Munich aged 16.
Indeed, he's the only player to represent England without having previously lived there. But winning 42 Three Lions caps legitimises his inclusion.
Born in Calgary, having also represented Wales at youth level, Hargreaves cleaned up on the silverware front during his seven seasons in Munich - winning four Bundesliga titles and several German Cups.
Yet his most impressive achievement came in Europe.
Then a 20-year-old, yet to be capped by England, he played 120 minutes in central midfield alongside captain Stefan Effenberg as Bayern beat Valencia on penalties at San Siro in 2001.
Several British players previously lost European Cup finals for foreign clubs - Kevin Keegan with Hamburg, Laurie Cunningham at Real Madrid, Steve Archibald with Barcelona and Chris Waddle at Marseille.
But Hargreaves became only the third to win it - and only two have done so since. Dortmund's Paul Lambert in 1997 was the first, we'll get to the others in a moment.
4. Jude Bellingham - Borussia Dortmund & Real Madrid
Well done for those of you who guessed. Yes, Jude Bellingham has joined the list of British players to win the Champions League for a foreign club.
Bellingham, a teen sensation at Birmingham, followed Sancho's playbook by first moving to Dortmund, where he blossomed into one of the most sought-after midfielders in Europe.
Bellingham became Dortmund's youngest ever goalscorer and also the youngest English player to start a Champions League match. Three productive seasons in Germany was enough evidence for Real Madrid to agree a deal worth more than £100m for him.
He hit the ground running, scoring 23 goals in all competitions as Madrid won both La Liga and the Champions League, and finished third in that year's Ballon d'Or.
3. Harry Kane - Bayern Munich
It was a tight call between Bellingham and Harry Kane. The midfielder boasts the accolade of becoming European champion, after all, but Kane's individual form at Bayern Munich is simply staggering and nudges him into third spot.
To date, Kane has scored 101 Bundesliga goals in 98 games - that figure stands as 152 goals in 154 games overall for Bayern Munich.
The Three Lions captain has shattered all kinds of records in Bavaria. He won the European Golden Shoe in his debut season, the first Englishman since Kevin Phillips to do so, and is the fastest player in Bundesliga history to hit a century of goals.
Oh, and Kane finally won the team silverware he craved for so long, too. He now has two Bundesliga titles and a German Cup to his name, though the Champions League - and potentially a Ballon d'Or - remain the ultimate target.
2. Steven McManaman - Real Madrid
Was Steven McManaman underappreciated? He perhaps didn't earn the number of England caps his talent deserved. In fact, the last of those 37 Three Lions outings came before he won a second Champions League with Real Madrid, despite pleas from club team-mates such as Zinedine Zidane that he should be given a recall.
The marauding winger's move to Madrid in the summer of 1999 was unique - he was the first English player since Laurie Cunningham in 1982 to feature for Los Merengues and the first to move to the Bernabeu directly from the Premier League.
It came at a time when Spanish football was harder to consume for UK audiences, before the peak Revista de la Liga era, making McManaman, renowned for his dribbling and creativity, something of an enigma.
But the Bootle-born midfielder enjoyed an impressive four-season stint in Spain, scoring a volley against Valencia in the Champions League final win of 2000 and coming off the bench to collect another winner's medal two years later, adding to two La Liga successes.
1. Gareth Bale - Real Madrid & LAFC
There is, however, one clear leader when it comes to the best British exports since the turn of the century - and potentially of all time.
Gareth Bale, the Welsh marvel, who has more Champions League winner's medals than the rest of this list combined. Five of them, in fact, across a nine-year spell that saw Real Madrid dominate Europe's showpiece competition.
Bale's commitment to Los Blancos' cause was sometimes questioned - he did make it clear Wales, and golf, were his priorities - but his return was still impressive.
The flying forward scored 106 goals in 258 games, with three of those coming in Champions League finals, including an outrageous overhead kick in 2018.
His short stint before retirement in Los Angeles was less memorable, but still yielded a Supporters' Shield and MLS Cup triumph, where he scored a last-gasp leveller before LAFC won on penalties.

A video showing smoke emerging from a skyscraper is being shared on social media (here, here, here) with the claim that it shows Iranian missile attacks on Israel. Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows the damage caused by Iranian missiles launched at Israel in 2026.
Fact: This video shows a fire that broke out at Marina Pinnacle, a 67-storey skyscraper also known as Tiger Tower, in Dubai in June 2025. Hence, the claim made in the post is False.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to a video posted on X featuring similar visuals by nexta tv in June 2025. The post was captioned, “Dubai skyscraper engulfed in massive fire — nearly 4,000 people evacuated from the building. Fortunately, there were no casualties. Rescue teams responded quickly and assured that the residents of the complex are now safe.”
Taking this as a clue, we conducted a relevant keyword search and found media reports featuring the viral visuals (here, here, and here). According to these reports, a 67-storey skyscraper known as Marina Pinnacle, also called Tiger Tower, had caught fire. The Dubai Civil Defence took six hours to completely extinguish the blaze. The Dubai Media Office reported that there were no casualties.
We also reviewed the location of Marina Pinnacle in Dubai on Google Street View and found that the buildings and other visual details match those seen in the viral video.
To sum up, an old video of the Dubai Skyscraper Fire is being falsely shared as a video of an Iranian missile strike on Israel.

Are Ethiopians marching back to war in Tigray?
- Published
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
Why has fighting broken out now?
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
Who are the TPLF?
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
Why has the peace deal faltered?
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
Who is backing the TPLF?
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
What is the government's position?
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
What do we know about the bombing in Tigray?
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
What is being done to stop the fighting?
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Could the fighting spread?
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

Jeremy Strong, now infamous for his dedication to method acting, recently admitted he doesn’t feel the “need to apologize” to those he works with who may feel he is taking the process “too seriously” on a recent episode of The New Yorker Radio Hour podcast.
The actor, who stepped into the role of tech billionaire Mark Zuckerberg for Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” out Oct. 9, was asked by podcast host and New Yorker editor-in-chief David Remnick how much he feels his method approach is helpful to the director and fellow castmates when filming, or, on the opposite end of the spectrum, how much it might throw them off.
“I think I can’t really speak to that,” Strong began. “Of course, it is never my intention to interfere with anyone else’s experience or anyone else’s way of working. First, do no harm, right? But commit to fucking what you’re doing, and utterly.” Remnick then interjects to ask whether Strong gets frustrated with others on set who may not be so committed, to which the “Succession” actor responds, “No, just meaning that I’m just there to commit utterly to serving the material.”
Popular on Variety
He continued: “So, if some people feel that I’m taking it too seriously, or it changes the molecules in the room in a way that makes something uncomfortable, I guess that’s something that I don’t feel that I need to apologize for, because I believe, and I think the directors that I work with all believe, that it’s in service of the material, and I personally think that a lot of the reactions to it are of a personal nature.”

Haryana-NCR petrol pumps to deny fuel to vehicles without valid PUC

Petrol pumps in Haryana-National Capital Region (NCR) districts will be required to verify pollution under control (PUC) certificates before refuelling of vehicles from October 1. Vehicles without a valid PUC certificate will be denied fuel under the Centre’s air pollution control measures.

Deep Dive

As sure as the sun rises, Crohn’s disease is most definitely not juvenile idiopathic arthritis. But government policy doesn’t seem to understand that.
I’m a pharmacist, and I started a specialty pharmacy in the small town of Sidney, Neb. My pharmacy patients drive miles and hours across the sun-drenched Nebraska prairie to see me at my pharmacy. They are often overjoyed to arrive at my counter to pick up medications like Rinvoq. No longer do they have to deal with remote mail-order pharmacies — they can come to my pharmacy anytime to speak with me and pick up their medications for things like Crohn’s disease in person.
While I am glad to sell my patients their Rinvoq, there is a downside that I never tell them: I sometimes sell them their medications at a staggering loss to the pharmacy.
The reason for that loss has nothing to do with my patient’s disease. Rinvoq carries an FDA orphan designation for juvenile idiopathic arthritis, a childhood arthritis that many of my patients do not have. Because my hospital is a critical access hospital, manufacturers can prevent me from buying any orphan-designated drug at the government discount price, no matter what it is being used to treat. The designation follows the molecule, not the diagnosis, so a Crohn’s prescription gets handled as though it were a juvenile idiopathic arthritis prescription.
The problem here is 340B, a government drug discount program that allows the sale of discounted medications to places like hospitals and certain kinds of clinics (i.e., “covered entities”) and allows them to keep the profit to help with things like medication access, service expansion, staffing, operations, and patient care.
When the Affordable Care Act brought hospitals like mine into the program in 2010, it came with a caveat. Some of the newly added covered entities, critical access hospitals among them, were shut out of 340B pricing on drugs carrying an orphan designation at the manufacturers’ discretion, meaning drugs the Food and Drug Administration has designated to treat a rare disease or condition affecting fewer than 200,000 people in the United States.
While this seems simple enough, many of these medications have more than a single use, and if a medication has an orphan designation, it does not have to be sold be sold at 340B discount prices even if it is currently being used for a non-orphan indication, depending on the manufacturer.
The Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) has tried to fix this before. In 2013 the agency issued a rule saying the exclusion should apply only when an orphan drug is actually used for the rare condition it was designated for. A federal court vacated that rule in May 2014, holding that HRSA lacked the authority to issue it. HRSA reissued the same position as interpretive guidance, and in October 2015 the same court struck that down as well, this time finding it contrary to the plain language of the statute.
Congress had written the exclusion around designation, and the court said only Congress could rewrite it around use.
Practicality was part of that fight. HRSA’s guidance told covered entities they could not buy orphan drugs through 340B unless they could track the indication, and in 2013 almost no small hospital could. That objection is now expiring.
Which brings me to what HRSA published on Aug. 3. The agency announced a 340B rebate pilot that takes effect Jan. 1, 2027. Instead of buying at a discount, covered entities will buy at full wholesale price, dispense the drug, submit claims-level data, and wait for a rebate.
Manufacturers can choose whether to take part. Covered entities like my pharmacy cannot. Once HRSA approves a manufacturer’s plan, my pharmacy has no option to keep buying those drugs the old way, and the savings will arrive as approved by the manufacturer after the medication has left my counter in a patient’s hands. That is a hard thing to ask of organizations with famously small margins, if there is any margin worth mentioning.
The pilot itself is narrow. It reaches only the drugs on Medicare’s negotiated price list for 2026 and 2027, which HRSA estimates at under 5.5% of 340B sales, and Rinvoq is not among them.
But HRSA has reserved the right to expand the model, and the agency puts the reporting cost to covered entities at roughly $34,000 a year per entity. The manufacturers are footing the bill for the IT platform of this new program to get the data and transparency they have been seeking for years. The data feed will carry the details of every transaction, including what was dispensed, how much was dispensed, and how it was covered. It is the exact machinery that did not exist in 2013, but could today if one more data field is included in the requested data feed.
This brings us back to how Crohn’s is not juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
Rinvoq has nine FDA-approved indications, and two of these carry orphan designations, juvenile idiopathic arthritis and giant cell arteritis. The 2021 Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General report that reviewed 40 high-spending Medicare medications found that, for Xgeva and Prolia, the share of dispensed units for their orphan indications amounted to around 1%. Orphan drug protections apply narrowly to the rare disease and do not apply when the same drug is developed for a common disease.
A patient today drives 45 minutes to my specialty pharmacy that they utilize as their local pharmacy. Their Rinvoq is for Crohn’s, but because the medication carries an orphan designation for a childhood arthritis, federal law treats their Crohn’s prescription as though it were one, and I lose money filling it.
I am not asking to be left out of it. If my pharmacy has to build the reporting anyway, I want the data to be worth what it costs us.
That takes two things. HRSA can add the diagnosis to the claims data it is already going to collect, which is one more field on a transmission being built regardless.
Congress has to do the rest, by amending the orphan exclusion so that it turns on what a drug is treating rather than on what it was once designated to treat. The court has already said that second half is Congress’ job, and the usual objection — that nobody could tell the difference — is about to stop being true.
Transactions like these have contributed to pharmacy deserts and shrinking pharmacy choice. Soon my patients may find themselves on hold all over again with a remote specialty pharmacy they never chose. Crohn’s is not juvenile idiopathic arthritis. My patient knows it, their gastroenterologist knows it, and starting in 2027 the claims data could know it too. All that is left is for the law to catch up.
John Mildenberger, Pharm.D., M.B.A., is the specialty pharmacy manager, senior clinical lead pharmacist, and community pharmacy compliance officer at Sidney Regional Medical Center in Sidney, Neb.

The Republic of Ireland’s press conference on Saturday on the eve of its second Nations League match against Israel in Serbia was cut short as head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions from Israeli journalists.
Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in Hungary in its first match on Tuesday following a turbulent build-up in which the Irish squad voted to fulfil the fixture despite unease amongst the team over the war in Gaza.

With the return leg taking place on Sunday in Backa Topola after the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) refused to host the match at home for security reasons, it was the Ireland manager’s pre-match press conference that gave rise to new tensions.
One journalist questioned Hallgrimsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday during a Flydubai flight from the UAE to Israel, which Emirati judicial authorities and Israeli officials have described as a “terrorist act”.

Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.
Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.
But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.
Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.
Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.
Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”
But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.
Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.
On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.
Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.
The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.
Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”
He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.
The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.
Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

Ovulation. Endometriosis. And especially: menopause. These once taboo words — among others — have become part of our daily vocabulary and conversations, a sign of greater interest in, and knowledge of, women’s health.
Yet even as women’s health has been receiving more attention than perhaps ever before, women remain poorly represented in clinical trials, and female health poorly understood compared to male health. Much of the attention remains focused on the reproductive aspects of women’s health.
This led the journal Science to plan a special issue dedicated to women’s health, published Thursday. “Biomedical science has come a long way over the years, and it has become increasingly clear that there are sex-dependent differences in many diseases that do not involve reproduction and that occur at all ages,” according to the introduction.
The issue was edited by an all-female team (Yevgeniya Nusinovich, Sacha Vignieri, Joana Osório, and Sarah Ross), which named political attacks on women’s rights and health care, as well as funding cuts affecting research in this area, as urgent motives behind their planning.
“The importance of doing clinical trials specifically in women has gained recognition over the years, and it’s something that should continue to be elevated, including as research funding cuts are targeted at this and other women-specific research, threatening the quality of women’s future healthcare,” they said.
Beyond reproductive health
The issue features reviews of research that aim to highlight recent findings on the impact of sex-dependent biological differences beyond reproduction, as well as deep dives into the latest discoveries about menopause and the pregnant body.
Women experience functional pain at about twice the rate of men, with persistent pain in the pelvic area often becoming a debilitating factor in their daily lives. The issue takes stock of recent research that identified sex-specific mechanisms of pain. The review highlights the impact of sex hormones, immune-neural interactions, the gut microbiome, and the role of ovarian hormones in pain, though it also highlights the deficit in efforts to understand female pain.
“Women are desperately waiting for concrete answers that might help eliminate the common ‘all in your head’ approach to their illnesses,” the authors of the review wrote.
Another review focuses on the impact of XX and XY chromosomes on aging and disease, making the argument that their impact is so significant that sex chromosomes should always be considered when developing precision medicine strategies.
Other contributions do take on issues of reproductive health. They call for a rethinking of menopause research and treatment, with an approach more tailored to the individual; investigating the immune system’s role in preparing for and carrying out a pregnancy; and considering the role of the ovary’s postmenopausal function.
Nusinovich, a senior editor at Science, said she considers research on post-reproductive health to be different from reproductive investigations “because the focus here is not on improving reproductive success but on considerations for a woman’s own health.” She said she considered including other medical conditions unrelated to reproduction in which sex differences play a role, such as cardiovascular and metabolic disease, “but it didn’t seem like there would be enough new biological insights (with mechanisms, not just clinical observations) for entire coherent review articles.”
The dearth of this research highlights the existing gaps. “We tend to focus on women in their reproductive years, and a lot of that I do think is driven by what institutions are willing to fund,” said Tiarney Ritchwood, a professor in the department of public health at Wake Forest University School of Medicine who focuses on health equity. “But I do think that the greater discussion on women outside of the reproductive years is really important.”
For other experts, however, including a strong focus on reproductive health is inevitable.
“There is still so much we don’t know about women’s health simply because sex is often considered an extraneous variable,” said Nicole Woitowich, executive director of the Northwestern University Clinical and Translational Sciences Institute who did not take part in the issue. “For many years, women’s health was synonymous with reproductive health. I’m glad we’ve broadened this perspective to consider the influence of sex across human physiology. Yet, pregnancy and menopause, for example, remain unique aspects of women’s health and we are just beginning to understand how these events can shape our long-term health and well-being.” Woitowich recently researched the reporting of sex differences in NIH-funded papers.
The attention to menopause is especially welcome, said Omisade Burney-Scott, a menopause justice advocate pushing to make menopause care inclusive through her platform, the Black Girl’s Guide to Surviving Menopause. Still, Burney-Scott said, the journal article is lacking some perspectives — including discussion of early menopause due to gender-affirming care, or a medical intervention — that shows the limitations of current research. “We must take into account the significant impact of environmental factors, such as systemic oppression (racism, classism, homophobia, transphobia, carcerality) on menopause health outcomes,” said Burney-Scott, who was not involved in the issue.
Women’s health needs funding, not just attention
For the editors, the value of the issue also resides in showing how much there is to learn about women’s health. “Out of all the special issues I’ve encountered, this one stood out to me as highlighting a ton of open questions and things that are just beginning to be studied, especially in the article on chronic pain, pointing to many opportunities for future productive research,” said Nusinovich.
The experts STAT spoke with agreed that a high-profile journal such as Science dedicating an issue to women’s health sends a strong signal to the scientific community. “It will contribute to increased awareness and even potentially increase research in this area, hopefully in the years beyond the reproductive ones,” said Ritchwood, “but none of this goes anywhere if there’s no funding dedicated to it.”
Unless there is a broader dissemination of these findings — and, just as importantly, a clear call to fund women’s health research — the impact will remain limited, she said. “The public is not reading Science, so it can’t just be something that we just communicate to ourselves. … Are we going to see it in Vogue, or something that the public is actually looking at?” she said.
Paula Schneider, the CEO of the Institute Advancing Women’s Health, a global nonprofit that focuses on improving women’s clinical care in midlife and after, noted that there is a lag in adopting new knowledge in clinical practice.
“Research is only half the equation. Even the evidence we already have on women’s midlife health too often doesn’t make it into clinical practice,” she said. “We need to close the gap between what’s known and what’s done, so that as discoveries like these arrive, women know what to ask, doctors know how to answer, and the system knows what to do next.”

In a setback for publishers worried about the effects of AI search, a US federal judge has dismissed lawsuits filed by Chegg and Penske Media against Google. The companies accused Google of antitrust violations in products like AI overviews, which have led to decreasing traffic at numerous sites. However, US District Judge Amit Mehta has ruled that Google’s conduct is not illegal under antitrust law.
The lawsuits were filed in 2025, and Google requested a dismissal earlier this year. Chegg, an education and learning platform, claimed in its lawsuit that Google illegally scraped its educational content. This allowed Gemini models to essentially recreate that content and reduce the site’s traffic. Penske, which owns publications like Rolling Stone and Variety, filed a similar case that alleged lost traffic. Specifically, the publisher claimed it was unfair that sites indexed for organic search would also have their content harvested for AI answers, with no way to opt out.
These arguments did not sway the judge, who noted that Google’s implicit agreement with websites is not legally relevant. “Plaintiffs have pleaded only that they have an ‘expectation’ that Google will send them search traffic if they make their content available for free,” wrote Mehta. “But an expectation is not an agreement. It is simply how a general search engine works.”
Since Google never had a formal arrangement with either Chegg or Penske, antitrust law doesn’t apply. And Mehta is aware of the legal issues surrounding search. He also heard the DOJ’s long-running search antitrust case against Google, eventually finding that Google violated the law. However, the government didn’t get the harsh penalties it wanted in that case.

What to know about Brazil's election pitting Lula against Flávio Bolsonaro
- Published
Brazilians are voting on Sunday in a general election in which the two front-runners for the presidency bear very familiar names.
The incumbent, veteran left-wing leader Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva, will be challenged by 11 candidates, the most prominent of whom is right-winger Flávio Bolsonaro.
In the last election four years ago, Lula narrowly defeated Flávio Bolsonaro's father Jair, but the tumultuous aftermath of the election, which saw Jair Bolsonaro convicted of plotting a coup after thousands of his supporters stormed the Brazilian Congress, has had a lasting impact on the nation's political life and this election.
Here's what you need to know.
The man not on the ballot
Jair Bolsonaro, the right-wing former army captain who governed Brazil from 2019 to 2023, will not be running for president in this election.
Not only is the 71-year-old barred from standing for office, he is also serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after he lost the 2022 election to Lula.
Due to recurrent health problems, he is currently under house arrest rather than in a cell, but he has had restrictions imposed on him prohibiting him from posting on social media or making public statements.
Despite these restrictions, his shadow - and sometimes his moving and talking image - looms large over this election.
At the event where Flávio Bolsonaro officially launched his presidential campaign, an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro endorsed his son's candidacy.
When pressed by the Supreme Court about the deepfake, Jair Bolsonaro's lawyers may have denied he had given his permission for its use, but there is nevertheless little doubt that Flávio Bolsonaro has the backing of his father.
What do the polls say?
While there are 12 candidates running for the presidency, there are only two who have reached double figures in the opinion polls, and they are Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro.
BBC Brasil's poll tracker shows them both hovering around the 40% mark, with Lula slightly ahead of Bolsonaro.
The other 11 candidates are polling at 4% or less.
If none of the candidates gains 50% of valid votes in the first round on 4 October, the top two contenders will proceed to a run-off election on 25 October.
The opinion polls suggest a run-off is highly likely - but with a relatively high number of voters still undecided just days before the election, an outright win cannot be entirely ruled out.
BBC Brasil's poll aggregator suggests that at the end of September, 9% of voters were either still undecided, or planning to spoil their ballot, cast a blank ballot or not go to the polls at all.
Brazilians who are 16 years of age or older are entitled to vote and it is compulsory for those aged between 18 and 70 who are literate, with a fine imposed on those who do not cast a ballot.
Almost 160 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this election and, with polls typically surveying just thousands of people, the end result can differ considerably from the indications given by surveys.
What does Lula stand for?
Lula, the 80-year-old candidate for the left-wing Workers' Party, has been president three times already.
He served two consecutive terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - and was widely praised for lifting millions out of poverty during this time with the help of a cash-transfer programme called Bolsa Família.
The former metalworker left office with record approval ratings of over 80%, but his party was later rocked by huge corruption scandals.
Lula himself spent more than 18 months in prison between 2018 and 2019 after being convicted of corruption and money laundering, charges he has always denied.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for the presidency in the 2022 election, in which he beat Jair Bolsonaro by 1.8 percentage points.
When he started his third term in office, he vowed it would be his last, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 later this month.
There is no doubt he remains a towering figure in the left. But while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.
His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
During Lula's latest term in office, relations with his US counterpart Donald Trump have been rocky.
Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".
In another thinly veiled reference to both his rival Flávio Bolsonaro and those in the Trump administration who would like to see the right-wing candidate win, the Brazilian leader has also warned that he would not tolerate "foreign and local enemies of democracy" interfering with the polls.
What is Bolsonaro promising?
Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, is Jair Bolsonaro's eldest son and has been serving as a senator since 2019.
The younger Bolsonaro is running for the right-wing Liberal Party (PL) and, while he is widely seen as less confrontational than his father, he is appealing to the followers of the older Bolsonaro by promising to broadly continue in his footsteps.
During his time in the Senate, the trained lawyer has advocated a tough-on-crime stance, calling for longer sentences and laxer gun laws, arguing that "decent citizens" should be able to defend themselves from criminals.
He has successfully lobbied for the US to declare Brazil-based criminal gangs Comando Vermelho (CV) and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) as Foreign Terrorist Organizations, a move that was opposed by Lula.
The younger Bolsonaro has also courted evangelicals and the agricultural industry as part of his campaign.
He has said that he will cut what he says are unnecessary regulations and "get the state off farmers' backs".
Quizzed in an interview with Globo in August on whether he still believed - as he had said in 2019 - that climate change did not exist, he acknowledged that there had been "extreme climate events", but insisted that these events were "cyclical".
Flávio Bolsonaro has actively courted Trump and members of his administration by portraying himself as a loyal ally during a meeting at the White House in May.
More recently, he promised to join the US-led anti-crime alliance that the Trump administration has dubbed "Shield of the Americas", should he be elected.
What are the main issues worrying voters?
Up until a few months ago, Brazilians told pollsters that crime and security were their main concerns.
But in the weeks leading up to the election, a scandal involving a jailed banker accused of orchestrating one of Brazil's largest financial fraud cases has pushed corruption to the top of the list.
The banker, Daniel Vorcaro, is well connected and has ties to many powerful people in Brazil - both on the political right and left.
Flávio Bolsonaro acknowledged asking Vorcaro to bankroll a biopic about his father after voice recordings emerged in which he could be heard asking for 134 million reais ($25.9m; £19.5m).
Police have since then opened an investigation into Flávio Bolsonaro for suspected corruption and money laundering over the financing of the film.
But pollsters say Lula's campaign was also hurt by the Vorcaro scandal, after alleged links emerged between the disgraced banker and an ally of Lula, the Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes.
Moraes is the man who presided over Jair Bolsonaro's trial and has made a number of subsequent rulings about the conditions of his detention.
A police report suggested that Vorcaro had made numerous calls and sent a number of messages to a phone number which officers say is linked to Moraes.
The investigators say Vorcaro asked the person with whom he was communicating for help avoiding arrest.
Moraes has denied any wrongdoing but these latest revelations mean that, in the crucial weeks before the election, attention shifted away from the allegations against Flávio Bolsonaro to those against the Supreme Court justice.
Lula has tried to distance himself from Moraes, saying that "no one is above the law", but his rival has already pounced on the allegations against the judge to make political hay.
"Voting for Lula means voting for Moraes," Flávio Bolsonaro told his supporters at a rally, using the right's intense dislike of the judge to shore up his own support.

Srinagar, Sep 22: The Jammu and Kashmir National Conference Additional General Secretary and Rajya Sabha Member Choudhary Mohammad Ramzan Tuesday said that the discontinuation of the December 5 holiday commemorating the birth anniversary of Sher-e-Kashmir Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah and attempts to obstruct the elected government’s efforts to restore the holiday, raise serious questions about respect for the democratic mandate and public sentiment.
He said the manner in which BJP legislators reacted to the proposal in the Assembly to restore the holiday on Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s birth anniversary reflected their narrow-mindedness, communal outlook and hostility towards the National Conference.
Choudhary Ramzan, as per a party statement, said Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s stature and legacy do not depend on any official holiday. He said the changes made to official holidays associated with July 13, Martyrs’ Day, and Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah’s birth anniversary are viewed by the National Conference in the context of its historical legacy and the memory of those who sacrificed their lives for the political rights of the people. He stressed that the martyrs of July 13, 1931, hold an important place in Jammu and Kashmir’s political history and that their sacrifices cannot simply be erased from public memory.
