Odisha rape accused injured in police encounter after firing at cops
The victim lodged a first information report on Thursday at Nayapalli police station, alleging that an unidentified masked man entered her rented house
A man accused of raping a 26-year-old woman at gunpoint in Odisha’s Nayapalli was injured in a police encounter in Chandaka on Saturday after he allegedly opened fire at a police team while trying to escape, police said.
The accused, Sridhar Panda from Ganjam district, sustained two bullet injuries to his left foot and was admitted to Capital Hospital in Bhubaneswar for treatment, Bhubaneswar deputy commissioner of police Saravana Dr Vivek M Saravana said.
“The accused fired two rounds at the police while attempting to escape. The police fired in self-defence,” Dr Saravana said, adding that Panda will be arrested after his recovery.
According to police, Panda was traced to Chandaka during the investigation into the alleged rape. When a police team attempted to apprehend him, he allegedly opened fire and tried to flee, following which the police fired at him.
The victim lodged a first information report on Thursday at Nayapalli police station, alleging that an unidentified masked man entered her rented house in Behera Sahi on Wednesday evening when she was alone and threatened her with a gun before allegedly raping her.
According to police, the accused flashed a lighter styled as a gun, or a fake gun and then tied the victim up using her scarf. He also smashed her mobile phone.
“The accused had two cases of mobile theft against him earlier and had recceed the house to steal a mobile phone. But when he saw the girl alone, his motive changed,” a senior official said.
The accused allegedly held the gun to her head and threatened to shoot her if she raised an alarm. He then fled the house after the alleged assault.
Police said CCTV footage showed the accused walking from the area towards CRP Square, where he boarded an Ama Bus. He later allegedly stole a motorcycle and fled. Investigators have been examining CCTV footage along the route to trace his movements.
A scientific team visited the scene and collected samples as part of the investigation.
The Odisha State Commission for Women on Friday took suo motu cognisance of the incident and directed the Bhubaneswar DCP to submit a report within 15 days.
Panda was being treated at Capital Hospital and would be formally arrested after his recovery, police said.

iPhone Duo vs. iPad Mini: Which Apple device is right for you?
The iPhone Duo could replace your tablet, but there's something to be said for having a separate device.
The iPhone Duo is slated to arrive October 23, and on the surface, the new foldable has a lot of overlap with Apple's smallest iPad, the iPad Mini. The Duo's interface is very iPad-esque, with a similar screen size and better hardware. However, whether the iPhone Duo can truly replace an iPad depends significantly on what you need from such a device.
Ditching your tablet for a foldable phone comes with both pros and cons, especially around more complex or longform tasks. From what we've seen, the Duo manages to bridge the gap between the two technologies fairly competently. Notably, a new iPad Mini is rumored to arrive sometime soon, and reportedly brings tech specs more on par with the Duo. Since that day hasn't arrived yet, for the purpose of this discussion, we're going to compare the iPhone Duo with the most recent seventh-generation model of iPad Mini from 2024.
How the iPad Mini and Duo compare
One of the biggest deciding factors between the Duo and Mini is the vast price difference. The iPad Mini starts at $600 for the 128GB model and goes up to $900 for 512GB, with cellular-equipped models costing an extra $150. The Duo starts at $2,000 for the 256GB model and goes all the way up to $3,200 for 2TB of storage. You could purchase the new 256GB iPhone 18 Pro ($1,200), plus an iPad Mini, and it would still cost less than a Duo. With such a significant price difference, you should be absolutely certain you're interested in the iPhone Duo before purchasing. Consider trying it out in an Apple Store first to see how it feels.
Specs-wise, the Duo comes out on top in processing power, boasting an A20 Pro chip versus the Mini's A17 Pro, a 7-core GPU compared to the iPad's 5-core and 12GB of RAM compared to eight. The Duo's camera is also substantially better, with both a 48 megapixel main and ultra wide lens, compared to the Mini's 12MP wide camera. However, this stat isn't particularly compelling — if you decide to invest in an iPad over the Duo, you presumably have a phone with a better camera.
The iPad Mini wins in display size, with an 8.3-inch display compared to the Duo's 7.6-inch inner display. However, both of the iPhone Duo's screens are ProMotion displays that reach up to 120Hz, while the iPad Mini's screen is 60Hz.
Some might prefer the capabilities of iPadOS, too: although the iPhone Duo's software is different from a normal iPhone, it's still not the same as the iPadOS. At most, the Duo's OS can support an app on each half of the inner screen, while the iPad has much more robust multitasking. If you use the Apple Pencil a lot, the Duo's limited compatibility is also a point to consider, as the phone will only support the USB-C version of the device, not the Pencil Pro. Said support also won't be there at launch, but will arrive later in 2026.
Which device is the better fit for you?
These tech specs paint a clear picture: the current model of iPad Mini only has the upper hand in screen size, the unique capabilities of iPadOS and better Pencil support. If two-screen multitasking is enough for you, you don't use the Apple Pencil Pro and price isn't an issue, in theory you should get the iPhone Duo. That being said, it's worth considering that the true evolution of the Duo's crease won't become clear for a long time — it might be best to wait and see how it fares.
However, not everything is answered by a side-by-side spec comparison. A large part of what determines which of these two is better for you comes down to whether you like to separate your tech. For some people, having an iPad is ideal for spending time locked in on a project or book without the many distractions that often come with a phone. It also means you won't drain your phone battery during long iPad sessions. Conversely, if you want to switch quickly between a typical phone view and an expanded one, then just as quickly close it back up to make a phone call, a Duo is the way to go.

Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
- Published
Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months.
The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police.
Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer.
The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.
Here's what we know.
Busisiwe Mahlangu
Case 1
Busisiwe Mahlangu's body was found in Kempton Park on 15 July 2026, the first of a string of bodies found in Ekurhuleni within a two-month period. The 37-year-old was found naked with her hands bound with cable ties.
Police arrested a suspect, believed to be her partner, two days after her murder. He has been in police custody since then and has not been linked to the other deaths that followed.
Itumeleng Kekana
Case 2
Itumeleng Kekana, 32, was the second woman whose body was found in the same area on 3 August 2026.
The young mother disappeared in July and her body was found badly bruised, partially clothed and dumped on a bridge in Kempton Park.
No arrests have been made so far.
Nomfesane Mjobo
Case 3
Nomfesane Mjobo's body was found on 26 August, also in Kempton Park.
Few details around her death have been released but like most of the victims, she was found partially or fully naked with bruises.
No arrests have been made.
Unknown woman
Case 4
Police confirmed the discovery of an unknown woman, in her 20s, on 7 September. The woman's body was found floating in a river in Olifantsfontain wearing only her underwear.
No further details have been shared about her death and no arrests have been made.
Gracious Nkomo
Case 5
Gracious Nkomo was the fifth woman whose body was discovered, again in the Kempton Park area.
Her partially clothed body was found on 10 September along a road close to South Africa's busiest airport. No arrests have been made in the 28-year-old's death.
Elizabeth "Tsontso" Moselakgomo
Case 6
Elizabeth Moselakgomo was the sixth woman to be found, after a highly publicised nationwide search for her. The 38-year-old went missing while out for a daily run near her home in Kempton Park.
Her body was found badly bruised and partially clothed on 12 September. It was the discovery of her body that really raised the alarm about the spate of killings. No arrests have been made in her case.
Unidentified woman
Case 7
Police confirmed the discovery of another body just two days after Moselakgomo was found. The body was found in Olifantsfontein on 14 September, but police have withheld her name as her family has not yet been informed.
No arrests have been made.
Dineo Motapane
Case 8
The body of Dineo Motapane, 38, was discovered on 15 September just two days after she was last seen alive.
Motapane's battered and partly burned body was found on the side of the road in Springs, another part of Ekurhuleni.
She leaves behind a young child. No arrests have been made in her case.
Jabulile Ntimba
Case 9
The body of Jabulile Ntimba, in her 30s, was discovered half-naked and wrapped in a sheet on the side of a road in Boksburg on 17 September. This was the ninth body found in Ekurhuleni.
According to police, it appears Ntimba was killed because of a possible love triangle. Three people, two women and a man, were initially arrested for her grisly murder but the man was released due to insufficient evidence.
The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice.
Ntombifuthi Nxumalo
Case 10
The body of Ntombifuthi Nxumalo, the 10th body found in Ekurhuleni, was discovered at a cemetery in the Tembisa neighbourhood north-east of central Johannesburg on 26 September. She was found naked with serious head injuries as well as stones near her body.
This has led to police believing she may have been stoned to death.
A 36-year-old man was arrested a day after Nxumalo's death after he had travelled to another province. He faces a murder charge.
Unidentified woman
Case 11
The body of a yet-to-be identified woman was found in Springs on Sunday - the 11th body found in Ekurhuleni.
The grim discovery was made by a security company patrolling the area.
The woman was found in an open field, but no further details have been shared.
No arrests have been made.
Boitumelo Gift Mashita
Case 12
Boitumelo Gift Mashita was shot and killed on Monday in Tembisa Ekurhuleni. The 23-year-old woman was on her way to work when she was gunned down and her belongings were taken.
Police say her estranged husband, who they suspected of being responsible for her murder, was later found dead inside his vehicle in Midrand.
Police have not found any link between this case and the discovery of the other bodies.
While most of the bodies were found in the same area, police confirmed the discovery of another body about 39 miles (63 km) away from Ekurhuleni on 20 September.
The body of a young woman, believed to be in her 20s, was found wrapped in a duvet in a dam in Soweto, south-west of Johannesburg.
It's unclear if her murder is linked to those in Ekurhuleni.
President Cyril Ramaphosa said the killing of these women and others was a "stain on our national conscience".
South Africa has one of the highest homicide rates, with 5,427 people murdered between April and June this year alone.
South African police statistics do not differentiate victims by gender but the South African Human Rights Commission said last week that 569 women were killed between April and June this year. This works out as an average of six women killed each day.
Police have set up a task team to investigate these murders and have offered a reward of 400,000 rand ($24,000; £18,000) for information that could lead to arrests.

The posters, just like the women holding them, were taking no prisoners.
“Girls don’t need curfews, rapists need consequences,” read one. “Lock your dicks rather than your women at home,” read another.
As hundreds of women walked from the gates of their university campus into the streets of Delhi – where sexual harassment, assault, catcalling and molestation are a constant, daily threat – they shouted together, in a chorus of rage and defiance: “We want justice.”
The fury that has erupted on India’s university campuses over the past week has been double-edged. The trigger was a series of brutal rapes that have taken place in Delhi in recent weeks, including the alleged gang rape of a 17-year-old in a public park close to Delhi university, by three men who posed as police officers.
Just a week earlier, another 17-year-old was gang raped and murdered in Delhi’s Swaroop Nagar neighbourhood, after she went to meet friends. The accused allegedly raped her, stabbed her to death and dumped her body in a field, where it was discovered days later half eaten by dogs.
Rapes of an 11-year-old and a six-year old were also reported in the same month. Last month, a 16-year-old was allegedly raped by the bus driver and conductor after she boarded a sleeper bus in Delhi.
Women who have taken part in protests on Delhi university campuses have condemned these alleged violent rapes on minors as disgusting and unforgivable – but they have also been at pains to emphasise that they are not out of the ordinary.
Fourteen years have passed since Delhi’s infamous Nirbhaya rape case, when a woman was gang raped on a bus and died from her injuries. But while it provoked international outrage and a slew of legislation and government promises, women say that nothing has changed; for them, India’s streets, particularly in Delhi, remain as unsafe as ever. According to statistics, a women is raped in India every 20 minutes – though the real scale is believed to be far worse due to chronic underreporting.
This week, the supreme court said the five successive rape cases “starkly underlined a systematic failure” and they could not help but “draw painful parallels to the Nirbhaya incident of 2012”.
Vaishnavi Dhruw, 21, a history student at Delhi university, was among the female protesters at the “smash the patriarchy” protest march on Wednesday afternoon. “I don’t know a single woman who lives in this city and feels safe,” she said.
While some of the key demands of the protest have been better lighting and policing, Dhruw emphasised that for anything to change, the country requires a deep societal shift where men no longer feel they have ownership over women’s bodies.
“We are not marching for safety, we are here to protest for our freedom, for the most basic right to walk in our own streets,’ she said. “Again and again, women are told to stay indoors, to not go out at night, to cover ourselves, to protect ourselves. When will society tell men in our country not to rape?”
Much of the anger driving the protests has also been prompted by the response by the authorities to the rapes, which women say once again has only been to police their freedoms. Women in Delhi were told to stay out of parks at night, and classes were temporarily halted at one of Delhi’s most prestigious female colleges. Many hostels where female students stay impose strict curfews preventing them from going out at night.
“Instead of going after criminals, you’re going to tell women to sit at home,” said Aranya Rathore, 25, a student at Delhi University. “A demand for more surveillance is not a solution. In fact, it’s going to curtail our freedom more.”
Female students say a lot of their time is taken up by safety logistics – from wearing modest clothes to reorganising their days to ensure they do not travel alone or at night and always having a trackable live location on their phones. There is widespread awareness that should anything happen, the onus of blame – both within the family home and more widely in society – tends to fall on women; as one poster at Wednesday’s march pointed out, “no one ever asks what the rapist was wearing”.
Yet despite their best efforts, many women said it was almost impossible to avoid harassment. Ananya Wig, a 26-year-old a graduate of Delhi University and the founder of Her Huq, a gender-equality initiative, said she has experienced harassment both around university campuses and in public spaces.
She recounted an incident where a driver rolled down his car window and began masturbating as she and female friends got off a rickshaw and walked through the college gates. “This wasn’t at night, it was in the middle of the day,” she said. “I’ve always lived in Delhi and the city has not changed.”
The protests have brought into focus a dilemma faced by many Indian women, who are being educated in greater numbers than any time in the country’s history and have better job opportunities than ever before – but still have to navigate the constant debilitating threats to their safety and the conservative pressures from their families.
“I know so many girls, not just 10 years ago, but even today, who end up choosing educational institutions and jobs and other employment opportunities depending on how close they are from their home,” said Wig. “Not on the basis of their marks, not on the basis of their aspirations, but simply, ‘OK, the shorter the distance is, the more likely it is that I will be safe.’”
Many of the Delhi university students who took part in the marches said that sexual harassment had become prevalent on campus, and have demanded better accountability mechanisms for reporting assault. The university has not responded.
“Delhi University is one of the most prestigious universities in India right now but there are various cases of women being assaulted by professors, sometimes unfortunately also for grades,” said Devyani Sarkar, 24, who is studying for her masters in English at Delhi University. “It’s despicable, but it’s also a living truth.”
Many on the marches said that it was no coincidence the protests took place in the aftermath of India’s “cockroach” movement, which saw hundreds of thousands of young Gen Z Indians take to the streets over education reform.
“My generation is not afraid to stand up and protest. We know that society has to change,” said 17-year-old Subhani. “The days of women being silent is over.”

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

Brazil presidential vote pits Trump ally against Lula, who is seeking 4th nonconsecutive term
Brazilians are heading to the polls for a high-stakes presidential election
SAO PAULO -- Brazilians vote Sunday in a high-stakes presidential election pitting incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, ideological opposites who are each seen as having a shot at an outright victory.
If no candidate gets more than 50% of the vote, the top two vote-getters will head to a runoff on Oct. 25 in Latin America's economic powerhouse. Ten other candidates are expected to garner much smaller numbers of votes on Sunday.
Bolsonaro, 45, is the son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro and an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump. Lula, who at 80 is one of the world’s oldest heads of state, is running in his seventh presidential election and has strengthened Brazil's ties with Beijing.
Trump allies have found support in recent years in some Latin American countries, including Argentina, Colombia and Peru.
Almost 159 million Brazilians are eligible to vote in this tense political showdown.
Where Bolsonaro has leaned into his ideological alliance with Trump, Lula has criticized Washington. He has often spoken about risks of U.S. intervention in the Brazilian elections after the Trump administration imposed high tariffs against Brazilian exports, revoked the visa of the country’s ambassador in D.C. and sanctioned a Supreme Court justice who chaired the probe that ended up resulting in the sentencing of Jair Bolsonaro, Lula's predecessor.
Flávio Bolsonaro has touted his proximity to the White House and insisted Brazil needs to strike better deals with the Trump administration, including the rare minerals economy. Brazil estimates its deposits to hold up to 21 million tons, second only to China. Bolsonaro also has campaigned on releasing his father from his 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup and bringing him back to politics.
Bolsonaro denies he's being helped by the U.S. government. "That narrative won't stick, sorry,” he said at a September campaign event.
Brazilians will also elect 27 state governors, members of state legislatures, all 513 federal congressmen and 54 of the country’s 81 senators in Sunday's vote.
Thomas Traumann, a political consultant based in Rio de Janeiro, says last-minute mistakes by either candidate or by their allies could make all the difference for undecided voters.
“ Polarization in Brazil created a trap. There’s no third candidate. You only have two options, and they fight each other in an atmosphere that becomes worse and worse,” Traumann said. “It is much more a competition of accusations than a competition of proposals.”
Four years ago, Lula beat Jair Bolsonaro by 2.1 million votes — a margin of just under 2 percentage points. At the time, Brazilians were upset with the then-president’s handling of the coronavirus pandemic, his repeated threats against democracy, his attacks on the electronic voting system, and the poor shape of the nation’s economy as inflation was on the rise.
Now, the incumbent faces a tough battle due to an affordability crisis and a corruption scandal that ensnared the same justice who led the investigation into Bolsonaro.
Carlos Melo, a political science professor at Insper University in Sao Paulo, says some voters have grown weary of Lula, who is seeking a fourth nonconsecutive term as president. He is one of the oldest presidents on the continent, along with Trump and Nicaragua's Daniel Ortega, both of whom also are 80.
“Many in the Lula campaign were not expecting such a difficult election a few weeks ago, and it is clear to them that the present election is a tough battle and the next ones, without Lula, could be even more so,” Melo said.
Bolsonaro has seen his political career tainted by several corruption accusations, the latest of them involving a disgraced banker paying him millions of dollars, allegedly to produce a movie on his father's life. More recently, he has been under fire from Roman Catholics who fear he might make too many concessions to his evangelical base.

Hamam al-Hammami, the flydubai co-pilot accused of trying to crash a passenger jet bound for Tel Aviv, told investigators after the plane landed in Saudi Arabia that he wanted to deliberately bring it down and was 'not afraid of death', according to a Wall Street Journal report.
The 29-year-old Omani national is now under investigation as to how he became radicalised, and how someone whose extremist interests had already drawn the attention of authorities was later allowed back into the cockpit.
From a love of flying to radicalisation
According to the Wall Street Journal, Hammami's first aviation employer, state-owned Oman Air, banned him from flying after authorities discovered that he was visiting extremist websites.
People briefed on his background told the newspaper that he was subsequently put through a deradicalisation programme and reassigned to a desk job.
After leaving Oman Air, Hammami eventually found work in the UAE, and Flydubai hired him in February 2026. It remains unclear what information about his earlier history was available to the airline or whether Oman was ever asked to provide it. The WSJ reported that Oman received no requests from other countries for information to vet him for employment.
Investigators are also looking at Hammami's time in Syria.
Born to an Omani father and Syrian mother, Hammami spent part of his youth in Syria during the country's civil war. 
According to people familiar with the investigation cited by the WSJ, authorities are examining whether he began to radicalise while there, when Islamist rebels were fighting Bashar al-Assad's government.
Hammami’s social media also provides a substantial online record that predates the flydubai attack.
More than 3,000 screenshots from Hammami's deleted X account remain available through the Internet Archive.
The posts include deeply conservative and misogynistic views, including statements opposing women working and expressing a preference for religious women who wear the veil.
One post described Hammami creating a fake account to contact Saudi women. In another, he wrote that his wife should not work.
The material does not by itself establish when he became violent or whether his views directly caused the flydubai attack. But investigators are examining the posts alongside his earlier extremist-web activity and his time in Syria to establish whether they form part of a broader process of radicalisation.
The flydubai attack
On September 30, Hammami attacked Captain Smit Machchhar aboard flydubai Flight 1073, using a cockpit crash axe before trying to take control of the aircraft.
The plane plunged more than 16,000 feet in roughly 30 seconds before the badly injured captain managed to open the cockpit door. Passengers and crew then overpowered Hammami, while two off-duty pilots on board helped stabilise and land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia.
After the emergency landing, a Saudi official briefed on his interrogation told the WSJ that Hammami acknowledged that he wanted to deliberately crash the aircraft and was not afraid of death.
The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Israel are investigating whether he acted alone or had links to outside groups, especially Iran.

'He's taught us courage': Friend on Indian pilot hailed as a hero
- Published
When Captain Dharav Gosalia first heard what had happened to his old friend Smit Machchhar, he had one immediate reaction.
"I had goosebumps."
The two men have known each other since they were about 20, when they were neighbours in Ghatkopar, a Mumbai suburb, and began their flying training in New Zealand.
Machchhar was Gosalia's senior. They later spent six years as colleagues at SpiceJet, flying Boeing 737s, before their careers took them in different directions. Machchhar moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022. Gosalia went on to fly Boeing 777s for Air India.
"We have been in touch with messages," Gosalia says. "If there are some routes we have to fly, we discuss destinations and family on WhatsApp and phone."

Sometimes their paths crossed in the air, too. In 2024, Gosalia was flying to London through Dubai airspace when he recognised Machchhar's voice on the radio. Machchhar was flying to Mumbai.
"We greeted each other," he recalls.
On Wednesday, Machchhar was captain of a Flydubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv when another pilot attacked and stabbed him in the cockpit. The Boeing 737 Max was diverted to Tabuk in north-western Saudi Arabia, where Machchhar was taken to hospital.
He remains in a stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Riyadh.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called Machchhar a "true hero", saying he saved the lives of 174 people and prevented a "catastrophic mid-air disaster".
For Gosalia, however, the man at the centre of the extraordinary incident is still "Smit Mac" – the nickname used by his friends and colleagues - and a "very brilliant person".
"Outgoing person, jovial. Very jovial," he adds.
They would meet during layovers in places such as Milan and Bangkok, and play tennis-ball cricket when they were back in Mumbai. Machchhar also helped younger pilots, teaching new recruits and passing on what he had learnt.
"He is a very disciplined flier," Gosalia says.
That discipline was reinforced by years of training, including from former Indian Air Force pilots who moved into commercial aviation.
"That training gives you more focus, more discipline, and more focus on motor skills," Gosalia says.
One part of that training, he says, is known among pilots as "chair flying": rehearsing an emergency procedure while sitting in a chair, mentally running through the sequence and moving your hands to where the relevant switches and controls would be in the cockpit.
The idea is to make those movements instinctive when something goes wrong and there is little time to think.
Machchhar had plenty of experience to draw on. He had more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.
Gosalia says the exact sequence of Wednesday's confrontation will become clearer from the aircraft's flight data and cockpit recordings. But whatever happened inside the cockpit, he says, Machchhar had to make decisions under an extraordinary kind of pressure.
"What happened to him, what he did – he was the commander on the flight," Gosalia says.
For a pilot, there are procedures for an engine failure, a fire or a loss of cabin pressure. There is no conventional checklist for another person trying to overpower you in the cockpit.
And that, Gosalia says, is where courage matters.
"How much courage plays a role? A lot," he says. "This was a threat to life."
Then comes the thought that perhaps best explains why the incident has affected him so deeply.
"Smit has taught us courage. Now we will do the same thing if something like this happens."

Malaysia begins controversial repatriation of asylum seekers to Myanmar
- Published
The Malaysian government has started repatriating around 5,000 asylum seekers from Myanmar, under a controversial deal agreed with Myanmar's military ruler Min Aung Hlaing.
Three ships from the Myanmar navy are scheduled to leave Malaysia later today carrying the first 1,476 returnees.
Human rights groups have condemned the repatriation, saying the returnees face violence, persecution and forced conscription into the Myanmar army.
Malaysia has described the repatriation as voluntary, but has barred the UN refugee agency from seeing or screening the returnees, who have been kept in detention centres.
According to Malaysian prime minister Anwar Ibrahim, these returnees will include Rohingyas: a persecuted Muslim minority who have sought sanctuary in Malaysia in large numbers after being driven out of Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens.
Anwar, whose popularity has fallen sharply this year, says he is responding to growing public hostility towards the large Rohingya population in Malaysia and has no choice but to negotiate with the Myanmar government over their return.
But the move signals a striking shift in attitude.
Anwar, a former political prisoner, has previously presented himself as a defender of human rights and freedom, and called for more to be done to help the Rohingyas. Under him, Malaysia has refused to recognise Min Aung Hlaing's regime, and has been one of the strongest voices in South East Asia pushing for a negotiated end to Myanmar's civil war.
What has changed?
Two things. First, increased economic strain on lower-income Malaysians since the Covid pandemic, which has stirred resentment of the Rohingyas.
Second, the febrile state of Malaysian politics since 2018, when a historic election unseated the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), the ethnic Malay party which had monopolised power for more than 60 years, leading to a revolving door of unstable coalition governments.
Shifting sentiments
For many years there was strong public sympathy among Malaysians for their fellow Muslims in Myanmar.
In August 2017, a brutal campaign by the Myanmar military drove three quarters of a million Rohingyas out of their homes in Rakhine State and into neighbouring Bangladesh. In the years since, dire conditions in Bangladeshi refugee camps have driven those with enough money to make the perilous sea journey to Malaysia in search of sanctuary and work.
While the Malaysian navy and coastguard have long tried to block Rohingya boats from landing in Malaysia, many gotten in via other routes, and for a long time were tolerated. More than 200,000 are now believed to live there, most eking out basic livings from manual labour.
Sentiment among Malaysians started to shift during the pandemic, which hit the country's economy hard. At a time of heightened public fear over the new coronavirus, accusations against Rohingya migrants spread on social media, with demands for their deportation.
In response, the then-government hardened its attitude, saying Malaysia could accept no more refugees and ordering raids on communities believed to be harbouring illegal immigrants.
Much the same has happened in 2026.
In May, an online complaint claimed that Rohingyas had failed to dispose of animal waste properly after the Muslim Eid al Adha festival, igniting a viral social media campaign falsely accusing Rohingya leaders of demanding land and citizenship in Malaysia.
Shortly thereafter, an online petition on Change.org calling for Rohingyas to be kicked out of Malaysia received more than 400,000 signatures, before being taken down.
A PM under pressure
Given Anwar's one-time reputation as a champion of liberal values, he might have been expected to push back against this wave of hate and disinformation. He has said the Rohingyas should be treated humanely.
"We can arrest them, but do not beat, intimidate or humiliate them," he said in a recent podcast interview - although this is exactly what human rights groups have accused Malaysian officials of doing in immigration detention centres.
Nonetheless, Anwar insists that the Rohingya must be expelled.
"They have clearly become a burden," he said in the same interview. "A security burden, an economic burden and a source of hostility among the people."
Some of his former supporters have accused him of betraying his principles. The former head of the Malaysian Anti Corruption Commission, Latheefa Koya, says his decision is "disgraceful, amoral, and shames the nation in the eyes of the international community".
Anwar, though, is under great political pressure. Once described as a perpetual prime minister-in-waiting, he finally got the top job in 2022, but only by forming an uneasy coalition with his one-time adversaries UMNO. Since then he has seen his own popularity plunge and his party lose seats in recent local elections. He must call a general election by early 2028.
"He is in a corner, at his weakest point", says Tricia Yeoh, Director of the Asian Institute for Policy and Engagement at the University of Nottingham Malaysia.
"He has been forced to make concessions to his UMNO partners... There have been several corruption scandals, and his own party is divided. And after four years of telling voters this is what is required to maintain his fragile coalition, they are no longer willing to go along with that narrative."
Instead, Yeoh says, ethnic Malays, who make up more than half of the electorate, are responding to the well-trodden UMNO narrative that they need special support and protection from the state - the kind of racial politics which she says feeds fear and resentment of outsiders.
"It's the same narrative you hear in the rest of the world, about immigrants taking jobs, that we should not be spending our public funds on facilities for them."
Forced home
However, it is not clear how any Rohingyas can be repatriated to Myanmar, where they are not recognised as citizens.
Rohingyas are not permitted to travel inside Myanmar, and are only allowed to live in Rakhine State, which borders Bangladesh. But nearly all of Rakhine State is now under the control of the insurgent Arakan Army, and subject to sustained bombardment by the Myanmar air force. On Monday, the day before the repatriation, the Arakan Army said two bombs killed 49 people at a market in the town of Kyauktaw.
The only place Rohingyas could conceivably be returned to is the state capital Sittwe - but it is besieged and isolated, and even there Rohingyas are confined to wretched camps which are critically short of food and medicine. Rights groups also fear that any men in the group could be forcibly conscripted into the army to fight in the civil war.
Neither Malaysia nor Myanmar have explained how these formidable obstacles can be overcome, nor how their planned repatriation can be consistent with humanitarian principles.
"We all dream of being able to return home one day," said Nur Sadek, a Rohingya refugee rights advocate, "but we want to return because it is safe and because we choose to — not because we are forced to.
"For me, the most important thing is that Rohingya and other refugees affected by this decision are listened to and treated with dignity."

Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.

Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.

Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.
Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".
I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"
More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24.
"I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.
She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.
Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.
Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot.
"Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.
Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.
But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach.
"I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.
Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.

Pink Saheli Smart Card now mandatory for free bus travel for Delhi women
Delhi has made the Pink Saheli Smart Card compulsory for women and transgender residents seeking free bus travel. The move ends paper tickets and shifts the scheme fully to an NCMC-based system.
The Delhi government has notified that women residents can avail free travel on DTC and cluster buses only through the Pink Saheli Smart Card, officials said on Sunday.
The change has been made under the Delhi Transport Corporation (Free and Concessional Passes) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2026.
Under the new arrangement, eligible women residents of Delhi will be able to travel free in both AC and non-AC DTC and cluster buses only by using the NCMC-based Pink Saheli Smart Card.
They will, however, continue to have the option of buying a ticket at the applicable fare for their journey.
According to a notification issued by the Delhi Transport Department, "Female passengers who are residents of Delhi can travel free in Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) and cluster buses, both AC and non-AC, only with the use of Pink Saheli Smart Card (NCMC). However, they will have the option to purchase a ticket at the applicable fare for the journey."
The notification also said that women who are not eligible for the free travel facility can travel on DTC and cluster buses by purchasing tickets at the applicable fare.
The notification added that the provisions will also apply to transgender persons who are residents of Delhi. The Transport Department had earlier directed that the Pink Saheli Smart Card would be mandatory for availing the free travel facility from September 30.
Launched in March this year, the NCMC-based card replaced the paper-based pink tickets that had earlier been issued by the government after several extensions.
Officials said the government will focus on creating awareness about the smart card through depot and in-bus announcements, social media, print media and other channels.
Officials said around 19 lakh women have availed of the smart-card facility since its launch earlier this year.
They added that women who have not yet registered will continue to have access to the registration and card issuance process, as the government rolls out the revised system for free travel.

Flydubai co-pilot attacked captain with axe, UAE official says
- Published
The co-pilot of the Flydubai plane travelling to Israel attacked the pilot with a crash axe in an attempt to take control of the aircraft, the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.
The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv carrying more than 170 people plunged more than 17,000ft (5,200m) two and a half hours into its journey.
Capt Smit Machchhar said he was lying on the cockpit floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside."
Passengers aboard the aircraft were then able to enter the cockpit and overpower the attacker, while on-duty crew travelling on the flight landed the plan safely.
A crash axe is usually kept in the cockpit in case of emergencies.
The UAE attorney general told state media that investigations were ongoing to determine the full circumstances and motives of the incident.
The co-pilot who launched the attack was an Omani national, according to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday that, after being subdued, the attacker called out to the crew, "Kill me, kill me!"
He added: "So, it's clear that he was suicidal… It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane."
He also said the attacker "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination".
The UAE has begun investigating whether the "incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose", according to the country's state news agency.
Machchhar, who was stabbed in the attack, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.
He was in "good health and recovering well", the Indian embassy in the UAE said on Thursday.
The pilot said: "I am confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again."

When Vikash Dhorasoo played for the French national team at the 2006 FIFA World Cup, there were very few people who believed that an Indian could excel on football’s world stage. Ever since Dhorasoo made his debut for Les Bleus, the belief has grown that Indian footballers can do well at the world level.
“It is a shame that we don’t find any Indian players at that level today. I don’t have any doubts that gems do exist within Indian football,” the former AC Milan and Paris Saint-Germain midfielder, who is currently in the city at the invitation of the All India Football Federation (AIFF), told Sportstar.
Dhorasoo, who recently acquired a UEFA Pro Licence in coaching, says that he would love to coach Indian players or an Indian club if the opportunity was right. He will be meeting AIFF officials later in the week to discuss a possible involvement with Indian football.
“I will always be ready to come and help find a way to create new methods, especially because there are a lot of things to do and invent for Indian football.”
The famed Les Bleus midfielder said that it would be great if the Indian government opened the doors to OCI/PIO by agreeing to dual citizenship, at least for sportspersons, and allowed the Indian diaspora to contribute to the development of sports.
Ahead of the Indian men’s team’s meeting with the giant of world football, Brazil, in a FIFA friendly here on Saturday, Dhorasoo pointed out that France played Brazil in a friendly in June 1997 and gained an insight into the game before winning the 1998 FIFA World Cup by beating the same opponent in the final.
“When you go to Brazil, it is football that comes to you. After that friendly, France again played against Brazil, this time in the final. You could tell that they had learned a lot and considered themselves differently than they had before.”
Q: What brings you to India?
A: I was honoured to be invited by the Indian Federation for this great and symbolic game for Indian football. It is an opportunity for me, first, to cheer for India and to keep following the evolution of the game and Indian football from the front row.
It was also a way for me to contact my former AC Milan coach, Carlo Ancelotti, who is now coaching Brazil. It was amazing to reconnect with him.
You recently acquired the UEFA Pro coaching licence; what does that mean for your coaching career?
I just graduated as a professional coach with a UEFA licence, so it means a lot to me to be there in that way. Most importantly, it is always something special to come back to my ancestors’ land. My great-grandfather was from India, and India has always been part of my culture and my DNA.
Would you like any offer to be involved in coaching India?
Maybe one day, and bring the national team to the World Cup. It is a dream for everybody, for me and for all Indian people. But for the moment, I am at the beginning of my story with coaching. Maybe I will start in France. I hope to work with a big team, at a high level, because I want to be a coach at the highest level.
I am in the market now, so I have to wait. I have to continue learning about football, watch a lot of matches and be ready to take on a big post with a big team.
There is a very good possibility [of coaching in India]. It is a big opportunity, and maybe it will be soon, very soon. It is one of my goals also to become a coach in India. It would be a great pleasure, and I have a lot of things to give to Indian football.
Did AIFF invite you or did you communicate an interest to come to India?
They knew that I wanted to come to see this match, and when they knew that, they contacted me to organise everything, including my flight to India. It was a mix of everything - my desire to come and their desire to make this project a reality.
I am following Indian players and players of Indian origin, and I hope there will be many more who come through. Every time I hear about a player of Indian origin, or see a name that looks like an Indian name, it intrigues me.
Do you follow Indian footballers?
Obviously I do. India is very far away, but I come to India regularly. I am interested in Indian football, and I try to become more and more interested because I know that Indian football has to develop and will develop in the next few years. I follow the Indian team, like Ryan Williams, who scored against Panama. Then there is Apuia (Lalengmawia Ralte); I love his skill. He is a technical player, like I was, so I like watching him.
I know that for this match against Brazil, the coach has selected young players to bring a bit of novelty and refresh the team. I am glad that the coach has made a list of young players who could bring new energy and start writing a new page for Indian football, especially after the good result the Under-17 team had against Spanish teams [in 2023] and the fact that the Under-20 team qualified for the Asian Cup.
If a lot of players around the world can play for India, it could be very good for the level of Indian football, and maybe it could also help the other players from India to increase their level.
How do you see the OCI scenario? Do you think the Indian government should allow dual citizenship especially to sportspersons?
I am not in a position to give the Indian government or Indians any indication of what to do with policy. My understanding is that it would be an interesting perspective to think about finding a way to allow athletes from the Indian diaspora to bring their talent to the national team.
Football is a global game. Everyone knows it. The perspective of having India performing at the World Cup would be something huge, both for football and for India and the Indian diaspora.
Either way, I hope India will find a way to get there and increase the level of the team, because it will be huge for everyone.
I want to insist on the fact that it is not only about bi-national players bringing their talent to the team. It is also, and mainly, about structural work in Indian football. It must be focused on youth categories, on having young boys and girls reach that level and giving Indian football the opportunity to progress in a structural way.
The football culture in India is big, especially around Kolkata (Bengal) and Kerala, so it is not as if we are starting from a blank page. I think we really need to work with the youth - the young footballers - to raise the level, have more matches, face big teams and learn.
The match against Brazil will be a good opportunity to evaluate and see what we can do to get to that level. But I am sure that in the next 10, 15 or 20 years, India will produce great talents.
Indian footballers do not play in the big leagues around the world. Is it the reason why Indian football is not succeeding internationally?
It is a shame that we don’t find any Indian players at that level today, because I have no doubt that gems exist within Indian football. It is always a matter of time, of course, a matter of working, and a matter of having young players playing important games. But to me, there is no doubt that in the coming years we will find great players here.
If we look at the dynamics right now, whether it is the youth categories or even the ownership of European clubs, there are perspectives for Indian football. In France, we have the National Technical Directorate of French Football, which thinks a lot about how to train coaches and how to pass that on to the younger generation.
It is obviously not about taking our project and bringing it to India. It is about how we can bring skills and create exchanges so that everyone can progress together.
In any case, it takes resources, methods and time, but there are lots of things to do and invent. And, of course, I am also at the service of India if there is a need to help in many ways.
If I am allowed to make a comparison with France in terms of methods, in France, football has a National Technical Directorate that is designed to train coaches and provide a structural direction for youth football.
My point is not to take the French model and bring it to India. My point is to create bridges between methods and the talent pool and try to find a way to do better together.
Of course, I will always be ready to come and help find a way to create new methods, especially because there are a lot of things to do and invent for Indian football.
But again, I have no doubt that we will find gems here.
If you take the example of French football, 20 years ago it was about finding players who would physically dominate the game. It didn’t work well, and they changed direction.
That is a way for me to say that you can choose the football you want to create, but it takes time.
For me, it is a good initiative. It can be a starting point for something. It puts football in the spotlight. We bring Brazil; that is not nothing.
I hope the stadium will be full. I hope people will watch the match, be interested in it and want to pass that interest on to their children, so that their children want to go and play football.
That is how we are going to develop football, by putting the spotlight on this match and communicating as much as possible, so that everyone wants to watch it.
I hope that the Indian national team playing against Brazil, for example, can have an impact on grassroots football and help people encourage their children to keep believing in their potential.
I think that is good, and they must keep going in that direction because it is a good celebration and, somehow, it is also a way to evaluate ourselves.
I hope that the players who play against Brazil will have a great experience. It will be a difficult match, but they will learn a lot from it.
It will be a huge moment, and for everyone who is on the pitch, it will also be an incredible learning experience. They will learn a lot in 90 minutes playing against Brazil.
I played with a lot of Brazilian players, great Brazilian players. Also, Carlo Ancelotti was my coach at AC Milan, so it will be a good moment.
In France, 20 years ago, maybe more, France played against Brazil in a friendly match. It was a great moment for everybody. We were a big team in France, but playing against Brazil is always very special.
When you go to Brazil, it is football that comes to you. A year later, France played against Brazil, this time in the final. You could tell that they had learned a lot and considered themselves differently than they had before.
That is a great thing. The inspiration that the French team got from playing Brazil paid off in the final.

Watch: Couple describe relief at rescue after whale destroys their yacht
A couple have spoken of their relief to be rescued after a sperm whale collided with their yacht.
Jeremy and Jemma Cooper told the BBC that they were 500 nautical miles off the coast of New Zealand when the boat, the Tai Tam, lurched port side and they knew they'd "been hit by something" - only to see a pod of six sperm whales swimming behind the boat.
As their boat took on water and eventually sank, the Coopers and two other sailors aboard the vessel evacuated to a life raft. Seventeen hours later they were rescued by a container ship.
The couple told the BBC that, despite their ordeal, they would be out on the water again soon.
