The Newport-Mesa Unified School District in Costa Mesa, California, announced it placed a teacher — whom it did not identify — on administrative leave for posting a video of herself saying the U.S. flag made her "uncomfortable" and suggesting to one student, possibly jokingly, that he recite the Pledge of Allegiance to a pride flag displayed on her classroom wall. However …
The video was recorded in 2021, a fact some people omitted from their "breaking" social media posts in 2026. No evidence showed the teacher, who taught English at Back Bay High School, "forced" any students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag, as was falsely claimed in memes and posts using fake, AI-generated images.
A district spokesperson said at the time, "The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues." The statement didn't identify the teacher by name, nor did it specify whether she departed the school because she resigned or because she was fired. People who claimed she was fired didn't offer evidence to support it.
A rumor that a California school district fired a teacher for forcing students to recite the Pledge of Allegiance while facing an LGBTQ+ pride flag circulated online in September 2026.
For example, on Sept. 29, a Facebook user posted a meme (archived) showing three images of a woman smiling, laughing and wearing a rainbow-striped shirt and jacket. Pride flags also appeared on the wall in the background. The meme read, "A California teacher has been fired after forcing students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag. Do you believe she deserved to be fired?"
(David J Harris Jr. via Facebook)
The same user previously shared (archived) the same rumor in late August 2026 with a different image and marked it "BREAKING." Other people shared the same meme, or a similar one, on Instagram (archived), X (archived) and other platforms.
We found these posts contained a mixture of truth, falsehood, speculation and artificial intelligence.
The Newport-Mesa Unified School District in Costa Mesa, California, did once announce (archived) it had placed a teacher — whom it did not identify — on administrative leave for posting a video in which she could be heard saying the U.S. flag made her "uncomfortable" and suggesting to one student, possibly jokingly, that he recite the Pledge of Allegiance to a pride flag displayed on the classroom wall.
However, this all took place in 2021, a fact some people omitted from their "breaking" social media posts in 2026. No evidence supported the claim that the teacher, who was reportedly named Kristen Pitzen and worked as an English teacher at Back Bay High School, "forced" any students to pledge allegiance to the pride flag. Images used in the above meme and other posts that supposedly depicted the educator were in fact AI-generated and inauthentic.
At the time of the incident, a district spokesperson said, in part, "The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues." The statement didn't identify Pitzen by name, nor did it specify whether she departed the school after submitting a resignation or whether she was fired. People who posted the claim she was fired didn't share evidence that the district had terminated her employment.
Via Messenger, Snopes contacted an account possibly belonging to Pitzen to ask questions. We will update this article if we receive further information.
Here are the facts
On Aug. 27, 2021, an educator — reportedly Pitzen, who was listed at the time as an English teacher for Back Bay High School in Costa Mesa — allegedly shared a video on her personal TikTok account in which she said she had packed her classroom's U.S. flag away and appeared to indicate she didn't intend to display it again.
In the clip, she laughed when recalling a story in which a student said her class was reciting the Pledge of Allegiance without a flag, then pointed the camera at a pride flag on her wall. She said she told him, "We do have a flag in the class that you can pledge your allegiance to." She laughed at several moments during the video, suggesting she may have been at least partly joking. No students or other staff were visible in the clip.
People then reposted the video and named Pitzen as its originator, with some X users organizing and calling for her firing that same day. Some users claimed her (now-defunct) TikTok handle on the account on which she shared the video and other clips was @mrsgillingsworth. We could not independently verify whether she truly owned the handle or if the videos originated from a different account.
In the video, she says the following:
Ok, so during third period, we have announcements and they do the Pledge of Allegiance. I always tell my class, "Stand if you feel like it. Don't stand if you feel like it. Say the words if you want. [You] don't have to say the words." So, my class decided to stand but not say the words. Totally fine.
Except for the fact [laughing] that my room does not have a flag. It used to be there but I took it down during COVID because [whispering] it made me uncomfortable. And I packed it away and I don't know where and I haven't found it yet. [laughing] But my kid today goes, "Hey, it's kind of weird that we just stand and then, you know, we say it to nothing." And I'm like, "Oh, well, you know I've gotta find it. Like I'm working on it. I got you." [laughing, shaking head]
In the meantime, I tell this kid, "We do have a flag in the class that you can pledge your allegiance to." And he like looks around and he goes, "Oh, that one?" [laughing, pointing to pride flag]
Following a wave of social media backlash, someone posted on the district's Facebook page the next day — a Saturday — posting (archived) that a teacher had been placed on administrative leave after causing "alarm and concern related to saluting the American flag." The post did not identify Pitzen by name.
(Newport-Mesa Unified School District - NMUSD via Facebook)
On the following Monday, Aug. 30, the district reportedly published a statement saying the teacher (still not identified) was "no longer in the classroom." The statement appeared in news articles, including in the Los Angeles Times:
We are aware that one of our teachers posted a video on her personal social media that caused alarm and concern related to saluting the American flag. We assure you that we take matters like this seriously. Showing respect for our nation's flag is an important value that we instill in our students and an expectation of our employees. The teacher is no longer in the classroom. We follow due process and our investigation continues.
Via email, district spokesperson Annette Franco confirmed the authenticity of the statement. We also asked whether the district fired the teacher mentioned in their statement — or whether the educator resigned. Without naming the teacher, Franco told us, "I can confirm that she is no longer with the District." We also requested comment from current Back Bay High School principal Scott Mazurier, who started at the school in 2024 and was not present during the incident. We will update this article if we receive more details.
The school district's policies include information about "patriotic exercises," including "the reciting of the Pledge of Allegiance." One part of the policy documentation says, "Individuals may choose not to participate in the flag salute for personal reasons."
For further reading, we previously reported about a video allegedly showing a kindergarten teacher saying she had been fired for helping students discover their gender identity.

Amazon's Prime Day has returned for its fall edition, and the Amazon Alexa-powered devices are already on sale. But are the sales actually any good?
There's already the question of whether you want Alexa in your house, and now it's a question of whether the sales are more of a mind game than a real discount. That's thanks to Amazon raising prices across its device categories at the end of August, leaving us with the same product lineup but a worse case to recommend it. Some devices are already on sale right now ahead of Amazon's Prime Big Deal Days for $40 off, but went up in price by $20 just a few weeks ago, cutting that discount into something that feels barely worth the spend.
If you're interested in Amazon's device sales but want the real picture of what the discount is and which devices are worth it, I've got you covered. I've been testing Amazon Alexa speakers since they launched in 2012, and I am also WIRED's resident Kindle tester, which gives me almost too much insight into the price games Amazon plays with these devices. Here's my full breakdown.
Which Amazon Devices Are on Sale Already, and Which Aren’t
Right now, Amazon's Alexa-powered Echo speakers and Fire TV sticks are currently on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days next week (October 6-7). These devices saw price hikes at the end of August, so some of the deals aren't as good as in the past. They do seem to be permanent price changes, though, so if you're certain you want one of these models, this is the best time to buy.
So far, most Kindles aren't on sale yet, but all three Kindle Kids models (the Kindle Kids, the Kindle Paperwhite Kids, and Kindle Colorsoft Kids) are already on sale. (Amazon also announced new versions of these Kindles today, along with the rest of its lineup, so it's up to you whether you want the current on-sale model or to preorder the new one!) If you're looking for a Paperwhite and Scribe, they aren't on sale yet as of this writing. Neither are Eero routers.
But I expect most of those models will be discounted once the event begins. Both Kindle and Eero products also saw price hikes at the end of August, so I recommend buying them only on sale (even if the sales aren't as good as they used to be, since they're similar discounts but on higher prices).
The Best Early Amazon Device Deals
Not all deals are great, especially given the recent price increases. If you're set on getting a new Amazon Alexa-powered speaker, though, here are the discounts (and devices themselves!) that are still worth it.
The Best Early Kindle Deals
If you're shopping for a Kindle, this is the best time to buy since most were hit with price increases. You won't get as good a deal anymore, but it's much better to buy it at a discount on the new price than the full, higher price for the same product. There's also new Kindles that were just announced, so it's up to you if you want to grab an older on-sale model (which all work great!) or wait for the new one.
As of this writing, only Kindle Kids models are on sale ahead of Amazon Prime Big Deal Days, but only one is a good deal after taking the price changes into account.
Other On-Sale Amazon Devices We’ve Tested
Looking for a different device during Amazon's sale event? We've tested several other Amazon Echo and Fire TV devices that are also on sale right now. Here's what else you can consider, and what the discount looks like.
- Amazon Echo Dot Max for $80 ($40 Off): If you're looking for a small speaker with bigger sound than the older Echo Dot, the Echo Dot Max has impressive sound for its size, plus a built-in smart home hub. Its price did increase $20, though, so it feels like it's just $20 off even if it looks like $40.
- Amazon Echo Show 8 (4th Gen) for $125 ($75 Off): While this model is on sale, I prefer the older Echo Show 8 (though it seems rarely available anymore) and the Echo Show 11 since both have better sound. It's a good discount, even off the original $180 price tag, but I'd just spend $25 more and get the better Echo Show 11 if you're set on a new Amazon Alexa-powered smart display.
- Amazon Echo Show 15 for $250 ($100 Off): The Echo Show 15 and Echo Show 21 are on sale and both double as a Fire TV device, with a massive screen, a flat back for mounting, and an included Alexa Voice Remote. I don't love the TV experience, but it works, and the homepage fits a ton of widgets if you want to see multiple at once. Both sizes are discounted, but both models also cost more now, so it's not as good as you'd think for the same device.
- Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max for $45 ($40 Off): If you love Amazon Prime as your streaming service, this is the favorite we've tested of Amazon's Fire TV streaming devices. It's not a crazy discount since it went up $25 in August, but it's still a really affordable streaming stick during this same event.
- Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Kids for $170 ($60 Off): The Paperwhite Kids has everything we like about a Kindle Paperwhite, but adds a cover to protect it from any drops by your kiddo's hands and comes with six months of Kids+ content, which is like Kindle Unlimited but designed for kids. It's a good device, but the discount isn't as good as before; it used to retail for $180, so it's really only $10 off what it used to cost. But you won't find it new for cheaper.
- Amazon Kindle Kids for $123 ($57 Off): This is the cheapest Kindle Kids device, with a 6-inch screen similar to the cheapest Kindle, and it still comes with a colorful cover and six months of Kids+ content like the Paperwhite Kids above. It has the smallest discount out of the Kids devices, and it used to retail for $130, so it's only $7 off the original price. The other Kids models are a better buy.
Which Amazon Device Prices Went Up?
Amazon raised prices across several of its device categories at the end of August. It's not a shocking move, but it hit many affordable products and makes for a worse sale season since we're getting discounts on a higher price tag for no other improvements. Here's a quick breakdown of most of the price changes to help you navigate what sales are good and which are really just bringing you back to the old price.
Either way, I'd only buy an Amazon device on sale now, but it is unfortunate the sales just won't be as good anymore on these existing devices. I expect most, if not all, of these devices to go on sale at some point during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days.

Badenoch says Tories want to have policies 'for everybody' as she defends plan to let people earning £1m to get free childcare
Kemi Badenoch recorded her interview with Laura Kuenssberg yesterday. It is playing out on the programme now.
In it, Badenoch defended her plan to extend free childcare to high earners. (See 9.08am.)
She said:
What we want to see is that people who work harder don’t get punished for doing so. If you earn £100 a pound over £100,000, you could lose £10,000, £20,000 worth of childcare. And we don’t want people to stop working because of that.
Asked if she would be happy for someone earning £1m to be able to get free childcare, Badenoch said it did not matter what people were earning.
But she said the policy was aimed at people caught by the cliff edge.
The kind of people that we’re really targeting [might be] a deputy headteacher who wants to become a head teacher. She goes from £85,000 to £110,000. She’s got three kids. All of a sudden she’s losing tens of thousands of pounds.
Asked why the Tories were not proposing a means test, so the very rich would not qualify, Badenoch said:
I believe that the number of people who have very small children who are earning tens of millions of pounds is negligible.
But she also said she wanted the Tory conference to show that the party had “policies for everybody, whether you don’t earn, whether you earn a little, whether you’re an a bit, whether you earn a lot”.
She went on:
We want everyone in this country to know that if you are out there working, the Conservative party has got a plan for you.
This is from Lee Harpinfrom Jewish News, who is at the Green party conference in Brighton but not allowed into the hall for the policy debate on the ‘Zionism is racism’ motion. The Greens always restrict the sessions debating policy to party members.

Badenoch publishes The Right Way, 100-page guide to her political philosophy
Kemi Badenoch has published a 100-page guide to her political philosophy. It is called The Right Way, and it is in part modelled on a pamphlet published by the Tories soon after Margaret Thatcher became leader in the 1970s. That one was called The Right Approach and drafted by Keith Joseph.
In her foreword, Badenoch says that the 30,000-word booklet is not a policy document; it is a statement of principle.
She explains.
In February 2026, the former head of MI6, Sir Alex Younger, addressed the Conservative parliamentary party. When I interviewed him on stage, he started with a warning: once you are in government, there is no time to construct first principles. If you have not worked out how you think before the crises arrive, you end up reacting to them one by one.
This is where the last Conservative governments went wrong, before they went wrong about anything else. We do not intend to make this mistake again. The Right Way is our answer to the challenge the now late Sir Alex Younger posed.
Good government enters office knowing how it thinks. A manifesto full of suggested policies for current, visible problems is not enough. Many problems a government ends up dealing with are not known at the time of the election. What is essential for success is a settled way of approaching the problems nobody predicted, how to recognise trade-offs, what government should do itself, what it should leave alone, and how to decide when circumstances, and indeed the world, change.

Badenoch says current triple lock 'right policy' - but declines to say Tories will always keep it
In her BBC interview, Kemi Badenoch was asked if she could say she would never change the pensions triple lock. Laura Kuenssberg asked her if she could say she would never touch it.
Badenoch did not quite give that assurance. Instead, she replied:
The triple lock is our policy. We believe that this is the right policy for pensioners. That is what we have planned, that is what we have promised.
There is nothing that has happened that has made me change my mind. That is our policy.
Given that Andy Burnham has said that he wants to legislate to end the pensions triple lock before the next election, it is possible that the choice for Badenoch when that election happens won’t be whether or not to keep the triple lock, but whether or not to restore it to the more generous version it was before Burnham amended it.

I just think that whether it’s Nigel Farage or even Keir Starmer who had his home firebombed, that there is a threat to politicians that is increasing and we just need to crack down on this.
Let’s build the prison spaces so that we can put people who are making these threats and threatening politicians. But what I want the public to know is that my priority really is their safety.
In her BBC interview, Badenoch rejected suggestions that the Tories were regaining their “nasty party” reputation under her leadership.
She said:
It’s the common sense party. That’s what we’re doing.
And, quite frankly, if we were doing so well the old way, then why did we have such a terrible issue in 2024?
I am a classic old-school Conservative. I believe in common sense: people working hard and being rewarded for that effort.
We look after those who can’t look after themselves. Welfare should be a safety net, not a lifestyle. But this is an amazing country and I want us to look to the future and see what we can do, not just hark back to the past.
Badenoch also said her values were timeless.
Personal responsibility is not a 1980s idea. These are the things that keep us going and we need that, the principles are timeless.
Badenoch claims pensions triple lock should stay because pensioners 'have contributed'
On Friday the Times revealed that Katie Lam, the communities secretary, told a meeting in private earlier this year that the state pension system needs a fundamental overhaul.
Speaking in June, when she was a frontbencher but not yet in the shadow cabinet, Lam was asked at a meeting with activists if she thought the pensions triple lock was sustainable. She replied:
Ultimately I think what we will need in the end is an entirely new pension system.
I mean, a baby that is born today has a 20% chance of living to be 100 and I don’t think we can fund one in five people half of their lives, you know, for the first 20 and the last 30 years. But obviously if you are 90 you probably can’t go out and get a job right, so I think you have to be realistic about how you would taper that and bring that in across the population.
I just think the whole system as it stands can’t stand for very much longer.
Asked about Lam’s comments, Badenoch said her shadow minister was right to say what mattered was growth. She went on:
The fact is, the triple lock and pensions are things that people have contributed to.
Conservatives believe that if you have contributed, then you deserve to get your state pension.
What we don’t want to see is people going after the elderly, chasing after vulnerable and disabled people, and then the extremely large cohort of people who can work, who are not working, [being] left alone [ie, not having their benefits cut].
Badenoch claims rising costs of pensions triple lock would not be problem if economy growing more quickly
Badenoch gave a similar answer when Kuenssberg asked her to defend her support for the pensions triple lock.
She said she accepted there were “good people” on both sides of the argument about keeping or changing the triple lock. But she said, as party leader, she had decided the Tories would stick with it. She went on:
The reason why is because what is going wrong in our economy is not lots of elderly people earning £10,000, £12,000 a year on the state pension. It is the huge number of people who can work, who don’t work.
Kuenssberg said 55% of welfare spending is now going on pensions, and that in 2017, when Badenoch was first elected, the Tories were promising to change the triple lock.
Badenoch replied:
We’ve had different policies at different times. We go with what the leader does. I am the leader now and what I am saying is that our economy is not growing. Changing and moving around the triple lock does not create growth.
In fact, if we were growing at 2 or 3%, nobody would be talking about the triple lock.

Conservatives claim ‘major victory’ as Tory conference begins after Labour scraps plans to curb jury trials
Good morning. Anthony Seldon recently published the latest in his long and invaluable series of inside stories of premierships, Sunak at 10, and he gave it the subtitle “The last Conservative prime minister?” When the book was being planned in the early days of Kemi Badenoch’s leadership of the Conservative party, it did look as though the Tories might be finished as a party of government. But now Seldon, and his co-author Tom Egerton, aren’t so sure. Their book concludes: “At the time of writing in July 2026 … the Tory party still needs to engage in a process of deep self-reflection to understand why it failed in government, and tore itself so destructively apart, if it is ever to regain power. But at this point in time we believe it is unlikely that Sunak will have been the last Tory prime minister.”
That is a victory, of sorts, for Badenoch. For most of last year there were doubts that she would still be leader by the time of the next election. But she gave a successful party conference speech, her response to the budget was much admired, and her personal approval ratings with Tory members and right-leaning voters shot up. After two years as opposition leader, Iain Duncan Smith was booted out. Two years in, Badenoch’s position as leader is safe and it is even conceivable that she could stay on if the Conservatives were to lose the next election (in part because any Tories who favour a radically different policy approach are being purged from the candidates list).
But that does not mean Badenoch’s leadership is going well. At the last election the Conservatives won 24.4% of the GB vote. According to the Politico poll of polls, they have been consistently polling below that since the end of 2024 and they are currently on 19%.
The Conservative conference starts today and, explaining her strategy in an interview in the Times, Badenoch said: “Last year was about telling the party who I was. Now the party is going to be showing the country who we are: a strong team of people who actually like each other.” The Tories have already announced quite a lot of conference-related policy.
But she has not got the news space all to herself. It is the final day of the Green party’s conference in Brighton and this morning activists are expected to debate their ‘Zionism is racism’ motion. The proposal has split the party, and critics claim that it is antisemitic. Whatever happens, it will affect how the Green party is seen.
And this morning Labour has announced a major U-turn – abandoning most of the Keir Starmer/David Lammy plans to restrict access to jury trials. Haroon Siddique has the story here.
In the past, there was an unofficial ‘gentleman’s agreement’ that the government did not make big news announcements during the opposition party’s conference. But that era (like two-party politics) is over, and Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has successfully kept Badenoch off the top of this morning’s news cycle.
Still, the Tories can claim this as a victory. This is from Nick Timothy, the shadow justice secretary.
This is a major victory for everyone who fought to defend trial by jury, and Conservatives led that fight from day one. Labour has been forced to abandon its central attack on jury trials in the crown court.
But Timothy also claimed the U-turn did not go far enough.
Labour are restricting juries by the back door, scrapping the right to elect one and dumping those cases on magistrates whose backlog is at a record high.
Nearly 81,000 cases are stuck in the crown court, yet there is no commitment to get courts sitting more often, but Labour did find the time to write into law a review of how its reforms treat people of different backgrounds.
Here is the agenda for the day.
8.30am: Alex Norris, the justice secretary, is interviewed on Sky’s Sunday with Helen Lewis.
9am:Kemi Badenoch is interviewed on the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg. (The interview has been pre-recorded.) Norris is being interviewed too.
Morning: The Green party debates the controversial ‘Zionism is racism’ motion on the final day of its conference this morning.
2pm: John Belsley, president of the National Conservative Convention, opens the proceedings at the Tory conference in Birmingham. The session is on the theme of “resisting separatism” and the speakers include Alex Burghart, the deputy leader and shadow Northern Ireland secretary; Mims Davies, shadow Welsh secretary; Harriet Cross, shadow Scottish secretary; Darren Millar, leader of the Welsh Conservatives in the Senedd; and Russell Findlay, the Scottish leader.
Mid afternoon: Badenoch delivers her opening speech to the conference.
4pm:James Cleverly, who wants to be the Tory candidate for London mayor in 2028, is speaking at a fringe event.

Scientists rush to solve mystery of dead baby whales washing up on shore of Argentina
Changes in marine conditions linked to climate change or El Nino could be to blame

An investigation has been launched over the mystery of why baby whales are washing up dead on the coast of Argentina.
The country’s Patagonian coast has seen scores of the calf carcasses washing ashore around Peninsula Valdes, on the country’s Patagonian coast.
The area is a major breeding ground for southern right whales in Argentina’s Chubut province.
Hunted to the brink of extinction in the 19th and 20th centuries, the whales now gather in the peninsula’s sheltered waters to give birth and nurse their young.
“We're looking into the whale calf deaths based on 23 years of monitoring that we have of this same population. That's what allows us to say that this is an unusual event," said Marcela Uhart, a veterinarian with the One Health Institute at the University of California, Davis, who is leading the investigation as head of the Southern Right Whale Health Monitoring Program.
The leading hypothesis is that the whale calves are suffering infections from marine bacteria that can enter their bodies through injuries inflicted by kelp gulls, Uhart said.
For decades, the seabirds have pecked at whales surfacing to breathe, gorging on their skin and blubber. Adults learn to surface with only their heads exposed, keeping their backs underwater and out of reach of the gulls. Calves can't do that maneuver, leaving them vulnerable to attacks.
The carcasses have been washing ashore around the gulf city of Puerto Madryn, including near the central waterfront where they alarm residents and tourists. Residents have reported hundreds of them, but researchers declined to give a death toll, saying that would become clear after the season ends around late November.
Uhart and a team of biologists, veterinarians and park rangers have been searching the area for the dead calves from shore and with boats, planes and drones.
The work is gruesome: They photograph and examine the bodies, racing against decomposition to collect skin and organ samples for testing at a veterinary school farther north, in the city of Tandil. Bacteria have already been detected in those tissues, but researchers are still culturing samples to identify the microbes and determine whether infection was the cause of death, she said.
Even if bacteria are to blame, researchers must still determine why they have become so deadly this year.
Changes in marine conditions like warming sea temperatures, potentially linked to climate change or El Nino, could contribute to “this perfect storm where this bacteria is powerful enough to overcome the immunity of the babies and cause their deaths,” Uhart said. “So to the extent that we can, we'll try to identify at least what factors may be triggering this event and making it so massive.”
Right whales got their name from whalers who considered them the “right” animals to hunt because they swam slowly, stayed close to shore and floated when killed, according to the International Whaling Commission, a global body tasked with regulating whaling.
Although illegal hunting continued into the 1970s, southern right whales have gradually rebounded since gaining international protection in 1935. But their recovery remains threatened by the same pressures facing whales worldwide: declining food supplies, fishing gear entanglements, oil spills and ship strikes.
If losses on this scale recur, they could slow the population’s recovery. By pinpointing what is killing the calves, researchers hope to find ways to protect the vulnerable population.
“If the cause relates to something that we are doing as humans, then we need to change that,” Uhart said. “We don’t want to endanger these whales again.”

Nine scandals that rocked the sporting world
- Published
Manchester City being found guilty of fuelling an era of glittering Premier League success via a network of sponsorship deals, found by an independent commision to be a "sham", has shaken the world of sport.
But it isn't the first time.
The lure of glory and riches on the biggest stages have tempted plenty of others to cheat.
BBC Sport looks back on nine more sporting scandals, stretching back more than a century.
Lance Armstrong's great lie
Cancer survivor. Cycling legend. American hero. Cheat.
Lance Armstrong had spent years vehemently and aggressively insisting that he had won all seven of his Tour de France titles between 1999 and 2005 without the help of performance-enhancing drugs.
His story was remarkable. Aged 25, Armstrong had been diagnosed with testicular cancer, with doctors warning he was likely to die given the disease had spread to other parts of his body.
He not only survived, but returned to dominate top-level cycling. His Livestrong Foundation was wildly successful, selling millions of yellow wristbands to raise money to support fellow cancer sufferers.
However, as the evidence and former team-mates allegations against him stacked up, Armstrong was stripped of his Tour de France titles.
Armstong eventually confessed to cheating in a blockbuster interview with talk show host Oprah Winfrey.
"I made those decisions, they were my mistake and I'm here to say sorry," he said, adding that the culture in professional cycling made using drugs non-negotiable.

  - Published18 January 2013
South Africa's golden boy undone by love of money
Hansie Cronje was the golden boy of South African sport.
Good looking and charming, he led the nation's cricket team with style and authority.
President Nelson Mandela singled out Cronje in 1996 for the "excellent manner" in which he captained the Proteas.
However, Cronje's love of money, combined with a fast-growing betting industry and the organised crime it attracted, proved his downfall.
Cronje entertained the offers of match-fixers, calling team meetings to discuss the possibility of throwing matches and sharing thousands of dollars in inducements.
Most infamously, Cronje contrived to lose a rain-affected Test against England in 2000.
With South Africa still in the midst of their first innings on the final day, Cronje convinced England counterpart Nasser Hussein that in the interest of sporting entertainment each side should forfeit an innings, producing a sudden run-chase and giving England a shot at victory.
Cronje was praised for his Corinthian spirit. In reality, he had been motivated by a bribe of £5,000 to ensure the match did not end in a draw.
Cronje was undone when an Indian police wiretap of a bookmaker caught him in discussions about fixing matches.
Cronje confessed in early 2000, was banned from cricket for life and died in a plane crash two years later at the age of 32.

F1's 'Crashgate' erupts in Singapore
There was something particular about turn 17 of the Marina Bay Street Circuit.
In 2008, before the inaugural Singapore Grand Prix was held at the circuit, Renault driver Nelson Piquet Jr knew it did not have any overhead cranes to lift a damaged car from the track. There were no side entrances to allow a stranded driver to be pushed out of danger's way by marshalls either.
On lap 14 Piquet found himself in exactly in that unfortunate position. And, despite his initial claim that he had made a "simple mistake", the Brazilian had put himself there deliberately.
When Renault dropped him in 2009, Piquet Jr revealed that he steered himself into a concrete wall to crash his car. The safety car was deployed as officials cleared debris off the track.
Crucially, Piquet Jr's team-mate Fernando Alonso was the only frontrunner to have stopped for fuel and new tyres at the point of the crash.
As Alonso's rivals went into the pits, the Spaniard, benefitting from the reduced gaps caused by the safety car, moved up the field and went on to win the race.
While Alonso was cleared of any wrongdoing or knowledge of the plot, Renault team principal Flavio Briatore and chief technical officer Pat Symonds were banned from F1 for several years.

Under the cover of darkness - the Premier League fix
Frank Lampard wheeled away in celebration after his well-hit shot from the edge of the penalty area beat Kevin Miller in the Crystal Palace goal in the 65th minute of a Monday evening Premier League game in November 1997.
As he was mobbed by team-mates, Upton Park was plunged into darkness.
The following month similar happened at Selhurst Park. Thirteen seconds into the second half - with Wimbledon and Arsenal goalless - the lights went off. The Christmas lights in nearby Croydon were raised as a possible cause.
The actual cause was more sinister.
An Asian betting syndicate had pulled the plug, using a remote control circuit breaker, to get each match abandoned at a scoreline which would maximise their profits.
The gang were foiled in their attempts to pull the deception for a third time. They had bribed a security guard at Charlton Athletic to allow them to plant a device at The Valley before Liverpool's visit in February.
However, a suspicious member of staff at the club tipped off police.
Four men were given sentences of between 18 months and four years for their involvement.
Taking the urine in Sochi
No expense was spared for the Winter Olympics in Sochi in 2014.
With a budget of $50bn (£38bn) - more than 25 times Vancouver's 2010 Winter Olympics spend - organisers created two entirely new resorts, bristling with security and military personnel.
But building facilities from scratch also gave the Russian hosts a chance to design an elaborate way around anti-doping measures.
A secret tunnel allowed a Russian secret service agent, disguised as a sewer engineer, to swap out his compatriots' urine samples, which contained traces of banned substances.
A special method had been developed to remove the tamperproof lids of sample bottles, which were then refilled with 'clean' urine that had been frozen before Russian athletes began doping programmes.
Forty-three Russian athletes were banned for life, 28 of whom successfully appealed against the full extent of their punishment.
Russia was banned from competing at the following Winter Olympics in South Korea, although athletes who could demonstrate their clean record were permitted to compete under a neutral flag.

A drama on ice
A camera crew caught the aftermath of the attack on Nancy Kerrigan in January 1994.
The 24-year-old figure skater was captured clutching her leg and repeatedly wailing "why?".
Kerrigan had been training at a rink in Detroit before the American national championships. As she stepped off the ice, a man rushed towards her and struck her on the leg with a telescopic baton.
Kerrigan's 'why' was soon answered.
The bodyguard and ex-husband of Kerrigan's rival Tonya Harding had hired a man to break Kerrigan's leg. They hoped to rule her out of the forthcoming Winter Olympics in Lillehammer, boosting Harding's chances.
It didn't work. Kerrigan recovered from heavy bruising in time to make the USA team, alongside Harding.
Amid a media frenzy, Harding, struggling with a broken lace on her boot, finished eighth in the Olympic final.
Kerrigan took silver.
The competition broke viewing records in the US.
Harding was banned for life from the sport after admitting attempting to conceal the identity of Kerrigan's assailant after the attack.
Harding's ex-husband Jeff Gillooly, the attacker he hired and a getaway driver all spent time in prison for their part in the crime.

The White Sox's dirty secret
"Say it ain't so Joe."
The headline written in the Chicago Daily News summed up the disbelief of a city, a nation and a sport when it emerged that superstar Joe Jackson and seven of his Chicago White Sox team-mates had apparently taken bribes to lose the 1919 World Series, baseball's biggest game.
First baseman Chick Gandil was the ringleader, while star pitcher Eddie Cicotte was the key figure.
A fee of $100,000 - worth about $1.6m today - was agreed with the head of a betting syndicate, with the money to be shared among the eight conspirators.
Cicotte's pitch, deliberately hitting Maurice Rath on the back, was a sign to his team-mates, and gamblers in the know, that the fix was on.
After the White Sox lost the series 5-3 to the Cincinnati Reds, the White Sox's suspicious owner Charles Comiskey sent word that the players needed to collect their pay cheques from him in person.
None of the eight fixers did. They left the stadium without their money. Rumours spread, followed by an investigation, and soon the players were in the dock.
Although a criminal court failed to convict the players, they were banned from Major League Baseball for life.
Jackson insisted until his death in 1951 that he was not involved and that, despite receiving $5,000, he had been deceived into signing a confession.

A betrayal of Paralympic trust
At half-time in their first match at the 2000 Paralympics the coach of Spain's intellectual disability basketball team told them to stop scoring so quickly and let their opponents shoot more.
He knew the vast majority of the team were there under false pretences.
Of the 12 players in the squad, 10 had no intellectual impairment at all, but were keen amateur players who had been recruited months before the Sydney Games to supplement the team.
Spain, perhaps unsurprisingly, won gold convincingly, beating Russia 87-63 in the final.
The scam unravelled because one of the ringers was also a journalist.
Realising he was in the midst of an incredible scoop, Carlos Ribagorda played in Sydney and then published an article detailing the scandal on his return.
The team were stripped of their medals and the incident led to a total ban on athletes with an intellectual disability from the 2004 and 2008 Paralympics, destroying the careers of thousands of sportspeople around the world.

The wiretaps that sunk a superstar squad to Serie B
When public prosecutors tapped telephone calls at Italian football giants Juventus in 2004, they were hunting for evidence of doping.
What they believed they found was corruption on a far more systematic scale.
They thought they had evidence of Juve general manager Luciano Moggi pressurising referee officials to favour certain clubs, including his own. Moggi denied the claims.
However, Juve, AC Milan, Fiorentina, Lazio and Reggina were all implicated in influencing referees.
All were given points deductions, but only Juventus ultimately dropped into the second tier of Italian football.
There was a split in the club's superstar squad.
Zlatan Ibrahimovic and Patrick Vieira joined rivals Inter Milan for a combined £23m, Fabio Cannavaro and Emerson went to Real Madrid for £13.7m, Lilian Thuram and Gianluca Zambrotta joined Barcelona for £13m, and Adrian Mutu went to Fiorentina for £5.5m.

Despite beginning the season with a nine-point penalty and an opening-day draw with minnows Rimini, Juventus were promoted at the first attempt.
The club still lay claim to the 2004–05 and 2005–06 titles that were stripped from them, counting 38 rather than the official 36.

Travel plans? Here's what to know as measles exposures reach trains and games
The U.S. is in the midst of the worst measles resurgence in decades. Recent outbreaks in several states and exposures in places like bars, sports stadiums and on public transit have some people questioning the safety of travel or how they should prepare for upcoming plans.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists over 3,600 confirmed measles cases in the U.S. as of Sept. 24 — and two deaths as of Sept. 28. Almost all of those cases have been among unvaccinated individuals.
The CDC notes the number of deaths is subject to change as more information becomes available and after it completes more reviews. It's important to note that the Pennsylvania Department of Health has counted four measles-associated deaths so far. The CDC has disputed whether measles actually caused those deaths.
In the last two weeks, Pennsylvania, Ohio and New York have had the most cases, according to the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health U.S. measles tracker.
The true number of cases across the country is likely higher, according to Dr. Paul Offit, director of the Vaccine Education Center at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia and a professor of pediatrics at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania.
"I think if anything, we're underestimating how many people are actually being exposed, and how many people are being infected, and how many people are being hospitalized and dying," he said.
He said that's because many children, parents or adults may not seek medical care if they get infected.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Dr. Kalyani McCullough, who leads the Vaccine Preventable Disease Epidemiology & Control Section of the Immunizations Branch of the California Department of Public Health, said it's important for people to know that measles is not "just a fever and a rash."
"It can affect a lot of different parts of the body, and it can have long-lasting effects as well," she said. "Both with immune amnesia, which means that the measles virus can actually reduce immunity to other infections after being infected with measles."
"So I think it's just important for people to realize that getting measles can have some pretty serious consequences," McCullough said.
How do you protect against measles?
People who've had two doses of the MMR vaccine are considered protected against measles.
The disease is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, sneezes or breathes. And you don't have to come in direct contact with someone who has measles to get infected; you just have to be within their airspace within two hours of them being there.
Offit said one person with measles can infect about 15 to 18 other people, if they're susceptible. Offit says "susceptible," in this case, means people who've either never had measles, or who are unvaccinated.
For people in that category, up to 9 out of every 10 exposed will get measles.
What does it mean if there have been measles exposures in my state?
Some states that aren't currently experiencing large measles outbreaks have notified residents of possible exposures.
While an outbreak is a group of cases in one area during a certain time period, an exposure is when a person comes into contact with someone who has measles, according to George Mason University College of Public Health epidemiologist Amira Roess.
The California Department of Public Health notified people of potential exposures after an infected and unvaccinated train and bus passenger traveled across the U.S. and through multiple California counties.
The City of St. Louis Department of Health also encouraged residents to monitor for symptoms after an individual who visited local bars and a sports stadium tested positive for measles.
Measles can be difficult for epidemiologists to track because symptoms — like a fever, cough and rash — usually begin seven to 14 days after a person is exposed or as late as 21 days later.
Once a person is confirmed to have measles, epidemiologists interview that person and try to figure out the places they visited and people they saw while they were contagious. In the case of measles, that's typically four days before the telltale rash appears, according to McCullough.
"So it's a really labor-intensive process," she said.
She said anyone exposed to measles is usually advised to seek medical advice and isolate themselves if they develop symptoms within three weeks of exposure. People who are unvaccinated may be asked to quarantine and may be monitored by public health officials to see if they get sick.
What should I do if I'm traveling soon?
All the experts who spoke to NPR said the first and most effective step to protect yourself against measles is to make sure you're fully vaccinated.
That means having had two doses of the MMR vaccine — commonly done in childhood. You can check with your healthcare provider if you aren't sure about your vaccine status. They may recommend a booster depending on your records and recent health.
Offit said this recommendation holds for travelers coming into the U.S. from other countries as well.
"I think anybody who is traveling from another country into the United States should make sure they're up to date on their vaccines, because it's dangerous to be in the United States now if you are not fully immune to measles," he said.
Offit noted many people who are immunocompromised cannot be vaccinated if they haven't been already. Those people may rely on herd immunity — protection from a disease when a certain percentage of people in a community are vaccinated. For measles, this threshold is 95%. Last school year, kindergarten vaccination coverage dipped to 92.4%, according to the CDC.
Children typically get their first dose of the MMR vaccine at around 12 months. But McCullough says if parents are planning to travel internationally with infants or babies 6-11 months old, the CDC's recommendation is to get an early dose of the vaccine.
But the experts we spoke to said that if you have your vaccines, you don't need to worry.
"If you've been relatively healthy and you are up to date on your vaccines, and you are up to date on your doctor's visits, then you will be fine," Roess said. "I'm not worried about those individuals."
Roess also said people can wear masks in busy areas if they are concerned.

The Karnataka government has flagged the disparity between the institutional landing costs and the Maximum Retail Prices (MRP) of high-value medicines, cancer drugs, antibiotics and hospital consumables supplied to hospitals across the State.
The department has raised the issue with the Union Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA). Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader, in a letter dated September 23, wrote to the Union Health Minister seeking action.
Massive markup
Recent investigations by the Karnataka Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) have revealed that pharmaceutical companies are supplying medicines to hospitals at heavily discounted institutional (landing) prices, while patients are being billed at or near the printed MRP, resulting in markups ranging from 10 times to over 52 times the actual procurement cost.
During inspections, the FSDA found extreme pricing anomalies in 253 drugs. For the cancer drug Cytax 100 mg, the landing cost was ₹342, while the MRP was ₹3,836, reflecting a markup of 11.2 times.
In the case of Gufipol, manufactured by Criticare, the markup was as high as 52.6 times, or 5,165%.
| Drug/Consumable | Landing Cost (₹) | MRP (₹) | Mark-up | 
| Gufipol (Criticare) | 86 | 4,528 | 52.6 times | 
| Guficycline-50 injection (GUFI) | 160 | 7,110 | 44.4 times | 
| Terlitis (AEQU) | 118 | 4,416 | 37.4 times | 
| Taxocare 120 mg (Intas) | 1,000 | 21,617 | 21.6 times | 
| Canmab 440 mg | 6,600 | 57,457 | 8.7 times | 
| Bevatas 400 mg injection | 5,850 | 62,690 | 10.7 times | 
| Cytax 100 mg (cancer drug) | 342 | 3,836 | 11.2 times | 
| Adult Nebuliser Mask | 44.50 | 950 | 21.3 times | 
| IV Set | 14.75 | 295 | 20 times | 
| Polysafety PRO IV Cannula | 33.21 | 548 | 16.5 times | 
11-point letter
The Karnataka government has requested the Centre to mandate transparency in institutional pricing by requiring hospitals to display both the landing cost and MRP on patient bills, expand the list of drugs under price control under the Drug Price Control Order (DPCO), and regulate trade margins on essential high-value medicines and consumables.
The State has also sought the constitution of an inter-ministerial expert group, a national data study, and amendments to, or supplementation of, the Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013.
Other demands include rationalisation of trade margins, mandatory cost-to-MRP transparency, expansion of the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM), and creation of an audit and enforcement mechanism.
Drive to continue
Another special verification drive was conducted on September 25 and 26, 2026, at various wholesale premises, hospitals and other establishments in Bengaluru and district headquarters across Karnataka. According to the FSDA, preliminary observations indicate substantial differences between the landing cost, the MRP and the actual sale price of certain high-cost drugs, medical devices and hospital consumables. The inspections covered more than 768 consumable items and 189 high-cost drugs. The findings will be brought to the notice of the Central Government, the FSDA said in a statement.
According to the FSDA, the special verification exercise will continue in a phased manner. In the next phase, enforcement and verification activities will focus, among other categories, on antiretroviral drugs, higher-generation and critical antibiotics, medical devices and hospital consumables with substantial financial implications for patients.
Khader unveils SuMi
Health and Family Welfare Minister U.T. Khader released the new mascot for the Karnataka State AIDS Control Society on Thursday.
The mascot, SuMi, short for Suraksha Mitra, was selected from around 1,500 entries. The winning mascot was designed by Navya of Athena College of Nursing, Mangaluru.
The competition was organised by the AIDS Control Society to raise awareness about HIV/AIDS. It was conducted across all districts for people above the age of 16.

How to customize Camera Control on your iPhone
Make your iPhone’s camera behave exactly how you want
Are you getting everything you can out of the button at the lower right of your iPhone 16, 17, and 18 series? The button is the phone's Camera Control, which can be customized to support your mobile photography workflow.
To clear up any confusion, Camera Control refers to the capacitive button on the right side of your iPhone, which understands a range of gestures, including single- and double-clicks and swipe gestures. You use it to open the camera, take pictures, record videos and work with the advanced photography settings on your iPhone.
Perfect for one-handed photography, Camera Control's default inputs are:
- Click the button once to launch the Camera.
- Swipe to use different photography tools such as exposure or zoom while in the app
- Click again to take the image.
- Long-press to capture video.
- Double-click to launch Visual Intelligence, which lets you use the camera to ask Siri questions about your surroundings.
How to customize the Camera Control button
You can change the default behaviors in Settings > Camera > Camera Control. This takes you to a pane of many options, including two important sections you should explore first: Launch Camera and Controls, alongside several smaller tweaks.
For Launch Camera, tap Camera to choose which supported app to open when you press the Camera Control button. Camera is enabled by default, but you'll find other options if the relevant app is installed. These may include Instagram, which makes your iPhone an instant story creation tool, Code Scanner to scan QR codes or Magnifier, which turns your iPhone into a high-powered digital magnifying glass. You may also see other third-party apps, some of which may be grayed out pending full support.
The Controls section includes a range of settings you should explore, including Camera Adjustments. When activated, this makes Camera Control even more useful. When your Camera app is active, light presses or swipes on the button will let you explore camera options and adjustments.
Customize lets you decide what gestures Camera Control supports while in that mode, including support for light presses and swipes. It also lets you enable and disable the six adjustments potentially supported by Camera Control, which include:
- Zoom
- Exposure
- Depth
- Cameras
- Styles
- Tone
Tap to enable and disable the tick beside the function, or press and hold the burger icon (three horizontal lines) beside each item to move it into your preferred order. In the future, when taking a picture, you'll be able to swipe the Camera Control to move through those different adjustments in the order you define.
Exploring additional Camera Control options
Along with the above-referenced features, Camera Control also allows:
- Single Click or Double Click: Double Click can be best to avoid accidental camera activations.
- Require Screen On: When enabled, this toggle-based control will prevent accidental Camera activation when your iPhone is locked.
- Lock Focus and Exposure: When this is active, Camera Control will maintain focus and exposure so long as you continue to touch it.
- Launch Visual Intelligence: When active, press and hold the Camera button to open Visual Intelligence, which lets you ask Siri about your surroundings.
There are several additional customizations available in Settings > Accessibility > Camera Control. Here you can disable the button completely and define the force and speed required to make the button respond to a press, choosing between Default, Slow and Slower.
I've found setting button behaviors to Slow helps stop accidentally opening the Camera when handling my device, and trimming the camera adjustments to Zoom, Exposure and Styles helps me focus on the image, not the controls I don't frequently use.
That's the point of Camera Control, really — configure it to support your workflow while making it much, much easier to take photos, videos and use Visual Intelligence with one hand.

Republic of Ireland news conference ends abruptly amid accusations

For more than 11 minutes of Saturday's pre-match news conference, Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson fielded questions centred on Sunday's Nations League Group B3 'home' game against Israel in Serbia.
The Icelander revealed that Dara O'Shea - captain in place of the injured Nathan Collins - was not with the squad, as his wife was due to give birth. He may arrive back in Backa Topola prior to Sunday's 19:45 BST kick-off.
Hallgrimsson also gave his thoughts on the strain of this four-game international window and reflected on Thursday's 2-2 draw against Austria.
As the first section of the media conference, which is allowed to be broadcast live, was ending, the mood soured.
One reporter tried to quiz Hallgrimsson on his thoughts about the incident on Wednesday when a co-pilot attacked a pilot on a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv, before passengers managed to overpower the attacker and successfully take control of the plane.
The Republic of Ireland manager was also asked by another journalist about alleged racism by Irish players during last Sunday's 3-0 win over Israel in Hungary and refused to give up the microphone.
Promptly, the news conference was brought to a close by Football Association of Ireland (FAI) head of communications Kieran Crowley after calling those allegations "completely untrue".
The allegations of racism by an Irish player comes after it was confirmed the FAI is investigating reports of racist abuse directed towards Republic of Ireland striker Adam Idah by Israel fans in Debrecen.
Minutes before the news conference was brought to an abrupt halt, Hallgrimsson insisted he would not be drawn on either matter and would not "get involved in that as others will process that".
"It is a game with a lot of emotions attached," Hallgrimsson said.
"I haven't read anything and it's not something I want to get involved with. It goes to a process, both in our department and with Uefa.
"Something was reported by both teams so I just hope we can focus on football and football will be the winner after this.
"I have not gone into details looking at this as I have enough to think about."
- Second Israel game won't be a friendly - Hallgrimsson

The Republic of Ireland boss revealed the team have taken to a group prayer before leaving the dressing room before recent games "just to cool our heads before we go on to the pitch" and said that has been led by midfielder Conor Coventry whom he joked is now known within the squad as "Brother Coventry".
It has been a challenging international window for the Republic of Ireland with the Israel double-header dominating discourse in Irish football.
Since the teams were drawn together in February, a 'Stop The Game' campaign was launched by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine to boycott the fixtures in protest of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war.
'Togetherness is stronger than individuals' - Hallgrimsson

There were protests during the game against Austria in Dublin on Thursday, with tennis balls thrown on to the pitch and a protester briefly interrupting the game when he ran on to the turf, waving a Palestine flag.
Hallgrimmson said under the circumstances, it will be a "a big win for this group and the association if we go through undamaged".
"The most pleasing thing for me is to see the togetherness and how they stand up for each other. Whatever they have done, they have done it with respect to the situation, to each other and after this, this bond of brothers will be stronger than ever. All the obstacles this group will face in the future will be lesser than it is.
"When we look back, this camp will be a moment we grew the most and stepped up as leaders, supported each other and stuck together. The power of togetherness is stronger than individuals."

The 31 Best STEM Toys for the Techie Kids in Your Life
Featured in this article
Anyone who has ever watched a toddler methodically take apart a Tupperware drawer knows that many children are natural-born engineers. Your job as a parent is to nurture their creativity … and clean up the mess afterward. I've tested tons of STEM toys with my kids over the years, some with help from other parents on the WIRED Reviews team and some with help from my wife, who is a teacher and can road-test them in the classroom.
Wrap up a few of these STEM toys (also called STEAM toys; we love you too, arts!) for your future scientist to assemble, squish, or dismantle. Hopefully, they'll thank you for the early encouragement when they're older. Be sure to check out our assortment of other buying guides, including the Best Subscription Boxes for Kids, Best Speakers for Kids, and How to Build the Lego Collection of Your Dreams.
Updated October 2026: I've added Gravity Maze, an Engine-Building Kit, and Rush Hour Deluxe.
- Creative Kit Plus Plus Mini Interlocking Building Blocks Set There’s something super-satisfying about these tactile building blocks. They come in a range of appealing colors and have a slightly squishy form that makes them delightful to build with and pull apart. Because the pieces are all the same, children don’t have to spend ages searching for a specific block as they do with Lego. They can pick by color or just experiment, and it’s as easy to create bracelets and headbands as it is to construct robots and bridges. These building blocks were very popular in the classroom with 7- and 8-year-olds. Some kids had fun just playing without something specific in mind, while others planned scenes and put their engineering skills to use to realize them. There are also some instruction booklets with suggestions. For kids aged 5 years and up.
- Sound Stage Qubs Qubitunes We’re in love with this screen-free play stage and speaker for kids. The cute wooden design includes a slot to insert a cartridge and a circular sound stage divided into four sections where you can pop characters on top to change the audio it plays. This basic functionality allows for a clever variety of add-on packs, from stories about quirky characters in the Groblies ($20) to a cooking game called Bernard’s Kitchen ($20) with different ingredients. My favorite is the Little Maestro set ($20) featuring players in an orchestra covering Mozart, Vivaldi, Beethoven, and Bach. The stereo speakers are quite good, it has a headphone port, and the Qubitunes can be recharged via USB-C for up to six hours of play. My wife has this in the reward area of her classroom, and it’s the most popular option with 7- and 8-year-olds. For kids aged 3 years and up.
- Wind-Up Flashlight Ambessa DIY Kinetic Flashlight Kids can build this wind-up flashlight themselves and learn all about electronic components and kinetic energy in the process. The thoughtful design includes 10 separate parts, and there are 16 steps to follow to assemble it. No batteries are required, and the kit is designed to be easy to disassemble and use again, making it perfect for a classroom setting. Our testers were delighted that simply winding the completed flashlight brought it to life (three minutes of winding provides 30 minutes of light). For every kit purchased, the maker, Ambessa, donates one to a refugee child out of school. For kids aged 8 years and up.
- Knight School Particula GoChess Mini I have been struggling for a few years to get my now 7- and 9-year-old interested in chess, and the GoChess Mini works wonderfully. This lightweight, portable board is beautiful to use—the pieces have a nice matte finish and are pleasingly weighty. Once you charge the Bluetooth-enabled board and connect it to the app, you can either play against remote players, against yourself, or get AI-enabled assistance to help guide your moves. You can scale the amount of assistance, whether it’s a little or a lot, and different-colored lights show you the advisability of different moves as you pick up each piece. One evening of charging results in weeks of playtime; my kids will play for hours and discuss each move as they go. It’s great.—Adrienne So Particula also offers a Harry Potter-themed GoChess Mini Board ($350) which appears in my best smart chess boards guide. For kids aged 6 years and up.
- Marble-Powered Computer Upper Story Turing Tumble Turing Tumble is a wonderful way to teach kids coding fundamentals. It combines the simple pleasure of marble runs with a beautifully illustrated sci-fi comic book packed with challenging puzzles. The board resembles a pachinko game, and you have to slot in different pieces to divert the blue and red balls and get the required pattern at the bottom. My 9-year-old spent hours working through the puzzles, reconfiguring this marble-powered computer. As the challenges grew tougher, the whole family joined in to find solutions. Well-designed, satisfying, and rewarding, this is a good pick for most kids. For kids aged 8 years and up.
- Coding Ball Sphero Bolt The Sphero Edu app is packed with computer science lessons and activities for different age groups. Bolt has an 8 x 8 LED board on top, various sensors inside (compass, light sensor, gyroscope, accelerometer), and supports infrared communication. My wife is a teacher and uses this in the classroom to teach basic coding skills, giving students challenges like navigating a maze. She says many kids grasp the concepts much faster than they might with a book or screen, because they can see the Bolt moving in physical space. For kids aged 9 years and up.
- Marble Puzzle ThinkFun Gravity Maze Kids love marble runs, and ThinkFun combines the joy of dropping marbles with a clever logic puzzle design in Gravity Maze. There are 60 challenge cards ranging in difficulty, and you must figure out how to place the available pieces to build a 3D maze that guides the marble to your target tower. For kids aged 8 years and up.
- Endless Building Fun Valtech Magna-Tiles The return on investment with Magna-Tiles staggers me. It's been years, and at 6 and 8 years old, my children can still occupy themselves with these for hours. Translucent Magna-Tiles click together to form both two-dimensional shapes and three-dimensional objects. Younger kids can make a house with a backyard and fences, or ice cream cones. With an older kid, the sky is the limit—or, rather, your credit card is, since there are wheelbarrows full of expansion sets you can buy. My daughter can currently build a full village in an afternoon for her stuffed animals. If these are too pricey, there are alternatives that work just as well, like Picasso Tiles, which are $23 for 60 pieces. —Adrienne So For kids aged 3 years and up.
- Robo Fun Robotical Marty the Robot V2 Combining coding with robotics can be a great way of engaging kids, and Marty the Robot V2 is an irresistibly charming biped with nine servo motors inside that enable him to walk, kick, wave, sidestep, and even waggle his eyebrows. There’s a customized microcontroller inside, various sensors, Bluetooth connectivity, and a speaker, so there’s plenty of potential for kids to code various routines and an extensive knowledge base with lessons and tutorials. Robotical has designed Marty for kids of all ages, so at the basic level, you can use color cards (green to move forward, for example) to control him. Older kids can use Scratch, a simplified coding program with drag-and-drop blocks on a connected Android or iOS device, and when they’re ready to advance, they can move on to Python. Marty is cute and fun but very expensive, though it’s mainly geared toward use in schools, and there are lots of good resources for educators. For kids aged 5 years and up.
- Construction Capers Geomag Classic Magnetic Building Set My entire household found this magnetic construction set irresistible, and there has been a new 3D structure on the coffee table every morning. The kit comprises glow-in-the-dark magnetic rods (crafted from recycled plastic), steel spheres, and plastic bases in different shapes. You also get storage boxes to put everything away in. There’s a guide in the box with a few suggested structures, but creating your own is a big part of the appeal. There are sets of various sizes. For kids aged 3 years and up.
- Early Engineering National Geographic 4-Cylinder Engine Building Kit You can build a four-cylinder engine with this 175-piece kit. It’s fun to assemble, but there are lots of fiddly pieces (tiny screws and springs), so younger kids may need supervision. Once built, simply insert three AA batteries (not included), push the button, and it comes to life, with moving pistons, valves, gears, and light-up LEDs to help kids understand how engines work. The instruction booklet also includes a brief potted history. For kids aged 10 years and up.
- A Twist on a Classic Particula GoCube No one needs a Bluetooth-enabled Rubik's Cube, but once you get your hands on a GoCube you probably won't be able to put it down. Smart sensors inside the beautiful, glowing cube connect to a companion app on your phone and sense where each block is positioned. You can learn algorithms and strategies that will help you get your solve-time down. And if you give everyone you know a GoCube, you can also stage live competitions with friends and family! —Adrienne So For kids aged 8 years and up.
- Sand Castles Kinetic Sand My kids love this moldable sand and have happily spent countless hours over the years making tabletop structures. It behaves like wet sand and never dries out, so you can shape it with your hands or use tools and molds to make castles. It comes in many colors and clumps together easily but doesn’t stick to your hands or surfaces. While it’s generally easy to clean up, it’s a good idea to confine play to a tray or table and supervise your kids, or you may end up picking tiny bits of pink sand out of your carpet. For kids aged 3 years and up.
- Remote-Controlled Robot Wonder Workshop Dash This super-cute robot looks like it rolled straight out of a Pixar movie. With a big, expressive eye atop three balls, it zips around with real personality, which helps it successfully combine play and learning in a way that all educational STEM toys aim for but many fall short of. Dash has lived with us for several years now and of all the coding robots I've tried, it remains my favorite. It’s a durable toy that works on a simple level like a remote-controlled car, but it also ties in with various apps to play games, solve puzzles, and create programs. Lego connectors for Dash’s head add to the creative possibilities. Wonder Workshop also offers some optional accessories. For kids aged 6 years and up.

Congress legislator from Bandipora constituency, Nizamuddin Bhat, Tuesday alleged that Jammu and Kashmir’s dual power structure has spawned a “devil’s authority”, creating administrative paralysis.
Talking to Greater Kashmir outside the Assembly complex, MLA Bandipora said the civil secretariat stands divided with no hierarchy and no link between authority and subordination.
“There is one elite class which is controlled by the Lok Bhavan and another class of officers which is controlled by the popular government. Naturally, there are two types of decisions,” he said.
“This is the first problem, and the second problem is the lack of power with the elected government,” he added.
MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the Lieutenant Governor earlier held absolute authority before the formation of the popular government.
“He made the law. He broke the law. He could do whatever he wanted to do because there was one single authority. This is the nature of democracy. Now they (elected government) is in power but with limited authority,” he said.
He said authority now stands divided at administrative, political, constitutional and legal levels.
“You have divided the law as well because there is one constitution which is in J&K. We are being attributed to the Reorganisation Act. When there are two laws, there is no need to go to the second law,” he said.
About the Wular Lake, MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the lake was the largest clean water body in the world once, hosting a larger community. “But when human fiddling, population boom and negligence at the administrative or environmental level came, our natural assets suffered,” he said.
He rejected the popular notion that the lake was fed by the Jhelum, Kishan Ganga or their tributaries, calling them merely flowing streams. “Wular’s source is not in Jhelum, not in Kishan Ganga, not his tributaries. Jehlum passes through the middle. When Jehlum has a level, it comes to the level of Wular. When Jehlum weakens, the ground is visible below. So that is not the source,” he said.
The actual source, he said, was a natural, gushing, oozing spring in the Watlab area that cleaned the lake and maintained its water level as well.
MLA Nizamuddin Bhat said the Wular project was conceived at Rs 360 crore, with Rs 307 crore allocated in 2011 and Rs 120 crore released, leading to the formation of the Wular Development Authority (WDA).
“Then that Wular Development Authority was also divided. So there too, devil authority was formed again. To save this lake, Rs 360 crore was not enough money to make an authority, create human resources, infrastructure, then add inhabitants of the lake. That cannot be done in Rs 360 crore,” he said.
Asked about the Manasbal and Wular development authorities, both linked to tourism and equipped with monetary and human resources, MLA Bandipora Nizamuddin Bhat said the core question remains unanswered.
“Why has Wular lost its size and the level of the water? Why has that declined?” he asked.
He said the government has not adopted the scientific approach it should have and has failed to stop human fiddling.
“Sand mafia is either growing on Jhelum or is growing on Walur. Look at the banks of Wular; they are so deep. The sound of fish is also gone. The sound of sandals is also gone. The water is also unclean, ugly,” he said.
MLA Bhat said he raised the issue at various forums.

The 52nd episode of The Health Wrap by The Hindu examines the growing use of artificial intelligence in healthcare, including its potential applications in drug and vaccine development, medical imaging and clinical decision-making.
Ramya Kannan, Health Editor, The Hindu, speaks to Abdul Gaffur, infectious diseases expert, Apollo Hospitals, Chennai, about the opportunities and limitations of AI in healthcare and the questions its growing use raises for patients and healthcare professionals.
Artificial intelligence is increasingly being explored across healthcare and medical research. The episode discusses how AI could help researchers identify potential drug candidates, analyse large volumes of information and accelerate some stages of medical research.
The conversation also looks at the possible use of AI in vaccine development and other areas of biomedical research. While these applications could support research, the discussion examines the need to consider the limitations of AI-generated outputs and the importance of scientific and clinical validation.
A key focus of the episode is the use of AI for health-related information. AI systems can produce answers that appear confident and authoritative but may contain incorrect information. The episode discusses why patients should be cautious about relying on AI-generated responses for medical advice and why such information needs to be assessed against reliable medical sources and professional advice.
The discussion also examines the use of AI in clinical care. AI-powered clinical intelligence could potentially bring together information from radiology, laboratory investigations, pharmacy records and medical records to support doctors in screening and triaging patients.
The episode looks at how such systems could assist healthcare professionals without replacing clinical assessment. It also considers the importance of understanding the limitations of AI when it is used in decisions that can affect patient care.
Data is another aspect of the discussion, particularly as healthcare AI systems may involve large amounts of medical information. The episode considers questions around the use of health data and the need for appropriate safeguards as AI becomes more integrated into healthcare.
The conversation also touches on the potential misuse of AI in biology and why advances in artificial intelligence need to be considered alongside questions of safety and responsible use.
The discussion focuses on both the potential applications of AI in healthcare and the limitations that need to be considered as these technologies are increasingly used in research, clinical settings and the communication of health information.
