On paper, director Tom McCarthy‘s latest film, A Statement might appear to be a dense polemic, hardly the stuff of exciting moviemaking. It centers on a 1980 Florida conference dealing with the effects of Carbon Dioxide emissions on the environment, gathering politicians, academics, scientists and environmentalists from around the U.S. to talk about the subject for four sessions over two days, and tasked with coming up with an agreed-upon statement on how to deal with the problem. The screenplay is largely taken from actual transcripts of the meeting, and is an adaptation by McCarthy and his co-writers Thomas Bidegan and Noé Debré of the Nathaniel Rich book, “Losing Earth: A Recent History”. Ready to line up for this one, folks?
Even though the density of the subject matter made my eyelids droop Trump-style a bit in the beginning, I have to say just trust in McCarthy whose very urgent Spotlight won the 2015 Best Picture Oscar and whose filmography includes such rich character studies as Win Win, The Station Agent, and The Visitor. His movies are all about people, and so, not surprisingly, is this one. Although this is all largely set around a large table in the St. Pete Beach Ce Sar Hotel conference room, and deals with a lot of dialogue around various conceits that might sail over your head, thanks to a smart approach to the basic material and the outstanding cast of wonderful actors hired to bring it to life, this becomes anything but a polemic. It is an entertaining, sly, humorous, enlightening, and even moving story of an effort by a group of mere human beings trying to come together for the good of the planet and deliver a simple statement on how to save us from ourselves. It is a quirky and unexpected period piece about a time when we weren’t so divided that it could be possible to have a civil discourse, even on a hot button topic. Ah, the good old days.
Watch on Deadline
Taking place in late October of 1980, just days before Ronald Reagan would defeat Jimmy Carter to become President, the timing of this conference in retrospect was crucial. The dawning impact of climate change was just coming into view (a global climate conference preceded this one a year earlier), but it was a time well before it would become such a polarizing political issue pitting us against each other on an issue about which there should be no argument. Seeing it play out now 46 years later, it is a bit mind boggling to see how far we haven’t come under a President and current administration that twice has canceled us out of the Paris Climate Agreement and enthusiastically welcomed the return of fossil fuels, coal, no regulations, and free reign for corporate America. Viewed now this film’s simple truths and debate over these inconvenient truths take on an importance and realization that not only have we not made much progress after four and a half decades, but we are sailing backwards to oblivion. If that sounds depressing, think again. A Statement, with its modest ambitions, comes just at the right time to remind us that no matter how divided we can be, we do share a common humanity – or once did – that hopefully can make a difference. The actual end result of this conference may not have been encouraging at the time, but by focusing on the people and disparate personalities who at least tried to come together in a room with potato salad and cold coffee we get the feeling all is not lost – even now when it all seems so dire. Guess I am an eternal optimist. I have to be. This is actually, oddly, a feel good movie in its own peculiar way.
Beware: A Statement does not follow a familiar usual three act structure for a movie. It all takes place at this hotel, where there is also a wedding going on that will figure delightfully as the weekend progresses, but basically the participants enter the room, introduce themselves, and start talking serious issues, no back stories on any of them. The Master Of Ceremonies here is ever confident Tom Jorling (Paul Rudd), assisted by atmospheric science expert Robert Cunningham (Noah Robbins) in keeping it all on track and power- pointing all the ideas that come up. Among the most prominently focused on here are an engaged activist with Friends Of The Earth, Rafe Pomerance (Evan Peters); Department Of Energy Carbon expert Dr. David Slade (Paul Giamatti) who may be out of a job after the election; a didactic M.I.T. Nuclear Engineer Dr. David Rose (John Turturro) with a lot of definite opinions; Public Health scholar Anne Marie Crocetti (Amy Ryan) who doesn’t say much until she does; legal scholar from Commission on Air Quality Edith Brown Weiss (Tatiana Maslansky) who may not be board; and personable but skeptical staff member John Perry (Jason Clarke), all among many others we meet and hear from.
Somehow, with major help from ace cinematographer Stuart Dryburgh, McCarthy keeps this all on track as a movie, a story of us, a group of unique personalities, strangers who come together with one purpose but also, in the end, show us we are, first and foremost more alike than not. A Statement is truly cinematic, even if the bones of it looks like it could have been a play. Reminiscent in some ways of Sidney Lumet’s landmark first feature, 12 Angry Men, McCarthy finds an exciting way to shoot this tight room without ever being rote. Although using the actual transcript can be challenging the filmmaker has found a clever way in as a human experience, and when you have actors on the level of Rudd, Giamatti, Turturro, Ryan, and on and on delivering the text we are in good hands.
McCarthy and his writers also smartly take us out of the conference room at the end of day one and invent interactions between the group into the night that also lets us get to personally know some of these people who likely will not see each other again. A lot of it is quite amusing. Who knew the M.I.T. guy Turturro plays could also be a hell of a wedding party crasher, or that the terrific scene-stealing Robbins’ atmospheric science expert Rob would hook up, so to speak, with the older stenographer Bernadette (played by the magnificent Nina Arianda). Their budding connection is ultimately quite a touching one. Ryan’s character is a largely quiet participant given a come-to-jesus moment toward the end that rivals Atticus Finch. Maslansky delivers the tough love from her character with deep conviction that keeps us riveted. The can-do-no-wrong Giamatti scores again here as the Energy Department veteran who has been to 300 of these types of conferences and has another lined up in December, just par for the course for a dedicated public servant hoping to make a difference in his – and our – humdrum life.
You get the feeling everyone in this room hopes to make a difference, and what they each have to say should be heard, but it is, in the end, the human comedy McCarthy untangles in bringing all of them together for a single collective goal that makes A Statement such a rewarding and heartfelt experience. I wanted to spend more time with this bunch, i was sorry to see them all go off to their own lives somewhere, maybe with a bit more knowledge that the mission that brought them to this Florida beach hotel conference room is one still worth pursuing.
Interestingly on the same weekend Alejandro G. Inarritu’s Digger opens, a divisive satire with a sober message about the devastating costs of ignoring the climate crisis, that film feels, to use earthquake terminology, like an aftershock to a calamity for the human race who stuck their heads in the sand and ignored the warnings. A Statement , very different in tone and attitude, and taking place right at the beginning when something could still be done, is the foreshock. Attention must be paid.
A Statement had its World Premiere today at the New York Film Festival and will be released in 2027. It is a gem. Producers are Jonathan King, David Levine, Jim Whitaker, Rae Baron, McCarthy, Jonathan Schwartz, Nick Shumaker, Bard Dorros and Mary Aloe.

Festival: New York Film Festival
Distributor: Sony Pictures Classics
Director: Tom McCarthy
Screenplay: Thomas Bidegan, Noé Debré and McCarthy
Cast: Paul Rudd, Evan Peters, Amy Ryan, Paul Giamatti, John Turturro, Tatiana Maslansky, Jason Clarke, Noah Robbins, Zach Woods, Nina Arianda, Mary Catherine Garrison, Michael Chernus, Tom McPherson, Dylan Baker, Michael Cerveris, Alan Eisenberg, Christopher Denham, Adrian Martinez.
Running Time: 1 hour and 44 minutes

Why am I suddenly buying up every 3D Blu-ray I can find after 3D became one of the biggest tech flops of all time?
3D movies are finally worth watching
It took decades, but the technology is finally ready.
3D movies are finally worth watching
It took decades, but the technology is finally ready.
The technology’s finally ready for 3D movies to shine, more than 15 years since James Cameron’s Avatar wowed me on the big screen and went on to become the highest-grossing film worldwide. Video glasses are giving me the experience I’ve always desired.
I’ve always loved 3D movies, but viewing them was awkward. Walking into a movie theater with a pair of polarized glasses, I would only get half the resolution and roughly half the brightness, since those glasses had to split one reflected image between my two eyes. Almost every 3D technology cuts something you care about in half, whether it’s resolution (see also: Nintendo 3DS) or the refresh rate and flicker you get with active shutter glasses.
But what if you had a full screen for each eye? That’s what video glasses can provide.
Last year, I began testing a pair of Xreal One Pro glasses, which primarily give you a gigantic flat screen, like a private theater, for whatever you plug in. But that screen doesn’t technically need to stay flat. If you press and hold the right button, Xreal can give you independent left and right views for side-by-side (SBS 3D) content. With proper content, you get a full 1080p view for each eye.
There are SBS 3D toggles in popular video player apps for VR headsets like the Meta Quest and Steam Frame, too — and the Apple Vision Pro and upcoming Meta VR Glasses let you natively stream 3D films.
They’re breathtaking.
The water in Moana, a glass-covered clock in Zootopia 2, the helmets in Gravity, suiting up in giant robots in Pacific Rim, lightcycles in Tron: Legacy, comic book panels coming to life in Into the Spider-Verse — there’s just so much more depth to see.
When the ocean parts to let Moana through, it no longer feels like looking at a flat wall of water. It’s a living chunk of ocean with life swimming inside. The Lego Movie went from “wow those are some realistic-looking CG Lego bricks on a flat screen” to “I just got teleported into an entire Lego diorama.” In Avatar, the holographic displays in the ops room are mind-blowing. Even the flat rectangular monitors have 3D layers within.
Cockpits and helmets and Tron: Legacy lightcycles and Mad Max: Fury Road’s convoy of battling vehicles — anything with transparent glass is a treat. There’s distinct detail on the faces inside the glass, the structures outside, beads of water or scratches on the glass itself, even reflections of the outside world, depending on the film.
Billie Eilish’s new concert film, shot by James Cameron with 16 twin cameras including four remote-controlled AGITO camera rigs, looked incredible in the Meta VR Glasses during a brief demo. He got up close and personal with the concert, like few VR concert recordings do. In a demo with the Google / Xreal Aura, I watched a tiny bit of the interactive nature documentary Galapagos: The Last Eden and was entranced by the gorgeous baby seals, the grains of sand in their shiny fur, the fuzzy depth of the hair on their skin.
Regardless of the hardware, it almost feels like I can reach out and touch a character’s face in 3D, feel their emotions and wrinkles and scars more vividly, once they have depth.
Or, in the case of Werner Herzog’s cult-classic 3D documentary Cave of Forgotten Dreams, I could appreciate how the world’s oldest surviving art isn’t flat — the 32,000-year-old cave paintings took form thanks to their three-dimensional canvas. “A bulging rock is now a bulging neck of a bison that attacks you,” Herzog explained to us earlier this year.
When I fired up Gravity for what I thought would be a brief test, late at night in bed, I wound up watching the entire film. It all feels a bit like when I bought my first decent set of headphones — I never knew what I was missing, but now I want to revisit all my favorites to experience them more deeply.
Not all 3D content is equal. Few live-action movies were truly filmed with twin cameras in recent years. In fake or poorly converted 3D movies, you’ll often see a “billboard” effect where it looks like there are flat layers of people or objects in the background instead of true depth.
But the biggest catch is that 3D movies aren’t easy to just buy and play. Even though 3D films are still coming to theaters, you can’t necessarily stream them or buy a high-quality copy. 4K Blu-ray doesn’t support 3D at all. 3D Blu-rays were the last discs to offer 3D, and as FlatPanelsHD pointed out last year, that means most physical 3D movies are stuck in the past at 1080p, 24fps, without HDR.
Even 3D Blu-rays aren’t necessarily easy to find: I had to nab a copy of Cave of Forgotten Dreams off eBay, and paid a pretty penny to ship a rare-ish copy of Into the Spider-Verse from Thailand.
Here’s the good news: The leading headset makers are starting to convince Hollywood it’s time to stream their 3D collections instead.
In 2024, the Apple Vision Pro launched with by far the best 3D movie experience yet, now with 4K, HDR, spatial audio, some (Avatar) films at 48fps, HEVC encoding, free 3D upgrades for many films you’d already purchased in 2D, and exclusive access to the largest catalog of 3D films in existence on Disney Plus. (Modern Disney animated films are natively rendered in digital 3D, and most Disney-owned Marvel films got a 3D conversion to jazz up their theatrical appeal.)
Soon, you’ll no longer need a $3,500 Apple headset to watch those films or convert them from old discs — you’ll be able to stream them with a $350 Meta Quest 3S or $600 Quest 3, as well as the new $1,300 Meta VR Glasses, Meta director of entertainment Sarah Malkin confirms to The Verge.
Meta’s headset will offer 3D movies to subscribers in the Disney Plus, HBO, Paramount Plus, and Peacock apps, she says, with some of that starting later this fall.
And by the time the Meta VR Glasses launch in spring, there will be “hundreds of 3D films available” to rent or buy though Meta’s TV app, as well as some free 3D content. They shouldn’t cost more than traditional movies, either, she says: “Our 3D movies will also be in line with typical pricing for 2D Ultra High Definition (UHD) films.”
(In case you’re wondering, she also says the Meta VR Glasses’ three-hour battery life quote should cover a full 3D movie “watched in Theater mode if starting with the device fully charged.”)
In the meanwhile, I’m experiencing 3D the hacky way: by ripping discs. Every time I walk into a thrift store, I hunt for a 3D Blu-ray or two. I pop them into an old external USB Blu-ray reader, then let MakeMKV spend half an hour per movie to produce a 30-to-40GB multi-view (MVC) file. I pop that into BD3D2MK3D for another 50 minutes per movie to spit out a high-quality 3840 x 1080 “Full-SBS” file that’s half the size of the MVC.
I drop that onto an SD card, pop it into the Steam Deck, plug in the Xreal glasses, fire up VLC Media Player, then flip the glasses into 3D mode. It’s a lot of friction, but for me, the payoff is worth it.
Even though I’m mostly watching old movies, it feels like a taste of the future. But you know what they say: Everything old is eventually new again.

ChatGPT wants to be your new virtual fitting room.
OpenAI on Thursday rolled out two shopping features globally, allowing users to virtually try on clothing and accessories and save their favorite finds for later.
The new Try On button lets shoppers upload a selfie or full-body photo to see how products might look on them. Users can also upload screenshots of items or celebrity outfits and ask ChatGPT to find similar pieces available for purchase.
Both features are powered by OpenAI's new ChatGPT Images 2.5 model, which the company said delivers more realistic lighting and textures.
I tested the function, from a simple necklace try-on to a complicated full-body costume, and included a cat in the mix to see if the AI could also dress our four-legged friends.
Here's what it excelled at — and where things began to get weird.
Starting with accessories
I started simple with a selfie and a request to find me products that could recreate a silver necklace stack I found on Pinterest, and a little moon pendant in particular, as a centerpiece.
The AI quickly found options for the moon pendant at various price points and gave me two options: I could try on the pendant, or I could try on the entire layered necklace look.
I tested out both looks. The proportions seemed correct and extremely realistic, and could convince me to make a purchase, even though I prefer to shop for jewelry in person.
Testing a full-body outfit
I pulled out another Pinterest save for a concert outfit inspiration, and chose a dressing room selfie with a simple background to try it on.
The AI categorized the style I'm seeking as "whimsigoth" and recommended products consistent with the branding, including garments from Disturbia and Free People.
I tried on both a single mesh top and a complete outfit. The result was nearly perfect. Even the wide lace sleeve that fell down my arm was perfectly placed.
The wedding dress
The AI did really well so far, so I decided to ask for more complicated outfits, and here is when we started to enter dicey territory.
Though I won't be getting married anytime soon, I love vintage wedding dresses from the 1970s, and was curious what one would look like on me.
The AI seemed to prefer brand-new products and surfaced real vintage items last, and I was surprised to find only one Etsy listing among a mix of brands I had never heard of.
I eventually asked to try on a 1970s ivory lace wedding dress, but the virtual rendering did not accurately represent it. The real dress was mostly made of satin and had solid sleeves, but the virtual try-on turned the dress into a full-length lace gown with cake-like layers and sheer sleeves. The original dress was also not meant to trail on the floor as the AI depicted.
I would not call this a successful virtual try-on.
A potential Halloween costume
To push the AI even more, I decided to ask for my dream Halloween outfit, complete with fairy wings.
ChatGPT recommended a combination of a Victorian-style white maxi dress and a pair of moth wings, so I asked to try them on together, but it did not turn out ideal.
Not only do the chunky wings look significantly different from the airy, semi-transparent, blush-colored moth wings I asked to try on, but the AI also began to "upgrade" my body so the dress would look more flattering, giving me exceedingly long legs.
I am fairly short and often can't manage to fit into a maxi dress like the AI wishes I could, so I would recommend always trusting the product measurements over the virtual try-on, which may not reflect actual proportions.
It works on cats
I was wondering if the AI was pet-friendly, so I ran a separate try-on test for my fluffy orange cat with an adorable Halloween collar, and now it's sitting in my shopping cart.
At the end of the day, ChatGPT may have given me longer legs and a wedding dress I didn't order, but it has at least one clear advantage over a real fitting room: I can bring my cat.

ixigo backed e-intercity bus operator Fresh Bus reported a 2.4X jump in its FY26 operating revenue to ₹63.5 Cr from ₹26.3 Cr as it expanded its electric fleet and route network. The startup’s top line grew on the back of a rapid expansion of its bus fleet and routes, founder and CEO Sudhakar Reddy Chirra told Inc42. The expansion also led to the startup’s bottom line for the fiscal swelling 33% to ₹43.6 Cr from ₹32.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal. The startup’s bottom line was weighed down by a sharp increase in expenditure over the fiscal. Its total expenses rose 81.4% YoY to ₹107.2 Cr from ₹59.1 Cr in the year-ago period. The jump in expenses in FY26 was primarily linked to the expansion of the fleet, according to Chirra. Lease costs rise with the number of buses, while maintenance, captain salaries, tolls and distribution expenses increase as operations scale, he said. Fresh Bus’ Growth Plans The startup is now targeting a revenue of ₹180 Cr in revenue in FY27, while reducing its loss to around ₹25 Cr-₹30 Cr, Chirra said. Chirra claims that the startup became contribution-margin positive in March 2026, with a current contribution margin of 15%-17%, according to Chirra. He expects Fresh Bus to turn profitable around April-June 2027. The startup is looking to improve its bottom line by reducing up to 30% of its costs by doubling down on larger bus fleets. This will benefit increasing fare rates as well customer stickiness, the founder believes. Founded in 2019, Fresh Bus operates electric buses on intercity routes. It leases buses from fleet providers including Vertelo and Drivn and offers users a digital platform to search for and book tickets. The startup claims to have completed 25 Lakh journeys for 9 Lakh passengers. At the end of the fiscal year, Fresh Bus operated 100 e-buses across 10 routes, primarily in South India. It intends to double this number to 200 by the end of FY27 and broaden its route options to 16. Beyond FY27, Fresh Bus plans to reach 500 buses by March 2028, initially focusing on southern India before expanding westward and then into the north. It expects to reach 1,000 buses across the three regions by March 2029. The startup currently operates at 85-90% occupancy, with around 1.6-1.7 Lakh seats offered each month, Chirra said. Established routes such as Bengaluru-Tirupati, Bengaluru-Chennai and Hyderabad-Vijayawada have repeat ratios of more than 55%. Moving forth, the startup is planning to deepen its presence in southern India, with routes including Chennai-Madurai, Chennai-Tanjavur, Chennai-Trichy, Bengaluru-Trichy, Bengaluru-Madurai and Bengaluru-Tanjavur planned by March. In August, Fresh Bus and ChargeZone expanded their partnership to support 400 additional electric buses, taking the fleet supported by ChargeZone's charging network to 500 buses. ChargeZone will add 30 MW of charging capacity to the 10 MW already dedicated to Fresh Bus. The expanded network is expected to connect 20 cities and 17 additional towns across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana over the next 15 months Fresh Bus had last raised ₹87.5 Cr in Series A funding in August 2024, with participation from Maniv Mobility, Shell Ventures, Alteria Capital and Riverwalk Holdings. The company had said the capital would be used to add 150 electric buses and expand its route network. In August 2026, ixigo agreed to sell a 17.39% stake in Fresh Bus to Twelve Stone LLP for ₹36.6 Cr. Moreover, it recognised a ₹11.22 Cr share of loss from Fresh Bus in FY26.

Prosecutor says 2 Iranian men scouted a UK synagogue for a chlorine bomb plot
Two Iranian men have been accused of plotting to bomb a Manchester synagogue
LONDON -- Two Iranian men conducted surveillance of a Manchester synagogue that was the site of a deadly attack a year ago as part of a plot to bomb it this year, a prosecutor said Saturday.
Salam Ahmadyan, 36, and Rahman Salehi, 34, researched attacking the Heaton Park Congregation Synagogue in Manchester in northwest England and the Jewish Museum in nearby Cheetham Hill, the court was told.
Ahmadyan and Salehi were arrested last month and charged Friday with engaging in conduct in preparation for terrorist acts.
Neither entered a plea during an appearance in Westminster Magistrates’ Court, where Judge Nina Tempia ordered them held until an Oct. 23 appearance at the Central Criminal Court in London.
Prosecutor Mark Luckett said the duo were directed by a third person believed to be in Iran who coordinated plans and provided instructions on making a homemade chlorine bomb.
The defendants were observed carrying out "a hostile reconnaissance within Manchester’s Jewish community," Luckett said.
The Heaton Park synagogue was the site of an attack on Yom Kippur, the holiest day of the Jewish calendar, on Oct. 2, 2025, when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, crashed his car into the gates and then began a knife attack while wearing a fake suicide belt.
Congregation members Melvin Cravitz, 66, and Adrian Daulby, 53, died in the attack and three other men were seriously wounded. Al-Shamie, who allegedly pledged allegiance to the Islamic State group, was killed by police.
Ahmadyan and Salehi entered the U.K. without authorization in the past six years after crossing the English Channel by boat, the court was told. Salehi was granted asylum and Ahmadyan has a pending asylum claim.
Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat. She also said it was unconnected to a suspected terror plot at U.S.-runRAF Fairford air base, which some officials have said was linked to Tehran.
“I’m aware that the news of this alleged plot coming during the High Holy Day period has caused a great deal of concern," Evans said. “It also coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing antisemitic incidents across the U.K., so we are very aware that this will likely increase what were already heightened concerns amongst the Jewish community."

The Kindle will turn 20 in 2027. Amazon says it plans to celebrate the milestone throughout the year, but to kick things off, it's starting with an entirely refreshed Kindle lineup.
On Thursday, the company introduced a handful of new Kindle models: a new 6-inch base Kindle, a 7-inch Kindle Paperwhite, and a 7-inch Kindle Colorsoft. You can buy Signature Editions of the latter two and Kids versions of the entire range, which include artist-designed kids cases, a year of Amazon's worry-free guarantee for damage, and a year of Kids+, the company's subscription service that offers unlimited access to ad-free, child-appropriate books.
The highlight is Amazon's use of aluminum for the Kindle's construction rather than traditional plastic. The starting tier is plastic, but you can upgrade to an all-aluminum model (Amazon uses 80 percent recycled aluminum) if you prefer that Kindle model and you just want something more robust.
It can get a little confusing with all the different SKUs, so here's a quick rundown:
Lighter and Premium
The base Kindle, the aluminum version, and the Kids Kindle are on sale starting today. The Paperwhite and Colorsoft are available for preorder on a rolling basis and will launch at the end of October.
The base Kindle's screen offers 30 percent faster page turns than its predecessor, Amazon says. The build is a whole millimeter thinner at 6.8 mm, and Amazon cut the weight by around 18 grams to 140 grams. The Kindle Paperwhite and Colorsoft are both similarly lighter (204 grams) and thinner (6.8 mm), retain the waterproof design, and feature adjustable warm reading lights. The screen refreshes 30 percent faster than the base Kindle, and the screen has a higher pixel density that makes text appear sharper.
Upgrading to the Signature Edition for both nets you the aluminum build, an ambient light sensor that adjusts brightness automatically, an accelerometer that lets you turn the screen to landscape orientation and have the pages adjust accordingly. The upgrade also adds the ability to use a double-tap gesture to turn pages.
Uniquely, the Signature Editions feature pogo pins that let you charge via Amazon's new $60 dock, which props the device up as it charges. There's also a new Page-Turn Cover ($80)—a case with physical page-turn buttons that magnetically attaches to the back of the devices and pairs via the pogo pins, which Amazon says offers page-turn buttons to the vocal minority that still loves them (around 5 percent of Kindle users) without adding unnecessary bulk to the device.
Don't worry, you don't need the case, the Signature Edition, or even a new Kindle if you just want page-turn buttons. Amazon is debuting its own Kindle Click, a $35 page-turn accessory that pairs over Bluetooth for the non-Signature (and older) Kindle models.
Kindle Ablaze
The Kindle business is booming. Amazon's Kevin Keith, vice president of product, says Kindles have seen double-digit growth over the last three years, with 2025 being the highest sales year in more than a decade. He says 60 to 65 percent of people buying new devices have never had a Kindle before, with Gen Z, millennials, and even Gen Alpha driving the lion's share. This past January saw the highest single-month Kindle reading volume in history.
At the same time, Kindles are more expensive than ever. “Memory pricing is a little bit crazy,” Keith says, referring to the memory shortage behind the general price bump on all electronics. Amazon upped prices of existing Kindles earlier this year; the new devices match those prices.
Part of the redesign aims to lower overall manufacturing costs and standardize the hardware. Take the refreshed display on the base Kindle—Keith says many of the improvements trickle down from the development of the Kindle Scribe. For the first time, the base Kindle has a display that sits flush with the body, just like its pricier counterparts. (It previously had a raised plastic bezel around the screen.) That whole front panel is also available in a new color: Ube (purple).
While Amazon has made Kindles with colorful fronts (like the matcha green Kindle from 2024), it hasn't done this with flush displays. That's because simply coloring the front would make the Ube color, for example, scatter around the screen as the frontlight reflects it, casting a purple hue on the display. To counter this, Keith says Amazon developed a new “edge-to-edge” color technology that prints two different colors under the cover lens: the Ube color backed by a layer of black. The black absorbs the light, which solves the problem. Amazon says it perfected this tech in the Scribe and ported it down here.
Color is important. Keith says alternative colors typically make up just 15 to 20 percent of sales—the rest being classic options like black or white—but the matcha green model captured a surprising 55 percent. Amazon also chose that color because, at the time, it noticed a general increase in the popularity of matcha in drinks and sweets (it also noted that folks on #BookTok are reading in coffee shops). Hence the new ube color, which is based on the popular purple yam of the same name.
“We've been tracking food trends, and two years ago, ube just exploded—ube was growing 200 percent year over year,” says Chris Green, Amazon's vice president of design. “We expect it to do far better than the matcha.”
For the aluminum housing, instead of milling the device's frame from a block of aluminum and using a lot of water in the process, Amazon stamps a flat sheet, which then goes into a forge that presses down to create the backplate and sides. The process supposedly takes seconds compared to the hours it can take to machine a single aluminum device frame (like an iPhone or MacBook) saving material and energy. It helps lower the Kindle's carbon footprint, which is now equivalent to 11 hardcover books.
Green says these improvements bring down the device's density. The density of the average human body is around 1 gram per cubic centimeter; an iPhone is around 2.2 grams per cubic centimeter. The new Kindles are around 1.2 grams. Lowering that number can help make the hardware “disappear” during prolonged use.
“I truly want people to never think about the Kindle,” Green says. “I just want them to think about the magical world that the author has created inside of this device.”
For Green, who has designed nearly all of Amazon's hardware in his 19-year tenure at the company (and yes, he says he's embarrassed by the Fire Phone), chasing that 1.2-grams-per-cubic-centimeter target is all about getting the gadget out of the way so the Kindle can mimic the analog calm of physical print.
“More people are reading on paper, more people are reading on Kindles,” Green says. “Is it a backlash to AI? Probably. People are trying to find things more authentic—we're in a crisis of authenticity.” Surveys have shown that overall leisure reading is down across the US, but the people who are reading are buying more than ever.
As for the 20th anniversary of the Kindle in 2027, Keith says the company may roll out a significant refresh to the Kindle's user interface, though he didn't share more. Expect special anniversary editions of some Kindles. When I asked whether we could expect the return of the Kindle Oasis—an asymmetrical e-reader with physical page-turn buttons—Green chuckles.
“The first Oasis was one of my passion projects,” he says. “I loved that. I really, really loved that product. But I was a vocal minority on that—most of the people wanted slabs.”
So, probably not.

“In what world,” New York Gov. Kathy Hochul asked on Friday, “would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang raped while she was intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?”
The Cornell case, explained
A timeline of how a student went ignored at Cornell.
Hochul was speaking about the case of a former Cornell student who said she was raped by several members of the university’s Chi Phi fraternity in 2024. At the time, the district attorney filed no criminal charges.
The case has rocked the nation and forced a renewed reckoning over how sexual assault is dealt with in higher education. While the district attorney has defended his handling of the case, many politicians and legal experts are now examining whether certain details of the alleged victim’s account were neglected, and prosecutors have reopened the case.
Amy Wang is a staff reporter at the Washington Post who’s been covering the story over the past week. She spoke with Today, Explained co-host Noel King about what allegedly happened on the night in question, what happened afterward, and what we still don’t know.
Since the two spoke, New York state Attorney General Letitia James has also been assigned to oversee the case and said it is now “an active criminal investigation.” As new information comes to light, further legal action could be taken.
Below is an excerpt of the conversation between King and Wang, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.
In October of 2024, a young woman went to a fraternity house near Cornell University’s campus. Who is this young woman, and why did she go to the frat house that night?
The young woman is only identified in documents as Jane Doe, so we don’t know her name. She was, at the time, 20 years old. She was a sophomore at Cornell. And around 11 pm on the night of October 19, 2024, this Jane Doe goes to a bar on campus, and then, after that, goes to the Chi Phi fraternity house to hang out with a friend.
She said that she was already pretty intoxicated at that point, and she’d had maybe 10 drinks in about three hours. Her friend at the fraternity house hands her a beer. After that is where she alleges that another member of the fraternity pressured her into taking drugs, specifically ketamine and marijuana, and drinking more alcohol. She alleges that two members of the fraternity assaulted her, and that one of them later sent a Snapchat message out to active Chi Phi members. The message is pretty graphic, but essentially invites them to join in, and several did.
In about three weeks, this young woman was going to go to the Cornell campus police and report what happened that night. But in the interim, what was going on? What was happening?
We now know, based on reporting by the New York Times and CBS News, this young woman was a member of a campus sorority, so she went to a member of her sorority and was trying to make sense of what happened. She was still processing it in real time. She wasn’t using, according to their reporting, the word “rape” or “assault.” And she was also seeing rumors circulating around campus about what had taken place at the fraternity house and was growing concerned about how they portrayed her.
She, in the interim, also received a text message from one of the seven men at the fraternity essentially apologizing for how things went down the other night. She is not yet accusing them of assault, but is chatting, even seeks to reassure him in that first message.
On October 22, she then makes an appointment at the campus health clinic because she had what she thought was a UTI and wanted to be tested because she told the doctor that she had gone through a traumatic experience.
According to the New York Times reporting, you could see her thinking about what happened kind of evolve over those few weeks. She at some point says that this is starting to ruin her life, and she’s sleeping and crying and she’s feeling ashamed. She’s just really grappling with what had taken place, trying to make sense of it. By November 3 is when, according to these investigative documents that were obtained by the Times, she kind of comes to this conclusion that what happened at the party at Chi Phi was assault.
She texts one of the seven fraternity members and says, “This was not consensual. I was given more ketamine than I can remember,” and that she was uncomfortable. A few days later, November 7th, 2024, according to these documents, she goes to the ER and asks for a rape kit. And the following day is when she goes to Cornell University Police.
When she goes to the police, how does she characterize what happened to the police? What does she tell them?
What she tells the police is that she believes she was assaulted, and she tells the police that it had started out as something that was consensual. And then at the end she says, “I can say with 100 percent confidence I was raped.” She tells police she was extremely uncomfortable and that she kept taking ketamine in part because she thought she might black out and pass out. She had thought of at least two of the men as her friends. After the events of that night, she is then confronted with rumors that were spreading across campus, sort of depicting her as loose and blaming her essentially.
What happens after Jane Doe talks to the police? What do they do?
When she talks to Cornell University Police, they summarize what she said in a six-page statement that she then signs. And that is the statement that is submitted to the Tompkins County district attorney.
And the district attorney would be the person who would bring charges or decide not to bring charges. What does he decide?
Yes, so the district attorney decides not to bring charges in 2024 based on, he has said, the sworn statement that she signs to police.
The DA says no charges for the seven men. Were they disciplined in any way?
We don’t know exactly how each of the men were disciplined. Cornell has said that they faced a range of disciplinary measures, including expulsions and suspensions. One of the details that had gone particularly viral about this is that the disciplinary measures included for some of the students to write essays. Cornell has not denied that, but it has specifically denied that the students only had to write essays as a disciplinary measure. The university has cited privacy laws and said it really can’t release any more specifics about how individual students were punished or not punished.
What did Jane Doe do after first talking to the police and then learning the DA wasn’t going to press charges?
After she goes to police, we know she remains on campus and she has to continue seeing some of these men. And she also participates in the school’s Title IX investigation, which takes place over several months and concludes at some point in 2025.
I want to ask you about the DA. He is out in public defending his decision to not press charges in 2024. How is he defending himself?
The DA is a big part of the story. This is the Tompkins County District Attorney. His name is Matthew Van Houten. And he has said that in 2024, based on the written statement from Jane Doe, they did not have what they needed to press criminal charges.
It’s important to note that we, as in the public, we’ve not actually seen a copy of Jane Doe’s sworn statement. The DA issued a press release in which he summarizes that statement. And in that summary, he describes her characterization of this as voluntary and conscious and consensual. That is at odds with some of the investigative documents that we’ve seen reported since then, including that transcript of Jane Doe’s interview with Cornell Police in which she very confidently says that she believes she was raped and even says that she was physically hit during that night.
The DA said that he did not see, before the lawsuit, the screenshot of the Snapchat message where the frat members are talking pretty crudely about the situation, and he also says he didn’t see the transcript of the interview between Jane Doe and police.
We now know the names of the seven men who were there that night. Have they said anything?
The seven men themselves have not publicly said anything, and the lawyers for three of those seven men have publicly denied the allegations. One of them says that his client went into the room, but immediately left and didn’t participate in the assault.
This is a story that is developing very quickly, and it seems like new information is coming out just about every day. What do we know about what happens next?
So there’s at least two things going on here. There is the reopened criminal investigation.
Separately, there’s the civil lawsuit that Jane Doe filed last month, and that is not dependent in any way on how the criminal investigation goes, but that will also proceed against the university, the seven fraternity members, and the fraternity itself.

$40K for mucking out pigs and harvesting corn: The farm schools cashing in on college applications
Forget summer camp. Some high school students are spending their summers studying soil, raising animals and learning agriculture – experiences their families hope will help them stand out in college admissions

Some American parents are paying thousands of dollars to send their kids to farm school – where they hope the phone-free experience of mucking out pigs, harvesting crops and chopping wood will give them an edge in the hyper-competitive world of college admissions.
At Vermont’s Mountain School of Milton Academy, 10th-, 11th- and 12th-grade students spend a semester living and learning on a 418-acre campus, with most students in their junior year. The program combines traditional academics with farm work and campus chores, and includes a strict break from technology. Tuition is nearly $40,000, according to the school’s website.
The cost covers room and board, activities, field trips and community programming. Students continue academic classes, including AP Calculus, while spending about eight hours a week on farm work and chores such as harvesting crops, caring for livestock, washing dishes and cleaning classrooms.
About 50 students attend each semester, according to U.S. News & World Report, and about 30 percent receive financial aid, the school’s director told The Wall Street Journal. The hands-on work is designed to teach students the practical tasks involved in maintaining a community. Some arrive with little or no farming experience and have to learn basics such as planting seeds and identifying plant roots, while others learn proper harvesting techniques and ways to avoid back injuries.
The semester also includes a four-day wilderness trip, giving students time in nature without the digital devices they typically use at home and school. A few students told the WSJ in September that they saw the unusual experience as worthwhile, rather than resenting the chores or tech restrictions.
“It’s fun,” student Max Sherman said about washing dishes, while Cassie Scott got excited about being outdoors and told the outlet: “This is the closest I’ve been to nature in a while. I’m literally hugging a tree.”
Meanwhile, student Estela Whitney, responsible for feeding food scraps to piglets and making sure they had water, recalled a lesson she learned once after arriving hours late and finding the animals hungry.
“I’m going to be a lot more careful to not make that mistake again,” Whitney said.
Some students and their parents hope these schools will give them an edge in the fiercely competitive college-admissions process.
At Olney Friends School in Barnesville, Ohio, students use the school’s 350-acre organic farm as an extension of the classroom, according to its website. They apply biology, chemistry, math and environmental science to real farm work, from testing soil and planting crops to caring for animals and managing resources.
The hands-on work also helps students develop practical skills such as responsibility, teamwork, problem-solving and resilience. Farm chores offer a break from screens while teaching students about sustainability and where their food comes from. Much of the farm’s produce eventually makes its way into school meals.
“This type of authentic education is what universities are increasingly looking for in college applicants,” the Olney website states.
Meanwhile, Stephen Turban, co-founder and director of Lumiere Education, sees value in agriculture-focused summer programs for high school students. The program pairs students with Ph.D. mentors to conduct research and write original academic papers.
In a November 2025 article, Turban, who studied statistics at Harvard, worked at McKinsey and pursued a PhD at Harvard Business School, highlighted 15 agriculture summer programs for high school students. The programs, offered by colleges and universities across the US, cover topics including agricultural research, animal science, sustainable farming, food systems, environmental science, food technology and agricultural business.
“Taking part in an agriculture program can also strengthen your college applications. It shows early initiative in exploring an important and evolving field, along with skills in research, data collection, and problem-solving,” Turban wrote. “Colleges value students who can connect academic study with real-world application, and agricultural programs show that you’ve already started doing that.”
But admissions consultant Adam Nguyen questioned whether attending these schools actually gives students an edge in the college-admissions process.
“Admissions officers don't reward expensive randomness. That will backfire, for sure,” he told the WSJ.
Farm schools also offer students a rare break from their phones. Many require the surrender of devices upon arrival, with internet access limited and technology largely reserved for schoolwork.
At the Vermont school, faculty member Bruce Brough said students once worried most about encountering bears during the solo trip. Now, he said, they are more concerned about being alone with their thoughts.
Myers added that the “solo” experience encourages students to consider: “Who am I when I don't have a screen?”

Hidaka, Hokkaido – The pressure cooker hardships of COVID-19 lockdowns produced diamonds that continue to shine years after the fact.
Disheartened by lackluster convenience store, street food and home delivery options while cooped up in his Paris home during the pandemic, chef Walter Ishizuka set his imagination to how simple B-kyū gurume (cheap and casual yet delicious food) could deliver superlative epicurean experiences.
And so in 2022, Yabai Sando was born — a “Paris Japanese sando house” (using the Japanese word for “sandwich”) in the French capital’s upscale Odeon neighborhood. There, Ishizuka serves chicken katsu (cutlets), tamago (egg), tuna tataki (seared) and wagyu katsu on pillowy, crustless Japanese shokupan bread and with fine-dining flourishes like yuzu aioli and black sesame and ginger wasabi sauces.

On Friday, Amazon committed to donating more than $1 billion over the next five years to communities neighboring data centers.
In a press release, Amazon Web Services’ CEO Matt Garman said that communities would decide how to prioritize funds across “education, job training, energy affordability, water, and energy preservation, and local priorities.”
Laying out other community commitments, Amazon also promised to ensure data centers wouldn’t increase power bills or wipe out local water supplies. Regarding the latter, Amazon promised to be “water positive” by 2030, while claiming that 75 percent of projects have already met this goal.
Rolling out these commitments, Amazon seemed bent on convincing Americans that the swelling data center backlash is based on lies. Echoing Donald Trump’s claims that foreign disinformation campaigns are fueling widespread protests, Garman urged that calls for data moratoriums must end or else American frontier AI might fall behind China’s.
According to Garman, US rivals are trying to “trick us into slowing down,” and Amazon’s commitments are meant to reassure Americans that everything’s okay and that we should instead plow ahead, as Trump endlessly advocates.
However, advocates at Stand.Earth—a global nonprofit that’s been fighting for environmental protections in communities hosting data centers—told Ars that Amazon is the one being “misleading” by spreading “corporate propaganda.” Seemingly in crisis mode as billions of dollars in data center projects have been blocked nationwide, Amazon’s promised donations represent “a flailing attempt at damage control for the harm its data center build-out has already caused,” Stand.Earth said.
Most problematic, Stand.Earth suggested, is Amazon’s plan to back a power plant that experts expect will become the largest source of US climate pollution. Glaringly, Amazon’s data center commitments don’t mention the power plant and scarcely address pollution, apart from promising to exclusively rely on back-up generators that use the lowest possible emissions.

Effects of preventive treatment for tuberculosis could start to wane after just one year of completing the antibiotics course in high-burden settings, while the protection lasts for at least eight and 13 years in medium and low-burden countries, a study has found.
Findings published in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine show that tuberculosis preventive treatment (TPT) offered a strong protection during the first 12-24 months across settings with all levels of TB burden.
Consisting of antibiotic medicines that can prevent inactive TB infections from developing into active disease, TPT is considered an important public health tool for protecting individuals and countries from the deadly infectious disease.
Preventive treatment can include medications, such as isoniazid and rifapentine -- typically prescribed for four months -- and is critical for the World Health Organization's goal to end the global TB epidemic by 2035.
TPT has been shown to be highly effective, but how long this protection lasts -- and whether its duration varies by region or community risk level -- remains unclear, researchers at the US' Boston University and the University of California, Berkeley, said.
They estimated TB risk among people with TB infections in 24 countries and found that TPT offered strong initial protection, but long-term protection varied depending on the burden of TB disease in each area.
"Of 4,66,523 participants from 47 studies, we included 84,128 individuals from 44 cohort studies across 24 countries. TPT was highly protective within the first year but declined over the course of follow-up in all settings, with greater effects observed in low-burden and medium-burden settings," the authors wrote.
The results showed that high-burden countries should consider combining TPT with other interventions to achieve the long-term benefits these medications are capable of providing, they said.
Lead author Lauren Linde, an epidemiology doctoral student at Boston University's school of public health, said, "In this study, our results corroborated something that was already well-established -- TPT is highly effective at preventing TB progression among close contacts and people who have been infected with TB."
"However, our finding that the initial effect of TPT declined so rapidly in very high-burden settings strengthens the case for not placing too much emphasis on TPT in isolation from other interventions that address ongoing community transmission," Linde said.

An allegation of sexual assault against a Delhi Police officer during a protest at Jantar Mantar has triggered protests outside Parliament Street Police Station, with journalists, protesters and lawyers demanding action on the complaint. The allegation was made by an independent journalist who said she was covering the detention of AISA activist Neha Bora when the incident allegedly took place. The allegations against the police officer have not been independently verified. Here is what happened and what is known about the controversy so far. In a video message posted by CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, the journalist alleged that ACP Vivek Bhagat groped and pushed her while she was covering the detention at Jantar Mantar. "It's been more than three hours that I have been sitting inside Parliament Street Police Station," she said. She alleged that Bhagat "groped me and then pushed me". The journalist said she had gone to Parliament Street Police Station to lodge a complaint but had been waiting for several hours without an FIR being registered. The allegations against the officer have not been independently verified. Delhi Police has now said that complaints of sexual harassment were made by three female journalists against police officers during the October 3 protest in New Delhi. In a post on X, Delhi Police said: "On 03-10-26, during the protest in New Delhi area, while being in law and order situation, allegations of sexual harassment were made by three female journalists against police officers." "New Delhi District has received their complaints and the same are transferred to Crime Branch for fair and impartial enquiry," the police said. The police statement does not detail the allegations made in the three complaints or identify the officers named in them. The allegation prompted hundreds of journalists to gather outside Parliament Street Police Station in support of the journalist. CJP member Saurav Das said journalists, protesters and lawyers would return to the police station and demand a copy of the FIR. "We will tell the police that time's up and now we want the copy of the FIR over Rosie's complaint," he said. Das alleged that Delhi Police was protecting the officer named in the complaint and said police had sought time to examine video footage of the incident. "The police have said that they just need a little time to look at the video footage and so on," he said. He argued that a complaint of sexual assault should result in immediate police action. "But the police, the Delhi police, are protecting their predator. We will absolutely not tolerate this," Das said. He said protesters had nevertheless agreed to give police time to examine the footage. "Whereas it does not take more than half an hour to watch the video," he said. "But even then we want to give the Delhi police the time they want to take." The allegation has also drawn criticism from Congress MP and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi. In a post on X, Gandhi questioned why an FIR had not been registered after hours of protests. "A female journalist has accused a police officer of misconduct at Jantar Mantar. For hours, hundreds of journalists have been sitting there with just one demand: that an FIR be registered. Isn't that the police's basic duty? They haven't even done that," Gandhi wrote. Gandhi also referred to allegations that protesters had been detained at Jantar Mantar, women protesters had faced misconduct and journalists had been dragged and had their cameras snatched. "Women across Delhi, students, are gripped by fear for their safety, staging satyagraha — but the very police responsible for protecting women are raising hands against them. And a government that fears registering even one woman's complaint — what exactly is it protecting?" he added. He also questioned Union Home Minister Amit Shah, noting that Delhi Police comes under the Ministry of Home Affairs. "Amit Shah ji, where are you? You have to answer for this," he wrote. CJP co-convener Ashutosh Ranka said hundreds of journalists were protesting outside Parliament Street Police Station over allegations against Delhi Police officials. "100s of journalists are protesting outside Parliamentary street police station, alleging harassment and assault by @DelhiPolice officials," he wrote. CJP member Ratna Singh separately alleged that a woman had been sexually harassed by a male police official and claimed that a Delhi Police DCP had asked her not to escalate the matter. The controversy unfolded during demonstrations near Jantar Mantar over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. Delhi Police detained several protesters, including AISA president Neha Bora. Senior advocates Prashant Bhushan and Kapil Sibal were also among those who attempted to move beyond police barricades during the protest. Delhi Police registered three FIRs in connection with the wider protest — two at Parliament Street Police Station and one at Connaught Place Police Station. The controversy came amid a wider political dispute over the Election Commission's handling of electoral-roll revision. A report in The Indian Express said Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised objections on at least 14 occasions over 10 months concerning electoral rolls, voter registration and the Commission's technology systems. The Election Commission rejected the suggestion that these objections amounted to institutional dissent, saying operational queries, inputs and suggestions during the draft stage were part of its standard administrative and decision-making process. The ECI said decisions on the SIR schedule were unanimous. The immediate focus is on the complaint made by the journalist against the police officer and the demand by protesters for an FIR. The police response, including the examination of video footage cited by officials, is likely to remain central to the dispute. For now, the allegations against the officer remain allegations and have not been independently established. One imam in Houston has been videoed with some of his supporters calling for Muslim business owners to stop selling haram products, like pork, alcohol and lottery tickets, that are prohibited under Islamic religious law.
As far as Snopes could tell, the request was coming from one individual imam and is not a coordinated or widespread movement. The imam's messaging is directed toward Muslim business owners, not all business owners, and is framed as a request rather than an order. No such wider order has been issued.
Under the First Amendment, all American have the right to freedom of speech and freedom of religion.
In September 2026, a claim spread online that Muslims in Texas are ordering local businesses to stop selling products Islam considers "haram" (forbidden), such as pork, alcohol and lottery tickets, within 30 days.
Multiple Facebook users posted similar captions saying Muslims have "taken to the streets in Houston" and other Texas cities, going "store to store" issuing "threats" of protests or more "if there's a continued noncompliance" (archived, archived).
Snopes readers searched our site and contacted us looking for more information regarding the rumor.
In short, the claim is exaggerated.
Footage does show one Houston imam, Qasim ibn Ali Khan, protesting with signs and asking Muslim convenience store owners to stop selling products deemed haram. One video posted on Khan's TikTok account in May 2025 (screenshotted), that features no signs of being generated using artificial intelligence, shows him telling employees at two Houston convenience stores that he planned to demonstrate if the staff did not remove haram products within 30 days. He did not specify where he planned to hold such demonstrations, only saying they would take place "around the city." Therefore, there is an element of truth to the claim.
Khan posted a follow-up video in July 2025 (screenshotted) showing him and his supporters protesting outside one of the convenience stores that features in the May 2025 clip.
It was not possible to determine whether the stores removed their haram products.
Similarly, it was not possible to find evidence of an "order" being issued — Khan specifically says in first the recording that he has no power to enforce his request — nor evidence of a coordinated, widespread movement to get businesses to stop selling haram products. Furthermore, Khan's rhetoric in the video shows he was making a request of specifically Muslim-owned businesses.
As such, we rate the claim mostly false.
Snopes attempted to contact Khan for comment, but got no response. We will update this article if we hear back.
Forbidden products across religions
Each of the world's religions, and the denominations within them, have different interpretations of religious law.
Using dietary restrictions as an example, Christian denominations rarely impose restrictions on what people can eat, though some practice abstinence from drinking alcohol. Hinduism promotes, but does not mandate, vegetarianism; Jainism requires vegetarianism, among other restrictions; observant Jews must follow kosher; and Islamic dietary law requires Muslims to not drink alcohol or consume pork.
As stated above, the grouping of forbidden practices in Islam is called "haram." In contrast, approved practices are called "halal," which is why some food products have a halal mark.
Texas Republicans, Islam and the First Amendment
Ahead of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, Republicans in Texas have made the idea that Muslims wish to implement Shariah law (Islamic religious law) in the United States a talking point in their campaigns.
(It should be noted: the phrase Shariah law can be interpreted in various ways to mean different things. In this case, Republicans appear to mean fundamentalist Shariah law, the strictest form, which applies Shariah principles to all matters of justice).
On Sept. 6, 2026, Amy Mekelburg — who is known for posting anti-Muslim videos online and who founded an organization the Southern Poverty Law Center considers an anti-Muslim hate group — posted one of Khan's TikTok videos to X. The footage shows Khan speaking outside a purportedly Muslim-owned convenience store. It's likely this is the origin of the claim that Muslims were ordering a ban on haram products.
In the clip, Khan says he asked the store to stop selling products deemed haram and that Muslim merchants should have "a higher standard," but he also states that he and his followers have no authority to force anyone to stop selling haram products:
We can't stop them, of course, this is the United States of America, and people have the freedom to sell what they want, as long as they're supported by the United States government.
Khan is correct — the First Amendment guarantees both freedom of speech and freedom of religion. As Texas Gov. Greg Abbott reportedly said during a September bill signing, according to the Texas Council for American-Islamic Relations, "Texas law and Texas courts govern those businesses and those neighborhoods. No ranting imam can change that."
In the video, Khan also says his request is being made specifically to Muslim business owners, not all businesses, as suggested in the social media posts spreading the claim in question:
Of course, you have the right to sell what you want, but as a Muslim, you should have higher principles, higher code of ethics that are supported by the Quran and the Sunnah [teachings] of Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
Despite thorough searches, it was not possible to find evidence of a widespread campaign making similar requests to businesses, Muslim-owned or otherwise.

The Jammu and Kashmir government has approved the diversion of 51.501 hectares of forest land for 33 projects in Uri over the 2024-25 to 2026-27 financial years, with 20.9352 hectares allocated for the Srinagar-Baramulla-Uri Road, the Legislative Assembly was informed Tuesday.
The figures were disclosed by the Minister for Forest, Ecology and Environment Department, Javed Ahmad Rana in response to an unstarred question by Uri National Conference MLA Sajjad Shafi, who sought details of forest and agricultural land affected by government and private construction in the constituency.
The Ministry said the projects were cleared under the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Abhiniyam and related rules.
These projects include work by the Jal Shakti Department, the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) and the Uri-II Stage-II hydroelectric project.
The government said the diversions were in the public interest and subject to “statutory environmental safeguards, conditions and compensatory measures” to minimise and mitigate their impact.
“Under the applicable provisions, user agencies must provide equivalent non-forest or State forest land for compensatory afforestation,” it said.
If such land is unavailable, the government said afforestation is carried out over twice the diverted area on degraded forest land.
Approved plans provide for 1,000 plants per hectare and 10 years of maintenance.
Depending on the project, agencies must also fund slope stabilisation, muck disposal, wildlife mitigation, Catchment Area Treatment and biodiversity management measures.
The Ministry said compensatory, mitigation and strip plantations have been undertaken near developmental and hydropower projects in Uri through CAPEX and CAMPA schemes, wherever feasible.
The response also lists the Uri-I Stage-II hydropower project and several water-supply schemes in Boniyar and Uri among the projects involving forest-land diversion.
Plantation and compensatory afforestation sites have been identified under approved plans, and the respective user agencies or companies are required to bear the costs, the Ministry said.

20 December 2024 was a crucial moment for Luxembourg in supporting WHO and strengthening global public health, to make progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals in 2025–2028. A Strategic Partnership Framework (SPF) with the Ministry of Development Cooperation and Humanitarian Affairs was signed amounting to €46.5 million – the largest-ever agreement WHO has had with Luxembourg. Furthermore, the first-ever multiyear agreement with the Ministry of Health and Social Safety €1 million was launched, as the country’s first voluntary contribution to WHO.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General greets with Luxembourg's Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety and Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. © MAE Luxembourg
“From now till 2028, this contribution will help finance priority areas in Luxembourg’s collaboration with WHO” said Martine Deprez, Minister of Health and Social Safety during the bilateral meeting, “notably for sanitary crisis preparedness and response and the fight against health inequalities, with a special focus on gender.”
The amount of €46.5 million contains fully flexible and thematic funding, and allocations for the Universal Health Coverage Partnership, tropical disease research and polio eradication. The fully flexible funding enables WHO to allocate the money to the areas of highest need.
“By signing two new partnership agreements, we have reaffirmed Luxembourg's continued support for the WHO and its mission,” said Xavier Bettel, Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Cooperation and Foreign Trade. “This reflects our strong commitment to promoting global health and multilateralism. We launch these agreements with WHO because we believe the best way to avoid is to prevent.”
To support the achievement of WHO’s priorities, the strategic partnership framework with Luxembourg includes support for WHO’s core work to develop, deliver and implement high-quality technical products – the guidelines, norms and standards on which many countries rely.
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General, remarked how symbolic it was that the agreements were signed on the International Day of Solidarity. They are “a strong statement of solidarity by Luxembourg, not just with WHO, but with the people of the world”, said Dr Tedros.
Xavier Bettel, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus and Martine Deprez at the signing ceremony. © MAE Luxembourg
WHO and Luxembourg continue their historical strategic partnership, collaborating to fulfill a shared mission to promote, provide and protect health.

Watch: Luxury prison in Indonesia demolished after public outcry
A prison compound in Indonesia has been demolished after public outcry following the discovery of luxury apartments on its grounds.
Investigators reported finding luxury facilities in Cibinong Prison in Bogor, near Jakarta, allegedly used by favoured inmates during a surprise inspection on 23 September.
The units contained amenities including air conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. Investigators also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction and luxury vehicles in the complex.
Officials said the residences appeared to house inmates, although prison officials claim they were for staff.
The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia's prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery.

This year, members of Seattle Mountain Rescue have been setting off into the wilds of the US Pacific Northwest wearing an unusual piece of kit.
They’ve been hiking into the wilderness with powered assistive devices attached to their hips and legs. Designed to increase lower-body strength when climbing or carrying heavy loads, these pieces of equipment are being tested to see if they can boost rescuers’ speed and endurance when it matters most—during searches for stranded people.
Devices like these are called human exoskeletons. They attach to parts of the body to create an external—or “exo”—mechanical structure. This powered frame enhances the wearer’s physical capabilities.
In physically demanding fields, workers are increasingly using these devices during strenuous tasks. IKEA has used SuitX exoskeletons for several years now. These assist warehouse workers with handling heavy materials. Ford, Boeing, and Mazda Toyota have also all adopted the tech on some of their assembly lines.
In Finland, a recent project called ExoPELA assessed whether exoskeletons could reduce muscle load and strain in rescue and firefighting work. It found noticeable benefits for users in certain real-world tasks.
And in early 2026, the Ukrainian military revealed its soldiers had been using Hypershell exoskeletons on the front lines to help with carrying artillery shells. According to test results, soldiers wearing the devices “become less fatigued, work faster, and maintain combat effectiveness for longer,” Colonel Vitalii Serdiuk told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper in March.
Multiple consumer and clinical devices, designed for everyday assistance, rehabilitation and exercise, are also now available. Some estimates have valued the total sector at around $500 million (£370 million) currently, and predict it could double or triple in size by the mid-2030s.
Exoskeleton technology has progressed significantly over the past decade. This has largely been thanks to robotic motors, sensors, and control systems becoming more affordable and accessible. However, the concept of augmenting human performance with exoskeleton-like devices dates back much earlier.

Injured Assefa narrowly misses world record in Berlin
- Published
An injured Tigst Assefa hobbled over the line at the Berlin Marathon on Sunday after looking set to smash the women's world record.
The Ethiopian still won with the third-fastest time in history in two hours 11 minutes four seconds.
But the 29-year-old, a silver medallist at the Paris Olympics two years ago, had been cruising to a new record before fading in the final stages.
Kenyan athlete Ruth Chepngetich's time of 2:09:56, set at the 2024 Chicago Marathon, remains the world record time, though that result is overshadowed by the three-year doping ban she received in 2025.
Assefa, the 2026 London Marathon winner, started rapidly and led the field by a minute at the 15km mark. She was ahead of the record pace at 35km and is a renowned fast finisher - but began to suffer clear discomfort and her pace slowed.
However she still broke the Berlin course record of 2:11:53 that she set in 2023 - which was also her previous personal best.
In addition, she improved on her time of 2:15:41 at the London Marathon earlier this year.
"We have to bow our heads to this performance. She was on a world record course for most of the race but then something happened to her tendon," said race director Mark Milde.
"To finish like this, I've never seen something like this. The pain is hard to imagine.
"With a heavy heart, we saw her set a course record, but it could have been a lot more."
The top five finishers were all from Ethiopia, with Bedatu Hirpa second and Dera Dida third.
Guye Adola - another Ethiopian - won the men's race with a time of 2:02:50.

Amazon has made a series of new public commitments to communities where it’s building data centers, including making an official announcement that it no longer uses nondisclosure agreements in its arrangements with county officials.
In a blog post published Friday, CEO Matt Garman detailed the steps the company says it’s already taking around data centers. In addition to stopping the use of NDAs, Garman says $1 billion will be invested over the next five years in communities that house the company’s data centers. The money will go toward free community college programs, workforce training, and energy efficiency upgrades for schools, homes, and community buildings.
In the post, Garman acknowledged how the fierce backlash against data centers across the country is hampering the AI buildout.
“Right now there are over 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country,” he wrote. “If these measures are enacted, the U.S. could be writing its own losing ticket to [the AI] race, and the consequences would last generations. As a country, we can’t afford to find ourselves in that position.”
Nondisclosure agreements have become a key point of contention amid the massive data center buildout. Typically, local officials who sign NDAs with data centers looking to develop projects in their area are unable to share information with the public, including the energy and water use of certain projects. Many NDAs bar officials from revealing even basic information—like the tech companies involved in building out the data center. In July, the New York Times reported on how secret agreements at all levels of government were crucial in building out plans for Hyperion, its massive data center in Louisiana.
There has been a rush of recent local legislation attempting to address the secretive paperwork. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, and Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer have all cracked down on data center NDAs in recent executive orders. Multiple states, including New York, New Jersey, Indiana, and Ohio, have considered recent legislation banning the practice.
At the federal level, a bipartisan group of lawmakers recently introduced the No Secrets for Data Centers Act in the House. Earlier this week, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-MD), one of the bill’s sponsors sent letters to Amazon, Google, Meta, and Oracle demanding information on their use of data center NDAs; Amazon told the Wall Street Journal that it was no longer using NDAs. (Google, Meta, and Oracle did not return the Journal’s request for comment.)
Amazon has been at the center of some high-profile controversies around NDAs. In Tucson, Arizona, Amazon was revealed last year to be the tenant of a controversial data center thanks to a public records request from a local outlet; an NDA had been in place barring county officials from sharing the identity of the end tenant. (Amazon has since exited that project.) In South Bend, Indiana, where the company has invested more than $13 billion into a massive data center campus, some elected officials have claimed that local government employees have been unable to answer questions about the project due to signing NDAs with the company.
Thanks to the opaque nature of data center financing and construction, end tenants like Amazon are often not the companies directly interfacing with government officials. As the Houston Chronicle reported last month, a top official in Wharton County, Texas, signed an NDA not with Amazon, but with contractor VisionFirst Advisors, which prevented him from sharing details about the Amazon project.
Amazon did not respond to WIRED’s queries about whether the promises around NDAs also extend to its contractors.
Much of the new blog from Garman is also dedicated to dispelling what he calls “misinformation and outright lies” around data centers and their water use, energy use, the use of diesel generators, and impacts on communities. “This build out is so important geopolitically that there are widespread reports of various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the U.S. about data centers to trick us into slowing down,” he wrote.
As WIRED has reported, the idea that China is intentionally seeding widespread dissent and misinformation around data centers is a consistent message coming from the White House and tech leaders. Experts, however, say that this narrative is widely overblown, and that there is little evidence of Chinese misinformation driving the data center backlash.
