A writ petition has been filed in the Madras High Court challenging the constitutional validity of Tamil Nadu government’s ‘Vettri Payanam’ (victorious travel) scheme which offers no-fare travel for women and transwomen passengers in 12,695 government buses across the State.
A private bus operator N. Kalamani from Bhavani Taluk in Erode district has approached the Court complaining the scheme would severely affect private transporters who may suffer heavy losses and have no option but to wind up their business.
The petitioner claimed private bus operators would not only stand to lose women passengers but also the men because families would naturally prefer to travel together in government buses in which the women need not pay any fare.
The writ petition, urging the Court to declare the Vettri Payanam scheme as unconstitutional, has been listed for hearing before the first Division Bench of Chief Justice Sushrut Arvind Dharmadhikari and Justice G. Arul Murugan on Monday (October 5, 2026).
Explaining her case in detail, the petitioner said, she was a widow who had two daughters to take care of. She held permits to operate buses on the 47-km route from Erode to Vellithiruppur and another 88-km route from Kakapalayam to Andhiyur.
The petitioner had employed about 15 people and their families too were dependant on her transport business. She feared hardly any passenger would step into her buses on the two routes since significant number of government buses were operated in those routes.
She said, the State government had come forward to spend a whopping amount of ₹6,000 crore a year for compensating the State transport corporations towards the Vettri Payanam scheme aimed at benefitting 84.32 lakh women on a daily basis.
However, a request made by the Federation of Bus Operators Associations of Tamil Nadu to Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay on July 22, 2026 for extending the scheme to private bus operators too did not yield the desired result, she claimed.
Ms. Kalamani said, not collecting any fare from women passengers in government buses alone would go against the principle of ensuring a level playing field in the bus transport sector and thereby violate Article 14 (right to equality) of the Constitution.
Though ‘Vettri Payanam’ was an expansion of the existing ‘Vidiyal Payanam’ scheme introduced by the previous DMK regime, the petitioner said, the previous scheme was limited in its scope and did not affect the private operators to a great extent.
The petitioner also relied upon various provisions of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 as well as the Tamil Nadu Motor Vehicle Rules, 1989 to contend that collection of fare from the passengers was mandatory and that the government could not announce no-fare travel.
Further, claiming the scheme had been implemented on the basis of an announcement made by the Chief Minister under Rule 110 in the Legislative Assembly and without issuing any Government Order, the petitioner said, such act offends Article 161 of the Constitution.
She urged the Court to declare the Chief Minister’s announcement, published by the Information and Public Relations Department (DIPR) on August 24, 2026 as unconstitutional and also grant an interim stay to it until the disposal of her writ petition.

Ajay Devgn starrer Drishyam The Conclusion has added another major milestone to its phenomenal box office run. The Abhishek Pathak directorial has crossed the Rs. 100 crore mark at the worldwide box office, grossing Rs. 145.46 crore globally within two days of its release.
The film has been driven by a strong performance in the domestic market, where it has collected Rs. 112.98 crore in India net over its first two days. The corresponding India gross stands at Rs. 134.50 crore. With an additional Rs. 10.96 crore coming from overseas markets, Drishyam The Conclusion has taken its worldwide gross to Rs. 145.46 crore.
The worldwide milestone comes on the back of a spectacular opening in India. The film opened to Rs. 62.03 crore on Friday before maintaining its momentum on Saturday with an estimated Rs. 50.95 crore. Its two-day India net total of Rs. 112.98 crore has already made it the second-fastest Rs. 100 crore grosser of 2026, behind only Dhurandhar The Revenge.
The overseas contribution, meanwhile, has added further strength to the film's global tally. With Rs. 10.96 crore coming from international markets, Drishyam The Conclusion has comfortably crossed the Rs. 100 crore worldwide mark while still being at the very beginning of its theatrical run.
The achievement marks a significant jump for the Drishyam franchise. The first two films had established a strong following among audiences, but Drishyam The Conclusion has taken that popularity to a completely different level, registering blockbuster numbers almost immediately after its release.
With Rs. 145.46 crore already accumulated worldwide, the Ajay Devgn-led thriller is now heading into Sunday with considerable momentum. The film's worldwide tally is expected to climb sharply as the first weekend progresses, setting the stage for another strong week ahead.

This week, SpaceX celebrated the first orbital launch of its new Starship rocket. I’m not sure many people, at least those outside of SpaceX, expected it to take 14 flights of Starship before it technically reached low-Earth orbit, but Monday morning’s launch finally added that to SpaceX’s list of accomplishments with its new super-heavy rocket. Starship had gone 99 percent of the way to orbit before, only held back by safety concerns around the possibility of stranding the huge rocket in space.
What was most notable for SpaceX with this Starship flight was that it unlocked a massive growth potential for Starlink, with the first 26 of the network’s new-generation Starlink V3 satellites successfully deployed Monday.

Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.
Rocket Lab scores its biggest launch contract yet. Rocket Lab has signed what it calls its largest Electron launch service agreement to date, a 20-mission agreement with Synspective, Aviation Week & Space Technology reports. Synspective is a Japanese company with a growing fleet of radar Earth-imaging satellites. It is one of Rocket Lab’s most loyal customers, with the company’s light-class Electron rocket having launched 13 of Synspective’s StriX radar sats since 2020. The most recent Rocket Lab launch for Synspective occurred last Friday, September 25.
Dedicated launch … Rocket Lab’s Electron launch vehicle is sized for dedicated launches of payloads like Synspective’s StriX satellites. The latest agreement extends Synspective’s total bookings with Rocket Lab to 47 launches, including the 13 already flown. “Signing 20 launches in a single deal is a massive vote of confidence not just in Electron but in the launch cadence, mission reliability, and orbital precision that Rocket Lab consistently delivers,” Rocket Lab’s founder and CEO, Peter Beck, said in a statement.
Portuguese company acquires what’s left of Orbex. A Portuguese space technology business has snapped up the assets of Orbex, the Scottish rocket maker that collapsed earlier this year, the Scotsman reports. The buyer, Omnidea, plans to establish its UK operations at Orbex’s former manufacturing facility in Scotland, having agreed to a deal to acquire the assets and intellectual property (IP) of the defunct rocket developer. An initial team of ex-Orbex employees will join the business, with Omnidea planning to recruit further as the operation develops.
No Prime resurrection … Omnidea, once a partner of Orbex, says it plans to use its new Scotland base as a center for “structures development and fabrication” and as a “hub for flight and ground system electronics.” Omnidea is a supplier of propulsion, fluid control, avionics, and thermal management components in the European space industry, but the company is also exploring other markets. It looks like Orbex’s Prime rocket, which never ventured near a launch pad, is still dead.
Rocket Report
Keep up with the latest in space exploration and rocket launches.
Crew-13 launches toward ISS. A four-person crew rocketed into orbit Thursday from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida, heading for a six-month expedition on the International Space Station, Ars reports. Riding a Falcon 9 rocket and Dragon spacecraft, the four crew members departed from Space Launch Complex-40 at Cape Canaveral at 11:10 am EDT. Nine minutes later, they were in orbit to begin closing in on the space station for docking Thursday evening.
Some notes … This mission is nothing particularly new for SpaceX (it’s the company’s 21st human spaceflight launch). But it is noteworthy for a few reasons. The commander, Jessica Watkins, became the first Black woman to lead a mission into space. Her crewmate, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, went to space while he and his wife are expecting their third child later this year.
It’s rare, but astronauts have been off the planet for their child’s birth before. Most recently, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, set to command the Artemis III mission next year, was flying aboard the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 2009 when his wife gave birth to their daughter in Houston. This launch was delayed several weeks to fix a leaky valve on Dragon’s propulsion system, work that involved cutting out the suspect valve and welding in a new one, an unusual but apparently successful repair method.
Canadian company pursues medium-lift rocket. More countries are becoming interested in developing their own access to space, including those that have historically paid US companies to launch their satellites. Canada is no different, and the Trump administration’s seeming obsession with lobbing threats and tariffs across the northern border has only crystallized Canadian interest in sovereign access to space.
This spring, the Canadian government announced the first awards to three companies—NordSpace, Reaction Dynamics, and Canada Rocket Company—to support work on rockets with “light lift” capability. Now, one of these rocket developers, Canada Rocket Company, says it is skipping over the small launch segment and going straight to a more ambitious medium-lift rocket, Ars reports.
R-2 V2? … Canada Rocket Company is following the lead of several US launch providers in going for a bigger rocket. “The advice we got from having spoken with about 150 engineers, from the director of Starship engineering all the way down to some entry-level folks, is that you’re not going to be able to de-risk a rocket development program by building a smaller rocket,” said Hugh Kolias, chief executive of the Canada Rocket Company, in an interview with Ars.
The company’s R-2 rocket somewhat resembles SpaceX’s Falcon 9 in renderings, with nine engines and landing legs that signal a future path toward reuse of the first stage. It could carry up to 12.5 metric tons to low-Earth orbit. If all goes well, Kolias said, the company could be ready to launch by 2032.
SpaceX rideshare launch deploys 130 payloads. An artificial intelligence prototype from Google, a methane-tracker, pharmaceutical manufacturing labs, and more hitched a ride onboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Vandenberg Space Force Base, California, on Thursday afternoon, Spaceflight Now reports. The rideshare mission, known as Transporter-18, carried 130 payloads into a polar Sun-synchronous orbit. It was SpaceX’s second launch of the day, following the successful flight of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission from Florida a few hours earlier.
Bread and butter … Much of the growing ecosystem of commercial satellite startups sees SpaceX’s rideshare launches as key enablers to their businesses, offering relatively inexpensive access to space on a predictable schedule. These kinds of launches, at least on Falcon 9, will likely go away in a couple of years as SpaceX transitions to the much larger Starship rocket. But for now, a bevy of satellite companies continue relying on Falcon 9 launches. The customers on Transporter-18 ranged from tech powerhouses like Google to scrappy startups like Starfish Space, alongside top remote sensing companies such as Planet Labs and ICEYE.
Starship reaches new heights in low-Earth orbit. SpaceX’s Starship rocket thundered into the sky over South Texas early Monday. It was the 14th test flight of the world’s most powerful launch vehicle. This time, however, the rocket’s massive upper stage squeezed out some extra oomph from its Raptor engines and accelerated to orbital velocity, Ars reports.
On all of Starship’s previous flights, SpaceX intentionally dialed back the full capability of the rocket to fly a suborbital trajectory, slow enough for Earth’s gravity to pull the vehicle back into the atmosphere before it could complete a full lap around the planet. After several successful suborbital flights in a row, SpaceX officials decided this launch should go all the way to low-Earth orbit. And it did.
Debuting Starlink V3 … What’s more, SpaceX packed 26 of the company’s newest generation of Starlink broadband satellites into the rocket’s cargo bay. One by one, the flat-packed satellites—too large to fit inside SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 rocket—were released from Starship’s payload deployer using a system of pulleys and cables to eject the satellites overboard like a Pez dispenser spits out candy. SpaceX cut a planned 10-hour test flight to three hours after one of the ship’s Raptor engines failed during ascent, but the vehicle was still able to make a pinpoint splashdown at one of its backup return sites north of Hawaii.
NASA will pay to human-rate ULA’s Vulcan rocket. NASA announced on Monday that it will exercise options to purchase two additional flights on Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft, as well as financially support the company in its efforts to return the crewed vehicle to flight and find a new rocket after the Atlas V vehicle retires, Ars reports. NASA is making the moves to preserve a path for its astronauts to low-Earth orbit as SpaceX nears retirement of its Falcon 9 rocket and Crew Dragon spacecraft. When that happens, Boeing’s troubled Starliner spacecraft will likely be the only commercial means of launching US crews to orbit.
A post-Atlas future … During a news conference on Monday, Dana Weigel, manager of NASA’s Low Earth Orbit Program, said the space agency would pay $359 million to Boeing to help the company complete a rebuild of the reaction control system thrusters that have overheated in flight. It would also certify United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket for human missions. NASA also said it would exercise options to order two additional crewed missions on Starliner, bringing its total spaceflights on the vehicle to six. Any future Starliner flights beyond that would require a new rocket, like ULA’s Vulcan, as the Atlas V rocket is no longer in production.
SpaceX completes three launches in 13 hours. SpaceX pulled off two Falcon 9 rocket launches and a Falcon Heavy mission in less than 13 hours Thursday, marking one of the busiest days ever for the company’s launch teams. The action began, as noted previously in the Rocket Report, with a Falcon 9 launch from Cape Canaveral, Florida, carrying the next four-person crew to the International Space Station. A few hours later, another Falcon 9 lifted off from California on a rideshare mission. The launch of SpaceX’s triple-body Falcon Heavy rocket with a classified National Reconnaissance Office payload from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, rounded out the triple-header Thursday night.
And four landings … This was the first time a Falcon Heavy rocket has launched a payload for the NRO, the US government’s spy satellite agency. Little is publicly known about the payload except that it launched into a highly inclined orbit, flying northeast from Florida’s Space Coast. To add an extra flourish to the launch triple-header, SpaceX returned both Falcon 9 boosters to their launch sites in Florida and California and landed both side boosters from Falcon Heavy back at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. That makes three launches and four landings (plus a Dragon docking at the ISS) in one day.
Blue Origin foresees growing launch cadence. As Blue Origin continues to recover from a New Glenn pad explosion in May, the company is seeking permission to significantly increase the vehicle’s launch rate, Space News reports. This is a big surprise, but a draft environmental assessment released this week puts some numbers to Blue Origin’s plans. The company is seeking permission from the FAA to increase the rate of New Glenn launches from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station’s Launch Complex 36 from 12 to 50 per year.
Reuse built in … The proposal would include 50 launches of the rocket and 50 landings of the rocket’s first stage on a drone ship in the Atlantic Ocean. It would also allow up to 100 static-fire tests, one for each stage of the rocket for each launch. The proposal also covers recovery of the rocket’s payload fairing, which Blue Origin has not attempted on any of the three launches of New Glenn to date.

Canada scores a dairy win on U.S. soil as farmers grumble about Trump's trade war
Both sides in trade dispute have been 'needless, pointless and childish,' says one retiree
On the most elite stage in the world of competitive dairy, a Canadian teenager and her "favourite cow" scored two major wins while on U.S. soil.
Never heard of competitive dairy? Let me assure you, it's a really big deal. One win — let alone two — at the World Dairy Expo in Madison, Wisc., can be life changing for farmers and their cows.
It can boost the value of an animal by tens of thousands of dollars. Future offspring can become more valuable too. And of course, there's an element of national pride, especially when Canada and the U.S. are locked in a trade war.
Alyson Doiron, a 16-year-old high school student from Cap-Sante, Que., glows as she poses for photos with her aforementioned favourite cow — Arolene Dempsey Ella, who goes by "Ella" for short, was the five-year-old cow awarded the top prize at the International Junior Holstein Show.
"She's an easy cow to work with. We love her so much," Doiron told CBC News.
Doiron cheered and cried as she was given the prestigious honour on Ella's behalf, at the Expo on Sunday. Even though this is a global gathering, the actual competitions are between animals from Canadian and American farms, due to health and safety regulations.
"This means a lot to me," she said with a nod to her home province. "It just proves that in Quebec, the [cow] show is really really strong," she said.
Sore point for some Americans
In the arena where the cows are judged, Canadian, American and Mexican flags hang in the rafters. It is a reminder, as constant as the smell of manure, that cross-border competition and co-operation are valued in this space.
"I think it's important for us to be here," said Brian Carscadden, the executive senior manager and part owner of Blondin Sires, a Quebec-based dairy company that has milk production and artificial insemination operations.
"If you think of the Westminster Dog Show, it's not unlike that. If you can win that, you've got a dog that's worth some money. It's the same here with your cow."
Carscadden and his team drove more than 1,500 kilometres from St. Placide to Madison, with 25 cows in trailers in tow. He says his business has not been affected by the trade war yet, and that it does not come up often in conversations at the Expo.
"There's jokes here and there," from his American friends, he said, along with "the odd snide remark … that makes things interesting."
"I always advise my Canadian colleagues that it's not our country, it's not our politics, don't talk about it."
Americans at the Expo are far more direct.
The trade war is a sore point for some, including voters who are connecting dots between U.S. President Donald Trump's broad economic agenda and increases in the cost of living.
"There is no lowering of grocery prices, no lowering of gas prices. I mean obviously it's all going higher and it makes me struggle," said Paula Lawver.
She's a single mom from a farming community in Indiana, and is at the Expo with a group of students from her son's high school. She describes herself as a conservative voter with conservative values, but does not consider herself a Republican.
She calls the dispute with Canada "nonsense," and says it will influence her vote in the midterm elections this November. Lawver says she will not support candidates in favour of tariffs and trade wars.
Seth Muck, a farmer from New York state, says he too may reconsider how he votes in the midterms.
He says in the past he's voted "hard, hard Republican, hard conservative." But after feeling the impact of Trump's global trade agenda, he's considering backing candidates with a "bit more moderate-type agenda."
Muck says his cash crops and farm inputs have been affected the most, noting that the price of fertilizer is double what he paid last year. Though he still holds out hope that economic conditions could improve.
"Perhaps it's going to take a bit … like ripping off a Band-Aid," he said.
Even among those willing to be more patient with Trump and his economic vision, CBC News did not find any Americans at this Expo supportive of the heated rhetoric that has upended the Canada-U.S. relationship.
"I think it's needless, pointless and childish. Both sides," said Gary Craugh, a retired farmer from Wisconsin.
Another retired farmer from Wisconsin, John Galgowski, says he's baffled by it all.
"I throw up my hands and go, 'Why are we doing this?'"
Galgowski does not support the Trump administration, and says the way the country has been run since Trump returned to office has only reaffirmed his position.
"It's just bad times," he said.
The way these voters described their experience is very different from how the Trump administration is framing the moment.
- Trump says 'very bad' Canada is being 'taught a little lesson' as trade action escalates
- U.S. bans on imported Canadian motorcycle, dairy, alcohol products take effect as trade war drags on
About 120 kilometres from the Expo, in Milwaukee, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer hosted a gathering of G20 trade ministers, where he unapologetically advocated for the "America first" trade agenda, arguing that the strategy is working.
"American workers and their families are better off now than they were before President Trump took office," Greer said as he read from prepared remarks.
Greer's defence of the Trump administration's policies suggests there are no plans to change course anytime soon.
Which means the trade war with Canada is poised to grind on.
Ella's big day
Even if the country-to-country tensions won't go away, Canada did score one more win at the World Dairy Expo.
On Friday, Doiron proudly paraded Ella in front of the judges on the arena floor, competing for one of the week’s largest titles: Supreme Junior Show Champion.
It’s a moment that almost didn’t happen. Doiron says she helped raise Ella, but when her parents unexpectedly sold the cow, she was devastated.
“I was so mad at my parents, because she was just the cow I liked,” she said, recalling the way she loved all of Ella's spots as a kid.
Doiron was determined to be reunited with her favourite cow, and when the opportunity arose, she re-purchased Ella, despite objections from her parents. “I need to bring this cow home,” she told her mom.
The reunion was clearly meant to be.
In front of a packed arena, Doiron and Ella’s big moment finally arrived — the heifer was named Supreme Junior Show Champion, a victory for all of Canada.

Trump administration reverses stance on integration of people with disabilities
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
For nearly 50 years, the federal government has said people with disabilities should live, work and learn in the most integrated setting possible rather than be segregated in institutions like nursing homes.
The Trump administration just took its most concrete step yet to reverse that position.
Last week, a federal judge agreed to strip out mentions of "integration" from federal regulations tied to Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, a landmark civil rights law that prohibits disability discrimination. The judge did so after the Justice Department declined to defend its own rules in a lawsuit brought by several states challenging the legality of those rules.
Part of what is so striking about Texas v. Kennedy is that the federal government was originally the defendant in that lawsuit, brought by states fighting what's known as the integration mandate. Then, it switched sides and agreed with the states that the requirement should be undone.
Bruce Darling, president and CEO of the Center for Disability Rights, says when he heard about the ruling, it felt "like a knife in your chest. Because what we're hearing, what people are hearing, is that the federal government has made a determination that [disabled people] don't have a right to live in freedom, that they can be locked up against their will."
The court's decision removes regulations from Section 504 that explicitly required federally funded programs to provide services in the "most integrated setting."
"That lack of clarity will impact people's rights. It will likely impact what states do and how they behave," says Jennifer Mathis, a disability rights lawyer who helps lead the Bazelon Center for Mental Health Law.
Mathis says it's important to note that the court's decision did not undo integration protections tied to the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) or those established by decades of case law, including the landmark Supreme Court decision known as Olmstead.
"My concern is that right now, where we're at is disabled people have a right to integration on paper. It is in the law, but whether it gets practically enforced is a serious question," Darling says. His organization is putting its energy behind a proposed law that would cement protections around integration, while others are working with states to strengthen their disability laws.
The Justice Department did not respond to multiple requests from NPR asking why it is changing course after decades of legal and bipartisan support for community-based services.
After 50 years, the government changes its position
In 1973, Congress passed the first civil rights law for people with disabilities: Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act. But it took advocates years of fighting — until 1977 — to get actual regulations that would make that law enforceable.
The Department of Health and Human Services, under President Joe Biden, updated the regulations in 2024 so it would be clearer to states what they had to do to uphold the law. "They thought it was important to do that so those rights would be as clear as possible," Mathis says.
In recent months, the federal government, under President Donald Trump, began to publicly change its position: First, in June, the Justice Department issued an opinion saying it no longer interpreted disability law to "require states to treat mentally disabled patients in the most integrated setting appropriate to their needs." The memo even noted its position is "out of step with the common understanding" of the Olmstead decision.
Then in July, the Justice Department announced it would stop relying on its own longstanding guidance explaining how it enforces the integration mandate.
These actions led up to the federal government switching sides in Texas v. Kennedy. Finally, last week, a federal judge agreed to throw out the integration mandate rules under Section 504, including language that was first introduced nearly 50 years ago.
Mathis says this kind of about-face is highly unusual. "It is pretty significant and pretty unprecedented to see the federal government asking a court to vacate its own rules."
That could leave more of the work of defining and enforcing the right to community living to people with disabilities, private litigators, advocacy organizations and the courts.
All this, says Mathis, comes at a time when states are already under immense pressure from the federal government to cut Medicaid spending, which pays for disabled people to get many of the services they need. "States are looking for things to cut," she says. Mathis worries that because the government has changed its stance on integration, states would be freer to cut spending on programs for community-based living.
How enforcement is already changing
One of the clearest examples of the effects of the federal government's changing position involves children with complex medical needs in Florida.
Back in 2013, the Justice Department sued the state of Florida, arguing that it failed to provide adequate services to children who needed in-home care. As a result, some of their families were forced to put their children in nursing facilities. Other children were at risk of the same.
The federal government won its case in 2023, and the state of Florida was required to provide these families the services they needed to keep their children at home. But in August, the government told the federal court to throw out its victory and allow Florida to have the case heard again in district court, citing the Justice Department's new opinion on the issue.
Mathis calls the reversal shocking. "To do that in a case that involves ripping children away from families, taking them out of the homes where they have families that want to take care of them, and to force those children to grow up in an institution, really is just unthinkable to me and is incredibly heartless."
The Florida case suggests that coming battles for community integration may increasingly play out not through federal enforcement, but case by case, in the courts.
What disability advocates are doing now
The disability rights community is rallying around a number of actions to try to combat the federal government's latest actions.
"There's nothing that is more cherished and hard-won than the right to live, work and participate and be included in your community," says Alison Barkoff, who worked on disability rights enforcement during the Obama administration and is now a health law and policy professor at George Washington University. She says the disability community is hard at work trying to protect those rights.
Thanks to recent advocacy efforts, Barkoff says some members of Congress have reaffirmed their commitment to the rights of people with disabilities to get services they need in their community. Just this week, a group of bipartisan lawmakers introduced a resolution asserting the federal government's longstanding interpretation of Olmstead. In July, 100 members of Congress signed a letter asking the Justice Department to rescind its June opinion.
There is also movement at the state level: Delaware already passed a law incorporating the regulations in Section 504 that were stripped from federal law. Barkoff says other states are moving in a similar direction: "I've probably gotten calls in the last week from at least a dozen state leaders across the country about how to codify the integration mandate … in state law. I see a lot of momentum," she says.
Bruce Darling of the Center for Disability Rights helped draft the Latonya Reeves Freedom Act, a bipartisan bill that would codify integration for disabled people into federal law. He says his organization has been working to convince lawmakers to sign onto it.
Although the bill has some bipartisan support, it has failed in the past and would have a difficult road ahead, facing an executive branch now challenging integration. But Darling says he's hopeful that members of Congress are now more aware of the challenges facing his community.
"I think that the issue has really come to a head now and folks can see that Olmstead is seriously at risk, that we need to do something," says Darling. "I don't know, I'm optimistic."

Zelensky vows Ukraine will strike Russian oil refineries after city bombardments
Ukrainian intelligence has reportedly gathered documentation that Putin has authorised a ‘new doctrine’ to expand Russia’s military strikes

President Volodymyr Zelensky has stated that Ukraine intends to intensify strikes against Russian oil refineries following a fresh campaign of bombardment by Moscow aimed at driving citizens out of Kyiv and major urban centres, while avoiding non-military targets.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian intelligence gathered documentation revealing that Russian leader Vladimir Putin has authorised a "new doctrine" expanding military strikes to encompass a significantly wider selection of non-military sites before winter sets in.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them to attack infrastructure, logistics, and especially to attack in the cities, in the villages, everywhere, roads, schools, hospitals," Zelenskiy told Reuters in an interview. "To pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities: this is the goal of the operation."
Zelensky explained that this strategic pivot stemmed from Putin's eagerness to project power as Russian forces suffer heavy casualties and yield territory in a crucial frontline sector.
While the Kremlin did not offer immediate comment on Saturday, Russia's Foreign Ministry released a statement advising foreign citizens to evacuate Kyiv, maintaining that Moscow will persist in carrying out systematic strikes in response to recent attacks launched by Ukraine against Russian territory.
Neither side admits to intentionally attacking civilians.
Zelensky confirmed that an ongoing Ukrainian counteroffensive, designated "Vivaldi", has successfully reclaimed roughly 140 sq km (54 sq miles) in the eastern Donbas region. Control over the whole of Donbas remains a core demand set out by Russia for any potential peace settlement.
US President Donald Trump's administration has moved in recent weeks to reboot diplomatic efforts aimed at resolving the four-year war, Europe's deadliest since World War Two.
Last month, the US leader appealed to Ukraine to cease strikes on Russian oil facilities, arguing that such actions were driving up global diesel costs.
However, speaking as air raid warnings echoed beyond the ornate halls of the presidential compound, Zelensky said there was no sign from Moscow that Putin harboured any genuine interest in diplomatic negotiations or a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
Throughout the past week, Kyiv has endured continuous bombardment from Russian missiles and uncrewed aerial vehicles aiming for power, communications, road, and railway networks. In an unprecedented move, Russian strikes also targeted bridges spanning the Dnipro river, which connect eastern and western Kyiv.
Although Ukraine will adapt its strategy in response to Moscow's tactics, Zelensky emphasised that non-military assets would not be struck indiscriminately.
"We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners etc: what gives money to them for this war," Zelensky said in English. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."
Following invitations extended to Putin by the Trump administration for December's G20 gathering in Miami and discussions regarding commercial agreements with Russian representatives, Zelenskiy implored Washington to refrain from normalising relations with Moscow prior to securing lasting peace.
While expressing willingness to sit down with Putin at the G20 for peace discussions, Zelensky cautioned the US against falling for "illusions" that Russian aggression would cease merely if Moscow secured control over Donbas.
"It's not fair just to normalise," said Zelensky, wearing his characteristic black T-shirt and military-style jacket. He stressed that restored economic and diplomatic links with Western powers must depend on Russia ending its combat operations: "Because peace is more important than any kind of economy."
Although Washington has suggested reviving three-way talks in the United Arab Emirates in the coming weeks, Zelensky highlighted that a precise date and venue for these technical discussions remain unconfirmed.
Officials in Kyiv have warned that Moscow has amassed hundreds of ballistic missiles in preparation for a winter campaign against power and water systems. During the previous winter, the harshest of the conflict, strikes repeatedly knocked out power and heating across large areas for days.
Since summer, Russian forces have also deployed dozens of swift, low-cost jet-powered Shahed drones daily against Ukraine, creating severe difficulties for air defence crews whose existing interceptor drones lacked the speed required to engage them successfully.
Zelensky explained that Ukraine had been compelled to rely on fighter jets, including F-16s and MiGs, to destroy roughly 60 per cent of the jet-powered drones, though stocks of 20 mm ammunition for these aircraft are becoming depleted.
Kyiv is actively pursuing alternative countermeasures, such as expanding electronic warfare jamming capabilities, according to Zelensky. By late October, the nation expects its initial delivery of compact, inexpensive air defence missiles engineered to intercept the upgraded Shahed models.
Zelensky recently disclosed that Ukraine is constructing five distinct interceptor drone designs targeting jet-powered Shaheds. Following a briefing with senior military leaders, he noted that initial trials on two prototype variants yielded a modest success rate near 30 per cent.
"We'll have to scale it," he said. "I hope that with all these things, with all these elements, we'll find a way."
This week, Ukraine confirmed the initial operational deployment of its indigenous FP-7 ballistic missile, which boasts an effective range of approximately 250 km (155 miles).
Zelensky revealed he had personally contacted defence firm Fire Point to urge executives to expedite development of the longer-range FP-9 missile, which the manufacturer claims can reach Moscow.
"I said to them, where is my FP-9?" said Zelensky, with a grin. "We need the FP-9. And the FP-9 will be (ready) this autumn, I'm sure."
Zelensky asserted that recent Russian drone overflights and hybrid operations across Europe represent a deliberate attempt to demoralise European publics and erode international assistance for Ukraine.
Certain European leaders are increasingly recognising this threat and taking a firmer stance, he noted.
Moscow dismisses these allegations as groundless claims fuelled by anti-Russian sentiment.
Following discussions with European leaders in Brussels this week, Ukraine secured the necessary financial support to purchase the drones required to sustain operations into early 2027, Zelensky said.
Ukrainian negotiators have collaborated with European allies to address a $27 billion shortfall in Kyiv's defence funding for the current year.
The strategy combines reshuffling domestic budgetary funds, receiving bilateral aid, and drawing on "money credits" from next year's allocation of a €90 billion EU loan package, Zelensky explained.
"We will close this (gap). I think this is absolutely a big success for our country," he said.

Quick Answer
Turn rough screen recordings into polished demos with tools that auto-zoom on clicks, follow and smooth the cursor, add clean framing, and highlight key actions. Options include Screen Studio, FocuSee, Screen Awesome, and ScreenCursor.
When you record a two-minute walkthrough of your app, for instance, a setting buried five menus deep, or a spreadsheet trick you are proud of, there is something that can leave you frustrated. You press play, and the cursor is dancing all around without highlighting what you actually wanted to show. Either the text is too small to read on a phone or the whole thing looks like security-camera footage of your desktop. The old-school way is to use a video editor, add zooms by hand, pan the camera to follow your cursor, and nudge keyframes for an hour. Thankfully, there is a newer batch of screen recorders that automatically do that part for you.
In this guide, we have covered four of them. They not only differ in price, platform, and functionality, but each one also has one detail that surprised me.
|  | Screen Studio | FocuSee | Screen Awesome | ScreenCursor | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Works on | Mac only | Windows and Mac | Chrome (also Edge, Brave and similar) | Chrome (Mac, Windows, Linux) | 
| Price | $9/mo billed yearly, or $29/mo | Free trial, paid plans | Free | $49 one-time (early pricing) | 
| Best for | Maximum polish on a Mac | All-in-one AI extras | Privacy and zero cost | Pay-once simplicity | 
Table of Contents
Why do raw screen recordings look so rough?
When you use any standard screen recorder, like the one built into your OS, it captures pixels and nothing else. It has no idea what mattered. It doesn’t know if you clicked a tiny button that you want the viewers to look at. The result? You get a full-screen recording of everything, including your cursor wandering here and there. Viewers watch these videos on laptops and phones, and since the important part is not zoomed in or clearly shown, they will miss it. A better screen recording would be one where:
- Zoom is on the action so people can actually read what you click.
- A camera that follows your cursor instead of leaving viewers guessing.
- A cursor that glides rather than jitters.
- A clean frame, such as a gradient background and rounded corners.
With all of the above, your screen recording not only looks professional but also provides clear instructions for viewers.
Screen recorders with auto cursor follow and zoom
Here are some of the best screen recorders that you can use for automatic cursor follow and zoom.
Screen Studio: The one the others get compared to
If you are on Mac, then Screen Studio is one of the best options for screen recording with automatic cursor follow and zoom. When you’re recording using Screen Studio, it looks at what you did, like where you clicked, and zooms in on the moments that matter. Every zoom is balanced and animated automatically; you don’t have to worry about handling them. The best part is that you can choose between two styles: Classic zoom is the one you usually see in polished product videos. Then there is Loupe zoom, which is a magnifier-style alternative. If you want to zoom somewhere the app did not automatically add one, you can drop it onto the timeline and point it where you like. Notably, the cursor gets the same treatment. Shaky movement is smoothed out into a steady glide, and clicks get a soft ripple. Fast movements pick up motion blur so they look filmed rather than captured. You also have the option to change the cursor’s size and style later. Some of the notable features of Screen Studio are:
- Edit by transcript: Delete a sentence from the transcript, and it disappears from the video. Filler words and long pauses can be cleared in one pass.
- One recording, many shapes: Record once, then switch the aspect ratio between wide (16:9), square (1:1), and vertical (9:16). Zooms can be re-aimed, layouts rearranged, and captions moved to stay readable. You can also choose the “Reel mode” that shows where Instagram’s or TikTok’s interface would cover your video, so you’re in the grey area where your inputs get hidden.
- Hide the private stuff: If the recording shows an API key or email address, you can mask it after the recording is complete, and the mask blends into the interface around it.
- iPhone and iPad framing: Plug your iPhone or iPad into a USB cable, pick the device, and record. Screen Studio wraps the footage in a matching device frame.
FocuSee: The Windows-friendly all-rounder
FocuSee comes from the house of iMobie and is a screen recording tool that works on both Windows and Mac. This already makes it the practical choice for many people working on either OS. FocuSee’s auto zoom follows your clicks and even your typing. This tool adds a spotlight to highlight areas worth noticing, making it much easier for anyone following your instructions. You can also choose a “3D Motion” mode that adds tilt and perspective that follows your cursor, for a more cinematic look. The cursor can fade out when you are not actively using it or don’t need it and reappears when you do. Similar to other screen recording tools, you can swap the cursor style and click animations. There are a bunch of features that deserve to be highlighted.
- A built-in teleprompter: You can show your script on screen while recording with the option to adjust the font size, speed, and position. If you tend to forget the script midway, this alone might sell you.
- An annotation suite: You can add text, shapes, arrows, callouts, spotlights, and blur effects. Moreover, you can stack several layers to walk viewers through a tricky step, or blur out something sensitive.
- An AI avatar: This one is for those who are camera-shy or do not want their face in the video. FocuSee can create a digital presenter, or in simple words, an AI avatar. It is a niche feature, but a handy one for company tutorials.
- Smart cleanup: You can remove filler words and silence with just one click, and also enhance voice and reduce noise with just a button.
- Background fixes for your webcam: It can blur or replace a messy room behind you after recording without needing a green screen.
- Add Subtitles: FocuSee supports speech recognition in over 50 languages, with accuracy above 98%. You can add your own subtitles and make it easier for the follower to go through the steps.
Screen Awesome: Free, and it can’t upload your recordings
Screen Awesome is a different kind of tool. It’s actually a free Chrome extension built by a developer named Nitinbhai Viras. On one hand, most apps say “we respect your privacy” and simply ask you to take their word; Screen Awesome does things a bit differently. Screen Awesome points you at Chrome’s own permission screen and requests no access to any website. It is not allowed to contact any server. That means it cannot upload your recordings, even if it wanted to. The best part is that you can verify this yourself in about 30 seconds. Head over to chrome://extensions, find Screen Awesome, click Details, and look at the Site access line. According to the developer, it reads none. On the extension’s settings page, there is a button that jumps you straight there. On top of this security, you get this tool for absolutely free. Here are some features that set Screen Awesome apart:
- Auto-zoom to clicks: While recording a browser tab, Screen Awesome notes where you click. A virtual camera follows each click and pans between them. You have the option to preview it, turn it off, or export the file. This works for tab recording.
- Serious annotation tools: Arrows, pen, highlighter, shapes, text, speech bubbles, step counters, emoji stamps, and a blur that destroys the pixels rather than just smudging them. You can edit all of these marks.
- Product-shot framing: You can place a recording on a backdrop with rounded corners, a soft shadow, and an optional browser window around it, and also change its aspect ratio to 16:9, etc.
- Formats: You can export your recording in MP4, WebM, or an animated GIF.
- Webcam and voice: Screen Awesome lets you mix in your microphone and the tab’s audio, and even add a movable webcam bubble while recording if you want to show your face.
ScreenCursor: Pay once, and record in Chrome
ScreenCursor is another screen recording tool that works as a Chrome extension. However, its approach is the opposite of Screen Awesome’s. Notably, it does one thing and tries to do it well, which is turning clicks into camera moves with as little fuss as possible. When you hit the record button, ScreenCursor waits three seconds before it starts. That gap is deliberate, and it exists because Chrome shows its own “sharing your screen” bar while recording, and unfortunately it cannot be switched off. With this delay, you get the time to collapse the bar before the screen recording starts. Every click, drag, and keystroke gets zoomed in. Each zoom happens a beat before the action; this way, viewers are already looking at the right spot, then the camera holds steady and follows your cursor. Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave lands on TIME100 Next list
- Published
Shoko Kawata, Japan's first mayor to take maternity leave, has been named one of the 100 most influential rising stars by TIME Magazine.
The recognition comes weeks after the 36-year-old gave birth to her first child on 15 September.
Earlier this year, Kawata, who is mayor of Yawata City in Kyoto prefecture, was plunged into a national debate about whether elected officials should take time off for childbirth.
Her decision to take maternity leave drew a mix of support and backlash across Japan, a country that is struggling to lift birth rates.
Some on social media said having a baby is tough and Kawata is doing her best. Japanese society has failed to design systems with pregnancy in mind, one claimed. Another said Kawata is setting a wonderful example by putting her family first and making it easier for other women to enter politics.
But critics argued that stepping away from public duties is "irresponsible", and that if Kawata wanted to get pregnant "she should have done so before taking office". One said top officials wanting to take extended leave "should resign".
Others insisted salaries should be cut during maternity leave.
In a sit-down interview with the BBC before giving birth, Kawata brushed off the criticisms, proudly declaring she enjoys her job and believes now is the time for her to have a child and start a family.
"If we were to criticise politicians taking maternity leave, it means we are effectively excluding all women in their 20s through 40s - women who are capable of becoming pregnant - from public office," she said.
While Japan provides maternity leave for city workers, there is currently no legal framework for local elected officials. So Kawata worked with her office to create a plan. She transferred her authority to her deputy mayor Shigeto Nose for 16 weeks, while working remotely when she could.
On 15 September, Mayor Kawata announced she gave birth to a baby girl. She posted a photo on X, external, thanking those who had supported her, and doubled down on her goal to advocate for social issues nationwide.
"As I face the countless challenges that lie ahead and learn what it truly means to be a parent, I want to reflect those experiences in real time into the policies I pursue," she wrote.
"I want to confront the many challenges facing parents and children today from that same perspective, as someone living through them myself, and think about how we can find a way forward together."

Why is this the only pink MacBook available right now?
Is one more too much to ask for?
Fancy a pink MacBook? Unfortunately, the options are scarce.
The MacBook Neo, Apple's latest addition to its laptop lineup, is the only personal computer available in the beloved rosy hue. Dubbed 'Blush' by the tech giant, this shade has garnered tons of love across social media, primarily among students.
While the budget-friendly laptop's color options turn heads, the device is best suited for casual users and note-taking. It simply doesn't have the power to tackle creative, pro-level work.
Ever since Apple quietly retired Rose Gold across all laptops, which may have never even truly cut it for pink purists, the brand has segued away from releasing its higher-end models in any vibrant shades. Sure, you can opt for a faint blue MacBook Air, but if you want to go all in on a Pro, you have no choice but to keep things traditional with Silver and Space Black.
While there's certainly an element of function-over-form at play here, why can't Apple merge both worlds and make a second pink MacBook?
A plea for pink
Bold colors have been on the rise among several devices, particularly smartphones. Most recently, Google's Pixel lineup has received many pink treatments, with the new 11 releasing in a striking shade of hot pink (called Hibiscus) reminiscent of the Motorola Razrs of old. Conversely, the reimagined, foldable Razr is available in Hot Pink, paying homage to the original design.
It's not like Apple doesn't know how to make fun colors. Two separate shades of pink douse the Phone 16 and 17e, with the latter more muted than the 16's bold, brighter look. The latest base-level iPad with A16 is available in a bold pink rivaled only by the same model's vibrant yellow variant, and the M4 iMac is available in a number of eye-grabbing colors, including pink.
Step up from those models to, say, the iPad Pro or MacBook Pro, and at best you'll find them in subtle, muted colors, on top of the typical grays and silvers.
Rose gold was a middle ground of sorts, bringing a splash of color to iPhones throughout the mid-2010s, MacBook Airs discontinued in 2019, and Apple Watches, which also ended this year. The Apple Watch Series 11 was the last showcase of the color, but with the Series 12 arriving this year, even that's gone. The most "colorful" option in that new lineup is a Night Blue, which is pretty dark, as the name suggests.
Recent Pro iPhones have given us a tiny bit of hope: The 17 Pro came in an uber-saturated orange, while the 18 Pro has the rich burgundy and subtle glacier blue options. With the rumored reimagining of the MacBook Pro range on the horizon, it's time for Apple to bring some color to its laptops, too.

Toyota, Aichi Pref. – South Korea won men’s soccer gold at the Asian Games on Saturday, beating host Japan 1-0 in the final to lift the gloom after a disastrous World Cup and a series of damaging controversies.
Swansea City’s Eom Ji-sung rifled in on the hour to give the South Koreans their fourth straight title in front of 30,000 fans at Toyota Stadium, near Nagoya.
Japan was looking to win gold for the first time since 2010 and was coached by Go Oiwa, who will take over the senior national team after next year’s Asian Cup.
The Asian Games are contested between Under-23 squads with three overage players.
“This goal was in all our hearts,” 24-year-old match-winner Eom said of the players’ determination to win the title again.
“We had to do a lot of defending tonight, but we always knew there would be one chance for us, and with the right timing and right service, it was me.”
South Korea endured a miserable World Cup in North America this year, going out in the group stage after a shock loss to South Africa.
Coach Hong Myung-bo quit, but his departure did little to quell public outrage over the disappointing campaign and added fuel to pre-existing questions about how he was hired.
Police raided Korea Football Association headquarters in August as part of an investigation into Hong’s 2024 appointment.
The KFA also apologized for allegations that it provided sexual entertainment for foreign referees.
Eom, who played in the dismal World Cup campaign, put a smile on South Korean faces with a brilliant goal, lashing home a left-foot shot against the run of play.
The win secured military exemptions for South Korea’s players.
Nearly every able-bodied South Korean male is required to perform at least 18 months of military service, but the government rewards Asian Games gold medals and Olympic medals of any color with an exemption.
This year’s squad followed in the footsteps of senior captain Son Heung-min and Atletico Madrid playmaker Lee Kang-in.
The South Koreans had players with European experience throughout their team, and Eom threatened with an early chance that went over the bar.
Japan, fielding a mostly home-based Under-21 team, suffered a setback when forward Uche Nwadike was stretchered off midway through the first half with a knee injury.
Japan went on to create the better chances, but Eom made the breakthrough to hand the Koreans the title, despite Japan hitting the post with a late chance.

Fact Check
While it is unclear that whether the police are claiming that the entire video of the event is AI-generated, or the portion where the cops are seen watching and recording the performance, Alt News found that one of the dancers present in the viral clip posted several videos of the event on her Instagram page, @queen__juhi_002__.

Below is a screen recording of a video posted by the dancer herself, where the performers are seen wearing the same attire as in the video posted by Rai.

We found another video on Facebook where the structure of the stage can be clearly seen and a red temple can be seen behind it.

Cornell president calls alleged gang rape 'deeply disturbing,' pledges greater transparency
Michael Kotlikoff addressed the Cornell community in an 8-minute video message
Cornell's president called the alleged gang rape of a student at a fraternity house in 2024 "deeply disturbing" Saturday, said it would weigh on the university for years to come and pledged greater transparency amid mounting outrage over the school's handling of the case.
In an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community, Michael Kotlikoff described the past week as one of the most difficult in the university's history and acknowledged troubling questions about the investigations that followed the allegations.
"My heart aches when I think of what she experienced," Kotlikoff said. "It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use."
Kotlikoff reaffirmed his commitment to supporting an independent review of Cornell's handling of the case called for by New York Gov. Kathy Hochul and said the school's Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also expressed support for Hochul's decision to turn the criminal investigation over to the state attorney general.
"I want to acknowledge something that can be difficult for an institution to say," Kotlikoff said. "We don't have all the answers, but we are committed to investigating and finding the answers our community deserves."
Scrutiny has mounted in recent days over Cornell's response to allegations that the woman was sexually assaulted by multiple fraternity members in 2024. The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, has sued the university and seven former students.
During a student assembly hearing Thursday that gave students an opportunity to voice concerns and discuss proposals to improve Cornell's response to sexual assault, several speakers called for Kotlikoff's resignation.
Hochul, asked at a news conference Friday whether she believed Kotlikoff should resign over the university's handling of the case, declined to take a position, saying she did not yet have enough information.
Kotlikoff acknowledged frustration that Cornell has not communicated enough, saying that has led to distrust. While citing "real legal and privacy limits" on what the university can disclose, he pledged greater transparency and more opportunities for students, parents and others to engage with university leaders.
He also committed Cornell's support to legislative efforts to change New York's sexual assault laws.
The case has renewed scrutiny of a state law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving people who voluntarily consume alcohol or drugs, even if they became too intoxicated to consent.
- Cornell 7: Governor vows to change N.Y. rape law that makes reporting hard when intoxication present
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten cited the law in defending his initial decision not to pursue charges, saying the woman's original statement to police described voluntary drug use and sexual activity.
Critics have long sought to close what they call the "voluntary intoxication loophole," which distinguishes between people incapacitated by drugs administered without their consent and those who voluntarily became intoxicated. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to the law.
Kotlikoff also called for a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life," saying Cornell would engage students, alumni and others in examining how to preserve the benefits of Greek life while strengthening accountability and transparency.
"Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.

The Asian Games in Japan closed on Sunday (October 4, 2026) after a fortnight lit up by record-smashing young stars but marred by mishaps, mediocre crowds and accusations of mismanagement.
More than 17,000 athletes and officials, a bigger number than the Olympics, descended on Nagoya and Aichi prefecture for the continent’s premier sporting spectacular.
Chinese swimming sensation Yu Zidi, just 13, stole the show with three gold medals, all in Games-record times.
She looks set to be a major medal threat at the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics.
The schoolgirl was named a Games MVP to cap an extraordinary showing that saw her scorch to gold in the 200m butterfly and do the 200m-400m individual medley double.
For all that, the shy teenager said: “I don’t think I am what people describe as a prodigy.”
Also in the pool, Japanese swimmer Shin Ohashi, only 17, smashed the men’s 200m breaststroke world record to delight the home crowd.
In athletics, where rain tumbled down over several days, the 20-year-old Thai sprinter Puripol Boonson did the 100m-200m double and was named men’s MVP.
On a dry evening, a celebratory closing ceremony full of colour and song saw Japan hand over hosting duties to Doha 2030.
‘Failure grade’
Top officials were on the defensive up until the last minute.
Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain Al-Musallam said “numbers are facts”, pointing to 50 world records broken at the Games after they opened on September 19.
“The athletes cannot perform if they don’t sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don’t have good transportation,” he said.
This 20th edition of the Games, which were first contested in 1951, did not have a traditional athletes’ village in a bid to save money.
Instead, participants were housed in wooden temporary units, on cruise ship the Costa Serena and in hotels.
Organisers said this was a template for future multi-sports events.
But it came with issues, with some teams complaining the units were too cramped and the beds too short.
More than that, the ballooning numbers of athletes and officials meant there were not enough beds for everyone.
One Thai Olympic official told AFP it was “like musical chairs” trying to get somewhere to sleep.
The sport, including a blockbuster cricket final won by India against arch-rivals Pakistan, did sometimes shine through.
North Korean weightlifter Ri Song Gum, a 140cm (4ft 7in) pocket powerhouse, set three new world marks in one day for gold.
But problems kept coming, including organisers playing North Korea’s national anthem for the South Korean hockey team.
There were athletes’ buses that did not turn up when they should, or did not arrive at all.
Two teams were sent to the wrong venue, delaying a volleyball match.
“If I were to give them a grade, it would be an F,” Ryu Seung-min, president of the Korean Sport and Olympic Committee, said.
Games organisers were on the back foot as well over attendances, with the opening ceremony taking place in front of thousands of empty seats.
At the women’s football semi-final between hosts Japan and South Korea there were 998 spectators in a 50,000 stadium.
Boy history-maker
Japanese Olympic Committee president Seiko Hashimoto admitted that “there were many problems”, but said the country wants to host more international events in future.
She said bad weather had turned some spectators off, but was eager to point out that some sports were well attended.
About 30,000 saw South Korea beat Japan 1-0 to clinch men’s football gold, although the occasion was tarnished somewhat when the South Korean flag failed to go up in the victory ceremony.
The hosts finished with 83 golds, a distant second in the medals table behind China with 169.
Japan’s tally included gold for Yuki Kurihara, who won an eSports competition aged 11, making him the youngest Games champion in history.
Several sports with ambitions of making the Olympics made their debut, including padel, MMA and virtual taekwondo.

Andhra Pradesh Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu and Union Rural Development Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan on Sunday (October 4, 2026) laid the foundation for the construction of three lakh houses across the state under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana-Gramin (PMAY-G) 2.0 at Burripalem in Tenali constituency. Mr. Chouhan said the Union government would sanction another six lakh houses for the State, in addition to the three lakh houses being taken up.
Addressing a public meeting later, Mr. Chouhan said another three lakh houses would be sanctioned by the time the ongoing construction was completed, and an additional three lakh houses would also be allocated to Andhra Pradesh. Mr. Naidu said the additional three lakh houses would come next year, taking the total allocation to nine lakh houses. The Union government would extend full support to the development of Andhra Pradesh, Mr. Chouhan said.
Mr. Naidu said the State government aimed to achieve 100% coverage under the housing programme by 2029. He said the Centre had initially sanctioned 75,000 houses to Andhra Pradesh under the regular quota, but three lakh houses were sanctioned following a special request made by the State government.
3D-printed houses
The two leaders also launched a pilot project for government-led 3D concrete-printed houses, described as the first such initiative in the country. A total of 177 houses using 3D concrete printing technology will be constructed at Burripalem and Obulanayudupalem under the pilot project.
Mr. Naidu said the present government had renewed its focus on providing quality houses to the poor. He said houses constructed using the technology were expected to maintain indoor temperatures around eight degrees Celsius lower than the outside temperature. If the pilot project proved successful, the government would take up the construction of 5,000 houses using the technology and seek to make Andhra Pradesh a model for 3D-technology-based housing, he added.
YSRCP cancelled six lakh houses: Naidu
Mr. Naidu alleged that the housing programme had suffered during the previous government between 2019 and 2024, claiming that six lakh houses meant for the poor had been cancelled and that irregularities had affected its implementation. He also alleged that house sites had been allotted at unsuitable locations, including tanks and hillocks, forcing nearly four lakh beneficiaries to return their sites.
The coalition government was committed to ensuring that welfare and development reached all sections of society, he said. Under the Pattabhishekam initiative, long-pending land issues had been resolved and house sites distributed to eligible poor families. House sites valued at ₹52,000 crore had been provided in Visakhapatnam, Vijayawada, Mangalagiri and other parts of the State, he said.
Referring to Burripalem, Mr. Naidu said the village was associated with the late actor Krishna, and noted that Union Minister of State for Communications and Rural Development Pemmasani Chandrasekhar was also from the region.
Centre’s support
Praising Mr. Naidu, Mr. Chouhan said the State was emerging as a leading State in the country under his leadership and described him as a visionary and dynamic leader. “Under Mr. Chandrababu Naidu’s leadership, Andhra Pradesh has become a shining, advanced and achieving State,” he said.
Mr. Chouhan said the Centre was providing ₹6,000 a year to farmers and the State government was adding another ₹14,000 under the Annadata Sukhibhava scheme, taking the total annual assistance to ₹20,000. He said the State government was working with the objective of making the benefits of welfare schemes reach every section of society.
Referring to rural infrastructure, he said villages could utilise the Viksit Bharat-Gramin Yojana (VBG-Ramji Yojana) for developing basic infrastructure such as drains, roads and drinking water facilities. He assured that the Centre would extend full cooperation to Andhra Pradesh in this regard.
Mr. Chouhan said the Modi and Chandrababu governments were working towards the comprehensive, 360-degree development of Andhra Pradesh. He criticised the Congress for bifurcating Andhra Pradesh without ensuring a capital and alleged that the State had subsequently been left without adequate support. The NDA governments at the Centre and in the State were now taking Andhra Pradesh forward on the path of development, he said.
He said he had visited Amaravati and was impressed by its development plans. Amaravati, he said, had the potential to emerge as a major centre for advanced technologies such as artificial intelligence, data centres and quantum computing. Stating that he was impressed by the scale of development planned for Amaravati and by Mr. Naidu’s interaction with people, he expressed confidence that Andhra Pradesh would emerge as the number one State in the country under Mr. Naidu’s leadership.

In September 2026, a screenshot (archived) circulated online that social media users claimed authentically showed a post from U.S. President Donald Trump that banned listening to the Canadian rock band Rush starting Oct. 1.
The screenshot circulated as the Trump administration banned nearly $1 billion worth of Canadian imports including alcohol, dairy and motorcycles in the latest move in a trade war that started over tit-for-tat tariffs.
The ban came into effect as Trump described the Canadian government as "very bad," but said they were being "taught a little lesson."
One Facebook user who shared a screenshot of the alleged post wrote, " I don't think this is real but it's very funny." The post, which allegedly came from an account called @realDonaldTrump, read:
Effective October 1, listening to the Canadian rock band RUSH will no longer be allowed in the United States. RUSH is a Canadian band, and Canada has been very unfair to our country for many years. Anyone caught listening to RUSH on the radio, streaming, or at home will be detained by ICE and deported to Canada. We will not support Canadian bands while they continue to take advantage of the United States. MAKE AMERICA LISTEN AMERICAN AGAIN!
The screenshot also circulated on Threads (archived), where some users expressed confusion over whether it was an authentic post from the president. Multiple Snopes readers contacted us to ask if it was real.
The post was fake, according to an Oct. 1, 2026, email from a spokesperson from the White House Press Office.
We also found no evidence of the post on Trump's X or Truth Social accounts, both of which use the handle @realDonaldTrump. Additionally, the screenshot appeared to mix Trump's profile picture on X with his verified pink checkmark emblem on Truth Social. Trump's X account does not have a pink checkmark emblem, nor does his Truth Social account use the profile picture shown in the post.
The source of the fake post was unclear.
At the time of this writing, Rush, which formed in Toronto, Canada, in 1968, was on a multi-state tour of the U.S. in September and October 2026. The band had 12 dates planned across seven states in the month of October alone.
For further reading, Snopes frequently debunks fake quotes attributed to Trump.

German Chancellor pledges support for Ukraine as Russia intensifies strikes on Kyiv
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has arrived in Kyiv to show support as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukrainian cities

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has arrived in Kyiv on Sunday to demonstrate support as Russia steps up strikes on Ukrainian cities.
Aerial warfare has intensified further, with Moscow targeting cities across Ukraine using difficult-to-intercept ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, while Kyiv has launched strikes against Russian commercial interests and oil infrastructure.
Merz said his trip to Kyiv, his second as chancellor, was intended to underscore Germany’s ongoing commitment to Ukraine.
"If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us," he said in a statement on Sunday, adding that he told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, "You can continue to count on our help."
Merz described the partnership between the nations as "not a one-way street," highlighting joint efforts by German and Ukrainian firms to build mutually beneficial technologies. "This makes us safer and stronger," he stated.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said discussions would concentrate on "strengthening Ukraine, our defense and resilience, and our shared European security."
Russia’s Foreign Ministry announced on Saturday that it would persist with "mass retaliatory strikes" against Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, urging foreign citizens and diplomats to leave the country—reiterating a similar warning previously issued in May.
A Russian drone hit Kyiv’s Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River once more on Sunday morning. Footage on social media showed the drone striking the bridge and exploding near crossing traffic. No casualties were immediately reported.
This latest attack followed earlier strikes this week that forced full or partial closures across three of Kyiv’s six Dnipro River road bridges, gridlocking traffic in Moscow’s ongoing effort to disrupt daily life in the capital. Russia has previously targeted apartment buildings, supermarket warehouses, petrol stations, and data facilities, among other sites.
More than 4-and-a-half years after Russia invaded its neighbour, there remain no clear indications that a peace settlement might be possible. Clashes along the roughly 1,250-kilometre (780-mile) front line winding across northern, eastern, and southern Ukraine have remained largely stagnant in recent months.
